3. [RFC 3596: DNS Extensions to Support IP Version 6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3596), S. Thomson et al., 2003. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: AAAA type 28, one 128-bit address in network byte order, IP6.ARPA. Note: `rfc-3596`.
4. [RFC 2782: DNS SRV](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2782), A. Gulbrandsen, P. Vixie, L. Esibov, 2000. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: type 33, `_Service._Proto.Name`, priority (lowest first), weight, port, target must not be an alias, "." means no service, use only when the protocol spec says so. Note: `rfc-2782`.
5. [RFC 9460: SVCB and HTTPS Resource Records](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9460), B. Schwartz, M. Bishop, E. Nygren, 2023. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: abstract "enable aliasing of apex domains, which is not possible with CNAME"; 1 CNAME can't carry configuration; 1.1 goals. Note: `rfc-9460`.
6. [CNAME flattening](https://developers.cloudflare.com/dns/cname-flattening/), Cloudflare docs (modified in 2026). Docs, primary: yes (for Cloudflare's behavior). Seen: flattening lets a CNAME be used at the zone apex by returning the final IP instead of the CNAME; dangling CNAME returns NODATA. Not cited; a vendor-specific workaround. Candidate if the article names the workaround.

#### `dns-caching` (short)

1. See `dns` #1 (RFC 1034): 3.6 TTL meaning and "lower it before a change"; 4.3.1 concentrating the cache; 6.2.1 cached TTLs age.
2. [RFC 2308: Negative Caching of DNS Queries (DNS NCACHE)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2308), M. Andrews, 1998. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: abstract "should no longer be seen as an optional part"; 2.2 NODATA = NOERROR + empty answer; 3 SOA in authority, negative TTL = min(SOA TTL, MINIMUM); 4 MINIMUM's three meanings, $TTL; 5 NXDOMAIN keyed by name, NODATA by name+type; 7.1 SERVFAIL cache at most 5 minutes; 7.2 dead server after 120 s. Note: `rfc-2308`.
3. [RFC 8767: Serving Stale Data to Improve DNS Resiliency](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8767), D. Lawrence, W. Kumari, P. Sood, 2020. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 4 new TTL definition, 7-day cap (604,800 s), stale TTL 30 s, only NOERROR/NXDOMAIN with AA refresh; 3 BIND, Knot, OpenDNS, Unbound already serve stale; 5 client response timer 1.8 s. Note: `rfc-8767`.
4. See `dns` #8 (Julia Evans 2020).
5. [systemd-resolved.service(8)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/systemd-resolved.service.8.html), systemd 262~devel. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "caching and validating DNS/DNSSEC stub resolver", stub on 127.0.0.53/54, nss-resolve, no ndots (names with a dot are FQDNs), caches /etc/hosts (highest priority), flushes on network change, `resolvectl flush-caches`. Note: `man7-systemd-resolved`.

**Disagreements and tensions**
- **What a TTL means.** RFC 1034/1035 (1987): how long a record may be cached before it "should be discarded". RFC 8767 (2020): how long before the source "MUST again be consulted", and a record may be used past it if refresh fails. Julia Evans (2020): some ISP resolvers keep records past the TTL anyway. So "the TTL is a hard expiry" is wrong in practice twice over.
- **How big a UDP answer can be.** RFC 1035: 512 bytes. RFC 6891 (2013): start at 4096, fall back to 1280-1410. DNS Flag Day 2020: default 1232. The advice got smaller, not bigger, because of fragmentation.
- **Is TCP optional?** RFC 1123's SHOULD was read as optional by some implementers; RFC 7766 (2016) made it MUST for everyone.
- **Search lists.** glibc (resolv.conf) tries short names with search domains using ndots; systemd-resolved ignores ndots and treats any dotted name as complete. Same name, different queries on different hosts.
- **Words.** "Resolver", "recursive server", "full resolver", "forwarder" and "lame delegation" are used loosely; RFC 9499 says so and discourages some terms.

**Couldn't open**
- Cloudflare Learning Center pages (https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/dns/what-is-dns/, .../dns-records/, .../dns-records/dns-cname-record/ and others): HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and curl. Not cited.

**Rejected**
- RFC 8020 (NXDOMAIN means nothing underneath) and RFC 8198 (aggressive use of DNSSEC-validated cache): downloaded but not read; too detailed for a short caching node. Revisit if `dns-caching` grows.
- RFC 9156 (QNAME minimisation, 2021): abstract and example tables seen (a root server no longer sees the full name). A privacy topic; left out to keep `dns` one concept.
- RFC 7858 (DNS over TLS, 2016, TCP port 853) and RFC 8484 (DNS over HTTPS, 2018): abstracts seen. Better in phase 3 next to TLS and HTTP.

**Gaps**
- No measured numbers for DNS lookup latency (cold vs warm cache). A small experiment (dig timings against a local stub, a public resolver, and +trace) would give `dns` and `dns-caching` real numbers. Not run.
- No primary source for how common TTL-ignoring resolvers are; only Julia Evans's anecdote and estimate.
- Nothing opened on glibc's own caching behavior (resolv.conf(5) is silent), nor on the JVM's DNS cache settings (Julia Evans links an AWS doc; not opened).
- DNSSEC isn't covered anywhere in phase 2.

### Added later: retransmission (deep), keepalive, bufferbloat, pacing

**Disagreements and tensions**
- Minimum RTO: RFC 6298 SHOULD 1 s; Linux 200 ms, and the kernel doc now calls ≤ 200 ms the recommended practice.
- Counting vs time: RFC 8985 replaces DupAck counting with a time window, at the cost of per-packet send times; it names ultra-low-RTT data centers (RTT below the clock granularity) as a case where the SACK-scoreboard approach (RFC 6675) needs less state.
- RACK accepts spurious retransmissions on short flows (reordering window zero or small) to recover faster; F-RTO/Eifel/DSACK exist to detect spurious retransmissions after the fact.
- Keepalive vs user timeout: Cloudflare's post says both "set TCP_USER_TIMEOUT to KEEPIDLE + KEEPINTVL * KEEPCNT" and "slightly lower than" that sum. RFC 5482 says with the UTO option the keep-alive timer must be larger than the user timeout. gRPC sets TCP_USER_TIMEOUT to its PING timeout.
- RFC 1122 says keepalives are "not universally accepted" and a failed probe must not mean death; every modern system that sits behind NAT or LBs needs them anyway.

**Couldn't open**
None.

**Rejected**
- RFC 5482 for tcp-keepalive (see above). socket(7) (duplicate of tcp(7)).

**Gaps**
- No source opened on what Linux does with the UTO option on the wire.
- No source on common cloud NAT gateway idle timeouts other than AWS NLB. The article uses NLB's 350 s as one example, dated.
- No measured number for how often RTOs are spurious on real paths.

**Disagreements and tensions**
- Endpoint fix (BBR) vs network fix (AQM). BBR keeps its own queue low, but loss-based flows in an unmanaged deep buffer still fill it (Cardwell 2016); RFC 7567 says endpoints alone can't control enough.
- Which AQM: RFC 7567 (BCP) recommends AQM but no algorithm; CoDel, FQ-CoDel and PIE are all Experimental.
- Pacing vs CPU: offload batching saves CPU but creates bursts (draft 5.6.3).

**Couldn't open**
- Gettys and Nichols, "Bufferbloat: Dark Buffers in the Internet" at queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=2071893 and cacm.acm.org/research/bufferbloat/: both HTTP 403.
- socket(7) on man7.org does not document SO_MAX_PACING_RATE (checked); used tc-fq(8) instead.

**Rejected**
- patchwork.ozlabs.org/patch/762784 (v1 of the internal pacing patch, "Superseded"): used the merged commit instead.
- Wikipedia "TCP pacing", martinuke0 blog on BBR, oneuptime qdisc blog: secondary, not needed.

**Gaps**
- No Google/Cloudflare/Fastly engineering post on pacing found in the time spent; the kernel commit and BBR paper stand in.
- Which distributions default to fq_codel or fq today (2026) wasn't checked; RFC 8290's list is from 2018. systemd's default qdisc setting not checked.
- Linux 4.13 and 4.20 release years not from a source (the commit year, 2017, is).

## Phase 3: Networking II, secure protocols and proxies

Researched by six parallel passes, one per group below.

### Crypto and TLS

#### `cryptographic-hashes` (short)

1. [Hash Functions](https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/hash-functions), NIST CSRC. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: the three properties an approved hash must have (collision, preimage, second preimage resistance); SHA-2 family list (FIPS 180-4) and SHA-3 (FIPS 202); SHA-1 deprecated in 2011 and disallowed for signatures after 2013; security strength table (SHA-1 collision resistance <80 bits, SHA-256 128 bits).
2. [Announcing the first SHA1 collision](https://security.googleblog.com/2017/02/announcing-first-sha1-collision.html), Stevens, Bursztein et al., Google Security Blog, 2017. Blog by the team that did it, primary: yes. Seen: two PDFs with the same SHA-1; about 9.2 quintillion SHA-1 computations; 6,500 CPU-years for phase one; still over 100,000 times faster than brute force; move to SHA-256 or SHA-3.
3. [FIPS 180-4](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.180-4.pdf), NIST, 2015. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: downloaded (36 pages), not read past the contents; the NIST page above covers the concept-level claims. Not used.

#### `symmetric-encryption` (short)

1. [RFC 5116](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5116), McGrew, 2008. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: AEAD interface (key, nonce, plaintext, associated data in; ciphertext out, or FAIL on decrypt); nonces must be distinct per key; 12-byte nonces recommended; GCM nonce reuse loses confidentiality (XOR of plaintexts) and integrity (hash key recovered, forgeries trivial); AES-128-GCM ciphertext is 16 bytes longer (the tag).
2. [RFC 8439](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8439), Nir and Langley, 2018. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: why a second cipher next to AES (standby cipher, AES slow without hardware, cache-timing attacks on AES software); ChaCha20 about three times faster than AES on platforms without AES hardware; not sensitive to timing attacks.
3. [crypto/cipher](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/cipher), Go 1.27.1 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: AEAD interface, nonce "unique for all time, for a given key"; NewGCMWithRandomNonce (Go 1.24) with a random 96-bit nonce and a limit of 2^32 messages per key; Overhead 28 bytes.
4. [NIST SP 800-38D](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-38d.pdf), Dworkin, 2007. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: section 8, IV uniqueness: probability of a repeated IV under one key no greater than 2^-32; "almost as important as the secrecy of the key". Not used (RFC 5116 says the same at concept level).
5. [A Detailed Look at RFC 8446](https://blog.cloudflare.com/rfc-8446-aka-tls-1-3/): see `tls` #3 (block vs stream ciphers, MAC-then-encrypt history).

#### `public-key-crypto` (short)

1. [A Detailed Look at RFC 8446 (a.k.a. TLS 1.3)](https://blog.cloudflare.com/rfc-8446-aka-tls-1-3/): see `tls` #3. Seen: hybrid cryptosystems; public key microseconds to milliseconds vs symmetric nanoseconds per operation; RSA key transport vs Diffie-Hellman; forward secrecy.
2. [RFC 7748](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7748), Langley, Hamburg, Turner, 2016. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: X25519 Diffie-Hellman step by step (32 random bytes each, exchange public values, both compute the same K, then derive a symmetric key with a KDF); all-zero check.
3. [RFC 8032](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032), Josefsson and Liusvaara, 2017. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: EdDSA advantages: no per-signature random number needed, small keys (32 bytes) and signatures (64 bytes) for Ed25519, about 128-bit security; a large quantum computer would break both Ed25519 and Ed448.

#### `hmac` (short)

1. [RFC 2104](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104), Krawczyk, Bellare, Canetti, 1997. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: MAC definition; H(K XOR opad, H(K XOR ipad, text)); key at least L bytes, random, refreshed; works with any iterated hash; breaking a MAC doesn't expose past messages.
2. [Length-extension attacks are still a thing](https://00f.net/2025/10/23/length-extension-attacks/), Frank Denis, 2025. Blog (libsodium author), primary: no. Seen: H(key || message) with SHA-256 is forgeable by appending data; real case in a CDN's token auth; fix is HMAC or a hash without length extension (BLAKE2/3, KMAC, SHAKE).
3. [crypto/hmac](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/hmac), Go 1.27.1 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: receivers should compare MACs with hmac.Equal to avoid timing side channels; example ValidMAC.

#### `tls` (deep)

1. [RFC 9846](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846), Rescorla, 2026. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: **obsoletes RFC 8446**; same version number, backward compatible; forbids TLS 1.0/1.1 and KeyShare reuse; figure 1 full handshake; three phases; CertificateVerify signs the transcript; Finished is a MAC over the handshake; HelloRetryRequest; record nonce from sequence number; AES-GCM key limit 2^24.5 records; mandatory cipher suites; SNI mandatory to implement; middlebox compatibility mode; ECH is RFC 9849.
2. [RFC 8446](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446), Rescorla, 2018. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: introduction (auth, confidentiality, integrity; handshake and record protocols). Superseded by RFC 9846; used only through RFC 9846's own history section.
3. [A Detailed Look at RFC 8446 (a.k.a. TLS 1.3)](https://blog.cloudflare.com/rfc-8446-aka-tls-1-3/), Nick Sullivan, Cloudflare, 2018. Blog from a team that helped build it, primary: yes. Seen: SSL to TLS history and RFC numbers; attacks on 1.2 (downgrade, padding oracles, RC4); RSA key transport removed; 2 round trips down to 1; client guesses key shares; ossification and middleboxes.
4. [RFC 9325](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9325), Sheffer, Saint-Andre, Fossati, 2022. BCP, primary: yes. Seen: TLS 1.0/1.1 MUST NOT; SNI must be supported, leaks the domain; host name validation is security-critical, without it TLS only proves key possession; ticket keys rotated regularly.
5. [RFC 9852](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9852), Salz and Aviram, 2026. BCP, primary: yes. Seen: new protocols using TLS must require TLS 1.3; TLS WG won't add PQC to TLS 1.2; TLS 1.2 can be configured securely but it's harder.
6. [crypto/tls](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/tls), Go 1.27.1 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: MinVersion default TLS 1.2, max TLS 1.3; TLS 1.3 cipher suites not configurable; X25519MLKEM768 in the default key exchanges since Go 1.24; InsecureSkipVerify warnings; ClientAuth types; session ticket keys rotated daily, dropped after 7 days.
7. [RFC 8996](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996), Moriarty and Farrell, 2021. Seen: abstract, TLS 1.0 and 1.1 moved to Historic. Not used (RFC 9325 and 9846 say the same).

#### `certificates-and-pki` (deep)

1. [RFC 5280](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280), Cooper et al., 2008 (updated many times since, most recently RFC 10007). Spec, primary: yes. Seen: certificates bind a public key to a subject, signed by a CA; can travel over untrusted channels; certification paths; path validation conditions; basicConstraints cA; subjectAltName; validity notBefore/notAfter; CRLs and their time granularity.
2. [RFC 8555](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8555), Barnes et al., 2019. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: DV vs OV/EV; manual issuance took webmasters 1-3 hours; http-01 (/.well-known/acme-challenge/, over HTTP not HTTPS) and dns-01 (_acme-challenge TXT with SHA-256 of key authorization); account keys.
3. [How CT works](https://certificate.transparency.dev/howctworks/), Certificate Transparency project (Google). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: precertificate and poison extension; SCT as promise to log within the MMD (usually 24 hours); Merkle tree logs, append-only; monitors; Chrome and Safari require at least 2 SCTs; roots, intermediates, chain verification.
4. [RFC 9162](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9162), Laurie, Messeri, Stradling, 2021. Spec, Experimental, primary: yes. Seen: CT v2, obsoletes RFC 6962; logs don't prevent misissuance, they make it detectable. Not used (the CT site covers the same for how it's deployed).
5. [TLS Baseline Requirements v2.3.0](https://github.com/cabforum/servercert/blob/main/docs/BR.md), CA/Browser Forum, 2026. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 6.3.2 validity schedule 398 / 200 / 100 / 47 days (2026, 2027, 2029); short-lived certificates (7 days or less from 2026) need not be revoked; OCSP optional and CRLs required since ballot SC063 (2023); revoke within 24 hours or 5 days.
6. [Ballot SC081v3](https://cabforum.org/2025/04/11/ballot-sc081v3-introduce-schedule-of-reducing-validity-and-data-reuse-periods/), CA/Browser Forum, 2025. Seen: vote tallies (all four browsers yes); rationale: certificates go stale, revocation doesn't work at internet scale. The schedule itself is only in the redline; used the BR instead. Not cited.
7. [OCSP Service Has Reached End of Life](https://letsencrypt.org/2025/08/06/ocsp-service-has-reached-end-of-life), Let's Encrypt, 2025. Blog from the CA, primary: yes. Seen: OCSP turned off, CRLs only; privacy reason; 340 billion requests per month at peak.
8. [Ending OCSP Support in 2025](https://letsencrypt.org/2024/12/05/ending-ocsp) and [Intent to End OCSP Service](https://letsencrypt.org/2024/07/23/replacing-ocsp-with-crls), Let's Encrypt, 2024. Seen: timeline, Must-Staple removed, stapling downtime risk, most OCSP clients fail open. Used the 2025 post only.
9. [6-day and IP Address Certificates are Generally Available](https://letsencrypt.org/2026/01/15/6day-and-ip-general-availability), Let's Encrypt, 2026. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: 160-hour certificates via the 'shortlived' profile; revocation unreliable; default going from 90 to 45 days.
10. [Certificate Lifetime Rationale](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/cert-lifetimes/) and [How It Works](https://letsencrypt.org/how-it-works/), Let's Encrypt docs. Seen: 90-day default since 2015, 45 days by 2028; multi-perspective validation. Not cited (the 2026 post covers lifetimes).
11. [RFC 6960](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6960), OCSP, 2013. Seen: header only. Not used.

#### `tls-resumption` (short)

1. [RFC 9846](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846): see `tls` #1. Seen: 2.2, 2.3, 4.7.1 (ticket lifetime at most 7 days), section 8 (anti-replay: single-use tickets, ClientHello recording, freshness checks; at most once per server instance), C.4 (don't reuse tickets across connections).
2. [Introducing Zero Round Trip Time Resumption (0-RTT)](https://blog.cloudflare.com/introducing-0-rtt/), Nick Sullivan, Cloudflare, 2017. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: about 40% of Cloudflare's HTTPS connections were resumptions; only GET without query parameters answered in 0-RTT; a header tells the origin about 0-RTT; later turned off by default.
3. [RFC 9325](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9325): see `tls` #4. Seen: 3.4 ticket keys changed regularly (e.g. weekly) and destroyed.
4. [RFC 8470](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8470), Thomson, Nottingham, Tarreau, 2018. Seen: abstract, 425 (Too Early), clients must retry on 425. Not used; belongs with the HTTP nodes.

#### `mtls` (short)

1. [RFC 9846](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846): see `tls` #1. Seen: 4.4.2 CertificateRequest; 4.5.1.3 empty client Certificate, server may continue or abort; 4.7.2 post-handshake auth; C.2 same certificate for client and server not well analyzed.
2. [SPIFFE Concepts](https://spiffe.io/docs/latest/spiffe-about/spiffe-concepts/), SPIFFE project docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: SPIFFE ID URI, trust domain, X.509-SVID vs JWT-SVID (JWTs replayable, X.509 preferred), short-lived keys rotated automatically via the Workload API, trust bundles.
3. [crypto/tls](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/tls): see `tls` #6. Seen: ClientAuth modes from NoClientCert to RequireAndVerifyClientCert; ClientCAs; VerifyPeerCertificate not called on resumed connections.

**Disagreements and tensions**
- Revocation. RFC 5280 treats CRLs as the X.509 way; OCSP was built to make checks timely. Let's Encrypt and the CA/B Forum now say both fail at internet scale (privacy, reliability, fail-open), and push short lifetimes instead. Revocation still exists (the BR still requires revoking within 24 hours or 5 days) but short-lived certificates need not be revoked at all.
- 0-RTT. The spec calls it a trade: a round trip saved for weaker guarantees (replay, no forward secrecy). Cloudflare launched it and later turned it off by default. Anti-replay at "at most once per server instance" still allows one replay per instance.
- Ticket key lifetime. RFC 9325's example is weekly rotation; Go rotates daily and keeps keys 7 days; RFC 9846 caps ticket lifetime at 7 days.
- TLS 1.2. RFC 9325 (2022) says TLS 1.2 MUST be supported; RFC 9852 (2026) relaxes that to MAY for new protocols and requires 1.3.

**Couldn't open**
- shattered.io: the domain now serves an unrelated content site that reuses the project's name. Used Google's 2017 post instead.

**Rejected**
- shattered.io (see above). FIPS 180-4 (not needed at concept level). RFC 6234, RFC 4231 (HMAC-SHA test vectors), RFC 6962 (replaced by 9162): downloaded, headers only.
- Cloudflare Learning Center pages were not tried (403 in phase 2).

**Gaps**
- No measured handshake cost or resumption rate of our own; the only rate (40% resumptions) is Cloudflare's from 2017.
- No source opened for Chrome's own root program or CT policy text, or for how browsers check revocation today (CRLite, CRLSets). "Browsers don't check OCSP" is left out for that reason.
- No source opened on password hashing (bcrypt, Argon2); `cryptographic-hashes` only says a plain hash is not the tool, without detail.
- No source on post-quantum signatures in certificates; only PQ key exchange (Go docs).

### DNS security and HTTP core

#### `dnssec` (short)

1. [RFC 4033](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4033), Arends, Austein, Larson, Massey, Rose, 2005. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: section 3 services (origin authentication and integrity, authenticated denial of existence); four new record types RRSIG, DNSKEY, DS, NSEC; CD and AD header bits; needs EDNS0 and the DO bit; key belongs to the zone, not to the name servers ("object security", not channel security); resolver needs at least one trust anchor; chain DNSKEY->[DS->DNSKEY]*->RRset from the root; NSEC chains describe the gaps between names; section 4: no confidentiality, no DoS protection; section 5: four states secure, insecure, bogus, indeterminate; bogus signalled to non-validating stubs as SERVFAIL (RCODE 2), secure via AD bit; section 7: a non-validating stub must trust its recursive and the channel to it; section 8: RRSIG inception/expiration, TTL can't extend it, signed zones need regular re-signing; section 12: NSEC zone walking, cryptographic DoS, misconfiguration can make whole zones unreachable, glue and NS at zone cuts not signed.
2. [RFC 9364](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9364), Paul Hoffman, BCP 237, 2023. Spec (best current practice), primary: yes. Seen: DNSSEC is RFCs 4033-4035 plus RFC 6840; third iteration (RFC 2065, 2535 before it); only standards-track method for origin authentication of DNS data; when written, fewer than 10% of website domain names signed and about a third of queries to recursive resolvers validated; near-universal signing of TLDs in the root; root signed in 2010; root trust anchor rolled in 2018 with RFC 5011; ECDSA and EdDSA now popular, RSA still among the most popular; CDS/CDNSKEY automate DS maintenance (RFC 7344, 8078).

Extra: [RFC 4034](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4034) and [RFC 4035](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4035), 2005. Downloaded, skimmed the table of contents only. Record formats and resolver algorithm; RFC 4033 covers what a short node needs. Not given notes.

#### `encrypted-dns` (short)

1. [RFC 7858](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7858), Hu, Zhu, Heidemann, Mankin, Wessels, Hoffman, 2016. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: DoT on TCP port 853, never cleartext on 853, never DoT on port 53; TLS handshake is the first exchange; messages keep the two-byte length prefix from RFC 1035; clients should pipeline and match responses by message ID; reuse connections; two profiles: opportunistic (no protection against an active on-path attacker) and out-of-band key-pinned (SPKI SHA-256 pins, backup pin); performance: extra RTT for TCP, TLS adds two more (TLS 1.2 era), resumption helps; security: traffic analysis by size and timing, padding (RFC 7830); DNSSEC and DoT are independent and solve different problems; scoped to stub-to-recursive.
2. [RFC 8484](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8484), Paul Hoffman, Patrick McManus, 2018. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: DoH maps each DNS query/response to one HTTP exchange over https; GET with base64url `dns` parameter or POST with `application/dns-message`; DNS ID 0 for cache friendliness; DNS errors (NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL) still come back as HTTP 2xx; freshness lifetime must not exceed the smallest answer TTL, Age must be subtracted; HTTP/2 is the minimum recommended version; port 443 and mixing with other HTTPS traffic make DoH hard to single out; in-server privacy: IP, connection reuse, TLS resumption, cookies, headers can all correlate; DoH doesn't give DNSSEC's integrity; filtering systems that rely on plaintext DNS stop working; bootstrapping the DoH server's own name.
3. [RFC 9250](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9250), Huitema, Dickinson, Mankin, 2022. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: DoQ, QUIC with ALPN "doq" on UDP port 853; same privacy as DoT, latency like UDP DNS; one query per QUIC stream so no head-of-line blocking; covers stub-to-recursive, recursive-to-authoritative and zone transfers; doesn't try to hide that the traffic is DNS.

Extra: [RFC 8310](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8310), Dickinson, Gillmor, Reddy, 2018. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: Strict Privacy profile (encrypted and authenticated or hard failure) vs Opportunistic Privacy. Not given a note; RFC 7858's two profiles are enough for a short node.
Extra: [RFC 7626](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7626), downloaded, not read (obsoleted by RFC 9076).

#### `http-semantics` (deep)

1. [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110), Fielding, Nottingham, Reschke (eds.), STD 97, 2022. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 1.2 history (HTTP since 1990; HTTP/1.1 1995/1997/1999/2014; all three versions share these semantics); 1.3 core semantics; 3.1-3.4 resources, representations, stateless, messages; 3.7 intermediaries (proxy, gateway = reverse proxy, tunnel); 5 fields (case-insensitive names, repeated lines combine with commas, Set-Cookie exception, proxies forward unknown fields); 6 message abstraction (control data, headers, content, trailers; framing per version); 7.2 Host; 7.6.1 Connection and hop-by-hop fields; 9 methods table, GET and HEAD required, 501 vs 405, 9.2.1 safe (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE), 9.2.2 idempotent (PUT, DELETE + safe), retries, "A proxy MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests"; 9.2.3 caching of GET/HEAD/POST; 9.3.1 content in GET has no meaning, smuggling risk; 15 status classes, unknown code treated as x00, 1xx interim; 15.4 301/302 POST-to-GET history, 307/308 preserve method; 401 vs 403, 404 may hide 403; 502, 503 + Retry-After, 504.
2. [RFC 9205](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9205), Mark Nottingham, BCP 56, 2022. Spec (best current practice), primary: yes. Seen: generic semantics, applications MUST NOT redefine methods or status codes; "A POST request MUST result in a 201" is brittle; status codes are generated by proxies, CDNs, captive portals, not only your app; use the most applicable code, 200/400/500 when in doubt, details in the body (problem details); GET should not have side effects because implementations retry it; OPTIONS limits; separate requests on one connection have no ordering relationship.
3. [RFC 5789](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5789), Dusseault, Snell, 2010. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: PATCH sends instructions, PUT sends a replacement; PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent; can be made safe to repeat with a conditional request (If-Match with a strong ETag).
4. [How to Think About HTTP Status Codes](https://www.mnot.net/blog/2017/05/11/status_codes), Mark Nottingham, 2017. Blog by an HTTP spec editor, primary: yes. Seen: two levels of meaning (class digit, specific code); status codes are generic, don't map app semantics onto them; lists of possible codes per endpoint are always incomplete (proxies, 421, 429, 500); specific effects handled by generic software (301 redirect, 401 auth, 429 slow down, 404 negative caching); 202 needs out-of-band outcome; 200/400/500 fine when unsure; put app detail in the body.
5. [A New Definition of HTTP](https://www.mnot.net/blog/2022/06/06/http-core), Mark Nottingham, 2022. Blog by a spec editor, primary: yes. Seen: why semantics were split from HTTP/1.1 into RFC 9110 (semantics), 9111 (caching), 9112 (HTTP/1.1); over 475 issues addressed; field name registry; don't memorise RFC numbers, the working group's spec page lists the current ones.

Extra: [RFC 6585](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585), Nottingham, Fielding, 2012. Opened: 429 Too Many Requests, MAY include Retry-After. Not given a note; mnot's post covers 429's role.
Extra: [RFC 9111](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111), downloaded, not read. Caching belongs to phase 9 (http caching).

#### `http-1-1` (deep)

1. [RFC 9112](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112), Fielding, Nottingham, Reschke (eds.), STD 99, 2022. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 2.1 message format (start line, field lines, empty line, body); 2.2 parse as octets not Unicode, bare CR forbidden, whitespace before first header is dangerous; 3 request line, lenient whitespace parsing can cause smuggling, recommended minimum 8000-octet request line; 3.2 Host required, 400 if missing or duplicated; 4 status line, ignore reason phrase; 5.1 no whitespace between field name and colon (400); 5.2 obs-fold deprecated; 6.1 Transfer-Encoding, chunked must be last, TE overrides CL (for historic progress-bar reasons), server must close after a request with both; 6.3 the eight-step body length algorithm; 7.1 chunked format, hex sizes, overflow warning, trailers; 8 incomplete messages; 9.2 responses matched to requests only by order; 9.3 persistent by default, Connection: close, HTTP/1.0 keep-alive; must read the whole body to reuse; 9.3.2 pipelining rules (responses in order, don't pipeline after non-idempotent); 9.4 concurrency, no fixed connection limit now; 9.5 idle timeout race; 9.6 staged close to avoid the TCP reset problem; 11.2 request smuggling; C.2.2 HTTP/1.0 Keep-Alive and hung proxies.
2. [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110). See http-semantics #1. Sections 6.1 (close-delimited framing can't tell complete from truncated), 7.6.1 (Connection, hop-by-hop list includes Transfer-Encoding), 9.2.2 (retrying idempotent requests on a dead persistent connection).
3. [HTTP Pipelining (Chromium design doc)](https://www.chromium.org/developers/design-documents/network-stack/http-pipelining/), The Chromium Projects. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: risks: broken servers, broken (transparent) proxies, front-of-queue blocking; mitigations tried (only HTTP/1.1, known length, keep-alive, no auth; blacklist per origin); status: option removed, known crashing bugs, many servers and middleboxes behave badly.
4. [curl says bye bye to pipelining](https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2019/04/06/curl-says-bye-bye-to-pipelining/), Daniel Stenberg, 2019. Blog by curl's maintainer, primary: yes. Seen: pipelining fragile and hard to debug in curl; never enabled by default in big desktop browsers; Firefox and Chrome dropped it; bad state of pipelining drove HTTP/2 multiplexing; disabled in curl 7.62.0, code removed in 7.65.0; multiplexing default since 7.62.0.
5. [RFC 9113](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113). Note exists. Section 1: pipelining only partially addressed concurrency and still has application-layer head-of-line blocking, so HTTP/1.x clients open several connections.

Extra: [RFC 7230](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7230), 2014. Downloaded; obsoleted by RFC 9110 and 9112. Not used, the current text is in RFC 9112.

**Disagreements and tensions**

- DNSSEC: the IETF calls it best current practice (RFC 9364) while the same document says deployment is low because its value "is often considered lower than the cost". Both are stated in one source.
- DoH vs network operators: RFC 8484 lists filtering systems breaking as an operational consequence; nothing opened argues either side further. Not expanded in the article beyond that.
- Status codes: RFC 9205 and mnot argue for coarse codes and detail in the body; common API practice maps many app errors to many codes. Covered as a tension in http-semantics.
- Pipelining: the spec still allows it (RFC 9112 9.3.2), while browsers and curl have removed it. The article says both.
- Transfer-Encoding with Content-Length: spec says TE wins, a server MAY reject and MUST close. Different servers choosing differently is the root of request smuggling (left to that node).

**Couldn't open**

- Nothing needed failed to open.

**Rejected**

- MDN pages: secondary, and RFC 9110 plus mnot cover the same ground from the people who wrote the specs.
- RFC 7230 (obsolete) and RFC 7626 (obsoleted by RFC 9076).

**Gaps**

- Firefox's removal of pipelining: only curl's post says "Firefox and Chrome dropped pipelining". No Mozilla source opened, so the article doesn't name a Firefox version.
- No source opened gives numbers for DNSSEC validation or DoH adoption beyond RFC 9364's "fewer than 10%" and "around a third", which are dated to when RFC 9364 was written (2023).
- No source with measured HTTP/1.1 keep-alive savings; the article says it saves a TCP (and TLS) handshake per request without numbers.

### HTTP/2, QUIC and streaming

#### `http2` (deep)

1. [RFC 9113](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113), M. Thomson, C. Benfield (eds.), 2022. Spec, primary: yes. Obsoletes RFC 7540 and 8740. Seen: 1 why (HTTP/1.1 pipelining's HOL blocking, many connections, verbose headers; TCP HOL not addressed); 2 overview (frames, streams, flow control, deprecated 7540 priorities, push); 3 starting (h2 via ALPN, h2c upgrade deprecated, prior knowledge, 24-octet client preface "PRI * HTTP/2.0"); 4.1 frame layout (9-octet header: length 24, type 8, flags 8, R, stream id 31); 4.2 max frame 16,384 default; 4.3 field blocks, HEADERS + CONTINUATION contiguous; 4.3.1 HPACK state per connection, table 4,096 bytes; 5 streams; 5.1 state machine (figure 2); 5.1.1 odd client ids, even server ids, no reuse, GOAWAY on exhaustion; 5.1.2 MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS, recommended ≥ 100; 5.2 flow control per stream and per connection, WINDOW_UPDATE, 65,535 initial, only DATA counted, hop-by-hop, BDP warning; 5.3 7540 priorities "not successful"; 6 frame types 0x0–0x9; 6.7 PING (8 octets, RTT, liveness); 6.8 GOAWAY last-stream-id; 8.1 message = HEADERS, DATA, trailers; 8.3 pseudo-headers; 8.4 push hard to use; 8.7 REFUSED_STREAM and GOAWAY make retry safe, PING for idle connections behind NAT/LB; 9.1 one connection per host; 9.1.1 connection coalescing, 421; 10.5 DoS list; 10.6 compression attacks.
2. [RFC 7541](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7541), R. Peon, H. Ruellan, 2015. Spec, primary: yes. HPACK. Seen: 1 why not DEFLATE (CRIME); static table (61 entries, appendix A), dynamic FIFO table, Huffman; 2.2 separate tables per direction; 4.1 entry size = name + value + 32; C.3.2 second request encodes four pseudo-headers as one byte each (82 86 84 be); 7.1 table probing, whole-value guesses; never-indexed literals.
3. [HTTP/2 Rapid Reset: deconstructing the record-breaking attack](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/), Lucas Pardue, Julien Desgats, Cloudflare, 2023. Engineering blog, primary: yes (their traffic and proxies). Seen: CVE-2023-44487; peak just above 201 million rps from about 20,000 machines; stream lifecycle walk-through; RST_STREAM frees the concurrency slot at once; MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS can't stop it; pcap: 525 requests in one packet, HEADERS 26 then 9 bytes (HPACK); lowering concurrency to 64 broke browsers that assume 100.
4. [Remove HTTP/2 Server Push from Chrome](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/removing-push), Barry Pollard, Chrome team, 2022. Engineering blog, primary: yes. Seen: push disabled by default from Chrome 106; used by 1.25% of HTTP/2 sites, later 0.7%; mixed results, regressions; 103 Early Hints and preload as replacements; push mostly never implemented for HTTP/3.
5. [RFC 9218](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9218), K. Oku, L. Pardue, 2022. Spec, primary: yes. Extensible priorities. Seen: 1 why the 7540 tree was dropped; Priority header, urgency 0–7 default 3, incremental flag; signals are only hints.

Extra: [How it works: The novel HTTP/2 'Rapid Reset' DDoS attack](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/how-it-works-the-novel-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack), Google Cloud, 2023. Seen: peak over 398 million rps; 100 streams per round trip vs one request per round trip for HTTP/1.1; recommends closing connections that exceed the stream limit; graceful GOAWAY too slow against abuse. Not used (Cloudflare's post covers the mechanism with a packet trace); good second source if the article grows.

#### `quic` (deep)

1. [RFC 9000](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000), J. Iyengar, M. Thomson (eds.), 2021. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 1 overview (UDP, integrated TLS, 0-RTT, streams, migration, only clients migrate); 2.1 62-bit stream ids, low two bits = initiator and direction; 4 flow control per stream and connection, stream count limits; 5.1 connection IDs, chosen by the receiver, routing through load balancers; 7 combined handshake (figures 4–6), CRYPTO frames; 8 anti-amplification 3x, Initial padded to 1200 bytes; 9 migration, NAT rebinding, path validation; 10.1 idle timeout, 10.1.2 PING every 30 s to keep middlebox state; 12.2 coalescing packets into one datagram; 12.3 three packet number spaces; 13 per-stream HOL; 14 min 1200-byte datagram, no IP fragmentation; 17 long and short headers.
2. [RFC 9001](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001), M. Thomson, S. Turner (eds.), 2021. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 1 TLS 1.3 gives 1-RTT and 0-RTT; 3 TLS handshake messages carried in QUIC instead of TLS records (figure 3 layers); 5.2 Initial keys derived from the client's Destination Connection ID, so anyone can read them; 5.4 header protection hides packet number; 7 Initial packets can be tampered with; 9.2 0-RTT replay, QUIC frames idempotent but application data isn't.
3. [RFC 9002](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9002), J. Iyengar, I. Swett (eds.), 2021. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 3 packet numbers never repeat, no retransmission ambiguity; 4 differences from TCP (separate spaces, monotonic numbers, more ACK ranges, ack delay, PTO, min cwnd 2); 7 NewReno-like default, sender may pick CUBIC etc.
4. [The QUIC Transport Protocol: Design and Internet-Scale Deployment](https://research.google/pubs/the-quic-transport-protocol-design-and-internet-scale-deployment/), Langley et al., Google, SIGCOMM 2017. Paper, primary: yes. Opened the abstract page and the PDF. Seen: user-space on UDP to escape kernel and middlebox ossification; Search latency down 8.0% desktop, 3.6% mobile; YouTube rebuffers down 18.0% / 15.3%; over 30% of Google egress, est. 7% of Internet traffic; Alt-Svc discovery and racing TCP with 300 ms head start; server CPU 3.5x TLS/TCP, optimized to about 2x; 4.4% of clients couldn't use QUIC (UDP blocked, mostly enterprise); the one-bit flags change that a firewall choked on. Describes Google QUIC, before the IETF version.

#### `http3` (short)

1. [RFC 9114](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114), M. Bishop (ed.), 2022. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 1.2 delegation to QUIC; 2 one request per bidirectional stream, control streams, QPACK; 3.1 h3 ALPN, fall back to TCP when UDP is blocked, Alt-Svc; 6.2.1 one unidirectional control stream each way; appendix A: stream concurrency by QUIC, all frames flow controlled, no RST_STREAM/PING/WINDOW_UPDATE/CONTINUATION, no priority signaling, settings sent once.
2. [RFC 9204](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9204), C. Krasic, M. Bishop, A. Frindell (eds.), 2022. Spec, primary: yes. QPACK. Seen: 1 HPACK would cause HOL blocking on QUIC; 2.1.2 blocked streams, Required Insert Count, SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS, encoder's trade-off.

Extra: RFC 9218 (see http2 #5): the Priority header and PRIORITY_UPDATE frames are how HTTP/3 signals priority.

#### `websockets` (short)

1. [RFC 6455](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455), I. Fette, A. Melnikov, 2011. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 1.1 why (polling problems); 1.2–1.3 Upgrade handshake example, Sec-WebSocket-Key + GUID + SHA-1 → Accept (checked the example value with openssl); 5.1 clients must mask, servers must not; 5.2 frame layout (FIN, opcode, mask, 7/16/64-bit length); 5.5.2 ping/pong as keepalive; 10.3 masking stops cache poisoning of proxies.
2. [RFC 8441](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8441), P. McManus, 2018. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: HTTP/2 has no Upgrade or 101; extended CONNECT with `:protocol: websocket` after SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL; one WebSocket per stream.
3. [The WebSockets API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSockets_API), MDN. Docs, primary: no. Seen: the browser WebSocket interface has no backpressure; WebSocketStream non-standard, one engine; WebTransport expected to replace it for many uses.

Extra: [RFC 9220](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9220), R. Hamilton, 2022. Seen: the same extended CONNECT for HTTP/3. Not used beyond a mention.

#### `server-sent-events` (short)

1. [HTML Standard, 9.2 Server-sent events](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html), WHATWG. Living standard, primary: yes. Seen: EventSource API (only url + withCredentials); `text/event-stream`, UTF-8 only; fields event, data, id, retry; blank line dispatches; comment lines; auto reconnect after a reconnection time, Last-Event-ID; 204 stops reconnects; non-200 or wrong type fails; comment every 15 s against proxies; chunking by another layer can hurt; per-server connection limits.
2. [Using server-sent events](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events), MDN. Docs, primary: no. Seen: 6 connections per browser and domain without HTTP/2, "Won't fix" in Chrome and Firefox; with HTTP/2 the stream limit is negotiated (default 100 per MDN).

**Disagreements and tensions**
- **MDN says HTTP/2 streams "default to 100".** RFC 9113 says the initial SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS is unlimited and only recommends servers set at least 100. Cloudflare's rapid-reset post shows the practical truth: clients assume 100 without waiting for SETTINGS. Articles say "servers usually allow at least 100", not "defaults to 100".
- **Stream-limit enforcement.** RFC 9113 treats going over the limit as a stream error; Google's rapid-reset post argues servers should close the whole connection.
- **QUIC numbers are Google QUIC.** The SIGCOMM 2017 paper measured Google's pre-IETF QUIC with its own crypto handshake. RFC 9000 QUIC uses TLS 1.3. The latency and CPU numbers are not measurements of IETF QUIC.
- **Server push.** RFC 9113 and RFC 9114 still define push; Chrome removed it (Chrome 106, 2022). The spec text itself says push is hard to use well.
- **Priorities.** RFC 7540's tree is deprecated in RFC 9113, HTTP/3 has no built-in priority signal; RFC 9218 replaces both with a header plus frames, and servers are free to ignore it.

**Couldn't open**
None.

**Rejected**
- Secondary explainers on HTTP/2 framing (e.g. web.dev's HTTP/2 introduction): the RFCs cover the mechanism directly.
- The HTTP/2 rapid reset CVE page on cve.org: the Cloudflare post explains more and is primary.

**Gaps**
- No source with current HTTP/3 or QUIC adoption numbers was opened; the articles give none.
- No first-hand source on how Linux UDP offloads (GSO/GRO) change QUIC's CPU cost; the article only gives Google's 2017 numbers, dated.
- No source for WebSocket connection counts per server or memory per connection; left out.

### RPC, pools and fuzzing

All pages below were opened with `curl -sL` and converted to text with
pandoc (the T-Reqs paper with pdftotext). Raw copies were kept in the
scratchpad while writing.

#### `protobuf` (short)

1. [Encoding](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/encoding/), Google (Protocol Buffers team), living doc (examples assume Edition 2023 or later). Spec, primary: yes. The wire format byte by byte. Seen: a message is a series of records, each a tag, then a payload; the tag is `(field_number << 3) | wire_type`; six wire types (VARINT, I64, LEN, SGROUP, EGROUP, I32, groups deprecated); the wire type lets "old parsers to skip over new fields"; `int32 a = 1` set to 150 encodes as `08 96 01`; field names and types live only in the .proto; missing fields are left out; packed repeated fields by default since Edition 2023; last value wins for a repeated singular field and message fields merge; no guaranteed field order and serialization "is not deterministic"; messages must be under 2 GiB. Already a source note (`protobuf-encoding`) from phase 1.
2. [Language Guide (proto 3)](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/), Google, living doc. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: field numbers 1 to 536,870,911, 19,000 to 19,999 reserved for the implementation; 1 to 15 take one byte, 16 to 2047 two; a field number "cannot be changed once your message type is in use"; reusing a number can cause parse errors, leaked PII, data corruption; `reserved` for deleted numbers; defaults (empty string, zero, false, first enum value) and implicit-presence scalars can't tell "set to zero" from "not set"; `optional` recommended; wire-safe changes (add field, remove field, add enum value), wire-unsafe (change number, move into existing oneof), compatible-but-lossy (int32 to int64); unknown fields kept by proto3 but lost through JSON; `service` blocks and gRPC.

Also opened: [Overview](https://protobuf.dev/overview/) (not a good fit for data over a few megabytes; messages not compressed; not self-describing), not used, the two above cover the node. [Proto best practices](https://protobuf.dev/best-practices/dos-donts/) redirected from `/programming-guides/dos-donts/`; opened, not used.

#### `grpc` (deep)

1. [gRPC over HTTP2 (PROTOCOL-HTTP2.md)](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/PROTOCOL-HTTP2.md), gRPC authors, master branch when this was written. Spec, primary: yes. The wire protocol. Seen: request = headers, length-prefixed messages, end of stream; response = headers, messages, trailers (or trailers only); `:method POST`, `:path /Service/Method`, `te: trailers` "used to detect incompatible proxies", `grpc-timeout` value of at most 8 digits plus a unit (H M S m u n); each message = 1-byte compressed flag + 4-byte big-endian length + message; DATA frame boundaries unrelated to message boundaries; status always in trailers, even OK; HTTP status 200 even on error; one HTTP/2 stream per call; RST_STREAM to gRPC code mapping (REFUSED_STREAM to UNAVAILABLE, safe to retry); GOAWAY carries last accepted stream id; calls not assumed idempotent, "Calls that cannot be proven to have started will not be retried"; full example unary call with frames.
2. [Core concepts, architecture and lifecycle](https://grpc.io/docs/what-is-grpc/core-concepts/), gRPC authors, page last modified 2026. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: four kinds of method (unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional); ordering guaranteed within a call; stubs generated from .proto; client and server make "independent and local determinations of the success of the call"; cancellation "not rolled back"; metadata keys, `-bin` suffix, `grpc-` prefix reserved; channels.
3. [Deadlines](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/deadlines/), gRPC authors, page last modified 2025. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: gRPC sets no deadline by default, so a client can wait "effectively forever"; server cancels the call when the deadline passes but the app must stop its own work; propagation automatic in Java and Go, opt-in in C++; deadline converted to a timeout on the wire to avoid clock skew; sequence diagram of client → user server → billing server with 2 s budget.
4. [Status codes and their use in gRPC (statuscodes.md)](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/statuscodes.md), gRPC authors, master branch. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 17 codes, 0 to 16; DEADLINE_EXCEEDED may be returned even if the operation succeeded; FAILED_PRECONDITION vs ABORTED vs UNAVAILABLE guidance for retries; table of codes the library itself generates; seven codes never generated by the library; "there is no fixed list of status codes on which it is appropriate to retry". The [grpc.io page](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/status-codes/) has the same code table but not the library-generated table.
5. [Performance best practices](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/performance/), gRPC authors, page last modified 2024. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: reuse stubs and channels; streams "cannot be load balanced once they have started"; each connection has a concurrent-stream limit and extra RPCs queue in the client; workaround is a pool of channels.
6. [gRPC Load Balancing on Kubernetes without Tears](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2018/11/07/grpc-load-balancing-on-kubernetes-without-tears/), William Morgan (Buoyant), Kubernetes blog, 2018. Blog, primary: no (vendor of Linkerd). Seen: HTTP/2's single long-lived connection breaks connection-level balancing, "All requests will get pinned to a single destination pod"; HTTP/1.1 doesn't suffer because it needs many connections that cycle; fixes: client-side balancing, headless services with many A records, or an L7 proxy.
7. [gRPC Web (PROTOCOL-WEB.md)](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/PROTOCOL-WEB.md), gRPC authors. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: browsers don't expose HTTP/2 framing; gRPC-Web works over any HTTP version; trailers sent as the last length-prefixed message with the top bit of the flag byte set; expected deployment is a translating proxy.

8. [Load Balancing in gRPC (load-balancing.md)](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/load-balancing.md), gRPC authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: balancing is per call; resolver gives addresses and a service config; `pick_first` is the default and sends all calls to one address; `round_robin` cycles over ready subchannels; look-aside `grpclb` deprecated in favour of xDS. Note `grpc-load-balancing` was created by another group; I re-opened the page and appended one claim.

Also opened: [gRPC Load Balancing](https://grpc.io/blog/grpc-load-balancing/), makdharma (Google), 2017. Proxy vs client-side vs lookaside balancing; L7 "can distribute the streams from one client among multiple backends". Not used; #6 says the same more directly. Keepalive: existing note `grpc-keepalive` (re-opened, quotes checked), cited from `connection-pooling`, not from `grpc`.

#### `connection-pooling` (short)

1. [net/http](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http), The Go Authors, go1.27.1. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "By default, Transport caches connections for future re-use"; `DefaultMaxIdleConnsPerHost = 2`; DefaultTransport has MaxIdleConns 100, IdleConnTimeout 90 s, dialer KeepAlive 30 s; MaxConnsPerHost counts dialing, active and idle, "dials will block"; the response body must be read to EOF and closed for reuse; Transport retries on a network error only if the connection was used before and the request is idempotent; DisableKeepAlives is "unrelated to the similarly named TCP keep-alives"; reuse Clients and Transports.
2. [About Pool Sizing](https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/About-Pool-Sizing), HikariCP wiki (Brett Wooldridge and contributors), last edited 2021. Wiki, primary: yes for HikariCP (the pool's authors), and it quotes the PostgreSQL formula. Seen: Oracle video: shrinking the pool cut response times "from ~100ms to ~2ms"; `connections = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count)`; "You want a small pool, saturated with threads waiting for connections"; pool-locking formula `T_n x (C_m - 1) + 1`; mixing long and short transactions is hardest, two pools can help; SSDs mean fewer threads, not more.
3. See `grpc` and phase 2 `tcp-keepalive`: [Keepalive](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/keepalive/) (existing note `grpc-keepalive`): long-lived connections "might be considered as idle by proxy or load balancers".

Also opened: [PgBouncer features](https://www.pgbouncer.org/features.html) and [PgBouncer config](https://www.pgbouncer.org/config.html): session, transaction and statement pooling modes. Not used here; belongs with phase 6's Postgres pooling.

#### `fuzzing` (short)

1. [Go Fuzzing](https://go.dev/doc/security/fuzz/), The Go Authors (Go 1.18+ docs). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: fuzzing "continuously manipulates inputs to a program to find bugs"; coverage guidance keeps inputs that expand coverage ("interesting"); seed corpus from `f.Add` and `testdata/fuzz`; failing inputs are minimized and saved as regression tests; 1-second per-input timeout; targets should be fast and deterministic, no global state; fuzzing runs until it fails or you stop it; `-fuzztime`; coverage instrumentation on AMD64 and ARM64 only.
2. [T-Reqs: HTTP Request Smuggling with Differential Fuzzing](https://seclab.nu/static/publications/ccs2021treqs.pdf), Jabiyev, Sprecher, Onarlioglu, Kirda, CCS 2021. Paper, primary: yes (they built the fuzzer). Seen: grammar-based generation plus string and tree mutations of the request line, headers and body; each of 10 servers (Apache, NGINX, Tomcat, ATS, HAProxy, Squid, Varnish, Akamai, Cloudflare, CloudFront) run as a reverse proxy in front of a feedback server; mismatched parsed body lengths are the "discrepancies"; pairs then stacked to verify smuggling; servers "may not be flawed when operating in isolation".

Also opened: [libFuzzer](https://llvm.org/docs/LibFuzzer.html) (in-process, coverage-guided) and [OSS-Fuzz](https://google.github.io/oss-fuzz/) (continuous fuzzing for open source). Not used; the Go docs cover coverage guidance for the lab's language.

**Disagreements and tensions**
- Protobuf: the docs call adding a field "wire-safe" but also warn that wire-safe changes can still break application code (exhaustive enum switches). And the implicit-presence default in proto3 hides "not set"; the guide now recommends `optional`.
- gRPC status codes: there is no official retry list; the docs say each app must pick. Deadlines: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED doesn't mean the work didn't happen.
- gRPC load balancing: the gRPC team presents proxy, client-side and lookaside as equal options; the Kubernetes blog (a proxy vendor) argues for a sidecar proxy.
- Pool sizing: HikariCP's "small pool" axiom vs Go's default of unlimited total connections and only 2 idle per host (our inference: a burst above 2 concurrent requests per host closes the extras afterwards and dials again later). Different layers (database vs HTTP) but people apply one rule to both.
- Fuzzing: which implementation counts as "right" in differential fuzzing is open; T-Reqs compares servers with each other, not with the RFC, and a disagreement is only a lead until checked.

**Couldn't open**
- arXiv abstract I tried for T-Reqs was the wrong id (a physics paper); used the authors' PDF instead.
- The Oracle Real-World Performance video linked from the HikariCP wiki (not a page; not watched). The 100 ms to 2 ms figure is cited as HikariCP reports it.

**Rejected**
- gRPC load balancing blog (2017): superseded by #6 for the one claim needed.
- PgBouncer docs: phase 6 material.
- libFuzzer, OSS-Fuzz: C/C++ focused; Go docs are enough for a short node.

**Gaps**
- No measured cost of a new TCP+TLS connection vs a pooled one; left qualitative. The lab could measure it.
- No primary source on how long idle timeouts are in common load balancers; left out.
- No source for protobuf vs JSON size or speed; left out.

### Proxies and CDNs

All pages below were opened (RFCs as plain text from rfc-editor.org;
HTML pages fetched with curl and read as text).

#### `reverse-proxy` (deep)

1. [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110), R. Fielding, M. Nottingham, J. Reschke (eds.), 2022. Spec, primary: yes. The definitions: proxy vs gateway ("a.k.a. reverse proxy") vs tunnel, and what an intermediary must do when forwarding. Seen: 3.7 figure of UA, A, B, C, O over four connections; "upstream/downstream" and "inbound/outbound" terms; 7.6 intermediaries must forward unrecognized protocol elements, must implement Connection and drop hop-by-hop fields, must not loop to themselves, may buffer instead of streaming; 7.6.3 Via: each intermediary appends itself, a gateway MUST send Via on inbound requests; 9.2.2 a proxy MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests; 15.6.3 502 and 15.6.5 504 defined in terms of a gateway or proxy. (Note already existed; appended.)
2. [Module ngx_http_proxy_module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html), nginx docs, read when nginx 1.31 was current. Docs, primary: yes. What a real proxy does by default. Seen: response buffering on by default, spills to temp files; request body buffering on by default (1.7.11); Host and Connection not passed by default, replaced with `$proxy_host` and `close` for HTTP/1.x; `proxy_http_version` default changed to 1.1 in 1.29.7 (was 1.0), version 2 added in 1.29.4; `proxy_next_upstream error timeout` by default, non-idempotent requests (POST, LOCK, PATCH) not passed to the next server once sent (since 1.9.13); retry only possible if nothing has been sent to the client yet; `proxy_read_timeout` 60s default, measured between two reads; `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for`.
3. [Module ngx_http_upstream_module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_upstream_module.html), nginx docs, 1.31. Docs, primary: yes. Upstream groups and connection caching. Seen: `keepalive` caches idle connections per worker process; since 1.29.7 enabled by default with 32 per worker (the `local` default means not shared across locations); it doesn't cap total connections; before 1.29.7 you had to set HTTP/1.1 and clear Connection; `max_fails`/`fail_timeout`.
4. [Life of a Request](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/life_of_a_request), Envoy docs, 1.40.0-dev. Docs, primary: yes. A modern L7 proxy's request path, step by step. Seen: terms downstream/upstream/cluster/endpoint/listener/filter; listener subsystem vs cluster subsystem bridged by the router filter; one downstream connection handled by exactly one worker thread for its lifetime; each worker keeps its own upstream connection pools; listeners warming/active/draining; TLS transport socket decrypts, HTTP/2 codec demultiplexes into streams, router picks a cluster, load balancing picks an endpoint, circuit breakers checked, new upstream connection if pool empty; response passes filters in reverse order.
5. [How we built Pingora, the proxy that connects Cloudflare to the Internet](https://blog.cloudflare.com/how-we-built-pingora-the-proxy-that-connects-cloudflare-to-the-internet/), Yuchen Wu and Andrew Hauck, Cloudflare, 2022. Blog, primary: yes. Why the proxy's own architecture matters for connection reuse. Seen: NGINX's upstream connection pool is per worker, so more workers means worse reuse; Pingora (Rust, multithreaded) shares pools; one customer's reuse ratio went from 87.1% to 99.92%, 160x fewer new origin connections; about 70% less CPU and 67% less memory for the same traffic.

#### `request-smuggling` (short)

1. [RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112), R. Fielding, M. Nottingham, J. Reschke (eds.), 2022. Spec, primary: yes. The framing rules smuggling abuses. Seen: 6.3 ordered body-length rules; rule 3: both TE and CL means TE wins, "ought to be handled as an error", an intermediary that forwards must remove CL first; 6.1 why TE overrides CL (old progress-bar senders), server must close the connection after such a request; an HTTP/1.0 message with TE is faulty framing; 11.2 defines smuggling and cites Linhart et al. 2005; 3 lenient whitespace parsing leads to smuggling. (Note already existed; appended.)
2. [HTTP Desync Attacks: Request Smuggling Reborn](https://portswigger.net/research/http-desync-attacks-request-smuggling-reborn), James Kettle, PortSwigger, 2019. Research write-up, primary: yes (the researcher who revived the attack). Seen: front-end and back-end reuse one connection for many users' requests; a disagreement on where a request ends leaves a "prefix" on the socket that is glued to the next user's request; CL.CL, CL.TE, TE.CL; obfuscated Transfer-Encoding headers (`Transfer-Encoding : chunked`, tabs, `xchunked`) that only one side recognises; timing-based detection; attack first documented by Watchfire in 2005; defence: HTTP/2 upstream, or no back-end connection reuse, or same server software; front-ends normalise, back-ends reject and close; HTTPS doesn't help.
3. [HTTP/1.1 must die: the desync endgame](https://portswigger.net/research/http1-must-die), James Kettle, PortSwigger, 2025. Research write-up, primary: yes. What changed in six years. Seen: WAF regexes and parser tightening hide the problem without fixing it; front-ends that downgrade HTTP/2 to HTTP/1.1 upstream add a fourth length interpretation (CL, TE, implicit zero, H2); a desync inside Cloudflare exposed over 24,000,000 websites, patched within hours; recommends upstream HTTP/2; lists nginx among vendors without upstream HTTP/2 when written; survival list for HTTP/1.1 (normalise and validate, disable upstream connection reuse, reject bodies on GET/HEAD/OPTIONS).

#### `client-ip-forwarding` (short)

1. [RFC 7239: Forwarded HTTP Extension](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7239), A. Petersson and M. Nilsson, 2014. Spec, primary: yes. The standard header and its trust problem. Seen: proxies make requests look like they come from the proxy's address; X-Forwarded-For/-By/-Proto are non-standard; `Forwarded: for=...;by=...;proto=...;host=...`; IPv6 must be quoted in brackets; first element is added by the first proxy; the last proxy isn't in the list, it's the TCP peer; obfuscated identifiers with a leading underscore; 7.4 converting X-Forwarded-For; 7.5 worked example with two proxies; 8.1 the header "cannot be relied upon to be correct", and whitelisting proxies still leaves the part before the first trusted proxy untrusted.
2. [The PROXY protocol, versions 1 & 2](https://www.haproxy.org/download/3.0/doc/proxy-protocol.txt), Willy Tarreau, HAProxy Technologies, last revised 2020. Spec, primary: yes. Client address for TCP proxies that don't parse HTTP. Seen: one header prepended to the connection; v1 is a text line like `PROXY TCP4 192.168.0.1 192.168.0.11 56324 443\r\n`, at most 107 characters; v2 is binary with a 12-byte signature; carries what getpeername()/getsockname() would have given; receiver MUST be configured for it and MUST NOT guess whether it's present, so a port can't be shared between public and trusted senders; MUST NOT be used on multiplexed connections carrying many clients' requests.
3. [X-Forwarded-For](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/X-Forwarded-For), MDN contributors, page last modified 2025. Reference, primary: no. The clearest practical rules. Seen: rightmost is the most recent proxy, leftmost the claimed client; if the server is reachable directly, no part of the list is trustworthy; multiple XFF headers must be joined into one list; pick by trusted proxy count or trusted proxy list, searching from the right; leftmost values only where spoofing doesn't matter.
4. [Module ngx_http_realip_module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_realip_module.html), nginx docs. Docs, primary: yes. How one proxy implements "trusted list from the right". Seen: `set_real_ip_from` trusted addresses; `real_ip_header` default X-Real-IP, can be X-Forwarded-For or proxy_protocol; `real_ip_recursive off` takes the last address, `on` takes the last non-trusted address; not built by default. Also the proxy module's `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` appends `$remote_addr`.

#### `zero-downtime-reload` (short)

1. [socket(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/socket.7.html), Linux man-pages 6.19. Man page, primary: yes. Seen: SO_REUSEPORT since Linux 3.9 lets several sockets bind the same address and port; must be set on every socket before bind; same effective UID required; for TCP it spreads accept() across per-thread listeners; when a socket leaves a reuseport group the last socket takes its place; BPF programs can pick the socket.
2. [Truly Seamless Reloads with HAProxy – No More Hacks!](https://www.haproxy.com/blog/truly-seamless-reloads-with-haproxy-no-more-hacks), Willy Tarreau, HAProxy Technologies, 2017. Blog, primary: yes. The whole history of the problem. Seen: 2006 soft reload with a brief window where no process held the port; SO_REUSEPORT on OpenBSD removed the gap; Linux 3.9's SO_REUSEPORT gives each socket its own queue, so connections waiting in the old process's queue are reset when it closes; about 2-3 RSTs per million connections per reload in their lab; workarounds: dropping SYNs, delaying SYNs with a qdisc (Yelp), GitHub's multibinder; the fix in HAProxy 1.8: pass listening file descriptors to the new process over a UNIX socket with SCM_RIGHTS (`expose-fd listeners`, `-x`).
3. [Graceful upgrades in Go](https://blog.cloudflare.com/graceful-upgrades-in-go/), Lorenz Bauer, Cloudflare, 2018. Blog, primary: yes. Same problem from the application side. Seen: a client is refused if no socket listens on the port or nothing calls accept(); plain exec can't be undone if the new config is bad, and the backlog can overflow while the new binary starts; SO_REUSEPORT creates a separate socket structure, so not-yet-accepted connections on the old socket get terminated; NGINX shares listeners by clearing FD_CLOEXEC and passing fd numbers in an environment variable; the tableflip library.
4. [Controlling nginx](https://nginx.org/en/docs/control.html), nginx docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: HUP: check config, open new listen sockets, roll back on failure, start new workers, old workers stop accepting and finish their clients; USR2 starts a new binary that inherits the listen sockets, WINCH drains old workers, old master keeps its listeners so you can roll back.
5. [Hot restart](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/operations/hot_restart), Envoy docs, 1.40.0-dev. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: new process fully initialises, then asks the old one for its listen sockets over a UNIX domain socket, then tells it to drain; `--drain-time-s` and `--parent-shutdown-time-s`; existing connections are never transferred, they finish or get closed; with reuse_port, sockets are passed by worker index so nothing is dropped from accept queues, unless concurrency decreases.

#### `cdn` (deep)

1. [RFC 9111: HTTP Caching](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111), R. Fielding, M. Nottingham, J. Reschke (eds.), 2022. Spec, primary: yes. The rules every CDN cache starts from. Seen: shared vs private cache; fresh vs stale, validation; the cache key is at least method and URI, and many caches use only the URI; Vary adds request headers to the key; section 3 list of when a response may be stored (no-store, private, Authorization); heuristic freshness, typical 10% of the time since Last-Modified; s-maxage for shared caches; unsafe methods invalidate the target URI; 7.1 cache poisoning via parser differences. Obsoletes RFC 7234.
2. [RFC 9213: Targeted HTTP Cache Control](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9213), S. Ludin (Akamai), M. Nottingham (Fastly), Y. Wu (Cloudflare), 2022. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: multiple cache layers (origin, same-network, CDN, browser) need separate instructions; `CDN-Cache-Control: max-age=60`; motivation: a publisher can purge its CDN so it gives the CDN a longer lifetime than browsers.
3. [Default cache behavior](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/concepts/default-cache-behavior/), Cloudflare docs, when this was written. Docs, primary: yes. What a big CDN does with no configuration. Seen: caches by file extension, not MIME type; does not cache HTML or JSON by default; list of extensions; doesn't cache with private/no-store/no-cache/max-age=0, Set-Cookie, or non-GET; default edge TTLs by status (200/206/301 120 min, 302/303 20 min, 404/410 3 min); request collapsing with a cache lock per data center.
4. [Tiered Cache](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/how-to/tiered-cache/), Cloudflare docs, when this was written. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: lower tiers near visitors ask upper tiers, only upper tiers ask the origin; fewer origin connections; Smart Tiered Cache picks the upper tier by measured latency to the origin; regional tier option.
5. [Caching content with Fastly](https://www.fastly.com/documentation/guides/concepts/edge-state/cache/) and [Purging](https://www.fastly.com/documentation/guides/concepts/edge-state/cache/purging/), Fastly docs, when this was written. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: first request for a cacheable resource at a POP goes to the backend, later ones are served from cache; follows RFC 9111; request collapsing, streaming miss, backend revalidation; cache is ephemeral and objects may be evicted before expiry; purge all (up to 2 minutes), URL purge and surrogate-key purge (around 150 ms); Surrogate-Key header stripped before delivery; soft purge marks stale instead of invalidating; warning that big purges spike origin traffic.
6. See `anycast` (RFC 7094 4.5): TCP anycast called architecturally unsafe, yet widely deployed for CDNs.

**Disagreements and tensions**

- **Normalise or reject?** Kettle 2019 says front-ends should normalise ambiguous requests and back-ends should reject them and close. RFC 9112 lets a server either reject TE+CL or use TE alone, as long as it closes the connection. Kettle 2025 says normalising and rejecting has failed in practice and only upstream HTTP/2 fixes the class.
- **nginx and upstream HTTP/2.** Kettle 2025 lists nginx as lacking upstream HTTP/2; the nginx docs now show `proxy_http_version 2` added in 1.29.4. The article says the docs show it, versioned.
- **HAProxy blog vs Envoy docs on SO_REUSEPORT.** HAProxy 2017 found that plain SO_REUSEPORT drops queued connections on reload and moved to fd passing. Envoy uses reuse_port and also passes the sockets, by worker index, so the queues survive. The common ground: passing the listening socket is what closes the gap, SO_REUSEPORT alone doesn't.
- **Forwarded vs X-Forwarded-For.** RFC 7239 standardised Forwarded in 2014; MDN says it's "much less frequently used" than XFF. nginx's realip module works with XFF, X-Real-IP or PROXY protocol, not Forwarded.
- **Retrying at the proxy.** RFC 9110 forbids automatic retry of non-idempotent requests by proxies; nginx allows it with `non_idempotent`.
- **Cache HTML?** RFC 9111 says caching is the default when nothing forbids it; Cloudflare doesn't cache HTML or JSON by default whatever the headers say, until a rule says so.

**Couldn't open**

- None of the chosen pages failed. The Linhart et al. 2005 Watchfire paper (cited by RFC 9112) wasn't opened; not cited.

**Rejected**

- RFC 7230 (downloaded): obsoleted by RFC 9110/9112; not needed.
- Cloudflare "The sad state of Linux socket balancing" (opened, 2017): about SO_REUSEPORT load spread, not reloads. Better for `load-balancing` or phase 4 event loops.

**Gaps**

- No source opened on HAProxy's own reverse-proxy docs (the configuration manual is very large); nginx and Envoy cover the proxy's behaviour.
- No source for how many PoPs any CDN runs today; the article gives no count.
- No source for CDN hit ratios in general; the only number is Pingora's connection reuse ratio for one customer.
- GitHub's multibinder post was named in the HAProxy blog but not opened.

### Load balancing

#### `load-balancing` (deep)

1. [Load Balancing in the Datacenter](https://sre.google/sre-book/load-balancing-datacenter/), Alejandro Forero Cuervo, *Site Reliability Engineering* chapter 20, Google/O'Reilly, 2017. Book chapter from the builders, primary: yes. Seen: the goal is equal CPU on the least and most loaded task, and the gap is reserved-but-wasted capacity (1,000 CPUs reserved, 700 usable example); simple flow control (active-request cap, 100 is "reasonable"); three backend states from the client's view (healthy, refusing connections, lame duck); lame-duck shutdown steps after SIGTERM, drain interval "between 10s and 150s"; long-lived connection pools; subsetting (20 to 100 backends per client), random subsetting spreads badly (300 clients, 300 backends, 30% subset: 63% to 121% of average; 10% subset: 50% to 150%), deterministic subsetting code; policies: simple round robin (up to 2x CPU spread), least-loaded round robin (sinkholing by fast errors, still about 2x), weighted round robin with backend-reported utilization. Query costs vary 1000x or more; one Java backend averages 15 ms CPU but some queries take 10 s.
2. [Load Balancing at the Frontend](https://sre.google/sre-book/load-balancing-frontend/), Piotr Lewandowski, *SRE* chapter 19, 2017. Primary: yes. Seen: balancing at several levels; DNS load balancing (multiple A/AAAA records, little control; recursive resolvers hide the user; TTL caching; 512-byte reply limit); VIPs served by a network load balancer; least-loaded breaks for stateful protocols so the balancer must track connections or hash; `id(packet) mod N` remaps almost everything when N changes; consistent hashing (1997) with connection tracking as the normal path; forwarding by NAT, by L2 rewrite with Direct Server Response, or by GRE encapsulation (24 bytes overhead for IPv4+GRE, MTU issue).
3. [Maglev: A Fast and Reliable Software Network Load Balancer](https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/44824.pdf), Eisenbud et al., NSDI 2016. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: routers spread packets to Maglev machines by ECMP; each VIP announced by BGP; GRE to the endpoint; Direct Server Return; serving Google since 2008; connection tracking table keyed by 5-tuple hash; tracking alone fails when the set of Maglevs changes (ECMP reshuffles) or the table fills (SYN flood); Maglev hashing favours even spread over minimal disruption; lookup table size M prime, M > 100 x N for at most 1% imbalance, default 65537; health checks per backend pool, deduplicated by IP.
4. [Unimog - Cloudflare's edge load balancer](https://blog.cloudflare.com/unimog-cloudflares-edge-load-balancer/), David Wragg, Cloudflare, 2020. Engineering blog, primary: yes. Seen: an L4LB looks at packets up to layer 4 of the OSI model; L4LB is cheap because it never touches the payload, but it can only choose which server gets a connection; L7LBs are proxies; one misdirected packet gets a RST and breaks the connection ("much worse than a dropped packet"); ECMP alone breaks connections on rehash, has group size limits and no dynamic weights; Unimog runs on every server in XDP, measures load and adjusts shares with a control loop; mixed hardware generations mean equal connection counts don't give equal load; costs under 1% CPU; GUE encapsulation makes a 1500-byte packet 1536, so jumbo frames inside.
5. [GLB: GitHub's open source load balancer](https://github.blog/engineering/infrastructure/glb-director-open-source-load-balancer/), Theo Julienne, GitHub, 2018. Engineering blog, primary: yes. Seen: GLB Director is an L4 LB in front of haproxy/nginx; ECMP hashing and its connection breakage when servers change; LVS directors need connection state and sync; GLB instead keeps no flow state: a 65k-row table of primary and secondary server per row, built with rendezvous hashing; a packet the primary doesn't know is forwarded to the secondary ("second chance"); draining by swapping primary and secondary; GUE encapsulation; Direct Server Return; DPDK.
6. [Load Balancing in gRPC](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/load-balancing.md), gRPC project docs (repo master). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: balancing per call, not per connection; resolver returns addresses plus service config; LB policy makes subchannels and picks one per RPC; `pick_first` is the default, `round_robin` optional; `grpclb` look-aside is deprecated in favour of xDS.

Extra: [Using nginx as HTTP load balancer](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/load_balancing.html), nginx docs. Seen: round-robin default, least-connected, ip-hash for stickiness, weights, passive health checks (`max_fails` default 1, `fail_timeout`). Used by `load-balancing-algorithms` and `health-checks`.

#### `l4-vs-l7` (short)

1. [ITU-T X.200 (07/94): OSI Basic Reference Model](https://www.itu.int/rec/T-REC-X.200-199407-I/en), ITU-T, 1994 (same text as ISO/IEC 7498-1:1994). Spec, primary: yes. Free PDF opened from the ITU page. Seen: 6.1.2 lists the seven layers with their numbers (Application layer 7 ... Transport layer 4, Network layer 3, Data Link layer 2, Physical layer 1); 7.4.2.3 transport protocols are end to end. This is the source for "L4" and "L7".
2. [Unimog](https://blog.cloudflare.com/unimog-cloudflares-edge-load-balancer/). See load-balancing #4. L4LB inspects up to layer 4; can't take part in TLS or HTTP; L7LBs are proxies that can modify data; the 4-tuple spans the IP (layer 3) and TCP (layer 4) headers.

3. [gRPC Load Balancing on Kubernetes without Tears](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2018/11/07/grpc-load-balancing-on-kubernetes-without-tears/), William Morgan (Buoyant), 2018. Already a note (`morgan-grpc-lb-kubernetes-2018`). Blog, primary: no. HTTP/2 multiplexing pins every call to one backend behind a connection-level balancer; HTTP/1.1 escapes it by cycling connections; fix by balancing requests.

Extra: [Outlier detection](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/outlier), Envoy docs (1.40.0-dev). The TCP proxy "does not understand any protocol above the TCP layer" so it only sees connection failures, while the HTTP router also sees 5xx. A neat L4/L7 difference; used in `health-checks`. HAProxy's `observe layer4|layer7` makes the same split.

#### `load-balancing-algorithms` (deep)

1. [The Power of Two Choices in Randomized Load Balancing](https://www.eecs.harvard.edu/~michaelm/postscripts/tpds2001.pdf), Michael Mitzenmacher, IEEE TPDS 12(10), 2001. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: supermarket model (Poisson arrivals, n servers, pick d at random, join the shortest); d = 2 gives an exponential improvement over d = 1, d = 3 only a constant factor more; rule of thumb that two choices do almost as well as perfect global knowledge; simulations with 100 and 500 queues; Table 2 (500 queues, arrival rate 0.99): average time 100.00 for d = 1 (prediction), 5.5413 for d = 2, 3.9518 for d = 3, 3.0012 for d = 5 (tables are images in the PDF, read from the rendered page 1101).
2. [Supported load balancers](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/load_balancers), Envoy docs (1.40.0-dev). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: weighted round robin; client-side WRR from ORCA load reports (qps / (utilization + eps/qps * penalty)); least request = P2C by default (2 random choices, cites Mitzenmacher), "resistance to herding"; with unequal weights, weight / (active + 1)^bias; ring hash (Ketama), 1/N of requests move when a host changes; Maglev table 65537, faster than ring hash but about double the keys move; random beats round robin without health checks.
3. [Load Balancing in the Datacenter](https://sre.google/sre-book/load-balancing-datacenter/). See load-balancing #1. Round robin, least-loaded round robin with the sinkhole trap and the limits of local counts, weighted round robin.
4. [HAProxy 3.2 Configuration Manual](https://docs.haproxy.org/3.2/configuration.html), HAProxy (3.2.25). Docs, primary: yes.
