Seen: `balance roundrobin` (dynamic weights, 4095 server limit, default), `static-rr`, `leastconn` ("recommended where very long sessions are expected ... not very well suited for protocols using short sessions such as HTTP", counts queued connections), `first`, `source` (hash of client IP; many clients move when server count changes), `random(<draws>)` default 2 draws, "Power of Two Random Choices", avoids hammering when servers are added; `slowstart`.
5. [ngx_http_upstream_module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_upstream_module.html), nginx docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `least_conn` (1.3.1/1.2.2), `random [two [method]]` (1.15.1, default method least_conn), `least_time` (open source since 1.31.0), `zone` shares run-time state between worker processes, `max_fails` / `fail_timeout` (default 1 and 10 s), `resolve` (open source since 1.27.3), SRV `service=`.
6. [Maglev](https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/44824.pdf). See load-balancing #3. Section 3.4 Maglev hashing: preference lists, backends take turns filling a prime-sized table; evenness over minimal disruption.

Extra: [Slow start mode](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/slow_start), Envoy docs. Seen: new endpoints ramp weight up over a window; not effective when all endpoints are new. Not used; HAProxy's `slowstart` covers the idea.

#### `health-checks` (short)

1. [Health checking](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/health_checking), Envoy docs (1.40.0-dev). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: active checks per cluster (HTTP expects 200, gRPC, L3/L4 connect or echo, Redis, Thrift), with interval and failure/success thresholds; passive = outlier detection; health-check filter modes including pass-through with caching to spare the service; `x-envoy-immediate-health-check-fail` for fast draining; a host can vanish and come back as a different service on the same IP, hence `service_name_matcher`; degraded state.
2. [Outlier detection](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/outlier), Envoy docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: passive checking from real traffic; locally vs externally originated errors; consecutive 5xx, gateway failures, success rate, failure percentage; `max_ejection_percent`; ejection time grows with each ejection up to `max_ejection_time`; hosts come back automatically; an active check pass unejects a host (can be premature).
3. [Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes/), Kubernetes docs (v1.37). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: readiness failure removes the Pod IP from EndpointSlices; liveness failure restarts the container; wrong liveness probes can cascade under load; exec/gRPC/HTTP (200 to 399)/TCP checks; defaults period 10 s, timeout 1 s, failureThreshold 3, successThreshold 1; readiness may check dependencies.

Extra: HAProxy `inter` (default 2000 ms), `rise` (default 2), `fall` (default 3), `observe layer4|layer7`, `agent-check` from HAProxy 3.2 manual (load-balancing-algorithms #4). nginx passive checks (`max_fails`, `fail_timeout`). [Panic threshold](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/panic_threshold), Envoy docs: below 50% available hosts (default), Envoy ignores health and balances over all hosts (or none). Used in `load-balancing`.

#### `service-discovery` (short)

1. [Service](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/), Kubernetes docs (v1.37). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Pods are ephemeral and change IPs; a Service selects Pods and the controller keeps EndpointSlices updated; cluster IP (virtual IP) handled by kube-proxy; headless Services return Pod IPs in DNS A/AAAA records instead; discovery by environment variables (needs the Service created first) or DNS (`my-service.my-ns`); SRV records for named ports (`_http._tcp.my-service.my-ns`); EndpointSlices hold up to 100 endpoints by default; old Endpoints API truncates past 1000.
2. [Service discovery](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/service_discovery), Envoy docs (1.40.0-dev). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: static, strict DNS (every IP is a host, refreshed asynchronously, default 5000 ms), logical DNS (first IP only, for big round-robin DNS services), original destination, EDS (xDS API, preferred, carries weights and zones); Envoy's stance that discovery needn't be fully consistent, with the 2x2 discovered/health-check matrix (health check beats discovery data).
3. [What is service discovery?](https://developer.hashicorp.com/consul/docs/use-case/service-discovery), HashiCorp Consul docs. Docs (vendor), primary: yes for Consul. Seen: service catalog as source of truth; instances register and deregister, unhealthy ones removed; consumers query by DNS; client-side vs server-side discovery patterns.
4. [RFC 2782](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2782). Already a note (`rfc-2782`). SRV gives host and port with priority and weight. Covered by `dns-records`; linked instead of cited.

Extra: [gRPC Name Resolution](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/naming.md), gRPC docs. Seen: URI scheme picks the resolver, `dns` default, resolvers can watch and push updates, results carry per-address attributes for the LB policy. Not used; `grpc-load-balancing` covers the resolver-to-policy handoff.

**Disagreements and tensions**

- **Least connections for HTTP.** HAProxy's manual recommends `leastconn` for long sessions and says it's not well suited to short HTTP sessions; nginx pitches `least_conn` for requests that take longer to complete; Google found least-loaded round robin about as bad as plain round robin at scale (2x spread) because each client only sees its own requests. Envoy's default least-request is P2C, not a full scan.
- **Minimal disruption vs even spread.** Maglev chose even spread and accepts more reshuffling; Envoy's docs measure about double the keys moving with Maglev vs ring hash. GLB and Unimog add a second-chance hop or connection tracking so reshuffles don't break flows.
- **Strongly vs eventually consistent discovery.** Envoy says operating ZooKeeper/etcd/Consul at scale is painful and discovery doesn't need full consistency (health checks win); Consul presents a replicated catalog as the source of truth.
- **Health checks can make things worse.** Kubernetes warns that wrong liveness probes cascade under load; Envoy adds a panic threshold (ignore health below 50% available) for the same reason; Google's active-request cap "backfired" and made all backends unreachable.

**Couldn't open**

- Consul DNS docs at developer.hashicorp.com/consul/docs/discover/dns: the page loaded a version picker with no content. Used the Consul service discovery overview instead.
- Cloudflare's OSI model learning page (blocked earlier, not retried). ITU-T X.200 used instead.

**Rejected**

- ISO/IEC 7498-1 itself: paywalled; X.200 is the same text and free.
- Envoy slow start page: fine, but HAProxy's `slowstart` covers the one idea used.

**Gaps**

- No measured numbers for least connections vs P2C vs round robin with one slow backend. That's the phase 3 lab's algorithm comparison; until it runs, the articles use Mitzenmacher's model numbers only.
- No source opened on the Linux IPVS scheduler list or Katran; mentioned only by name via Unimog.
- Consistent hashing proper (Karger 1997, rendezvous hashing) not opened; the articles lean on Maglev, Envoy and GLB descriptions only.

### HTTP caching

#### `http-caching` (deep)

1. [RFC 9111: HTTP Caching](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111), R. Fielding, M. Nottingham, J. Reschke (editors), 2022 (STD 98, obsoletes 7234). Spec, primary: yes. The rules. Seen: 2 reuse is the default, cache key is at least method and URI (many caches use URI only), caches may store 404s, redirects, 206s; 3 the storage checklist (no-store, private in shared caches, Authorization, needs public/private/Expires/max-age/s-maxage/extension/heuristic status); 3.5 must-revalidate, public, s-maxage allow shared caching with Authorization; 4 reuse conditions, Age must be generated, unsafe methods written through, request collapsing allowed; 4.1 Vary matching, `Vary: *` never matches; 4.2 fresh = lifetime > age; 4.2.1 precedence s-maxage, max-age, Expires − Date, heuristic; 4.2.2 heuristic "typical" 10% of time since Last-Modified, old query-string ban "not widely implemented"; 4.2.3 Age arithmetic; 4.2.4 stale only when disconnected or allowed (RFC 5861 named); 4.3 validation, If-None-Match beats If-Modified-Since, 304 freshens stored headers, 5xx during validation may be treated as no answer; 4.4 invalidation only in caches the request passes through; 5.2 can't target one cache; 5.2.1 request directives advisory; 5.2.2 max-age, must-revalidate (504 when disconnected), no-cache, no-store ("not a reliable or sufficient mechanism for ensuring privacy"), private, public, s-maxage; qualified no-cache/private "not widely implemented"; 5.3 Expires ignored when max-age present, "0" = already expired; 5.4 Pragma deprecated; 7.1 poisoning, 7.2 timing and double keying, 7.3 Set-Cookie does not inhibit caching. Note: `rfc-9111` (appended).
2. [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110), same editors, 2022. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 8.8.1 strong vs weak validators (hash is enough for strong; one-second mtime and gzip-shared tags are weak); 8.8.3 ETag syntax, W/ prefix; 9.2.3 GET, HEAD, POST have caching semantics, most caches do GET and HEAD only; 9.3.3 POST responses cacheable only with explicit freshness and matching Content-Location; 12.5.5 Vary "expands the cache key"; 13.1.2 If-None-Match weak comparison, 304 for GET/HEAD; 13.1.3 If-Modified-Since ignored when If-None-Match present; 15.1 heuristically cacheable codes (200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414, 501); 15.4.5 304 must carry Cache-Control, Date, ETag, Vary, no content. Note: `rfc-9110` (appended).
3. [RFC 5861: HTTP Cache-Control Extensions for Stale Content](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5861), M. Nottingham (Yahoo!), 2010, informational (independent submission). Spec, primary: yes. Seen: stale-while-revalidate (serve stale while revalidating without blocking; example max-age=600, stale-while-revalidate=30; both at 600 means up to 20 minutes from cache; sparse traffic falls outside the window and blocks); stale-if-error (errors = 500, 502, 503, 504; example with Age: 900 and error written through after 1800 s); security: trigger background revalidation from a real request. Note: `rfc-5861`.
4. [RFC 8246: HTTP Immutable Responses](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8246), P. McManus (Mozilla), 2017, standards track. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: reloads issue conditional requests that return 304 for versioned URLs; `immutable` = won't change while fresh; skip conditional requests except force reload; only while fresh; proxies should skip too; example max-age=31536000, immutable; ignore it outside HTTPS. Note: `rfc-8246`.
5. [The State of Browser Caching, Revisited](https://mnot.net/blog/2017/browser-caching), Mark Nottingham, 2017 (www.mnot.net/blog/2017/03/16/browser-caching redirects here). Blog, primary: yes for his test results (he edits the caching spec and wrote the tests). Seen: Web Platform Tests via Fetch on Firefox, Chrome, Safari TP, Edge Insider; all got max-age/Expires, no-store, no-cache, 304 header updates and Vary right; heuristic freshness and caching of non-200 codes varied a lot by browser; request directives patchy (Chrome only max-age=0); only Firefox invalidated Location/Content-Location; browsers kept one Vary variant at a time. Note: `mnot-browser-caching-2017`.
6. [HTTP caching (MDN)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching), MDN contributors, page last modified 2026. Docs, primary: no (secondary explainer). Seen: private/shared, proxy vs managed caches, HTTPS makes most path proxies tunnel; heuristic caching as a workaround; Age example (604800 − 86400 = 518400); why max-age replaced Expires; Vary on User-Agent kills reuse, use private not Vary: Cookie; no-cache vs no-store, no-store doesn't delete an existing entry and costs bfcache; kitchen-sink header; reload sends max-age=0 plus validators, force reload sends no-cache; Chrome skipped immutable and stopped revalidating subresources on reload; no way to delete from intermediate caches, Clear-Site-Data browser only; request collapse reuses even no-cache responses; patterns (no-cache default, cache busting with immutable, no-cache for HTML). Note: `mdn-http-caching`.
7. [Caching content with Fastly](https://www.fastly.com/documentation/guides/concepts/edge-state/cache/), Fastly docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen (for this node): follows RFC 9111; automatic conditional revalidation of stale objects; stale-while-revalidate revalidations issued asynchronously; stale-if-error supported. Note: `fastly-caching` (appended).
8. [Default cache behavior](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/concepts/default-cache-behavior/), Cloudflare docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: no caching with Set-Cookie, private, no-store, no-cache or max-age=0; GET only; extension-based, no HTML/JSON by default. Note: `cloudflare-default-cache-behavior` (unchanged; used for the Set-Cookie contrast with RFC 9111 7.3).
9. [RFC 9213: Targeted HTTP Cache Control](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9213), Ludin, Nottingham, Wu, 2022. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: re-opened; CDN-Cache-Control, layered caches. Note: `rfc-9213` (unchanged).
10. [Caching Tutorial for Web Authors and Webmasters](https://www.mnot.net/cache_docs/), Mark Nottingham. Tutorial, primary: yes-ish (author of the spec). Seen: browser, proxy and gateway caches; "use URLs consistently" as the golden rule; Pragma doesn't work; Expires clock problems; validators; implementation notes for Apache 1.3, IIS 4, Netscape Enterprise Server. Not cited: old (server notes from the late 1990s), and MDN plus the RFCs cover the same ideas.
11. [Two HTTP Caching Extensions](https://www.mnot.net/blog/2007/12/12/stale), Mark Nottingham, 2007. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error were built at Yahoo! for back-end HTTP services, implemented in Squid; argues for Cache-Control over per-cache configuration. Not cited (RFC 5861 carries the mechanism); good history if the article grows.

**Disagreements and tensions**
- **Set-Cookie.** RFC 9111 7.3: Set-Cookie does not stop caching. Cloudflare: a response with Set-Cookie isn't cached. MDN: a cookie alone doesn't make a response private. So never rely on a cookie to keep a response out of a shared cache; say `private`.
- **no-store vs no-cache as the default "don't cache".** RFC 9111 defines both; MDN recommends `no-cache` (plus `private`) over `no-store` because no-store loses the back/forward cache and doesn't remove an old entry. Nottingham (2017) found both work in all tested browsers.
- **max-age=0, must-revalidate vs no-cache.** Often called equivalent; MDN says the combination is a pre-HTTP/1.1 workaround and no-cache is enough. RFC 9111 4.2 also allows an Expires in the past to force validation.
- **immutable.** RFC 8246 (Mozilla) defines it; MDN says Chrome didn't implement it and changed reload behavior instead.
- **Heuristic freshness.** RFC 9111 allows it and suggests 10%; Nottingham calls it what got web caching started; MDN calls it a workaround and says to always send Cache-Control. Browser support for heuristic caching of non-200 codes varied (2017).
- **Qualified private/no-cache.** Defined in RFC 9111, but the RFC itself says they're usually treated as unqualified.

**Couldn't open**
- Nothing: every page listed was opened.

**Rejected**
- Caching Tutorial (mnot.net/cache_docs): out of date (see #10).
- RFC 7234 (obsoleted by RFC 9111): not opened; no reason to cite a replaced spec.

**Gaps**
- No current (2026) primary source on browser caching behavior per browser; Nottingham's results are from 2017. The WPT results dashboard for fetch/http-cache would be the source, not opened.
- No measured numbers (304 sizes, hit ratios); the lab is on hold.
- Cache eviction before expiry is stated in RFC 9111 5.3 and Fastly, with no numbers.

## Phase 4: Concurrency and I/O models

Researched by 4 parallel passes, one per group below.

### Shared memory

#### `concurrency-vs-parallelism` (short)

1. [Concurrency is not Parallelism (slides)](https://go.dev/talks/2012/waza.slide), Rob Pike, Google/Go team, 2012. Talk, primary: yes. Seen: concurrency = composition of independently executing processes, parallelism = simultaneous execution; "dealing with" vs "doing" lots of things at once; structure vs execution; drivers (concurrent) vs dot product (parallel); prime sieve slower on 4 processors; gopher designs: concurrent design isn't automatically parallel, is still correct with zero parallelism, is parallelizable; goroutines multiplexed onto OS threads, a blocked goroutine blocks its thread only; buffered-channel load balancer; "Concurrency enables parallelism". Slides only; the Vimeo video wasn't watched.
2. [Parallelism Is Not Concurrency](https://existentialtype.wordpress.com/2011/03/17/parallelism-is-not-concurrency/), Robert Harper, Carnegie Mellon, 2011. Blog, primary: no. Seen: concurrency = nondeterministic composition (events you don't control), parallelism = asymptotic efficiency of deterministic programs; PRAM criticized as a programming model; Quicksort as naturally parallel; work and depth; Brent's principle O(max(w/p, d)); functional programming for parallelism. Comments push back (efficient parallel systems are nondeterministic in practice).
3. [Concurrency: An Introduction (OSTEP ch. 26)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf). Note exists (ostep-concurrency-intro). Two reasons for threads: parallelism across CPUs and not blocking on I/O; the race on one CPU via an interrupt.

Extra: [Concurrency is not parallelism (Go blog)](https://go.dev/blog/waza-talk), Andrew Gerrand, 2013. Opened: one paragraph summarizing the talk, links to slides and video. Not given a note; the slides say everything it does.

#### `race-condition` (deep)

1. [The Go Memory Model](https://go.dev/ref/mem), The Go Authors (2022 revision). Spec, primary: yes. Seen: data race definition (write concurrent with another access, unless all atomic); DRF-SC; racy Go limited to observed values for word-sized reads, multiword races (interfaces, slices, maps, strings) can corrupt memory; C/C++ racy programs undefined; TSan via -race halts on a race; happens-before = sequenced-before + synchronized-before; synchronizing operations list; broken idioms (double-checked locking, busy wait); compiler must not introduce writes or re-read locals; these optimizations are allowed in C/C++.
2. [Common Concurrency Problems (OSTEP ch. 32)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf), Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau, version 1.20. Book chapter, primary: no. Seen: Lu et al.'s study of MySQL, Apache, Mozilla, OpenOffice: 105 bugs, 74 non-deadlock, 31 deadlock; atomicity violation (MySQL proc_info check then fputs); order violation (Mozilla mThread); 97% of non-deadlock bugs are one or the other; fixes: lock around both, condition variable for order.
3. [How to miscompile programs with "benign" data races](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/hotpar11/tech/final_files/Boehm.pdf), Hans-J. Boehm, HP Labs, HotPar 2011. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: data race definition; catch-fire semantics (Ada 83, Posix, C, C++) vs Java's attempt; every kind of "benign" race from earlier work shown to break under reasonable compilers or hardware; double-checked locking; torn 32-bit counter with 16-bit writes reading zero; compiler re-reading a shared variable instead of spilling; redundant same-value writes; disjoint bit manipulation.
4. [CWE-367: TOCTOU Race Condition](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/367.html), MITRE, CWE list 4.20. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: definition (check state, state changes before use); TOCTTOU alternate term; setuid access()/fopen() symlink example (names, not handles); mitigations: don't check first, lock before the check, recheck after use; child of CWE-362; CVEs including browser sandbox add-on swap (CVE-2015-1743).
5. [open(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/open.2.html), man-pages 6.19. Note exists (man7-open), claims appended. Seen: O_CREAT|O_EXCL fails with EEXIST if the path exists and doesn't follow symlinks; NFS without O_EXCL makes lock files racy (link(2) workaround); O_APPEND positions and writes in one atomic step; O_CLOEXEC race with fork+execve.
6. [Concurrency: An Introduction (OSTEP ch. 26)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-intro.pdf). Note exists (ostep-concurrency-intro). The counter race, critical section, mutual exclusion.

Extra: [Data Race Detector](https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector), The Go Authors. Opened: the -race flag, report format, typical races (loop counter, accidentally shared variable, unprotected global, primitive unprotected variable, unsynchronized send and close). Not given a note; belongs to `race-detector`.

#### `mutex` (short)

1. [Locks (OSTEP ch. 28)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-locks.pdf), Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau, version 1.10. Book chapter, primary: no. Seen: lock as a variable (free/held); POSIX mutex; coarse vs fine-grained; criteria: correctness, fairness, performance; disabling interrupts; failed flag lock (Figure 28.2); test-and-set, compare-and-swap, LL/SC, fetch-and-add (ticket lock); spin waste; priority inversion aside; yield; queues with park/unpark; Linux futex_wait/futex_wake and glibc's lowlevellock (high bit plus waiter count); two-phase locks.
2. [sync package documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/sync), The Go Authors, go1.27.1. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: most of sync is low level, prefer channels; don't copy; Mutex zero value unlocked; unlock n synchronizes before lock m; TryLock (Go 1.18) often a sign of a deeper problem; unlock of unlocked mutex is a run-time error; not tied to a goroutine; RWMutex: waiting writer blocks new readers, no recursive read locking, no upgrade/downgrade; Cond vs channels; Map, Once, Pool, WaitGroup.
3. [src/internal/sync/mutex.go](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golang/go/master/src/internal/sync/mutex.go), The Go Authors, master branch. Code, primary: yes. Seen: state int32 + sema uint32; fast path one CAS; normal vs starvation mode comment (1 ms threshold, direct handoff, normal mode faster, starvation mode for tail latency); active spinning in lockSlow when runtime_canSpin.

Extra: [futex(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/futex.7.html), man-pages. Opened: futexes are a kernel building block for fast user-space locks; most programs use them through libraries such as NPTL; a futex is identified by a piece of memory shared between threads or processes. Not given a note; OSTEP covers what a short node needs.

#### `deadlock` (short)

1. [Common Concurrency Problems (OSTEP ch. 32)](https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~remzi/OSTEP/threads-bugs.pdf). See race-condition #2. Seen for this node: L1/L2 opposite-order example, only deadlocks with an unlucky switch; dependency graph cycle (Figure 32.7); why: large code bases and encapsulation (Java Vector.AddAll); Coffman's four conditions (1971); prevention per condition: total/partial lock order (Linux mm comment, v5.2), order by address, global prevention lock, trylock with livelock and random delay, lock-free CAS; avoidance by scheduling (Banker's algorithm) limited; detect and recover in databases; Dijkstra's "deadly embrace".
2. [Runtime locking correctness validator (lockdep)](https://docs.kernel.org/locking/lockdep-design.html), Ingo Molnar, Arjan van de Ven, Linux kernel docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: lock classes; L1 -> L2 dependencies; same class twice (recursion deadlock); inverse orders; cycles of any complexity; irq-safe/unsafe rules; proves possible deadlocks from component chains seen once, without the deadlock happening; per-chain 64-bit hash to check once; MAX_LOCKDEP_KEYS 8191; recursive vs non-recursive readers, a waiting writer blocking a second read lock.
3. [Understanding Real-World Concurrency Bugs in Go](https://songlh.github.io/paper/go-study.pdf), Tengfei Tu, Xiaoyu Liu, Linhai Song, Yiying Zhang, Penn State / Purdue, ASPLOS 2019. Paper, primary: yes. Seen for this node: Go's built-in deadlock detector reports only when no goroutine can progress; found 2 of the reproduced blocking bugs; misses partial blocking and waits on non-Go resources.

#### `memory-model` (deep)

1. [Hardware Memory Models](https://research.swtch.com/hwmm), Russ Cox, 2021. Blog, primary: no. Seen: flag program prints 1 on x86, can print 0 on ARM/POWER; Lamport's sequential consistency (1979); litmus tests; x86-TSO with per-core FIFO write queues; store buffering allowed on x86; barriers; Dekker/Peterson; history of Intel's model (2007 white paper, TLO+CC, real hardware violating it, x86-TSO adopted); ARM/POWER per-core memory copies; message passing, IRIW, load buffering allowed; coherence holds everywhere; ARMv8 multicopy atomic; gap between allowed and observed; Adve and Hill 1990 weak ordering / DRF-SC.
2. [Programming Language Memory Models](https://research.swtch.com/plmm), Russ Cox, 2021. Blog, primary: no. Seen: compiler register caching and reordering break the flag program; atomics as synchronizing atomics; DRF-SC in languages; compiled languages weaker than any hardware (not even coherent); compilers must not introduce races (Boehm 2004); Java 1996 model flaws, JSR-133 in Java 5.0 (2004); out-of-thin-air; C++11 seq_cst / acquire-release / relaxed; DRF-SC or catch fire; acquire/release allows store buffering; relaxed has no ordering; C++14 dropped formal OOTA rules; Rust 1.0 and Swift 5.3 adopted C++ model; ARMv8 ldar/stlr; JavaScript SC-only atomics and defined racy semantics.
3. [The Go Memory Model](https://go.dev/ref/mem). See race-condition #1. Seen for this node: happens-before rules for go statement, channels (buffered, unbuffered, close, semaphore), mutex, RWMutex, Once, atomics (SC, like C++ seq_cst and Java volatile), finalizers; incorrect compilation examples.
4. [sync/atomic package documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/sync/atomic), The Go Authors, go1.27.1. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "require great care"; prefer channels or sync; the Go proverb; swap, CAS, add, load, store semantics; atomics synchronize and are sequentially consistent; typed wrappers (Bool since go1.19).

Extra: [std::memory_order](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/atomic/memory_order.html), cppreference. Opened: the memory_order values (relaxed, consume, acquire, release, acq_rel, seq_cst) and their definitions. Not given a note; Cox's plmm covers the orderings in plain words and Go has only seq_cst.
Extra: [What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory](https://www.akkadia.org/drepper/cpumemory.pdf). Note exists (drepper-cpumemory); coherence/MESI is in `cpu-cache`, which the article links instead of re-citing.

#### `lock-free-structures` (short)

1. [An Introduction to Lock-Free Programming](https://preshing.com/20120612/an-introduction-to-lock-free-programming/), Jeff Preshing, 2012. Blog, primary: no. Seen: lock-free as a progress property (no "locking up": deadlock, livelock, worst-enemy scheduling); X = 1 - X example; Herlihy and Shavit's definition; suspended thread can't block others; RMW operations line up on one address; CAS loop pattern; failed CAS means another thread succeeded; ABA warning; sequential consistency via C++11 atomics or Java volatile; acquire/release; x86 loads acquire, stores release; code that works on x86 and fails elsewhere; is_lock_free.
2. [Simple, Fast, and Practical Non-Blocking and Blocking Concurrent Queue Algorithms](https://www.cs.rochester.edu/u/scott/papers/1996_PODC_queues.pdf), Maged Michael, Michael Scott, University of Rochester, PODC 1996. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: blocking vs non-blocking vs wait-free; delays from preemption, page faults, cache misses; CAS defined (IBM System 370); races found in earlier published queues (lost items); Valois reference counting runs out of memory; ABA and modification counters (double-word CAS or indices); the non-blocking queue with dummy node and the two-lock queue; single lock faster for one or two processors; 12-node SGI Challenge experiments (not used).
3. [sync/atomic package documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/sync/atomic). See memory-model #4. CompareAndSwap semantics in Go; all atomics sequentially consistent.

Extra: OSTEP ch. 32 (see race-condition #2) shows a CAS-based atomic increment and list insert and notes lock-free code can still livelock. Used in `deadlock`, not re-cited here.

#### `message-passing` (short)

1. [Share Memory By Communicating](https://go.dev/blog/codelab-share), Andrew Gerrand, Go blog, 2010. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: traditional threads share memory under locks; Go's channels pass references so one goroutine has the data at a time; CSP roots; "Do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating."; URL poller with mutex vs channels.
2. [Understanding Real-World Concurrency Bugs in Go](https://songlh.github.io/paper/go-study.pdf). See deadlock #3. Seen for this node: 171 bugs in Docker, Kubernetes, etcd, gRPC, CockroachDB, BoltDB; message passing as easy to get wrong as shared memory; about 58% of blocking bugs from message passing, 42% from shared memory, although shared-memory primitives are used more; far fewer non-blocking bugs from message passing; Kubernetes leaked goroutine (unbuffered send after select timeout, fixed with a buffer of 1); race detector found 7/13 traditional and 3/4 anonymous-function non-blocking bugs over 100 runs, and why it misses some.
3. [The Go Memory Model](https://go.dev/ref/mem). See race-condition #1. Channel send/receive/close happens-before rules, buffered channel as semaphore.

Extra: [Effective Go](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go), The Go Authors. Opened: the "Share by communicating" section and channels as semaphores. Not given a note; the blog post and memory model cover it.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Concurrency vs parallelism: Pike defines the difference as structure vs execution; Harper as nondeterministic composition vs deterministic speedup. Both agree they differ. The article gives both.
- Message passing vs shared memory: Go's docs and blog say channels are the better default; Tu et al. find message passing causes more blocking bugs than locks in real Go code, and fewer non-blocking ones. Both sides in `message-passing`.
- "Benign" data races: earlier work classified some races as harmless; Boehm (and the Go and C++ memory models) say none are safe at the source level.
- What a racy program means: C/C++ undefined ("catch fire"), Go limited outcomes but multiword corruption, Java and JavaScript define racy behavior (for security). Covered in `memory-model`.
- Acquire/release atomics: C++ offers them for speed; Cox argues they're less useful than seq_cst and badly named; Go and JavaScript offer only seq_cst.
- Mutex fairness: Go's normal mode favors throughput, starvation mode favors tail latency; spin locks promise no fairness at all.

**Couldn't open:**

- Lamport, "How to Make a Multiprocessor Computer That Correctly Executes Multiprocess Programs" (1979), Microsoft Research PDF: the URL returned a small HTML page instead of the PDF. Not cited; the definition comes via Cox's quote.
- The Waza talk's .slide source on GitHub (golang/talks raw path returned 404); the rendered slides on go.dev opened fine.

**Rejected:**

- cppreference memory_order: C++-specific detail beyond what a Go-focused article needs.
- futex(7): the short mutex node explains futexes in one paragraph from OSTEP.
- Go blog "Concurrency is not parallelism" and Effective Go: summaries of sources already used.

**Gaps:**

- No source opened with measured costs (uncontended mutex lock, CAS, contended lock, channel send in ns), so none of the articles give numbers. The lab's phase 4 build could measure these.
- No source opened on database check-then-act beyond the framing; `race-condition` links `lost-update` (phase 8) for it.
- No Go-specific source on memory reclamation in lock-free code (does the GC remove ABA via reuse?); the article doesn't claim either way.
- Coffman et al. 1971 and Adve and Hill 1990 not opened; cited only through OSTEP and Cox, and named as such.

### I/O models

#### `non-blocking-io` (short)

1. [open(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/open.2.html), Michael Kerrisk and man-pages contributors, man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: O_NONBLOCK: open and later I/O don't make the caller wait; the flag doesn't change what select/poll/epoll report; it has no effect on regular files and block devices, which still block briefly for device activity.
2. [recv(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/recv.2.html), Michael Kerrisk and man-pages contributors, man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: with no data a receive waits unless the socket is nonblocking, then -1 and EAGAIN or EWOULDBLOCK; check for both; returns what's available, not the full amount; MSG_DONTWAIT is per call while O_NONBLOCK sits on the open file description and affects every holder.
3. [accept(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/accept.2.html): already a note (`man7-accept`). Seen again: on Linux the accepted socket doesn't inherit O_NONBLOCK.
4. [read(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/read.2.html), [write(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/write.2.html), [connect(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/connect.2.html), [F_GETFL(2const)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/F_GETFL.2const.html), [socket(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/socket.2.html), man-pages 6.19. Seen: EAGAIN on read and write for nonblocking fds; partial writes; connect returns EINPROGRESS and you wait for writability then read SO_ERROR; F_SETFL can change O_NONBLOCK; SOCK_NONBLOCK saves the fcntl call. Read for background; not cited (open and recv carry the article).

#### `io-multiplexing` (deep)

1. [select(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/select.2.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: WARNING that select only handles fd numbers below FD_SETSIZE (1024) "and this limitation will not change"; sets are modified in place and must be rebuilt each call; on Linux select can report a socket readable and the read still blocks (bad checksum), so use O_NONBLOCK; first appeared in 4.2BSD.
2. [poll(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/poll.2.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: array of struct pollfd (fd, events, revents) passed every call; negative fd is skipped; Linux 2.1.23; epoll does the same job with more features.
3. [epoll(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/epoll.7.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: epoll instance with an interest list and a ready list; epoll_create1/epoll_ctl/epoll_wait; the pipe example of ET vs LT (2 kB written, 1 kB read, second wait may hang); use ET with nonblocking fds and wait only after EAGAIN; LT is "simply a faster poll"; events combined between waits; registration is on the open file description, so a closed fd with a dup keeps reporting; starvation advice; about 160 bytes per watch on 64-bit; Linux 2.5.44.
4. [epoll_ctl(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/epoll_ctl.2.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: default is level-triggered; EPOLLONESHOT (2.6.2) disables the fd after one event until EPOLL_CTL_MOD; EPOLLEXCLUSIVE (4.5) wakes one or more instead of all epoll instances attached to the same fd.
5. [epoll_wait(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/epoll_wait.2.html), man-pages 6.19. Seen: history (2.6; epoll_pwait2 5.11). Not cited; epoll(7) covers it.
6. [Kqueue: A generic and scalable event notification facility](https://people.freebsd.org/~jlemon/papers/kqueue.pdf), Jonathan Lemon, FreeBSD Project, BSDCon 2000 (year from Kegel's page; the PDF doesn't print it). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: select/poll pass the whole list every call, two copies across the boundary, O(N) walks, three passes when the call sleeps; the root cause is that they're stateless; "a few hundred" active out of thousands, "95% of the copies unnecessary"; events level-triggered by design so partial reads still get notified; one kevent() call both registers and retrieves; registering is twice the cost of a poll() call for a single descriptor.
7. [kqueue(2)](https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?query=kqueue), FreeBSD 15.1 manual. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: kevents identified by (ident, filter); filters aggregate events; EV_CLEAR resets state after retrieval (edge-like); EVFILT_READ on a listen socket reports the backlog size; first appeared in FreeBSD 4.1. Not cited (Lemon's paper covers the design).
8. [Epoll is fundamentally broken 1/2](https://idea.popcount.org/2017-02-20-epoll-is-fundamentally-broken-12/) and [2/2](https://idea.popcount.org/2017-03-20-epoll-is-fundamentally-broken-22/), Marek Majkowski, 2017. Blog, primary: no. Seen: epoll created by Davide Libenzi in 2002; two design issues (multithreading, registering the file description not the fd); step-by-step LT thundering herd and ET starvation when threads share an accept socket; EPOLLEXCLUSIVE (4.5+) as the fix; EPOLLONESHOT emulation. Part 1 used.
9. [The C10K problem](http://www.kegel.com/c10k.html): already a note (`kegel-c10k`). Seen: readiness is a hint; LT vs ET named by Lemon; /dev/poll, rtsignals and epoll history. Not cited here (c10k node's).
10. [Go runtime source](https://github.com/golang/go/tree/release-branch.go1.26/src/runtime): already a note (`go-runtime-source`). Used for one example: the netpoller registers each socket edge-triggered for read and write.

#### `io-uring` (deep)

1. [Efficient IO with io_uring](https://kernel.dk/io_uring.pdf), Jens Axboe, 2019 (document version 0.4). Paper/design note, primary: yes. Seen: why Linux aio failed (O_DIRECT only, submission can block, 104 bytes copied per I/O, two system calls per I/O); design: single-producer single-consumer rings, SQ and CQ; sqe and cqe layouts, user_data; CQ twice the SQ; completions in any order; io_uring_setup/enter/register; IOSQE_IO_DRAIN and IOSQE_IO_LINK; fixed files and buffers; IOPOLL; SQPOLL with idle sleep and IORING_SQ_NEED_WAKEUP; 1.7M 4k IOPS polled vs aio 608K; buffered reads in page cache served inline. **kernel.dk's TLS certificate didn't match the host when opened; read through the Wayback Machine copy of the same URL.**
2. [io_uring(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/io_uring.7.html), liburing project, via man7.org. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: programming model; one CQE per SQE (with exceptions: CQE_SKIP_SUCCESS, multishot); res holds -errno; completion order is not submission order; don't have two sends or two receives in flight on one TCP socket; SQ polling; batching many SQEs into one io_uring_enter; Spectre/Meltdown made system calls dearer; pointer lifetimes.
3. [io_uring_setup(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/io_uring_setup.2.html), liburing project, via man7.org. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: rings shared, no copies; SQPOLL: kernel thread, no system calls while busy, sleeps after sq_thread_idle; SQPOLL needed root before 5.11, CAP_SYS_NICE in 5.11, no privilege from 5.13; EPERM when io_uring_disabled is 2, or 1 without CAP_SYS_ADMIN or io_uring_group.
4. [io_uring and networking in 2023](https://github.com/axboe/liburing/wiki/io_uring-and-networking-in-2023), Jens Axboe, liburing wiki, 2023. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: networking apps are readiness-based; swapping epoll for io_uring notifiers cuts system calls but misses the gains, the event loop has to change; submit_and_wait; multishot accept (5.19), multishot receive (6.0); provided buffers (ring-mapped 5.19) because completion-based receives need a buffer up front; -ENOBUFS; SOCK_NONEMPTY; task_work and COOP_TASKRUN / DEFER_TASKRUN.
5. [Learnings from kCTF VRP's 42 Linux kernel exploits submissions](https://security.googleblog.com/2023/06/learnings-from-kctf-vrps-42-linux.html), Tamás Koczka, Google Security Blog, 2023. Blog, primary: yes (Google runs the program and the servers). Seen: 60% of submissions exploited io_uring, about 1 million USD paid for io_uring alone; disabled on ChromeOS, unreachable to Android apps via seccomp, disabled on production Google servers; "safe only for use by trusted components".
6. [Documentation for /proc/sys/kernel/](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/sysctl/kernel.html), Linux kernel docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: io_uring_disabled 0/1/2 and io_uring_group; "shrinks the kernel's attack surface".
7. [Linux 5.1](https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_5.1), Kernel Newbies. Release notes, primary: no. Seen: io_uring merged in 5.1 (2019) for fast buffered and unbuffered async I/O; the old aio only did O_DIRECT; liburing created alongside.
8. [Linux 6.6](https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_6.6): already a note (`kernelnewbies-linux-6-6`). Seen: "Add a sysctl to disable io_uring system-wide"; faster async direct I/O. Not cited (kernel docs cover the sysctl).
9. [Ringing in a new asynchronous I/O API](https://lwn.net/Articles/776703/), Jonathan Corbet, LWN, 2019. Seen: the proposal as first posted; three mmap calls; CQ twice the SQ; buffered I/O from page cache without a context switch. Not cited (Axboe's own doc is newer and says to prefer it).

#### `thread-per-connection` (short)

1. [SEDA: An Architecture for Well-Conditioned, Scalable Internet Services](https://www.sosp.org/2001/papers/welsh.pdf), Matt Welsh, David Culler, Eric Brewer, SOSP 2001. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: Figure 1 thread-per-request design; overheads (cache and TLB misses, scheduling, lock contention); Figure 2 throughput climbing then collapsing as threads grow, response time unbounded (4-way 500 MHz Pentium III, Linux 2.2.14); bounded thread pools avoid collapse but make clients queue in the network with arbitrary waits; event-driven design with one thread per CPU.
2. [Measuring context switching and memory overheads for Linux threads](https://eli.thegreenplace.net/2018/measuring-context-switching-and-memory-overheads-for-linux-threads/): already a note (`bendersky-thread-overheads-2018`). Seen: 8 MiB virtual stacks mostly unbacked; 10,000 threads practical in 2018.
3. [net/http](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http): already a note (`go-net-http`). Seen: Serve creates "a new service goroutine for each" connection.
4. [Inside NGINX: How We Designed for Performance & Scale](https://blog.nginx.org/blog/inside-nginx-how-we-designed-for-performance-scale), Owen Garrett, NGINX, 2015. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: the blocking thread/process-per-connection model, the light-connection-on-a-heavy-object point, and why it doesn't scale to thousands. Also used for `event-loop`.
5. [The C10K problem](http://www.kegel.com/c10k.html): see `io-multiplexing` #9. Seen: section 4, 2 MB stacks and 512 threads on 32-bit. Left to the c10k node.

#### `thread-pool` (short)

1. [ThreadPoolExecutor](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/ThreadPoolExecutor.html): already a note (`java-threadpoolexecutor`). Seen again: "Thread pools address two different problems"; core vs maximum pool size and when threads get added; three queuing strategies; rejection policies.
2. [Executors](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html), Java SE 21. Seen: newFixedThreadPool uses "a shared unbounded queue"; newCachedThreadPool reclaims threads idle for sixty seconds. Not cited (the ThreadPoolExecutor page says the same).
3. [About Pool Sizing](https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/About-Pool-Sizing): already a note (`hikaricp-pool-sizing`). Seen: past core count, more threads only help while others block; the cores*2 + spindles starting point; test around it.
4. [Thread pool work scheduling](https://docs.libuv.org/en/v1.x/threadpool.html), libuv v1.x docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: global pool for file system, getaddrinfo and user work; default 4 threads, UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE up to 1024 (since 1.30.0); 8 MB stacks since 1.45.0.
5. [SEDA](https://www.sosp.org/2001/papers/welsh.pdf): see `thread-per-connection` #1. Seen: bounded pools and unfairness; SEDA's per-stage thread pool controller.

#### `event-loop` (deep)

1. [Design overview](https://docs.libuv.org/en/v1.x/design.html), libuv v1.x docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: one loop per thread, not thread-safe; non-blocking sockets polled with epoll/kqueue/event ports/IOCP; the 13 steps of a loop iteration (timers, pending, idle, prepare, poll with a computed timeout, check, close); network I/O on the loop thread, file I/O on a thread pool.
2. [The Node.js Event Loop](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/event-loop-timers-and-nexttick), Node.js project. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: phases (timers, pending, poll, check, close); libuv 1.45.0 (Node 20) moved timers after poll. Not cited (libuv's own page is the source of the phases).
3. [Don't Block the Event Loop](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/dont-block-the-event-loop): already a note (`nodejs-dont-block-event-loop`). Seen: one loop plus k workers; blocked thread serves nobody else; fairness is the app's job; partitioning vs offloading.
4. [Inside NGINX: How We Designed for Performance & Scale](https://blog.nginx.org/blog/inside-nginx-how-we-designed-for-performance-scale), Owen Garrett, NGINX, 2015. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: master plus one single-threaded worker per core; each worker handles many connections nonblocking as state machines; the chess grandmaster analogy; context switches only when there's no work.
5. [Redis client handling](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/clients/): already a note (`redis-client-handling`). Seen: non-blocking sockets and multiplexing; one read() per readable event for fairness.
6. [Event library](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/reference/internals/internals-rediseventlib/), Salvatore Sanfilippo, Redis docs (written c. 2010, flagged as possibly out of date). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: ae.c, aeCreateFileEvent via epoll_ctl, aeProcessEvents picks the nearest timer, epoll_wait with that timeout, serverCron. Not cited (old; redis-client-handling covers the model).
7. [redis.conf](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/redis/redis/unstable/redis.conf), Redis, unstable branch. Code/config, primary: yes. Seen: THREADED I/O: "Redis is mostly single threaded"; io-threads for socket reads, writes and parsing; off by default; use with 4+ cores. Cited for the one line on Redis's I/O threads; `redis-internals` should reuse it.
8. [Redis FAQ](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/get-started/faq/). Seen: CPU rarely the bottleneck; run several instances for more cores; "As of version 4.0" threaded actions. Not cited (dated wording).
9. [Why Threads Are A Bad Idea (for most purposes)](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/papers/threads.pdf), John Ousterhout, Sun Labs, 1995 (slides). Talk, primary: yes. Seen: event loop waits and invokes short handlers without preemption; long handlers freeze the app; events avoid locks and context switches on one CPU; threads needed for true CPU concurrency.
10. [Why Events Are A Bad Idea](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/hotos03/tech/full_papers/vonbehren/vonbehren.pdf): already a note (`vonbehren-events-bad-idea-2003`). Seen: duality; stack ripping; "free" synchronization only on one CPU.
11. [Why does one NGINX worker take all the load?](https://blog.cloudflare.com/the-sad-state-of-linux-socket-balancing/), Marek Majkowski, Cloudflare, 2017. Blog, primary: yes (Cloudflare runs NGINX). Seen: three layouts (one listener one worker, shared listener, SO_REUSEPORT per worker); blocking accept is FIFO across workers, epoll wakeups are LIFO so the busiest worker gets most connections; SO_REUSEPORT balances but a stuck worker's queue stalls, worse tail latency.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Threads vs events. Ousterhout (1995) says use events except where you need real CPU parallelism; SEDA (2001) shows threaded servers collapsing past some thread count; von Behren et al. (2003) say the collapse is a flaw of thread implementations, not of threads, and events make you rip your stack apart by hand. Modern runtimes (Go's netpoller, Java virtual threads) took the "cheap threads over an event loop" side; nginx, Node and Redis stayed with explicit loops.
- Level vs edge triggered. Lemon made kqueue level-triggered by default for correctness with partial reads; epoll offers both, and edge-triggered only works if you always drain to EAGAIN. Majkowski and epoll(7) show both modes misbehave when several threads share one epoll set on one socket.
- Readiness vs completion. Axboe's networking guide says moving an epoll loop to io_uring by only swapping the notifier gives fewer system calls but not the real gains; the loop has to change to completion style, which needs buffers up front (hence provided buffers).
- io_uring and security. Kernel developers kept adding features; Google disabled it on its production servers and ChromeOS after 60% of kernel exploit submissions used it. The kernel added a sysctl to turn it off.
- Shared accept queue vs SO_REUSEPORT. Shared queue: bad balancing with epoll (LIFO) but a better tail; per-worker queues: even load but one stuck worker delays its whole queue.

- Nothing else failed.

- Redis event library page: flagged by Redis as describing c. 2010 code.
- Node event loop phases page: libuv's design page is the primary source for the same loop.

- Majkowski part 2 (close/dup problem): epoll(7)'s Q&A says the same from the primary source.

**Gaps:**

- No primary source opened for Windows IOCP or Solaris event ports beyond one line in libuv.
- No source for io_uring performance on sockets versus epoll (Axboe's numbers are block I/O); the article doesn't claim a network speedup.
- No current source on thread-per-connection limits on a modern 64-bit Linux beyond Bendersky (2018).
- No source for how many threads a thread pool "should" have beyond HikariCP (for DB connections) and the Java docs' qualitative trade-offs; the article keeps it qualitative.

### I/O models (async/await, green threads, C10K)

#### `async-await` (deep)

1. [Async in depth (Tokio tutorial)](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial/async), Tokio project. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: the `Future` trait (`poll`, `Pin`, `Context`); a Rust future is the computation itself, not a background job; calling an async fn prints nothing until awaited; the `MainFuture` enum the compiler generates (State0, State1(Delay), Terminated); poll advances as far as possible, returns Ready or Pending; nested futures; the executor polls the outer future; mini-tokio busy loop; wakers; forgetting to wake after Pending hangs the task; a future may be polled with a different waker each time.
2. [Why async Rust?](https://without.boats/blog/why-async-rust/), without.boats, 2023. Engineering blog, primary: yes (drove the Rust async/await design 2017 to 2019). Seen: two costs of OS threads (kernel switches, preallocated stacks); cooperative vs preemptive; stackful vs stackless; goroutines as green threads; function coloring; Rust removed green threads late 2014 (RFC 230); segmented stacks abandoned by Rust and Go (hot split); Go copies stacks; FFI cost, C# aborted a green-threads experiment; most languages compile async/await to CPS; Rust's poll-based futures; "perfectly sized stack"; Pin; curl CVE from hand-written state machine; MVP 2019, Tokio 1.0 2020; async/await not right for every language.
3. [What Color is Your Function?](https://journal.stuffwithstuff.com/2015/02/01/what-color-is-your-function/), Bob Nystrom, 2015. Blog, primary: no. Seen: red/blue allegory and five rules; red = async; promises and async/await keep the split; colorless languages have switchable call stacks (Go, Lua, Ruby, threaded Java); CPS; await tells the compiler where to split; color spreads to main; Go parks goroutines on I/O.
4. [Async: What is blocking?](https://ryhl.io/blog/async-what-is-blocking/), Alice Ryhl, 2020. Blog, primary: yes (Tokio maintainer). Seen: cooperative scheduling; "never spend a long time without reaching an .await"; three one-second `std::thread::sleep` timers take 3 s under join!, 1 s with tokio sleep; default runtime one thread per core; 10 to 100 µs rule of thumb; spawn_blocking pool "around 500 threads"; rayon for CPU work; dedicated thread for forever-tasks.
5. [PEP 492: Coroutines with async and await syntax](https://peps.python.org/pep-0492/), Yury Selivanov, 2015. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: Python 3.5; assumes an asyncio-style event loop; generator-based coroutines before (PEP 342/380); calling returns a coroutine object; RuntimeWarning if never awaited; every await chain ends in a yield; C#, ECMAScript 7 proposal, Hack, Dart, Scala, C++ as prior art; why a separate `async` keyword (refactor removing the last await).

Extra: [RFC 230: remove runtime](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rust-lang/rfcs/master/text/0230-remove-runtime.md), Rust RFC, 2014. Opened the summary and motivation: libgreen moved out of tree, std::io welded to native threads; 1:1 vs M:N; a page fault in M:N blocks the whole worker thread. Not cited (boats summarizes it); good second source for green-threads.

#### `green-threads` (deep)

1. [Go runtime source, src/runtime (Go 1.26)](https://github.com/golang/go/tree/release-branch.go1.26/src/runtime), The Go Authors. Source code, primary: yes. Seen: proc.go header (G, M, P; M may be in a syscall without a P; spinning threads; rejected designs); runtime2.go `runq [256]` and `runnext`; findRunnable checks global queue when `schedtick%61 == 0`, `runqsteal`; `forcePreemptNS` 10 ms; retake hands off a P stuck in a syscall after more than one sysmon tick (at least 20 µs); entersyscall used for cgo too; preempt.go (sync safe points via the stack bound check, async via signals); stack.go (`stackMin = 2048`, prologue guard check, grow by doubling and copying, shrink by half under a quarter); netpoll.go / netpoll_epoll.go (edge-triggered epoll, goroutines parked on pollDesc semaphores).
2. [Scalable Go Scheduler Design Doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TTj4T2JO42uD5ID9e89oa0sLKhJYD0Y_kqxDv3I3XMw/edit), Dmitry Vyukov, 2012. Design doc, primary: yes. Opened via the text export (golang.org/s/go11sched redirects here). Seen: old scheduler's global mutex; Vtocc at 70% CPU on 8 cores with 14% in futex; M:running-M ratio up to 100:1; introduce P, exactly GOMAXPROCS; steal half from a random victim; spinning instead of prompt park/unpark.
3. [Go 1.14 Release Notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.14), The Go Authors, 2020. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: goroutines asynchronously preemptible; loops without calls no longer deadlock the scheduler or delay GC; not on windows/arm, darwin/arm, js/wasm, plan9; more signals, more EINTR from slow syscalls.
4. [JEP 444: Virtual Threads](https://openjdk.org/jeps/444), Ron Pressler, Alan Bateman, 2023 (JDK 21). Spec, primary: yes. Seen: thread-per-request goal; Little's law motivation; asynchronous style loses loops, try/catch, stack traces, debuggers, profilers; early Java green threads were M:1, lost to 1:1; virtual threads M:N; blocking java.* I/O becomes non-blocking call plus suspend; not faster threads; don't pool, use semaphores; thread-local caching trap; work-stealing FIFO ForkJoinPool; no time sharing; not cooperative; filesystem ops capture carrier, scheduler compensates; pinning in synchronized and native, not compensated; stacks as heap stack chunks; invisible to the OS; new thread dump format.
5. [JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning](https://openjdk.org/jeps/491), Patricio Chilano Mateo, Alan Bateman, JDK 24. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: synchronized no longer pins; remaining cases: native code calling back into Java and blocking, class loading, class initializers.
6. Why async Rust? (see async-await #2): segmented vs copied stacks, FFI cost, Rust's removal of green threads.

Extra: [Measuring context switching and memory overheads for Linux threads](https://eli.thegreenplace.net/2018/measuring-context-switching-and-memory-overheads-for-linux-threads/), Eli Bendersky, 2018 (already a note). Goroutine switch about 170 ns vs 1.2 to 1.5 µs for a thread switch; left to `context-switch` and `thread`, which already cite it. Why Events Are A Bad Idea (see c10k #2) also fits here as history.

#### `c10k` (short)

1. [The C10K problem](http://www.kegel.com/c10k.html), Dan Kegel, 1999 (last updated 2014, minor fix 2019). Web page, primary: yes (named the problem). Seen: 1000 MHz / 2 GB / gigabit arithmetic for 20,000 clients; cdrom.com at 10,000 clients in 1999; I/O strategies (blocking + threads, non-blocking + readiness, async + completion, in-kernel); user-level threads listed; readiness is a hint; non-blocking has no effect on disk files; 2 MB stacks give 512 threads on 32-bit Linux; stacks can't grow; M:N hard, most moving to 1:1; NPTL above ~32,000 threads needs max_map_count; Linux 2.4 threads-max 2047 on RH8.
2. [Why Events Are A Bad Idea (for high-concurrency servers)](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/hotos03/tech/full_papers/vonbehren/vonbehren.pdf), von Behren, Condit, Brewer, HotOS 2003. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: thread problems are implementation artifacts; user-level thread package to 100,000 threads; Lauer and Needham duality (1978); stack ripping; fixing events is switching to threads; dynamic stack growth proposal; Knot vs Haboob on 2x2000 MHz Xeon, Linux 2.4.20, poll(): ~700 vs 500 Mbit/s, Haboob out of memory above 16,384 clients.
3. Measuring context switching and memory overheads for Linux threads (see green-threads Extra). Seen again: 10,000 threads with 8 MiB stacks, ~80 GiB virtual, ~80 MiB resident; 400 KiB touched each gives ~2.6 GiB; memory per task is a concurrency cost, not a thread cost; 32-bit default 2 MiB stack and 3 GiB gives ~1,500 threads; ~32K thread cap on his 64-bit machine.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- **Threads vs events.** Kegel (at the time) recommended moving off thread per client for 10,000 clients; von Behren et al. argue threads lose only because of poor implementations; Bendersky (2018) finds 10,000 OS threads practical. The articles present it as a cost question: per-connection memory and switching, not the model.
- **Stackless vs stackful.** Rust (boats) argues stackless async/await was the only option for a language without a GC that must be cheap to call from C, and says it isn't right for every language; Java (JEP 444) chose virtual threads to keep stack traces and debuggers; Nystrom argues colored functions are the price of async/await.
- **Is Java's scheduler cooperative?** JEP 444 says virtual threads are "not cooperative" (no explicit yields) but also have no time slicing; a CPU-bound virtual thread holds its carrier. The article says both.
- **Tokio numbers age.** The 10 to 100 µs rule and "around 500" blocking threads are from a 2020 post; the article dates them.

**Couldn't open:**
None.

**Rejected:**
- Go blog and third-party "Go scheduler explained" posts: the runtime comments and Vyukov's doc are primary and cover it.
- MDN pages on JavaScript async functions and promises: not needed once Nystrom and PEP 492 covered the shape; no JS-specific claims made.
- Stephen Toub's "How async/await really works in C#" (not opened); the C# history is kept to one line from PEP 492.

**Gaps:**
- No source opened for JavaScript's promise semantics (eager start) or Node's event loop; the async-await article makes no JS-specific claims beyond Nystrom's.
- No measured memory per goroutine or per virtual thread beyond Go's 2 KiB minimum stack; the green-threads article gives no per-connection memory figure. The phase 4 lab will measure it.
- No source for per-socket kernel memory (socket buffers) in the c10k article; left out.
- C# async/await history (year introduced) not sourced; left out.

### Load on a server + Tools the build uses

All pages below were opened with `curl -sL` and converted to text with
pandoc (the Reactive Streams spec and the TSan algorithm page as raw
markdown from GitHub). Quotes in the source notes were checked by
script against those downloads.

#### `cpu-bound-vs-io-bound` (short)

1. [Don't Block the Event Loop (or the Worker Pool)](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/dont-block-the-event-loop), Node.js project. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: one event loop plus a pool of k workers; "Node.js is fast when the work associated with each client at any given time is small"; worker pool takes I/O with no non-blocking OS version (fs, dns.lookup) and CPU-heavy work (crypto.pbkdf2, crypto.scrypt, zlib); fairness is the application's job; bound input to bound worst-case time; REDOS; partitioning vs offloading; "4 logical cores and 5 Workers, one of these Workers cannot make progress"; I/O tasks progress while the thread isn't running; one pool for both kinds can hurt.
2. [threading](https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html), Python Software Foundation, Python 3.14.7. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: GIL lets one thread run Python code at a time; processes for multi-core; threads still fit I/O-bound work; 3.13 free-threaded builds can disable the GIL, not by default (PEP 703).
3. [getrusage(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/getrusage.2.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: ru_utime and ru_stime; ru_nvcsw (voluntary, "usually to await availability of a resource") and ru_nivcsw (preempted or time slice exceeded), both since Linux 2.6. Existing note `man7-getrusage`, appended.

Also considered: existing note `hikaricp-pool-sizing` ("More threads only perform better when blocking creates opportunities for executing"); not cited, the Node page says the same at the concept level. `java-threadpoolexecutor` (below) also says I/O-bound tasks leave room for more threads.

#### `latency-percentiles` (short)

1. [Service Level Objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/), Chris Jones, John Wilkes, Niall Murphy with Cody Smith, Google SRE book, 2016. Book chapter (free online), primary: yes. Seen: averages hide bursts (200 req/s in even seconds vs steady 100); "Most metrics are better thought of as distributions rather than averages"; figure 4-1, typical request about 50 ms, 5% 20 times slower, average shows no change over the day; high percentiles = plausible worst case, median = typical; users prefer lower variance; queueing makes the tail worse at high load; latency data skewed, mean and median can differ; don't assume normal; SLO example "99% (averaged over 1 minute) of Get RPC calls will complete in less than 100 ms".
2. [Histograms and summaries](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/), Prometheus authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: φ-quantile is the value at rank φ·N; summaries can't be aggregated, `avg(...{quantile="0.95"}) // BAD!`; histograms aggregate via histogram_quantile(); every quantile is an estimate; classic bucket 200-300 ms gives p95 295 ms for data near 220 ms, native histogram 228 ms; summary error in φ, histogram error in value; native histograms now recommended.

#### `backpressure` (deep)

1. [Backpressuring in Streams](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/modules/backpressuring-in-streams), Node.js project. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: definition (buildup behind a buffer); Unix pipes and TCP call it flow control; experiment gzipping ~9 GB with `write()` patched to return true: similar run time, max RSS ~87.81 MB vs ~1.52 GB, GC firing pattern changes; `write()` returns false past highWaterMark, wait for 'drain'; rules for custom streams; the `readable.on('data', ...write)` anti-pattern; gives the default highWaterMark as 16 kB (outdated, see #2).
2. [Stream](https://nodejs.org/api/stream.html), Node.js v26.10.0 API docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Buffering section; highWaterMark "is a threshold, not a limit"; pipe() exists to limit buffering between different speeds; default 64 KiB for byte streams on non-Windows, 16 KiB on Windows, raised in v22.0.0.
3. [Reactive Streams for the JVM, README/spec](https://github.com/reactive-streams/reactive-streams-jvm/blob/master/README.md), Reactive Streams (Kaazing, Lightbend, Netflix, Pivotal, Red Hat, Twitter and others), 1.0.4. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: rule 1.1 (never more onNext than requested), 2.1 (demand via request(n)), 3.17 (2^63-1 means unbounded); subscriber-controlled queue bounds P - N; sources that can't be slowed must buffer or drop; request(1) is stop-and-wait, bigger demand amortizes.
4. [Queues Don't Fix Overload](https://ferd.ca/queues-don-t-fix-overload.html), Fred Hebert, 2014. Blog (author of Erlang in Anger), primary: no. Seen: the sink metaphor; choose between blocking input (back-pressure) and dropping (load-shedding); implicit backpressure is slowness; a queue makes failures rarer but bigger; ask the bottleneck for permission.
5. [Redis client handling](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/clients/), Redis. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: non-blocking multiplexed clients, TCP_NODELAY; one read() per event for fairness; maxclients 10,000; output buffer limits (normal 0 = none, Pub/Sub hard 32 MB soft 8 MB/60 s, replicas 256 MB / 64 MB/60 s), connection closed at the limit; 1 GB query buffer hard limit; client eviction (7.0) off by default; keepalive 300 s since 3.2.
6. [send(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/send.2.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: a message that doesn't fit the send buffer blocks, or fails with EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK on a non-blocking socket; select tells you when you can send again; send with zero flags is write.

Also opened: [reactive-streams.org](https://www.reactive-streams.org/) home page (JDK 9 Flow "1:1 semantically equivalent"); not cited. Existing note `rfc-9113` (HTTP/2 per-stream and per-connection flow control); not cited to keep the node at 6 sources, see Gaps.

#### `bounded-queues` (short)

1. [ThreadPoolExecutor](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/ThreadPoolExecutor.html), Oracle, Java SE 21. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: three queuing strategies (direct handoff, unbounded, bounded); unbounded growth "when commands continue to arrive on average faster than they can be processed"; big queue + small pool vs small queue + big pool; I/O-bound tasks allow more threads; rejection policies AbortPolicy (default), CallerRunsPolicy ("simple feedback control mechanism"), DiscardPolicy, DiscardOldestPolicy ("rarely acceptable").
2. [The Go Programming Language Specification](https://go.dev/ref/spec), The Go Authors, go1.27. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: unbuffered channels need both sides ready; buffered sends block only when full; nil channel never ready; select picks a ready case, else default, else blocks.
3. [listen(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/listen.2.html): existing note `man7-listen` (phase 2). Seen: backlog = queue of established connections waiting for accept; when full, ECONNREFUSED or the SYN is ignored for a retry.

#### `graceful-shutdown` (short)

1. [Pod Lifecycle](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/), Kubernetes docs. Docs, primary: yes. Existing note `kubernetes-pod-lifecycle`, re-opened. Seen: preStop, then TERM to process 1 (or STOPSIGNAL); endpoint marked not ready at the same time; 30 s default grace period; one-off 2 s extension for preStop; KILL after; custom stop signals alpha since v1.33.
2. [net/http](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http), The Go Authors, go1.27.1. Docs, primary: yes. Existing note `go-net-http`, appended. Seen: Server.Shutdown (go1.8) closes listeners, then idle connections, then waits; context bounds it; ListenAndServe returns ErrServerClosed at once, so main must wait; hijacked connections not waited for; RegisterOnShutdown (go1.9); SetKeepAlivesEnabled(false) for servers shutting down; Close is the abrupt version.

Also opened: [Explore Termination Behavior for Pods And Their Endpoints](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/services/pods-and-endpoint-termination-flow/): terminating endpoints show ready false, serving true, terminating true, so a load balancer can drain. Not cited. Existing `cloudflare-graceful-upgrades-go-2018` and `man7-signal` considered; the first belongs to `zero-downtime-reload`, the second to `signals`.

#### `race-detector` (short)

1. [Data Race Detector](https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector), The Go Authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: definition of a data race; -race on test/run/build/install; report format with the previous conflicting access; GORACE options (exitcode 66, halt_on_error, history_size); `race` build tag; "only finds races that happen at runtime"; typical races (loop counter, shared err, map, plain int, send vs close); cgo and C compiler required; overhead memory 5-10x, time 2-20x; defer/recover leak.
2. [ThreadSanitizer](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ThreadSanitizer.html), LLVM/Clang docs (main branch). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: instrumentation + runtime; slowdown 5-15x, memory 5-10x; -fsanitize=thread; uninstrumented code causes misses or false positives; not for production; still beta; adaptive delay (off by default) perturbs scheduling to expose races.
3. [ThreadSanitizerAlgorithm](https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/ThreadSanitizerAlgorithm), Google sanitizers wiki. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: every access instrumented (`__tsan_read4(addr)`), atomics via `__tsan_atomic_`; each 8-byte word maps to N = 2, 4 or 8 shadow words (TID, clock, IsWrite, size, offset); race = different threads, overlapping bytes, no happens-before; random eviction, "tiny probability to miss a data race".
4. [src/runtime/race/README](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/runtime/race/README), The Go Authors. Code, primary: yes. Seen: "It is based on ThreadSanitizer race detector, that is currently a part of the LLVM project"; per-platform .syso files built from pinned LLVM commits.

Also opened: [runtime/race package page](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/race) (go1.27.1), nothing beyond the README. Not cited.

#### `resp-protocol` (short)

1. [Redis serialization protocol specification](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/protocol-spec/), Redis. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: RESP1 in 1.2, RESP2 standard since 2.0, RESP3 opt-in since 6.0 via HELLO; port 6379; first byte = type; CRLF terminator; RESP2 types + - : $ * and RESP3 additions; 512 MB bulk limit; $-1 and *-1 nulls vs RESP3 `_`; clients send arrays of bulk strings; LLEN example; pipelining; inline commands; length prefixes mean no scanning or escaping; calls itself "a binary protocol that uses control sequences encoded in standard ASCII".
2. [Redis pipelining](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/using-commands/pipelining/), Redis. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: 250 ms RTT caps a lock-step client at 4 requests/s; loopback RTT sub-millisecond; server queues replies in memory, batch ~10k; fewer read()/write() calls; up to 10x baseline; Ruby example 1.185 s vs 0.251 s over loopback; read-compute-write needs scripting.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- RESP: the node note called it a "text protocol"; the spec calls it a binary protocol with ASCII control bytes. Both are fair (ASCII framing, binary-safe payloads). Note reworded.
- Node.js default highWaterMark: the backpressure guide says 16 kB; the API docs say 64 KiB since v22 (non-Windows). The guide is out of date.
- Race detector overhead: Go docs say 2-20x time, 5-10x memory; Clang says 5-15x time, 5-10x memory (plus 1 MB per thread). Different programs and languages, same runtime.
- Queues: Java's docs present an unbounded queue as fine for independent tasks such as a web server, while Hebert argues a queue in front of overload only delays failure. The Java page also warns about unbounded growth; the difference is burst vs sustained load.
- Graceful shutdown in Kubernetes: SIGTERM and endpoint removal happen at the same time, not in order. The docs don't say how long to keep accepting after SIGTERM; no primary source gives a number.

**Couldn't open:**
- Nothing failed. PEP 703 was not opened (the Python docs' one-line statement is what's cited).

**Rejected:**
- rfc-9113 for backpressure: would be a seventh source; the per-stream window point was cut from the article.
- hikaricp-pool-sizing for cpu-bound-vs-io-bound: same point as the Node page, about database pools rather than CPU vs I/O in general.
- Kubernetes endpoint termination tutorial: detail on EndpointSlice conditions, more than a short node needs.

**Gaps:**
- No measured cost of a Go `-race` run on the lab server, and no measured p99 numbers; the lab will produce both.
- No primary source for how long to delay closing the listener after SIGTERM, or how fast common load balancers react to an endpoint going not ready.
- No primary source for Go-specific backpressure patterns in an epoll loop (high/low water marks); the article gives it as a design rule derived from Node's pattern and send(2).
- `race-detector` cites 4 sources and `bounded-queues` 3, above the 1-2 for a short node.

## Phase 5: APIs and contracts

Researched by 4 parallel passes, one per group below.

### Design

All pages below were opened with `curl -sL` and converted to text with
pandoc (READMEs read as raw Markdown from GitHub). Quotes in the notes
were checked by script against those copies.

#### `api-design` (deep)

1. [AIP-121: Resource-oriented design](https://google.aip.dev/121), Google API Improvement Proposals, Google. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: resources (nouns) first, few standard methods (Get, List, Create, Update, Delete), custom methods when those don't fit; "borrows many principles from REST"; design order resources → relationships → schema → methods; mirroring the database schema is "an anti-pattern"; same resource schema across all methods; every resource must support Get and List (except singletons); custom methods are POST with the verb in the URI, not new HTTP verbs; strong consistency after a management-plane method returns; stateless protocol, client owns application state; references must form a DAG, a cycle costs a third call.
2. [AIP-122: Resource names](https://google.aip.dev/122), Google. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: names are URI paths without the leading slash (`publishers/123/books/les-miserables`), alternating plural camelCase collection ids and resource ids; users store the name; full URI adds host and `v1`, but the version isn't in the name because names persist across versions; references by name string, never embedding (lifecycle, permissions, coupling); names vs ID tuples.
3. [AIP-136: Custom methods](https://google.aip.dev/136), Google. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `:archive` / `books:sort` / `:translateText` patterns; verb-noun names, no prepositions (GetBookByAuthor → SearchBooks with an author field); GET for reads, POST for side effects; no "Async" in names; declarative tools can't use custom methods.
4. [AIP-180: Backwards compatibility](https://google.aip.dev/180), Google. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: source, wire and semantic compatibility; adding is fine, no new required request fields; removing/renaming breaking; type changes break generated code even when wire-compatible; raising string length limits, changing defaults, changing value format (IPv4 → IPv6), serializing defaults differently are all breaking; enum values in responses need care; adding pagination later breaks; "indicative" not complete.
5. [Microsoft Azure REST API Guidelines](https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines/blob/vNext/azure/Guidelines.md), Microsoft Azure HTTP/REST Stewardship Board, vNext branch. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: URL pattern, "model resource state, not behavior"; same JSON schema across PUT/PATCH/GET/POST; PATCH with JSON Merge Patch, PUT for create/replace; required fields only in v1; 400 for unknown fields; actions `users/Bob:grant` as POST, no action for CRUD, disallow `:` in ids; collections with `value` and `nextLink`, adding paging later is breaking, document skipped/duplicated items, avoid `count`; required `api-version` query parameter with date values, no version in path, no breaking changes, previews retired after 90 days; extensible enums. (Another group appended error, LRO and conditional-request claims to the same note.)
6. [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110). Existing note. Sections 9.3.3 (POST → 201 + Location) and 9.3.4 (PUT creates or replaces), for the standard-method mapping.

Also opened: [Cloud API design guide: resources](https://cloud.google.com/apis/design/resources), which now redirects to the AIP index; the AIPs above replace it. [RFC 9205](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9205) (existing note) was re-opened for rest.

#### `rest` (deep)

1. [Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, chapter 5](https://ics.uci.edu/~fielding/pubs/dissertation/rest_arch_style.htm), Roy Fielding, UC Irvine, 2000. Paper (PhD dissertation), primary: yes. Seen: REST derived by adding constraints to the null style (client-server, stateless, cache, uniform interface, layered system, optional code-on-demand) with the property and cost of each; four interface constraints; resource as a time-varying membership function, "authors' preferred version" example; representation = bytes + metadata, media type; connectors (client, server, cache, resolver, tunnel), components (origin server, gateway, proxy, user agent); caches can decide cacheability because the interface is generic; REST not tied to one protocol; "the most efficient network request is one that doesn't use the network"; pull not push. Chapter 6 not read.
2. [REST APIs must be hypertext-driven](https://roy.gbiv.com/untangled/2008/rest-apis-must-be-hypertext-driven), Roy Fielding, 2008. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: frustration that any HTTP interface is called REST; six rules (not tied to one protocol, no protocol changes, describe media types, no fixed resource names or hierarchies, no typed resources, enter with only a bookmark); "choose some other buzzword"; his comments define hypertext as information plus controls, and query results as lists of links.
3. [Richardson Maturity Model](https://martinfowler.com/articles/richardsonMaturityModel.html), Martin Fowler, 2010. Blog, primary: no. Seen: levels 0-3 with a doctor's-appointment example (POX tunnel, resources, verbs + 201/409, hypermedia links); POST/PUT ≠ create/update; the Web rarely uses PUT/DELETE; safe/unsafe split and status codes are what the Web proves; no standard for hypermedia controls; "level 3 RMM is a pre-condition of REST".
4. [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110). Existing note. Safe and idempotent methods, statelessness, intermediaries.
5. [RFC 9205](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9205), Mark Nottingham, BCP 56, 2022. Existing note, appended. Seen now: 3.2 don't squat on URL paths, use links; 4.4 "/app/v1" common for single-deployment APIs but inappropriate in IETF specs; 4.4.1 discovery documents; 4.16 breaking changes through new link relations, media types or header fields.
6. Microsoft Azure REST API Guidelines. See api-design #5. What "REST" means to a large provider in practice (level 2 with fixed URL patterns).

#### `graphql` (deep)

1. [GraphQL specification, 2025 edition](https://spec.graphql.org/September2025/), GraphQL Specification Project (GraphQL Foundation), 2025. Spec, primary: yes.
