Seen: created 2012, open standard work since 2015; first example queries Facebook's implementation; principles (product-centric, hierarchical, strong typing, client-specified response, introspective); no transport required; operations query/mutation/subscription; resolvers ("internal function provided by objectType"), often async; normal execution may be parallel because non-mutation fields must be side-effect free; top-level mutation fields serial; non-null error propagation; response with data + errors, partial data; request errors have no data; field deprecation; OneOf input objects (new since the 2021 edition, also opened).
2. [GraphQL over HTTP](https://graphql.github.io/graphql-over-http/draft/), GraphQL over HTTP working group, current working draft. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: POST JSON body {query, operationName, variables, extensions}; GET for queries only, mutation over GET → 405; `application/graphql-response+json`; clients read the body, not the status; 400 for unparseable, 422 for validation failures; 200 even with execution errors; new "294 Partial Success" for data + errors, not registered with IANA.
3. [Learn GraphQL: Performance](https://graphql.org/learn/performance/), GraphQL Foundation. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "as cacheable as any API that enables parameterized requests"; GET + persisted queries (hash) for HTTP caching and CDNs; N+1 defined, batching with DataLoader; demand control (paginate lists, depth and breadth limits, complexity analysis); JSON with gzip; monitoring.
4. [Learn GraphQL: Caching](https://graphql.org/learn/caching/), GraphQL Foundation. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: no URL-like primitive per object; globally unique `id` (type name + id, base64), or client-derived from `__typename`.
5. [DataLoader](https://github.com/graphql/dataloader), GraphQL Foundation, main branch. Code (README), primary: yes. Seen: port of Facebook's 2010 "Loader"; coalesces loads within one tick of the event loop; batch function contract (same length and order); "four round-trips ... at most two"; per-request memoization cache, not a replacement for Redis/Memcache; per-request instances to avoid leaking data between users.
6. [Rate limits and query limits for the GraphQL API](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/overview/rate-limits-and-query-limits-for-the-graphql-api), GitHub. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: points per query; 5,000 points/hour for users (more for Enterprise Cloud apps, 1,000 per repository for GITHUB_TOKEN); cost formula (requests per connection assuming full pages, ÷100, round), worked example 5,101 requests → 51 points; `first`/`last` required, 1-100; 500,000 node limit; 10-second timeout; secondary limits.

Also opened: [Learn GraphQL: Security](https://graphql.org/learn/security/) (trusted documents, depth/breadth/batch limits, rate limiting in the business layer, complexity analysis, introspection and error masking), [Learn GraphQL: Schema Design](https://graphql.org/learn/schema-design/) ("strong opinion on avoiding versioning", every field nullable by default), [Learn GraphQL: Pagination](https://graphql.org/learn/pagination/) (connections). Not given notes: the six above cover the article; Security and Schema Design would be good for a later `graphql` revision or for `rate-limiting`.

#### `openapi` (short)

1. [OpenAPI Specification v3.2.1](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.2.1.html), OpenAPI Initiative (Linux Foundation), 3.2.1 patch release. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: language-agnostic description of HTTP APIs; tools for docs, codegen, tests; major.minor = feature set, minor versions may occasionally break; JSON or YAML; bodies needn't be JSON; `openapi` vs `info.version`; `webhooks`; paths templating (no `/` in values), path params always required; `operationId` unique; Schema Object a superset of JSON Schema (2020 draft); Components; QUERY method and `querystring` parameters new in 3.2 (absent from the 3.1.1 text, also opened); revision history from Swagger 1.0 to OpenAPI 3.2.1.
2. [OpenAPI Generator](https://github.com/OpenAPITools/openapi-generator), OpenAPI Tools community, master at 7.26.0. Code (README), primary: yes. Seen: generates clients, server stubs (Go: net/http, Gin, Echo), docs and config; supports 2.0 and 3.0 descriptions; not affiliated with the OAI; untrusted descriptions can inject code; migration guide from Swagger Codegen.

#### `pagination` (short)

1. [Paging Through Results](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/fetch-next-page), Markus Winand, Use The Index, Luke (online book). Book chapter, primary: no. Seen: offset vs seek method; offsets drift on insert and slow down with depth; seek uses the last row's values and an index; deterministic order with a unique tie-breaker; row values `(a, b) < (x, y)`, PostgreSQL since 8.4; approximations for other databases; no arbitrary pages, backwards needs reversed comparisons; infinite scroll doesn't need either.
2. [AIP-158: Pagination](https://google.aip.dev/158), Google. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `page_size`/`page_token`/`next_page_token`; default and max coercion; short pages allowed; empty token is the only end signal; opaque tokens ("if users are able to deconstruct these, they will do so"), base64 not enough, tokens aren't authorization; three-day expiry rule of thumb; adding pagination later is breaking (75-item example); `skip`.
3. Microsoft Azure REST API Guidelines. See api-design #5. `nextLink`, document skipped/duplicated items, avoid counts.

Also opened: [We need tool support for keyset pagination](https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset), Markus Winand (offset drift picture, framework support list); [Evolving API Pagination at Slack](https://slack.engineering/evolving-api-pagination-at-slack/), Slack Engineering (offset reads offset + count rows; cursor on a unique sequential column; why Slack moved to cursors). Not given notes; #1 and #2 cover a short node. Slack's post would be a good primary source if pagination grows.

#### `api-versioning` (short)

1. [Hyrum's Law](https://www.hyrumslaw.com/), Hyrum Wright. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: the law; "no such thing as a private implementation"; bug-for-bug compatibility; performance becomes implicit interface; tests detect but can't remove; named by Titus Winters.
2. [APIs as infrastructure: future-proofing Stripe with versioning](https://stripe.com/blog/api-versioning), Brandur Leach, Stripe, 2017. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: `verified` boolean → `status` example; safe vs breaking changes; major versions in URL or Accept header and their cost; date-named rolling versions, account pinned on first request, `Stripe-Version` header; version change modules applied backwards; changes with side effects avoided; almost a hundred breaking upgrades in six years; API review to get it right first.
3. [Stripe API reference: Versioning](https://docs.stripe.com/api/versioning), Stripe, current when this was written. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: since the "acacia" release (2024), monthly non-breaking versions and a breaking major release twice a year; Stripe-Version header; webhook endpoints get their own version; open vs closed enums, keep a fallback branch.
4. Microsoft Azure REST API Guidelines. See api-design #5. Required `api-version` query parameter with dates, no version in the path, no breaking changes.

Also opened: [AIP-185: API Versioning](https://google.aip.dev/185), Google (major version first in the path, updated in place, no minor versions; alpha/beta channels, 180-day beta deprecation; newer interface-based versioning with date versions in an `X-Goog-Api-Version` header). A note was drafted and then removed to keep a short node to four sources; worth a note if `api-versioning` is revisited. [Upgrade your integration](https://docs.stripe.com/upgrades), Stripe (per-request override, SDK pins, two webhook endpoints during an upgrade). Not used.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- What "REST" means: Fielding requires hypertext (and says so bluntly); the Richardson model, Microsoft's guidelines and most real APIs stop at level 2 with fixed URL patterns. Google's AIPs say they "borrow" from REST and are written for RPC APIs.
- Where the version lives: Google puts `v1` in the path (AIP-185), Microsoft forbids that and requires an `api-version` query parameter, Stripe uses a header plus an account pin. Google's newer IBV and Microsoft both use dates, like Stripe.
- Stripe changed its own scheme: the 2017 post argues against big breaking releases; the current docs describe two breaking major releases a year.
- GraphQL caching: graphql.org says GraphQL is "as cacheable as any API that enables parameterized requests"; the same page concedes URL limits force persisted queries, and the caching page says there's no URL-like cache key. The tentative note ("why caching gets harder") and graphql.org disagree in tone; the article presents both.
- GraphQL status codes: older practice and the draft both send 200 with execution errors; the draft now proposes an unregistered 294 for partial success.
- Unknown fields: Microsoft rejects them with 400; GraphQL and protobuf ecosystems tolerate or ignore extras. Only Microsoft's side is cited.
- Enums: Google allows adding response enum values with caution; Microsoft and Stripe want enums marked extensible/open and clients to have fallbacks.

**Couldn't open:**

- Nothing needed failed to open. cloud.google.com/apis/design/resources redirected to the AIP index.

**Rejected:**

- Zalando RESTful API Guidelines: downloaded (very long), not read closely; Google and Microsoft cover the same ground from larger API programs.
- Google Cloud API design guide: now redirects to the AIPs.
- AIP-131/132/133 (per-method AIPs): only AIP-131 downloaded; AIP-121's table is enough for a deep node that isn't about any single method.
- GraphQL spec 2021 edition: superseded by the 2025 edition.

**Gaps:**

- No primary source on how common hypermedia (level 3) APIs are; the rest article doesn't claim numbers.
- No source on design-first vs code-first OpenAPI workflows; the openapi article gives advice without claiming either is standard.
- No measured cost of offset vs keyset pagination with a written-down setup; Winand's chart has no setup, so the article stays qualitative. The phase 6 lab could measure it with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
- GraphQL depth/complexity limits: only GitHub's real numbers were used; the community cost-directive draft wasn't opened.

### Design

#### `schema-evolution` (deep)

1. [Language Guide (proto 3)](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/), Google (Protocol Buffers team), living doc. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "Updating A Message Type": ProtoJSON and text format have different safe-change rules; three tiers: wire-unsafe (changing a field number, moving fields into an existing oneof), wire-safe (add fields, remove fields if the number isn't reused, add enum values, some oneof/extension moves) and wire-compatible but conditionally safe (int32 to int64 compatible but lossy; sint32/sint64 only with each other); "any wire-safe changes may be a breaking change to application code" (exhaustive switch on an enum); roll out lossy changes by writing only old-range values until every endpoint has the new schema; don't make wire-compatible changes to schemas published outside your organization; proto3 keeps unknown fields; reserve deleted names for JSON. Note: `protobuf-proto3-guide` (appended).
2. [Proto Best Practices](https://protobuf.dev/best-practices/dos-donts/), Google (Protocol Buffers team), living doc. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: clients and servers are never updated at exactly the same time, one may be rolled back; never reuse a tag number (old serialized data in logs); reserve deleted numbers and names; enum alias rename in three steps (add below and deprecate, swap once all parsers have it, delete once all serializers have it); don't change a field's type; don't add a required field (removed from proto3); first enum value should be FOO_UNSPECIFIED = 0 because old clients see unknown values as unset; don't change a field's default (version skew), proto3 removed custom defaults; repeated to scalar loses data; different messages for RPC and storage. Note: `protobuf-best-practices`.
3. [Specification (Apache Avro 1.12.0)](https://avro.apache.org/docs/1.12.0/specification/), Apache Avro project. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: binary data has no field names or types, so the writer's schema must always be available; files store the writer's schema, RPC must guarantee it; record encoding is just the concatenation of field values in declared order (example `36 06 66 6f 6f`); Schema Resolution: writer's vs reader's schema, fields matched by name, writer-only fields ignored, reader-only fields take the reader's default or it's an error, int promotable to long/float/double, enum default for unknown symbols, union matching; aliases rewrite the writer's names to the reader's; single-object encoding (`C3 01` marker plus an 8-byte schema fingerprint) for records stored "for several weeks in an Apache Kafka topic". Docs index lists 1.12.0 as the newest version. Note: `avro-specification`.
4. [Schema evolution in Avro, Protocol Buffers and Thrift](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2012/12/05/schema-evolution-in-avro-protocol-buffers-thrift.html), Martin Kleppmann, 2012. Blog, primary: no (he didn't build these formats, but it's the classic comparison). Seen: one Person record in JSON (82 bytes), protobuf (33 bytes), Avro (32 bytes); protobuf: tag numbers, skip unknown fields by wire type, never reuse a tag, rename freely; `required` adds a validation check that makes changes risky; Avro: no tags, parse needs the writer's schema, reader and writer schemas resolved by name; add a field only with a default, remove only if it had one; adding a type to a union needs readers updated first; renaming needs aliases in readers first; how readers find the writer schema (file header, negotiated per connection, version number per record plus a schema registry); "every field in a record is tagged" in protobuf vs the whole record/file/connection tagged with a schema version in Avro. Pre-proto3 (still has `required`). Note: `kleppmann-schema-evolution-2012`.
5. [Schema Evolution and Compatibility for Schema Registry on Confluent Platform](https://docs.confluent.io/platform/current/schema-registry/fundamentals/schema-evolution.html), Confluent docs. Docs, primary: yes (they build Schema Registry). Seen: BACKWARD (new schema reads data from the last schema), FORWARD (last schema reads data from the new), FULL (both), NONE; transitive variants check against every earlier version, the plain ones only against the last; default is BACKWARD, chosen so consumers can rewind to the start of a topic; FORWARD means you "need to anticipate all future changes"; upgrade order: BACKWARD upgrade consumers first, FORWARD producers first, FULL any order; an Avro field added with a default is backward compatible, without one it isn't; incompatible change (Number to String) means new topic and migrate; table of allowed changes per format; Protobuf best practice is BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE because adding message types isn't forward compatible. Note: `confluent-schema-evolution`.
6. [Rules and categories (buf breaking)](https://buf.build/docs/breaking/rules/), Buf. Docs, primary: yes (Buf builds the checker). Seen: four categories from strictest to most lenient, FILE (default), PACKAGE, WIRE_JSON, WIRE; FILE/PACKAGE protect generated code (deleting a deprecated enum value is wire compatible but breaks compiling code); WIRE_JSON recommended minimum because protobuf's JSON encoding breaks when field names change; WIRE only when you know only binary is decoded; WIRE/WIRE_JSON fit when you control all clients or read your own old data from disk; per-rule list (ENUM_VALUE_NO_DELETE_UNLESS_NAME_RESERVED etc.). Note: `buf-breaking-rules`.

#### `error-design` (short)

1. [RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457), M. Nottingham, E. Wilde, S. Dalal, 2023 (obsoletes RFC 7807). Spec, primary: yes. Seen: `application/problem+json`; members type, status, title, detail, instance; type is the primary identifier and defaults to `about:blank`; status is advisory and must match the real HTTP status; detail should help the client fix the problem and must not be parsed; extensions (the `balance`/`accounts` and `errors` with JSON Pointer examples); clients must ignore unknown extensions; 422 example for validation errors; multiple different problems: report the most urgent one; generic problems are better as plain status codes; problem types may specify Retry-After; security: don't leak stack dumps; status member and real status can disagree when an intermediary changes the code. Changes from 7807: a registry of problem types, multiple-problem guidance, non-dereferenceable type URIs. Note: `rfc-9457`.
2. [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110). See `http-semantics` (phase 3). Sections 15.5 and 15.6: both 4xx and 5xx bodies should say whether the condition is temporary or permanent; 10.2.3 Retry-After (HTTP-date or seconds, with 503 and 3xx); 409 Conflict ("might be able to resolve the conflict and resubmit"); 422 Unprocessable Content. Note: `rfc-9110` (appended).
3. [Microsoft Azure REST API Guidelines](https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines/blob/vNext/azure/Guidelines.md), Microsoft (Azure API Stewardship Board), vNext branch. Docs, primary: yes for how Azure designs its APIs. Seen (Handling Errors): two kinds of errors, ones customer code should recover from at runtime and bugs the customer must fix; `x-ms-error-code` header whose value is part of the contract and can't change; unique codes for recoverable errors, reused codes for usage errors; body `{error: {code, message, target, details, innererror}}`; only the top-level code is contract, other fields can change; don't make developers rely on fields in the message, `Retry-After` is what they should back off on; don't list specific error codes in OpenAPI. Note: `microsoft-azure-api-guidelines`.

Extra: [AIP-193: Errors](https://google.aip.dev/193), Google. Opened: google.rpc.Status with a required ErrorInfo (reason, domain, metadata); (reason, domain) must be stable; message text becomes contract once clients parse it; partial errors discouraged. Not given a note; RFC 9457 and Azure cover the same points for HTTP.
Extra: [AIP-194: Automatic retry configuration](https://google.aip.dev/194), Google. Opened: retry only UNAVAILABLE automatically; never INVALID_ARGUMENT, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, DATA_LOSS; RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED usually not (quota may take hours); ABORTED retried at a higher level. Not given a note: gRPC-specific; `grpc-status-codes` already has similar retry guidance if the article needs it.
Extra: [Considerations for Service Design](https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines/blob/vNext/azure/ConsiderationsForServiceDesign.md), Microsoft. Opened: usage errors vs runtime errors; changing the status code or top-level error code is a breaking change; design errors away with idempotency and conditional requests. Not given a note; the Guidelines page has the same rules.

#### `validation-at-boundary` (short)

1. [Parse, don't validate](https://lexi-lambda.github.io/blog/2019/11/05/parse-don-t-validate/), Alexis King, 2019. Blog, primary: yes for the idea (she coined the slogan). Seen: `head` on a possibly-empty list; weaken the return type (`Maybe`) vs strengthen the argument (`NonEmpty`); validateNonEmpty returns `()` and throws away what it learned, parseNonEmpty returns a refined type; a parser "consumes less-structured input and produces more-structured output"; parse at the boundary so checks never have to be repeated; shotgun parsing (LangSec) spreads checks through processing code and can act on part of the input before finding the rest invalid; "make illegal states unrepresentable"; push the burden of proof upward "as far as possible, but no further"; footnote: sometimes authorize before parsing to avoid denial of service. Examples in Haskell. Note: `king-parse-dont-validate-2019`.
2. [Input Validation Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Docs, primary: no (community guidance, but the standard reference). Seen: validate as early as possible, from all untrusted sources including partner feeds; not the primary defence against XSS or SQL injection; syntactic vs semantic validation; allowlist over denylist (O'Brian example); JSON Schema, type conversion with strict errors, min/max ranges and lengths, regex anchored with `^...$`; ReDoS; client-side validation can be bypassed, server-side is required; free-form Unicode: normalize, allowlist categories; files: size limits, check before unzipping, random names; email: basic checks then let the mail server decide, 254-character limit. Note: `owasp-input-validation`.

#### `conditional-requests` (short)

1. [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110). See `http-semantics`. Section 13: conditionals on PUT/DELETE prevent the "lost update" problem; If-Match uses strong comparison; `If-Match: *` and `If-None-Match: *` (don't create over an existing resource); false If-Match means don't perform the method, 412, or a 2xx if the change seems to have been applied already (risky for non-cooperating clients); If-Unmodified-Since as the date-based fallback, ignored when If-Match is present; 13.2.1 preconditions are evaluated after normal checks and just before the method runs; a server that isn't the origin must forward them; 13.2.2 evaluation order; 8.8.3.2 strong vs weak comparison table; 15.5.13 412. Note: `rfc-9110` (appended).
2. [Microsoft Azure REST API Guidelines](https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines/blob/vNext/azure/Guidelines.md). See error-design #3. Section Conditional Requests: honor every precondition header; ETags preferred over dates because dates can't tell apart updates less than a second apart; table of PUT/PATCH/DELETE outcomes (412 on mismatch, new ETag on success); prefer a hash of the whole resource over a version number, because a retried conditional update would otherwise look like a conflict; different ETags per content encoding. Note: `microsoft-azure-api-guidelines`.
3. [How to prevent object overwrites with conditional writes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-writes.html), Amazon S3 User Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: If-None-Match `*` (only `*`) fails with 412 if the key exists; If-Match compares ETags, 412 on mismatch; PutObject, CompleteMultipartUpload, CopyObject; with several conditional writes to one key the first to finish wins, the rest get 412; 409 when a concurrent delete wins, PutObject can be retried; in-progress multipart uploads aren't considered; bucket policies can require conditional writes; needs SigV4. Note: `aws-s3-conditional-writes`.

Extra: [RFC 6585](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585), Nottingham, Fielding, 2012. Opened: 428 Precondition Required, used to force clients to send conditional requests; "The 428 status code is optional; clients cannot rely upon its use to prevent 'lost update' conflicts." Not given a note to keep the short node at three sources; worth adding if the article grows.

#### `long-running-operations` (short)

1. [AIP-151: Long-running operations](https://google.aip.dev/151), Google API Improvement Proposals. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: return a `google.longrunning.Operation` instead of the final response, like a future or promise; operation_info names a response type and a metadata type (progress, partial failures); rule of thumb 10 seconds for "a significant amount of time"; resource being created shows in List/Get with a state enum; parallel operations: queue, reject with ABORTED, or let the latest preempt; operations may expire, rule of thumb 30 days; errors before start are normal errors, failures during execution go in `Operation.error`; changing response or metadata type is breaking; validate-only returns a done operation. Note: `google-aip-151`.
2. [Microsoft Azure REST API Guidelines](https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines/blob/vNext/azure/Guidelines.md). See error-design #3. Section Long-Running Operations & Jobs: LROs exist because services don't want long-lived connections (>1 second) and load-balancer timeouts; make it an LRO if p99 > 1 second; validate as much as possible up front; `operation-location` header with the status monitor URL; client may pass `Operation-Id` for retries, 409 if reused with a different request; DELETE and POST actions return 202 even when already finished; status monitor has id, status (NotStarted, Running, Succeeded, Failed, Canceled), error, result; polling GET returns `retry-after` while not terminal; keep the status monitor at least 24 hours; cancel as a POST `:cancel` action (Considerations page); no PATCH as LRO. Note: `microsoft-azure-api-guidelines`.
3. [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110). See `http-semantics`. Section 15.3.3: 202 is "intentionally noncommittal", HTTP has no way to re-send a status code from an asynchronous operation, the body should point to a status monitor. Note: `rfc-9110` (appended).

Extra: [Considerations for Service Design](https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines/blob/vNext/azure/ConsiderationsForServiceDesign.md), Microsoft. Opened: the status monitor is a separate, short-lived resource; four LRO kinds; cancel via POST on the monitor. Not given a note; the Guidelines page has the rules.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- **Which status to start an LRO with.** RFC 9110 and Azure use 202 with a status monitor; Azure says return 202 even when the work already finished, but uses 201 for PUT-creates with extra processing and for PUT-started actions. AIP-151 is RPC-first and returns an Operation object from the method, with no special status code.
- **Retry on a conditional update.** RFC 9110 allows a server to answer 2xx when a failed If-Match looks like it was already applied, and warns it's risky for non-cooperating clients. Azure avoids the issue by preferring content-hash ETags over version numbers, so a retried identical update still matches.
- **Backward vs forward first.** Confluent defaults to BACKWARD so consumers can re-read a topic from the start; the protobuf docs treat adding fields as safe in both directions. Kleppmann (2012) notes Avro unions need readers updated before writers. The right order depends on who upgrades first.
- **Required fields.** Kleppmann's 2012 post still has protobuf `required`; proto3 removed it and the best-practices page calls it harmful. Buf still checks that optional fields aren't made required.
- **Error detail formats.** RFC 9457 (problem+json), Azure (`{error:{code,...}}` plus a header) and Google (google.rpc.Status with ErrorInfo) all say the same thing: status for generic software, a stable machine code in the body. They disagree on shape, and none is universal.
- **Validation as security.** OWASP says input validation isn't the primary defence against injection; King's parse-don't-validate is about correctness and types, not attacks. The node should say both.

**Couldn't open:**

- Nothing needed failed to open. Avro's `++version++` docs URL resolves too, but the article pins 1.12.0.

**Rejected:**

- AIP-193, AIP-194 and the Azure Considerations page: opened, used for understanding, not cited (see Extras).
- MDN status code pages: secondary; RFC 9110 and RFC 9457 cover it.
- Kleppmann's DDIA chapter 4: not opened (book), so not cited; his 2012 post covers the same ground.

**Gaps:**

- No source with measured numbers on schema evolution failures or how often version skew happens; the article uses the Kleppmann byte counts only.
- No primary source for "callbacks instead of polling" for LROs beyond the webhooks node; the article only points there.
- No JSON Schema-focused source for evolving plain JSON APIs; Confluent's JSON Schema tables (open vs closed content model) are the only one opened.

### Doing it once, even when it's retried

#### `timeouts` (short)

1. [Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter](https://d1.awsstatic.com/builderslibrary/pdfs/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter.pdf), Marc Brooker, Amazon Builders' Library, 2019. Blog by the team that built it, primary: yes. Seen: read as the PDF (the web page now redirects to builder.aws.com, which renders only with JavaScript). Timeout = max wait; waiting holds memory, threads, connections, ephemeral ports; set a connection and a request timeout on every remote call, even across processes on one box; too high wastes resources, too low causes retries and can turn a small latency rise into an outage; pick an acceptable false-timeout rate (0.1%) and use the matching downstream percentile (p99.9); fails over the internet and when p99.9 is close to p50; SO_RCVTIMEO unsuitable as end-to-end; some timeouts skip DNS or TLS; the 20 ms timeout that included new TLS connections after deployments, fixed by connecting at startup.
2. [The complete guide to Go net/http timeouts](https://blog.cloudflare.com/the-complete-guide-to-golang-net-http-timeouts/), Filippo Valsorda, Cloudflare, 2016. Blog, primary: no (Cloudflare didn't build net/http). Seen: deadlines are absolute and don't reset on progress; server ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout and their exact spans (HTTPS differs); slow clients leak file descriptors; ListenAndServe and http.Get have no timeouts (Go 1.6/1.7); streaming can't use absolute write timeouts; Client.Timeout covers dial to body including redirects; Dialer.Timeout, TLSHandshakeTimeout, ResponseHeaderTimeout, ExpectContinueTimeout; idle timeout by resetting a timer per read; contexts propagate cancellation.
3. [Addressing Cascading Failures](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/), Mike Ulrich, Google SRE book, 2016. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: see `retries-with-backoff` #3. For timeouts: picking a deadline (none or huge lets old problems eat resources; short makes expensive requests fail); missing deadlines wastes work; deadline propagation (30, 23, 19 s); bimodal latency example (1,000 threads, 5% hang, 100 s deadline, 19.6% served); deadlines orders of magnitude above mean latency are bad; fail fast.

Extra: [gRPC deadlines guide](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/deadlines/), note `grpc-deadlines` already exists (no default deadline). Not cited, to keep the short node at three sources.

#### `idempotency` (deep)

1. [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110), Fielding, Nottingham, Reschke (eds.), 2022. Spec, primary: yes. Note exists. Section 9.2.1/9.2.2: safe and idempotent defined as intended effect; PUT, DELETE and safe methods idempotent; the response to a retry may differ; clients shouldn't auto-retry non-idempotent requests, proxies must not.
2. [RFC 5789](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5789), Dusseault, Snell, 2010. Spec, primary: yes. Note exists, appended. Section 2: PATCH neither safe nor idempotent; can be issued so it's idempotent; conditional request so it fails if the resource changed; some patch formats corrupt a resource applied to the wrong base.
3. [Making retries safe with idempotent APIs](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/), Malcolm Featonby, Amazon Builders' Library. Blog by the team that built it, primary: yes. Seen: EC2 RunInstances example; after a timeout the caller can't know; hashing parameters to detect duplicates fails (two identical instances may be wanted); caller-provided client request identifier (ClientToken); record token and do the work atomically (ACID); ResourceAlreadyExists is idempotent but surprising, so return a semantically equivalent response; SDK/CLI generate and reuse the token; late-arriving retry after termination still answered with the original result; token retention = resource lifetime plus a margin; same token different parameters = validation error; cost isn't right for every API.
4. [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency), Brandur Leach, Stripe, 2017. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: three failure points of a call; ambiguous failures; idempotent = side effects once; PUT DNS record example; charging needs idempotency keys; server behaviour per failure case; Idempotency-Key on POST; exponential backoff (2^n) and jitter against the thundering herd; Stripe Ruby library retries with keys.
5. [Implementing Stripe-like Idempotency Keys in Postgres](https://brandur.org/idempotency-keys), Brandur Leach, 2017. Blog by a Stripe engineer, primary: yes. Seen: see `idempotency-keys` #3. For idempotency: local ACID-only endpoints can map a request to one transaction; foreign state mutations (idempotent by nature, made idempotent with a key, or not at all); once a foreign call is made you're committed; Kafka writes count as foreign calls.
6. [net/http](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http), The Go Authors, go1.27.1. Docs, primary: yes. Note exists. Transport retries after a network error only on a used connection and only idempotent requests (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, or with Idempotency-Key).

#### `idempotency-keys` (deep)

1. [The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field, draft 07](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header-07), Jayadeba Jena, Sanjay Dalal, IETF HTTPAPI WG, 2025. Spec (Internet-Draft), primary: yes. Seen: datatracker lists it as an expired Internet-Draft. Header is a Structured Field String; key unique, not reused with a different payload; UUID recommended; server may expire keys and should publish the policy; optional fingerprint; completed duplicate gets the earlier result; concurrent duplicate gets a conflict (409); missing key 400; reused key with different payload 422; implementations list (Stripe, Adyen, Dwolla, Interledger, WorldPay, Yandex, http4s, Finastra, Datatrans); security: low-entropy keys leak other clients' cached results, validate the key, scope the lookup with client attributes.
2. [Idempotent requests](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests), Stripe API reference. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: stores status and body of the first request, success or failure, including 500s; V4 UUIDs; up to 255 characters; no sensitive data in keys; may prune after 24 hours, then a reused key is a new request; parameters compared, mismatch errors; results saved only once execution begins, so validation failures and concurrent conflicts aren't saved; all POSTs accept keys, GET and DELETE don't need them.
3. [Implementing Stripe-like Idempotency Keys in Postgres](https://brandur.org/idempotency-keys), Brandur Leach, 2017. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: key table schema (unique on user_id + key, locked_at, request params, response code/body, recovery_point); upsert in SERIALIZABLE, locked key gets 409; atomic phases between foreign calls; recovery points; transactionally staged jobs for email; completer; reaper (~24 h general, 72 h suggested); failure walkthrough ("Murphy in action"); non-idempotent foreign calls marked failed; no non-ACID stores; hidden form field against double submit.
4. [Making retries safe with idempotent APIs](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/). See `idempotency` #3.

Extra: [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency). See `idempotency` #4; cited there, not here.

#### `retries-with-backoff` (deep)

1. [Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter](https://d1.awsstatic.com/builderslibrary/pdfs/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter.pdf). See `timeouts` #1. For retries: partial and transient failures; retries are selfish; capped exponential backoff and the cap problem; limit retries; 3 retries at 5 layers = 243x; retry at a single point; circuit breakers modal, local token bucket instead (AWS SDK, 2016); side-effect APIs need idempotency; 4xx vs 5xx blurred by eventual consistency; jitter on all timers and periodic jobs; consistent per-host jitter for scheduled work; retry only while the dependency is healthy.
2. [Exponential Backoff And Jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/), Marc Brooker, AWS Architecture Blog, 2015. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: OCC contention simulation (10 ms mean delay); work grows with N²; capped exponential backoff formula; backoff leaves clusters and gaps; full, equal and decorrelated jitter formulas (as images of code); no-jitter is the clear loser; with 100 clients full jitter cuts calls by more than half; equal jitter slowest; decorrelated more calls; N² unchanged; update note says most AWS SDKs now do backoff with jitter in standard and adaptive modes.
3. [Addressing Cascading Failures](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/). See `timeouts` #3. For retries: naive retry loop growing 100, 200, 300 QPS; retries keep backends overloaded; randomized exponential backoff; limit per request; server-wide budget (60/min); 4 attempts at 3 layers = 64; separate retriable and non-retriable errors; retry graphs look like symptoms.
4. [Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/), Alejandro Forero Cuervo, Google SRE book, 2016. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: retry immediately when only a few tasks are overloaded; per-request budget of three attempts; per-client retry ratio below 10% (3x vs 1.1x worst case); attempt counter in metadata and "overloaded; don't retry" error; retry only at the layer directly above the rejecting one.
5. [Retry (gRPC guide)](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/retry/), gRPC authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: retry replays call history; committed once response headers arrive; retries on but no default policy; transparent retry rules; policy fields (maxAttempts, initialBackoff, maxBackoff, backoffMultiplier, retryableStatusCodes); ±20% jitter; retry throttling (maxTokens, tokenRatio, pause below half); hedging exists.
6. [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency). See `idempotency` #4. Backoff proportional to 2^n, jitter, thundering herd.

#### `delivery-guarantees` (deep)

1. [Kafka design: Message Delivery Semantics, Using Transactions](https://kafka.apache.org/43/design/design/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: the three definitions; producer and consumer halves; read the fine print of exactly-once claims; producer network error is ambiguous; before 0.11.0.0 at least once; idempotent producer (producer ID + sequence number); save-then-process = at most once, process-then-save = at least once; keyed updates idempotent; offsets written in the same transaction as output; for external systems store offsets with the output instead of 2PC; default at least once; at most once by disabling retries and committing first; only the producer is transactional; transactional.id aborts the previous instance's transaction; share groups count delivery attempts.
2. [Exactly-once Semantics are Possible: Here's How Apache Kafka Does it](https://www.confluent.io/blog/exactly-once-semantics-are-possible-heres-how-apache-kafka-does-it/), Neha Narkhede, Confluent, 2017. Blog by Kafka's builders, primary: yes. Seen: at least once/at most once/exactly once from the producer's side; exactly once needs system and application to cooperate; three failure cases (broker, RPC, client) and zombie producers; idempotent producer like TCP sequence numbers but persisted in the log; transactions across partitions, read_committed; exactly once for stream processing = results reflected once; scope limited to Kafka Streams' internal processing; non-deterministic operations; benchmark (3% producer throughput cost at 1 KB, 100 ms transactions; Kafka 0.11).
3. [You Cannot Have Exactly-Once Delivery](https://bravenewgeek.com/you-cannot-have-exactly-once-delivery/), Tyler Treat, 2015. Blog, primary: no. Seen: exactly-once delivery impossible between any two machines; ack before processing = at most once, after = at least once; exactly once is faked with idempotency or dedup; send state not instructions (directions example); leans on Two Generals and FLP, disputed in its own comments (FLP assumes reliable links; it's about termination, not safety).
4. [Amazon SQS at-least-once delivery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues-at-least-once-delivery.html), AWS docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: copies on several servers; an unavailable server keeps its copy when you delete, so you can get it again; design consumers to be idempotent.
5. [Exactly-once processing in Amazon SQS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/FIFO-queues-exactly-once-processing.html), AWS docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: FIFO queues don't introduce duplicates for a SendMessage retried within the 5-minute deduplication interval; content-based dedup (SHA-256 of the body, not attributes) or explicit deduplication ID. Says nothing about consumer crashes.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Exactly once: Treat (2015) says exactly-once delivery is impossible; Narkhede (2017) says exactly-once semantics are possible. They differ on what "delivery" means: from the sender's side it's at most or at least once; the processed effect can be once with cooperation from the receiver. The `delivery-guarantees` article explains the disagreement this way. Treat's use of FLP is disputed in his own comments; the article doesn't lean on FLP.
- How much jitter: AWS's "full jitter" picks 0 to the whole backoff; gRPC applies ±20%. Both covered in `retries-with-backoff`.
- Circuit breakers vs retry token buckets: Amazon finds breakers modal and hard to test and prefers a local token bucket; breakers are "widely promoted". Covered; phase 13's `circuit-breakers` should take it up.
- Where to retry: Amazon says a single point in the stack; Google says the layer directly above the rejecting one, with a "don't retry" error upward. Compatible, different emphasis.
- Which result to store under an idempotency key: Stripe stores the first result including 500s; Brandur's design stores only final results and resumes the rest; EC2 returns a semantically equivalent (not identical) response.
- Key retention: Stripe 24 h minimum, Brandur 24 h generally and 72 h suggested, EC2 the resource's lifetime plus a margin, the IETF draft leaves it to the server.
- Status codes for idempotency-key errors: the draft suggests 400, 409, 422; APIs differ.

**Couldn't open:**

- [Idempotence Is Not a Medical Condition](https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=2187821), Pat Helland, ACM Queue, 2012. Blocked by a Cloudflare JavaScript challenge. Not cited.
- The builder.aws.com version of Brooker's Builders' Library article renders only with JavaScript; used the official PDF instead.

**Rejected:**

- MDN and generic blog explainers on backoff and idempotency: secondary, and the AWS, Google and Stripe sources are from the people who built the systems.
- RabbitMQ's publisher-confirm docs (quoted in Treat's post): not opened directly, so not cited.
- Confluent's benchmark numbers: from Kafka 0.11 and a vendor; kept in the note, not used in the article.

**Gaps:**

- No source opened for HTTP `Retry-After` handling on the client side beyond RFC 9110's 503 note; left to `rate-limiting` and `error-design`.
- No source settles how an idempotency-key lock left by a crashed process should expire; `idempotency-keys` says so.
- No measured numbers for backoff or jitter beyond Brooker's simulation; articles use none of its figures except "more than half" for 100 clients.
- Go's current default timeouts weren't re-checked against pkg.go.dev; `timeouts` pins the no-timeout claim to Go 1.7 via the Cloudflare post.
- The SQS FIFO page doesn't say what happens to a retry after five minutes; the article says it isn't covered rather than that it duplicates.

### Doing it once, even when it's retried + Protecting the API

#### `dead-letter-queue` (short)

1. [Using dead-letter queues in Amazon SQS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html), AWS, SQS Developer Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: DLQ is a queue that source queues target for messages not processed successfully; useful for debugging; same account and Region; redrive policy with maxReceiveCount (receives before the move; 1 means one failure moves it; set it high enough for retries); standard queues with maxReceiveCount above 3 push a message received 3+ times to the back of the queue; redrive allow policy (all, up to 10 named source queues, or deny all); don't use a DLQ with FIFO if you can't break order; standard queues keep the original enqueue timestamp so the DLQ's retention should be longer than the source's (1 day + 4 day example), FIFO resets it. Note: `aws-sqs-dead-letter-queues`.
2. [Configuring a dead-letter queue redrive](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-configure-dead-letter-queue-redrive.html), AWS, SQS Developer Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: redrive moves messages back to the source queue by default, or to another queue of the same type; velocity control, custom max 500 messages per second, start small and ramp up; oldest first; redriven messages interleave with new ones, even in FIFO; redriven messages get a new message ID and enqueue time; no filtering or editing during redrive; a redrive task runs at most 36 hours, 100 active tasks per account; StartMessageMoveTask, ListMessageMoveTasks, CancelMessageMoveTask. Note: `aws-sqs-dlq-redrive`.
3. [Dead-letter topics](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/handling-failures), Google Cloud, Pub/Sub docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Pub/Sub forwards undeliverable messages to a dead-letter topic after a configured number of delivery attempts (default 5, min 5, max 100); set on the subscription, not the topic; the count is approximate and best effort, can reset to zero, so a message can be delivered more times than the maximum; the original message is wrapped and gets attributes (source delivery count, source subscription, original publish time); the message is removed from the source subscription after forwarding; a DLQ topic needs its own subscription; dead_letter_message_count metric. Note: `gcp-pubsub-dead-letter-topics`.

#### `request-signing` (short)

1. [AWS Signature Version 4 for API requests](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_sigv.html), AWS, IAM User Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: three steps (canonical request, signature from credentials, Authorization header); AWS repeats the process and compares; SigV4 derives a key scoped to one service, one Region, one day; SigV4a uses ECDSA so AWS stores only public keys; why sign: identity, integrity in transit, replay protection with a five-minute window; SDKs do it for you. Note: `aws-sigv4`.
2. [Create a signed AWS API request](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_sigv-create-signed-request.html), AWS, IAM User Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: canonical request = method, canonical URI, sorted and encoded query, lowercased sorted trimmed headers, signed header list, hex SHA-256 of the payload; host and x-amz-* headers required; don't sign hop-by-hop headers that proxies change; write your own UriEncode because platform ones differ; string to sign = algorithm, timestamp, credential scope (date/region/service/aws4_request), hash of canonical request; signing key from four chained HMAC-SHA256 calls starting with "AWS4"+secret; signature = HMAC-SHA256(signing key, string to sign) in lowercase hex. Note: `aws-sigv4-create-signed-request`.
3. [RFC 9421: HTTP Message Signatures](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421), Backman, Richer, Sporny (eds.), IETF, 2024. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: TLS protects one connection, not an end-to-end path through TLS-terminating gateways; detached signatures over chosen components; HTTP lets intermediaries reorder, combine and re-case fields, so strict canonicalization; Signature-Input and Signature fields; parameters created, expires, nonce, alg, keyid, tag; unsigned parts can be changed (insufficient coverage); replay: cover enough, nonce, created/expires; body not covered directly, needs Content-Digest, and the verifier must check the digest against the body; symmetric keys let a verifier impersonate a signer, prefer asymmetric; algorithms include hmac-sha256, ecdsa, ed25519, rsa-pss. Note: `rfc-9421`.
4. [Standard Webhooks specification](https://github.com/standard-webhooks/standard-webhooks/blob/main/spec/standard-webhooks.md), Standard Webhooks contributors, version 1.0.0. Spec (community), primary: yes. See webhooks #1. Used here for the `msg_id.timestamp.payload` signing scheme, the `webhook-` headers, constant-time compare and timestamp tolerance.

Extra: [Stripe webhooks](https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks). See webhooks #2; the timestamp-in-signature and five-minute tolerance are cited from there in the webhooks article, not here.

#### `webhooks` (deep)

1. [Standard Webhooks specification](https://github.com/standard-webhooks/standard-webhooks/blob/main/spec/standard-webhooks.md), Standard Webhooks contributors, version 1.0.0. Spec (community, by webhook providers), primary: yes. Seen: webhooks are a "reverse API", server to server; payload shape (type, timestamp, data), thin vs full payloads and their trade-offs, keep payloads under about 20 kB; signature over `msg_id.timestamp.payload`, HMAC-SHA256 (`v1`) or ed25519 (`v1a`), secrets 24 to 64 bytes, `whsec_` prefix; headers `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp`, `webhook-signature`; space-separated list of signatures for zero-downtime key rotation; re-serialising parsed JSON breaks signatures; constant-time compare; timestamp tolerance; webhook-id as idempotency key; retry schedule over several days with exponential backoff and jitter (10 attempts, last one at about 75.5 hours); disable endpoints that keep failing and tell the owner by email; 2xx = success, 3xx failure, 410 = disable, 429/502/504 = throttle, honour Retry-After; request timeout 15 to 30 s; HTTPS; static source IPs; SSRF through customer-chosen URLs, smokescreen proxy and a separate subnet; fan-out to many endpoints; failure visibility and manual replay; endpoint management API. Note: `standard-webhooks-spec`.
2. [Receive Stripe events in your webhook endpoint](https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks), Stripe docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: HTTPS endpoints, up to 16 per account; signing secret `whsec_` per endpoint; verify with the raw body; return 2xx fast before complex logic; redirects count as failures; TLS 1.2 or higher; retries up to three days with exponential backoff in live mode; manual resend 15 days (Dashboard) or 30 days (CLI); no ordering guarantee, don't use `created` to order; duplicates happen, log event IDs; process through an async queue because of spikes (beginning of the month); exempt the route from CSRF; roll secrets, old one can stay valid up to 24 hours, one signature per secret; timestamp in the Stripe-Signature header, signed, libraries default to a five-minute tolerance, tolerance 0 disables the check; a new timestamp and signature for each retry; IP allowlist. Note: `stripe-webhooks`.
3. [Best practices for using webhooks](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/using-webhooks/best-practices-for-using-webhooks), GitHub docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: subscribe to the minimum events; use a webhook secret, not credentials in the URL; HTTPS and SSL verification; IP allow list from GET /meta; respond with 2xx within 10 seconds or GitHub counts a failure; queue and process asynchronously; check event type and action, new ones get added; redeliver missed webhooks after downtime; X-GitHub-Delivery is unique per event and stays the same on redelivery (replay protection). Note: `github-webhooks-best-practices`.
4. [Handling failed webhook deliveries](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/using-webhooks/handling-failed-webhook-deliveries), GitHub docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: GitHub does not automatically redeliver failed deliveries; manual redelivery, or a scheduled script that lists deliveries through the REST API and redelivers the failed ones; no API for Marketplace or Sponsors webhooks. Note: `github-webhooks-failed-deliveries`.
5. [Validating webhook deliveries](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/using-webhooks/validating-webhook-deliveries), GitHub docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: X-Hub-Signature-256 is an HMAC-SHA256 hex digest of the payload with the secret; X-Hub-Signature (SHA-1) kept for legacy only; never use `==`, use a constant-time compare; handle payload as UTF-8; proxies and load balancers must not change the payload or headers; test vector given. Note: `github-webhooks-validating`.
6. [Verify webhook deliveries](https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/build/webhooks/ignore-duplicates), Shopify docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: raw body needed for HMAC (body-parser middleware breaks it); duplicates after timeouts or retries, dedupe on X-Shopify-Webhook-Id, X-Shopify-Event-Id shared across subscriptions; 200 range only counts as success, 3xx is an error; one-second connect timeout, five-second total; keep-alive reuse; queue and reconcile; 8 retries over 4 hours, then the subscription is deleted (Admin API ones) and warning emails sent. Note: `shopify-webhooks-verify`.
7. [About webhooks](https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/build/webhooks), Shopify docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: webhooks vs polling; no ordering guarantee within a topic or across topics (products/update before products/create); order by X-Shopify-Triggered-At or updated_at; don't rely only on webhooks, run reconciliation jobs with updated_at filters. Note: none; the ordering and reconciliation points are also in #6 and #2, so one Shopify note is enough. Not cited.
8. [Troubleshoot webhooks](https://shopify.dev/docs/apps/build/webhooks/troubleshooting-webhooks), Shopify docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: retries up to eight times in four hours with a growing interval, subscription removed after that; five-second response time. Not cited; #6 carries the same numbers.

#### `rate-limiting` (short)

1. [RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585), Nottingham, Fielding, IETF, 2012. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 429 Too Many Requests means too many requests in a given amount of time; SHOULD explain, MAY include Retry-After; doesn't define how to identify the user or count (per resource, per server, across servers; credentials or cookie); 429 MUST NOT be cached; under attack, answering each request with 429 costs resources, dropping connections may be better; also 428 Precondition Required. Note: `rfc-6585`.
2. [Scaling your API with rate limiters](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters), Paul Tarjan, Stripe, 2017. Blog by the team that runs it, primary: yes. Seen: why (one user's spike, runaway scripts, low-priority traffic, internal trouble); rate limiter vs load shedder (whole-system state); four limiters: request rate (N per second, with bursts), concurrent requests (20 in flight), fleet usage load shedder (reserve 20% for critical requests, 503), worker utilisation load shedder; token bucket per user in Redis; fail open if the limiter breaks; 429 vs 503; kill switches; dark launch first. Note: `stripe-rate-limiters-2017`.
3. [RateLimit header fields for HTTP](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers/), Polli, Martinez, Miller, IETF HTTPAPI working group, draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers-11. Internet-Draft (work in progress), primary: yes. Seen: no standard way today for servers to tell clients their quota; defines RateLimit-Policy (q, qu, w, pk) and RateLimit (r, t, pk); quota units requests, content-bytes, concurrent-requests; doesn't mandate an algorithm; effective window is delay-seconds so it doesn't need clock sync and avoids everyone retrying at one timestamp; Retry-After takes precedence; remaining quota is a hint, not a promise; ignore on cached responses; intermediaries may retry and consume quota; if 401/403 count against quota, a client can probe another user's traffic; Appendix A: common X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset headers with different meanings per vendor. Note: `ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers`.
4. [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110), section 10.2.3. Note exists (`rfc-9110`, already carries 10.2.3). Seen: Retry-After is an HTTP date or delay-seconds; meaning with 503 and 3xx. Not cited in the article; RFC 6585 and the RateLimit draft cover what it needs.

#### `rate-limiting-algorithms` (deep)

1. [How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains](https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/), Julien Desgats, Cloudflare, 2017. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: stock nginx module is per server, which breaks when traffic spreads across servers; anycast keeps one client IP at one PoP, so a counter per PoP (Twemproxy + memcache shards, consistent hashing); fixed window resets let spikes through; storing every timestamp is accurate but costly; leaky bucket accurate but two parameters to tune and needs non-atomic steps on memcached; sliding window counter: previous count weighted by the remaining fraction plus the current count (42 × 0.75 + 18 = 49.5 for a 50/min limit); on 400 million requests from 270,000 sources, 0.003% wrongly allowed or limited, 6% average difference, no false positives; two numbers per counter, one INCR; increments done asynchronously and mitigation decisions cached in memory; 400,000 requests per second attack on one domain mitigated. Note: `cloudflare-rate-limiting-2017`.
2. [Rate Limiting, Cells, and GCRA](https://brandur.org/rate-limiting), Brandur Leach, 2015. Blog by a Stripe/Heroku engineer who maintains Throttled, primary: partly (he maintains the library). Seen: uses (shared capacity, security, revenue); naive expiring bucket lets a script burn the whole limit at once and locks it out, and makes the server absorb hourly bursts (GitHub's 5,000/hour example); leaky bucket with capacity τ and leak rate T, smooth; the naive leaky bucket needs a background drip process that can fall behind; GCRA from ATM cells keeps one theoretical arrival time (TAT) per key, no drip; clock drift across machines matters, use the store's clock (Redis TIME); Throttled (Go) implements it. Note: `brandur-rate-limiting-gcra-2015`.
3. [throttled rate.go](https://github.com/throttled/throttled/blob/master/rate.go), Throttled authors. Source code, primary: yes. Seen: GCRARateLimiterCtx; emission interval = period between equally spaced requests; delay variation tolerance = emission interval × (max burst + 1); limit = burst + 1; new TAT = max(now, TAT) + quantity × interval; reject when now < newTAT − tolerance; RetryAfter from the difference; compare-and-swap loop against the store with a TTL; quantity lets you limit bytes, 0 peeks; PerMin(60) = 60 at once then one per second. Note: `throttled-rate-go`.
4. [Module ngx_http_limit_req_module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_limit_req_module.html), nginx docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "leaky bucket" method per key; rate in r/s or r/m; burst queues excess requests and delays them to the rate; `nodelay` serves the burst at once; `delay=` (1.15.7) for two-stage limiting; default reject status 503 (`limit_req_status`); dry-run mode (1.17.1); state 64 or 128 bytes per key, a 1 MB zone holds about 16,000 or 8,000 states, LRU eviction when full; `sync` for shared state is commercial only. Note: `nginx-limit-req-module`.
5. [Local rate limit (Envoy)](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/configuration/http/http_filters/local_rate_limit_filter), Envoy docs, 1.40.0-dev. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: token bucket (max_tokens, tokens_per_fill, fill_interval); 429 plus x-envoy-ratelimited; bucket per Envoy process by default or per downstream connection; optional Retry-After = seconds until the next token, at least 1 s; descriptors for per-route and per-client buckets; a rejected request can still consume tokens of another descriptor. Note: `envoy-local-rate-limit`.
6. [Scaling your API with rate limiters](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters). See rate-limiting #2. Token bucket per user in Redis; request-rate plus burst; concurrency limiter as a different shape.
7. [Throttle requests to your REST APIs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-request-throttling.html), AWS, API Gateway Developer Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: token bucket, a token per request; rate = tokens added per second, burst = bucket capacity; best-effort targets, not guaranteed ceilings; 429 when exceeded; layered limits (AWS Region-wide, per account, per stage/method, per client via API keys in usage plans). Note: `aws-api-gateway-throttling`. Cited in `api-gateway`, not here (six sources were enough).

Extra: [tc-tbf(8)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/tc-tbf.8.html), Linux man-pages (iproute2). Opened: token bucket filter for packets, tokens roughly bytes, bucket size = burst, packets queue when empty, peakrate as a second bucket. Not given a note: a traffic shaper, not a request limiter; the article sticks to request limiting.

#### `api-gateway` (short)

1. [Pattern: API Gateway / Backends for Frontends](https://microservices.io/patterns/apigateway.html), Chris Richardson, microservices.io. Pattern catalogue by the author who named it, primary: yes (for the pattern). Seen: single entry point for all clients; routes some requests, fans out others (API composition); a different API per client, Netflix example; Backends for Frontends variant, one gateway per kind of client; benefits (hides partitioning and instance locations, fewer round trips for mobile, protocol translation); drawbacks (another moving part, an extra network hop); authenticates and passes a token to services; uses service discovery and circuit breakers. Note: `microservices-io-api-gateway`.
2. [What is Amazon API Gateway?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/welcome.html), AWS, API Gateway Developer Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: managed service for REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs; "front door" for backends (EC2, Lambda, any web app); traffic management, authorization and access control, monitoring, API version management; IAM, Lambda authorizers, Cognito; canary releases; logging; WAF integration. Note: `aws-api-gateway-overview`.
3. [Throttle requests to your REST APIs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/api-gateway-request-throttling.html). See rate-limiting-algorithms #7. Per-client limits keyed by API key in usage plans.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- **Which status for "slow down".** RFC 6585 defines 429 for rate limiting; nginx's `limit_req` rejects with 503 by default; Stripe returns 503 from its load shedders and says to choose between 429 and 503 per case; the RateLimit draft's appendix notes servers use 429 or 403. The articles say 429 for per-client limits, 503 for "the whole service is overloaded".
- **Leaky bucket means two things.** nginx calls its limiter a leaky bucket and queues (delays) excess requests; Cloudflare and Brandur describe it as a counter that drains and rejects when full, which is the same as a token bucket turned upside down. The algorithms article explains both readings.
- **Symmetric vs asymmetric signatures.** Standard Webhooks and RFC 9421 both say prefer asymmetric keys (a verifier holding the HMAC key can forge); every big provider opened (Stripe, GitHub, Shopify, AWS SigV4) uses HMAC. AWS added SigV4a (ECDSA) for multi-Region.
- **Replay protection in webhook signatures.** Stripe and Standard Webhooks sign a timestamp; GitHub signs only the body and points to the X-GitHub-Delivery ID for replays.
- **Automatic retries.** Stripe retries for up to three days, Shopify 8 times over 4 hours then deletes the subscription, GitHub doesn't retry at all; Standard Webhooks recommends several days.
- **DLQ and order.** AWS says don't use a DLQ with FIFO queues when order matters; the lab wants per-endpoint order and a DLQ. The webhooks and DLQ articles say what you give up.
- **Pub/Sub's attempt count is approximate**, so "after N tries" is a target, not an exact rule.

**Couldn't open:**

- Stripe's "manual verification" steps (the `t=` and `v1=` format of Stripe-Signature) are in a collapsed part of the page that didn't come through in the fetched text. Not cited; the article describes Stripe's scheme only as far as the note goes.
- Nothing else failed. (The Cloudflare sliding-window calculation, 42 × 0.75 + 18 = 49.5, is in a formatted block the text converter dropped; it was read from the page's HTML.)

**Rejected:**

- tc-tbf(8): a packet shaper; see rate-limiting-algorithms Extra.
- Shopify "About webhooks" and "Troubleshoot webhooks": same facts as the verify page, one note is enough.
- Vendor blog posts from webhook-as-a-service companies: secondary, and Standard Webhooks is the same people writing the spec.

**Gaps:**

- No primary source on keeping per-endpoint order in a webhook sender (every provider opened says it doesn't guarantee order). The webhooks article explains why from the delivery model and says the providers don't promise it; the lab's decision record will have to measure the cost.
- No source for the sliding log algorithm beyond Cloudflare's one-line description ("store the timestamp of every request").
- The GCRA ATM Forum spec itself wasn't opened; GCRA is described from Brandur and the Throttled source.
- No numbers for gateway latency overhead; the api-gateway article says "an extra hop" without a figure.

## Phase 6: Databases I, using Postgres well

Researched by 5 parallel passes, one per group below.

### The model

#### `relational-model` (deep)

1. [A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks](https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~zives/03f/cis550/codd.pdf), E. F. Codd, IBM Research, CACM 13(6), 1970. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: scanned PDF (course mirror at UPenn; OCR text layer has errors, quotes chosen from clean lines). 1.2 three data dependencies in the systems of the day: ordering, indexing, access path; the parts/projects example where a program written for one of five tree structures fails on at least three others; 1.3 relation defined as a set of n-tuples, array representation (row order immaterial, rows distinct), users should see domain-unordered "relationships" with role names; primary key, nonredundant key, foreign key (may reference the same relation); nonsimple domains (relations as values); 1.4 normalization removes nonsimple domains (employee/jobhistory/salaryhistory/children example, figure 3); 1.5 a data sublanguage based on first-order predicate calculus, "symmetric exploitation"; 2.2 strong and weak redundancy, employee(serial#, name, manager#, managername) example; redundancy in the stored set costs storage and update time for faster queries; 2.3 consistency as a property of the instantaneous state, checking slows writes.
2. [What Goes Around Comes Around](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~yanlei/courses/CS691LL-f06/papers/SH05.pdf), Michael Stonebraker and Joseph M. Hellerstein, Red Book 4th ed., 2005. Paper, primary: yes (Stonebraker built INGRES and Postgres). Seen: nine eras of data models; IMS and CODASYL lessons 1-6 (data independence, record-at-a-time forces manual optimization); section IV Codd's threefold proposal (tables, set-at-a-time DML, no storage proposal), the "great debate" and SIGMOD '74, System R and INGRES prove it can be implemented, VAX, DB/2 on MVS in 1984, SQL becomes the de facto standard, lessons 7-10; section V normalization theory "dead in the water", E-R diagrams won schema design, lesson 11 "functional dependencies are too difficult for mere mortals".
3. [What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around...](https://db.cs.cmu.edu/papers/2024/whatgoesaround-sigmodrec2024.pdf), Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo, SIGMOD Record 53(2), 2024. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: RM and SQL still dominant, SQL absorbs good ideas; MapReduce, KV stores, document, column-family, text search, array, vector and graph databases each reviewed; KV stores push joins into the application; document DBs repeat OO/XML arguments, denormalization/prejoining problems (duplicated data, not always faster, no data independence); almost every NoSQL system added a SQL interface by the end of the 2010s, MongoDB Atlas in 2021; SQL standard added JSON in 2016; the optimizer is the hardest part of a DBMS; ORMs and developers querying directly.
4. [Lecture #01: Relational Model & Algebra](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/01-relationalmodel.pdf), Andy Pavlo, CMU 15-445/645 Fall 2024 notes. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: flat-file strawman (CSV per entity) and its integrity, implementation and durability problems; early DBMSs tied logical and physical layers; Codd 1969; three ideas (simple structures, physical storage left to the DBMS, high-level language); structure, integrity, manipulation; data independence; relation is unordered; NULL; primary key, foreign key, constraint; procedural vs declarative DML; relational algebra operators with SQL equivalents; the "filter before join is faster, same answer" example; document and vector models.

Extra: [PostgreSQL 18 tutorial, Concepts](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-concepts.html). Opened: tables as named collections of rows with typed columns; columns have a fixed order but SQL does not guarantee row order. Not given a note; the CMU notes cover the same ground.

#### `sql` (deep)

1. [SELECT (PostgreSQL 18 docs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: the ten-step "general processing of SELECT" (WITH, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY/HAVING, SELECT list, DISTINCT, UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT, ORDER BY, LIMIT, locking); output column names usable in ORDER BY and GROUP BY but not WHERE or HAVING; NULLS LAST default for ASC (nulls sort as larger); LIMIT without ORDER BY gives an unpredictable subset, "not a bug"; Postgres evaluates output expressions after sort and limit when it can; LEFT/FULL OUTER JOIN definitions; compatibility section (LIMIT is nonstandard, OFFSET ... FETCH is SQL:2008).
2. [Comparison Functions and Operators (PostgreSQL 18 docs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-comparison.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `7 = NULL` yields null; IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM; "Do not write expression = NULL"; transform_null_equals; row-valued IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are not inverses.
3. [Subquery Expressions (PostgreSQL 18 docs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-subquery.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: NOT IN returns null (not true) when the subquery has a null and no match; NOT IN is equivalent to <> ALL.
4. [Table Expressions (PostgreSQL 18 docs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: FROM list with several tables is a cross join; WHERE keeps a row only if the condition is true (false or null discards it); join types defined; ON vs WHERE for outer joins; NATURAL is risky under schema change.
5. [NULL Handling in SQLite Versus Other Database Engines](https://www.sqlite.org/nulls.html), D. Richard Hipp, SQLite. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: the standard is ambiguous on NULLs; SQLite matched other engines by experiment; table across SQLite, PostgreSQL, Oracle, Informix, DB2, MS-SQL, MySQL and others; NULLs distinct in UNIQUE but not in DISTINCT or UNION; Informix and MS-SQL treat NULLs as indistinct in UNIQUE; test script comment "capricious and cannot be deduced by logic".
6. [Lecture #02: Modern SQL](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/02-modernsql.pdf), Andy Pavlo, CMU 15-445/645 Fall 2024 notes. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: SQL from IBM System R, first called SEQUEL; editions SQL:1999 to SQL:2023 with headline features; SQL-92 as the minimum; DML/DDL/DCL; relational algebra uses sets, SQL uses bags; aggregates, GROUP BY rule, HAVING, ANY_VALUE in SQL:2023.

7. [Planner/Optimizer (PostgreSQL 18 docs, 51.5)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/planner-optimizer.html). See joins #1. One query, many plans, same result.

Extra: [SEQUEL: A Structured English Query Language](https://s3.us.cloud-object-storage.appdomain.cloud/res-files/2705-sequel-1974.pdf), Chamberlin and Boyce, 1974. Opened; scanned, OCR text too garbled to quote reliably. Seen: aimed at non-specialist users, set-oriented table lookups instead of row-at-a-time, equivalent in power to first-order predicate calculus. Not given a note.

#### `joins` (deep)

1. [Planner/Optimizer (PostgreSQL 18 docs, 51.5)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/planner-optimizer.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: the three join strategies (nested loop, merge, hash) and when each is attractive; hash join loads the right relation into a hash table; multi-table queries are a tree of two-input joins; near-exhaustive search of join orders below geqo_threshold, genetic search above; join pairs without a join clause considered last.
2. [Controlling the Planner with Explicit JOIN Clauses (PostgreSQL 18 docs, 14.3)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-joins.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: join orders give the same result but "hugely different execution costs"; orders grow exponentially, exhaustive search impractical beyond about ten tables; outer joins constrain order, only FULL JOIN completely; explicit inner JOIN is the same as a FROM list; join_collapse_limit.
3. [Table Expressions (PostgreSQL 18 docs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html). See sql #4. Join types with the t1/t2 example, ON vs WHERE in outer joins, USING and NATURAL.
4. [Lecture #12: Join Algorithms](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/12-joins.pdf), Andy Pavlo, CMU 15-445/645 Fall 2024 notes. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: joins reconstruct normalized tables; early vs late materialization; I/O cost model; naive, block and index nested loop with costs; sort-merge (good when already sorted or output must be sorted; worst case all keys equal); hash join build/probe, only for equi-joins, Bloom filter; Grace hash join partitions to disk, 3(M+N); comparison table (1.4 hours down to 0.45 s under stated assumptions); "hash joins are almost always better than sort-based" with exceptions.
5. [Hash Join Optimization (MySQL 8.0 Reference Manual)](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/hash-joins.html), Oracle. Docs, primary: yes. Seen (curl with browser headers; plain curl got an error page): hash joins from MySQL 8.0.18; block nested loop removed in 8.0.20; before 8.0.20 needed an equi-join condition; outer, semi and anti joins from 8.0.20; memory capped by join_buffer_size, spills to disk files, can fail on open_files_limit.
6. [Nested Loops (Use The Index, Luke)](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join/nested-loops-join-n1-problem), Markus Winand. Book site, primary: no. Seen: nested loops explained as a driving query plus one query per row; ORMs produce "nested selects", the N+1 problem; a real join does the same index lookups but saves network round trips; eager fetching; good when the driving query returns few rows.

Extra: [Hash Join (Use The Index, Luke)](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join/hash-join-partial-objects), Markus Winand. Opened: no need to index join columns for a hash join, only independent predicates; smaller side goes into the hash table; selecting fewer columns shrinks it. Not given a note; the article keeps to six sources.
Extra: [Sort-Merge Join (Use The Index, Luke)](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join/sort-merge-join). Opened: symmetric, zipper, rarely used unless inputs are already sorted. Not given a note.

#### `normalization` (deep)

1. [A Simple Guide to Five Normal Forms in Relational Database Theory](https://www.bkent.net/Doc/simple5.htm), William Kent, CACM 26(2), 1983. Paper, primary: no (a tutorial, reviewed by Codd and Fagin). Seen: normal forms as record-design guidelines against update anomalies; bias toward assuming non-key fields are updated often, penalizes retrieval, no obligation to fully normalize; 1NF (fixed fields, no repeating groups); 2NF PART/WAREHOUSE/WAREHOUSE-ADDRESS with its four problems; 3NF EMPLOYEE/DEPARTMENT/LOCATION; functional dependencies need unique identifiers (John Smith addresses); 4NF employee/skill/language and the maintenance policies; 5NF agent/company/product; unavoidable and inter-record redundancies; conclusion: performance impact must be assessed. (plain http:// returned an error page; https:// with a browser user agent worked.)
2. [A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks](https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~zives/03f/cis550/codd.pdf). See relational-model #1. Section 1.4 (normalization of nonsimple domains, the first "normal form"), 2.2 (strong redundancy, manager name example), 2.3 (consistency and the cost of checking).
3. [What Goes Around Comes Around](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~yanlei/courses/CS691LL-f06/papers/SH05.pdf). See relational-model #2. Section V: the list of normal forms (2NF, 3NF, BCNF, 4NF, project-join NF) with their original papers, and why normalization theory lost to E-R design in practice.
4. [Description of the database normalization basics](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/office/troubleshoot/access/database-normalization-description), Microsoft (Access troubleshooting docs). Docs, primary: no. Seen: normalization to remove redundancy and inconsistent dependency; 3NF "highest level necessary for most applications"; vendor-code-1/vendor-code-2 repeating fields; customer address in many tables; exception: full 3NF not always practical; student/advisor/class worked example. Claims "Fourth normal form, also called Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)", which conflicts with Stonebraker/Hellerstein and Kent, who list BCNF and 4NF separately.
5. [Lecture #12: Join Algorithms](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/12-joins.pdf). See joins #4. Opening: normalization minimizes repetition, so joins are needed to reconstruct tables.

#### `denormalization` (short)

1. [Materialized Views (PostgreSQL 18 docs, 39.3)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/rules-materializedviews.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: a materialized view persists a query's result like a table, can't be updated directly, refreshed with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW; often much faster to read but "not always current"; sales_summary example refreshed nightly; indexes on the view; file_fdw spell-check example with timings.
2. [What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around...](https://db.cs.cmu.edu/papers/2024/whatgoesaround-sigmodrec2024.pdf). See relational-model #3. Section 2.3: document databases argue denormalized nesting avoids N+1 queries; the three problems with denormalization/prejoining (duplicates when not one-to-many, not necessarily faster, no data independence).

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- How far to normalize. Kent says there's no obligation to fully normalize once performance counts; Microsoft's Access docs call 3NF enough for most applications and full 3NF sometimes impractical; Stonebraker and Hellerstein say normalization theory was "dead in the water" for practitioners and E-R design won. Codd in 1970 only defined what later became first normal form.
- Microsoft's page equates 4NF with BCNF; Kent and Stonebraker/Hellerstein treat them as different forms. The article doesn't define BCNF (no source opened defines it) and doesn't repeat the error.
