- Denormalization for speed: document-database vendors argue nesting is faster; Stonebraker and Pavlo argue prejoins aren't necessarily faster and lose data independence. Codd already noted in 1970 that stored redundancy trades update time and space for query time.
- Sets vs bags: Codd defines relations with distinct rows; SQL tables allow duplicates (CMU notes). SQL also treats NULLs as distinct in UNIQUE but not in DISTINCT, which SQLite's author calls puzzling; engines differ (Informix, MS-SQL).
- Hash join build side: Postgres docs say the right relation is loaded into the hash table; CMU notes build on the outer (left) table. It's naming, not substance: the build side is the smaller input chosen by the planner. The article says "the smaller input".
- Hash vs sort-merge: CMU notes say hash joins are almost always better; Winand says the same but notes merge join's symmetry for full outer joins. MySQL had no hash join at all before 8.0.18.

**Couldn't open:**

- [50 Years of Queries](https://cacm.acm.org/research/50-years-of-queries/), Donald Chamberlin, CACM, 2024: HTTP 403 by curl and WebFetch; ACM DL PDF returned an HTML block page. Would have been the primary source on SQL's design and its NULL regrets.
- Codd, "Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model" (1971/1972): no open copy found; 2NF and 3NF are taken from Kent's tutorial instead.
- DDIA chapter 2 and Date's books: not opened, not cited.

**Rejected:**

- Wikipedia pages on normalization and joins: secondary; Kent and the Postgres docs cover the same ground from better sources.
- The SEQUEL 1974 paper as a cited source: the scanned text is too garbled to quote word for word.

**Gaps:**

- No opened source defines BCNF, so the normalization article only names it.
- No source for when each SQL standard edition shipped beyond the CMU list (SQL:1999 to SQL:2023); no primary ISO source (the standard is paywalled).
- Postgres 15's UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT: not opened here; belongs to `constraints`.
- No measured cost of a join vs a denormalized read; the CMU cost table is a worked example with assumed page counts, not a measurement. A lab run (phase 6 planner experiments: N+1 vs one join) would fill this.

### The model

#### `primary-keys` (short)

1. [RFC 9562: Universally Unique IDentifiers (UUIDs)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9562), K. Davis, B. Peabody, P. Leach, IETF, 2024. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: obsoletes RFC 4122; 2.1 first motivation is "poor database-index locality" of v4, B-tree effects "can be dramatic", lists ULID, Snowflake, KSUID and others as prior art; 5.4 v4 = 122 random bits; 5.7 v7 = 48-bit Unix ms timestamp then 74 random bits, optional sub-ms fraction or counter, SHOULD prefer v7 over v1/v6; 6.2 counters and monotonicity; 6.11 v6/v7 sort as raw bytes, index locality difference "one order of magnitude or more" (no benchmark given); 6.13 store as 128-bit binary not 288-bit text, DB-generated UUIDs give best monotonicity in one database, natural keys that "seem unique and unchanging" later change, advice: time-based surrogate keys; 8 UUIDs must not be security capabilities, use v4 when creation order must not leak. Note: `rfc-9562`.
2. [PostgreSQL documentation, 5.5 Constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen (for this node): primary key = unique + not null, builds a unique B-tree index, one per table, theory says every table needs one but Postgres doesn't enforce it, default target of foreign keys; ON UPDATE CASCADE copies a changed key into referencing rows. Note: `postgres-ddl-constraints`.
3. [PostgreSQL documentation, 5.3 Identity Columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-identity-columns.html), version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: GENERATED ALWAYS / BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY from an implicit sequence, OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE, identity is NOT NULL but not unique on its own (sequence can be reset or bypassed). Note: `postgres-identity-columns`.
4. [PostgreSQL 18 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/18.0/), 2025. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `uuidv7()` added, `uuidv4()` alias; also NOT ENFORCED CHECK/FK, NOT VALID not-null, temporal constraints (WITHOUT OVERLAPS, PERIOD). Note: `postgres-18-release-notes`.
5. [PostgreSQL documentation, 8.12 UUID Type](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-uuid.html) and [9.14 UUID Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-uuid.html), version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: uuid type follows RFC 9562, 128-bit; sequences "only unique within a single database"; gen_random_uuid()/uuidv4(), uuidv7([shift]), uuid_extract_timestamp, uuid_extract_version. Not cited (release notes carry the version fact; kept the short node to four sources).
6. [Don't Do This](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This), PostgreSQL wiki. Wiki, primary: yes-ish (community). Seen: "Don't use serial", use identity columns for new applications; serial only for pre-10 or shared sequences. Not cited (identity docs cover it).
7. [PostgreSQL documentation, 9.17 Sequence Manipulation Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-sequence.html), version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: nextval values are never reclaimed on abort, so sequences have gaps (also from ON CONFLICT); not "gapless". Not cited; worth adding if the node grows.

#### `constraints` (short)

1. [PostgreSQL documentation, 5.5 Constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html), version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: types too coarse; CHECK is a row-level Boolean, passes on NULL, must not read other rows (dump/restore can fail), assumed immutable; NOT NULL tip "majority of columns"; UNIQUE builds a B-tree index, NULLs distinct by default, NULLS NOT DISTINCT, implementation-defined across databases; PK; FK referential integrity, NO ACTION (default, deferrable) / RESTRICT (not deferrable) / CASCADE / SET NULL / SET DEFAULT (with column lists), when to cascade, ON UPDATE, MATCH FULL, referencing side not indexed automatically; EXCLUDE. Note: `postgres-ddl-constraints`.
2. [PostgreSQL documentation, CREATE TABLE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtable.html), version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: DEFERRABLE only for UNIQUE, PK, EXCLUDE, FK; not arbiters for ON CONFLICT; NOT ENFORCED for FK and CHECK, planner may still assume it; WITHOUT OVERLAPS behaves like EXCLUDE USING GIST. Note: `postgres-create-table`.
3. [PostgreSQL documentation, ALTER TABLE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-altertable.html), version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: ADD CONSTRAINT scans the table and locks out updates until commit; NOT VALID (FK, CHECK, not-null) plus VALIDATE CONSTRAINT under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE; CHECK/NOT NULL scan but no rewrite. Note: `postgres-alter-table` (also useful for `ddl-locks`).
4. PostgreSQL 18 release notes, see `primary-keys` #4. Used for when NOT ENFORCED and WITHOUT OVERLAPS arrived.

#### `ctes` (short)

1. [PostgreSQL documentation, 7.8 WITH Queries (Common Table Expressions)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-with.html), version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: CTE as a temporary table for one query; regional_sales / top_regions example; RECURSIVE form and working-table evaluation ("evaluated iteratively"); parts explosion example; SEARCH DEPTH/BREADTH FIRST; CYCLE clause; LIMIT trick not for production; materialization: once per query, no pushdown into multiply-referenced CTEs, folded when non-recursive, side-effect-free and referenced once, MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED, big_table self-join example; data-modifying CTEs run to completion, share one snapshot, RETURNING is the only channel, don't modify a row twice. Note: `postgres-queries-with`.
2. [PostgreSQL 12 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/12.0/), 2019. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: automatic but overridable CTE inlining; before 12 CTEs were never inlined and always evaluated first. Note: `postgres-12-release-notes`.

#### `window-functions` (short)

1. [PostgreSQL documentation, 3.5 Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-window.html), version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: rows keep identity; OVER, PARTITION BY, ORDER BY; empsalary outputs for avg over partition, row_number, sum() OVER () and running sum; default frame (start through last peer, whole partition without ORDER BY); only in SELECT list and ORDER BY because they run after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING; sub-select to filter; WINDOW clause. Note: `postgres-tutorial-window`.
2. [PostgreSQL documentation, 9.22 Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-window.html), version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: table of row_number, rank, dense_rank, percent_rank, cume_dist, ntile, lag, lead, first_value, last_value, nth_value; any ordinary aggregate works with OVER; peers; last_value frame trap; RANGE/ROWS/GROUPS; running-sum default; IGNORE NULLS and FROM LAST not implemented. Note: `postgres-window-functions`.
3. [PostgreSQL documentation, 4.2.8 Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-expressions.html), version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: frame syntax (ROWS/RANGE/GROUPS, offsets, EXCLUDE). Not cited; the article avoids exact frame syntax. Cite it if the node grows a frames section.

#### `data-models` (deep)

1. [What Goes Around Comes Around... And Around...](https://db.cs.cmu.edu/papers/2024/whatgoesaround-sigmodrec2024.pdf), Michael Stonebraker, Andrew Pavlo, SIGMOD Record 53(2), 2024. Paper (survey and argument), primary: no for the systems it covers. Seen: 2.1 MapReduce; 2.2 KV = simplest model, opaque blob, get/set/delete, more predictable performance for less function, bad for multi-field records, KV stores morphing into JSON record stores; 2.3 document model, the two NoSQL marketing messages, the three old problems with pre-joining, almost every NoSQL added SQL by end of 2010s (PartiQL, CQL, AQL, SQL++), many added ACID, SQL standard JSON type in 2016, "schema later"; 2.4 column-family is not columnar, one level of nesting, Cassandra/HBase copied Bigtable's limits; 2.8 property graphs, pointer chasing vs joins, graph as Node/Edge tables, "vanilla" SQL not expressive enough, SQL:2023 SQL/PGQ, DuckDB SQL/PGQ up to 10x a graph DBMS (cited study); 2.9 summary. Note: `stonebraker-pavlo-what-goes-around-2024` (created in parallel by another agent; claims appended).
2. [Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf), DeCandia et al., Amazon, SOSP 2007. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: services needing only primary-key access (carts, sessions, preferences, best sellers); RDBMS "far from ideal", replication chose consistency over availability; query model: blobs by key, no multi-item operations, no relational schema, objects usually under 1 MB. Note: `decandia-dynamo-2007` (phase 11 can reuse it).
3. [Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//archive/bigtable-osdi06.pdf), Chang et al., Google, OSDI 2006. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: not a full relational model; sparse, distributed, persistent, sorted map (row, column, timestamp) to bytes; Webtable and reversed URLs; row-level atomicity; lexicographic row order, tablets; column families declared up front; no cross-row transactions. Note: `chang-bigtable-2006`.
4. [NoSQL design for DynamoDB](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-general-nosql-design.html), AWS DynamoDB Developer Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: RDBMS flexible but "don't scale well in high-traffic situations" (vendor framing); design around the most important queries; don't design until you know the questions; few tables; data shaped as it's queried; keep related data together; use sort order; spread keys to avoid hot spots; GSIs. Note: `aws-dynamodb-nosql-design`.
5. [Best Practices for Data Modeling in MongoDB](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/best-practices/), MongoDB manual 8.3 (current when opened). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: embed vs reference table (has-a, read together, updated together, archived together vs high cardinality, unbounded growth, written at different times, independent child); duplication trade-offs; single-document atomicity; distributed transactions cost more and don't replace schema design. The old embedding-vs-references URL redirects here. Note: `mongodb-data-modeling`.
6. [What is a graph database](https://neo4j.com/docs/getting-started/graph-database/), Neo4j Getting Started. Docs, primary: yes (vendor, marketing tone). Seen: nodes with labels and properties; relationships with start, end, one type, direction, properties; "Graph databases do not use JOINs"; unsourced "millions of connections per second". Note: `neo4j-graph-database-concepts`.
7. [Data Modeling in MongoDB (overview)](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/), MongoDB manual 8.3. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: polymorphic collections, "data that's accessed together should be stored together", relational vs document table. Not cited (#4 and #5 cover it).

#### `jsonb` (short)

1. [PostgreSQL documentation, 8.14 JSON Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html), version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: json keeps text and reparses, jsonb binary, slower in, faster to process, indexable; drops whitespace, key order, duplicate keys; prefer jsonb; numeric mapping and precision warning; JSON null vs SQL NULL; 8.14.2 design advice (fixed-ish structure, co-exist with relational, whole-row lock, atomic datums); containment and top-level-only existence; GIN jsonb_ops vs jsonb_path_ops, expression indexes; subscripting. Note: `postgres-json-types`.
2. [When To Avoid JSONB In A PostgreSQL Schema](https://www.heap.io/blog/when-to-avoid-jsonb-in-a-postgresql-schema), Dan Robinson, Heap, 2016. Blog, primary: no (user of Postgres, not a builder). Seen: jsonb since 9.4; no statistics on fields inside jsonb, hardcoded 0.1% estimate, nested loop, 584 s vs ~300 ms on the author's laptop; enable_nestloop = off in production; 79 MB vs 164 MB; ~30% disk saved by moving 45 fields to columns; jsonb good for many optional values. Old (Postgres 9.x era). Note: `heap-avoid-jsonb-2016`.
3. [PostgreSQL 14 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/14.0/), 2021. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: extended statistics on expressions. Note: `postgres-14-release-notes`.
4. [PostgreSQL documentation, CREATE STATISTICS](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createstatistics.html), version 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: univariate expression statistics "similar to an expression index without the overhead of index maintenance". Not cited (release notes carry the version); cite it if a lab run tests statistics on a jsonb field.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- **Do non-relational models converge on SQL?** Stonebraker and Pavlo (2024) say yes: NoSQL systems added SQL and ACID, the SQL standard added JSON, KV workloads can be matched by relational systems. The DynamoDB guide says relational queries don't scale well under heavy traffic and schema should follow access patterns. Neo4j says joins are expensive and graphs avoid them; the survey cites a study where SQL/PGQ in DuckDB beat a graph database by up to 10x.
- **Embedding.** MongoDB recommends embedding for data read together (fewer joins, single-document atomicity). The survey lists three old problems with pre-joining (duplication for non-one-to-many, not always faster, no data independence).
- **UUIDv7 vs v4.** RFC 9562 prefers time-ordered keys for locality but says to use v4 when creation order must not leak. The "order of magnitude" locality gain is stated without a benchmark.
- **Natural keys.** RFC 9562 advises against name-based natural keys; the Postgres docs are neutral and only require unique + not null.
- **CTE materialization.** Before PostgreSQL 12 every CTE was a fence; since 12 most are inlined. Old advice goes both ways (avoid CTEs for speed, or use them as a deliberate fence).
- **jsonb statistics.** Heap (2016) says the planner has no statistics on jsonb fields; PostgreSQL 14 added expression statistics that might address it. Not tested.

- Nothing: every page listed was opened.

- MongoDB "embedding-vs-references" URL: redirects to the best-practices page (#5), not a separate source.
- Neo4j "millions of connections per second": no setup, not used as a number.
- Citus "Choosing NoSQL: hstore, json or jsonb" (linked from Heap): not opened, not needed.

**Gaps:**
- No measured numbers for UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7 insert cost in Postgres; the lab could run it (phase 6 planner experiments).
- No primary source on natural vs surrogate keys beyond RFC 9562 section 6.13; DDIA and database textbooks not opened.
- No current test of jsonb planner estimates or of expression statistics on jsonb fields; Heap's numbers are from 2016 on the author's laptop.
- Cassandra and HBase docs not opened; wide-column is covered only by Bigtable and the survey.

### Making queries fast

All PostgreSQL manual pages below were read at version 18.6 (the "current" docs).

#### `indexes` (deep)

1. [PostgreSQL docs, 11.1 Introduction (Indexes)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-intro.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `test1` example, full scan without an index vs walking "a few levels deep into a search tree"; book-index analogy; the system keeps the index in sync and the planner decides when to use it; ANALYZE needed for statistics; indexes help UPDATE, DELETE and joins; `indexed-column indexable-operator comparison-value` form; CREATE INDEX blocks writes (not reads) by default, CONCURRENTLY exists with caveats; keeping the index synchronized adds overhead to every write, indexes can prevent HOT, drop unused ones.
2. [PostgreSQL docs, 65.1 B-Tree Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/btree.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: 65.1.4.1 structure: multi-level tree, each level a doubly linked list of pages, metapage, leaf vs internal pages, over 99% of pages are leaves; page splits cascade upwards, a root split adds a level; 65.1.4.2 bottom-up index deletion against version churn from UPDATEs (since PG 14 simple deletion was the only kind before); 65.1.4.3 deduplication into posting lists, on by default.
3. [PostgreSQL docs, 66.7 Heap-Only Tuples (HOT)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/storage-hot.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: MVCC means updates add new row versions and may need new index entries; HOT applies when no indexed column changes (BRIN excepted) and the page has room; then no new index entries; fillfactor raises the odds; pg_stat_all_tables counts HOT updates.
4. [The Search Tree (B-Tree) Makes the Index Fast](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/anatomy/the-tree), Markus Winand, Use The Index, Luke. Book chapter online, primary: no. Seen: leaf nodes in arbitrary disk order, a balanced tree over them; branch entries hold the biggest value of each leaf; traversal; depth grows logarithmically; real indexes with millions of rows have depth four or five, six is rare; hundreds of entries per node; maintenance overhead for writes.
5. [Slow Indexes, Part I](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/anatomy/slow-indexes), Markus Winand. Book chapter online, primary: no. Seen: three steps of an index lookup (tree traversal, following the leaf chain, fetching table rows); only the first is bounded; "degenerated index" myth; a range scan plus one table access per row is why an index lookup can still be slow.
6. [Why Uber Engineering Switched from Postgres to MySQL](https://www.uber.com/blog/postgres-to-mysql-migration/), Evan Klitzke, Uber, 2016. Engineering blog, primary: no (users of Postgres, not builders). The live page returned "Not Acceptable" to curl; read through the Internet Archive copy. Seen: based on Postgres 9.2; write amplification: one update to an indexed column writes the new tuple plus an entry in every index (12 indexes, 12 writes), each also in the WAL, which then inflates replication traffic.

Extra: [Insert](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/dml/insert), Markus Winand. Opened: number of indexes is the dominant factor for insert speed, each index is a multiplier, leaf splits up to the root. Not given a note; the Postgres B-tree page and HOT page cover the write cost with primary sources. Its chart ("a factor of a hundred" for the first index) has no stated setup.
Extra: [The Leaf Nodes](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/anatomy/the-leaf-nodes), Markus Winand. Opened: doubly linked leaf list, logical order independent of physical order, table is an unsorted heap. Covered by #4; no note.

#### `index-types` (short)

1. [PostgreSQL docs, 11.2 Index Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-types.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: B-tree, Hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN, BRIN (plus the bloom extension); B-tree default, operators `< <= = >= >`, BETWEEN, IN, IS NULL, anchored LIKE; hash stores a 32-bit hash code, equality only; GiST/SP-GiST are frameworks, geometric operators, nearest-neighbour ORDER BY `<->`; GIN is an inverted index for multi-part values like arrays; BRIN stores summaries (min/max) per block range, good when values correlate with physical order.
2. [PostgreSQL docs, 65.5 BRIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/brin.html), 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: designed for very large tables with natural correlation to physical location; order-date example; lossy, rows rechecked; very small index; `pages_per_range` trades index size for precision.
3. [PostgreSQL docs, 65.4 GIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/gin.html), 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: 65.4.4.1 updating GIN is slow because one row produces many index inserts; pending list and `fastupdate`; searches must also scan the pending list; 65.4.5 for bulk loads drop and recreate.
4. [PostgreSQL 10 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/10.0/), 2017. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: WAL support for hash indexes, now crash-safe and replicated, old warning removed; hash indexes must be rebuilt after pg_upgrade from earlier versions.

Extra: [PostgreSQL docs, 65.6 Hash Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/hash-index.html). Opened: stores only the 4-byte hash, can be much smaller than a B-tree for long values such as UUIDs and URLs, lossy scans. Not given a note; #1 has the needed facts.

#### `composite-indexes` (short)

1. [PostgreSQL docs, 11.3 Multicolumn Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html), 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `(major, minor)` example; B-tree, GiST, GIN, BRIN support several key columns; up to 32 columns; the exact rule (equality on leading columns plus one inequality on the first column without equality bounds the scan; later columns are checked in the index); skip scan: dynamic equality on a leading column when it has few distinct values; GIN and BRIN don't care about column order; use sparingly, more than three columns rarely helps.
2. [Greater, Less and BETWEEN](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/searching-for-ranges/greater-less-between-tuning-sql-access-filter-predicates), Markus Winand. Book chapter online, primary: no. Seen: date-of-birth plus subsidiary example drawn as leaf pages; column order changes the scanned range; "index for equality first, then for ranges"; debunks "most selective column first".
3. [PostgreSQL 18 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/18.0/), 2025. Docs, primary: yes. Note exists. Seen: skip scan for B-tree added (Peter Geoghegan), usable when early columns have no or non-equality conditions.

Extra: [Concatenated Indexes](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/the-equals-operator/concatenated-keys), Markus Winand. Opened: telephone directory analogy, leftmost prefix rule, reversing the primary key column order instead of adding a second index. Not given a note; #1 and #2 cover it.
Extra: [PostgreSQL docs, 11.5 Combining Multiple Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-bitmap-scans.html). Opened: bitmap AND/OR of separate indexes, when two single-column indexes beat one composite, skip scan makes `(x, y)` usable for `y` if x has at most several hundred distinct values. Not given a note (used for research only).

#### `covering-indexes` (short)

1. [PostgreSQL docs, 11.9 Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-index-only-scans.html), 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: all Postgres indexes are secondary; ordinary index scans touch index and heap, heap access is random; index-only scan needs an index type that stores values (B-tree always, GIN never) and only indexed columns in the query; visibility map check, only a win when many pages are all-visible; INCLUDE payload columns, not part of the key, uniqueness only on key columns; include-column cautions (size limit, bloat, pointless on fast-changing tables); B-tree, GiST, SP-GiST support INCLUDE; suffix truncation; expression and partial index quirks (9.6+).
2. [A Close Look at the Index Include Clause](https://use-the-index-luke.com/blog/2019-04/include-columns-in-btree-indexes), Markus Winand, 2019. Blog, primary: no. Seen: three layers (tree, leaf list, table); rough read counts per layer; index-only scan gains of one or two orders of magnitude when many rows; INCLUDE columns live only in leaf nodes; leaf order ignores them, so no help for sorting or uniqueness; documents intent, safer to extend later; he avoids the term "covering index".

Extra: [Index-Only Scan: Avoiding Table Access](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/clustering/index-only-scan-covering-index), Markus Winand. Opened: SUM(eur_value) example, gains depend on rows read and clustering factor, adding a WHERE column can silently break an index-only scan, Postgres B-tree entry limit 2713 bytes. Not given a note; #1 and #2 cover what the short article needs.

#### `partial-indexes` (short)

1. [PostgreSQL docs, 11.8 Partial Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-partial.html), 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: index over a subset defined by a predicate; excluding common values; unbilled orders example; the query's WHERE must imply the predicate, only simple implications recognised; matching at plan time, so parameterized clauses don't match; partial unique index (one successful test per subject and target); don't replace partitioning with many partial indexes.
2. [Partial Indexes](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/partial-and-filtered-indexes), Markus Winand. Book chapter online, primary: no. Seen: queue table `messages` with `processed = 'N'`; the partial index shrinks in rows and columns; index size can stay flat while the table grows; SQL Server calls them filtered indexes; Oracle and Db2 need emulation.

#### `query-planner` (deep)

1. [PostgreSQL docs, 51.5 Planner/Optimizer](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/planner-optimizer.html), 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: many plans give the same result, pick the one expected to run fastest; paths vs plans; scan plans per relation (seq scan always, index scans where operators match, or for ORDER BY / merge joins); three join strategies; join order search, near-exhaustive below `geqo_threshold`, genetic optimizer above; joins without a join clause considered last.
2. [PostgreSQL docs, 19.7 Query Planning](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-query.html), 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: enable_* switches only discourage; cost constants on an arbitrary scale, only ratios matter; defaults seq_page_cost 1.0, random_page_cost 4.0 (low because most random reads assumed cached), cpu_tuple_cost 0.01, cpu_index_tuple_cost 0.005, cpu_operator_cost 0.0025; effective_cache_size 4GB default, estimate only; geqo_threshold 12; from_collapse_limit 8; plan_cache_mode custom vs generic plans.
3. [PostgreSQL docs, 14.1 Using EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html), 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: plan tree of nodes, top line's total cost is what the planner minimises; cost units; worked cost of a seq scan (345 pages, 10000 rows, 445); filters add cpu_operator_cost; bitmap scan vs index scan choice as selectivity changes; LIMIT changes the plan; nested loop, hash and merge join examples switch as selectivity changes.
4. [Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System](https://courses.cs.duke.edu/compsci516/cps216/spring03/papers/selinger-etal-1979.pdf), Selinger, Astrahan, Chamberlin, Lorie, Price, IBM, SIGMOD 1979. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: System R optimizer; COST = PAGE FETCHES + W * (RSI CALLS); statistics refreshed by UPDATE STATISTICS, not on every write; selectivity factors table (1/ICARD, 1/10 fallback, product of factors); interesting orders; n factorial join orders reduced by building best plans for growing subsets; nested loops and merging scans; costs often wrong in absolute value but the right plan picked in most cases.
5. [How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really?](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol9/p204-leis.pdf), Leis, Gubichev, Mirchev, Boncz, Kemper, Neumann, PVLDB 9(3), 2015. Paper, primary: yes (researchers measuring PostgreSQL and others). Seen: Join Order Benchmark on IMDB, 113 queries; all estimators produce large errors, misestimates by 1000x or more, errors grow with joins, systematic underestimation due to the independence assumption; PostgreSQL 9.4 picks nested loops on tiny cost differences, risky under underestimates; cost model matters far less than cardinality estimates (median error 38%, tuned 30%); exhaustive enumeration beats heuristics.

#### `table-statistics` (short)

1. [PostgreSQL docs, 14.2 Statistics Used by the Planner](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/planner-stats.html), 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: reltuples and relpages in pg_class, updated by VACUUM, ANALYZE, CREATE INDEX, scaled to current size; pg_statistic / pg_stats; MCVs and histogram bounds; default_statistics_target 100; extended statistics (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv) with CREATE STATISTICS; zip/city example; independence assumption.
2. [PostgreSQL docs, 69.1 Row Estimation Examples](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/row-estimation-examples.html), 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: worked selectivity: histogram bucket interpolation for `unique1 < 1000` (1007 rows), MCV lookup for `stringu1 = 'CRAAAA'` (30 rows), non-MCV fallback (15 rows), MCV + histogram combined; ANALYZE samples randomly.
3. [PostgreSQL docs, 24.1 Routine Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/routine-vacuuming.html), 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: 24.1.3 ANALYZE gathers stats, autovacuum runs it when enough rows changed, it doesn't know if the change matters; timestamp-column example of a moving max; partitioned parents and temp tables not analyzed automatically; analyze threshold formula.
4. [PostgreSQL docs, 19.10 Vacuuming (autovacuum parameters)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-vacuum.html), 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: autovacuum_analyze_threshold 50 rows, autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor 0.1 (10% of the table).
5. [PostgreSQL 18 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/18.0/). Note exists. Seen: pg_upgrade keeps optimizer statistics, except extended statistics; functions to set statistics by hand; vacuumdb `--missing-stats-only`.

Extra: [PostgreSQL docs, ANALYZE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-analyze.html). Opened: random sample for large tables, estimates change slightly between runs, target 0 disables stats for a column, the largest target sets the sample size. Not given a note.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- "Covering index": the Postgres manual uses the term for an index built with INCLUDE for index-only scans; Winand avoids it and says what matters is whether a query can run as an index-only scan. The article uses the term the way the Postgres docs do and says the scan is the thing that matters.
- Composite column order: a common rule of thumb is "most selective column first"; Winand shows equality-before-range matters more, and the Postgres manual's exact rule agrees. Skip scan (PostgreSQL 18) softens the leftmost-prefix rule when the leading column has few distinct values.
- Write cost of indexes: Uber's post (Postgres 9.2) says every update writes to every index; the Postgres manual's HOT section says updates that change no indexed column skip new index entries when the page has room. Both are true; Uber's example changes an indexed column.
- Cost model vs estimates: the Postgres manual spends pages on tuning cost constants and warns that changing them from a few experiments is risky; Leis et al. find the cost model matters much less than cardinality errors.

**Couldn't open:**

- uber.com returned "Not Acceptable" to curl; the same article was read via the Internet Archive and cited at its original URL.

**Rejected:**

- Winand's insert chart numbers: no setup stated, so not used.
- Blog posts that repeat the Postgres manual (pganalyze, Crunchy, Cybertec explainers): not opened for citation, the manual is primary.

**Gaps:**

- No source with measured numbers for index write overhead in current Postgres. The indexes article describes the cost without numbers.
- No source opened for MySQL/InnoDB clustered indexes beyond Winand's passing mentions; the articles stay on Postgres.
- The Selinger PDF is a scan-derived text on a course site (Duke); ACM DL not opened.

### Making queries fast + Running Postgres

#### `explain` (deep)

1. [14.1. Using EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, docs for 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. The main source. Seen: a plan is a tree of nodes, scan nodes at the bottom; the four numbers (start-up cost, total cost, rows, width); costs in arbitrary units, conventionally page fetches; `seq_page_cost` 1.0 and `cpu_tuple_cost` 0.01, worked example 345 pages + 10000 rows = 445; upper nodes include children's cost; rows is rows emitted, not scanned; Seq Scan with Filter, Bitmap Index/Heap Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan, Sort, Incremental Sort, Limit, Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join, Materialize, SubPlan, InitPlan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query; actual time in ms, rows and loops are per-loop averages; "Rows Removed by Filter"; "Rows Removed by Index Recheck" for lossy GiST; Index Searches line; BUFFERS implied by ANALYZE; wrap data-changing statements in BEGIN/ROLLBACK; Planning Time vs Execution Time; SERIALIZE; caveats: no network cost, timing overhead, toy tables don't extrapolate, LIMIT and merge join make actual < estimate without an error, BitmapAnd/Or report zero rows.
2. [EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-explain.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, docs for 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. The command reference. Seen: option list (ANALYZE, VERBOSE, COSTS, SETTINGS, GENERIC_PLAN, BUFFERS, SERIALIZE, WAL, TIMING, SUMMARY, MEMORY, FORMAT); BUFFERS meaning of hit, read, dirtied, written; buffer counts of an upper node include children; `TIMING OFF` for row counts without clock overhead; planner picks smallest start-up cost for EXISTS; stale statistics need a manual ANALYZE; EXPLAIN ANALYZE profiling overhead.
3. [F.3. auto_explain](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/auto-explain.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, docs for 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Plans for slow queries in production. Seen: logs plans of statements slower than `auto_explain.log_min_duration` (default -1, off); `log_analyze` times every statement, "extremely negative impact"; `log_timing` off to cut the cost; `sample_rate`; superuser only.
4. [PostgreSQL 18 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/18.0/), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, 2025. Docs, primary: yes. What changed in EXPLAIN. Seen: BUFFERS automatically included in EXPLAIN ANALYZE; index lookups per index scan node reported; fractional row counts; disabled nodes shown; pg_overexplain extension; async I/O subsystem (io_method).
5. [Explaining the unexplainable](https://www.depesz.com/2013/04/16/explaining-the-unexplainable/), Hubert "depesz" Lubaczewski, 2013 (updated 2022). Blog by the author of explain.depesz.com, primary: no. Seen: cost unit is one sequential page fetch, not seconds; start-up vs total cost with a Sort example; plans run top-down, each node pulls rows from its children; Hash must read all its input before returning a row; Limit stops a Seq Scan early; loops times actual time equals total time; a node run 26,000 times at 0.003 ms each; `enable_*` settings are for testing, not production. Output format predates "Execution Time" (shows "Total runtime"), so used for concepts only.
6. [Using EXPLAIN](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Using_EXPLAIN), PostgreSQL wiki. Wiki, primary: no. Seen: list of visualisers (explain.depesz.com, pgMustard, PEV) and old tutorials; stale statistics and small memory defaults as common causes of bad plans. Not used (a link list).

#### `n-plus-one` (short)

1. [Active Record Query Interface, section 16: Eager Loading Associations](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_record_querying.html), Rails core team, Rails guides v8.1.4. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: 10 books and their authors = 1 + 10 = 11 queries; `includes`, `preload` (2 queries with `WHERE authors.id IN (...)`), `eager_load` (1 query with LEFT OUTER JOIN); `strict_loading` raises on lazy loads; `:n_plus_one_only` mode.
2. [Fetch modes](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/db/fetch-modes/), Django project, Django 6.1. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: new in 6.1; FETCH_ONE (default) gives 1+N queries and names it the N+1 problem; FETCH_PEERS batches the missing field for all instances from the same QuerySet into 1 extra query; FETCH_RAISE raises FieldFetchBlocked; mode copied to related objects.
3. [Database access optimization](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/db/optimization/), Django project, Django 6.1. Docs, primary: yes. Used for `orm`, not `n-plus-one`. Seen: query in a loop; FETCH_PEERS, select_related and prefetch_related; callable attributes query every time; templates call callables and hide the difference; profile after every change. (An older version's line about network latency compounding the cost is gone in 6.1.)
4. [QuerySet API reference](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/models/querysets/), Django 6.1. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: select_related uses a JOIN and is limited to single-valued relations; prefetch_related runs one extra query per relation and joins in Python; select_related() with no arguments deprecated in 6.1; QuerySets are lazy and evaluated on iteration, len(), bool(), list(). Also used for `orm`.

#### `orm` (short)

1. [OrmHate](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/OrmHate.html), Martin Fowler, 2012. Blog, primary: no. Seen: the problem is in-memory/relational mapping, hard because it's two-way; complaints: complex, leaky abstraction, naive database interaction; ORMs handle 80-90% of the mapping, the rest needs someone who knows the database; Active Record gives "manholes" down to SQL; read-only access is easier without an ORM (CQRS); rolling your own is worse.
2. See `n-plus-one` #3 (Django database access optimization, used): lazy QuerySets, cached vs callable attributes, `explain()`, `connection.queries`, RawSQL and raw SQL as escape hatches, profile first.
3. See `n-plus-one` #1 (Rails guide): what a Relation does (build SQL, run, instantiate, callbacks); one interface across databases.
4. See `n-plus-one` #4 (QuerySet API reference): when QuerySets hit the database.

#### `full-text-search` (short)

1. [12.1. Introduction](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch-intro.html), PostgreSQL docs 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: LIKE and regex lack stemming, ranking and index support; parse into tokens, normalise into lexemes, drop stop words; tsvector, tsquery, `@@`; `rats` doesn't match `rat` without normalisation; `<->` phrase operator; configurations (parser + dictionaries).
2. [12.2. Tables and Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch-tables.html), PostgreSQL docs 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: search without an index is too slow for most applications; GIN expression index needs the 2-argument to_tsvector; stored generated tsvector column; trade-offs of the two.
3. [12.3. Controlling Text Search](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch-controls.html), PostgreSQL docs 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: ts_rank and ts_rank_cd; weights A-D with defaults {0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 1.0}; setweight for title vs body; normalization flags for length; ranking functions use no global information; ranking reads the tsvector of every match, "can be I/O bound"; websearch_to_tsquery.
4. [12.9. Preferred Index Types for Text Search](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch-indexes.html), PostgreSQL docs 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: GIN preferred, an entry per lexeme with a compressed list of locations; GIN doesn't store weights, so weighted queries recheck; GiST is lossy, a fixed signature (124 bytes default), false matches recheck the row.
5. [12.11. Limitations](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch-limitations.html), PostgreSQL docs 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: lexeme under 2 KB, tsvector under 1 MB, 256 positions per lexeme, positions up to 16,383.

#### `postgres-architecture` (short)

1. [Glossary](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/glossary.html), PostgreSQL docs 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: definitions of postmaster, backend, auxiliary processes (autovacuum launcher, background writer, checkpointer, logger, startup, WAL archiver, receiver, summarizer, writer), background workers, instance, shared memory and shared buffers, dirty page.
2. [51.2. How Connections Are Established](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/connect-estab.html), PostgreSQL docs 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "process per user" model; postmaster spawns a backend per connection; backends talk through semaphores and shared memory; the backend parses, plans, executes.
3. [19.4. Resource Consumption](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html), PostgreSQL docs 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: shared_buffers default typically 128 MB, 25% of RAM as a start, more than 40% unlikely to help because Postgres also relies on the OS cache; work_mem 4 MB per sort or hash operation, many per query; io_method default `worker`, io_workers default 3.
4. [PostgreSQL reconsiders its process-based model](https://lwn.net/Articles/934940/), Jonathan Corbet, LWN, 2023. News, primary: no. Seen: Linnakangas' proposal to move to threads; Freund on cross-process context switches and TLB misses; Tom Lane: "a disaster"; about 2,000 global variables; would take more than one release.
5. [1.2. Architectural Fundamentals](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-arch.html), PostgreSQL docs 18.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: client/server, server forks a new process per connection. Not used (connect-estab says the same in more detail).
6. See `explain` #4 (PostgreSQL 18 release notes): async I/O subsystem, io_method.

#### `sqlite` (short)

1. [Appropriate Uses For SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/whentouse.html), SQLite developers. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "SQLite competes with fopen()"; fits devices, application files, low to medium traffic websites (under 100K hits a day, conservative), caches, per-user database files on a server; one writer at a time, unlimited readers; avoid many clients over a network filesystem (locking bugs, corruption); size limit 281 TB; checklist: network between data and app, many concurrent writers, big data.
2. [SQLite Is Serverless](https://www.sqlite.org/serverless.html), SQLite developers. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: no server process, the application reads and writes the file itself; no setup; downside: a stray pointer in the app can corrupt the database, and no single process to coordinate finer locking; classic vs "neo-serverless".
3. [Write-Ahead Logging](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html), SQLite developers. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: WAL since 3.7.0 (2010); readers don't block writers and vice versa; all processes must be on one host (shared memory), no network filesystems; extra -wal and -shm files; checkpointing.
4. See `sqlite-file-format` (existing note, WAL frame format). Not needed here.

#### `db-connection-pooling` (short)

1. [PgBouncer features](https://www.pgbouncer.org/features.html), PgBouncer authors, 1.26. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: session, transaction and statement pooling; the SQL feature map (SET/RESET, LISTEN, WITH HOLD cursors, PREPARE/DEALLOCATE, PRESERVE ROWS temp tables, LOAD, session advisory locks never work in transaction mode; protocol-level prepared plans need max_prepared_statements); 2 kB per client connection.
2. [PgBouncer configuration](https://www.pgbouncer.org/config.html), PgBouncer authors, 1.26. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: pool_mode default session; default_pool_size 20 per user/database pair; max_client_conn 100; max_prepared_statements default 200, rewrites names to PGBOUNCER_n and re-prepares on whichever server connection the client lands on; "cached plan must not change result type" after DDL, fix with RECONNECT; server_reset_query DISCARD ALL, not used in transaction mode.
3. [PgBouncer changelog](https://www.pgbouncer.org/changelog.html), PgBouncer authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: 1.21.0 added protocol-level prepared statements; 1.24.0 made max_prepared_statements 200 by default. Used for version facts only.
4. [Analyzing the limits of connection scalability in Postgres](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/adforpostgresql/analyzing-the-limits-of-connection-scalability-in-postgres/1757266), Andres Freund, Microsoft, 2020. Blog by a Postgres core developer, primary: yes. Seen: new connection costs TLS, latency and Postgres work; per-connection memory under 2 MiB with huge pages; catalog cache bloat (593 MB after touching 100k tables); work_mem per operation; idle connections slow active ones through GetSnapshotData (one active connection more than 2x slower with thousands idle); cross-process context switches; transaction pooling rules out prepared statements and temp tables; fixes promised for Postgres 14.
5. [Number Of Database Connections](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Number_Of_Database_Connections), PostgreSQL wiki. Wiki, primary: yes (community). Seen: the throughput "knee"; reasons (disk, work_mem RAM, lock contention, context switches, cache lines, O(N^2) structures); (cores × 2) + effective spindles; no built-in pooler by design. Old (9.2 era); already cited through HikariCP in `connection-pooling`. Used lightly.
6. See `connection-pooling` (phase 3): HikariCP pool sizing.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- **Is max_connections itself the problem?** The wiki and most advice say keep connections low. Freund shows that a high max_connections alone costs little; it's many established connections (even idle ones) that slow the rest, through snapshot building. His later work in Postgres 14 targeted that.
- **Pooler inside or outside the server.** The wiki says the community decided against a built-in pooler on purpose. Freund argues a different connection model (few processes serving many connections) is what really fixes the limit, and says it's a huge project. The LWN thread-model debate shows developers split on even the step to threads.
- **ORMs: tool or trap.** Fowler defends them as the lesser evil for two-way mapping and says the last 10-20% needs SQL knowledge; the Django docs are full of ways to see and fix the SQL the ORM writes. Both agree you can't treat the database as hidden.
- **Eager load with a join or with a second query.** Rails' `includes` picks separate queries or a LEFT OUTER JOIN depending on conditions; Django's select_related joins only single-valued relations and prefetch_related uses a second query, because joining a "many" relation multiplies rows.
- **EXPLAIN ANALYZE overhead.** The docs warn timing can slow a query down a lot on machines with slow clock calls; auto_explain with log_analyze times every statement. TIMING OFF keeps row counts.

**Couldn't open:**

- Freund's Microsoft post returned an empty page to WebFetch; its text was read from the JSON embedded in the page downloaded with curl.
- pgMustard blog and glossary pages returned only a shell (89 words); not cited.

**Rejected:**

- PostgreSQL wiki "Using EXPLAIN": a link list, no content to cite.
- 1.2. Architectural Fundamentals: same fact as 51.2 with less detail.

**Gaps:**

- No source with a measured cost of one Postgres connection setup (fork plus authentication) in time. Freund names TLS, latency and Postgres costs in that order but gives no number. Left out.
- No source for how Elasticsearch or other search engines compare to Postgres full-text search (global statistics like BM25, typo tolerance). The article only says what Postgres lacks, from its docs; the comparison belongs to `search-architecture` (phase 17).
- No source for pg_trgm (fuzzy matching); not opened.
- Postgres 14's snapshot scalability fix is only described as planned in Freund's post; its follow-up post wasn't opened.
- Supavisor, Odyssey and PgCat (other poolers) not opened.

### Changing the schema

#### `schema-migrations` (short)

1. [Active Record Migrations](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_record_migrations.html), Rails core team, Rails Guides for Rails 8.1. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: each migration is a new "version" of the database; file names start with a UTC timestamp that sets the order; `schema_migrations` table records every version that ran; don't edit a migration that already ran elsewhere, write a new one; each migration is wrapped in a transaction on databases with transactional DDL, `disable_ddl_transaction!` turns that off; `db/schema.rb` is a snapshot and "the authoritative source for rebuilding", migrations are not; old migrations can fail to replay when they depend on app code; old files can be pruned.
2. [How Flyway works](https://documentation.red-gate.com/fd/how-flyway-works-184127223.html), Redgate, Flyway docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `flyway_schema_history` table created on first run; migrations found on disk or classpath, applied in version order; versions lower than the current one are ignored by default; pending migrations = available but not applied; every change, DDL or DML, is a new migration.

Extra: [Why database migrations](https://documentation.red-gate.com/fd/why-database-migrations-184127574.html), Redgate. Opened: the problem (which scripts ran where, how to build a new database), and three goals (recreate from scratch, know the state, migrate deterministically). Research only, covered by #2.
Extra: [Django migrations](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/topics/migrations/). Downloaded, skimmed; not used (Rails covers the same ground for a short node).

#### `ddl-locks` (short)

1. [Explicit Locking, 13.3](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: eight table lock modes, all table-level despite names; modes differ only by what they conflict with; conflict table 13.2; SELECT takes ACCESS SHARE; INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE take ROW EXCLUSIVE; CREATE INDEX takes SHARE; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, VALIDATE, ANALYZE take SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE; CREATE TRIGGER takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE; many ALTER TABLE forms take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; only ACCESS EXCLUSIVE blocks plain SELECT; locks held to end of transaction; lock waits are indefinite unless a deadlock is found.
2. [ALTER TABLE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-altertable.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: ACCESS EXCLUSIVE unless noted; strictest lock of all subcommands wins; ADD FOREIGN KEY takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on both tables; VALIDATE CONSTRAINT takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE; non-volatile default is stored in metadata, no rewrite; volatile default, stored generated, identity, constrained domain = rewrite; type change usually rewrites table and indexes unless binary coercible; rewrites can need double the disk; DROP COLUMN only hides the column; rewriting forms are not MVCC-safe. Also opened the PostgreSQL 10 and 11 versions of the page (a DEFAULT forced a rewrite until 11) and 17 (NOT VALID only for FK and CHECK until 18).
3. [Client Connection Defaults, 19.11](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: lock_timeout aborts a statement that waits longer than the limit for any lock, applies to each lock attempt separately, 0 (off) by default; statement_timeout likewise off by default.
4. [Zero-downtime Postgres migrations - the hard parts](https://gocardless.com/blog/zero-downtime-postgres-migrations-the-hard-parts/), Chris Sinjakli, GoCardless, Postgres 9.4 era. Engineering blog, primary: yes (their outage). Seen: about 15 s of API downtime from a fast ALTER that waited behind a slow SELECT; lock queue: later lock requests that conflict with the queued ACCESS EXCLUSIVE queue behind it; worked example with three transactions; fixes: no long transactions, log_lock_waits, lock_timeout in migrations; open psql transaction as a cause.

#### `zero-downtime-migrations` (deep)

1. [ParallelChange](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ParallelChange.html), Danilo Sato, martinfowler.com, 2014. Article, primary: yes (names the pattern). Seen: expand, migrate, contract; each phase can be released on its own; database refactorings follow the pattern, the migrate phase is the period both schemas exist; downside: supplier supports two versions, and skipping contract leaves you worse off.
2. [Online migrations at scale](https://stripe.com/blog/online-migrations), Jacqueline Xu, Stripe, 2017. Engineering blog, primary: yes. Seen: four steps (dual write, move reads, move writes, remove old data); ramp dual writes by percentage; lazy copy on update, then backfill from an offline job over snapshots; GitHub Scientist compares old and new reads in production; never more than a few hundred lines of code changed at once; hundreds of millions of Subscriptions objects.
3. [Strong Migrations README](https://github.com/ankane/strong_migrations), Andrew Kane, v2.8.0. Docs/code, primary: yes (tool author). Seen: "dangerous" = blocks reads or writes for more than a few seconds after the lock, or likely app errors; safe recipes for removing a column (ignore it in the ORM first), renaming a column (six steps), backfilling (batch, throttle, outside a transaction), SET NOT NULL via CHECK NOT VALID + VALIDATE; short lock timeout plus long statement timeout for migrations (10 s and 1 h in its example); experimental lock-timeout retries.
4. [ALTER TABLE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-altertable.html). See ddl-locks #2. NOT VALID + VALIDATE, SET NOT NULL skips the scan with a valid CHECK.
5. [CREATE INDEX](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createindex.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: a plain build locks out writes but not reads; CONCURRENTLY does two scans in three transactions, waits for older transactions, can't run inside a transaction block; a failed build leaves an INVALID index that still costs updates; a unique index enforces uniqueness before it's usable.
6. [Zero-downtime Postgres migrations - the hard parts](https://gocardless.com/blog/zero-downtime-postgres-migrations-the-hard-parts/). See ddl-locks #4. The standard rules (don't rename in use, don't rewrite under an exclusive lock, index concurrently) and why they weren't enough.

#### `triggers` (short)

1. [Overview of Trigger Behavior, 37.1](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/trigger-definition.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: BEFORE/AFTER/INSTEAD OF, row vs statement level; trigger function takes no arguments and returns `trigger`; runs in the same transaction as the statement, an error rolls back both; row AFTER triggers fire at end of statement and their events are queued; BEFORE is cheaper when you don't need the final row; BEFORE can return NULL to skip the row; alphabetical order for several triggers; cascading triggers with no depth limit; transition tables for statement-level triggers.
2. [Trigger Functions, 41.10](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/plpgsql-trigger.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: NEW, OLD, TG_OP variables; example 41.4 audit trigger writing every change to `emp_audit`; example 41.7 same with transition tables, "significantly faster" when a statement changes many rows.
3. [Why triggerless?](https://github.com/github/gh-ost/blob/master/doc/why-triggerless.md), gh-ost authors (GitHub). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: MySQL triggers are interpreted stored routines, so each write pays the extra write plus interpretation; triggers compete for locks with the writes that fired them; they can't be paused mid-migration without losing data; GitHub saw near or full lock-downs in production. (MySQL-specific; the Postgres cost has no source here.)

#### `online-schema-change` (deep)

1. [pt-online-schema-change](https://docs.percona.com/percona-toolkit/pt-online-schema-change.html), Percona, Percona Toolkit 3.7.1. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: empty copy, alter it, copy rows in chunks sized to `--chunk-time` (default 0.5 s), triggers mirror writes, atomic RENAME swap, drops the old table; needs a primary key or unique index for the DELETE trigger; won't work if the table already has triggers; foreign keys that point at the table need `rebuild_constraints` or the risky `drop_swap`; pauses on replica lag and load; sets short lock wait timeouts so it loses lock fights; ANALYZE before swap to avoid missing statistics.
2. [Why triggerless?](https://github.com/github/gh-ost/blob/master/doc/why-triggerless.md). See triggers #3.
3. [Triggerless design](https://github.com/github/gh-ost/blob/master/doc/triggerless-design.md), gh-ost authors (GitHub), gh-ost v1.1.11. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: pt-osc is synchronous (three AFTER triggers write to the ghost table in the same transaction); Facebook OSC is asynchronous via a changelog table; gh-ost reads the row-based binlog as a fake replica instead; single writer alternates row copy and binlog apply; true pause; can migrate on a replica; cut-over complicated by the backlog.
4. [Cut-over step](https://github.com/github/gh-ost/blob/master/doc/cut-over.md), gh-ost authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: MySQL won't let a connection RENAME tables it holds locked; Facebook OSC does two renames with a moment when the table doesn't exist; gh-ost uses a two-connection lock + atomic RENAME with a sentry table, and on timeout falls back to the pre-cut-over state and retries.
5. [pgroll concepts](https://github.com/xataio/pgroll/blob/main/docs/concepts.md), Xata, pgroll v0.16.3. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: expand/contract in two commands (start, complete); a Postgres schema of views per version so old and new clients both work; breaking column changes = duplicate column + backfill + triggers both ways; old schema and columns dropped on complete. From the CLI docs: `--lock-timeout` default 500 ms, backfill batch 1000 rows by default; README: Postgres 14 or later.
6. [pg-osc README](https://github.com/shayonj/pg-osc), Shayon Mukherjee, pg-osc v0.9.10. Docs/code, primary: yes. Seen: shadow table + audit table filled by a trigger; copy, build indexes, replay audit rows, swap under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE when about 20 rows are left; ACCESS EXCLUSIVE taken twice; kills competing backends optionally; foreign keys re-added NOT VALID then validated; needs a primary key and enough disk for a second copy; Postgres 9.6+.

Extra: [gh-ost: GitHub's online migration tool for MySQL](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/gh-ost-github-s-online-migration-tool-for-mysql/), Shlomi Noach, GitHub, 2016. Opened: MySQL ALTERs block by default; replica-then-promote costs operations; InnoDB Online DDL serializes on replicas and can't be throttled; pt-osc migrations became "risky operations" at GitHub. Research only; the gh-ost docs cover the claims used.
Extra: [gh-ost README](https://github.com/github/gh-ost). Opened: all tools make a ghost table, alter it empty, copy rows, propagate changes, swap. Research only.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- **Lock for CREATE TRIGGER.** Postgres docs (13.3) say CREATE TRIGGER takes SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE, which lets reads through. pg-osc's README says it takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE to add its trigger. Probably pg-osc locks explicitly, but its README doesn't say why, so the article states only what each source says.
- **Foreign key lock levels have changed.** GoCardless (Postgres 9.4 era) says ADD FOREIGN KEY took ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on both tables. The Postgres 18 docs say SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on both. The lock-queue lesson still holds, because SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE also conflicts with writes.
- **Triggers vs log-based capture.** gh-ost argues triggers are the main risk of online schema change on MySQL; pgroll and pg-osc on Postgres still use triggers. No source here measures trigger cost on Postgres.
- **Lock timeout values.** strong_migrations' example uses 10 s, pgroll's default is 500 ms. Different trade-offs of how long other queries may queue.

**Couldn't open:**

- [PostgreSQL at Scale: Database Schema Changes Without Downtime](https://medium.com/paypal-tech/postgresql-at-scale-database-schema-changes-without-downtime-20d3749ed680), Braintree/PayPal: blocked (Cloudflare challenge with curl, HTTP 403 with WebFetch).
- pgroll.com docs and the introductory blog post: rendered by JavaScript, no text in the HTML. Used the same docs from the GitHub repo instead.
- Flyway "Migrations" concept page: 404 at the URL tried.

**Rejected:**

- Django migrations docs: fine, but one framework is enough for a short node.
- Facebook OSC note (facebook.com): not opened; its design is described in gh-ost's docs, which are cited instead.

**Gaps:**

- No source with numbers for trigger overhead on Postgres. The article says there's a cost and why, without a number.
- No primary source on MySQL's own Online DDL (INSTANT/INPLACE); only gh-ost's blog view of it.
- The lock queue itself is not described in the Postgres manual; the source is GoCardless's incident write-up.

## Phase 7: Databases II, storage engines

Researched by 4 parallel passes, one per group below.

### Pages and trees

#### `storage-engine` (short)

1. [Lecture #03: Database Storage (Part I)](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/03-storage1.pdf), Andy Pavlo, Carnegie Mellon University, 2024. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: disk-oriented architecture (pages on disk, buffer pool, execution engine gets pointers); DBMS vs OS and why mmap is a bad idea for writes; the OS doesn't know file contents; some systems use many files, SQLite one; page ids mapped to file and offset; fixed-size pages; hardware 4 KB vs OS 4 KB vs database 1-16 KB pages and torn pages; heap files (linked list vs page directory); page header fields; slotted pages; tuple header and record ids. Note: `cmu-15445-storage1`.
2. [Lecture #04: Database Storage (Part II)](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/04-storage2.pdf), Andy Pavlo, Carnegie Mellon University, 2024. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: problems of slotted pages updated in place (fragmentation, whole-block I/O, random I/O); log-structured storage (memtable, sorted immutable SSTables, newest-to-oldest reads, compaction, write amplification); index-organized storage; overflow pages; data representation; catalogs. Note: `cmu-15445-storage2`.
3. [Alternative Storage Engines](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/storage-engines.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: storage engines handle SQL operations for table types; pluggable, loadable into a running server; InnoDB default and recommended; InnoDB stores data in clustered indexes; MyISAM table-level locking; MEMORY engine formerly HEAP. Note: `mysql-storage-engines`.
4. [Table Access Method Interface Definition](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tableam.html), PostgreSQL documentation, version 18. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: table access methods as Postgres's pluggable storage interface (TableAmRoutine callbacks, pg_am); new AMs need TIDs of block number plus item number to support indexes; heap is the reference implementation. Not used (the version that added it isn't on the page; MySQL shows pluggable engines more plainly).

#### `database-pages` (short)

1. [Database Page Layout](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/storage-page-layout.html), PostgreSQL documentation, version 18 (section 66.6). Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: every table and index an array of fixed-size pages, usually 8 kB, chosen at compile time; five parts (24-byte header, 4-byte item identifiers, free space, items from the end, special space); header fields pd_lsn, pd_checksum, pd_lower, pd_upper, pd_special, pd_prune_xid; item identifiers never move so CTID = page + item index stays valid while rows are compacted; B-tree sibling links in special space; heap row header 23 bytes, xmin/xmax/ctid, null bitmap; decoding needs pg_attribute. Note: `postgres-page-layout`.
2. [Lecture #03: Database Storage (Part I)](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/03-storage1.pdf): see `storage-engine` #1. Seen: the general slotted page and the three meanings of "page".
3. [Database File Format](https://www.sqlite.org/fileformat2.html), SQLite developers. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: sections 1.2 and 1.6: page size a power of two 512-65536; b-tree page regions (header 8 or 12 bytes, cell pointer array of 2-byte offsets in key order, unallocated space, cell content packed toward the end, reserved region); freeblocks and fragments; overflow pages. Note: `sqlite-file-format` (appended).
4. [Database File Layout](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/storage-file-layout.html), PostgreSQL documentation, version 18. Seen: one file per table/index, 1 GB segments, free space map and visibility map forks. Not used in the end (a note was started and removed as uncited).

#### `b-plus-tree` (deep)

1. [The Ubiquitous B-Tree](http://carlosproal.com/ir/papers/p121-comer.pdf), Douglas Comer, ACM Computing Surveys 11(2), 1979. Survey paper, primary: no. Seen: B-tree the de facto standard for database indexes; cost = number of secondary storage accesses; Bayer and McCreight at Boeing; "B" never explained; order d nodes at least half full; balancing; height bound; plain B-tree bad at sequential "next"; B+-tree: keys only in leaves, leaves linked (sequence set), copy of key promoted on leaf split, index unchanged on delete while leaf half full; "B*-tree" misused. Read from a personal-site copy; the ACM DL refused the download. Note: `comer-ubiquitous-btree-1979`.
2. [Lecture #08: Indexes & Filters I](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/08-indexes1.pdf), Andy Pavlo, Carnegie Mellon University, 2024. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: B+tree definition and invariants; B-tree vs B+tree; B-link sibling pointers; insert (copy up vs push up), delete (redistribute, merge); clustered indexes; node size; merge threshold and thrashing; variable-length keys; intra-node search; prefix compression, dedup, suffix truncation, pointer swizzling, bulk load, B-epsilon trees. Note: `cmu-15445-indexes1`.
3. [Lecture #10: Index Concurrency Control](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/10-indexconcurrency.pdf), Andy Pavlo, Carnegie Mellon University, 2024. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: locks vs latches; latch implementations; latch crabbing, "safe" nodes, optimistic variant; leaf scans and no-wait. Note: `cmu-15445-index-concurrency`.
4. [Efficient Locking for Concurrent Operations on B-Trees](https://www.csd.uoc.gr/~hy460/pdf/p650-lehman.pdf), Philip Lehman and S. Bing Yao, ACM TODS 6(4), 1981. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: abstract (one link pointer, no read locks, constant number of locks per updater), introduction, storage model (fixed-size pages). Read from a course copy of the ACM PDF. Note: `lehman-yao-blink-1981`.
5. [src/backend/access/nbtree/README](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/REL_18_STABLE/src/backend/access/nbtree/README), PostgreSQL developers, REL_18_STABLE. Source code docs, primary: yes. Seen: L&Y right-links and high keys, moving right; heap TID as tiebreaker; page-level read locks because buffers are shared; left links for backward scans; root split; split by bytes; page deletion only of empty pages, never merges (and why); rightmost-leaf fastpath; WAL logging of splits in two records and missing downlinks fixed on later inserts; suffix truncation from Bayer and Unterauer (1977); dedup. Compared with master: only a few lines differ. Note: `postgres-nbtree-readme`.
6. [B-Tree Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/btree.html), PostgreSQL documentation, version 18. Official docs, primary: yes. Existing note `postgres-btree` (unchanged): leaf vs internal pages, over 99% leaves, splits cascade, bottom-up deletion since 14, dedup on by default.
7. [The Physical Structure of an InnoDB Index](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-physical-structure.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: B-trees except spatial (R-trees); 16KB default page; 1/16 left free; pages about 15/16 full on sequential inserts, 1/2 to 15/16 on random; innodb_fill_factor for sorted builds; MERGE_THRESHOLD 50% default. Note: `mysql-innodb-physical-structure`.
8. [CREATE INDEX](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createindex.html), PostgreSQL documentation, version 18. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: B-tree fillfactor default 90, range 10-100, 50-90 smooths splits. Note: `postgres-create-index` (appended).
9. [The Search Tree (B-Tree) Makes the Index Fast](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/anatomy/the-tree), Markus Winand. Book chapter (free web), primary: no. Existing note `winand-search-tree` (unchanged): depth 4-5 for millions of rows, hundreds of entries per node.
10. [Clustered Indexes and the WITHOUT ROWID Optimization](https://www.sqlite.org/withoutrowid.html): see `heap-files` #2. Seen (for this node): rowid tables are leaves-only "B*-trees", WITHOUT ROWID tables keep content in inner nodes, which lowers fan-out.

#### `heap-files` (short)

1. [Clustered and Secondary Indexes](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-index-types.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: clustered index stores the rows, normally the primary key; fallback to first NOT NULL unique index, then hidden 6-byte monotonically increasing row id; clustered access saves I/O; secondary index records hold the primary key; long primary keys bloat secondaries. dev.mysql.com returns an error page to browser user agents; curl's default got the page. Note: `mysql-innodb-index-types`.
2. [Clustered Indexes and the WITHOUT ROWID Optimization](https://www.sqlite.org/withoutrowid.html), SQLite developers. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: ordinary tables keyed by rowid, INTEGER PRIMARY KEY aliases rowid, other primary keys are separate unique indexes (text stored twice, two searches); WITHOUT ROWID is a clustered index (about half the space, nearly twice as fast in their example); rule of thumb rows under 1/20 of a page. Note: `sqlite-without-rowid`.
3. [Database Page Layout](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/storage-page-layout.html): see `database-pages` #1. Seen (for this node): any row on any page; CTID.
4. [Heap-Only Tuples (HOT)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/storage-hot.html), PostgreSQL documentation, version 18. Existing note `postgres-hot` (unchanged): updates can need new index entries; HOT when no indexed column changes and the page has room.
5. [Why Uber Engineering Switched from Postgres to MySQL](https://www.uber.com/blog/postgres-to-mysql-migration/), Evan Klitzke, 2016. Existing note `uber-postgres-to-mysql-2016`. Not cited here; the HOT docs carry the mechanism. Belongs to `amplification`.

#### `buffer-pool` (deep)

1. [Lecture #06: Buffer Pools](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/06-bufferpool.pdf), Andy Pavlo, Carnegie Mellon University, 2024. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: frames, page table vs page directory, pin counts and dirty flags, write-back cache, locks vs latches, four reasons not to use mmap, what the DBMS does better, LRU cost, CLOCK, sequential flooding, LRU-K, two-list LRU-2 approximation, dirty-page fast/slow path, background writing, I/O priorities, most DBMS use O_DIRECT and Postgres uses the page cache, multiple pools, prefetching, scan sharing, bypass. Note: `cmu-15445-buffer-pool`.
2. [src/backend/storage/buffer/README](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/REL_18_STABLE/src/backend/storage/buffer/README), PostgreSQL developers, REL_18_STABLE. Source code docs, primary: yes. Seen: pins vs content locks and the access rules; BufMappingLock, partitions since 8.2, single BufMgrLock before 8.1; free list plus clock sweep with usage counts; ring buffers (256KB seq scan, VACUUM via vacuum_buffer_usage_limit, 16MB bulk writes capped at 1/8 of shared_buffers); WAL flush before reusing a dirtied ring buffer; background writer. Master (19 development) removes the free list and adds a share-exclusive lock mode. Note: `postgres-buffer-manager-readme`.
3. [The LRU-K Page Replacement Algorithm For Database Disk Buffering](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~natassa/courses/15-721/papers/p297-o_neil.pdf), Elizabeth O'Neil, Patrick O'Neil, Gerhard Weikum, SIGMOD 1993. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: abstract; 1.1 LRU uses only the last reference; example 1.1 (B-tree leaf pages vs record pages, LRU keeps about half of each); example 1.2 (sequential scans swamp the cache). Text layer has OCR errors; quotes limited to clean sentences. Note: `oneil-lru-k-1993`.
4. [Buffer Pool](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-buffer-pool.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: up to 80% of memory on dedicated servers; linked list of pages; midpoint insertion LRU; 3/8 old sublist; read-ahead pages; scans can still evict hot pages. Note: `mysql-innodb-buffer-pool`.
5. [Making the Buffer Pool Scan Resistant](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-performance-midpoint_insertion.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: innodb_old_blocks_pct default 37 (3/8), range 5-95; innodb_old_blocks_time default 1000 ms; benchmark before changing. Note: `mysql-innodb-midpoint-insertion`.
6. [InnoDB Startup Options and System Variables](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-parameters.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: innodb_flush_method default O_DIRECT on Unix where supported, still fsyncs; O_DIRECT_NO_FSYNC data-loss warning. Note: `mysql-innodb-parameters`.
7. [Resource Consumption](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html), PostgreSQL documentation, version 18. Existing note `postgres-runtime-config-resource` (unchanged): shared_buffers 128MB default, 25% starting point, over 40% unlikely to help, io_method.
8. [PostgreSQL 18 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/18.0/). Existing note `postgres-18-release-notes` (unchanged): the asynchronous I/O subsystem.
9. [Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your Database Management System?](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2022/papers/p13-crotty.pdf), Crotty, Leis, Pavlo, CIDR 2022. Existing note `crotty-mmap-cidr-2022` (unchanged).
10. [Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your DBMS?](https://www.symas.com/post/are-you-sure-you-want-to-use-mmap-in-your-dbms), Howard Chu. Existing note `chu-mmap-response` (unchanged).

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- **Merge or not.** The textbook B+tree (CMU, Comer) keeps every node at least half full and merges on underflow. InnoDB merges below a 50% threshold. Postgres never merges partly full pages, only deletes empty ones, because moving items could make an opposite-direction scan miss them. CMU notes eager merging can thrash.
- **Crabbing vs B-link.** CMU teaches latch crabbing with an optimistic variant; Postgres uses Lehman and Yao right-links and high keys, and still takes short page read locks because its buffers are shared (L&Y assumed private copies).
- **Trust the OS page cache or not.** CMU ("the OS is not your friend") and Crotty et al. say the DBMS should manage its own memory; most engines use O_DIRECT (InnoDB's default on Unix). Postgres deliberately uses the page cache as a second level and keeps shared_buffers at about 25% of RAM; InnoDB often gets up to 80%. Chu argues the OS sees whole-machine memory pressure and a read-only mmap avoids most of the problems.
- **Naming.** "B-tree", "B+tree" and "B*-tree" are used loosely: Postgres calls its B+tree a B-tree, SQLite calls its leaves-only tables B*-trees, and Comer (1979) already called "B*-tree" the most misused term.
- **Eviction.** CLOCK (Postgres clock sweep with usage counts), two-list LRU with midpoint insertion (InnoDB), LRU-K (paper): three answers to the same scan and frequency problems.

**Couldn't open:**
- ACM Digital Library PDFs for Comer (1979), Lehman and Yao (1981) and O'Neil et al. (1993): 403 to curl. Used mirror copies on a personal site and university course pages instead; URLs recorded in the notes.
- dev.mysql.com returned a "Technical Difficulties" page to a browser user agent; curl's default user agent got the real pages.
- CMU 15-445 Fall 2024 "08-trees.pdf" doesn't exist (empty); the B+tree lecture is `08-indexes1.pdf`.

**Rejected:**
- Bayer and McCreight's 1972 paper (a copy was downloaded from infolab.usc.edu but not read closely); Comer covers the original B-tree for the article's level.
- Postgres table access method chapter (see `storage-engine` #4).
- Postgres TOAST docs (read: 2 kB threshold); overflow belongs in `database-pages` only briefly, and SQLite's overflow pages covered it with a source already in use.
- Postgres master-branch READMEs as the cited version: they describe unreleased (19 development) behavior. Used REL_18_STABLE.

**Gaps:**
- No measured numbers from this project (lab on hold): no page fill, split rates, buffer hit rates or eviction comparisons. The fanout example in `b-plus-tree` is a labelled hypothetical (100 keys per page).
- No primary source opened for RocksDB or another LSM engine; `storage-engine` names the LSM family only through the phase's own `lsm-tree` node.
- Graefe's "Modern B-Tree Techniques" not opened; it would be the best single source on production B-tree tricks.
- No source on 2Q, ARC or other eviction policies beyond LRU-K, CLOCK and InnoDB's two lists; left to phase 9's `eviction-policies`.
- No source opened on Postgres's `CLUSTER` command or on other databases' use of "clustered" for sorted heaps, so `heap-files` doesn't discuss it.
- Postgres TOAST (out-of-line storage of big values) isn't covered by any node.

### Logging and recovery

#### `write-ahead-log` (deep)

1. [Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-intro.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18 (read as 18.6). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: 28.3 the rule (data files change only after WAL records are flushed); no data-page flush per commit; roll-forward "REDO"; only the WAL is flushed at commit, sequential so cheaper; one fsync can commit many small transactions; PITR by replaying archived WAL onto a base backup; journaled filesystems not needed for data files.
