2. [WAL Internals](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-internals.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: LSN is a monotonically increasing byte offset, used to measure replication and recovery progress; pg_wal, 16 MB segments, 8 kB pages, record headers in access/xlogrecord.h; segment names from 000000010000000000000001; WAL on a separate disk is advantageous; drives that falsely report writes subvert the WAL; recovery reads pg_control, then the checkpoint record, then redoes forward; full page images make pages changed since the checkpoint consistent; pg_control is less than one page so not subject to partial writes.
3. [Asynchronous Commit](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-async-commit.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: synchronous commit waits for WAL flush; the flush dominates short transactions; async commit risks data loss not corruption; replay in commit order; per-transaction choice; risk window three times wal_writer_delay; DROP TABLE and PREPARE TRANSACTION always synchronous; fsync = off can corrupt; commit_delay is a synchronous method.
4. [ARIES](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs345d-01/rl/aries.pdf), C. Mohan, D. Haderle, B. Lindsay, H. Pirahesh, P. Schwarz, IBM, ACM TODS 17(1), 1992. Paper, primary: yes. Seen (scanned PDF, text layer): 1.1 WAL protocol, in-place updates vs shadow paging, page LSN in every page, commit forces the log to the commit record's LSN, LSNs are log addresses, log as ever-growing sequential file, CLRs redo-only; 1.4 steal/force definitions and what each implies for undo/redo; 2 why steal is still desirable; 3 overview of the three passes; 4.2 page_LSN; 5.4 fuzzy checkpoints, master record, no pages forced at checkpoint; 6 restart processing; 10.1 why selective redo and undo-before-redo break with WAL and record locking, figures 15 and 16.
5. [Lecture #20: Database Logging](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/20-logging.pdf), Andy Pavlo, CMU 15-445, 2024. Lecture notes, primary: no. Seen: undo and redo; steal/force and NO-STEAL+FORCE limits; shadow paging; SQLite's pre-2010 journal; WAL as STEAL+NO-FORCE and why almost every DBMS uses it; commit rule; record contents (txn id, object id, before/after values, checksum); group commit; physical, logical, physiological logging; CDC from the log; blocking checkpoints.
6. [WAL Performance](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/WAL-Performance), RocksDB team (Meta). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: sync = false is the default and isn't crash safe; manual_wal_flush; SyncWAL; sync = true fsyncs before returning; group commit (one WAL write, one fsync, 1 MB cap, no deliberate delay); two I/Os per fsync on a new file; recycle_log_file_num; 40-byte write amplified to 8 KB (about 200x).

Extra: [Redo Log](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-redo-log.html), MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual 17.6.5. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: redo encodes changes by records affected; ever-increasing LSN; innodb_redo_log_capacity; 32 redo files in #innodb_redo; checkpoint LSN stored in the file header, recovery starts at the latest checkpoint LSN; ALTER INSTANCE DISABLE INNODB REDO_LOG for bulk loads only. Not given a note; Postgres covers the article.
Extra: [Database Page Layout](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/storage-page-layout.html), PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: pd_lsn (8 bytes), "next byte after last byte of WAL record for last change to this page". Not given a note; a good concrete page-LSN example if `database-pages` wants it.

#### `group-commit` (short)

1. [WAL Configuration](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-configuration.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: XLogInsertRecord and XLogFlush; group commit leader sleeps commit_delay inside XLogFlush while followers queue; commit_siblings guard; start commit_delay at half of pg_test_fsync's single 8 kB flush; too high hurts throughput; with commit_delay = 0 groups form from commits arriving during the previous flush; "gangway effect" at higher client counts; only helps with concurrent commits and a commit-rate bottleneck.
2. [WAL Performance](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/WAL-Performance). See write-ahead-log #6.

Extra: [Write Ahead Log settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html). See full-page-writes #1. commit_delay default 0, commit_siblings default 5, and the PostgreSQL 9.3 change (leader waits, followers wait only for the leader's flush).

#### `checkpoints` (short)

1. [WAL Configuration](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-configuration.html). See group-commit #1. Seen: checkpoint definition, dirty pages flushed and a checkpoint record written, redo record, old segments recycled or removed; significant I/O load; checkpoint_timeout 5 min and max_wal_size 1 GB defaults; skipped if no WAL; CHECKPOINT command; frequency trade-off; full-page-write cost after each checkpoint; checkpoint_warning; checkpoint_completion_target 0.9 spreads writes, longer checkpoints keep more WAL; checkpoint_flush_after and the end-of-checkpoint fsync stall; restartpoints on standbys.
2. [Lecture #21: Database Crash Recovery](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/21-recovery.pdf), Andy Pavlo, CMU 15-445, 2024. Lecture notes, primary: no. Seen: non-fuzzy checkpoints, "slightly better" blocking checkpoints, fuzzy checkpoints with CHECKPOINT-BEGIN/END, ATT and DPT, recLSN, MasterRecord.

Extra: [InnoDB Checkpoints](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-checkpoints.html), MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual 17.11.3. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: InnoDB uses fuzzy checkpointing, flushing modified pages in small batches; recovery scans forward from the checkpoint label; large log files may reduce checkpoint I/O. Not given a note; two sources were enough for a short node.

#### `full-page-writes` (short)

1. [Write Ahead Log settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: full_page_writes (why, once per checkpoint, risks of turning off, default on); wal_log_hints; wal_compression (pglz, lz4, zstd, default off); synchronous_commit modes; fsync; wal_writer_delay 200 ms; commit_delay, commit_siblings; checkpoint settings and defaults.
2. [Reliability](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-reliability.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: caching layers and write-back caches; many SSDs don't honour flushes by default; 512-byte sectors, Postgres writes 8192 bytes (16 sectors); full page images repair partial writes; ZFS can turn them off; BBU doesn't help unless full 8 kB pages; CRC-32C on every WAL record; FPIs always checksummed.
3. [Doublewrite Buffer](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-doublewrite-buffer.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual 17.6.4. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: pages flushed from the buffer pool go to doublewrite files first; good copy used in recovery; not twice the I/O ops (one sequential chunk, one fsync); ON, DETECT_AND_RECOVER, DETECT_ONLY, OFF; auto-disabled on Fusion-io atomic writes; file layout (flush list and LRU files, #ib_16384_0.dblwr); encryption and compression. Only opened with a browser user agent (plain curl gets an error page).

Extra: [Atomic writes without tears](https://lwn.net/Articles/974578/), Jake Edge, LWN, 2024. Note already exists (`lwn-atomic-writes-without-tears`, from phase 1). Not cited here; the torn-writes node carries it.

#### `crash-recovery` (deep)

1. [ARIES](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs345d-01/rl/aries.pdf). See write-ahead-log #4. Sections 3, 5.4, 6 and 10.1 used.
2. [Lecture #21: Database Crash Recovery](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/21-recovery.pdf). See checkpoints #2. Seen: ARIES origin; pageLSN, flushedLSN, recLSN, lastLSN, MasterRecord; commit and TXN-END; abort with prevLSN, CLRs, undoNextLSN; analysis, redo (skip rules), undo (largest lastLSN first, CLRs); crash during recovery; figure 4.
3. [WAL Internals](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-internals.html). See write-ahead-log #2.
4. [InnoDB Recovery](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-recovery.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual 17.18.2. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: PITR from the binary log; recovery from corruption needs a backup; crash recovery steps (tablespace discovery, redo before connections, rollback of incomplete transactions in a background thread, change buffer merge, purge); rollback can take 3-4x the transaction's run time; lock conflicts with recovered transactions; don't delete redo logs.
5. [Atomic Commit In SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/atomiccommit.html), SQLite developers. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: hardware assumptions (sector writes not atomic, linear, fsync works, deletion atomic, powersafe overwrite since 3.7.9); rollback journal steps 3.1-3.12; commit = journal deletion; hot journals and rollback 4.1-4.6; super-journal for multi-file commits; things that go wrong. Parts describe 3.5.0-era behaviour.
6. [Write Ahead Log (WAL)](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/Write-Ahead-Log-%28WAL%29), RocksDB team (Meta). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: every write goes to memtable and WAL; WAL rebuilds the memtable; default "process crash consistency"; one WAL for all column families; WAL deleted once all column families flushed past it; max_total_wal_size; disableWAL.

Extra: [WAL Recovery Modes](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/WAL-Recovery-Modes). Note already exists (phase 1). Referenced through `append-only-log`, not cited again.
Extra: [Basic Operations](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/Basic-Operations), RocksDB wiki. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: writes async by default; a process crash alone loses nothing with sync = false, a machine crash can lose the last few updates; fdatasync by default, use_fsync option. Not given a note.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- SQLite's default: CMU's logging notes say SQLite used a rollback journal "prior to 2010" and then switched to a WAL; SQLite's own docs (`sqlite-wal`, `sqlite-atomic-commit`) say the rollback journal is still the default and WAL is an option since 3.7.0. The article follows SQLite's docs.
- "Flushing the WAL": RocksDB's WAL overview says the default "flushes the WAL after every user write" for process crash consistency, while WAL Performance says the default doesn't sync and isn't crash safe. Both are true (flush to the OS, not fsync); the write-ahead-log article calls this out.
- Checkpoint pacing: Postgres writes every dirty page at a checkpoint (spread over the interval), while ARIES forces no pages at checkpoint time and relies on background writing. Mentioned in checkpoints only as blocking vs fuzzy; the ARIES detail stayed out of the short node.
- Selective redo: System R redid only committed work; ARIES (10.1) argues this is wrong with WAL and record locking. Explained in crash-recovery.

**Couldn't open:**

- `https://cs.stanford.edu/people/chr101/cs345/aries.pdf` (404). Used the Stanford course copy and a Berkeley copy (`people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~brewer/cs262/Aries.pdf`) instead; both are scans with an OCR text layer, so quotes were checked against the text and OCR slips corrected.
- MySQL manual pages return an error page to plain curl; opened with a browser user agent. Not a real failure.
- `https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/19-logging.pdf` and `20-recovery.pdf` (404; the lecture numbers are 20 and 21 this year).

**Rejected:**

- DDIA and Database Internals chapters on the WAL: not opened, so not cited.
- MySQL InnoDB Checkpoints and Redo Log pages as article sources: redundant with Postgres and CMU for the short nodes.
- Blog explainers on ARIES: the paper and CMU notes cover it from the source.

**Gaps:**

- No source opened says why InnoDB's redo log can't repair a torn page on its own (the reason it needs the doublewrite buffer). The article only states what the doublewrite buffer does.
- No source opened states that Postgres needs no undo pass because of MVCC. Left out of crash-recovery.
- No measured cost of full-page writes or the doublewrite buffer. The LWN note has a spoken "60-100%" figure for MySQL; not used.
- No numbers for group commit gains; nothing measured on this machine (lab on hold).

### Log-structured engines

#### `log-structured-hash-table` (short)

1. [Bitcask: A Log-Structured Hash Table for Fast Key/Value Data](https://riak.com/assets/bitcask-intro.pdf), Justin Sheehy, David Smith, Basho, 2010. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: six pages; origin in Riak's pluggable backends and Eric Brewer's "hash table log merging" insight vs LSM trees; one writer process per directory; one active file, closed at a size threshold and never reopened for writing; entry layout crc, tstamp, ksz, value_sz, key, value (figure p. 2); deletes are tombstones removed at the next merge; keydir hash table maps key to file_id, value_sz, value_pos, tstamp; a get is one lookup and at most one seek, OS read-ahead helps; merge rewrites live values of immutable files and writes hint files (key, position, size); startup scans data files or hint files to rebuild the keydir; data files are the commit log, recovery needs no replay; keydir must fit in RAM; no compression; API with sync-on-put option; early numbers only (5000-6000 writes/s on a laptop).
2. [Bitcask (Riak KV 2.2.3 docs)](https://docs.riak.com/riak/kv/2.2.3/setup/planning/backend/bitcask/index.html), Basho, Riak KV 2.2.3. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: the "latest" URL serves 2.2.3; strengths list (one seek per read, fast bounded crash recovery checking the last record or two by CRC, easy backup); weakness: all keys in memory; default backend of Riak; sync strategies none (default), o_sync, interval; merge policy and merge windows; merge triggers fragmentation (default 60% dead keys) and dead bytes (default 512 MB); thresholds for which files join a merge; deletes are a tombstone plus removal from the keydir; hint files with optional CRC; object expiry.

#### `skip-list` (short)

1. [Skip Lists: A Probabilistic Alternative to Balanced Trees](https://15721.courses.cs.cmu.edu/spring2018/papers/08-oltpindexes1/pugh-skiplists-cacm1990.pdf), William Pugh, CACM, 1990 (copy hosted by CMU 15-721). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: probabilistic balancing vs balanced trees; bad worst case but no input triggers it reliably (250 elements, 3x expected time, under one in a million); 1⅓ pointers per element; figure 1 building from every-2nd to every-2^i-th pointers to random levels; search, insert (update vector, splice) and delete algorithms (figures 2-4); randomLevel with p and MaxLevel (figure 5); MaxLevel 16 for 2^16 elements at p = 1/2; analysis; choosing p: 1/4 recommended unless variability matters; adversary who sees levels can force the worst case; concurrent version simpler than for balanced trees.
2. [leveldb db/skiplist.h](https://github.com/google/leveldb/blob/main/db/skiplist.h), LevelDB authors, code. Code, primary: yes. Seen: writes need an outside mutex, reads lock-free; nodes never deleted while the list lives; nodes published with release stores; no duplicate inserts; kMaxHeight 12; kBranching 4. Also opened db/memtable.h, which declares the memtable table as this SkipList.
3. [MemTable (RocksDB wiki)](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/MemTable), RocksDB team. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: memtable role, read before SST files; options (write_buffer_size 64 MB default, max_write_buffer_number 2); skip list default; HashSkipList, HashLinkList, Vector and their costs (prefix-crossing scans need copy and sort); flush triggers; concurrent insert on by default, skip list only; comparison table with ~1.33 pointers per entry.

#### `lsm-tree` (deep)

1. [The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree)](https://www.cs.umb.edu/~poneil/lsmtree.pdf), Patrick O'Neil, Edward Cheng, Dieter Gawlick, Elizabeth O'Neil, Acta Informatica, 1996 (authors' preprint). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: abstract (B-tree index doubles I/O of a TPC-A-style transaction; defer and batch index changes; finds may lose efficiency); five-minute-rule motivation; two-component C0/C1 design; log record first, C0 rebuilt from the log; C0 insert has no I/O; rolling merge with emptying and filling multi-page blocks, written to new disk space; C1 packed 100% full; finds search C0 then C1, multi-component needs every Ci; deletes as delete node entries that annihilate during merge; predicate deletion; cost analysis and concurrency/recovery sections skimmed.
2. [LSM-based Storage Techniques: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.07527), Chen Luo, Michael J. Carey, arXiv v3, 2019. Paper (survey), primary: no. Seen: 2.1 history (in-place vs out-of-place, differential files 1976, Postgres log-structured storage, LFS, LSM 1996, stepped merge → tiering, rolling merge not used today, equal size ratios optimal); 2.2.1 memory and disk components, anti-matter entries, immutable disk components, skip-list or B+-tree memtables, SSTables, point lookup newest to oldest, range queries via priority queue, leveling vs tiering (figure 3); 2.2.2 Bloom filters (formula, 10 bits/key ≈ 1%), partitioning (figure 4, LevelDB's partitioned leveling, sequential keys need no merge), partitioned tiering (vertical and horizontal grouping); 2.2.3 concurrency, WAL, no-steal, redo-only recovery, metadata log; 2.3 cost model and table 1; 3.x improvements, write stalls.
3. [Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//archive/bigtable-osdi06.pdf), Chang et al., OSDI 2006. Paper, primary: yes. Note already existed; appended. Seen: section 4 SSTable (immutable sorted map, 64 KB blocks, index at end loaded on open, one seek per lookup); 5.3 tablet serving (commit log with group commit, memtable, merged view for reads, recovery from redo points); 5.4 minor, merging and major compactions, deletion entries; 6 per-block compression (two-pass scheme, 10-to-1 on Webtable), Bloom filters per locality group.
4. [leveldb Implementation notes](https://github.com/google/leveldb/blob/main/doc/impl.md), LevelDB authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: log files (~4 MB), memtable, sorted tables with deletion markers, level 0 overlapping, compaction into level 1 at more than four files, 2 MB files, 10^L MB per level; MANIFEST and CURRENT; level-0 flush steps; compaction picking, output file cut rules, rotation through the key space, what's dropped; timing (26 MB worst case, write-rate slowdown as a fix); number of files; recovery; garbage collection of files.
5. [RocksDB Overview](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/RocksDB-Overview), RocksDB team. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: forked from LevelDB 1.5; memtable, SST file and log; WAL and per-write fsync choice, batch commit; per-block checksums, blocks never modified; compaction's role; flush drops duplicates; write throughput depends on compaction speed, multi-threaded compaction up to 10x on SSD; leveled, universal and FIFO styles; stalls; compaction filter; bottommost compression (90% of data); block cache compressed and uncompressed; prefix iterators and the range-scan problem.
6. [MemTable (RocksDB wiki)](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/MemTable). See skip-list #3.

#### `bloom-filter` (short)

1. [RocksDB Bloom Filter (RocksDB wiki)](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/RocksDB-Bloom-Filter), RocksDB team. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: may-exist vs definitely-not; one filter per SST file; bits per key and diminishing returns list; Ribbon filter since 6.15.0 (~30% less space, 3-4x CPU); filters ~10% of RAM; filters rebuilt on compaction, not combined; old block-based format (per 2 KB), full filters with cache-line-local probes, format_version=5 in 6.6 with 64-bit hash; prefix vs whole-key filters; statistics for the observed FP rate; partitioned filters; optimize_filters_for_memory; the cache-local FP math (0.95% vs 0.84%).
2. [LSM-based Storage Techniques: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.07527). See lsm-tree #2. Section 2.2.2: insert and test, no false negatives, false positives cost I/O not correctness, (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k, optimal k, 10 bits/key ≈ 1%.
3. [leveldb util/bloom.cc](https://github.com/google/leveldb/blob/main/util/bloom.cc), LevelDB authors. Code, primary: yes. Seen: k = bits_per_key × 0.69 rounded down, clamped 1-30; minimum 64-bit filter; double hashing from one 32-bit hash (cites Kirsch and Mitzenmacher 2006); k stored in the filter's last byte; lookup stops at first zero bit.

Extra: [leveldb documentation](https://github.com/google/leveldb/blob/main/doc/index.md), section Filters: 10 bits per key cuts unneeded reads about 100x; custom comparators need matching filter policies. Has a note (used by block-compression).

#### `block-compression` (short)

1. [Bigtable](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//archive/bigtable-osdi06.pdf). See lsm-tree #3. Section 6, Compression: per-block compression so small parts are readable, some space lost; two-pass scheme at 100-200 MB/s encode and 400-1000 MB/s decode on hardware of the time; 10-to-1 on Webtable vs 3-to-1 or 4-to-1 for Gzip, thanks to key locality.
2. [leveldb documentation (doc/index.md)](https://github.com/google/leveldb/blob/main/doc/index.md), LevelDB authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: block size ~4096 uncompressed bytes, bigger for scans, smaller for point reads, 1 KB to a few MB; per-block compression on by default, off for incompressible data; block cache holds uncompressed blocks, OS cache compressed ones; key layout for locality; filters.
3. [Compression (RocksDB wiki)](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/Compression), RocksDB team. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: data and index blocks compressed, filters not; Snappy default, LZ4 almost always better; bottommost_compression with ZSTD; heavy compression everywhere cuts write amplification; compression_per_level; missing library falls back to no compression; dictionary compression.
4. [Zstandard README](https://github.com/facebook/zstd/blob/dev/README.md), zstd maintainers. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: benchmark table (zstd 1.5.7, brotli, zlib, lz4 1.10.0, snappy 1.2.1 and others; Core i7-9700K, Ubuntu 24.04, lzbench, Silesia); decompression speed roughly constant across levels; small data compresses badly; trained dictionaries.

Extra: [Dictionary Compression (RocksDB wiki)](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/Dictionary-Compression), opened: 4 KB blocks too small for the compressor's own dictionary; dictionary sampled per SST file. Not given a note; the block-based table format page covers the same point.
Extra: leveldb `include/leveldb/options.h` and `table/table_builder.cc`, opened: Snappy default with Core 2-era speeds; compression dropped if it saves less than 12.5%. Not used (old numbers; the 12.5% rule only in code).

#### `sstable` (short)

1. [leveldb File format](https://github.com/google/leveldb/blob/main/doc/table_format.md), LevelDB authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: layout (data blocks, meta blocks, metaindex, index, footer); BlockHandle as varint offset and size; index keys as separators; footer with padding and magic number; filter meta block per 2 KB; stats block. Also opened table/format.h for the 5-byte block trailer (type + CRC) and the footer length.
2. [leveldb table/block_builder.cc](https://github.com/google/leveldb/blob/main/table/block_builder.cc), LevelDB authors. Code, primary: yes. Seen: prefix-compressed keys, restart points every K keys, restart array for binary search, entry layout, trailer. Also options.h for block_restart_interval = 16.
3. [Rocksdb BlockBasedTable Format (RocksDB wiki)](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/Rocksdb-BlockBasedTable-Format), RocksDB team. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: forked from LevelDB's format; meta blocks for filter, index, compression dictionary, range deletions, properties; full and partitioned filters; block-based filter deprecated; default properties; compression dictionary built at bottommost-level compaction from 64-byte samples; range deletions in their own block, dropped only at the bottom.
4. [Bigtable](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//archive/bigtable-osdi06.pdf). See lsm-tree #3. Section 4: the original SSTable.

#### `compaction` (deep)

1. [LSM-based Storage Techniques: A Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.07527). See lsm-tree #2. Sections 2.1-2.3: leveling and tiering, partitioned leveling and tiering, cost model.
2. [leveldb Implementation notes](https://github.com/google/leveldb/blob/main/doc/impl.md). See lsm-tree #4. Compactions and Timing sections.
3. [Name that compaction algorithm](https://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2018/08/name-that-compaction-algorithm.html), Mark Callaghan, 2018. Blog, primary: no (RocksDB-side engineer, his own taxonomy). Seen: leveled, tiered, tiered+leveled, leveled-N, time-series; per-level write amp up to fanout; all-to-all vs some-to-some; where leveled is competitive (key-order inserts, skew); tiered's four problems; RocksDB's leveled is tiered+leveled because L0 is tiered; Fluid LSM; ScyllaDB hybrid. The RocksDB wiki's Compaction page copies this text.
4. [Leveled Compaction (RocksDB wiki)](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/Leveled-Compaction), RocksDB team. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: structure, L0 to L1, picking by score, parallel compactions and subcompactions, dynamic level bytes (default since 8.4, 90% in last level, migration since 8.2), intra-L0, TTL, periodic compaction.
5. [Universal Compaction (RocksDB wiki)](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/Universal-Compaction), RocksDB team. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: goal (lower write amp); why tiered writes less; spiky; double size issue; sorted runs in time order; placement of outputs; picking algorithm, major vs minor.
6. [Compaction overview (Apache Cassandra 5.0)](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/5.0/cassandra/managing/operating/compaction/overview.html), Apache Cassandra. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: why compaction, how it works, kinds (minor, major, user-defined, scrub, cleanup, anticompaction...); strategies UCS (recommended for new workloads), STCS (default), LCS, TWCS; tombstones, gc_grace_seconds 864000 (10 days), zombies, tombstone must meet its data in one compaction. Page shows a "prerelease" banner even under /doc/5.0/.

Extra: [Describing tiered and leveled compaction](https://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2018/10/describing-tiered-and-leveled-compaction.html), Mark Callaghan, 2018. Opened: compaction as a per-level property, (c, f, r) tuples, stepped merge. Not given a note; #3 covers what the article needs.
Extra: [Compaction (RocksDB wiki)](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/Compaction), opened: copies Callaghan's taxonomy, adds FIFO and option defaults (level0_file_num_compaction_trigger 4, target_file_size_base 64 MB). Not given a note.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Leveled write amplification: worst case T per level (Luo, Callaghan), "tends to be less than the fanout in practice" (Callaghan), "often larger than 10" in total (RocksDB). All three stated in the article; the numbers are in `amplification`.
- What "LSM tree" means: Callaghan notes it used to imply leveled; he and Luo include tiered. The original paper's rolling merge isn't what any engine does today (Luo).
- Cassandra keeps STCS as the default while recommending UCS for new workloads.
- RocksDB keeps Snappy as its default compressor while saying LZ4 is almost always better (compatibility).
- Names clash: universal vs size-tiered vs tiered; "major" and "minor" compaction mean different things in Bigtable, Cassandra and RocksDB universal.

**Couldn't open:**

- Burton Bloom's 1970 CACM paper: the ACM PDF returned an HTML page and a mirror returned nothing usable. Not cited.
- Kirsch and Mitzenmacher, "Less hashing, same performance" (cited in LevelDB's bloom.cc): not tried.

**Rejected:**

- Wikipedia's Bloom filter page (linked from the RocksDB wiki): secondary; Luo and RocksDB cover the formula.
- Designing Data-Intensive Applications chapter 3 and Database Internals: not opened, so not citable.
- DataStax Cassandra 3.0 compaction docs (linked from the RocksDB wiki): old; the Apache 5.0 page is current.

**Gaps:**

- No source with block-sized compression ratios; the zstd table is whole-corpus, and the article says small blocks compress less without a number.
- No measured write-stall or compaction-debt numbers; the lab's YCSB run is where those should come from.
- Sarkar et al., "Constructing and analyzing the LSM compaction design space" (VLDB 2021) and Dayan et al. (Monkey, Dostoevsky) not opened; they'd deepen the compaction article's cost section.
- ScyllaDB's incremental compaction and Cassandra's UCS internals not read.

### Comparing and testing engines

All pages below were opened with `curl -sL` and converted to text with
pandoc (PDFs with pdftotext). Raw copies were kept in the scratchpad
while writing.

#### `amplification` (deep)

1. [Read, write & space amplification - pick 2](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2015/11/read-write-space-amplification-pick-2_23.html), Mark Callaghan, Small Datum blog, 2015. Blog, primary: yes (RocksDB/MyRocks performance at Facebook). Seen: "An algorithm can optimize for at most two from read, write and space amplification"; the metrics assume a workload and a configuration (RAM, database size, storage) and don't replace big-O; definitions of read-amp (work per logical read: comparisons, bytes, seeks, decompression), write-amp (work per write), space-amp (database size over data size); read-amp split for point, range and missing-key queries, bloom filters don't help range queries; B-tree pays its read cost at once, an LSM defers it to compaction; flash GC adds write-amp when data of different lifetimes shares a logical erase block; parallel reads improve response time but not efficiency.
2. [Read, write & space amplification - B-Tree vs LSM](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2015/11/read-write-space-amplification-b-tree.html), Mark Callaghan, Small Datum blog, 2015. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: caching assumptions for read-amp, one disk read per point query for both under them; B-tree write-amp 33 for a 128-byte row on a 4,096-byte page; LSM per-level ~10 in theory, ~7 in practice, total 24 for levels 0 to 4; B-tree leaves 50 to 70% full, space-amp 1.5 to 2; InnoDB ~20 bytes/row metadata; compressed-page waste (16 KB to 5 KB in an 8 KB slot); leveled 1.1 to 1.2, size-tiered ~2 plus temporary; compression can take space-amp below 1; measure by normalizing iostat/vmstat by QPS, run at least 12 hours; MyRocks half the space-amp and write-amp of InnoDB. Comments: compaction reads belong to write-amp in the author's view.
3. [Designing Access Methods: The RUM Conjecture](https://openproceedings.org/2016/conf/edbt/paper-12.pdf), Athanassoulis, Kester, Maas, Stoica, Idreos, Ailamaki, Callaghan, EDBT 2016. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: read, update and memory overheads defined as read, write and space amplification ratios with minimum 1.0; toy array proofs that perfecting one blows up another (append-only log for updates, dense array for space, key-addressed array for reads); the conjecture "set an upper bound for two ... also sets a lower bound for the third"; figure 1 triangle placing hash, B-tree, skip list, LSM, bloom filters, sparse indexes; table 1 of I/O costs. The Harvard copy (stratos.seas.harvard.edu) returned Access Denied; the OpenProceedings copy opened.
4. [Optimizing Space Amplification in RocksDB](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2017/papers/p82-dong-cidr17.pdf), Dong, Callaghan, Galanis, Borthakur, Savor, Stumm, CIDR 2017. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: space was the bottleneck on Facebook's flash servers; B-tree pages 1/2 to 2/3 full in production, space-amp worse than 1.5; LSM worst case ~1.111 with 10x levels, over 2 with fixed targets when the last level is small; dynamic level sizes; multiplier trades write-amp against read and space (10 in most installations, some 8); larger blocks compress better but cost read-amp; per-level compression, ~90% of data in last level; RocksDB ~50% less space than compressed InnoDB and writes 10 to 15% as much.
5. [RocksDB Tuning Guide](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/RocksDB-Tuning-Guide), RocksDB team, wiki, last edited 2023 (118 revisions). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "Amplification factors" section with working definitions; 10 MB/s in, 30 MB/s disk = 3; write-amp 50 on a 500 MB/s disk caps writes at 10 MB/s; observe via rocksdb.stats or iostat; iostat reads include compaction; 500 GB leveled example, space 1.14 and write ~33; range read-amp = L0 files + non-empty levels; universal compaction lowers write-amp, raises read, always raises space, can double space temporarily; bloom 10 bits/key ~1% FP; block size trades memory and space against read-amp.
6. [Read-only benchmarks with an LSM are complicated](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2021/02/read-only-benchmarks-with-lsm-are.html), Mark Callaghan, Small Datum blog, 2021. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: QPS varies up to 5x with LSM tree shape on read-only, CPU-bound RocksDB; read-amp split into IO (pages from real storage) and CPU; an LSM is 10 to 20 trees in his configs; bloom filters don't eliminate cost; ~5x worst case without bloom, ~2x with; read-only tests freeze the tree shape.
7. See `storage-benchmarks` #3 (Benchmarking the leveldb family): write-amp up to ~50 on a large database, sequential loads give write-amp 1 or 2.

Also opened: [Leveled Compaction](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/Leveled-Compaction) (RocksDB wiki): intra-L0 compaction adds 1 to write-amp against "usually ... larger than 10" for leveled; not used, the tuning guide covers the numbers and `compaction` owns the mechanism.

#### `storage-benchmarks` (short)

1. [Benchmarking Cloud Serving Systems with YCSB](https://courses.cs.duke.edu/fall13/cps296.4/838-CloudPapers/ycsb.pdf), Cooper, Silberstein, Tam, Ramakrishnan, Sears, Yahoo! Research, SoCC 2010. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: performance tier = latency versus offered throughput until saturation; uniform, zipfian, latest distributions (figure 1); Table 2 with workloads A to E; loading takes longer than runs, runs 30 minutes; reload if writes fragment data; client reports average, p95 and p99; setup: 6 servers, 8 GB RAM, RAID-10, 120 million 1 KB records, 20 GB per server "more than it could cache entirely in RAM"; Cassandra, MySQL and PNUTS synced every update, HBase didn't; single RAID-10 array with no dedicated log disk for fairness; HBase compactions applied periodically; tuning help from each system's developers. The ACM copy returned 403; this is a Duke course mirror.
2. [Core Workloads](https://github.com/brianfrankcooper/YCSB/wiki/Core-Workloads), YCSB wiki, last edited 2020. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: six workloads A to F with example applications; F (read-modify-write) isn't in the paper; A and B updates are blind writes; recommended order load, A, B, C, F, D, delete, reload, E because D and E insert.
3. [Benchmarking the leveldb family](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2014/07/benchmarking-leveldb-family.html), Mark Callaghan, Small Datum blog, 2014. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: problems show only in a steady state on a large database; write-amp up to ~50; peak ingest = storage write rate / write-amp; L0 to L1 falls behind and stalls Puts; per-interval stats; same RNG seed leaves data in the OS cache between runs and understates write-amp; checksum verification off hides a CPU cost; readahead too high ruins IO-bound tests; sequential inserts skip compaction (write-amp 1 or 2); empty memtable inflates read QPS; "steady state" means compaction in progress; load X, then X random writes; trust drops with the number of products compared.

Also opened: [workloads/workloada to workloadf](https://github.com/brianfrankcooper/YCSB/tree/master/workloads) raw files: proportions and distributions match the wiki; each ships with `recordcount=1000`, a tiny default dataset. Not cited (research only). [How I do performance tests for RocksDB](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2022/08/how-i-do-performance-tests-for-rocksdb.html), Callaghan, 2022: benchmark step order (fillseq, read-only, overwritesome, flush_mt_l0, read-while-writing, overwrite) to avoid inheriting compaction debt; four cache setups (byrx, byos, iobuf, iodir). Not used; a good lab reference. [Benchmark(et)ing](http://smalldatum.blogspot.com/2014/06/benchmarketing.html), Callaghan, 2014: checklist of context to report (hardware, versions, aged file structures, how full the device is, buffered or direct IO). Not used; overlaps #3 and phase 9's `benchmarking-pitfalls`.

#### `model-based-testing` (short)

1. [Using Lightweight Formal Methods to Validate a Key-Value Storage Node in Amazon S3](https://www.amazon.science/publications/using-lightweight-formal-methods-to-validate-a-key-value-storage-node-in-amazon-s3), Bornholt and 11 others, AWS, SOSP 2021. Paper, primary: yes. Seen (PDF linked from the page): executable reference models in Rust, 1% of the code, the LSM index's model is a hash map; property-based tests apply each operation to model and implementation, compare, check invariants; background ops (reclaim, reboot) as no-ops in the model; in-memory disk; tens of millions of sequences before each deployment; 16 issues prevented; argument biasing (Get prefers keys already Put), production distributions had no effect; coverage metrics; minimization 61 ops to 6; non-determinism (Rust HashMap order) breaks minimization; IO failure injection with a relaxed check; DirtyReboot crash operations and a persistence property; block-level crash enumeration found no extra bugs and was much slower.
2. [rapid](https://pkg.go.dev/pgregory.net/rapid), Gregory Petrosyan and contributors, v1.3.0. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Go property-based testing with automatic minimization and persistence of failures; state machine ("stateful" or "model-based") tests via `T.Repeat` and `StateMachine`; `""` action runs around every action for invariants; no coverage feedback unlike `testing.F.Fuzz`, but `MakeFuzz` turns a rapid test into a fuzz target; queue example with a slice as the model.

Also opened: [Hypothesis stateful testing](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/stateful.html) (Hypothesis 6.168.3 docs): rule-based state machines, bundles, preconditions, invariants, an example comparing a database to an in-memory dict. Not used; rapid covers the same idea in the lab's language.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Write-amp sums for leveled LSMs differ: Callaghan's 2015 worked example gives 24 (L0 to L1 ~1, ~7 per level in practice); the RocksDB tuning guide gives ~33 (L0 to L1 = 2, 10 per level); the 2014 LevelDB post says up to ~50 for a large database with uniform keys. Different level counts and assumptions, not errors.
- What read-amp counts: RUM counts bytes read over bytes wanted; the RocksDB guide counts disk reads per query; Callaghan (2021) adds CPU read-amp and says it's usually the real problem on cached workloads.
- Compaction reads: Callaghan puts them under write-amp; `iostat` physical reads (the RocksDB guide's suggested measure) mix them into reads.
- MyRocks vs InnoDB: the 2015 post says half the write-amp; the 2017 paper's fleet review says RocksDB writes 10 to 15% of what InnoDB writes. Different measurements (Linkbench vs production review).
- "Compaction settled" in the storage-benchmarks note vs Callaghan's definition of steady state as compaction running, not finished.
- ShardStore found block-level crash enumeration added nothing over coarse dirty reboots; tools like the phase 1 crash harness take the block-level view. Their result on their system, not a general rule.
- Workload biasing: ShardStore trusts default randomness except where there's evidence; rapid biases toward small values and edge cases by default.

**Couldn't open:**
- RUM paper at stratos.seas.harvard.edu (Access Denied) and the eecs.harvard.edu copy (not a PDF); used OpenProceedings.
- YCSB paper at dl.acm.org (403); used the Duke course mirror.
- The FAST 2016 paper on per-level LSM write amplification linked in Callaghan's comments (not tried; would explain the ~7 vs 10).

**Rejected:**
- RocksDB Leveled Compaction wiki: mechanism belongs to `compaction`.
- "How I do performance tests for RocksDB" and "Benchmark(et)ing": good, but a short node can't take more than 3 sources; the leveldb-family post covers the storage-specific traps.
- Hypothesis stateful docs: Python; rapid fits a Go lab.

**Gaps:**
- No measured amplification numbers for Pebble or SQLite; the lab's comparison has to produce them.
- No source on how big "several times RAM" should be for a benchmark dataset; YCSB used 20 GB per 8 GB server and that's all the article says.
- No primary source on YCSB's newer workloads or the maintained YCSB release; the core workloads page is the reference.
- Nothing on model-based testing of concurrent engines beyond "use a linearizability check"; that's phase 11.

## Phase 8: Databases III, transactions

Researched by 5 parallel passes, one per group below.

### Transactions and what they promise

#### `transaction` (deep)

1. [PostgreSQL 3.4 Transactions (tutorial)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-transactions.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, version 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: bank transfer example (Alice, Bob, branch totals); all-or-nothing; intermediate states invisible; updates logged to permanent storage before reported complete; all updates visible at once at commit; BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK; every statement has an implicit BEGIN/COMMIT; some client libraries send BEGIN/COMMIT for you; savepoints, ROLLBACK TO, RELEASE; releasing or rolling back to a savepoint releases later ones; after an error the block is "in aborted state", only ROLLBACK TO or a full rollback recovers.
2. [PostgreSQL BEGIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-begin.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, version 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: autocommit definition (commit per statement, rollback on error); a transaction block is faster because start/commit needs "significant CPU and disk activity"; isolation level, read-only, deferrable modes; BEGIN inside a block only warns; nest with savepoints; BEGIN is an extension of START TRANSACTION.
3. [MySQL 8.4, 17.7.2.2 autocommit, Commit, and Rollback](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-autocommit-commit-rollback.html), Oracle. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: all InnoDB user activity is in a transaction; autocommit on by default; autocommit=0 means a transaction is always open; session ending without commit rolls back; some statements commit implicitly; COMMIT/ROLLBACK release locks.
4. [SQLite, Transaction](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html), SQLite developers. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: no reads or writes outside a transaction; implicit transactions commit when the last statement finishes; BEGIN doesn't nest; many readers, one writer; read-to-write upgrade can fail with SQLITE_BUSY; DEFERRED (default), IMMEDIATE, EXCLUSIVE; some errors roll back only the statement, others the whole transaction.
5. [The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations](https://jimgray.azurewebsites.net/papers/thetransactionconcept.pdf), Jim Gray, Tandem/VLDB, 1981. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: transaction from contract law; three properties (consistency, atomicity, durability), no isolation; commit or abort; unprotected, protected and real actions (cash dispensers can't be undone); compensating transactions; nested and long-lived transactions as open problems.
6. [Lecture #16: Concurrency Control Theory](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/16-concurrencycontrol.pdf), Andy Pavlo, CMU 15-445, Fall 2024. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: transaction as unit of change; strawman one-at-a-time with copying the DB file; scope only inside the DB (email can't be rolled back); client defines boundaries; aborts self-inflicted or by DBMS; ACID with logging vs shadow paging; transaction consistency is the application's job; pessimistic vs optimistic; conflicts, conflict and view serializability, dependency graph.

Extra: [PostgreSQL psql](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/app-psql.html), version 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: AUTOCOMMIT variable (off means implicit BEGIN), ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK works by an implicit SAVEPOINT before each command. Not given a note; BEGIN and the tutorial cover the article.
Extra: [PostgreSQL SAVEPOINT](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-savepoint.html), version 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: savepoint rolls back commands after it; same-name savepoints shadow older ones. Not given a note; the tutorial covers it.

#### `acid` (short)

1. [Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery](https://cs-people.bu.edu/mathan/reading-groups/papers-classics/recovery.pdf), Theo Haerder, Andreas Reuter, ACM Computing Surveys vol. 15 no. 4, 1983. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: section 1.1 defines atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability and names them ACID ("the ACID test of the system's quality"); consistency is by definition (each successful transaction commits only legal results); isolation justified by being able to reset a transaction; durability; bad committed transactions removed only by countertransactions; "transaction" name from Eswaran et al. 1976. Copy hosted by a Boston University reading group.
2. [Lecture #16: Concurrency Control Theory](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/16-concurrencycontrol.pdf). See transaction #6. Sections 3 to 7: each letter and how a DBMS gets it (logging or shadow paging for A and D; concurrency control for I; "transaction consistency is the application's responsibility").

Also relevant, see transaction #5: Gray's 1981 paper lists only C, A and D.
Extra: [When is "ACID" ACID? Rarely.](http://www.bailis.org/blog/when-is-acid-acid-rarely/), Peter Bailis, 2013. See isolation-levels #5; the "I" is rarely serializable by default.

#### `isolation-levels` (deep)

1. [PostgreSQL 13.2 Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, version 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: standard's four levels and four phenomena; Table 13.1 with "Allowed, but not in PG"; Read Uncommitted = Read Committed; sequences not rolled back; Read Committed per-statement snapshot, updater waits and re-evaluates WHERE on the new row version, hits/DELETE example; Repeatable Read snapshot at first statement, "could not serialize access due to concurrent update", retry, is snapshot isolation, pre-9.1 Serializable meant this; Serializable = SSI, mytab example, non-blocking SIRead predicate locks, 40001, read data not valid until commit, performance tips.
2. [PostgreSQL 13.5 Serialization Failure Handling](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html), version 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: 40001, 40P01, unique violations that are hidden serialization failures, retry the whole transaction including logic, no automatic retry, many attempts under contention.
3. [MySQL 8.4, 17.7.2.1 Transaction Isolation Levels](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-transaction-isolation-levels.html), Oracle. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: all four SQL:1992 levels, default REPEATABLE READ; consistent reads use snapshot from first read; locking reads/UPDATE/DELETE lock ranges with gap or next-key locks; don't mix locking and non-locking statements at RR ("typically in such cases you want SERIALIZABLE"); READ COMMITTED fresh snapshot per read, no gap locks, phantoms; READ UNCOMMITTED dirty reads; SERIALIZABLE turns plain SELECT into FOR SHARE when autocommit is off.
4. [A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/tr-95-51.pdf), Berenson, Bernstein, Gray, Melton, O'Neil, O'Neil, SIGMOD, 1995. Paper, primary: yes. Seen (from the arXiv copy, https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0701157; the Microsoft URL gave 403 to curl): phenomena ambiguous; broad vs strict; P0 dirty write missing; H1 inconsistent analysis; phenomena are disguised locking; P4 lost update; snapshot isolation and first-committer-wins; A5A read skew, A5B write skew, H5; RR and SI incomparable; SI passes all three strict ANSI anomalies yet isn't serializable.
5. [When is "ACID" ACID? Rarely.](http://www.bailis.org/blog/when-is-acid-acid-rarely/), Peter Bailis, 2013. Blog by a database researcher, primary: no. Seen: textbook isolation = serializability; 3 of 18 databases default to serializable, 9 offer it; table of default and max levels (Postgres 9.2.2 RC/S, MySQL 5.6 RR/S, Oracle 11g RC/SI). Old versions.
6. [Hermitage](https://github.com/ept/hermitage), Martin Kleppmann and contributors, started 2014. Test suite, primary: no (note already existed, marked no). Seen: table of "so-called" vs actual level per database (Postgres RC = monotonic atomic view, RR = snapshot isolation; MySQL RR default = monotonic atomic view, lost update possible; Oracle serializable = SI; SQL Server levels); Adya anomaly names; standard's definition "flawed"; serializability rarely used.

Extra: [Hermitage: Testing the "I" in ACID](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2014/11/25/hermitage-testing-the-i-in-acid.html), Martin Kleppmann, 2014. Blog, primary: no. Seen: Bitcoin exchange race as motivation; System R team offered weaker levels for performance; levels are a leaky abstraction defined by implementation. Not given a note; the repo README covers the claims used.
Extra: [PostgreSQL SET TRANSACTION](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-set-transaction.html), version 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: level can't change after the first query; READ ONLY DEFERRABLE for reports; default_transaction_isolation. Not given a note.

#### `serializability` (deep)

1. [Lecture #16: Concurrency Control Theory](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/16-concurrencycontrol.pdf). See transaction #6. Section 6: serial and equivalent schedules; conflict definition and the three conflict kinds (RW, WR, WW); conflict vs view serializability; dependency (precedence) graph, conflict serializable iff acyclic; blind writes; nested sets of schedules.
2. [Generalized Isolation Level Definitions](https://pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/icde00.pdf), Atul Adya, Barbara Liskov, Patrick O'Neil, ICDE, 2000. Paper, primary: yes. Seen (from the Internet Archive copy; pmg.csail.mit.edu refused connections): Berenson's fix is "disguised versions of locking"; ww, wr, rw dependencies incl. predicate versions; DSG over committed transactions; G0, G1c, G2-item, G2; PL-3 forbids all cycles; realistic implementations give conflict serializability.
3. [A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/tr-95-51.pdf). See isolation-levels #4. Section 2.1: conflicts, dependency graph, serializable = same graph as a serial history; H5 write skew as a non-serializable history.
4. [Serializability](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/serializable), Jepsen. Reference page, primary: no. Seen: "some total order"; multi-object incl. predicates; not totally or sticky available; no real-time or per-process order; can miss your own earlier writes; empty-read and reorder-to-end pathologies; ANSI 1999 wording; Adya's preventive reading too strict; Cerone and Crooks formalizations.
5. [Linearizability versus Serializability](http://www.bailis.org/blog/linearizability-versus-serializability/), Peter Bailis, 2014. Blog by a database researcher, primary: no. Seen: serializability multi-op multi-object with no real-time order; strict serializability; not composable; 2PL gives strict serializability, some MVCC doesn't; NULL-for-every-read is serializable; terms from two communities.
6. [PostgreSQL 13.2 Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html). See isolation-levels #1. Section 13.2.3: the mytab example as a real two-transaction cycle, "correct alone means correct in any mix".

Extra: [Weak Consistency (Adya PhD thesis)](http://pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/adya-phd.pdf), 1999. Couldn't open (see below).

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- What "consistency" means in ACID. Haerder and Reuter define it as "by definition" correct transactions; the CMU notes split database consistency (constraints) from transaction consistency (the application's job); Bailis says serializability is what guarantees it. The acid article explains the split; none of the sources contradicts the others.
- Whether ACID's I means serializable. Textbooks and Bailis say yes; every major database defaults to something weaker (Postgres and Oracle read committed, MySQL repeatable read). Both are stated in the isolation-levels article.
- How to read the SQL standard. Berenson et al. argue for the broad, preventive reading (which is locking in disguise); Adya argues that reading is too strict and redefines the levels as graph cycles; Jepsen agrees with Adya. Postgres's docs still present the standard's phenomena table, noting SI's anomalies were formalized after the standard.
- MySQL's REPEATABLE READ. The MySQL manual presents it as a strong default; Hermitage classifies it below snapshot isolation (lost updates possible). The manual itself warns against mixing locking and non-locking reads at that level.
- Whether serializable should be the default. Postgres's docs present it as the best performance choice for some environments and warn about retry and monitoring cost; no source opened gives numbers.

**Couldn't open:**

- Adya's PhD thesis (pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/adya-phd.pdf): connection refused on the MIT server for this writer (another agent has since made a note for it, adya-weak-consistency-1999). The ICDE 2000 paper was read from the Internet Archive instead.
- The Microsoft Research URL of Berenson et al. returned 403 to curl; the arXiv copy of the same tech report was read. (Another agent's note already uses the Microsoft URL.)
- CMU 15-445 Fall 2024 note "15-concurrencycontrol.pdf" is 404; the lecture is number 16 in that term.

**Rejected:**

- Papadimitriou, "The serializability of concurrent database updates" (JACM, 1979): paywalled, not opened.
- DDIA chapter 7: book, not opened.
- Kleppmann's Hermitage blog post: used for background only; the repo README carries the claims.

**Gaps:**

- No source opened gives the cost of a transaction start/commit in numbers (Postgres says only "significant CPU and disk activity"), or the throughput cost of serializable vs read committed. The phase 8 lab is meant to measure the latter.
- No source opened says which statements implicitly commit in MySQL (the list is on another page) or that DDL is transactional in Postgres. Left out of the articles.
- Current Oracle and SQL Server defaults come only from Hermitage and Bailis (old versions); the articles name only Postgres and MySQL defaults from their own current manuals.
- Strict serializability and real time are covered only from Bailis and Jepsen; `linearizability` (phase 11) should carry the detail.

### Anomalies

#### `dirty-read` (short)

1. [A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/tr-95-51.pdf), Berenson, Bernstein, Gray, Melton, O'Neil, O'Neil, Microsoft Research / SIGMOD, 1995. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: P1 (dirty read) in words and as a history; strict A1 (only when T1 aborts) versus broad P1 (any read of uncommitted data); history H1, a transfer seen half-done with no abort, caught only by the broad reading; P0 dirty write and why rollback by before-images needs it; Table 4.
2. [13.2 Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: dirty read definition; Table 13.1 "Allowed, but not in PG" for read uncommitted; Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed; a statement sees only data committed before it began.
3. [17.7.2.1 Transaction Isolation Levels](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-transaction-isolation-levels.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4 manual. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: READ UNCOMMITTED reads may use "a possible earlier version of a row", called a dirty read; default is REPEATABLE READ; READ COMMITTED takes a fresh snapshot per read and disables gap locks.
4. [Hermitage](https://github.com/ept/hermitage) (mysql.md): see `lost-update` #3. Seen: MySQL read uncommitted shows T1's uncommitted 101, then 10 again after rollback (G1a); G1b intermediate read.

#### `non-repeatable-read` (short)

1. [13.2 Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html): see `dirty-read` #2. Seen: nonrepeatable read definition; Read Committed takes a new snapshot per statement, so two SELECTs in one transaction can differ; Repeatable Read keeps one snapshot for the transaction.
2. [A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/tr-95-51.pdf): see `dirty-read` #1. Seen: P2 fuzzy read, A2 versus P2, history H2 (total of 140 with no re-read); read skew A5A; "Fuzzy Reads (P2) is a degenerate form of Read Skew where x=y".
3. [Hermitage](https://github.com/ept/hermitage) (postgres.md): see `lost-update` #3. Seen: G-single read skew script: read committed shows 2 => 18 after T2's commit, repeatable read shows 2 => 20.

#### `phantom-read` (short)

1. [13.2 Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html): see `dirty-read` #2. Seen: phantom read definition; Postgres Repeatable Read doesn't allow phantoms, which the standard permits.
2. [A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/tr-95-51.pdf): see `dirty-read` #1. Seen: P3 in words; A3 versus P3; ANSI P3 only covers inserts, the broad P3 any write to the predicate; H3 (active employees and a count); snapshot isolation has no A3 phantoms but allows the job-tasks P3 case (two 1-hour inserts under an 8-hour limit).
3. [17.7.4 Phantom Rows](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-next-key-locking.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4 manual. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: phantom definition; `id > 100 FOR UPDATE` example with rows 90 and 102 and an insert of 101; next-key lock = record lock plus gap lock; "lock" the nonexistence of a row; disabling gap locks brings phantoms back.
4. [Hermitage](https://github.com/ept/hermitage): see `lost-update` #3. Seen: PMP scripts (predicate read returns the newly inserted row at read committed, not at repeatable read).

#### `lost-update` (deep)

1. [A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/tr-95-51.pdf): see `dirty-read` #1. Seen: P4 defined; H4 (100, +20, +30, final 130); P4 allowed at READ COMMITTED; forbidding P2 forbids P4; cursor stability (P4C); first-committer-wins in snapshot isolation prevents P4; Oracle Read Consistency allows P4.
2. [13.2 Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html): see `dirty-read` #2. Seen: at Read Committed a second updater waits, then re-checks the WHERE clause against the new row version; `balance = balance + 100` safe; the hits/DELETE example; at Repeatable Read "could not serialize access due to concurrent update", retry the whole transaction.
3. [Hermitage](https://github.com/ept/hermitage), Martin Kleppmann and contributors, GitHub, 2014 onward (Postgres 9.3.5, MySQL 5.6.21 test runs). Test suite, primary: no. Seen: summary table; P4 scripts: Postgres read committed overwrites, repeatable read errors; MySQL repeatable read (default) doesn't prevent P4, serializable deadlocks one side.
4. [17.7.2.3 Consistent Nonlocking Reads](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-consistent-read.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4 manual. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: snapshot applies to SELECT, "not necessarily to DML statements"; UPDATE/DELETE hit rows committed after the snapshot; use READ COMMITTED or a locking read for the freshest state.
5. [13.4 Data Consistency Checks at the Application Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/applevel-consistency.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: SELECT FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE / LOCK TABLE when writes aren't serializable; FOR UPDATE locks only returned rows; the lock only lasts until commit; take locks before the Repeatable Read snapshot is frozen.
6. [13.5 Serialization Failure Handling](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: SQLSTATE 40001; also consider 40P01; unique violations after check-then-insert; retry the complete transaction including its logic; no automatic retry.
7. [Query Expressions: F()](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.2/ref/models/expressions/), Django Software Foundation, Django 5.2. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "Avoiding race conditions using F()": two threads lose an increment; F() makes the database compute from the current value; F() assignments persist across saves.
8. [ActiveRecord::Locking::Optimistic](https://api.rubyonrails.org/classes/ActiveRecord/Locking/Optimistic.html), Rails 8.1.4 API. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: lock_version column bumped per update, StaleObjectError; hidden form field across requests. Also opened the source (optimistic.rb on main): old lock_version merged into the update's conditions; affected_rows != 1 raises.

#### `write-skew` (deep)

1. [A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/tr-95-51.pdf): see `dirty-read` #1. Seen: A5B write skew history; H5 (x + y positive, both write -40); bank example; SI allows A5B, locking REPEATABLE READ doesn't, so they're incomparable; the job-tasks predicate example.
2. [Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL](https://drkp.net/papers/ssi-vldb12.pdf), Dan Ports and Kevin Grittner, VLDB, 2012. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: doctors on call (figure 1); write locks don't help because rows differ; 2PL and OCC would catch it; batch-processing read-only anomaly; workarounds (FOR UPDATE, LOCK TABLE, materialize the conflict with a dummy row, declarative constraints); rw-antidependencies; Adya's two-rw-edges observation; dangerous structures and false positives.
3. [SSI](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/SSI), PostgreSQL wiki (Kevin Grittner and others). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: write skew definition; black/white rows swap at REPEATABLE READ; overdraft ($900 from two $500 accounts); error text with "pivot"; trigger-enforced unique-like rule; prefer declarative constraints.
4. [13.2 Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html): see `dirty-read` #2. Seen: class/value sum example rolled back at Serializable; "could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies"; non-blocking predicate locks; explicit locks needed at lower levels; unique violations under Serializable.
5. [Hermitage](https://github.com/ept/hermitage): see `lost-update` #3. Seen: G2-item (disjoint rows) and G2 (predicate insert) at Postgres repeatable read; MySQL repeatable read allows G2-item; Oracle "serializable" is snapshot isolation.
6. [13.4 Data Consistency Checks at the Application Level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/applevel-consistency.html): see `lost-update` #5. Seen: read/write conflicts and cycles in the apparent order; Serializable everywhere needs no other effort; not extended to hot standby or logical replicas.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Names differ by vendor. "Repeatable read" is snapshot isolation in Postgres, something weaker in MySQL/InnoDB (lost update and write skew get through; Hermitage calls it monotonic atomic view), and a lock-based level in SQL Server. Oracle's "serializable" is snapshot isolation.
- Strict versus broad readings of the SQL-92 phenomena (Berenson et al.): the strict ones miss H1, H2, H3. The SQL standard itself wasn't opened (paywalled); everything about it here is second-hand through Berenson and the Postgres manual.
- Whether SELECT FOR UPDATE "fixes" write skew: it only works when the rows you check exist to be locked; it can't lock a row that isn't there (then you need a predicate or gap lock, a materialized conflict row, or SERIALIZABLE).
- Postgres Repeatable Read has no phantoms (Table 13.1), yet the broad P3 (job-tasks example) still happens under snapshot isolation. Both are true: the strict A3 is gone, the write-skew-shaped P3 isn't.
- Hermitage's data is old (Postgres 9.3.5, MySQL 5.6.21). The current Postgres 18 manual and MySQL 8.4 manual describe the same behaviour, but the MySQL results weren't re-run.

**Couldn't open:**
- The SQL standard (ISO/IEC 9075) text: paywalled. Hermitage links a PDF copy of the SQL:1999 foundation draft on a third-party site; not used.
- dev.mysql.com returned a "Technical Difficulties" page to a browser user agent; opened fine with curl's default user agent and with WebFetch.

**Rejected:**
- Kleppmann's blog post "Hermitage: Testing the 'I' in ACID" (2014): opened; background only, the repository has the facts.
- Adya's thesis and Adya/Liskov/O'Neil (ICDE 2000): not opened for this group; the G-names come through Hermitage and the Ports/Grittner summary. Belongs with `history-checking` and `serializability`.
- *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* chapter 7: not opened.

**Gaps:**
- No source opened for SQL Server's lock-based levels beyond Hermitage's table.
- No real Postgres history of our own yet; LAB.md wants one per anomaly node (lab on hold).
- Postgres 18 `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` row-lock details are in 13.3.2 (explicit-locking); not re-opened here, the locking group owns it.
- No source for how often lost updates or write skew happen in real apps; Ports/Grittner mention the Wisconsin courts and a citation, nothing measured.

### Locking

#### `two-phase-locking` (deep)

1. [The Notions of Consistency and Predicate Locks in a Database System](https://people.csail.mit.edu/tdanford/6830papers/eswaran-notions-of-consistency.pdf), K. P. Eswaran, J. N. Gray, R. A. Lorie, I. L. Traiger, IBM Research, 1976. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: abstract (consistency requires no new locks after releasing one; lock logical not physical subsets); section 2 definitions of well-formed and two-phase, figure 2 (T11 not two-phase, T12 two-phase), the theorem that well-formed two-phase transactions give only consistent legal schedules and its converse for unknown transaction sets, "two-phase restriction may be too strong" for known pairs, partitioning into disjoint classes; section 3 phantoms and the Napa example; predicate locks, conflict via mutual satisfiability, recursively unsolvable in general; simple predicates decidable. OCR scan on an MIT course page (ACM's copy is behind a login).
2. [Lecture #16: Two-Phase Locking](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2023/notes/16-twophaselocking.pdf), Andy Pavlo, Jignesh Patel, CMU, 2023. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: locks vs latches, S and X locks, lock manager and non-durable lock table; growing and shrinking phases; 2PL gives conflict serializability, cascading aborts, dirty reads and deadlocks still possible, rejects some serializable schedules; strong strict (rigorous) 2PL; universe of schedules; deadlock detection (waits-for graph, periodic, victim selection criteria, partial rollback) and prevention (wait-die, wound-wait, restarts keep timestamp); lock granularities, billion-tuple example, hierarchy levels, IS/IX/SIX. The Fall 2024 URL returned 404.
3. [README-SSI (PostgreSQL 18 source)](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/REL_18_STABLE/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README-SSI), PostgreSQL Global Development Group. Code docs, primary: yes. Seen: S2PL described as the primary historical technique (blocks writes on read data and all access on written data), cycles of blocking are deadlocks, "debilitating" under contention; SSI overview; apparent serial order is commit order under S2PL; predicate locking needed by both S2PL and SSI; multiple granularities with escalation; false positives from coarse locks and plan choice; SIREAD locks can't use intent locking; heap and index locking rules; B-tree leaf-page locks; whole-index lock for index AMs without support. Same text on master and REL_18_STABLE.
4. [Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL](https://drkp.net/papers/ssi-vldb12.pdf), Dan R. K. Ports, Kevin Grittner, 2012. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: Postgres had no serializable level because 2PL was seen as too expensive; nearly all other databases use S2PL with index-range locks for phantoms; readers-don't-block-writers mantra; commit order equals serial order under 2PL and OCC; InnoDB and Berkeley DB already had S2PL; B+tree SIREAD locks at page granularity, next-key locking planned; evaluation with their own simple S2PL for Postgres; RUBiS (85% read-only) throughput SI 435, SSI 422, S2PL 208 req/s. Note already existed; appended.
5. [Transaction locking and row versioning guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/sql-server-transaction-locking-and-row-versioning-guide), Microsoft. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: pessimistic vs optimistic control and when each fits; isolation levels (SERIALIZABLE keeps read and write locks to the end plus range locks); S locks released after the read below REPEATABLE READ; lock granularity and resource list; lock modes including U, intent (IS, IX, SIX, IU, SIU, UIX), key-range; escalation (5,000 locks, retry every 1,250, row straight to table, 24% memory, ~100 bytes a lock); optimized locking with TID locks; advice to batch large deletes. Read in the sql-server-ver17 view.
6. [Transaction Isolation Levels (MySQL 8.4)](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-transaction-isolation-levels.html), Oracle. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: SERIALIZABLE converts plain SELECTs to SELECT ... FOR SHARE when autocommit is off. Note already existed (mysql-innodb-isolation-levels), claim already there.

#### `lock-granularity` (short)

1. [Granularity of Locks and Degrees of Consistency in a Shared Data Base](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs245/readings/granularity-of-locks.pdf), J. N. Gray, R. A. Lorie, G. R. Putzolu, I. L. Traiger, IBM Research, 1976. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: concurrency vs overhead trade-off; lockable units coexisting; figure 1 hierarchy (database, areas, files, records); implicit locking of subtrees; intention mode tags ancestors; IS, IX, SIX, S, X with table 1 compatibilities and the partial order of figure 2; request root to leaf, release leaf to root; second half on degrees of consistency 0 to 3 (not used). OCR scan on a Stanford course page, heavily letter-spaced.
2. [Transaction locking and row versioning guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/sql-server-transaction-locking-and-row-versioning-guide). See two-phase-locking #5. Lock hierarchy, intent locks, escalation thresholds, batching large deletes.
3. [InnoDB Locking (MySQL 8.4)](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-locking.html), Oracle. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: S and X row locks; multiple granularity locking; IS and IX, FOR SHARE takes IS, FOR UPDATE takes IX; intention protocol; X/IX/S/IS compatibility matrix; intention locks block only full-table requests; record, gap, next-key, insert intention, AUTO-INC and spatial predicate locks. dev.mysql.com served an error page to a browser user agent and the real page to curl's default one.
4. [Explicit Locking](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: eight table-level modes (names with ROW are table locks), conflict table, savepoint release; row-level modes and their conflict table; row locks not kept in memory, no limit, disk writes; page-level buffer locks; deadlocks with the two-account example; advisory locks. Note already existed; appended.
5. [Lock Management](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-locks.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: deadlock_timeout (default 1s, why the check is delayed, relation to log_lock_waits); max_locks_per_transaction (64, objects not rows); max_pred_locks_per_transaction, _per_relation (promotion to relation), _per_page (default 2).
6. [src/backend/storage/lmgr/README](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/REL_18_STABLE/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README), PostgreSQL Global Development Group. Code docs, primary: yes. Seen: spinlocks, LWLocks, heavyweight locks, SIRead; partitioned lock table; fast path for weak relation locks since 9.2; deadlock detection (see deadlock-detection #2). Read for the fast-path point, which was cut from the article for length.

#### `deadlock-detection` (short)

1. [Explicit Locking, 13.3.4 Deadlocks](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html). See lock-granularity #4. The 11111/22222 example, unpredictable victim, consistent lock order, strongest lock first, retry.
2. [src/backend/storage/lmgr/README](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/REL_18_STABLE/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README). See lock-granularity #6. Seen: on by default; victim is the smallest by rows inserted, updated or deleted; can't see LOCK TABLES or other engines' locks; 200-transaction and 1,000,000-lock limits treated as deadlock; slowdown under high concurrency; innodb_deadlock_detect and innodb_lock_wait_timeout.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- 2PL vs SSI cost: the Postgres SSI README calls blocking under S2PL "debilitating" under contention, and Ports and Grittner's RUBiS run shows S2PL at under half of SI's throughput; but their S2PL was a simple implementation built for the comparison, not a tuned commercial lock manager. The article says so.
- What "strict 2PL" means: CMU's notes separate strict (about writes) from strong strict or rigorous (all locks held to commit); the Postgres README and Ports and Grittner use "strict two-phase locking (S2PL)" for holding all locks to commit. The article uses the Postgres usage and mentions the other names.
- Deadlock detection timing: Postgres checks only after deadlock_timeout (default 1 s) and says one second is about the smallest sensible value; InnoDB checks by default but lets you turn detection off on high-concurrency systems in favour of a timeout. CMU describes periodic background checks. Different trade-offs of CPU vs time-to-detect.
- InnoDB says the isolation level doesn't affect deadlock odds, while its gap locks (a source of range deadlocks) only apply at REPEATABLE READ and above for locking reads. Not resolved; the article doesn't repeat the isolation claim.
- Optimistic vs pessimistic: Kung and Robinson and Microsoft agree optimism fits rare conflicts and locking fits contention; nobody opened gives a crossover point.
