- No measured numbers for deadlock detection cost or for OCC retry rates under contention. No numbers given.
- Advisory lock key hashing (hashtext and friends) isn't documented on the pages opened; the article only says you must map strings to numbers yourself.
- The Gray et al. and Eswaran et al. scans are OCR with garbled letters, so a few useful sentences couldn't be quoted exactly.
- Postgres's lack of lock escalation for row locks is stated indirectly (row locks aren't in memory, no limit); no page says "Postgres never escalates row locks" in so many words.

### Multiversion

#### `mvcc` (deep)

1. [13.1 Introduction](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-intro.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Postgres uses MVCC; each statement sees a snapshot "as it was some time ago"; reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading, even at Serializable (SSI); table and row locks still available.
2. [66.6 Database Page Layout](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/storage-page-layout.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: heap row header with t_xmin (insert XID), t_xmax (delete XID), t_ctid (this or newer version), infomask bits; 23-byte header; CTID = page + item index; pd_prune_xid. Note already existed (postgres-page-layout).
3. [An Empirical Evaluation of In-Memory Multi-Version Concurrency Control](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol10/p781-Wu.pdf), Wu, Arulraj, Lin, Xian, Pavlo, PVLDB vol. 10, 2017. Paper, primary: no. Seen: four design decisions (protocol, version storage, GC, index management); Table 1 of real systems (Oracle 1984 delta, Postgres 1985 append-only O2N, InnoDB 2001 delta, Hekaton, HANA time-travel, HyPer); append-only O2N vs N2O trade-off; time-travel storage; delta storage (rollback segment in MySQL and Oracle); GC tuple-level (VAC, COOP) vs transaction-level; long-running transactions hurt GC; logical vs physical index pointers; MVCC first described in a 1979 dissertation, first implemented in InterBase from 1981.
4. [InnoDB Multi-Versioning](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-multi-versioning.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: rollback segment in undo tablespaces; DB_TRX_ID (6 bytes), DB_ROLL_PTR (7 bytes), DB_ROW_ID; insert vs update undo; commit regularly, even read-only; purge; clustered index updated in place, secondary indexes delete-marked. dev.mysql.com returned a "Technical Difficulties" page to curl; read via the Internet Archive copy.
5. [The Part of PostgreSQL We Hate the Most](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~pavlo/blog/2023/04/the-part-of-postgresql-we-hate-the-most.html), Andy Pavlo and Bohan Zhang, 2023. Blog, primary: no. Seen: three MVCC design questions; Postgres O2N chain and index entry per version; HOT; delta storage in MySQL/Oracle; zheap stalled; dead tuples mixed with live ones; vacuum doesn't return pages; secondary index logical ids in MySQL/Oracle; Uber's post got chain direction wrong; 20% scale factor; long-running transactions block autovacuum; Reed 1978 dissertation.
6. [Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL](https://drkp.net/papers/ssi-vldb12.pdf), Ports and Grittner, 2012. See `serializable-snapshot-isolation` #2. Section 5.1: xmin/xmax, snapshot as a set of visible transactions, update = delete + insert, Oracle updates in place with a rollback log; section 3: MVCC replaced a lock manager in 1999.

Extra: [66.7 Heap-Only Tuples](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/storage-hot.html) and [Uber: Why we switched from Postgres to MySQL](https://www.uber.com/blog/postgres-to-mysql-migration/). Notes already existed; cited for HOT and write amplification.

#### `snapshot-isolation` (deep)

1. [A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/tr-95-51.pdf), Berenson, Bernstein, Gray, Melton, O'Neil, O'Neil, 1995. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: section 4.2 defines SI (Start-Timestamp, never blocked reading, Commit-Timestamp, First-committer-wins prevents P4); H5 non-serializable; A5A read skew and A5B write skew; SI stronger than READ COMMITTED; SI vs locking REPEATABLE READ incomparable; SI allows the broad phantom (8-hour tasks) but not strict A3; InterBase 4 and Exchange; time travel; bad for long update transactions. Note already existed.
2. [13.2 Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html), PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: RR snapshot at first non-control statement; RR updater waits for first updater, proceeds on rollback, errors on commit ("could not serialize access due to concurrent update"); retry sees committed change; read-only never fails; read-only batch control-record anomaly; RR is SI; before 9.1 SERIALIZABLE meant SI. Note already existed.
3. [Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL](https://drkp.net/papers/ssi-vldb12.pdf), Ports and Grittner, 2012. See `serializable-snapshot-isolation` #2. Section 2: doctors write skew, three-transaction batch anomaly with a read-only report, Oracle's SERIALIZABLE is SI, the misconception about the three ANSI anomalies, workarounds.
4. [Snapshot Isolation](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/snapshot-isolation), Jepsen. Docs, primary: no. Seen: definition; write conflict rule; write skew and read-only anomaly; SI implies read committed; no real-time constraint; may miss own prior writes across transactions; papers disagree on strictness (Daudjee and Salem strong/weak, Adya's scheduler-dependent SI); Jepsen allows cycles with two adjacent rw edges.
5. [Hermitage](https://github.com/ept/hermitage), Martin Kleppmann and contributors. Code (test suite), primary: no. Seen: summary table: Postgres RR = SI (stops P4, G-single, not G2-item/G2); MySQL RR = monotonic atomic view (P4 not prevented); Oracle serializable = SI; SQL Server "snapshot" = SI; same guarantees, different implementations. Note already existed.
6. [Consistent Nonlocking Reads](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-consistent-read.html), Oracle, MySQL 8.4. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: snapshot fixed by first read at RR; no locks; DML doesn't use the snapshot and can hit rows committed after it; state that never existed. Note already existed; read via Internet Archive copy.

Extra: [Serializable Isolation for Snapshot Databases](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~kubitron/courses/cs262a-F13/handouts/papers/p729-cahill.pdf) (see `serializable-snapshot-isolation` #1) section 1 for a crisp First-Committer-Wins definition.

#### `serializable-snapshot-isolation` (deep)

1. [Serializable Isolation for Snapshot Databases](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~kubitron/courses/cs262a-F13/handouts/papers/p729-cahill.pdf), Cahill, Röhm, Fekete, SIGMOD 2008. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: SSI detects SI anomalies at runtime; readers and writers still don't block; vulnerable edges, dangerous structure, pivot; SIREAD locks don't block; inConflict/outConflict flags; prototype in Berkeley DB. Read from a Berkeley course copy (ACM copy paywalled).
2. [Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL](https://drkp.net/papers/ssi-vldb12.pdf), Ports and Grittner, PVLDB vol. 5, 2012. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: first production SSI (9.1); wr/ww/rw edges; Theorem 1 (two adjacent rw edges, T3 commits first); commit ordering and read-only snapshot ordering optimizations; safe snapshots, DEFERRABLE; conflict detection from MVCC data (write first) or SIREAD locks (read first); B-tree locks at page granularity, next-key planned; safe retry (abort T2); memory bounding (promotion, summarization); evaluation on 9.1 (under 7% vs SI; SIBENCH 10-20% CPU; DBT-2++ 5% in memory, failures under 0.25%; RUBiS 435/422/208 req/s). Note already existed.
3. [README-SSI](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/REL_18_STABLE/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README-SSI), PostgreSQL source (18). Code, primary: yes. Seen: 90% of the code is predicate locking; false positives but never an anomaly; Tin → Tpivot → Tout; roll back only if Tout commits first; read-only optimization; only SERIALIZABLE transactions protected; heap and per-index-type locking (B-tree leaf pages, GIN, GiST, hash); promotion; WAL replay stays at SI (R&D issue). Note already existed (another group); appended.
4. [13.2 Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html), PostgreSQL 18. See `snapshot-isolation` #2. Section 13.2.3: class/value example; SIReadLock in pg_locks; plan-dependent locks; DEFERRABLE the only blocking case; 40001; unique violations; tuning list (READ ONLY, pool, idle in transaction, max_pred_locks_*, sequential scans lock the relation).
5. [13.5 Serialization Failure Handling](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html), PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: 40001 always; retry whole transaction including logic; unique violation as a hidden serialization failure; no automatic retry. Note already existed.
6. [SSI](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/SSI), PostgreSQL wiki. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: write-skew scripts (black/white, overdraft), first committer wins among SSI conflicts, pivot error text. Note already existed.

Extra: [Making Snapshot Isolation Serializable](https://www.cse.iitb.ac.in/infolab/Data/Courses/CS632/2009/Papers/p492-fekete.pdf), Fekete, Liarokapis, O'Neil, O'Neil, Shasha, TODS 2005. Opened (course copy): dangerous structures in the static dependency graph; TPC-C shown serializable under SI; how to modify programs. Not given a note; Ports and Cahill cover the theorem the article needs.

#### `vacuum` (short)

1. [24.1 Routine Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/routine-vacuuming.html), PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: four jobs of VACUUM; plain vs FULL (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, extra disk); space not returned to the OS except trailing pages; steady-state goal; visibility map; XID wraparound (32 bits, modulo-2^32, 2 billion), freezing (flag bit since 9.4), aggressive vacuum, relfrozenxid; 40 million warnings, 3 million stop; recovery steps (end long transactions, drop slots, no single-user mode); multixacts; autovacuum launcher, threshold formula with the new max threshold, anti-wraparound vacuum not interrupted. Note already existed; appended.
2. [19.10 Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-vacuum.html), PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: autovacuum_vacuum_threshold 50, scale factor 0.2, max threshold 100,000,000, naptime 1 min, max_workers 3, freeze_max_age 200 million, vacuum_freeze_min_age 50 million, failsafe 1.6 billion and what it bypasses. Note already existed; appended.

Extra: [PostgreSQL 18 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/18.0/) (autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold is new) and [Purge Configuration](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-purge-configuration.html) (MySQL 8.4; purge threads, history list, purge lag; read via Internet Archive) for the undo-log comparison.

#### `long-running-transactions` (short)

1. [Four reasons why VACUUM won't remove dead rows from a table](https://www.cybertec-postgresql.com/en/reasons-why-vacuum-wont-remove-dead-rows/), Laurenz Albe (CYBERTEC), 2018, updated 2024. Blog, primary: no. Seen: xmin horizon definition; VACUUM VERBOSE "cannot be removed yet"; four causes (long transactions, replication slots, prepared transactions, hot_standby_feedback) each with a finding query and fix.
2. [19.11 Client Connection Defaults](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html), PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout (locks, bloat), transaction_timeout (not recommended in postgresql.conf), idle_session_timeout (idle outside a transaction is cheap), all off by default. Note already existed; appended.

Extra: [PostgreSQL 17 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/17.0/) (transaction_timeout added, old_snapshot_threshold removed); [27.2 Cumulative Statistics System](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/monitoring-stats.html) (pg_stat_activity state, xact_start, backend_xmin); [Purge Configuration](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-purge-configuration.html) (long read-only transactions grow the history list; mysqldump --single-transaction; autocommit off).

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Where MVCC starts: Pavlo and Zhang date Reed's dissertation 1978; Wu et al. say 1979. The article says "late 1970s" and mentions both.
- Postgres's MVCC age: Wu et al. list Postgres MVCC "since 1985" and Pavlo says multi-versioning was designed in from 1987; Ports and Grittner say the original POSTGRES storage manager used a conventional lock manager and MVCC replaced it in 1999. Both hold: old versions were kept (for time travel) before MVCC was the concurrency control. The article says it that way.
- Version chain direction: Uber's 2016 post says newest-to-oldest; Pavlo says oldest-to-newest, and the Postgres page-layout doc (t_ctid points to "this or newer") agrees with Pavlo.
- Pavlo calls the Wu et al. paper "our 2018 VLDB paper"; the PDF is PVLDB vol. 10, 2017. Cited as 2017.
- Postgres's MVCC design itself: Pavlo calls it the worst of the major databases; nobody opened argues the other side in depth. The article gives the criticism and InnoDB's own failure mode (undo growth).
- First-committer-wins (Berenson, Cahill) vs Postgres's behaviour: Postgres checks at update time and makes the second updater wait, then error if the first committed. Same outcome, different moment. Not given a name in the article (no source for "first-updater-wins").
- SI definitions vary (Jepsen: strong vs generalized SI, real-time ordering); relevant mainly for distributed SI.
- SSI cost: Ports and Grittner's numbers are PostgreSQL 9.1 on their hardware. Nothing newer was opened.

**Couldn't open:**

- dev.mysql.com pages directly (curl got a "Technical Difficulties" page). Read the Internet Archive copies of the same URLs instead; noted in each source note.
- Cahill's thesis (ses.library.usyd.edu.au returned an HTML page, no PDF). Not used.
- The CMU 15-721 copy of the Cahill paper (empty response). Used the Berkeley course copy instead.

**Rejected:**

- Cahill thesis: couldn't open, and the SIGMOD paper plus Ports and Grittner cover what's needed.
- Fekete et al. 2005: opened, not needed beyond what Ports and Grittner restate.
- WebFetch summaries of the MySQL pages: model-rewritten text, not usable for word-for-word quotes.

**Gaps:**

- No measured numbers for bloat or vacuum cost that we could stand behind (Pavlo's OtterTune figures, like 46% HOT, aren't reproducible). The vacuum and MVCC articles have no bloat numbers.
- No current (post-9.1) benchmark of SSI vs SI. The lab's done-when ("the throughput cost of serializable vs snapshot isolation is published") would fill this.
- No source opened on Oracle's undo or SQL Server's version store directly; Oracle's design is stated only via Wu et al. and Ports and Grittner.
- Replication slots and hot_standby_feedback are only covered by Albe's post; no Postgres doc page on them was opened.

### Checking

All pages below were opened with `curl -sL`; PDFs converted with
pdftotext, HTML with pandoc. Raw copies kept in the scratchpad while
writing.

#### `history-checking` (deep)

1. [Elle: Inferring Isolation Anomalies from Experimental Observations](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.10554), Kyle Kingsbury and Peter Alvaro, Jepsen and UC Santa Cruz, 2020 (arXiv v1; later PVLDB volume 14). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: hand-written checkers "find a small number of anomalies in a specific pattern of transactions"; serializability checking NP-complete in general, and real time can't prune it; Kingsbury's earlier constraint-solver checker intractable past "a hundred-odd transactions"; Adya's DSG needs the version order, which clients don't see and which can't be taken from real time; ww, wr, rw dependencies; G0, G1a, G1b, G1c, G-single, G2; recoverability (unique values) and traceability (append-only lists); blind register writes "destroy history"; sets are order-free; indeterminate transactions; process edges (strong session SI) and real-time edges (strict serializability); soundness theorem over clean interpretations; Tarjan SCC then BFS per component, filtered subgraphs per anomaly; garbage reads, duplicate writes, internal inconsistency; case studies of TiDB (G-single and lost updates from auto-retry; SELECT FOR UPDATE not locking new rows), YugaByte DB 1.3.1 (G2-item after leader election), FaunaDB 2.6.0 and Dgraph 1.1.1 (internal inconsistency); benchmark vs Knossos on a 24-core Xeon, c! permutations, Knossos stuck at 40+ processes; no predicates, so can't tell repeatable read from serializable. Source note `kingsbury-elle-2020`.
2. [Elle (README)](https://github.com/jepsen-io/elle), Jepsen (Kingsbury, Alvaro and contributors), main branch when this was written. Code, primary: yes. Seen: black-box checker; "~linear in history length, and ~constant ... with respect to concurrency"; three-transaction G1c demo with text explanation; list-append vs rw-register workloads; anomaly list; realtime and process edges; "Elle is not complete"; limits inference to linear or log-linear time on purpose; recommends checking anomalies by hand; optimized checker: 22 million transactions in about two minutes, about 60 GB heap; Knossos limited to a few hundred operations. Source note `jepsen-elle`.
3. [PostgreSQL 12.3](https://jepsen.io/analyses/postgresql-12.3), Kyle Kingsbury, Jepsen, 2020. Analysis, primary: no for Postgres, yes for Elle. Seen: list-append workload as comma-separated TEXT with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT; REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation and allows G2-item (about 140 cycles a minute in one history); SERIALIZABLE allowed G2-item (six cases in a two-minute run), always with a freshly inserted row; cause: SSI conflict check could credit the wrong XID; present from 9.5.22 to 13; isolationtester, Hermitage and the old bank test used hand-proven invariants; Elle can't check predicates, deletes, aggregates; SI forbids G-single but allows G2-item and G2. Source note `jepsen-postgresql-12-3`.
4. [Weak Consistency: A Generalized Theory and Optimistic Implementations for Distributed Transactions](https://publications.csail.mit.edu/lcs/pubs/pdf/MIT-LCS-TR-786.pdf), Atul Adya, MIT PhD thesis (LCS TR-786), 1999. Thesis, primary: yes. Seen: chapter 3 definitions of read-, anti- and write-dependencies (item and predicate), the Direct Serialization Graph over committed transactions, G0, G1a, G1b, G1c (P1 split in three), G2, G2-item, PL-2.99, PL-3 as conflict serializability, lost update DSG (figure 3-4); section 4.1 G-single and PL-2+. Source note `adya-weak-consistency-1999`.
5. [Cobra: Making Transactional Key-Value Stores Verifiably Serializable](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi20-tan.pdf), Cheng Tan, Changgeng Zhao, Shuai Mu, Michael Walfish, OSDI 2020. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: black-box serializability checking is NP-complete; strict variant easier but concurrency and clock drift bring back the hard case; unique ids per write; version order not exposed; polygraph with either-or constraints; acyclic compatible graph iff serializable; MonoSAT SMT solver plus GPU reachability pruning; fence transactions for an unbounded history; 10k transactions in 14 s, 2k txn/s sustained. Source note `tan-cobra-2020`.
6. [On the Complexity of Checking Transactional Consistency](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1908.04509), Ranadeep Biswas and Constantin Enea, arXiv v1 (OOPSLA 2019). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: read committed, read atomic, causal consistency polynomial to check; prefix consistency and snapshot isolation NP-complete; serializability NP-complete (Papadimitriou); polynomial when the number of sessions is fixed; unique values are "without loss of generality". Source note `biswas-checking-transactional-consistency-2019`.

Also opened: [Elle, PVLDB version](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p268-alvaro.pdf) (same method, wording differs from arXiv; quotes taken from arXiv). [Hermitage README](https://github.com/ept/hermitage) (hand-run anomaly tests across databases; a note `kleppmann-hermitage` was made by another group; not cited here). [Jepsen: Serializability](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/serializable) (serializability allows read-only transactions to see the empty state; note `jepsen-serializable` by another group; the same point is in #1, so not cited here).

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Shape the workload or solve the search: Elle picks list-append data so the version order is visible and the check is near linear; Cobra checks ordinary key-value workloads by handing the either-or write orders to an SMT solver. Theory (#6) says SI and SER are NP-complete in general, polynomial for a fixed number of sessions.
- Sound but not complete: Elle can't prove absence of bugs; indeterminate commits and the unread tail hide anomalies, and its README still asks you to hand-check every report.
- Repeatable read: Adya's PL-2.99 forbids G2-item; PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ (snapshot isolation) allows it, which the ANSI wording arguably permits. Jepsen calls the behaviour defensible.
- Biswas and Enea call Jepsen's older checks "ad hoc"; that predates Elle.

**Couldn't open:**
- [Generalized Isolation Level Definitions, ICDE 2000](https://pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/icde00.pdf): https timed out, http returned 403 Forbidden. Used the thesis (#4) instead. Another group has since made a note for it (`adya-generalized-isolation-2000`).
- [pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/adya-phd.pdf](http://pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/adya-phd.pdf): 403. Same thesis opened from the MIT LCS publications server.

**Rejected:**
- Elle talk video (linked from the README): not a page; not watched.
- elle-cli: linked from the README, not opened; not needed for the concept.

**Gaps:**
- No source for how long a history needs to be, or how many clients, to find a given anomaly with good odds. Left out; the lab can measure it.
- No source says which PostgreSQL minor release shipped the SSI fix (the report says only "the next minor release"). Left out.
- Nothing on checking predicate reads from the outside; both Elle sources list it as future work.

## Phase 9: Caching and performance

Researched by 5 parallel passes, one per group below.

### Caching

#### `caching` (deep)

1. [Caching challenges and strategies](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/caching-challenges-and-strategies/), Matt Brinkley, Jas Chhabra, Amazon Builders' Library, no year on the page. Blog, primary: yes (Amazon's own operating experience). Seen: "addicted to its cache" story and modal behavior; cache only helps if results are reused; eventual consistency is inherent; local caches: coherence between servers, load proportional to fleet size, cold start; external caches (Memcached, Redis): another fleet, different availability, fall back carefully (brownout), consistent hashing to add nodes, treat cached format like persistent format, format mismatch causes mass refresh; inline (read-through/write-through) vs side caches; TTL most common expiry, LRU most common eviction; emit hits, misses, size, downstream calls; soft and hard TTL (IAM client); negative caching with its own TTL; poisoning and timing side channels; thundering herd fixed with request coalescing; run load tests with caches disabled. Note: `aws-caching-challenges`.
2. [Caches, Modes, and Unstable Systems](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2021/08/27/caches.html), Marc Brooker, 2021. Blog, primary: no. Seen: cache in front of a DB gives two stable loops (full and empty), a metastable system; load tests rarely find the bad loop; "caches extract cacheability"; locality/skew assumptions aren't enforced; CPU caches are safe because slowness reduces offered load; good caches have feedback (back pressure, limited concurrency). Note: `brooker-caches-modes-2021`.
3. [Scaling Memcache at Facebook](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/nsdi13/nsdi13-final170_update.pdf), Nishtala et al., NSDI 2013. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: demand-filled look-aside cache; delete on write because deletes are idempotent; stale data as a tuned parameter; 521 items per popular page; consistent hashing; leases (64-bit token, one per 10 s per key, 17K/s to 1.3K/s peak DB queries); stale values; pools for churn; Gutter (about 1% of servers); mcsqueal invalidation from the commit log (only 4% of deletes hit cached data); cold cluster warmup with 2 s hold-off; remote markers across regions; LRU per slab class; lazy expiry; upgrades take over 12 hours; pool miss rates (Table 2); invalidation reliability nines (7.3). Note: `nishtala-memcache-2013`.
4. [A large scale analysis of hundreds of in-memory cache clusters at Twitter](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi20-yang.pdf), Yang, Yue, Rashmi, OSDI 2020. Paper, primary: yes (co-written by Twitter's cache lead). Seen: 153 Twemcache clusters, about 700 billion requests; look-aside; eight of top ten under 5% miss, six near or under 1%, a write-heavy one near 70%; max/min miss ratio under 1.5 for most; extremely low miss ratios are least robust; >35% of clusters write-heavy; TTL from minutes to days bounds the working set, expire before evict; approximate Zipf; FIFO often close to LRU; three use cases (storage, computation, transient). Note: `yang-twitter-cache-2020`.
5. [Key eviction](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/), Redis docs (latest; mentions Redis 8.6). Docs, primary: yes. Seen (for this node): hit ratio from INFO keyspace_hits and keyspace_misses; maxmemory. Note: `redis-eviction`. See also `eviction-policies` #5.
6. [Cache made consistent](https://engineering.fb.com/2022/06/08/core-infra/cache-made-consistent/), Lu Pan (Meta), 2022. Blog, primary: yes. Seen (for this node): TAO serves over a quadrillion queries a day; at 99% hits still over 10 trillion fills a day. See `cache-invalidation` #1.

#### `caching-patterns` (short)

1. [Cache-Aside pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center. Docs, primary: no. Seen: three-step read; write updates store then invalidates; cache-aside emulates read-through; expiry trade-off; no consistency guarantee, external processes change the store; staleness window after writes vs write-through; local caches diverge; not worth it when most requests miss; order note: update store before removing the cached item, else a reader re-adds the old value; example with 5-minute expiry. Note: `microsoft-cache-aside`.
2. [Caching Data Sources](https://docs.oracle.com/en/middleware/fusion-middleware/coherence/14.1.2/develop-applications/caching-data-sources.html), Oracle Coherence 14.1.2, chapter 15. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: read-through, write-through (put waits for the store, no write speedup), write-behind (delay, write-coalescing, write-combining, requeue on failure, must never fail or handle rollback, reordering, conflicts with external writers, cache is system of record until queue drains), refresh-ahead (factor of expiry, triggered on access near expiry, only helps with accurate prediction); cache-aside in a cluster causes duplicate DB visits or needs clustered locking. Note: `oracle-coherence-caching-data-sources`.
3. [Caching patterns (Database Caching Strategies Using Redis)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/database-caching-strategies-using-redis/caching-patterns.html), AWS whitepaper. Docs, primary: no. Seen: cache-aside (reactive, most common, only requested data, extra round trips on a miss) and write-through as app updating DB then cache (proactive, almost always combined with lazy loading, fills cache with unread data; add expiration). Note: `aws-database-caching-strategies`.
4. See `caching` #3 (Facebook look-aside, delete not update).

#### `cache-invalidation` (deep)

1. [Cache made consistent](https://engineering.fb.com/2022/06/08/core-infra/cache-made-consistent/), Lu Pan (Meta), 2022. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: definition of invalidation; TTL-only caches out of scope; x=42 fill vs x=43 invalidation race; versions fail if the newer entry is evicted; inconsistency can look like data loss (messaging split-brain story); dynamic caches mutate on fill and invalidation; Polaris measures a client-observable invariant with multi-timescale checks; TAO from six to ten nines within five minutes; consistency tracing; bug in error handler that dropped only older versions. Note: `meta-cache-made-consistent-2022`.
2. See `caching` #3 (delete on write, leases against stale sets, mcsqueal, replay from commit log, web server invalidates own cluster, replica regions and remote markers, measured invalidation latency).
3. [How Uber Serves Over 40 Million Reads Per Second from Online Storage Using an Integrated Cache](https://www.uber.com/blog/how-uber-serves-over-40-million-reads-per-second-using-an-integrated-cache/), Pozniansky, Patel, Narayanareddy (Uber), 2024. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: default 5-minute TTL, lowering it hurts hit rate without much consistency gain; conditional updates can't be invalidated in the write path; Flux tails MySQL binlog (CDC) to invalidate or upsert in Redis; consistent within seconds; no uncommitted data; stale write race fixed with row timestamp as version in a Lua script; explicit invalidation API for read-your-own-writes; Compare Cache shadow reads, 99.99% consistent; negative caching; 6M RPS at 99% hits; opt-in, strong flows bypass the cache. (curl needed browser Accept headers; the default fetch returned "Not Acceptable".) Note: `uber-cachefront-2024`.
4. See `caching-patterns` #1 (update store then delete; external processes).
5. See `caching` #1 (soft and hard TTL, negative caching, local cache coherence).

#### `cache-stampede` (short)

1. [Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention](https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~avattani/papers/cache_stampede.pdf), Vattani, Chierichetti, Lowenstein, PVLDB 8(8), 2015. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: definition and other names; size = rate × recompute time (10/s × 3 s = 30); cascading; fixes: external recompute, locking (extra write, lock TTL, not fault-tolerant), probabilistic early expiration (Perl CHI uses uniform); exponential gap is optimal and rate-independent; XFetch pseudo-code with delta and beta; Goodreads trace results (most stampedes size 1 or 2, none above 8 at 10 s recompute). Note: `vattani-cache-stampede-2015`.
2. [singleflight](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/singleflight), Go authors, x/sync v0.23.0. Code/docs, primary: yes. Seen: Do runs one call per key, duplicates wait and share results; DoChan; Forget. Note: `go-singleflight`.
3. See `caching` #3 (leases: token rate per key, waiting clients, stale values, 17K/s to 1.3K/s).
4. See `caching` #1 (request coalescing, in caches and proxies like Nginx and Varnish).

#### `eviction-policies` (deep)

1. [ARC: A Self-Tuning, Low Overhead Replacement Cache](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/fast03/tech/full_papers/megiddo/megiddo.pdf), Megiddo, Modha (IBM), FAST 2003. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: Belady's MIN as upper bound; LRU captures recency not frequency; LFU drawbacks; two LRU lists, directory of 2c pages (ghosts), adaptive split, constant time, scan-resistant, no tuning. The PDF's math font doesn't extract, so the hit-ratio numbers in the abstract couldn't be read. Note: `megiddo-arc-2003`.
2. [TinyLFU: A Highly Efficient Cache Admission Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.00727), Einziger, Friedman, Manes, arXiv v2 2015 (ACM TOS 2017). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: admission vs eviction; LFU best under a fixed distribution; LRU needs bigger caches; counting Bloom filter with minimal increment; CM-Sketch less accurate per space but faster; reset (halving); counters capped at W/C; doorkeeper Bloom filter; W-TinyLFU (window LRU, SLRU 80/20, 1% window in Caffeine 2.0), 8 bytes per entry, no ghosts; sample 10x cache size. Note: `einziger-tinylfu-2015`.
3. [FIFO Queues are All You Need for Cache Eviction](https://jasony.me/publication/sosp23-s3fifo.pdf), Yang, Zhang, Qiu, Yue, Rashmi, SOSP 2023. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: LRU's pointer and locking costs; one-hit wonders 26% whole-trace vs 72% in 10% windows (6594 traces); S3-FIFO design (S 10%, M 90%, G ghosts, 2-bit counters); 6x throughput vs optimized LRU at 16 threads; best on 10 of 14 datasets; Bloom-filter admission too blunt; TinyLFU with a 1% window closest competitor but worse than FIFO on some traces, 10% window helps; adversarial "twice with a gap" pattern for partitioned caches; flash caches use FIFO. Note: `yang-s3-fifo-2023`.
4. [Efficiency](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/wiki/Efficiency), Ben Manes, Caffeine wiki. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: LRU poor on full scans; ARC doubles keys and is patented (IBM license); LIRS triples keys; W-TinyLFU with hill-climbing window, 4-bit CountMinSketch, 8 bytes per entry, no retained evicted keys; charts against Belady's optimal on Wikipedia, Glimpse, database, search, OLTP traces. Note: `caffeine-efficiency`.
5. [Key eviction](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/), Redis docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: policies incl. allkeys-lru default advice, volatile-* act like noeviction without TTLs; sampled LRU (maxmemory-samples 5, pool since 3.0, close to true LRU on power-law); LFU since 4.0 with Morris counters, lfu-log-factor 10, lfu-decay-time 1; LRM since 8.6. Note: `redis-eviction`.
6. See `caching` #4 (FIFO often close to LRU; expire before evict).
7. [Why Aren't We SIEVE-ing?](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2023/12/15/sieve.html), Marc Brooker, 2023. Blog, primary: no. Seen: eviction trades accuracy, speed, metadata; SIEVE sets a bit on access like CLOCK; SIEVE authors conjecture it wasn't found because it isn't scan-resistant; scans matter for block and file caches; SIEVE-k worse on web KV traces, mixed on block; block traces are the residue after upstream caching. Note: `brooker-sieve-2023`.

#### `count-min-sketch` (short)

1. [An Improved Data Stream Summary: The Count-Min Sketch and its Applications](https://dsf.berkeley.edu/cs286/papers/countmin-latin2004.pdf), Cormode, Muthukrishnan, LATIN 2004 (hosted on a Berkeley course page). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: named for count then min; w = ⌈e/ε⌉, d = ⌈ln 1/δ⌉, pairwise-independent hashes; update adds to one counter per row; estimate is the min; Theorem 1 bound for non-negative counts; O(ln 1/δ) time. Note: `cormode-count-min-2004`.
2. [FrequencySketch.java](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/blob/master/caffeine/src/main/java/com/github/benmanes/caffeine/cache/FrequencySketch.java), Ben Manes, Caffeine source (master when v3.3.0 was the latest release). Code, primary: yes. Seen: 4-bit counters capped at 15; depth 4; table sized from maximum size; 93.75% confidence, error e/width; counters in one 64-byte block; reset halves counters; sample size 10x maximum; increments all four counters. Note: `caffeine-frequency-sketch`.
3. See `eviction-policies` #2 (reset, small counters, doorkeeper, conservative update).

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- **S3-FIFO vs W-TinyLFU.** The S3-FIFO paper finds TinyLFU (fixed 1% window) worse than FIFO on a share of traces and blames the small window; Caffeine's current W-TinyLFU adapts the window by hill climbing, which the paper's comparison didn't use. No independent comparison opened.
- **FIFO vs LRU.** Folklore and the ARC/TinyLFU papers treat LRU as more efficient than FIFO; the Twitter study finds FIFO often close to LRU at reasonable sizes, and S3-FIFO beats LRU-based designs. Brooker's SIEVE post: FIFO-style policies struggle with scans, which matter for block caches.
- **Delete vs update on write.** Facebook deletes (idempotent); AWS's "write-through" and Uber's CDC consumer upsert new values into the cache, with a version check to stop stale writes.
- **Invalidation source.** Application-driven deletes (Microsoft pattern) vs log-driven (Facebook mcsqueal, Uber Flux). Both big systems still add a synchronous delete for read-your-own-writes.
- **What "write-through" means.** Coherence: the cache writes the database. AWS: the application writes the database, then the cache.
- **Thundering herd vs stampede.** Facebook calls the hot-key invalidation problem a thundering herd; Vattani calls expiry-driven recompute a stampede; the graph's `thundering-herd` node is about retries.
- **Conservative update.** TinyLFU's paper uses minimal increment for its counting Bloom filter; Caffeine's sketch increments all four counters.

**Gaps:**

- No numbers on how big stampedes get in production beyond Facebook's 17K/s vs 1.3K/s and the Goodreads trace.

#### `redis-internals` (deep)

1. [Diagnosing latency issues](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/optimization/latency/), Redis. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: checklist (slow log, THP off, intrinsic latency, durability vs latency table); "Single threaded nature of Redis" (one request at a time via multiplexing, like Node.js, doesn't block on socket system calls, background threads for disk I/O since 2.4); slow commands (SORT, LREM, SUNION; KEYS in production is the classic cause; SCAN family since 2.8); fork cost (page table 24 GB / 4 kB * 8 = 48 MB; fork runs in the main thread; table of fork times, 62 ms for 6.9 GB on a physical Xeon, 1460 ms for 6.1 GB on old Xen EC2); THP after fork; swapping; AOF write and fdatasync, everysec delays write up to two seconds; active expiry every 100 ms sampling 20 keys, repeats above 25% expired; software watchdog. Note already existed (phase 1); appended.
2. [Redis FAQ](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/get-started/faq/), Redis. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: data types map to data structures; in-memory so dataset ≤ RAM; memory footprint examples (empty ~3 MB, 1M small keys ~85 MB, 1M 5-field hashes ~160 MB); 64-bit pointers 8 bytes; maxmemory errors; fork and overcommit_memory (3 GB dataset, 2 GB free fails); snapshots atomic because fork happens between commands; CPU rarely the bottleneck, "1 million requests per second" with pipelining (no hardware given); several instances to use cores; threaded actions since 4.0 (background delete). The multi-core answer predates 6.0/8.0 I/O threads.
3. [Memory optimization](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/optimization/memory-optimization/), Redis. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: special encoding of small aggregates since 2.2, up to 10x less memory (5x average); thresholds for ≤6.2 (ziplist) and ≥7.0 (listpack), 7.2 adds set listpack; automatic conversion; 32-bit builds; bitmaps (100 M users in 12 MB); hashes as a memory-efficient key-value store, O(N) linear array with length-prefixed pairs, better cache locality than a hash table.
4. [OBJECT ENCODING](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/object-encoding/), Redis. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: since 2.2.3; strings raw/int/embstr (44 bytes); lists linkedlist (old), ziplist (≤6.2), listpack (≥7.0), quicklist; sets hashtable/intset/listpack (≥7.2); hashes zipmap (old)/hashtable/ziplist/listpack; sorted sets skiplist/ziplist/listpack; streams radix tree of listpacks; automatic conversion to the general type.

Seen (unstable branch, same text at tag 8.10.2 for the parts used): THREADED I/O (mostly single-threaded, io-threads off by default, 4+ cores, reads/writes/parsing); LAZY FREEING (DEL blocks, UNLINK/ASYNC, lazyfree-lazy-* default no); encoding thresholds; SNAPSHOTTING defaults; APPEND ONLY MODE (appendfsync, no-appendfsync-on-rewrite 30 s, aof-use-rdb-preamble). Unstable also has a new "hash template" encoding (hash-min-template-entries, default 0) not in the docs pages. Note already existed (another group); appended.

Seen: "kinda" single-threaded, bio.c; DEL of 50M elements blocks for seconds; incremental work (eviction, expiry, rehashing) in a single-threaded server; adaptive incremental lazy free, then threaded; performance dominated by cache misses; removing robj sharing, less indirection made everything faster; UNLINK decides by free cost; unsharing makes threaded I/O possible. Year from the page's "4021 days ago"; the ETA section (3.4) is out of date.
7. [Async IO Threads, redis/redis PR 13695](https://github.com/redis/redis/pull/13695), ShooterIT and Redis contributors, 2024. Code (design write-up in the PR), primary: yes. Seen: 6.0 I/O threads (main thread blocked waiting, busy-waiting, TLS race); new design with per-thread event loops, main thread only executes commands; event-notified client queues (eventfd or pipe); pause/resume of I/O threads; least-clients assignment, INFO THREADS; replica/monitor/pub-sub/tracking clients stay on main; client eviction and defrag trade-offs; PING benchmark 1.61M ops/s, 15 I/O threads, Ryzen 7950X; low io-threads barely help GET/SET; top -H to find the bottleneck. Redis 8.0 release notes (raw.githubusercontent.com/redis/redis/8.0/00-RELEASENOTES) confirm it shipped in 8.0-M03 and io-threads-do-reads is gone.

#### `redis-persistence` (short)

1. [Redis persistence](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/persistence/), Redis. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: RDB/AOF/none/both; RDB pros/cons (parent never does disk I/O, faster restarts, lose minutes, fork stalls ms to 1 s); AOF pros/cons (fsync policies, background fsync thread, redis-check-aof, bigger files, pre-7.0 rewrite buffered and written twice); "use both for PostgreSQL-like safety", AOF alone discouraged; snapshot steps (fork, temp file, replace, copy-on-write); AOF since 1.1; multi-part AOF since 7.0 (base, incr, manifest); rewriting (100 INCRs), automatic since 2.4; appendfsync always/everysec/no, group commit, Linux flush every 30 s; truncated vs corrupted AOF; rewrite steps for ≥7.0 and <7.0; switching to AOF safely; no rewrite during BGSAVE; AOF preferred at load; backups (RDB never modified, rename(2)).
2. [redis.conf](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/redis/redis/unstable/redis.conf). See redis-internals #5. Default save points (3600/1, 300/100, 60/10000), stop-writes-on-bgsave-error, appendfsync modes, no-appendfsync-on-rewrite (up to 30 s), aof-use-rdb-preamble, process crash vs power outage loss for everysec.
3. [Diagnosing latency issues](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/optimization/latency/). See redis-internals #1. Fork cost table, THP, AOF write/fdatasync, the two-second everysec delay.

Seen: five steps from client to platter; process crash vs power failure; POSIX write vs fsync; AOF buffer written once per event loop iteration; appendfsync no still writes before replying; everysec worst case two seconds; comparison with other databases (2012-era). Not given a note: the current docs and redis.conf cover the same claims, and the post predates the multi-part AOF.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- How much everysec loses: the persistence page says "you can only lose one second worth of writes", while the latency page and the 2012 antirez post describe the write being delayed up to two seconds when fsync is slow. The article says "about 1 second, up to 2".
- Threads: the FAQ still says threading is "limited to deleting objects in the background" (as of 4.0), while redis.conf and the 8.0 PR describe I/O threads for reads, parsing and writes. The article follows the newer sources.
- Redis and Valkey both kept single-threaded command execution but built their new I/O threads separately; Valkey also moves epoll_wait around between threads and prefetches keys. Each team's benchmark is its own (PING on a Ryzen for Redis, SET on Graviton for Valkey), so they can't be compared.

### Finding the bottleneck

#### `use-method` (short)

1. [The USE Method](https://www.brendangregg.com/usemethod.html), Brendan Gregg, 2012 (updated 2017). Blog by the method's creator, primary: yes. Seen: "for every resource, check utilization, saturation, and errors"; definitions (utilization as busy time, with a second capacity-used definition; saturation as queued work; errors as counts); generic server resource list; example metric table and harder metrics (interconnects, controllers); about thirty metrics in total; known-unknowns; software resources (mutexes, thread pools, process and fd limits); interpretations (100% a bottleneck, trouble from about 70%, any saturation matters); five-minute averages under 80% hiding seconds at 100%; cloud and cgroup limits as resources; flowchart, errors first; "80% of server issues with 5% of the effort" (author's estimate); tools method anti-pattern; Apollo guidance computer example.
2. [PSI - Pressure Stall Information](https://docs.kernel.org/accounting/psi.html), Johannes Weiner, Linux kernel docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `/proc/pressure/{cpu,memory,io}`; "some" vs "full" lines; 10/60/300 s averages plus total stall time in µs; CPU full reported as zero since 5.13; poll()-able triggers with 500 ms to 10 s windows; per-cgroup `*.pressure` files; motivation (load shedding, sizing). No version given for when PSI was added.

Extra: [USE Method: Linux Performance Checklist](https://www.brendangregg.com/USEmethod/use-linux.html), Brendan Gregg. Opened: per-resource Linux commands (vmstat "r" > CPU count for CPU saturation, iostat %util and avgqu-sz, sar -n EDEV, ifconfig drops/overruns). Not given a note: uses older tools (ifconfig, dstat), and the short node only needs the method.

#### `red-method` (short)

1. [The RED Method: How to Instrument Your Services](https://grafana.com/blog/2018/08/02/the-red-method-how-to-instrument-your-services/), Julie Dam (Grafana Labs) reporting Tom Wilkie's talk, 2018. Blog, primary: no (Wilkie quoted, not the author). Seen: RED created by Wilkie in 2015; rate, errors, duration definitions; "USE doesn't really apply to services"; memory utilization is tricky for USE; "some distribution of latency"; consistency across services lets people go on call for code they didn't write; proxy for customer happiness, good for alerts and SLAs; four golden signals = RED + saturation; CPU vs quota as a saturation proxy; use RED and USE together.
2. [Monitoring Distributed Systems](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/), Rob Ewaschuk, Google SRE book ch. 6. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation); latency of errors vs successes, slow errors worse than fast ones; errors explicit, implicit and by policy; traffic as requests per second for web services; saturation as fullness of the most constrained resource, latency as a leading indicator, predictions of impending saturation; worrying about the tail (100 ms average at 1,000 rps with 1% at 5 s, as an illustration); exponential latency buckets by factors of about 3.

Extra: [Grafana dashboard best practices](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/dashboards/build-dashboards/best-practices/), Grafana docs. Opened: USE tells how happy machines are, RED how happy users are; USE reports causes, RED symptoms; alert on RED. Not given a note (restates the blog).

#### `flame-graphs` (short)

1. [Flame Graphs](https://www.brendangregg.com/flamegraphs.html), Brendan Gregg. Official page by the inventor, primary: yes. Seen: x-axis is the sorted sample population, not time; y-axis stack depth; width = frequency; top edge on-CPU; random warm colours; interactive hover, zoom, search with cumulative percentage; icicle graphs, flame charts (time on x, from Chrome's WebKit Web Inspector, can't show many threads), sunbursts; mislabelled flame charts; origin in a MySQL issue, switch from tracing to sampling; released 2011; `perf script report flamegraph`; getting good stacks is the hard part.
2. [CPU Flame Graphs](https://www.brendangregg.com/FlameGraphs/cpuflamegraphs.html), Brendan Gregg. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: perf report over 8,000 lines, first screen 3% of samples; description of boxes, axes, width, colours; call counts not known; samples can exceed elapsed time; capture, fold, render; grep the folded file; perf -F 99 -a -g; 99 and 199 Hz to avoid lockstep; bcc profile(8) aggregates in the kernel; missing frame pointers lose towers; JVM JIT symbols and frame pointer register; interrupt "hair"; NUMA rebalancing example on Ubuntu 14.04.

#### `ebpf` (deep)

1. [What is eBPF?](https://ebpf.io/what-is-ebpf/), eBPF.io. Project site, primary: yes (promotional in places). Seen: sandboxed programs in the kernel without source changes or modules; name no longer an acronym, cBPF vs eBPF; hooks (syscalls, function entry/exit, tracepoints, network events, kprobes, uprobes); usually used via Cilium, bcc, bpftrace; LLVM to bytecode; bpf() loads; verifier (privileges, no crash, runs to completion, bounded loops only if provably exiting, no uninitialised reads or out-of-bounds, complexity limit, "safety tool, not a security tool"); hardening (read-only, Spectre mitigations, constant blinding); JIT; maps (hash, array, LRU, ring buffer, stack trace, LPM); helpers; tail calls; CAP_BPF; toolchains bcc, bpftrace, Go, libbpf, Rust (aya).
2. [bpf(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/bpf.2.html), man-pages 6.19. Man page, primary: yes. Seen: one syscall for maps and programs; kernel statically analyses cBPF and eBPF; verifier determines termination and safety; events trigger programs, maps share data with user space; program type decides helpers; EINVAL for infinite loops or unknown calls; Linux 3.18; CAP_SYS_ADMIN before 4.4, limited unprivileged socket filters since; unprivileged_bpf_disabled; JIT per architecture with versions.
3. [eBPF verifier](https://docs.kernel.org/bpf/verifier.html), Linux kernel docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: two steps (CFG/DAG check, then simulate all paths); register types (PTR_TO_CTX, SCALAR_VALUE, map pointers); unwritten registers unreadable; pointer + pointer = scalar; bounds and alignment checks; stack read only after write; helper argument checks per program type; range tracking per register and stack slot; map lookups return OR_NULL until checked. Still says "DAG check to disallow loops".
4. [Bounded loops in BPF for the 5.3 kernel](https://lwn.net/Articles/794934/), Marta Rybczyńska, LWN, 2019. Article, primary: no. Seen: loops rejected before 5.3, unrolled by hand or pragma; limit raised from 4096 instructions to one million in 5.2; loops verified by simulating iterations as states; state pruning; 80% of saved states never matched; pruning points every ten instructions, up to 20% faster; register-to-register comparisons; precise scalar tracking by backtracking.
5. [bpftrace One-Liner Tutorial](https://bpftrace.org/tutorial-one-liners), Brendan Gregg, bpftrace project, 2018. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: 12 lessons; probes; tracepoint openat; tracepoints preferred for stable API; maps and count(); hist() power-of-2; kretprobe vfs_read; timing vfs_read by tid; profile:hz:99 and why 99; sched_switch stacks; block_rq_issue; BTF makes all kernel structs available.
6. [Off-CPU Analysis](https://www.brendangregg.com/offcpuanalysis.html), see profiling #4. Used for the perf vs eBPF overhead comparison and cpudist's anatomy.
7. [strace Wow Much Syscall](https://www.brendangregg.com/blog/2014-05-11/strace-wow-much-syscall.html), existing note gregg-strace-overhead-2014. Used for the strace comparison (442x worst case).

Extra: [Linux Extended BPF (eBPF) Tracing Tools](https://www.brendangregg.com/ebpf.html), Brendan Gregg. Opened: event sources (kprobes, uprobes, tracepoints, perf_events); bcc vs bpftrace front ends; one-liner tools (execsnoop, opensnoop, biolatency, tcpretrans); prerequisites Linux 4.4 and CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL; says the verifier doesn't allow loops. Not given a note; ebpf.io and bpftrace cover it more currently.
Extra: [A thorough introduction to eBPF](https://lwn.net/Articles/740157/), Matt Fleming, LWN, 2017. Opened: eBPF by Alexei Starovoitov, 64-bit registers and ten of them instead of two, exposed to user space in 2014, up to 4x faster than cBPF on some microbenchmarks, verifier stages and pruning, program types. Not given a note; history not needed in the article.
Extra: [bpftrace README](https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace), opened: LLVM backend and libbpf; probe types. Not given a note.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Loops in eBPF: Gregg's eBPF tools page and the kernel's own verifier page still say loops are disallowed; ebpf.io and LWN say bounded loops have been accepted since Linux 5.3. The article goes with 5.3 and flags the stale wording.
- Flame graph vs icicle layout: Gregg prefers flames, many tools default to icicles. The article says read them the same way.
- Frame pointers: compiler developers dropped them for speed (2004); profiler authors argue the cost (usually under 1%, up to 10% in microbenchmarks) is worth it. Fedora and Ubuntu 24.04 sided with profiling.
- USE vs RED: RED's creator says USE doesn't fit services and is awkward for memory; the two are presented as complementary (USE for causes, RED for symptoms).
- The USE method's "80% of server issues" is the author's estimate, not a measurement; the article labels it so.

**Couldn't open:**

- ACM Queue "Thinking Methodically about Performance" (USE, 2012) and "The Flame Graph" (2016): queue.acm.org and cacm.acm.org blocked the requests (Cloudflare / 403).
- Netflix tech blog "Linux Performance Analysis in 60,000 Milliseconds": the page returned a block page.
- Mytkowicz et al., "Evaluating the Accuracy of Java Profilers" (PLDI 2010): the ACM PDF returned an HTML block page; only the line quoted in Wakart's post is used.
- Weaveworks' original RED blog post: the domain returned nothing.

**Rejected:**

- Gregg's USE Linux checklist, eBPF tools page, LWN's 2017 eBPF introduction, runtime/pprof, async-profiler and Grafana's dashboard docs as cited sources: opened and useful, but the chosen notes cover the same ground more directly or more currently (listed as Extra above).

**Gaps:**

- No opened source gives the Linux version that added PSI; the use-method article gives none.
- No source gives perf's default sampling frequency or a measured CPU-profiling overhead for Go; the articles give none.
- No source opened says when CAP_BPF was added; not versioned.
- No experiment of our own: overhead numbers are Gregg's single test and are labelled as such. A lab run (strace vs bpftrace on the same read-heavy load) would fit the phase 9 profiling work.

### Queues and limits

#### `littles-law` (short)

1. [Little's Law as Viewed on Its 50th Anniversary](https://people.cs.umass.edu/~emery/classes/cmpsci691st/readings/OS/Littles-Law-50-Years-Later.pdf), John D. C. Little, MIT Sloan, 2011 (Operations Research 59(3)). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: definition of L, λ, W; proof over a finite window by the area under n(t) (L = A/T, λ = N/T, W = A/N), exact over a measured window; "An item in queue is also waiting"; holds without steady state, independent of queue discipline, without a service step, per class of item; "measurement business, not the forecasting business"; know two, get the third; §4.1 servers (W = latency), a Microsoft FAST Search load test of an Intel server where queues grew then requests were dumped after about 18 requests/second, and service rate fell as L grew. Note: `little-littles-law-50-years-2011`.
2. [Telling Stories About Little's Law](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2018/06/20/littles-law.html), Marc Brooker (AWS), 2018. Blog, primary: no. Seen: L = λW as long-term averages with λ and W independent; concurrency as a measure of capacity (threads, connections, file handles); W rises with L (Amdahl, USL); three client behaviours (closed: λ ∝ 1/W, Poisson: independent, timeout and retry: λ rises with W); "scary cliffs"; means hide percentiles; cron jobs as the biggest spike source; a difference-equation "story" model. Note: `brooker-littles-law-stories-2018`.
3. [Little's Law (chapter, Little and Graves)](http://web.mit.edu/sgraves/www/papers/Little's%20Law-Published.pdf), John D. C. Little, Stephen C. Graves, MIT. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: the URL returned an HTML page, not the PDF. Not cited.

#### `queueing-theory` (deep)

1. [Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems, chapter 1](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~harchol/PerformanceModeling/chpt1.pdf), Mor Harchol-Balter, CMU, 2013 (Cambridge University Press; free first chapter). Book, primary: yes. Seen: definition; queues in CPU, disk, routers, memory, lock queues, server farms; capacity planning as a main use; Markovian assumptions simplify but fail with highly variable or correlated job sizes; design examples: doubling λ needs less than double μ (λ = 3, μ = 5), a faster server barely helps a closed system of 6 jobs but helps the open one, one fast vs many slow depends on job-size variability and load, task assignment policies. Note: `harchol-balter-performance-modeling-2013`.
2. [Latency Sneaks Up On You](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2021/08/05/utilization.html), Marc Brooker, 2021. Blog, primary: no. Seen: ρ = λ/μ, idle 1 − ρ, E[N] = ρ/(1−ρ) (1 at 0.5, 99 at 0.99; printed with a typo), efficiency gains lost as ρ climbs back, high percentiles as a leading indicator of overload, defends mean latency for efficiency, M/M/1 assumptions, implicit queues. Note: `brooker-latency-sneaks-up-2021`.
3. [Surprising Economics of Load-Balanced Systems](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2020/08/06/erlang.html), Marc Brooker, 2020. Blog, primary: no. Seen: M/M/c at 80% per server; mean latency falls toward the service time as c grows; Erlang C: 87% vs 96.4% served without queueing at half load for 5 vs 10 servers; simulated p50/p99/p99.9 follow the mean; service times more like log-normal. Note: `brooker-load-balanced-economics-2020`.
4. [The most important thing to understand about queues](https://blog.danslimmon.com/2016/08/26/the-most-important-thing-to-understand-about-queues/), Dan Slimmon, 2016. Blog, primary: no. Seen: wait approaches infinity near maximum throughput; 100% utilization is equivalent to an unbounded queue; qsim simulation (Poisson, exponential, 1 task/s) turns "a little crazy around 80%", 20 s mean wait at 96%; three levers (capacity, demand, bound the queue). Note: `slimmon-queues-2016`.
5. [Kingman's formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingman%27s_formula), Wikipedia. Encyclopedia, primary: no. Seen: G/G/1 mean wait ≈ ρ/(1−ρ) × (ca² + cs²)/2 × τ; "VUT"; Kingman 1961; accurate near saturation. Note: `wikipedia-kingmans-formula`.
6. [Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 22: Addressing Cascading Failures](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/), Mike Ulrich, Google, 2016. Book, primary: yes. Seen (for this node): CPU overload raises in-flight requests and uses memory, threads, file descriptors and caches worse; queue 10x threads at 100 ms gives about 1.1 s; queues ≤50% of the pool for steady traffic; Gmail queueless servers. Note: `google-sre-cascading-failures` (appended).
7. [M/M/1 queue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M/M/1_queue), Wikipedia. Encyclopedia, primary: no. Seen: stability λ < μ, mean number ρ/(1−ρ), mean response time 1/(μ − λ) via Little's law. Not cited: the same results follow from Brooker #2 plus Little's law.

#### `amdahls-law` (short)

1. [Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities](https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~rezaul/Spring-2012/CSE613/reading/Amdahl-1967.pdf), Gene M. Amdahl, IBM, 1967 (IEEE SSCS News reprint, 2007, on a Stony Brook course page). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: no equations, one figure; housekeeping 40% of instructions, limit of five to seven times; parallel effort wasted unless sequential speed keeps up; two processors with shared memory: about 2.2x hardware for about 1.8x performance. Note: `amdahl-single-processor-1967`.
2. [Reevaluating Amdahl's Law](http://www.johngustafson.net/pubs/pub13/amdahl.htm), John L. Gustafson, Sandia, 1988 (year from his "Gustafson's Law" page). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: Speedup = (s + p)/(s + p/N), limit 1/s; speedups 1021, 1020, 1016 on 1,024 processors with s = 0.4–0.8%; p isn't independent of N; fix run time, not problem size; scaled speedup N + (1 − N)s'. Note: `gustafson-reevaluating-amdahl-1988`.
3. [A General Theory of Computational Scalability Based on Rational Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/0808.1431), Neil J. Gunther, Performance Dynamics, 2008 (arXiv v2). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: Amdahl p/(1 + σ(p−1)), Gustafson σ + (1−σ)p, USL p/(1 + σ(p−1) + κp(p−1)); σ contention, κ coherency; peak at √((1−σ)/κ), retrograde beyond; Table 1 examples (reservation systems, database updates); all are bounds of a machine-repairman queue. Note: `gunther-scalability-rational-functions-2008`.
4. [How to Quantify Scalability](http://www.perfdynamics.com/Manifesto/USLscalability.html), Neil J. Gunther. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: opened (first try returned 403, second worked); supplements his Guerrilla Capacity Planning book chapters on the USL. Not cited: the arXiv paper is the citable form.
5. [Amdahl's Law in the Multicore Era](https://research.cs.wisc.edu/multifacet/papers/ieeecomputer08_amdahl_multicore.pdf), Mark D. Hill, Michael R. Marty, 2008 (IEEE Computer). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: a corollary of Amdahl's law for chips built from base core equivalents; argues for both more parallelism and faster sequential cores. Not cited: about chip design, not services.
6. [Scalability! But at what COST?](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/hotos15/hotos15-paper-mcsherry.pdf), Frank McSherry, Michael Isard, Derek G. Murray, HotOS 2015. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: COST = the configuration that outperforms a single thread; many published graph systems never beat one thread. Not cited (would push a short node to four sources); good for "scaling isn't speed".

#### `capacity-planning` (short)

1. [Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 1: Introduction](https://sre.google/sre-book/introduction/), Benjamin Treynor Sloss, Google, 2016. Book, primary: yes. Seen: capacity planning = capacity and redundancy for projected demand; organic vs inorganic growth; forecast beyond the lead time; regular load tests correlating raw to service capacity; provisioning riskier than load shifting; a slowdown is lost capacity; capacity targets are at a response speed. Note: `google-sre-book-introduction` (appended).
2. [Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 22: Addressing Cascading Failures](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/), see `queueing-theory` #6. Seen (for this node): capacity planning coupled with load tests; N + 2 example (5,000 QPS per cluster, 19,000 peak, about six clusters); planning is not sufficient; growing on demand still needs planning; organic growth and request-profile changes as triggers; slack CPU; load test each component to its breaking point within committed limits.
3. [Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 21: Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/), Alejandro Forero Cuervo, Google, 2016. Book, primary: yes. Seen (for this node): "queries per second" as a poor capacity metric; measure capacity in resources (cores, memory); CPU usually enough, with GC turning memory pressure into CPU. Note: `google-sre-handling-overload` (appended).
4. [Site Reliability Engineering: Software Engineering in SRE](https://sre.google/sre-book/software-engineering-in-sre/), Dave Helstroom, Trisha Weir, Evan Leonard, Kurt Delimon, Google, 2016. Book, primary: yes. Seen: traditional capacity planning cycle (forecast, build plan, review, deploy), brittle to slips and efficiency changes, bin packing by hand; intent-based planning (Auxon) from "50 cores in X" up to "5 nines"; performance metrics from load tests; N + 2 as a priority trade-off. Not cited: tool-specific; worth it if the node grows.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Amdahl vs Gustafson: fixed work vs fixed time. Both formulas are right; they answer different questions (one request's latency vs throughput of many requests).
- Amdahl vs USL: Amdahl's throughput levels off; Gunther's USL (and Brooker 2018) say real systems often peak and fall because of coherency costs.
- Mean vs percentiles: Brooker (2021) says use mean latency for efficiency and calls "never use the mean" advice wrong; others treat percentiles as the only honest number.
- Model realism: Brooker calls M/M/c assumptions "reasonable, albeit wrong" (service times closer to log-normal); Harchol-Balter says Markovian assumptions can be very far from reality with variable or correlated job sizes; Little's own load-test example shows service rate falling as queues grow, which no fixed-rate model captures.
- Slimmon's simulated 20 s mean wait at 96% vs the M/M/1 formula's larger mean at 96%; one simulation run vs the exact mean. Articles use the formula and cite Slimmon only for the shape.
- Queue sizing: SRE book suggests queues at 50% of the pool or less for steady traffic, and none at all for Gmail; bursty services may need bigger ones.

**Couldn't open:**
- Little and Graves, "Little's Law" chapter (MIT URL served an HTML page, not the PDF).
- Kingman's 1961 paper "The single server queue in heavy traffic" (publisher paywall; not tried further).
- Karl Sigman's M/M/1 notes at columbia.edu (404).
- AWS Builders' Library "Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs" (page is rendered by JavaScript; curl got no text). Not retried with WebFetch.
- Amdahl's paper at the Berkeley n252 URL and the ACM DL (HTML pages, not the PDF); the Stony Brook copy opened.

**Rejected:**
- Wikipedia M/M/1 queue (see #7): redundant with Brooker plus Little's law.
- Hill and Marty (chip design), McSherry et al. (not needed for a short node), Gunther's USL web page (arXiv paper is citable).

**Gaps:**
- No primary source for Kingman's formula was opened; the node cites Wikipedia.
- No measured numbers of our own: the utilization and USL figures are drawn from formulas with example parameters, not from runs. The phase 9 load generator could measure a real latency-vs-utilization curve for the cache server and fit the USL to it.
- Nothing opened on forecasting methods for capacity planning (seasonality, confidence intervals).
- Brendan Gregg's Systems Performance chapter on queueing and capacity planning not opened.

### Measuring latency under load

#### `tail-latency` (deep)

1. [The Tail at Scale](https://www.barroso.org/publications/TheTailAtScale.pdf), Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso, Google, 2013 (CACM vol. 56 no. 2). Paper, primary: yes. The source for the whole idea. Seen: causes of variability (shared resources, daemons, maintenance like compaction and GC, queueing, power limits, SSD garbage collection up to 100× read latency, energy states); fan-out math (10 ms typical, 1 s p99 per server: 1% of single-server requests slow, 63% at 100 servers; 1-in-10,000 outliers and 2,000 servers gives almost 1 in 5); Table 1 from a real service (p99 for one leaf 10 ms, for all leaves 140 ms, for 95% of leaves 70 ms); reducing variability (service classes, shallow low-level queues, time slicing, synchronized background work, caching doesn't fix the tail); hedged requests after the p95 (about 5% extra load; BigTable 1,000 keys over 100 servers, hedge after 10 ms: p99.9 1,800 ms to 74 ms with 2% more requests); tied requests with cross-server cancellation (Table 2, p99.9 −38% idle, overhead under 1% disk); micro-partitions, selective replication, latency-induced probation, good-enough results, canary requests; mutations tolerate tail better (quorums). The CACM page (cacm.acm.org/research/the-tail-at-scale/) blocked us with a Cloudflare page; the author's PDF opened. Note: `dean-tail-at-scale-2013`.
2. [Tail Latency Might Matter More Than You Think](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2021/04/19/latency.html), Marc Brooker (AWS), 2021. Blog, primary: no. Seen: simulation with a bimodal service (99% around 10 ms, 1% around 100 ms); parallel fan-out makes the slow mode common as N grows; serial chains raise variance of the sum by a factor of 25 in his model; trimmed means cut off the tail that fan-out amplifies; still says measure the mean if you measure one thing. Note: `brooker-tail-latency-2021`.
3. [Tales of the Tail: Hardware, OS, and Application-level Sources of Tail Latency](https://drkp.net/papers/latency-socc14.pdf), Jialin Li, Naveen Kr. Sharma, Dan R. K. Ports, Steven D. Gribble (University of Washington), SoCC 2014. Paper, primary: yes (their measurements). Seen: servers on Linux (null RPC, Memcached, Nginx) have worse tails than queueing models predict; causes are background processes, non-FIFO scheduling, interrupt routing, CPU power saving, NUMA; tuned Memcached at 80% utilization on four cores: median 11 µs, p99.9 32 µs, versus naive single-core 100 µs and 5 ms; FIFO queueing gives the best tail; power saving hurts the tail at low utilization. Note: `li-tales-of-the-tail-2014`.
4. [gRPC Retry Design (proposal A6)](https://github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A6-client-retries.md), Noah Eisen and Eric Gribkoff, gRPC. Design doc, primary: yes. Seen: status line says implemented in Java, .NET, Node, and in Go and C-Core "except hedging"; hedgingPolicy with maxAttempts and hedgingDelay; original sent immediately, next after hedgingDelay, and so on; first good response cancels the rest; only for methods safe to run more than once; throttling via token count applies to hedges; maxAttempts capped at 5 by default on the client. Note: `grpc-proposal-a6-retries`.
5. [HTTP routing (request hedging)](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/http/http_routing), Envoy docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: hedge policy races upstream requests and returns the first acceptable response; "Currently" hedging only on per-try timeout, the timed-out request isn't cancelled. Note: `envoy-http-routing`.
6. [Achieving Rapid Response Times in Large Online Services](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//people/jeff/Berkeley-Latency-Mar2012.pdf), Jeff Dean, Berkeley talk slides, 2012. Talk, primary: yes. Seen: the same fan-out example (1 ms average, 1 s p99, 63% at 100 servers), "squash all variability" not tenable at scale, shared environments. Not cited: the 2013 paper has everything in fuller form.

#### `histograms` (short)

1. [HdrHistogram](https://github.com/HdrHistogram/HdrHistogram), Gil Tene and contributors, README (an excerpt of the Java Histogram javadoc). Code and docs, primary: yes. Seen: configurable range and significant digits; example 1 µs to 1 hour at 3 significant digits, around 185 KB fixed footprint; exponential buckets with linear sub-buckets like a float; recording is constant time with no allocation; histograms are additive, per-thread histograms summed by a reporting thread; recordValueWithExpectedInterval fills in missed samples (the 100-second pause example). Note: `hdrhistogram-readme`.
2. [Histograms and summaries](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/), Prometheus docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: summaries can't be aggregated, `avg` of quantiles marked BAD; histograms aggregate with histogram_quantile; errors: all requests near 220 ms land in a 200–300 ms classic bucket and p95 comes out at 295 ms, a native histogram with factor 1.1 gives 228 ms; after a 100 ms shift, classic says 443 ms against a true 320 ms; summary error is in rank, histogram error in value. Note: `prometheus-histograms` (existing; appended).
3. [Native Histograms (specification)](https://prometheus.io/docs/specs/native_histograms/), Prometheus authors. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: experimental from v2.40.0 behind a feature flag, stable from v3.8.0 but scraping must be switched on; standard exponential schemas −4 to 8, schema n+1 has twice the resolution of n, all standard schemas mergeable; bucket bounds (2^(2^−n))^i; custom-bucket schema −53 generally not mergeable; zero bucket. Note: `prometheus-native-histograms`.
4. [DDSketch: A Fast and Fully-Mergeable Quantile Sketch with Relative-Error Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10693), Charles Masson, Jee E. Rim, Homin K. Lee (Datadog), VLDB 2019. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: rank-error sketches give wide value error on heavy tails (0.005 rank accuracy at p99 means anywhere from 2 to 20 seconds in their 2M-request data); relative error defined; comparison table lists HDR Histogram as relative-error, bounded range, fully mergeable. Not cited: the short node has enough with HdrHistogram and Prometheus; a good source if `histograms` grows or `metrics` wants sketches.

#### `load-testing` (deep)

1. [Open Versus Closed: A Cautionary Tale](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi06/tech/full_papers/schroeder/schroeder.pdf), Bianca Schroeder, Adam Wierman, Mor Harchol-Balter (CMU), NSDI 2006. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: definitions of closed (fixed MPL, new request only after a completion plus think time), open (arrivals independent of completions), partly-open (sessions); Table 1 classifying generators of the time (httperf open, most others closed); mean response time in open can exceed closed by an order of magnitude at the same load; principles (i) closed lower mean response time, (ii) closed converges to open only slowly as MPL grows (MPL 1000 still differs), (iii) job size variability matters much more in open; partly-open behaves open under about 5 requests per session and closed above about 10; think time barely matters; closed generators underestimate response times in capacity planning. Note: `schroeder-open-versus-closed-2006`.
2. [Open and Closed, Omission and Collapse](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2023/05/10/open-closed.html), Marc Brooker (AWS), 2023. Blog, primary: no. Seen: simulation at ρ = 0.8: open has a much longer tail than closed; with a 0.1% 10 ms mode, single-client closed p99 under 1 ms, open over 25 ms; closed benchmark can underestimate p99 by at least 25×; the closed loop is the loop you write by default; retry after 15 ms timeout makes the queue grow without bound; stable production systems approximate closed by limiting concurrency or rate. Note: `brooker-open-closed-2023`.
3. [Open and closed models](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/scenarios/concepts/open-vs-closed/), Grafana k6 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: closed executors (constant-vus) start an iteration only after the last finishes; slow responses reduce the arrival rate, "known as coordinated omission"; arrival-rate executors are open; 1 iteration/s against a 6-second endpoint used 11 VUs. Note: `grafana-k6-open-vs-closed`.
4. [Breakpoint testing](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/testing-guides/test-types/breakpoint-testing/), Grafana k6 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: ramp load gradually until the system fails; also called capacity, point load, limit testing; turn off elasticity in cloud environments; failure has levels (degraded, troublesome, timeouts, errors, collapse); use ramping-arrival-rate so load keeps rising as the system slows; stop with a threshold. Note: `grafana-k6-breakpoint-testing`.
5. [Dropped iterations](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/using-k6/scenarios/concepts/dropped-iterations/), Grafana k6 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: arrival-rate executors drop iterations when no VU is free; early in a test, allocate more VUs; later, the SUT is slowing; `dropped_iterations` counter can go in a threshold. Note: `grafana-k6-dropped-iterations`.
6. [Load test types](https://grafana.com/docs/k6/latest/testing-guides/test-types/), Grafana k6 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: smoke, average-load, stress, soak, spike, breakpoint; ramp-up, plateau, ramp-down; avoid "rollercoaster" patterns; no naming consensus. Not cited: the breakpoint page covers what the article uses.
7. [Injection (Gatling docs)](https://docs.gatling.io/concepts/injection/), Gatling. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `injectOpen` (users per second) and `injectClosed` (concurrent users) as separate profiles. Not cited: shows the same split as k6; one tool's docs is enough.
8. [Telling Stories About Little's Law](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2018/06/20/littles-law.html), Marc Brooker, 2018. Blog, primary: no. Seen: L = λW; closed clients send less as latency rises (λ ∝ 1/W), Poisson clients don't, retries make λ rise with W. Note: `brooker-littles-law-stories-2018` (existing, made by the `littles-law` group; cited unchanged).
9. See `coordinated-omission` #2 (Prisyazhynyy): its worker-count arithmetic (rate ÷ per-worker rate) fits here too; not cited in this node to keep it at 6 sources.

#### `coordinated-omission` (short)

1. [wrk2](https://github.com/giltene/wrk2), Gil Tene, README. Code and docs, primary: yes (he named the problem and wrote the tool). Seen: constant-throughput load with `-R`, HdrHistogram recording; wrk measures from send to response, so each connection waits and "coordinates" with the server; wrk2 measures from when the request should have been sent; accurate to about ±1 ms due to sleep; 10-second calibration; example with a 1.4 s pause (^Z on httpd): corrected p99 1.27 s vs uncorrected 6.04 ms, "200x". Note: `tene-wrk2-readme`.
2. [On Coordinated Omission](https://www.scylladb.com/2021/04/22/on-coordinated-omission/), Ivan Prisyazhynyy (ScyllaDB), 2021. Blog, primary: no. Seen: definition quoted from Daniel Compton; open vs closed loaders; thread per request doesn't scale; N workers each sending sequentially is a closed loader; worker count = target rate ÷ per-worker rate (100,000 QPS, 10 ms p99 gives 1,000 workers); static vs dynamic schedule; queueing vs queueless; latency correction = now − intended time; YCSB on one ScyllaDB core: closed p99 read 249 µs; with a target, 819 µs; with `measurement.interval=both`, intended p99 read 665 ms. Note: `prisyazhynyy-coordinated-omission-2021`.
3. [HdrHistogram](https://github.com/HdrHistogram/HdrHistogram) README: see `histograms` #1. Seen for this node: recordValueWithExpectedInterval, the 100-second pause example (raw data says ~99.99% at 1 ms; corrected says ~50%).
4. See `load-testing` #2 (Brooker 2023) and #3 (k6 docs, which call closed-model arrival slowdown coordinated omission).

#### `benchmarking-pitfalls` (short)

1. [Active Benchmarking](https://www.brendangregg.com/activebenchmarking.html), Brendan Gregg, 2014. Methodology page, primary: yes (his method). Seen: "you benchmark A, but actually measure B, and conclude you've measured C"; passive vs active; run long in steady state and analyze with other tools while it runs; ask why the result is X not 2X; checklist (perturbed by neighbors, throttled by resource controls or network, single-threaded client, different versions, disk vs filesystem I/O, unrealistic workload); statistics on wrong results make them look trustworthy. Note: `gregg-active-benchmarking`.
2. [Benchmarking tips](https://llvm.org/docs/Benchmarking.html), LLVM docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: low noise needed but not sufficient (cites Mytkowicz); run many times; disable services, frequency scaling, Turbo Boost, ASLR; tmpfs instead of storage; `scaling_governor` to performance; `cset shield` to reserve cores; disable the SMT sibling; with all that, variation under 0.1%. Note: `llvm-benchmarking-tips`.
3. [Run a benchmark (pyperf docs)](https://pyperf.readthedocs.io/en/latest/run_benchmark.html), Victor Stinner and contributors, pyperf 2.10.0. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: calibration run, then 20 worker processes; each worker's first value is a warmup and ignored; many runs to average out ASLR and hash randomization; warmups set by looking at values; some benchmarks never stabilize (VM warmup paper); unstable-result warnings. Note: `pyperf-run-benchmark`.
4. [Producing Wrong Data Without Doing Anything Obviously Wrong!](https://users.cs.northwestern.edu/~robby/courses/322-2013-spring/mytkowicz-wrong-data.pdf), Todd Mytkowicz, Amer Diwan, Matthias Hauswirth, Peter F. Sweeney, ASPLOS 2009. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: UNIX environment size and link order change run time (often about 33%, once almost 300%) and flip conclusions about O3; bias is unpredictable across machines; none of 133 surveyed papers handled it; fixes are setup randomization and causal analysis.
