Note: `mytkowicz-wrong-data-2009`.
5. [Tune the system for benchmarks (pyperf docs)](https://pyperf.readthedocs.io/en/latest/system.html), pyperf 2.10.0. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: CPU isolation with `isolcpus` and pinning; Turbo Boost, P-states and C-states change frequency; `pyperf system tune`; check with a load script that isolated results match idle; "ASLR must not be disabled manually!". Not cited: the run page carries the ASLR point; kept here for the disagreement with LLVM.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- **Disable ASLR or keep it?** LLVM's tips say turn address randomization off to cut noise. pyperf says never disable it, and instead run many processes so its effect averages out. Mytkowicz et al. explain why: memory layout can bias a result in one direction, so pinning one layout gives low noise and a biased answer. Low noise and correct are different goals.
- **Mean or percentiles?** Brooker (2021) says if you measure one thing, measure the mean, while showing that fan-out makes the tail dominate. The SRE book and Prometheus push percentiles. Both agree one number isn't enough.
- **Open or closed in production?** Schroeder et al. say real web traffic is partly open. Brooker (2023) says stable production systems end up closer to closed because they cap concurrency or rate, and warns retries turn closed clients open. So "use an open-model load generator" is right for measuring latency against independent users, but not the whole story.
- **Correct or simulate?** wrk2 and YCSB's intended-time mode compute latency from the planned send time. HdrHistogram's expected-interval correction invents the missing samples after the fact. Prisyazhynyy prefers a static schedule with queueing plus correction; simulation is a fallback when requests aren't sent at all.
- **Hedging cost.** Dean and Barroso report small extra load (2% more requests in their BigTable test). gRPC and Envoy both warn the method must be safe to run twice, and gRPC Go had not implemented hedging when this was written.

**Couldn't open:**
- cacm.acm.org/research/the-tail-at-scale/ (Cloudflare block page). Used the author-hosted PDF instead.
- Gil Tene's talk "How NOT to Measure Latency" is a video; not opened, not cited.

**Rejected:**
- Dean's 2012 Berkeley slides: same fan-out example as the 2013 paper, less detail.
- Gatling injection docs and k6 "Load test types": fine, but duplicate what the cited k6 pages say.
- DDSketch: kept as a candidate for later (see `histograms` #4), not needed for a short node.

**Gaps:**
- No source that measures coordinated omission against a real HTTP server under current tool versions; wrk2's README example is from its 2014 README. The phase 9 lab (closed vs open loadgen on the same server) would fill this once the lab resumes.
- No primary source that lists the default latency method of today's popular tools (wrk, hey, k6, vegeta). Only k6 was checked.
- CPU frequency effects are stated qualitatively (LLVM, pyperf, Li et al.); no numbers for a current CPU.
- Hedging overhead numbers only come from Google (2013).

## Phase 10: Messaging and streams

Researched by 5 parallel passes, one per group below.

### Queues and logs

#### `message-queue` (deep)

1. [RabbitMQ tutorial 2: Work Queues (Python)](https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/tutorial-two-python), RabbitMQ team (Broadcom), RabbitMQ 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: work queues to avoid doing slow tasks in the request; round-robin dispatch by default ("blindly dispatches every n-th message to the n-th consumer"); auto-ack loses the in-progress message on a crash; manual ack = "processed, free to delete"; consumer death (channel, connection or TCP loss) requeues unacked messages; ack timeout 30 minutes by default; forgotten acks grow broker memory; durable queue + persistent messages, but no fsync per message; prefetch_count=1 for fair dispatch.
2. [Consumer Acknowledgements and Publisher Confirms](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms), RabbitMQ team, RabbitMQ 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: both publishers and consumers need confirmation; automatic ack = delivered once written to the TCP socket ("fire-and-forget"); basic.ack, basic.nack, basic.reject; requeue to original position if possible; requeue/redelivery loops; nack without requeue goes to a dead-letter exchange or is dropped; prefetch caps unacked deliveries per channel, 100-300 usually best, 1 most conservative and slow; quorum queues cap prefetch at 2,000; unacked deliveries requeued when the channel closes; consumers must be idempotent, `redeliver` flag; publisher confirms vs AMQP transactions (the page says transactions cut throughput "by a factor of 250", no setup given); confirms and consumer acks are independent.
3. [Queues](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/queues), RabbitMQ team, RabbitMQ 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: a queue is an ordered FIFO collection; publishes on several channels interleave; priorities and multiple consumers with redelivery reorder; keep order with a stream or single active consumer.
4. [Amazon SQS visibility timeout](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html), AWS. Docs, primary: yes. Note already existed; re-opened. Seen: received messages stay in the queue but invisible; default 30 s; reappears if not deleted; extend with ChangeMessageVisibility, heartbeat pattern; 12-hour cap from first receive; about 120,000 in-flight messages per standard queue; no absolute no-duplicate guarantee inside the timeout; too long a timeout slows retries.
5. [Amazon SQS standard queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues.html), AWS. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: at least once, duplicates and occasional reordering, best-effort order; message stored in several AZs before the send is acknowledged; use cases (background work after a user request, spreading tasks over workers).
6. [Queues Don't Fix Overload](https://ferd.ca/queues-don-t-fix-overload.html), Fred Hebert, 2014. Blog, primary: no. Note already existed; re-opened and quotes re-checked. Seen: queues absorb bursts but not sustained overload; pick backpressure or load shedding; failures become rarer and bigger.

Extra: [AMQP 0-9-1 Model Explained](https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/amqp-concepts), RabbitMQ team. Opened: exchanges, bindings, four exchange types, two ack modes, broker waits for a consumer before redelivering. Not given a note; tutorials 2 and 3 plus the confirms guide cover it.

#### `pub-sub` (short)

1. [Overview of the Pub/Sub service](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/pubsub-basics), Google Cloud. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: publisher, topic, subscription, subscriber; each subscription gets a copy of every message; subscribers sharing a subscription split its messages; a message is deleted after every subscription acks it; ackDeadline; acked, unacked, nacked states; fan-in, load-balanced and fan-out patterns.
2. [Subscription overview](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/subscription-overview), Google Cloud. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: only messages published after the subscription exists are delivered; many subscriptions per topic; topic retention and seek for replay; pull, push and export subscriptions; at least once with no ordering by default; redelivery possible even after a successful ack; subscriptions expire after 31 days idle by default; a re-created subscription has no backlog.
3. [RabbitMQ tutorial 3: Publish/Subscribe (Python)](https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials/tutorial-three-python), RabbitMQ team. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: work queue = one worker per task, pub/sub = every consumer; producers publish to exchanges, never directly to queues; fanout exchange copies to every bound queue; server-named exclusive temporary queues deleted on disconnect; messages dropped when no queue is bound.

Extra: [Publish-Subscribe Channel](https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/PublishSubscribeChannel.html), Gregor Hohpe, Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns. Book pattern page, primary: no. Opened: one input channel splits into one output channel per subscriber, each gets a copy once; Google Pub/Sub example with topics and subscriptions. Not given a note; Google's own page says the same with the subscription detail.

#### `log-based-messaging` (deep)

1. [The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction](https://web.archive.org/web/2025/https://engineering.linkedin.com/distributed-systems/log-what-every-software-engineer-should-know-about-real-time-datas-unifying), Jay Kreps, LinkedIn Engineering, 2013. Blog by Kafka's co-creator, primary: yes. The live LinkedIn URL returns 404; read through the Internet Archive. Seen: log = append-only, totally ordered records with sequential numbers; state machine replication principle; log as buffer between producers and many subscribers at their own pace; consumers added without touching the pipeline; "pub sub" implies little beyond indirect addressing; partitions totally ordered, no global order, single-sender order; log compaction; log-centric system design.
2. [Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing](https://notes.stephenholiday.com/Kafka.pdf), Jay Kreps, Neha Narkhede, Jun Rao, NetDB 2011. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: why JMS-era brokers didn't fit (per-message acks, no batching, short queues assumed, slow with backlogs); partition = logical log of segment files; offsets instead of message ids; acking an offset covers everything before it; stateless broker; time-based retention, typically 7 days then; rewind; consumer groups, partition as unit of parallelism, need more partitions than consumers; order only within a partition; at least once; ZooKeeper registries; performance comparison with ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ (numbers not used).
3. [Kafka design](https://kafka.apache.org/43/design/design/), Apache Kafka project, 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Note already existed (`kafka-design-delivery-semantics`); appended. Seen: "more akin to a database log"; page cache instead of in-process cache; per-consumer queue + B-tree in traditional brokers vs O(1) appends; pull vs push, long poll; Consumer Position (broker-side ack state vs one integer offset; rewind "violates the common contract of a queue"); The Share Consumer (share groups, per-record acks, 30 s acquisition lock, delivery counts); replication and ISR.
4. [Streams and Super Streams](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/streams), RabbitMQ team, RabbitMQ 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: append-only log with "non-destructive consumer semantics"; complement, not replace, queues; use cases: large fan-outs, replay, throughput, large backlogs; x-stream-offset (first, last, next, offset, timestamp); segment files, retention per segment; single active consumer; super streams (partitioned) since 3.11; feature matrix vs classic queues.
5. [KIP-932: Queues for Kafka](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-932%3A+Queues+for+Kafka), Andrew Schofield. Spec (KIP, accepted), primary: yes. Seen: consumer groups force over-partitioning; share groups for independent work items; not a new queue object, cooperative consumption on topics; acquisition locks, per-record ack/release/reject, delivery counts against poison messages; ordering: batches in offset order, redeliveries out of order.
6. [Competing Consumers](https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/CompetingConsumers.html), Gregor Hohpe, Bobby Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns. Book pattern page, primary: no. Seen: the pattern; on a pub-sub channel extra consumers only make copies; Kafka decides the consumer "a priori" through partitions, so an idle consumer can't help a busy one, and a group can't have more consumers than partitions.

Extra: [What is Pub/Sub?](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/overview), Google Cloud. Opened: Google argues per-message leasing beats partition-based scaling, which "limits the number of concurrent clients to the number of partitions". Not given a note; EIP and KIP-932 make the same point.

#### `kafka-architecture` (deep)

1. [Introduction](https://kafka.apache.org/43/getting-started/introduction/), Apache Kafka project, 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: brokers and Connect servers; event = key, value, timestamp, headers; producers never wait for consumers; topics multi-producer, multi-subscriber, not deleted on read, per-topic retention; partitions on different brokers, same key same partition, per-partition order; replication factor 3 common, replication per partition; figure of four partitions and two producers.
2. [Kafka design](https://kafka.apache.org/43/design/design/). See log-based-messaging #3. Load balancing (producer to leader, no routing tier, metadata from any broker, key hashing), asynchronous send (batching), Replication (leader and followers, followers fetch, leaders spread, controller, ISR, committed = visible, availability under network partitions not guaranteed), Replica Management (controller elects from ISR).
3. [Basic Kafka Operations](https://kafka.apache.org/43/operations/basic-kafka-operations/), Apache Kafka project, 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Note created by another group while this one was being written; appended. Seen: partition must fit on one server, count caps consumer parallelism, folder per partition, 249-character topic names; adding partitions moves keys, no redistribution, no shrinking; graceful shutdown; preferred replica and leader rebalancing; rack awareness.
4. [KIP-500: Replace ZooKeeper with a Self-Managed Metadata Quorum](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-500%3A+Replace+ZooKeeper+with+a+Self-Managed+Metadata+Quorum), Colin McCabe. Spec (KIP), primary: yes. Seen: ZooKeeper stored metadata and elected the controller; pushed updates left brokers divergent; metadata as an event log in Kafka; Raft quorum of controllers, active controller, hot standbys; brokers fetch metadata; two systems to deploy and secure; before/after diagram.
5. [KRaft](https://kafka.apache.org/43/operations/kraft/), Apache Kafka project, 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: process.roles broker/controller/combined; combined not for critical deployments; 3 or 5 controllers, majority needed; dynamic controller membership since 4.1; migration from ZooKeeper via bridge release 3.9.
6. [Upgrading](https://kafka.apache.org/43/getting-started/upgrade/), Apache Kafka project, 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: 4.0 supports only KRaft, ZooKeeper removed; KRaft production ready from 3.3; share groups preview in 4.1, production-ready in 4.2. Another group made the note first (`kafka-upgrade-notes`); claims appended there.

Extra: [KIP-480: Sticky Partitioner](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-480%3A+Sticky+Partitioner) (Justine Olshan) and [KIP-794: Strictly Uniform Sticky Partitioner](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-794%3A+Strictly+Uniform+Sticky+Partitioner) (Artem Livshits). Downloaded, skimmed. Not given notes; the producer config reference describes the current behaviour.

#### `message-ordering` (short)

1. [Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing](https://notes.stephenholiday.com/Kafka.pdf). See log-based-messaging #2. Section 3.3: in order within a partition, no guarantee across partitions; duplicates after the last committed offset.
2. [Producer Configs](https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/producer-configs/), Apache Kafka project, 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Note created by another group; appended. Seen: default partitioner (hash of key, sticky partition without key), RoundRobinPartitioner, partitioner.ignore.keys; retries + max.in.flight > 1 without idempotence reorder batches; idempotence on by default, needs max.in.flight <= 5, retries > 0, acks=all, silently off with conflicting settings; broker keeps 5 batches per producer.
3. [Basic Kafka Operations](https://kafka.apache.org/43/operations/basic-kafka-operations/). See kafka-architecture #3. Adding partitions sends keys elsewhere and can break per-key order.
4. [Order messages](https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/ordering), Google Cloud. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: ordering keys (up to 1 KB), much higher cardinality than partitions; no order across keys; redelivery replays later messages of the key; 1 MBps per key publish limit; ordered delivery costs availability and latency; hot keys; one outstanding batch per key for pull, one message for push; async work in callbacks must keep order.

Extra: [FIFO queue delivery logic](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/FIFO-queues-understanding-logic.html), AWS. Opened: order per message group ID, groups processed in parallel, next message in a group held until the current one is deleted or times out. Not given a note; would suit a comparison paragraph if the node grows.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Per-message leasing vs partitions. Google's Pub/Sub overview argues partitions limit consumer parallelism and force in-order processing; Kafka's design docs and Kreps argue partitions make acks cheap and order possible. KIP-932 (share groups) is Kafka conceding part of Google's point for work-queue use; RabbitMQ streams are the reverse move.
- "Rewind violates the common contract of a queue" (Kafka paper and design docs) vs RabbitMQ's position that streams complement queues rather than replace them. Both sides now ship both models.
- Durability: Kafka writes to the page cache without flushing and relies on replication; RabbitMQ also doesn't fsync every message but offers publisher confirms. Neither source gives a measured loss window.
- Kafka paper's "typically 7 days" retention is from 2011; the 4.3 docs just call it a per-topic setting. The article presents it as a historical figure.

**Couldn't open:**

- Jay Kreps, "The Log" at its original LinkedIn Engineering URL: 404 (and 404 through WebFetch). Read and cited through the Internet Archive copy.

**Rejected:**

- AMQP 0-9-1 Model Explained and EIP Publish-Subscribe Channel: opened, overlapping with sources already noted.
- KIP-480 and KIP-794: proposal detail superseded by the current producer config reference.
- DDIA chapter 11 (Stream Processing), which covers logs vs queues well: not opened, so not cited.

**Gaps:**

- No measured throughput or latency numbers for queues vs logs were used. The Kafka paper's 2011 benchmark against ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ is too old and too specific to quote. The lab comparison with Kafka (LAB.md phase 10) would fill this.
- No source for how long RabbitMQ takes to notice a dead consumer's connection (RabbitMQ only says "it takes a period of time"). The article gives no number.
- Kafka's hash function for keys isn't named in the 4.3 producer config page; the article says "a hash" only.
- No source opened for RabbitMQ streams' first release version; only super streams (3.11) are dated in the article.

### Inside a log broker

#### `log-segments` (short)

1. [Implementation, Log](https://kafka.apache.org/43/implementation/log/), Apache Kafka project, Kafka 4.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: one directory per partition; segment files named by first offset (`00000000000000000000.log`); appends to the last file, rolled at a size limit; reads locate the segment then the position; deletes one segment at a time by time (largest timestamp in the segment) or size (off by default); copy-on-write segment list so deletes don't block reads; startup recovery of the newest segment with CRC checks and truncation. **Stale in places**: still calls an offset a byte position and doesn't mention `.index` files.
2. [Topic Configs](https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/topic-configs/), Apache Kafka project, Kafka 4.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: `segment.bytes` 1 GiB, `segment.ms` 7 days, `retention.ms` 7 days ("an SLA on how soon consumers must read"), `retention.bytes` per partition and unlimited, `index.interval.bytes` 4096, `segment.index.bytes` 10 MiB preallocated, `file.delete.delay.ms` 1 minute, `flush.messages` not recommended (use replication).
3. [Kafka storage log package](https://github.com/apache/kafka/tree/4.3.0/storage/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/storage/internals/log), Apache Kafka project, 4.3.0 tag. Source code, primary: yes. Seen: LogSegment (`.log` + `.index` + time index), LogSegments (skip-list map by base offset, `floorEntry`), OffsetIndex (sparse, 8-byte entries of 4-byte relative offset + 4-byte position, memory-mapped binary search, no checksum, rebuilt after a crash), TimeIndex (12-byte entries), LogFileUtils (suffixes `.log`, `.index`, `.timeindex`, `.snapshot`, `.cleaned`, `.swap`).

#### `log-compaction` (short)

1. [Kafka design](https://kafka.apache.org/43/design/design/), Apache Kafka project, Kafka 4.3 docs, Log Compaction section. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: the user-email example; head (dense) vs tail (compacted); offsets never change and missing offsets read as the next one; tombstones (null value) removed after a while; order preserved; the cleaner's steps (pick the dirtiest log, build a key-to-last-offset map of the head, recopy, swap segment by segment); 24 bytes per map entry, 8 GB buffer about 366 GB of head at 1 kB messages; active segment never compacted; `max.compaction.lag.ms` not a hard deadline; inspired by LinkedIn's Databus.
2. [Topic Configs](https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/topic-configs/): see `log-segments` #2. Seen: `cleanup.policy` (delete, compact, both), `min.cleanable.dirty.ratio` 0.5 bounding duplicates at 50%, `delete.retention.ms` 1 day also bounding a full read from offset 0, `min/max.compaction.lag.ms`.
3. [Kafka storage log package](https://github.com/apache/kafka/tree/4.3.0/storage/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/storage/internals/log): see `log-segments` #3. Seen: SkimpyOffsetMap stores an MD5 hash of the key plus an 8-byte offset (the 24 bytes), no deletes; Cleaner keeps batches that only hold producer sequence information.
4. [Implementation, Message Format](https://kafka.apache.org/43/implementation/message-format/), Apache Kafka project, Kafka 4.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: compaction preserves each batch's first and last offset and sequence; empty batches can remain to keep a producer's last sequence; `baseTimestamp` can change on compaction.

#### `zero-copy` (short)

1. [Kafka design](https://kafka.apache.org/43/design/design/): see `log-compaction` #1, Persistence and Efficiency sections. Seen: page-cache-centric design; shared binary format for producer, broker, consumer and disk; the read/write path as four copies and two system calls; sendfile leaves only the copy to the NIC; data in the page cache once for many consumers; caught-up consumers cause no disk reads; sendfile not used with SSL; batches stay compressed end to end. Links an IBM article on Java zero-copy (couldn't open, see below).
2. [sendfile(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/sendfile.2.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: copy inside the kernel beats read plus write; in_fd must be mmap-able; offset argument; short writes; 0x7ffff000 bytes per call; TCP_CORK for headers; fall back on EINVAL/ENOSYS; file must stay unmodified until consumed; Linux 2.2; non-portable; splice needs a pipe on one side.
3. [Zero-copy networking](https://lwn.net/Articles/726917/), Jonathan Corbet, LWN, 2017. Secondary, primary: no. Seen: sendfile only works for data straight from a file; NIC scatter/gather; MSG_ZEROCOPY pins buffers and notifies through the error queue; setup overhead makes small sends a loss; no zero-copy when the kernel must transform data or compute checksums; patch author's 39% (netperf) and 5-8% (production).
4. [Rethinking splice()](https://lwn.net/Articles/923237/), Jonathan Corbet, LWN, 2023. Secondary, primary: no. Seen: splice to a socket reads page cache pages directly; writing the file before transmission ends can change what's sent; no way to know when it's safe; copy-on-write rejected; io_uring suggested for completions.
5. [Kernel TLS](https://docs.kernel.org/networking/tls.html), Linux kernel docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: handshake in user space, keys handed over with TLS_TX/TLS_RX; sendfile over kTLS in records up to 2^14 bytes; TLS_TX_ZEROCOPY_RO with device offload skips the in-kernel copy, and modified data would look like tampering.
6. [MSG_ZEROCOPY](https://docs.kernel.org/networking/msg_zerocopy.html), Linux kernel docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: copy avoidance for send on TCP, UDP and VSOCK; "generally only effective at writes over around 10 KB"; notifications on the error queue, coalesced as ranges. Not used (LWN covers it at the level the node needs); a good second source if the node grows.

#### `idempotent-producers` (short)

1. [KIP-98: Exactly Once Delivery and Transactional Messaging](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-98+-+Exactly+Once+Delivery+and+Transactional+Messaging), Apurva Mehta and others, Apache Kafka. Design proposal, primary: yes. Seen: PID per producer, sequence numbers from 0 per partition; broker accepts exactly last+1, lower is a duplicate, higher is fatal data loss; one session only; TransactionalId and epoch bump to fence zombies; fields per batch to amortize the cost; wraparound; cleaner must keep sequence ranges; original config forced max.inflight=1 and default off.
2. [Producer Configs](https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/producer-configs/), Apache Kafka project, Kafka 4.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: `enable.idempotence` default true, needs `acks=all`, retries > 0, in-flight ≤ 5 (broker keeps 5 batches per producer); conflicting settings silently disable it unless explicitly enabled (then ConfigException); reordering risk without idempotence; `delivery.timeout.ms` 2 minutes; `transactional.id`.
3. [Kafka storage log package](https://github.com/apache/kafka/tree/4.3.0/storage/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/storage/internals/log): see `log-segments` #3. Seen: ProducerStateEntry `NUM_BATCHES_TO_RETAIN = 5` and the exact-range duplicate match; UnifiedLog returns the original batch's offsets for a duplicate; ProducerAppendInfo `inSequence` (last+1, or wrap to 0) and OutOfOrderSequenceException; ProducerStateManager class comment on expiry and zombie fencing.
4. [Exactly-once Semantics are Possible](https://www.confluent.io/blog/exactly-once-semantics-are-possible-heres-how-apache-kafka-does-it/), Neha Narkhede, Confluent, 2017. Blog by the builders, primary: yes. Seen (already a note): like TCP sequence numbers but persisted in the replicated log, so a new leader also spots duplicates.
5. [KIP-679](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-679%3A+Producer+will+enable+the+strongest+delivery+guarantee+by+default), Cheng Tan and others, Apache Kafka. Design proposal, primary: yes. Seen: defaults change in 3.0, `enable.idempotence` false to true and `acks` 1 to all; compatibility cases with brokers before 2.8 and message format before v2; performance claim without numbers on the page.
6. [Broker Configs](https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/broker-configs/), Apache Kafka project, Kafka 4.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: `producer.id.expiration.ms` 1 day; IDs can expire sooner when retention deletes the last write; keep it at least `delivery.timeout.ms`.
7. [Implementation, Message Format](https://kafka.apache.org/43/implementation/message-format/): see `log-compaction` #4. Seen: `producerId`, `producerEpoch`, `baseSequence` in the batch header; duplicate check by first and last sequence.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Kafka's own docs disagree with its code. The Implementation/Log page still describes offsets as byte positions and a segment lookup without `.index` files; the 4.3.0 source has logical offsets and a sparse memory-mapped index. The articles follow the source.
- Idempotence limits changed: KIP-98 required one in-flight request; Kafka 4.3 allows five. The default flipped from off to on in 3.0 (KIP-679).
- How much zero-copy is worth. Kafka's design docs present sendfile as a large win; LWN notes that zero-copy gains in practice tend to disappoint, with the MSG_ZEROCOPY author reporting 39% on a benchmark but 5-8% in production.
- Whether splice was a good idea at all: Torvalds on record disliking it, io_uring proposed as the better interface, nothing settled.
- Durability: Kafka recommends not setting per-message fsync (`flush.messages`) and relying on replication, which is the opposite of the phase 1 advice to fsync before acknowledging. Belongs in `in-sync-replicas`, not here; mentioned only in passing.

**Couldn't open:**
- [Java zero-copy article](https://developer.ibm.com/articles/j-zerocopy/), IBM Developer (linked from Kafka's design docs): the page renders only navigation without JavaScript; neither curl nor WebFetch got the article body.

**Rejected:**
- Kafka's `PlaintextTransportLayer.java` / `SslTransportLayer.java` (clients module): opened; the plaintext path calls `FileChannel.transferTo` (sendfile), the SSL path reads into a buffer. Would support "Kafka uses sendfile" from code, but the design docs already say it; left out to keep the note count down.
- kernel-internals.org and crackingwalnuts.com zero-copy pages from search: third-party summaries, not opened; primary sources cover the claims.

**Gaps:**
- No source opened for Redpanda's or other brokers' segment formats, so the node is Kafka-only.
- No measured sendfile vs read/write numbers on our machine; the only numbers are for MSG_ZEROCOPY, from the patch author via LWN. The lab's broker could produce one.
- No source for how mmap compares to sendfile for sending; the article only says what each is for.
- Kafka's time index format and `.txnindex` are mentioned but not explained; transactions belong to `exactly-once-processing`.

### Consuming a log

#### `consumer-groups` (short)

1. [KafkaConsumer](https://kafka.apache.org/43/javadoc/org/apache/kafka/clients/consumer/KafkaConsumer.html), Apache Kafka 4.3 Javadoc. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: group.id; each partition to exactly one consumer in the group (four partitions, two processes, two each); rebalancing on join, leave, new partitions or regex-matched topics; group as one logical subscriber; queue vs pub-sub by group layout; ConsumerRebalanceListener; heartbeats and session.timeout.ms; max.poll.interval.ms livelock guard and the CommitFailedException after it; manual assignment disables group coordination.
2. [Consumer Configs](https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/consumer-configs/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: group.protocol classic or consumer, default classic; session.timeout.ms 45 s (classic only); max.poll.interval.ms 5 min; max.poll.records 500; default assignors [RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor]; group.instance.id for static membership; group.remote.assignor.
3. [From Eager to Smarter in Apache Kafka Consumer Rebalances](https://www.confluent.io/blog/cooperative-rebalancing-in-kafka-streams-consumer-ksqldb/), Sophie Blee-Goldman, Confluent, 2020. Blog by a Kafka committer, primary: yes. Seen: group coordinator broker; JoinGroup/SyncGroup with a client-side leader; eager protocol revokes everything (no member works, scales with partitions); incremental cooperative (Kafka 2.4) moves the barrier into a second rebalance; the assignor must be sticky. Benchmark charts have no numbers in the text.
4. [KIP-848](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-848%3A+The+Next+Generation+of+the+Consumer+Rebalance+Protocol), Jacot, Wang, Gustafson, Apache Kafka. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: GA in 4.0 with server-side assignors; client-side assignors not implemented; motivation (thick clients, group-wide barrier, cooperative can't commit mid-rebalance, complexity); declarative target assignment and reconciliation through heartbeats; group epoch; same at-least-once worst case.
5. [Kafka design](https://kafka.apache.org/43/design/design/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs: see `offsets-and-commits` #2. Seen: Static Membership section (ephemeral member ids reshuffle on deploys; fencing of duplicate instance ids); The Share Consumer section. Not cited here (the config reference covers static membership).

#### `offsets-and-commits` (short)

1. [KafkaConsumer](https://kafka.apache.org/43/javadoc/org/apache/kafka/clients/consumer/KafkaConsumer.html): see `consumer-groups` #1. Seen: offsets as id and position; not consecutive (compaction, transactions); position vs committed position; auto commit only at-least-once if a poll's records are finished before the next poll; commitSync after a DB insert repeats the batch on a crash; commit the next offset to read; storing offsets outside Kafka atomically with results; seek, seekToBeginning, seekToEnd.
2. [Kafka design](https://kafka.apache.org/43/design/design/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Consumer Position (one integer per partition because one consumer per partition per group; per-message acks lose or duplicate and cost state; rewind to re-consume after a bug); pull vs push; commit order sets at most once vs at least once; offsets stored as messages in an internal topic.
3. [Consumer Configs](https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/consumer-configs/): see `consumer-groups` #2. Seen: enable.auto.commit default true; auto.commit.interval.ms 5 s; auto.offset.reset earliest, latest, by_duration, none, and the warning that latest plus added partitions can lose messages.
4. [Broker Configs](https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/broker-configs/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: offsets.retention.minutes default 10080, rules for when committed offsets expire (group empty, or unsubscribed); share group delivery count limit 5 (2-10) and lock duration 30 s.

#### `consumer-lag` (short)

1. [Basic Kafka Operations](https://kafka.apache.org/43/operations/basic-kafka-operations/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe with CURRENT-OFFSET, LOG-END-OFFSET, LAG per partition; --members (one consumer with 0 partitions in the example); --state; --reset-offsets options; groups deleted when their last committed offset expires.
2. [Monitoring](https://kafka.apache.org/43/operations/monitoring/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: records-lag-max is measured from the current position, not the committed offset; lag is published by the consumer, not the broker; per-partition records-lag; advice: max lag under a threshold, min fetch rate above zero.
3. [Consumer Lag Evaluation Rules](https://github.com/linkedin/Burrow/wiki/Consumer-Lag-Evaluation-Rules), LinkedIn Burrow wiki. Docs by the tool's builders, primary: yes. Seen: no fixed threshold; a sliding window of 10 committed offsets (10 minutes with 60 s commits); rules OK / STALLED / WARNING (slow) / STOPPED, with worked examples; busy topics' lag goes up and down.

#### `exactly-once-processing` (deep)

1. [Kafka design](https://kafka.apache.org/43/design/design/): see `offsets-and-commits` #2. Seen: Message Delivery Semantics and Using Transactions: offset written in the same transaction as output; aborted transaction reverts the stored position but the consumer "does not automatically rewind"; read_uncommitted default shows aborted records; storing offsets with external output instead of 2PC; required settings (read_committed, auto commit off, transactional.id); reset position on abort or recreate clients; Kafka Streams is the simplest route; the transactional exception categories.
2. [Transactions in Apache Kafka](https://www.confluent.io/blog/transactions-apache-kafka/), Apurva Mehta and Jason Gustafson, Confluent, 2017. Blog by the builders, primary: yes. Seen: read-process-write; formal definition (A consumed iff B produced); three failure cases; offset commit as a write to the offsets topic; transactional.id epoch fencing; not atomic reads; coordinator and transaction log; two-phase commit with markers; transactional.id must map to fixed input partitions; overhead per transaction; 3% at 1 KB and 100 ms; latency vs commit interval; external side effects not covered.
3. [KIP-447](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-447%3A+Producer+scalability+for+exactly+once+semantics), Jason Gustafson and others, Apache Kafka. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: adopted in 2.6.0; mismatch between moving partitions and static transactional ids; one producer per partition didn't scale; group metadata (generation, member id) sent with the transactional offset commit; PendingTransactionException wait; zombie GC example; exactly_once_beta (now exactly_once_v2).
4. [Jepsen: Bufstream 0.1.0](https://jepsen.io/analyses/bufstream-0.1.0), Kyle Kingsbury, 2024. Independent test report, primary: no. Seen: Kafka transaction docs scattered; what a transaction is; exactly-once holds only under several assumptions; KAFKA-17582 (consumers don't rewind on abort unless rebalanced; intended; undocumented then); KAFKA-17754 (aborted reads, lost writes, torn transactions under pauses; no transaction number); KIP-890 expected to fix it; correction about auto-commit committing the penultimate poll.
5. [Upgrading](https://kafka.apache.org/43/getting-started/upgrade/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: KIP-848 GA in 4.0; KIP-890 in 4.0 bumps the producer epoch every transaction for 4.0 clients; TransactionAbortableException; share groups preview in 4.1, production-ready in 4.2.
6. [Configuring a Streams Application](https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/developer-guide/config-streams/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: processing.guarantee at_least_once (default) or exactly_once_v2 (brokers 2.5+); commit.interval.ms 30 s at-least-once, 100 ms exactly-once; exception handlers.
7. [KIP-98](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-98+-+Exactly+Once+Delivery+and+Transactional+Messaging), Apache Kafka. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: atomic multi-partition writes; "consumed only if the entire consume-transform-produce executed"; control messages as markers; transaction.timeout.ms; endless-transaction attack. Not cited (the Confluent post and the design docs cover it at this level).
8. [KIP-890](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-890%3A+Transactions+Server-Side+Defense), Justine Olshan, Apache Kafka. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: hanging transactions; a delayed message or EndTxn landing in the next transaction; epoch bump after every commit or abort; implicit AddPartitionsToTxn; server-side verification for old clients. Not cited (the upgrade notes give the shipped behaviour and version).
9. [Exactly-once Semantics are Possible](https://www.confluent.io/blog/exactly-once-semantics-are-possible-heres-how-apache-kafka-does-it/), Neha Narkhede, 2017: already a note (`confluent-exactly-once-2017`) used by `delivery-guarantees`. Not re-cited here.

#### `poison-messages` (short)

1. [Building Reliable Reprocessing and Dead Letter Queues with Apache Kafka](https://www.uber.com/blog/reliable-reprocessing/), Ning Xia, Uber, 2018. Engineering blog, primary: yes. Seen: a failing message blocks the batch because the offset can't be committed past it; retry topics with growing delays; commit after publishing to the retry topic; DLQ at the end; replay into the first retry topic; code bugs straight to the DLQ; separate retry flows per consumer group. curl got 406 with the default headers; opened with browser Accept headers.
2. [KIP-1034: Dead letter queue in Kafka Streams](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-1034%3A+Dead+letter+queue+in+Kafka+Streams), Gasparina, Greffier, Viale, Apache Kafka. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: adopted; built-in options are log-and-continue or fail (the default); why neither fits; errors.dead.letter.queue.topic.name; raw key and value; exception, stack trace, topic, partition, offset in headers.
3. [Configuring a Streams Application](https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/developer-guide/config-streams/): see `exactly-once-processing` #6. Seen: deserialization failures (corrupt data, wrong serializer, unknown type); FAIL vs CONTINUE; a hand-written DLQ write is a side effect outside Streams' guarantees; the DLQ config exists in 4.3.
4. [Upgrading](https://kafka.apache.org/43/getting-started/upgrade/): see `exactly-once-processing` #5. Seen: share groups (4.2): no whole-partition ownership, per-record acks, delivery counting, meant for one-at-a-time work, not ordered streams.
5. [Kafka Connect Deep Dive: Error Handling and Dead Letter Queues](https://www.confluent.io/blog/kafka-connect-deep-dive-error-handling-dead-letter-queues/), Confluent. Downloaded; skimmed only. Not used (Connect-specific).

#### `message-schemas` (short)

1. [Schema Registry Concepts](https://docs.confluent.io/platform/current/schema-registry/fundamentals/index.html), Confluent docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: registry outside the brokers; stores versioned schemas per subject with compatibility settings; storage in a Kafka topic with a single primary; IDs unique and increasing; schema vs subject vs version vs ID; identical schemas share an ID; why schemas (a contract like an API); Avro needs the schema to decode.
2. [Formats, Serializers, and Deserializers](https://docs.confluent.io/platform/current/schema-registry/fundamentals/serdes-develop/index.html), Confluent docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: subject name strategies (TopicNameStrategy default means one schema per topic; RecordName and TopicRecordName for several event types); auto.register.schemas, use.latest.version; missing schema ID fails deserialization; wire format (version byte 0, 4-byte big-endian ID, Protobuf message indexes, data); schema GUID in a header since Confluent Platform 8.1.1, header-first deserializers.
3. [Schema Evolution and Compatibility](https://docs.confluent.io/platform/current/schema-registry/fundamentals/schema-evolution.html) and [Apache Avro Specification](https://avro.apache.org/docs/1.12.0/specification/): already notes, used by `schema-evolution`. Not re-cited; the compatibility modes are linked through `[[schema-evolution]]`.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Exactly once. Kafka's docs and Confluent present transactions as exactly-once for read-process-write. Jepsen (2024) calls the transaction protocol "fundamentally broken" (KAFKA-17754) and says the guarantee rests on unstated assumptions. Kafka 4.0's KIP-890 changes the protocol in the way Kafka's engineers said would fix it; nobody opened here has re-tested it.
- Aborts and rewinding. KIP-98 says consumed means the whole consume-transform-produce ran; the Java consumer keeps advancing after an abort unless rebalanced (KAFKA-17582, intended). The Kafka 4.3 design docs now document the manual rewind.
- Auto commit. Confluent's docs (quoted by Jepsen) say auto commit can lose progress for the latest poll; readers told Jepsen the Java client commits the penultimate poll; the Javadoc says auto commit is at-least-once only if you finish each poll's records before the next poll. The articles follow the Javadoc.
- Lag alerting. Kafka's monitoring docs suggest a max-lag threshold; Burrow argues against any fixed threshold and reads the trend instead.
- Poison handling. Stop (Kafka Streams' default), skip, or set aside. KIP-1034 says neither built-in suits most cases; Uber's retry topics give up per-key order, which nobody in these sources discusses.
- Deserialization handler default. The Kafka 4.3 Streams config table lists LogAndFail for the deprecated setting and LogAndContinue next to the new one; KIP-1034 says fail is the default. Not cited either way.

**Couldn't open:**
- Uber blog with curl's default headers (406 Not Acceptable); opened with browser-like Accept headers, so it is cited.

**Rejected:**
- Kafka 4.3 introduction page (opened; consumer group basics are better in the Javadoc).
- KIP-98, KIP-890 (opened; covered by the design docs, the Confluent post and the upgrade notes).
- Confluent's Kafka Connect error-handling post (downloaded, not read; Connect-specific).

**Gaps:**
- No source opened on Flink's or other engines' exactly-once to external sinks; `exactly-once-processing` points to `transactional-sinks` for that.
- No measured cost of transactions newer than Confluent's Kafka 0.11 figure (3%, 2017).
- No source on how consumers cache registry lookups, or what happens when the registry is down; the article only says the registry is on the read path.
- No source on default share group settings beyond the broker config reference; no independent test of share groups.
- No source converting lag in messages to lag in time (Burrow and Kafka count messages); the article does the arithmetic in words only.

### Getting changes out of the database + Built on logs

#### `dual-writes` (short)

1. [Using logs to build a solid data infrastructure (or: why dual writes are a bad idea)](https://www.confluent.io/blog/using-logs-to-build-a-solid-data-infrastructure-or-why-dual-writes-are-a-bad-idea/), Martin Kleppmann, Confluent, 2015. Talk transcript, primary: no. Seen: dual writes defined as the application updating every store; two-client race leaves database X=B and index X=A with no error; denormalized counter update fails after inbox insert; transactions fix it only inside one database; 2PC often unsupported and of doubtful value; "permanent inconsistency", not eventual; alternative: one ordered log consumed by every store, each tracking its position; consumers are eventually consistent; CDC from one database works as well as writing to a log and keeps linearizable reads and constraints.
2. [Reliable Microservices Data Exchange With the Outbox Pattern](https://debezium.io/blog/2019/02/19/reliable-microservices-data-exchange-with-the-outbox-pattern/), Gunnar Morling, Debezium, 2019. Blog by the project's lead, primary: yes. Seen: Kafka can't join an XA transaction with the database; both failure orders; "modify only one resource and drive the other"; writing to Kafka first loses read-your-own-writes. See transactional-outbox #2.

#### `transactional-outbox` (deep)

1. [Pattern: Transactional outbox](https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html), Chris Richardson. Pattern page, primary: yes. Seen: context (send inside the transaction: might not commit; after: might crash); forces (no 2PC, if-and-only-if, order across instances); solution (outbox table, or a property of each record in NoSQL; message relay); results (sent iff commit, in order, relay may publish twice so consumers idempotent, developers may forget); relay styles: transaction log tailing, polling publisher; event sourcing as the alternative.
2. [Reliable Microservices Data Exchange With the Outbox Pattern](https://debezium.io/blog/2019/02/19/reliable-microservices-data-exchange-with-the-outbox-pattern/), Gunnar Morling, Debezium, 2019. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: outbox columns id, aggregatetype, aggregateid, type, payload; aggregate id as Kafka key for per-aggregate order; insert then delete in the same transaction so the table stays empty while the WAL still carries the insert; Debezium Postgres connector + EventRouter SMT; consumer dedup by event id stored in a message log table in the same transaction; at-least-once; events are part of the service's API; later update: Debezium ships an outbox event router SMT.
3. [Transactional outbox pattern](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/transactional-outbox.html), AWS Prescriptive Guidance. Docs, primary: no. Seen: flight/payment example; both failure orders; outbox table with timestamp and sequence number; relay sends to SQS and deletes on success (sample code); duplicates and idempotent consumers; claims order is preserved "by using timestamps and sequence numbers"; CDC variant with DynamoDB Streams.
4. [Transactionally Staged Job Drains in Postgres](https://brandur.org/job-drain), Brandur Leach, 2017. Blog, primary: no. Seen: enqueue inside a transaction lets a worker run before commit, and rollback leaves unrunnable jobs; enqueue after commit risks a crash in between; staging table plus single enqueuer under a lock, REPEATABLE READ so the DELETE matches the SELECT, at-least-once; better than working jobs straight from Postgres under load.
5. [How Postgres sequences issues can impact your messaging guarantees](https://event-driven.io/en/ordering_in_postgres_outbox/), Oskar Dudycz, 2022. Blog by an event-store maintainer, primary: no. Seen: sequence values taken before commit; gaps from rollbacks; a relay that tracks "last position" skips late-committing rows; gapless counter serialises writers; Marten's high water mark gap detection; filter by xid8 transaction id < pg_snapshot_xmin(pg_current_snapshot()); ordering then follows transaction start; long transactions delay the relay.
6. [Using logs to build a solid data infrastructure](https://www.confluent.io/blog/using-logs-to-build-a-solid-data-infrastructure-or-why-dual-writes-are-a-bad-idea/). See dual-writes #1. Used for: a log read from the database in commit order.

Extra: [Outbox Event Router](https://debezium.io/documentation/reference/stable/transformations/outbox-event-router.html), Debezium 3.6 docs. Opened: expected columns (id, aggregatetype, aggregateid, payload), routing to outbox.event.<aggregatetype>, not for MongoDB. Not given a note; Morling's post covers the design.
Extra: [System administration functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-admin.html), PostgreSQL 18. Opened: pg_logical_emit_message (transactional messages straight into the WAL for decoding plugins). A possible table-less outbox; not used in the article.

#### `logical-replication` (short)

1. [Logical Decoding Concepts](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/logicaldecoding-explanation.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: decoding WAL into tuples or SQL; slot = ordered stream from one database; crash-safe; position persisted only at checkpoint so changes can repeat; one slot per consumer, one receiver at a time; slots hold WAL and catalog rows even when idle, can force a wraparound shutdown; failover slot sync to hot standby; output plugins; exported snapshot at slot creation.
2. [Logical Replication](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/logical-replication.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: replication identity (usually PK) vs block-level physical; publish/subscribe; initial snapshot then in-order apply; use cases incl. across major versions and platforms; subscriber is an ordinary instance and can publish.
3. [Write Ahead Log settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: wal_level default replica, logical adds decoding info, set at server start. Note existed; claims appended.
4. [Replication settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-replication.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: max_replication_slots default 10; max_slot_wal_keep_size default -1 (unlimited); idle_replication_slot_timeout default 0, invalidation at checkpoint; wal_sender_timeout 60 s.
5. [PostgreSQL 17 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/17.0/). Note existed; appended: failover of logical slots, sync_replication_slots.

Extra: [Logical Replication Publication](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/logical-replication-publication.html), PostgreSQL 18. Opened: replica identity rules (DEFAULT, USING INDEX, FULL, NOTHING; UPDATE/DELETE error without one). Not given a note; Debezium's page covers what CDC needs.
Extra: [PostgreSQL 18 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/18.0/). Opened: idle_replication_slot_timeout is new in 18. Not cited; the article pins it to the 18 docs.
Extra: pages downloaded but only skimmed: warm-standby (26.2), protocol-logical-replication, logical-replication-failover, logicaldecoding-output-plugin, logicaldecoding-example.

#### `change-data-capture` (deep)

1. [Debezium connector for PostgreSQL](https://debezium.io/documentation/reference/stable/connectors/postgresql.html), Debezium 3.6. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: logical decoding since 9.4; decoderbufs or pgoutput (built in since 10); initial snapshot steps then stream from the noted LSN; LSN as Kafka Connect offset; topic per table; event key/value, before/after/op/source; op c/u/d/r/t/m; replica identity DEFAULT/NOTHING/FULL/INDEX, no PK means creates only; tombstone after delete; TOAST unchanged values omitted (~8 KB); incremental snapshots (chunks of 1024, snapshot window dedup, based on DDD-3); read-only incremental snapshots on PG 13+; transaction metadata; WAL growth, heartbeats, confirmed_flush_lsn vs restart_lsn; one slot per connector; exactly once normally, at least once on faults; never drop the slot; PG 15/16/17 failover behaviour.
2. [DBLog: A Watermark Based Change-Data-Capture Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.12597), Andreakis, Papapanagiotou, Netflix, 2020. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: requirements (trigger any time, pause/resume, no stall, no time travel, no locks, vendor neutral); comparison with Databus, Debezium (locks, then), Maxwell, MySQLStreamer; algorithm 1 low/high watermark chunk selection; figures 3 and 4; non-stale reads; used by tens of Netflix services.
3. [Bottled Water: Real-time integration of PostgreSQL and Kafka](https://www.confluent.io/blog/bottled-water-real-time-integration-of-postgresql-and-kafka/), Martin Kleppmann, 2015. Blog by the tool's author, primary: yes. Seen: snapshot + change stream = replication; triggers before 9.4; binlog, oplog, GoldenGate, Databus, Wormhole; logical decoding groups by transaction, commit order, no rolled-back changes; lockless snapshot; PK as Kafka key, null for deletes, log compaction; plugin in C needs superuser, leader only (in 9.4); duplicates on client restart.
4. [Incremental Snapshots in Debezium](https://debezium.io/blog/2021/10/07/incremental-snapshots/), Jiri Pechanec, Debezium, 2021. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: problems of all-or-nothing snapshots; Debezium 1.6; adopted DBLog's watermarks in the shared core; signalling table.
5. [Logical Replication Restrictions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/logical-replication-restrictions.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: no DDL, no sequences, no large objects, only tables; additive schema changes on subscriber first.
6. Kleppmann dual writes (see dual-writes #1) and Morling outbox (see transactional-outbox #2).

#### `event-sourcing` (deep)

1. [Event Sourcing](https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/EventSourcing.html), Martin Fowler, 2005. Pattern write-up (draft), primary: yes. Seen: definition; complete rebuild, temporal query, event replay; version control example; snapshots and system of record; reversing events (differences vs absolute values); external updates and queries during replay, gateways; code changes; accounting ledgers; when to use.
2. [CQRS Documents](https://cqrs.files.wordpress.com/2010/11/cqrs_documents.pdf), Greg Young, 2010. Long-form PDF, primary: yes. Seen: task-based UI; commands vs events, past tense; no delete; rolling snapshots; event storage on two tables (Events, Aggregates) with per-aggregate version and an optimistic concurrency check in a transaction.
3. [Event Sourcing pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/event-sourcing), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center. Docs, primary: no. Seen: complexity warning; per-entity streams, rehydration; projections; optimistic concurrency (seat example); intent vs state events; compensating events; versioning (tolerant readers, version ids, upcasting, in-place migration last resort); Kafka isn't an event store; snapshots every N events; idempotent handlers; crypto-shredding; when not to use; apply selectively.
4. [Don't Let the Internet Dupe You, Event Sourcing is Hard](https://chriskiehl.com/article/event-sourcing-is-hard), Chris Kiehl, 2019. Practitioner blog, primary: no. Seen: shared event streams couple services and become opaque; plumbing cost; UI must be task-based; stale events and lost fidelity; noisy audit log; projections cost N times; materialization lag; history table gets "80%" (his estimate); CQRS doesn't require event sourcing.

#### `cqrs` (short)

1. [CQRS](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CQRS.html), Martin Fowler, 2011. Bliki, primary: no. Seen: definition; shared vs separate databases (ReportingDatabase); fits task UIs, event sourcing, eventual consistency; use only in bounded contexts; majority of cases went badly; reporting database as the lighter alternative.
2. [CQRS Documents](https://cqrs.files.wordpress.com/2010/11/cqrs_documents.pdf). See event-sourcing #2. Seen: origin in Meyer's CQS; CustomerService split into write and read services; different consistency, storage (3NF vs 1NF) and scale needs; one model can't serve all.

Extra: [CQRS pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cqrs), Microsoft. Downloaded, not read closely; two sources were enough for a short node.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Outbox ordering: AWS says the outbox preserves order using timestamps and sequence numbers; Dudycz shows Postgres sequences are assigned before commit, so a position-tracking poller can skip or reorder rows. The article explains the gap and the fixes.
- Debezium's delivery claim: "exactly once" when operating normally, "at least once" on faults. The article tells readers to design for at least once.
- Event sourcing's value: Fowler and Microsoft list rebuilds, temporal queries and audit; Kiehl reports that event versioning erodes the exact history and that a history table gets most of the value. Microsoft itself opens with a strong warning. Covered in "Where it gets tricky".
- CQRS: Fowler says most projects he saw went badly and to use it only in parts; Young presents it as fixing a stereotypical architecture. Both views are in the article without naming sides.
- CDC vs outbox: capturing business tables directly exposes internal schema (Morling); capturing an outbox needs extra application code. Stated as a trade-off in both articles.

**Couldn't open:**

- Nothing needed failed to open.

**Rejected:**

- Secondary outbox tutorials from search results (dev.to posts, personal blogs): the primary pattern page, Debezium's post and Dudycz cover the same ground with more authority.
- Microsoft CQRS page: fine, but Fowler plus Young were enough for a short node.

**Gaps:**

- No source with measured relay latency or throughput (polling interval vs log tailing). The articles give no numbers.
- No primary source on MySQL binlog-based CDC beyond mentions in Bottled Water and DBLog.
- Kafka's own transactions as an alternative to the outbox (producer writes to Kafka and DB in one Kafka transaction isn't possible) aren't covered; `exactly-once-processing` may want to say why.
- DDIA chapters 11 and 12 (CDC, event sourcing) not opened.

### Jobs

#### `background-jobs` (deep)

1. [SELECT, the locking clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, version 18. Docs, primary: yes. Note already existed (postgres-sql-select). Seen: FOR UPDATE / NO KEY UPDATE / SHARE / KEY SHARE; NOWAIT errors, SKIP LOCKED skips rows that can't be locked at once; skipping gives an inconsistent view, fit for queue-like tables only; LIMIT stops locking once enough rows are returned; ROW SHARE table lock still taken; ORDER BY with a locking clause can return rows out of order at Read Committed.
2. [Postgres Job Queues & Failure By MVCC](https://brandur.org/postgres-queues), Brandur Leach, Heroku, 2015. Blog, primary: yes (his incident and test bench). Seen: why jobs go in Postgres (roll back with the transaction, invisible until commit); an idle analytics transaction stalled the queue, killing it cleared the backlog; que-degradation-test at about 50 jobs/s; lock time under 0.01 s rising about 15x; dead tuples near 100,000, VACUUM "247311 dead row versions cannot be removed yet"; indexes lack visibility info so every lock attempt walks dead entries; Que's recursive CTE with pg_try_advisory_lock; fixes tried: predicate specificity with last job id, lock jitter, locking several jobs, batching to Redis via a pending_jobs table; statement_timeout not enough, kill long transactions, don't share databases across teams. Postgres 9.4 era, before SKIP LOCKED.
3. [River: a Fast, Robust Job Queue for Go + Postgres](https://brandur.org/river), Brandur Leach, 2023. Blog by River's author, primary: yes. Seen: four failure modes of a Redis queue next to a Postgres transaction (runs before commit, runs after rollback until DLQ, lost in the gap after commit, partial state); NOTIFY is transactional; about 10k trivial jobs/s on a MacBook Air, explicitly not a benchmark; Ruby process-per-worker contention at Heroku; SKIP LOCKED in 9.5 as the key change; REINDEX CONCURRENTLY (12), B-tree dedup (13), expired-entry removal before splits (14); no whole-transaction timeout at the time.
4. [Solid Queue README](https://github.com/rails/solid_queue), Rails / 37signals, main branch. Code docs, primary: yes. Seen: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED polling on MySQL 8+, MariaDB 10.6+, PostgreSQL 9.5+; default in new Rails 8 apps; workers, dispatchers, scheduler, supervisor; the two polling queries shaped for a covering index; worker poll 0.1 s, dispatcher 1 s; heartbeats every 60 s, dead after 5 min, claimed jobs marked failed; heartbeats per process, a stuck job in a live process stays claimed; MySQL REPEATABLE READ gap-lock deadlocks, they run READ COMMITTED; concurrency controls via semaphores; separate database by default, same-transaction enqueueing called a sharp tool; Rails 8 enqueue_after_transaction_commit.
5. [Reliability](https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/wiki/Reliability), Mike Perham, Sidekiq wiki. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: basic fetch uses BRPOP and loses the job on crash; super_fetch (Pro) uses LMOVE to keep it; orphan recovery after a 60 s heartbeat expiry, "5 minutes or 3 hours"; poison pill after 3 recoveries in 72 hours; strict queue ordering starves; default scheduler not atomic (two round trips), reliable_scheduler uses Lua.
6. [Amazon SQS visibility timeout](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html), AWS. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: received message hidden, not removed; default 30 s; reappears if not deleted; no absolute guarantee against duplicates; heartbeat-extend with ChangeMessageVisibility; 12-hour cap from first receive; in-flight limit about 120,000 for standard queues; DLQ for repeated failures.

Extra: [PostgreSQL 17 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/17.0/). Note already existed. Used for transaction_timeout arriving in 17.
Extra: [Explicit locking](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html). Note already existed. Used for row locks lasting until transaction end.
Extra: [Sidekiq Best Practices](https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/wiki/Best-Practices), Mike Perham. Opened. Seen: small JSON args, pass ids not objects; idempotent and transactional jobs; "at least once, not exactly once". Not given a note; the Reliability page covers the mechanism.
Extra: [Celery tasks guide](https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/stable/userguide/tasks.html). Opened. Seen: default acks early (before running), acks_late acks after return and can re-run on crash; worker acks even with acks_late if the child is killed by a signal, task_reject_on_worker_lost to change that. Not given a note; would suit a follow-up on ack timing.
Extra: [River transactional enqueueing](https://riverqueue.com/docs/transactional-enqueueing). Opened. Same failure modes as the River blog; claims "tens of thousands of jobs per second". Not given a note.

#### `job-scheduling` (short)

1. [CronJob](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs/), The Kubernetes Authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: stable since v1.21; one CronJob like one crontab line; cron fields and step values; startingDeadlineSeconds and the 8-hour backup example; concurrencyPolicy Allow/Forbid/Replace; suspend and missed runs; history limits 3 and 1; timeZone stable since v1.27, CRON_TZ unsupported; "two Jobs might be created, or no Job", so jobs should be idempotent; scheduled-timestamp annotation since v1.32; controller checks every 10 s; more than 100 missed schedules and it won't start.
2. [Solid Queue README](https://github.com/rails/solid_queue). See background-jobs #4. Recurring tasks section: scheduler process, Fugit cron syntax with time zones, each task schedules the next, several schedulers made safe by a unique index on (task_key, run_at) written in the same transaction, only while finished jobs are kept, no guarantee for jobs on other backends. Dispatchers move due delayed jobs to the ready table.
3. [Periodic and cron jobs](https://riverqueue.com/docs/periodic-jobs), River docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: leader inserts periodic jobs from an in-memory schedule; resets on restart or election; runs can be skipped; unique jobs plus RunOnStart close the gap; durable periodic jobs in River Pro v0.15. Used for the leader-election design.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Same-database queues: River's authors call transactional enqueueing the right default for all but the largest apps; Solid Queue ships with a separate database because code comes to rely on it silently. Covered in the article.
- Postgres as a queue: Brandur's 2015 post shows how badly it can fail; his 2023 post argues for it again, citing SKIP LOCKED and index improvements. Both are in the article; the long-transaction risk is unchanged.
- Duplicate prevention for recurring jobs: many schedulers plus a unique key (Solid Queue) vs one elected leader (River). Kubernetes admits neither is perfect ("two or none").

**Couldn't open:**

- [What is SKIP LOCKED for in PostgreSQL 9.5?](https://www.enterprisedb.com/blog/what-skip-locked-postgresql-95), Craig Ringer (2ndQuadrant, now EDB). Returns an EDB 404 page. Not cited.

**Rejected:**

- Celery and Sidekiq Best Practices pages: opened and useful, but the article already had six core sources; recorded as extras.
- River transactional enqueueing page: repeats the River blog.

**Gaps:**

- No primary source measured SKIP LOCKED throughput against the older advisory-lock approach. The article gives no number for it.
- "A dead client's transaction is aborted and its row locks released" isn't stated in any note; the article only says a rolled-back transaction frees the lock.
- Nothing opened on Redis-based delayed jobs beyond "Sidekiq's default scheduler isn't atomic"; left out of job-scheduling.
- No source for spreading cron start times to avoid everything firing at midnight; that advice was cut.

## Phase 11: Distributed systems I, replication and partitioning

Researched by 7 parallel passes, one per group below.

### Why it's hard

All pages below were opened with `curl -sL` and read as text (HTML through
pandoc, PDFs through pdftotext); the ACM Queue and live AWS pages through
WebFetch where curl failed. Raw copies were kept in the scratchpad while
writing.

#### `distributed-system` (deep)

1. [Distributed Systems lecture notes](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2122/ConcDisSys/dist-sys-notes.pdf), Martin Kleppmann, University of Cambridge, 2021/22 course. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: sections 1 and 2 read in full; a distributed system is nodes that only communicate by messages; why distribute (inherently distributed, reliability, performance, too big for one machine); "Communication may fail (and we might not even know it has failed)"; partial failure; RPC and why a missing reply leaves the client unsure; two generals ("cannot reach certainty by exchanging any finite number of messages"); Byzantine generals and 3f + 1; system models (network, node, timing); causes of timing violations including GC pauses of minutes and packets delayed over a minute in one datacenter; fault vs failure; timeout failure detectors can't tell crash from delay. Already the best single source for this group.
2. [Challenges with distributed systems](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/challenges-with-distributed-systems/), Jacob Gabrielson, AWS Builders' Library. Blog, primary: yes (AWS engineer on AWS systems). Seen: the live page now redirects to builder.aws.com and renders with JavaScript (WebFetch got only the page header), so read through the Internet Archive's copy; offline, soft real-time and hard real-time systems; the eight steps of a request/reply and how each can fail; "timing out means that the result of the request is UNKNOWN"; fate sharing on one machine; test matrix "balloons from 10 to 200"; latent bugs; the amazon.com outage from one full disk and a load balancer that favoured fast empty replies.
3. [distribution (email)](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/distributed-system.txt), Leslie Lamport, DEC SRC, 1987. Email, primary: yes. Seen: the full short email with the "failure of a computer you didn't even know existed" definition and why he wrote it (his workstation depending on programs elsewhere).
4. [The network is reliable](https://aphyr.com/posts/288-the-network-is-reliable), Kyle Kingsbury and Peter Bailis, 2013. Blog survey, primary: no. Seen: Microsoft datacenter study (5.2 devices and 40.8 links failing per day, redundancy improves median traffic by only 43%); HP, Chubby, Google cluster numbers; application-level partitions from GC and overload; BCM5709 one-way NIC failure; GitHub's Pacemaker split and 90-second spanning-tree partition; MongoDB write loss on EC2; Twilio's Redis resync overload; CENIC's 508 partitions; "some networks really are reliable" at a price. Also under `network-partitions`.

Also opened: [A Note on Distributed Computing](https://scholar.harvard.edu/files/waldo/files/waldo-94.pdf) (Waldo et al., 1994): Access Denied, see Couldn't open. [MIT 6.5840](https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.824/) not opened this round; the Cambridge notes cover the same ground for this node.

#### `fallacies-of-distributed-computing` (short)

1. [The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing](http://nighthacks.com/jag/res/Fallacies.html), Peter Deutsch, page on James Gosling's site. List, primary: yes. Seen: the eight items and one sentence: all "prove to be false in the long run and all cause big trouble and painful learning experiences"; points to Rotem-Gal-Oz for detail.
2. [21 years and counting of 'eight fallacies of distributed computing'](https://blog.apnic.net/2025/12/08/21-years-and-counting-of-eight-fallacies-of-distributed-computing/), George Michaelson, APNIC blog, 2025. Blog, primary: no. Seen: history (Joy and Tom Lyon's first four, Deutsch three, Gosling the eighth); "Several online discussions ... mistakenly refer to Tom Lyon as Dave Lyon"; each fallacy from a network operator's view (loss, delay, jitter, queueing, topology changes, many admins, hidden costs, heterogeneous links); IP doesn't guarantee delivery.
3. See `distributed-system` #4 for evidence that fallacy 1 is false.

Also opened: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallacies_of_distributed_computing): list, effects, history crediting "Dave Lyon", Deutsch's later ninth fallacy, Richards and Ford's three more (2020). Not cited (secondary, and contradicts #2 on the name).

#### `failure-models` (short)

1. See `distributed-system` #1 (Kleppmann notes, section 2.3): network models (reliable, fair-loss, arbitrary), node models (crash-stop, crash-recovery, Byzantine), timing models (synchronous, partially synchronous, asynchronous); network models convert, node models don't; "If your assumptions are wrong, all bets are off!"
2. [Consensus in the Presence of Partial Synchrony](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Lynch/jacm88.pdf), Dwork, Lynch, Stockmeyer, JACM, 1988. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: definitions of fail-stop, omission, authenticated Byzantine, Byzantine; no consensus tolerating one crash in a fully asynchronous system; partial synchrony as unknown bound or bound after an unknown GST; late messages are not processor faults; safety holds even when fully asynchronous; N ≥ 2t + 1 for crash or omission, 3t + 1 for Byzantine; "authentication does not improve resiliency" under partial synchrony; Table I.

#### `network-partitions` (short)

1. [An Analysis of Network-Partitioning Failures in Cloud Systems](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi18-alquraan.pdf), Alquraan, Takruri, Alfatafta, Al-Kiswany, OSDI 2018. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: 136 failures in 25 systems; complete, partial and simplex partitions (Figure 1); 80% catastrophic, 90% silent, 21% lasting after heal; leader election most vulnerable (40%), two leaders at once the top flaw; 29% from partial partitions; 88% by isolating one node; 64% need no client or one-side clients; 83% reproduce on three nodes; 93% reproducible with fault injection; NEAT with OpenFlow or iptables.
2. [Post-incident analysis (GitHub)](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/oct21-post-incident-analysis/), Jason Warner, GitHub, 2018. Postmortem, primary: yes. Seen: 43 seconds of lost connectivity between the East Coast hub and data center; Raft-based Orchestrator failed MySQL primaries over to the West Coast; writes on both sides not on the other; 24 hours 11 minutes degraded; 954 unreplicated writes on one busy cluster; fix: no cross-region promotion.
3. See `distributed-system` #4 (Kingsbury and Bailis): catalogue of real partitions, one-way NIC failure, split brain in two-node clusters.

#### `process-pauses` (short)

1. [How to do distributed locking](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html), Martin Kleppmann, 2016. Blog, primary: no. Seen: the lease-plus-GC-pause diagram; HBase had this bug; stop-the-world pauses of minutes; checking before the write doesn't help; page faults, EBS, CPU contention, SIGSTOP; "Your processes will get paused."; packets delayed about 90 s at GitHub; fencing tokens (phase 12 material).
2. See `distributed-system` #1 (Kleppmann notes 2.3): a paused node doesn't notice, other nodes may declare it dead, a pause is not a crash.
3. [Live Migration of Virtual Machines](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/nsdi05/tech/full_papers/clark/clark.pdf), Clark et al., NSDI 2005. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: pre-copy then stop-and-copy; the source VM is suspended for the final copy; downtimes of 60 ms (Quake 3) and 210 ms (web server) on their cluster.
4. Existing note `man7-signal` re-opened: SIGSTOP stops, SIGCONT continues, SIGSTOP can't be caught; after stop and SIGCONT some Linux calls fail with EINTR.

#### `fault-injection` (deep)

1. [Jepsen](https://github.com/jepsen-io/jepsen), Kyle Kingsbury and contributors, main branch. Code and docs, primary: yes. Seen: README design (control node, DB nodes over SSH, clients, history, nemesis, checker); tutorial 05 (random halves partition, crashed ops "may or may not take place", stale reads found in etcd); `nemesis/combined.clj` (clock skew, crashes, pauses, partitions, file corruption; partition shapes one, majority, majorities-ring, minority-third, primaries); `nemesis.clj` (bridge grudge, SIGSTOP/SIGCONT pauses); `net.clj` (iptables DROP, tc netem for delay, loss, corruption, duplication, reorder, rate); `nemesis/time.clj` (disable NTP, bump and strobe clocks); containers can't test clock skew.
2. [Toxiproxy README](https://github.com/Shopify/toxiproxy), Shopify, v2.12.0. Code and docs, primary: yes. Seen: TCP proxy plus HTTP API; toxics latency, down, bandwidth, slow_close, timeout, reset_peer, slicer, limit_data, packet_loss; upstream vs downstream; toxicity; no root needed; < 100 µs overhead; MySQL on localhost bypasses it.
3. [tc-netem(8)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/tc-netem.8.html), iproute2 (netem by Stephen Hemminger). Man page, primary: yes. Seen: delay with jitter, correlation and distributions (pareto for long tails); random, Markov and Gilbert-Elliot loss; corrupt, duplicate, reorder, rate, slot; seed for reproducibility; limits (timer granularity, reorder needs delay, put on receiver ingress for TCP tests because of TSQ); acts on outgoing packets; selective impairment with prio and filters.
4. [An Analysis of Network-Partitioning Failures in Cloud Systems](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi18-alquraan.pdf), see `network-partitions` #1: mocking tests one side of one component; 93% reproducible with partition injection; small clusters suffice.
5. [Simple Testing Can Prevent Most Critical Failures](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/osdi14/osdi14-paper-yuan.pdf), Yuan et al., OSDI 2014. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: 198 failures in Cassandra, HBase, HDFS, MapReduce, Redis; 77% need more than one input, 90% at most three; 98% on three nodes or fewer; 92% of catastrophic failures from mishandled non-fatal errors; 35% trivial (empty handler, over-catch and abort, TODO); 58% catchable by simple tests of error handlers.
6. See `distributed-system` #4 for real faults worth imitating.

Also relevant, existing notes: `lazyfs-github`, `ramos-lazyfs-2024`, `kernel-dm-log-writes` (disk faults, via `crash-testing`).

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Are partitions rare? Some operators say modern networks are reliable; the surveys (Kingsbury and Bailis, Alquraan et al.) show they aren't, while admitting some expensive networks rarely partition. The data is thin because few companies publish.
- Who wrote the fallacies: Wikipedia says Bill Joy and "Dave Lyon"; the APNIC post says Tom Lyon and calls "Dave" a common error. The list's page on Gosling's site credits only Deutsch.
- "Byzantine" for bugs: the theory counts any deviation as Byzantine, but Kleppmann's notes reserve the word for deliberate misbehaviour, since a bug shared by all nodes breaks the 3f + 1 bound anyway.
- Jepsen's partition coverage: Alquraan et al. (2018) say Jepsen doesn't support all partition types; current Jepsen code has bridge and majorities-ring (partial) partitions, but no built-in one-way partition was seen.
- Where to inject: a proxy (Toxiproxy, no root, one connection at a time) vs the kernel (netem and iptables, root, whole interfaces). The netem man page says realistic TCP results need netem on the receiver's ingress.
- Pause length: Kleppmann cites minute-long stop-the-world pauses on large JVM heaps; modern collectors (ZGC, Go) target sub-millisecond pauses (existing notes `openjdk-zgc`, `go-gc-guide`). Pauses from other causes (VM migration, SIGSTOP, swap) don't go away.

**Couldn't open:**
- Waldo, Wyant, Wollrath, Kendall, "A Note on Distributed Computing" (1994) at scholar.harvard.edu: Access Denied.
- ACM Queue version of "The Network is Reliable" (queue.acm.org, id 2655736): Cloudflare 403 by curl and WebFetch; used the 2013 blog version instead.
- Rotem-Gal-Oz, "Fallacies of Distributed Computing Explained" (rgoarchitects.com PDF): connection timed out.
- AWS Builders' Library live page: redirects to builder.aws.com, which renders client-side; read via the Internet Archive copy of the original URL.

**Rejected:**
- Wikipedia on the fallacies: secondary, and wrong on Tom Lyon's name per the APNIC post.
- Medium and vendor explainers on the fallacies (Ably, Geek Culture): secondary, add nothing over #1 and #2.

**Gaps:**
- No primary source on how long VM live migration pauses are on today's public clouds; only the 2005 Xen numbers.
- No primary source for omission failures in practice (only the DLS definition); the article keeps it to the definition.
- No measured numbers for our own machine (netem accuracy, pause lengths). The phase 11 lab could measure both.
- Clock faults are only covered from the Jepsen side; `clock-skew` owns the rest.

### Replication

#### `replication` (deep)
