1. [Chapter 26. High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/high-availability.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: read-only servers are easy to combine, read/write servers are hard because every write has to reach every server; that "synchronization problem" is the core difficulty; some solutions let only one server modify data (primary, standby; warm vs hot standby); synchronous means not committed until all servers commit, so failover loses nothing and load-balanced reads agree; asynchronous allows delay, so some transactions can be lost on failover and reads can be stale; a fully synchronous solution over a slow network "might cut performance by more than half".
2. [26.1. Comparison of Different Solutions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/different-replication-solutions.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: shared disk, block-device (DRBD), WAL shipping (whole server, sync or async), logical (per table, can flow in several directions), trigger-based, SQL middleware (random(), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, sequences differ per server when statements are broadcast), async multimaster (conflicts resolved by users or rules, Bucardo), sync multimaster (Postgres doesn't offer it); feature matrix table 26.1; data partitioning listed as a separate thing.
3. [MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual, Chapter 19 Replication](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/replication.html), Oracle. Docs, primary: yes. Seen (via WebFetch, curl got a "Technical Difficulties" page): source and replicas; asynchronous by default, replicas need not be connected all the time; advantages: scale-out (all writes on the source, reads on replicas), running backups on a replica, analytics on a replica, long-distance distribution.
4. [Replication (MongoDB manual)](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/replication/), MongoDB Inc., MongoDB 8.0 era docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: replica set, one primary takes all writes and records them in the oplog; secondaries apply the oplog asynchronously; reasons: redundancy, read capacity, locality across data centers, copies for DR/reporting/backup; replication lag defined; flow control (`flowControlTargetLagSeconds`); `electionTimeoutMillis` 10 s default, median election time should not typically exceed 12 s; reads from secondaries may not reflect the primary.
5. [Distributed systems for fun and profit, chapter 4: Replication](http://book.mixu.net/distsys/replication.html), Mikito Takada, 2013. Book (free online), primary: no. Seen: sync = write N-of-N, as slow as the slowest server, can't lose a server; async = write 1-of-N, fast, weak durability; single-copy vs divergence-risking (multi-master) methods; primary/backup = log shipping, MySQL async by default; even sync primary/backup has an ambiguous-failure case; split brain; 2PC; can't tell a partitioned node from a dead one.
6. [Eventually Consistent, Revisited](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2008/12/eventually_consistent.html), Werner Vogels, 2008. Blog (Amazon CTO, ACM Queue article reposted), primary: yes. Seen: replication used for performance and availability, but clients see its consequences; strong vs weak vs eventual consistency, inconsistency window; RDBMS primary-backup sync vs async via log shipping; reading from backups gives eventual consistency; N/W/R and W+R>N; stickiness gives read-your-writes and monotonic reads.

Extra: [Chapter 26.4 Hot Standby](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/hot-standby.html), see replication-lag #4. Used here for "a DROP TABLE on the primary is applied on the standby" (replication isn't a backup).

#### `leader-follower-replication` (deep)

1. [26.2. Log-Shipping Standby Servers](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: standby in "continuous recovery mode" reading the primary's WAL; file-based shipping one 16MB segment at a time vs streaming; same hardware architecture and major version needed; base backup then catch-up; `standby.signal`, `primary_conninfo`, walsender and walreceiver; streaming async by default, delay typically under one second; WAL recycled before a standby gets it forces re-initialisation, fixed by `wal_keep_size`, slots, or an archive; slots can fill `pg_wal`, `max_slot_wal_keep_size`; cascading replication (async only); synchronous replication 26.2.8 (see sync-vs-async); monitoring by comparing LSNs; the WAL stream exposes privileged data.
2. [26.1. Comparison of Different Solutions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/different-replication-solutions.html). See replication #2. WAL shipping vs logical vs SQL-statement broadcast, and why broadcasting statements breaks with random() and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.
3. [MySQL 8.4, 19.2.1 Replication Formats](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/replication-formats.html), Oracle. Docs, primary: yes. Seen (WebFetch): statement-based (SBR) vs row-based (RBR) vs mixed; row-based is the default; SBR has issues with stored routines and triggers.
4. [Replication (MongoDB manual)](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/replication/). See replication #4. The oplog, secondaries applying it asynchronously, elections.
5. [Kafka design, Replication section](https://kafka.apache.org/43/design/design/), Apache Kafka project, Kafka 4.3. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: partition = unit of replication, one leader, followers pull like consumers (natural batching), identical logs and offsets; ISR; "a leader who chooses the ordering" as the simplest and fastest replicated log; majority quorum comparison (2f+1 vs f+1); Kafka doesn't require intact stable storage or fsync per write, a rejoining replica fully re-syncs; controller elects a new leader from the ISR, batching elections.
6. [Chapter 26.4 Hot Standby](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/hot-standby.html). See replication-lag #4. Read-only standby, what's refused, query conflicts.

Extra: [Why Uber Engineering Switched from Postgres to MySQL](https://www.uber.com/blog/postgres-to-mysql-migration/). Note exists from phase 6 (write amplification also becomes replication amplification). Not re-opened this time, so not cited.

#### `sync-vs-async-replication` (short)

1. [26.2. Log-Shipping Standby Servers, 26.2.8 Synchronous Replication](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby.html). See leader-follower #1. Seen: async by default, loss proportional to replication delay; synchronous waits for WAL on disk on primary and standby; minimum wait one round trip; `synchronous_commit` levels `remote_write`, `on`, `remote_apply`; per-transaction choice (the 10%/90% example); FIRST vs ANY in `synchronous_standby_names`; commits may never complete if a sync standby crashes; catch-up vs streaming state; a primary restart marks waiting transactions committed; locks held while waiting.
2. [MySQL 8.4, 19.4.10 Semisynchronous Replication](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/replication-semisync.html), Oracle. Docs, primary: yes. Seen (WebFetch): async, semisync and fully synchronous defined side by side; source waits until at least one replica has received and logged the events (relay log flushed), not applied; AFTER_SYNC default vs AFTER_COMMIT; slowdown at least one TCP round trip, best for close servers; timeout reverts to async and comes back when a replica catches up; after a crash and failover the old source should be discarded.

Extra: [Distributed systems for fun and profit, ch. 4](http://book.mixu.net/distsys/replication.html). See replication #5. The ambiguous failure in synchronous primary/backup (client told "failed", backup committed). Not cited, the Postgres and MySQL pages cover the same point.

#### `in-sync-replicas` (short)

1. [Kafka design, Replication section](https://kafka.apache.org/43/design/design/). See leader-follower #5. Seen: two liveness conditions (session with controller, not "too far" behind); `replica.lag.time.max.ms`; committed = all ISR have it; consumers only see committed messages; `acks` 0/1/all; `acks=all` means current ISR, not all assigned replicas; `min.insync.replicas`; unclean leader election off by default since 0.11.0.0; ISR vs majority vote (f+1 vs 2f+1, latency set by the slowest in-sync replica vs the fastest majority).
2. [Eligible Leader Replicas (Kafka operations docs)](https://kafka.apache.org/43/operations/eligible-leader-replicas/), Apache Kafka project, Kafka 4.3. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: ELR available from 4.0 (KIP-966 part 1), on by default for new clusters from 4.1; strict min ISR rule: high watermark can't advance while ISR < min ISR; election order; `eligible.leader.replicas.version`; min.insync.replicas moves to a cluster-level config.
3. [KIP-966: Eligible Leader Replicas](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-966%3A+Eligible+Leader+Replicas), Calvin Liu, Apache Kafka wiki. Design proposal, primary: yes. Seen: "last replica standing": unflushed data lost in an unclean shutdown of the last ISR member turns local loss into global loss; timeline with brokers 0, 1, 2 and min ISR 2; before the KIP min ISR only mattered for accepting acks=all; the ISR's two jobs (replication quorum and leader candidates) are split.

Extra: [Hands-free Kafka Replication](https://www.confluent.io/blog/hands-free-kafka-replication-a-lesson-in-operational-simplicity/), Neha Narkhede, Confluent, 2015. Blog by a Kafka author, primary: yes. Seen: slow, stuck and bootstrapping replicas; Kafka 0.8.2 used both `replica.lag.max.messages` and `replica.lag.time.max.ms`; message-count lag made replicas flap in and out of the ISR on traffic spikes; replaced by time-only lag. Not cited (a short node keeps to two or three sources); good background.
Extra: [Jepsen: Kafka](https://aphyr.com/posts/293-call-me-maybe-kafka), Kyle Kingsbury, 2013. Blog, primary: no. Seen: pre-0.8 design let the ISR shrink to the leader alone, then an out-of-ISR node could be elected, losing acknowledged writes; recommended a floor on ISR size and blocking when it empties; a comment notes unclean election could be disabled from 0.8.2. Historical; not cited.
Extra: [Kafka Replication (design wiki)](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/Kafka+Replication). Downloaded, not read; the current design docs cover it.

#### `replication-lag` (deep)

1. [Session Guarantees for Weakly Consistent Replicated Data](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs734/2000FA/cached%20papers/SessionGuaranteesPDIS_1.html), Douglas Terry, Alan Demers, Karin Petersen, Mike Spreitzer, Marvin Theimer, Brent Welch, Xerox PARC, PDIS 1994. Paper (HTML copy on a Cornell course page), primary: yes. Seen: the four guarantees (read your writes, monotonic reads, writes follow reads, monotonic writes) with formal definitions; the Grapevine password example; mail and calendar examples; session manager with read-set and write-set; version vectors to make it cheap; latching onto one server skips checks; guarantees can reduce availability; RYW doesn't promise anything about other sessions.
2. [Eventually Consistent, Revisited](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2008/12/eventually_consistent.html). See replication #6. Read-your-writes, session, monotonic read, monotonic write definitions; reading from backups is a classic eventual-consistency case; stickiness; client-side versions; "user-perceived consistency": the window must be shorter than the time to the next page load.
3. [26.2. Log-Shipping Standby Servers](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby.html). See leader-follower #1. Delay typically under one second; monitoring via `pg_current_wal_lsn`, `sent_lsn`, `pg_last_wal_receive_lsn`, `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn`, and what each gap points to; `remote_apply` gives "load balancing with causal consistency".
4. [26.4. Hot Standby](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/hot-standby.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: standby is "eventually consistent" with the primary; changes visible once the commit record is replayed; query conflicts (locks, DROP, vacuum cleanup) force either delaying WAL replay or cancelling queries; `max_standby_streaming_delay`; `hot_standby_feedback` and bloat; a long query can hold back replay so other sessions don't see recent changes.
5. [27.2 The Cumulative Statistics System](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/monitoring-stats.html), PostgreSQL 18. Note exists (pg_stat_activity); appended: `write_lag`, `flush_lag`, `replay_lag` in `pg_stat_replication`, replay_lag approximates visibility delay for an async standby, shows NULL after going idle.
6. [Mitigating replication lag and reducing read load with freno](https://github.blog/engineering/infrastructure/mitigating-replication-lag-and-reducing-read-load-with-freno/), Shlomi Noach and Miguel Fernández, GitHub, 2017. Blog by the builders, primary: yes. Seen: async MySQL, reads served from replicas; lagging replicas removed from the pool after a few seconds, sub-second lag expected; big writes split into 50-100 row chunks with throttling between; pt-heartbeat timestamp every 100 ms; "five seconds since last write" rule; comparing time since last write with max cluster lag moved ~30% of master reads to replicas; delaying indexing jobs until data replicated (under 600 ms at p95).
7. [Causal Consistency and Read and Write Concerns](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/causal-consistency-read-write-concerns/), MongoDB Inc., MongoDB 8.0 era docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: causally consistent client sessions; table of read/write concern combinations vs the four guarantees; only majority/majority gives all four, including during a transient two-primary period; `w:1` writes on an old primary roll back.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Majority quorum vs ISR: the Kafka docs argue ISR needs fewer copies (f+1) for the same f failures and that letting the client choose to block makes up for commit latency tied to the slowest in-sync replica. Jepsen (2013) argued majority quorums are the most available choice for small replica counts. Kafka's answer since then is `min.insync.replicas`, unclean election off by default (0.11.0.0), and ELR (4.0/4.1).
- "Synchronous" means different things: Postgres `on` waits for the standby's flush, `remote_write` only for its OS write, `remote_apply` for replay; MySQL semisync waits only for the relay log. Only `remote_apply` makes a replica read fresh.
- Semisync's durability promise lapses exactly under trouble: on timeout MySQL goes back to async. Postgres does the opposite: commits hang if the sync standby is gone.
- Hot standby tuning: short replay delay for HA vs long delay for reporting queries. The Postgres docs say it's one or the other per standby.
- Kafka doesn't fsync each write and relies on replicas; KIP-966 shows the gap that leaves when the last in-sync replica loses its page cache.

- ACM Queue's copy of "Eventually Consistent" (Cloudflare block); used the author's own repost instead.
- dev.mysql.com via curl ("Technical Difficulties" page); opened with WebFetch instead, so quotes came through WebFetch rather than a local download.
- Terry et al. PDF copies on utexas and berkeley pages (returned HTML errors); the Cornell HTML copy worked.

**Rejected:**

- DDIA chapter 5 (not opened, per the book rule).
- MySQL replication implementation page (IO/SQL threads): the Postgres walsender/walreceiver material covers the same idea.
- Confluent and Jepsen Kafka posts as citations for `in-sync-replicas` (kept as background, see above).

**Gaps:**

- No opened source gives Kafka's default for `replica.lag.time.max.ms` or `min.insync.replicas`; articles leave the numbers out.
- No measured numbers for sync vs async commit latency beyond "at least one round trip" and Postgres's "might cut performance by more than half" for a fully synchronous solution over a slow network.
- Leaderless and multi-leader are only mentioned in `replication` from the Postgres comparison page and Vogels; Dynamo's paper (note exists) wasn't re-opened here.

### Replication

#### `failover` (deep)

1. [26.3. Failover](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby-failover.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: old primary must be told it's no longer primary; STONITH, both think they're primary leads to data loss; optional witness server; Postgres ships no failure detection; degenerate state after failover; pg_rewind; regular switchovers test failover; pg_ctl promote / pg_promote().
2. [High availability with Redis Sentinel](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/sentinel/), Redis. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: no guarantee acknowledged writes survive (async replication); quorum is detection only, majority authorizes; no failover in minority partition; two Sentinels never enough; example 1 permanent split brain; example 2 partitioned old master loses C1's writes; min-replicas-to-write 1 + max-lag 10 makes it stop after 10 s; SDOWN/ODOWN; replica choice by priority then replication offset; configuration epochs, higher wins; returning masters reconfigured as replicas.
3. [Rollbacks During Replica Set Failover](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/replica-set-rollbacks/), MongoDB, manual 8.0. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: rollback on rejoin of old primary; usually after partition; lagging secondaries increase it; rollback BSON files; w:1 only primary; majority + journaling prevents rollback of acknowledged writes; w:majority default since 5.0; local reads can see rolled-back data.
4. [GitHub availability this week](https://github.blog/news-insights/the-library/github-availability-this-week/), Jesse Newland, GitHub, 2012. Engineering blog, primary: yes. Seen: Pacemaker/Percona Replication Manager; migration load failed health checks; cold buffer pool, fail back; maintenance mode; Pacemaker segfault split cluster, two elections despite majority config; stale node elected; Redis/MySQL id drift, events on wrong dashboards, 16 private repos exposed for seven minutes; failover made manual.
5. [Post-incident analysis (GitHub's 2018 MySQL failover)](https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/oct21-post-incident-analysis/), Jason Warner, GitHub, 2018. Engineering blog, primary: yes. Seen: 43 s cut, 24 h 11 min degradation; Orchestrator on Raft; West + cloud formed quorum, promoted West primaries; unreplicated East writes (954 on one busy cluster); couldn't fail back; cross-country latency; restore from backups took hours; replication catch-up power decay; fix: no cross-region promotion; binlogs kept for reconciliation.

#### `multi-leader-replication` (short)

1. [Replication and conflict model](https://docs.couchdb.org/en/stable/replication/conflicts.html), Apache CouchDB, docs 3.5. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: business card example (desktop/laptop); both revisions kept on both sides; deterministic winner, conflicts hidden from plain GET; single-node 409 via _rev; revision tree; merge and delete losers; sweeper window; compaction drops old bodies; store diffs in new revision.
2. [How DynamoDB global tables work](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/V2globaltables_HowItWorks.html), AWS. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: one replica per Region, every replica writable; MREC default, async within a second or less, last writer wins per item by internal timestamp; strong reads/conditional writes/transactions local only; RPO = replication delay; MRSC: sync to another Region, exactly three Regions, ReplicatedWriteConflictException, cross-Region latency.

#### `leaderless-replication` (deep)

1. [Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf), DeCandia et al., SOSP 2007. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: always writeable; preference list; N/R/W, R+W>N; W-1 acks; sloppy quorum, hinted handoff; vector clocks and semantic reconciliation; read repair; Merkle trees per key range; (3,2,2) common, R=1 W=N read engine, W=1; divergent versions 99.94% single version, caused by concurrent writers (robots).
2. [Dynamo (Cassandra architecture)](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/architecture/dynamo.html), Apache Cassandra, docs 5.0. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: multi-master with versioned data; LWW per column instead of vector clocks (LWW-Element-Set CRDT); NTP needed; consistency levels as R+W>N; writes always to all replicas; LOCAL_QUORUM; ANY with hints; read repair and hints best effort, repair guarantees; gossip membership.
3. [Hints](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/managing/operating/hints.html), Apache Cassandra, docs 5.0. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: coordinator stores hints; 3 h window; t0-t4 timeline; best effort; late replica out of sync until repair; hint replay idempotent via original timestamp.
4. [Replication Properties](https://docs.riak.com/riak/kv/latest/developing/app-guide/replication-properties/index.html), Basho, Riak KV docs 2.2.3. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: n_val 3, r/w quorum defaults, pr/pw 0; sloppy quorum vs strict (PR/PW); PW failure may still have written; DW; notfound_ok; quorum = floor(N/2)+1.
5. [Probabilistically Bounded Staleness for Practical Partial Quorums](http://www.bailis.org/papers/pbs-vldb2012.pdf), Bailis et al., VLDB 2012. Paper, primary: no. Seen: partial quorums R+W≤N; defaults then (Cassandra R=W=1, Riak R=W=2); expanding quorums; LinkedIn SSD vs disk (1.85 vs 45.5 ms for 99.9%); Yammer 230 → 43.3 ms for 202 ms window; 43.9% fresh right after write on disks; read repair as extra write.

#### `quorums` (short)

1. Dynamo paper: see `leaderless-replication` #1 (R, W, sloppy quorum, hinted handoff).
2. PBS paper: see `leaderless-replication` #5 (partial quorums, staleness).
3. [Jepsen: Riak](https://aphyr.com/posts/285-jepsen-riak), Kyle Kingsbury, 2013. Blog with test results, primary: no. Seen: LWW lost 71% of acknowledged writes with no partition; sloppy quorum lets both sides write; PR=PW=R=W=quorum still 92% loss because failed writes partially land and win by timestamp; partial availability per key; requests stall until fallbacks; CRDT set merge kept 100%; LWW safe only for immutable/full-state writes; LWW made default because siblings were hard.

#### `anti-entropy` (short)

1. Dynamo paper: see `leaderless-replication` #1 (read repair, Merkle trees).
2. [Read repair](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/managing/operating/read_repair.html), Apache Cassandra, docs 5.0. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: digest reads; blocking read repair and monotonic quorum reads; 4.0 read_repair NONE option; breaks write atomicity; no repair at ONE; background read repair removed in 4.0.
3. [Repair](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/managing/operating/repair.html), Apache Cassandra, docs 5.0. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: Merkle trees; incremental default, full occasionally; not automatic; suggested schedule; gc grace 10 days, repair every 7 or deleted data reappears.
4. [Epidemic Algorithms for Replicated Database Maintenance](https://bitsavers.org/pdf/xerox/parc/techReports/CSL-89-1_Epidemic_Algorithms_for_Replicated_Database_Maintenance.pdf), Demers et al., Xerox PARC, PODC 1987 (tech report CSL-89-1). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: anti-entropy defined; reliable but costly; background backup to direct mail; checksums; deletes resurrect, death certificates, when to drop them. (Note already created by another group; I appended.)
5. [Active Anti-Entropy](https://docs.riak.com/riak/kv/latest/learn/concepts/active-anti-entropy/index.html), Basho, Riak KV docs 2.2.3. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: read repair only reaches read objects; AAE since 1.3 for cold data; persistent on-disk hash trees updated in real time, regenerated weekly. Not used (short node already at 4 sources).

#### `conflict-resolution` (deep)

1. Dynamo paper: see `leaderless-replication` #1 (figure 3 version history, cart merge, deletes resurface, clock truncation at 10).
2. [Causal Context](https://docs.riak.com/riak/kv/latest/learn/concepts/causal-context/index.html), Basho, Riak KV docs 2.2.3. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: siblings vs timestamp (allow_mult), CRDT option, vector clocks vs dotted version vectors (2.0), sibling explosion can crash a node, read/modify/write cycle.
3. Jepsen: Riak: see `quorums` #3.
4. [The trouble with timestamps](https://aphyr.com/posts/299-the-trouble-with-timestamps), Kyle Kingsbury, 2013. Blog, primary: no. Seen: Cassandra wall-clock timestamps; clocks step back (NTP, leap seconds); later write with smaller timestamp gone forever; tombstones delete lower timestamps; logical clocks needed; measure skew.
5. Cassandra architecture: see `leaderless-replication` #2 (per-column LWW, NTP).
6. CouchDB: see `multi-leader-replication` #1.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Automatic vs manual failover: GitHub went manual after 2012; in 2018 it ran automated Raft-based failover and changed only where promotion may go.
- Last write wins: Cassandra and DynamoDB global tables make it the default; Riak's docs now recommend siblings; Jepsen shows LWW losing most concurrent writes. Cassandra calls its LWW a CRDT, which converges but still drops writes.
- Quorum staleness: PBS says partial quorums are usually fresh within tens of ms; Jepsen shows even strict quorums lose writes under partitions. Different questions (staleness vs loss), often confused.
- "Quorum" means different things: Sentinel's quorum is detection-only; Dynamo's is R/W; Riak's symbolic "quorum" is a majority.

### Replication

#### `crdts` (deep)

1. [A comprehensive study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types](https://inria.hal.science/inria-00555588/document), Marc Shapiro, Nuno Preguiça, Carlos Baquero, Marek Zawirski, INRIA RR-7506, 2011. Paper (research report), primary: yes. Seen: 1 intro (CRDT = convergent or commutative replicated data type, update executes immediately, no consensus so strong limits, unbounded growth and GC needs weak sync, ad-hoc reconciliation brittle, Amazon cart footnote); 2 system model; 2.2.1 state-based, causal history; 2.2.2 op-based, reliable broadcast in delivery order; 2.3.1 LUB is commutative, idempotent, associative, messages can be lost/reordered/duplicated; 2.3.2 concurrent ops commute, causal delivery needs no consensus; 2.4 state vs op trade-offs, "shipping deltas", op-based needs group membership; 2.4.1-2 each can emulate the other; 3.1 op counter, G-Counter (max merge loses an increment, add merge not idempotent, vector inspired by vector clocks, assumes no overflow and known replicas), PN-Counter, non-negative counter impossible locally (two replicas at 1 converge to -1), escrow; 3.2 LWW register (timestamps consistent with causality), MV register with version vectors, Amazon cart reappearing item (figure 10); 3.3 add/remove don't commute, naive set diverges (figure 11), G-Set, 2P-Set with tombstones, U-Set, LWW-element-Set, PN-Set anomalies, OR-Set with unique tags, add wins (figure 14); 4 GC: tombstones accumulate, stability needs known replicas that don't crash permanently; 7 conclusion.
2. [Conflict-free Replicated Data Types](https://inria.hal.science/hal-00932836/document), Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero, Zawirski, SSS 2011. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: abstract; 1 intro (SEC as "a solution to the CAP problem"); 2.2 EC definition (eventual delivery, convergence, termination), EC systems that roll back need consensus, SEC adds strong convergence; 3.1 CAP: SEC replica always available for reads and writes, partitioned subsets converge, tolerates n-1 crashes, no consensus; 3.3 SEC incomparable with sequential consistency, add-wins example with e and e′, alternatives (add wins, remove wins, highest IP wins, reset).
3. [Conflict-free Replicated Data Types](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.06358), Nuno Preguiça, Carlos Baquero, Marc Shapiro, 2018 (encyclopedia entry). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: definition; concurrency semantics vs synchronization model; happens-before; add-wins vs remove-wins vs LWW sets (figure 1); clock time + site id total order doesn't respect happens-before under skew, HLC; MV vs LWW register; counter with write; state-based conditions (semilattice, inflation, join); op-based generator/effector, causal delivery; delta-state, first contact needs full state, big-delta, digests; pure op-based; preservation of sequential semantics (2P-Set breaks it); add-wins states with no sequential explanation (figure 2); CAP favours availability, per-object causal consistency, session guarantees; auction close needs agreement; bounded counter / escrow; commercial users Riak, Redis, Akka, Roshi (LWW-element-set at SoundCloud); future: metadata linear in replicas, limits past a few hundred replicas; undo; security (deletes can wipe state); non-uniform replication; verification.
4. [Delta State Replicated Data Types](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1603.01529), Paulo Sérgio Almeida, Ali Shoker, Carlos Baquero, arXiv 1603.01529v1, 2016. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: abstract (small messages over unreliable channels); 1 intro: op-based needs reliable exactly-once causal broadcast, hard even over TCP, membership hard; state size grows with replicas (counter) or elements (set), full state fine for counters not large sets; Riak DT Maps as motivation; deltas keep join idempotent; deltas are state fragments and usually need causal merging; C++ reference library; 2 system model (lost, duplicated, reordered messages). Read sections 1-3 only.
5. [Interleaving anomalies in collaborative text editors](https://martin.kleppmann.com/papers/interleaving-papoc19.pdf), Martin Kleppmann, Victor B. F. Gomes, Dominic P. Mulligan, Alastair R. Beresford, PaPoC 2019. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: SEC properties restated; convergence necessary but not sufficient (lexicographic sort example); figure 2 "Hello Al Ciharcliee!"; Logoot and LSEQ interleave via dense position identifiers (figure 3), observed in open-source implementations; RGA has a lesser anomaly and a proposed fix; Treedoc and WOOT conjectured fine.
6. [Concepts: Data Types](https://docs.riak.com/riak/kv/latest/learn/concepts/crdts/index.html), Basho, Riak KV 2.2.3. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: types (counters, flags, HLL, maps, registers, sets); op-based interface over state-based convergence; counters can't give unique IDs; no custom merge; context like vector clock / dotted version vectors; convergence rules table (flags enable wins, registers newest timestamp, counters PN, sets add wins, maps add/update wins); no strong consistency.
7. [Develop applications with Active-Active databases](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/rs/databases/active-active/develop/develop-for-aa/), Redis, Redis Software docs, latest = v8.0 when read. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: multi-master + CRDTs behind normal commands; INCRBY 7 and 3 across two members read 10 after sync; comparison with active-passive, 2PC, quorum writes, LWW (LWW drops concurrent set adds), MVCC; Lua in effects mode; eviction; EXPIRE conflict (longer TTL wins, PERSIST wins); tombstones kept until all instances observed the delete; OOM; INFO CRDT section (vector clocks, crdt_gc_pending).

Extra: [About CRDTs](https://crdt.tech/), crdt.tech (Kleppmann's site). Opened: strong vs optimistic replication, CRDTs don't assume a central server unlike Google Docs/Trello/Figma. Not given a note; the papers cover it.
Extra: [Local-first software](https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/local-first/), Kleppmann, Wiggins, van Hardenberg, McGranaghan, Ink & Switch, 2019. Opened: CRDT section and findings (Automerge; server-centric users Cosmos DB, Redis, Riak, Roshi, OpenR; conflicts rarer than feared; full history grows and can't be truncated because someone may reconnect after six months). Not cited here; fits `realtime-sync` in phase 17.
Extra: [Riak KV Data Types (developing)](https://docs.riak.com/riak/kv/latest/developing/data-types/index.html), Basho. Opened: bucket types, allow_mult=true and last_write_wins=false required, context needed for removes (without it a remove can fail or remove updates the client never saw). Not given a note.
Extra: Redis Active-Active [strings](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/rs/databases/active-active/develop/data-types/strings/) and [sets](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/rs/databases/active-active/develop/data-types/sets/) pages. Opened: strings are LWW by OS time except when used as counters (59-bit counters); sets use OR-Set, add wins, observed remove. Not given notes; summarised in redis-active-active-develop's "My notes".
Extra: [Active-Active geo-distributed Redis](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/rs/databases/active-active/). Opened: overview, syncer, strong eventual consistency, vector clocks, optional causal consistency. Not given a note.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- "Conflict-free" vs clocks: the papers define CRDTs to need no synchronisation, yet the LWW register and Riak's registers pick winners by timestamp, and Redis strings use OS time. The article says clocks sneak back in wherever a type picks a winner by timestamp.
- The SSS paper calls SEC "a solution to the CAP problem"; the 2018 overview says more carefully that CRDTs favour availability over consistency. The article uses the second framing.
- Convergence as the goal vs usable results: the 2011 papers treat convergence as the correctness condition; Kleppmann et al. show converged text can still be garbage. Covered in "Where it gets tricky".
- State vs op-based: the RR says each can emulate the other; Almeida et al. argue op-based's exactly-once causal broadcast is hard in practice. Both stated.

**Couldn't open:**

- Nothing needed failed to open.

**Rejected:**

- Wikipedia's CRDT page and blog explainers: secondary; the defining papers are open.
- Automerge and Yjs docs: about client-side document CRDTs, which belong to `realtime-sync`.
- DDIA chapter 5 (conflict resolution, CRDT mention): book not opened for this project.

**Gaps:**

- No measured numbers on metadata or tombstone size in production; the article gives none beyond the 2018 overview's "more than a few hundred replicas".
- Riak's docs are frozen at 2.2.3 (Basho is gone). No current source on Riak's status was opened, so the article pins the version and says nothing more.
- Azure Cosmos DB's multi-region conflict resolution wasn't opened; it may be a second current production example.

### Partitioning

#### `partitioning` (deep)

1. [Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf), DeCandia et al., Amazon, SOSP 2007. Paper, primary: yes. Already a note (`decandia-dynamo-2007`). Seen: 4.2 incremental scaling needs dynamic partitioning; MD5 of the key gives a 128-bit identifier; the ring, a node owns the range between it and its predecessor; 4.3 key replicated on the N-1 clockwise successors, preference list skips positions to get distinct physical nodes; 6.1 load imbalance falls with load (out-of-balance ratio about 20% at low load, about 10% at high); 6.2 three partitioning strategies, partitioning and placement "intertwined" in strategy 1, bootstrapping took almost a day, strategy 3 (Q equal fixed partitions, Q/S tokens per node) best efficiency and three orders of magnitude less membership data; 6.4 client-driven routing avoids a hop.
2. [Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//archive/bigtable-osdi06.pdf), Chang et al., Google, OSDI 2006. Paper, primary: yes. Already a note (`chang-bigtable-2006`). Seen: row range dynamically partitioned into tablets, the unit of distribution and load balancing; tablets split at about 100 to 200 MB by default; ten to a thousand tablets per tablet server; three-level location hierarchy (root tablet, METADATA, user tablets) like a B+ tree, cached by clients; master assigns tablets and balances load; reversed URLs for locality.
3. [Sharding](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/sharding/), MongoDB manual 8.3. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: sharding for data sets and throughput beyond one server; vertical vs horizontal scaling; shard key picks the shard, resharding possible since 5.0; chunks with inclusive lower and exclusive upper bound; balancer; queries with the shard key are targeted, others broadcast; mongos routers and config servers.
4. [Distribution Layer](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/architecture/distribution-layer), CockroachDB docs (v26.3). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: one sorted key-value map split into ranges of contiguous keys; two-level meta ranges (meta1, meta2) locate ranges, cached on each node; split on size, merge small ranges; table and secondary index each start as one range; DistSender routes batches to leaseholders. Range size defaults are rendered client-side on this page; the numbers (split at 512 MiB, merge below 128 MiB) are on [Replication Controls](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/configure-replication-zones).
5. [Amazon DynamoDB: A Scalable, Predictably Performant, and Fully Managed NoSQL Database Service](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/atc22-elhemali.pdf), Elhemali et al., Amazon, USENIX ATC 2022. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: partition key hashed; each partition holds a disjoint contiguous part of the (hashed) key range, replicated by Multi-Paxos across AZs; split for size and for throughput; throughput divided among child partitions (3200 WCU table example); hot partitions and throughput dilution; bursting, adaptive capacity, then global admission control; split for consumption chooses the split point from observed key distribution, finishes in minutes, not for one hot item or sequential access.
6. [Table Partitioning](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-partitioning.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: splitting one large table into smaller physical pieces on one server; range, list and hash (modulus and remainder) partitioning; benefits for bulk loads and deletes (DROP or DETACH a partition); rule of thumb that it pays when the table exceeds the server's memory. The same word for a single-server feature.

#### `range-vs-hash-partitioning` (short)

1. [Hashed Sharding](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/hashed-sharding/), MongoDB manual 8.3. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: hashed shard key gives more even spread at the cost of broadcast range queries; equality queries still targeted; hashed keys ideal for monotonic fields (ObjectId, timestamps); with ranged sharding on a monotonic key the MaxKey chunk takes most inserts; compound hashed keys keep a ranged prefix; floats truncated to 64-bit integers before hashing. Companion page [Ranged Sharding](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/ranged-sharding/): close keys likely in the same chunk, efficient range reads, default method, good keys have high cardinality, low frequency, non-monotonic change.
2. [Hash-sharded indexes](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/hash-sharded-indexes), CockroachDB docs (v26.3). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: sequential keys make every write land at the end of one range, so load-based splitting can't find a split point; a hidden shard column spreads them over buckets; "an implementation of hash partitioning, not hash indexing"; small cost to range reads, which scan every bucket; more buckets than nodes gives diminishing returns; `shard_columns` hashes only a prefix.
3. [Partitions and data distribution](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.Partitions.html), DynamoDB Developer Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: partition key hashed to pick the partition, items not stored in sorted order across partitions; with a sort key, items sharing a partition key stay together in sort order (item collection) so a Query can read a range inside one key. The hybrid most systems use.

#### `consistent-hashing` (deep)

1. [Consistent Hashing and Random Trees](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall09/cos518/papers/chash.pdf), Karger, Lehman, Leighton, Levine, Lewin, Panigrahy, MIT, STOC 1997. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: motivated by hot spots on web caches; with `ax + b mod p`, changing the range remaps almost every item; properties balance, monotonicity (items move only to new buckets), spread and load across inconsistent client views; construction maps buckets and items to the unit interval, item goes to the closest bucket point, each bucket copied about log C times; binary search tree implementation.
2. [Dynamo](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf). See partitioning #1. 4.2 ring, clockwise walk, random positions give non-uniform load and ignore heterogeneity, virtual nodes ("tokens") fix both; 6.2 the three strategies and why they moved to fixed equal partitions.
3. [A Fast, Minimal Memory, Consistent Hash Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.2294), John Lamping and Eric Veach, Google, 2014. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: `h(key) mod 10` to `mod 12` rearranges everything, only 1/6 must move; jump hash in about 5 lines, no memory, buckets must be numbered 0..n-1 so only the last can be removed; Karger's ring with 1000 points per bucket gives standard error 3.2%, 10 points gives 1% of buckets below 0.37x or above 1.98x of average; ring memory 46 MB (version A) for 1000 buckets at 1000 points; jump spreads a new bucket's intake evenly from every old bucket, the ring from only a few; describes rendezvous hashing (highest hash wins, time linear in buckets).
4. [Consistent Hashing with Bounded Loads](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1608.01350), Mirrokni, Thorup, Zadimoghaddam, Google Research and University of Copenhagen, arXiv 2016 (v3 2017). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: plain consistent hashing and rendezvous balance no better than random assignment; with n clients and n servers many servers get Θ(log n / log log n); max load of plain ring likely Θ(log n) times average; capacity ⌈cm/n⌉ with c = 1 + ε, forward to the next non-full bin (linear probing); moves O(1/ε²) per update; used in Google Cloud Pub/Sub and at Vimeo (c = 1.25).
5. [Consistent Hashing with Bounded Loads (Google Research blog)](https://research.google/blog/consistent-hashing-with-bounded-loads/), Vahab Mirrokni and Morteza Zadimoghaddam, Google, 2017. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: plain-language version with a 6-balls, 3-bins worked example; Pub/Sub deployment; Vimeo implemented it in HAProxy and cut cache bandwidth by a factor of almost 8; ε trades uniformity against movement.
6. [Dynamo (Apache Cassandra architecture docs)](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/architecture/dynamo.html), Apache Cassandra. Already a note (`cassandra-architecture-dynamo`). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `hash mod 100` vs a token ring; walk the ring to RF distinct nodes; vnodes let small clusters add one node and take from many neighbours; costs of many tokens (more neighbours, more failure combinations, slower repair); Cassandra 2.x random tokens needed 256 per node, 3.x+ deterministic token allocator.

Extra: [Supported load balancers](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/load_balancers) (Envoy, already `envoy-load-balancers`): ring hash moves 1/N, Maglev about double. [Maglev](https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/44824.pdf) (already `eisenbud-maglev-2016`): evenness over minimal disruption, 65537-entry table. [Load Balancing at the Frontend](https://sre.google/sre-book/load-balancing-frontend/) (already `google-sre-lb-frontend`): `id(packet) mod N`. Used through the existing notes.

#### `rebalancing` (short)

1. [Dynamo](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf). See partitioning #1. 6.2: random tokens mean a joining node must scan other nodes' stores, bootstrapping ran at lowest priority and took almost a day in peak season, Merkle trees recalculated for many ranges, archiving hard; strategy 3 fixes Q equal partitions, moves a partition as a file; the cost is coordination on membership change.
2. [Redis cluster specification](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/reference/cluster-spec/), Redis Open Source docs. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 16384 hash slots, `CRC16(key) mod 16384`; hash tags `{...}`; adding, removing and rebalancing are all "move hash slots"; SETSLOT MIGRATING/IMPORTING, keys moved with MIGRATE while clients follow -ASK, then SETSLOT NODE; -MOVED for permanent moves; big keys are unwise to move under latency limits; multi-key ops may be unavailable during resharding.
3. [The Tail at Scale](https://www.barroso.org/publications/TheTailAtScale.pdf), Dean and Barroso, CACM 2013. Already a note (`dean-tail-at-scale-2013`). Seen: micro-partitions, many more partitions than machines; 20 per machine sheds load in about 5% steps; Bigtable machines manage 20 to 1,000 tablets; faster failure recovery.

Extra: [Balancer](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharding-balancer-administration/), MongoDB 8.3. A shard takes part in at most one migration at a time, at most n/2 parallel migrations; migrations start only past a threshold; balancing window; new shard causes imbalance; range migration steps (copy, catch up, update config metadata, delete after cursors close). Not cited, the Redis and Dynamo pair covers the mechanism.

#### `hot-spots` (short)

1. [Amazon DynamoDB (ATC 2022)](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/atc22-elhemali.pdf). See partitioning #5. Hot partitions and throughput dilution; bursting, adaptive capacity, global admission control; split for consumption at a point chosen from observed keys, done in minutes, useless for a single hot item or sequential keys.
2. [How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages](https://discord.com/blog/how-discord-stores-trillions-of-messages), Bo Ingram, Discord, 2023. Engineering blog, primary: yes. Seen: messages partitioned by (channel_id, bucket); small servers vs servers with hundreds of thousands of people; reads costlier than writes in Cassandra; one hot partition raised latency for the whole cluster with quorum reads; request coalescing in Rust data services, routed by consistent hash on channel ID; 177 Cassandra nodes to 72 ScyllaDB nodes.
3. [Using write sharding to distribute workloads evenly](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-sharding.html), DynamoDB Developer Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: random suffix 1 to 200 on a date key spreads writes, reads must query every suffix and merge; calculated suffix from an attribute you know lets you find one item again.

Extra: [Load-based splitting](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/load-based-splitting), CockroachDB v26.3: splits a range above 2500 QPS (default `kv.range_split.load_qps_threshold`), balance and split-crossing heuristics, 99% on one key vs 60% example, "no split key found" with "popular key" or "clear direction" reasons. [Burst and adaptive capacity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/burst-adaptive-capacity.html): 3,000 reads or 1,000 writes per second per partition, 300 s of unused burst, adaptive capacity isolates hot items. [How Discord Stores Billions of Messages](https://discord.com/blog/how-discord-stores-billions-of-messages), Stanislav Vishnevskiy, 2017: partitions over 100 MB, bucket by about 10 days of messages. Karger 1997 (consistent-hashing #1) was itself about web hot spots. Dean and Barroso's selective replication (rebalancing #3).

#### `partitioned-secondary-indexes` (short)

1. [Improving data access with secondary indexes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/SecondaryIndexes.html), DynamoDB Developer Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: global index has its own partition key and its own partitions, spans all base partitions, eventual consistency only, own throughput; local index shares the base partition key, scoped to one base partition, strong reads possible, 10 GB per partition key value, only at table creation. Companion page [GSI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GSI.html): updated asynchronously, "within a fraction of a second" normally, an under-provisioned index throttles table writes.
2. [Vindexes](https://vitess.io/docs/reference/features/vindexes/), Vitess docs (24.0). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: a Vindex maps a column value to a keyspace ID; primary Vindex is the sharding key; without a secondary Vindex VTGate scatters to all shards; lookup Vindex is a MySQL table, usually on another shard than the row; keeping it in step is a distributed transaction, consistent lookup Vindexes avoid 2PC with ordered commits and locking; shards still need ordinary local indexes.

Extra: [Secondary index (2i) concepts](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/developing/cql/indexing/2i/2i-concepts.html), Cassandra docs: indexes built locally on each node, poor performance, use SAI. [SAI concepts](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/developing/cql/indexing/sai/sai-concepts.html): coordinator queries token ranges in rounds with a concurrency factor until the limit is met. [Elasticsearch `_routing`](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/mapping-reference/mapping-routing-field): search fans out to every shard unless you pass a routing value. All local-index designs.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- **Minimal movement vs even load.** Karger and Dynamo's first design value moving few keys; Lamping and Veach show the ring's uneven buckets (1000 points per bucket still leaves about 1% of buckets 8% off); Maglev and Mirrokni et al. accept more movement for evenness or a hard cap; Dynamo itself ended up at fixed equal partitions.
- **How many vnodes.** Dynamo argues for many tokens per node for balance; Cassandra dropped its default from 256 (random tokens, 2.x) to 16 with a deterministic allocator, because more tokens mean more neighbours and more failure combinations that lose a range.
- **Splitting fixes hot spots, until it doesn't.** CockroachDB and DynamoDB both split hot ranges by load, and both say it can't help a single hot key or a sequential key. Discord fixed hot partitions above the database (coalescing), not in it.
- **Local vs global indexes.** DynamoDB offers both and makes the global one eventually consistent; Vitess makes the lookup consistent with careful commit ordering instead of 2PC; Cassandra calls its per-node indexes "globally-distributed" while saying 2i queries perform poorly because every node is asked.
- **Hash mod N is fine if N never changes.** Redis Cluster (16384 slots) and Elasticsearch (`hash(_routing) % num_primary_shards`) both use plain modulo over a fixed count, and move whole slots or split shards instead of changing N.

**Couldn't open:**

- Andrew Rodland's Vimeo post on bounded-load consistent hashing (medium.com returned a stub). The Google Research blog summarizes the result instead.
- Thaler and Ravishankar's rendezvous hashing report (CSE-TR-316-96): the PDF downloaded but the text layer is unreadable. Rendezvous hashing is described only through Lamping and Veach and Mirrokni et al.
- CockroachDB's distribution layer page renders its range size numbers with JavaScript; took them from the replication zones page.

**Rejected:**

- Elasticsearch shard split API page: the split rules depend on `number_of_routing_shards`, and from Elasticsearch 9.4.0 new indices use plain `hash % num_primary_shards` routing, so the split page and the routing page disagree for new indices. Too version-tangled for a short node.
- MongoDB balancer page: good, but Redis Cluster shows slot migration more clearly.
- Postgres partitioning for `range-vs-hash-partitioning`: single-server, used only in `partitioning` to explain the name clash.

**Gaps:**

- DDIA's partitioning chapter not opened (no official sample chapter found); the articles lean on papers and docs.
- No source measures how much data moves with modulo vs ring vs jump in one setting; the numbers come from Lamping and Veach's own measurements.
- No primary source found on Twitter-style celebrity hot keys; Discord's announcement case stands in.

### Consistency and time

#### `consistency-models` (deep)

1. [Consistency Models](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models), Jepsen. Docs, primary: no. Seen: clickable map of models (adapted from Bailis et al. and Viotti and Vukolić), arrows mean "implies", colours for total, sticky or no availability on an asynchronous network; single-object chain strict serializable > linearizable > sequential > causal > PRAM and writes follow reads > monotonic reads, monotonic writes, read your writes; sequential and stronger can't be totally available, read your writes and stronger at most sticky; definitions of process, operation, invocation and completion time on an imaginary clock, concurrency, crashed operations (concurrent with everything after), history; a model is a set of histories, stronger = subset; SI and RR incomparable.
2. [Replicated Data Consistency Explained Through Baseball](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/ConsistencyAndBaseballReport.pdf), Doug Terry, Microsoft Research technical report, 2011 (CACM 2013). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: six read guarantees (strong, eventual, consistent prefix, bounded staleness, monotonic reads, read my writes); Table 2 consistency/performance/availability ratings; sample game at 2-5 and Table 3 of possible scores per guarantee (18 for eventual, including 1-0 which never happened); participants: scorekeeper (read my writes gives strong effect), umpire (strong), radio reporter (consistent prefix + monotonic reads), sportswriter (bounded staleness), statistician, stat watcher (eventual); SimpleDB, App Engine and PNUTS offer per-read choice. The Microsoft URL blocks some user agents; curl with a browser UA worked. The CACM page came back empty.
3. [Eventually Consistent - Revisited](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2008/12/eventually_consistent.html), Werner Vogels, 2008. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: see `eventual-consistency` #1. For this node: client-side models, session variants listed as variations of eventual, stickiness, client-side version tracking, ACID consistency is a different thing.
4. [Strong consistency models](https://aphyr.com/posts/313-strong-consistency-models), Kyle Kingsbury, 2014. Blog, primary: no. Seen: register, histories, light cones; linearizability from invocation/completion bounds; CAS builds mutexes, queues, maps; sequential as time-skewed but process-ordered; causal via explicit dependencies; serializability has no time bounds; CAP's precise terms; other proofs rule out total availability for sequential, serializable, SI, RR, cursor stability; sticky gives causal, PRAM, RYW; lock service needs linearizability; CPUs not linearizable by default; mix stores (bulk in S3/Cassandra, pointer in etcd/ZooKeeper). A reader comment disputes causal > PRAM.
5. [Sequential Consistency](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/sequential), Jepsen. Docs, primary: no. Seen: total order consistent with each process's order; not totally or sticky available; a process may read arbitrarily stale state but never goes back; for side channels use linearizability; Lamport 1979.
6. [Writes Follow Reads](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/writes-follow-reads), Jepsen. Docs, primary: no. Seen: session causality definition; totally available.
7. [A Critique of the CAP Theorem](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.05393), Martin Kleppmann, 2015. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: see `cap-theorem` #5. For this node: Table 1 lowest latency per model (linearizable O(d) reads and writes; sequential |r| + |w| ≥ d; causal O(1)); causal is optimal if delay tolerance is the only consideration; eventual consistency provides no safety property.

Extra: [PRAM](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/pram) and [Monotonic Writes](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/monotonic-writes), Jepsen. Opened: PRAM is exactly RYW + MW + MR, sticky available; monotonic writes totally available. Not given notes; the models page and Vogels cover what the article says.
Extra: [Consistency in Non-Transactional Distributed Storage Systems](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1512.00168), Viotti and Vukolić, 2016. Downloaded, skimmed only. The formal survey Jepsen's map draws on. Not given a note.
Extra: [Highly Available Transactions: Virtues and Limitations](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1302.0309), Bailis et al., 2014. Downloaded; the text layer of the two-column PDF is badly interleaved (Table 3 of available, sticky and unavailable models unreadable). Not given a note; Jepsen's map summarises it.

#### `eventual-consistency` (short)

1. [Eventually Consistent - Revisited](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2008/12/eventually_consistent.html), Werner Vogels, 2008. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: definition ("if no new updates are made ... eventually all accesses will return the last updated value"); inconsistency window, bounded without failures by delay, load, replica count; DNS as the best-known example; RDBMS async read replicas; N, W, R and W + R ≤ N; session variants; stickiness and client-side versions; shopping cart merges after a partition; two reasons to accept inconsistency; user-perceived consistency on web sites. (Note already existed from another group; appended.)
2. [Replicated Data Consistency Explained Through Baseball](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2011/10/ConsistencyAndBaseballReport.pdf). See `consistency-models` #2. The 18 possible scores, scores that never existed, reading 2-5 then 1-3, stale read-modify-write gives a wrong score.

#### `causal-consistency` (short)

1. [Don't Settle for Eventual: Scalable Causal Consistency for Wide-Area Storage with COPS](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~dga/papers/cops-sosp2011.pdf), Lloyd, Freedman, Kaminsky, Andersen, SOSP 2011. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: ALPS properties; causal+ = causal + convergent conflict handling, strongest they could reach; photo and album example; three rules of potential causality; threads only communicate through the store; Carol and Dan 8pm/10pm conflict, plain causal can diverge forever; last-writer-wins via Lamport clock + node id; dependencies, nearest dependencies, dep_check blocks until present, reads never block; local ops linearizable, cross-datacentre replication in the background; get transactions (ACL and album); RTC vs causal+ and hidden (out-of-band) causality; earlier systems used per-replica logs with version vectors; low latency proven incompatible with linearizability.
2. [Causal Consistency](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/causal), Jepsen. Docs, primary: no. Seen: definition; lunch example; convergent causal; sticky available; real-time causal proven strongest in an always-available one-way convergent system; most "causal" systems are RTC or causal+; total availability means giving up causal and RYW; Lamport happens-before; Mahajan et al. and Viotti-Vukolić formal definitions.

#### `linearizability` (deep)

1. [Linearizability: A Correctness Condition for Concurrent Objects](https://cs.brown.edu/~mph/HerlihyW90/p463-herlihy.pdf), Herlihy and Wing, ACM TOPLAS 1990. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: abstract (takes effect instantaneously between invocation and response); two intuitive requirements; locality and nonblocking; FIFO queue histories H1 to H4, register histories; sequential consistency not local; linearizability as strict serializability restricted to single operations on single objects. Scanned PDF, text layer messy around figures.
2. [Linearizability](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/linearizable), Jepsen. Docs, primary: no. Seen: real-time definition; not totally or sticky available; scope of "an object" varies; strict serializability for many objects; Viotti-Vukolić decomposition.
3. [Strong consistency models](https://aphyr.com/posts/313-strong-consistency-models). See `consistency-models` #4.
4. [Please stop calling databases CP or AP](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2015/05/11/please-stop-calling-databases-cp-or-ap.html), Martin Kleppmann, 2015. Blog, primary: no. Seen: see `cap-theorem` #4. For this node: informal definition, Alice and Bob stale-replica example, must look like a single copy, CPU memory barriers, snapshot isolation intentionally non-linearizable (PostgreSQL SSI serializable but not linearizable), quorums don't reliably give linearizability (sloppy quorums, read repair), ZooKeeper reads and `sync`.
5. [Linearizability versus Serializability](http://www.bailis.org/blog/linearizability-versus-serializability/), Peter Bailis, 2014. Blog, primary: no. Note already existed. Used as is.
6. [KV API guarantees](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/learning/api_guarantees/), etcd v3.6 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: durability and strict serializability for KV calls; linearizable by default through Raft; "serializable" read mode may be stale; read-after-write example.
7. [A Critique of the CAP Theorem](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.05393). See `cap-theorem` #5. Section 4.2.1: linearizable latency at least u/2 (Attiya and Welch), simplified to O(d).

#### `linearizability-checking` (short)

1. [Testing Distributed Systems for Linearizability](https://anishathalye.com/testing-distributed-systems-for-linearizability/), Anish Athalye, 2017. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: sequential spec as code; linearization points; ad-hoc per-key asserts miss bugs; record-and-check; NP-completeness via subset sum; Knossos handled about a hundred events, Porcupine thousands in a couple of seconds; planted-bug comparison.
2. [Porcupine](https://github.com/anishathalye/porcupine), Anish Athalye. Code (README on master), primary: yes. Seen: model with Init/Step/Hash; histories as operations or call/return events; two register examples (one linearizable, one not); implements P-compositionality algorithm (Horn and Kroening) on Lowe's; 1,000x to 10,000x faster than Knossos on Jepsen data, millions with P-compositionality; visualizer per partition, longest partial linearization, illegal linearization points; state space explosion; ARM timestamps need barriers; users (etcd robustness tests, MemoryDB, MIT 6.5840 origin, others).
3. [Knossos](https://github.com/jepsen-io/knossos), Kyle Kingsbury. Code (README), primary: yes. Seen: invoke plus ok / fail / info completions; crashed processes; crashed write can linearize before a read; built-in register, CAS register, mutex models; true / false / :unknown (out of memory); graph search and WGL tree search in parallel; author's caution that results are "plausible but verify by hand".

#### `cap-theorem` (deep)

1. [Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services](https://www.comp.nus.edu.sg/~gilbert/pubs/BrewersConjecture-SigAct.pdf), Gilbert and Lynch, SIGACT News 2002. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: atomic (linearizable) data object; availability = every request to a non-failing node gets a response, no time bound; partition = arbitrary message loss; Theorem 1 and the G1/G2 proof; Corollary 1.1 (can't tell lost from delayed); any two achievable (central node, web caches); partially synchronous model and Theorem 2 (clocks don't help). The copy at users.ece.cmu.edu has broken font encoding in its text layer; the author's copy at nus.edu.sg is clean.
2. [Towards Robust Distributed Systems](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~brewer/cs262b-2004/PODC-keynote.pdf), Eric Brewer, PODC keynote slides, 2000. Talk, primary: yes. Seen: ACID vs BASE slide ("I think it's a spectrum"); CAP slide ("You can have at most two of these properties for any shared-data system"); forfeit P / A / C slides with examples (single-site DBs, 2PC; distributed DBs, locking, majority protocols; Coda, web caching, DNS).
3. [CAP Twelve Years Later: How the "Rules" Have Changed](https://www.infoq.com/articles/cap-twelve-years-later-how-the-rules-have-changed/), Eric Brewer, IEEE Computer 2012 (InfoQ repost). Blog, primary: yes. Seen: "2 of 3" misleading; CAP forbids only a tiny part of the design space; history (1998, 1999, PODC 2000); ACID vs BASE vs CAP; timeout as the partition decision; no global notion of partition; CA and forfeiting P unclear; hidden cost of forfeiting C is knowing invariants; partition mode and recovery; duplicate keys; credit card charges deferred; compensation; PNUTS and Facebook examples.
4. [Please stop calling databases CP or AP](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2015/05/11/please-stop-calling-databases-cp-or-ap.html), Martin Kleppmann, 2015. Blog, primary: no. Seen: narrow definitions (linearizability, any non-failing node, P not a choice); single register, only partition faults, no latency; two-datacenter proof; choosing C need not mean downtime; SLA availability vs CAP availability; single-leader, MongoDB, Dynamo-style stores, ZooKeeper (3.4.0 read-only mode) fit neither bucket; CP/AP a false dichotomy.
5. [A Critique of the CAP Theorem](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1509.05393), Martin Kleppmann, arXiv 2015. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: ambiguities in CAP's definitions and proof; trade-off known in the 1970s; lower bounds (Attiya-Welch for linearizability, Lipton-Sandberg for sequential), Table 1; delay-sensitivity framework; partitions as long delays.
6. [Strong consistency models](https://aphyr.com/posts/313-strong-consistency-models). See `consistency-models` #4. CAP's precise terms and the models beyond linearizability that also can't be totally available.

Extra: [Perspectives on the CAP Theorem](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer2.pdf), Gilbert and Lynch, 2012. Downloaded, read the abstract and introduction only. Not given a note.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- CP/AP labels: Brewer (2012) says "2 of 3" was misleading but keeps CAP as a design tool with partition modes; Kleppmann (2015) asks to retire CAP and the labels altogether and proposes delay-sensitivity instead. Both covered in `cap-theorem`.
- Where causal sits: Vogels lists causal, read-your-writes and monotonic consistency as variations of eventual consistency; Jepsen's map puts causal above PRAM and the session guarantees; a reader comment on Kingsbury's post argues causal (as he described it) can't be stronger than PRAM. Covered in `consistency-models`.
- "Strong consistency": Vogels and Terry use it informally; Jepsen and Kleppmann insist on naming the model. The articles use the precise names.
- Quorums and linearizability: Vogels says W + R > N can guarantee strong consistency; Kleppmann says sloppy quorums and read repair break linearizability in practice. `linearizability` warns; `quorums` (other group) should cover it in depth.
- etcd's "serializable" read mode means a possibly stale local read, not serializability in the transaction sense. Flagged in `linearizability`.

**Couldn't open:**

- Bailis and Ghodsi, "Eventual Consistency Today: Limitations, Extensions, and Beyond" (ACM Queue, 2013): queue.acm.org blocked (Cloudflare, then 403 via WebFetch); bailis.org's PDF link returned an error page. Would have added PBS numbers and the safety/liveness framing to `eventual-consistency`.
- Terry's CACM page (cacm.acm.org) returned no article text; the Microsoft technical report was used instead.

**Rejected:**

- HAT paper as a cited source: text layer unreadable; Jepsen's map carries its availability results.
- Viotti and Vukolić: formal, and the articles don't use the formal definitions.
- The garbled Gilbert-Lynch copy on users.ece.cmu.edu (same paper, unreadable text).

**Gaps:**

- No source opened with measured numbers for inconsistency windows or replica lag in a real system, so `eventual-consistency` has none.
- No primary source on Mahajan, Alvisi and Dahlin's real-time causal result was opened; the claim that RTC is the strongest always-available model rests on Jepsen and COPS citing it.
- Horn and Kroening's P-compositionality paper and Lowe's "Testing for linearizability" not opened; `linearizability-checking` describes splitting by key only as Porcupine's README does.
- Lamport's 1979 sequential consistency paper not opened; sequential consistency is described from Jepsen and Kingsbury.

### Consistency and time

#### `pacelc` (short)

1. [Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-pacelc.pdf), Daniel J. Abadi, IEEE Computer, 2012. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: CAP only constrains behaviour during partitions; replication alone creates a consistency/latency tradeoff; three replication options (all replicas at once, master first, arbitrary node first) and their sync/async variants; no way around it over a WAN; Cassandra quorum vs any-replica reads a factor of four or more apart (Rao et al.); PACELC definition; PA/EL Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak; PC/EC VoltDB/H-Store, Megastore, BigTable/HBase; PA/EC MongoDB (then); PC/EL PNUTS and why PC doesn't mean fully consistent; availability and latency blur; neither CAP nor PACELC explains everything.
2. [Write Concern](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/write-concern/), MongoDB manual 8.3. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: implicit default write concern is `w: majority`; majority of a three-member set is 2; `w: 1` writes can be rolled back if the primary steps down. Shows how the 2012 MongoDB label has aged.

Extra: [Problems with CAP, and Yahoo's little known NoSQL system](https://dbmsmusings.blogspot.com/2010/04/problems-with-cap-and-yahoos-little.html), Daniel Abadi, 2010. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: first statement of PACELC, PNUTS as PC/EL, WAN message costs "hundreds of milliseconds". Not given a note; the 2012 article supersedes it.

#### `clock-skew` (deep)

1. [RFC 5905](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5905), Mills, Martin, Burbank, Kasch, 2010. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: NTPv4 hierarchy from primary servers; typical accuracy (tens of µs primary, hundreds of µs on a LAN, tens of ms with long polls); UDP datagrams, TCP retries would add error; four-timestamp offset and delay formulas (section 8); dispersion grows at PHI 15 ppm, about 1.3 s a day; step threshold 125 ms, stepout 900 s, panic 1000 s; slew below the step threshold.
2. [clock_getres(2), clock_gettime(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/clock_gettime.2.html), Linux man-pages 6.19. Man page, primary: yes. Seen: CLOCK_REALTIME jumps and is slewed by NTP, ignores leap seconds; CLOCK_MONOTONIC counts from boot on Linux, no jumps, still slewed, stops on suspend, may return equal values; MONOTONIC_RAW (2.6.28) not slewed; BOOTTIME (2.6.39) counts suspend; CLOCK_TAI; leap seconds planned to be discontinued.
3. [Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf), Corbett et al., OSDI 2012. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: TrueTime returns an interval with bounded uncertainty; GPS and atomic-clock time masters per datacenter; error bound sawtooth about 1 to 7 ms over a 30 s poll; assumed drift 200 µs/s; drifting machines evicted; commit wait about 5 ms; bad CPUs 6 times more likely than bad clocks; tail spikes from network congestion and time masters down for maintenance; epoch is Unix time with leap smearing.
4. [How and why the leap second affected Cloudflare DNS](https://blog.cloudflare.com/how-and-why-the-leap-second-affected-cloudflare-dns/), John Graham-Cumming, Cloudflare, 2017. Blog (postmortem), primary: yes. Seen: Go time.Now() not monotonic then; clock went back a second during fast lookups; smoothed RTT went negative; rand.Int63n panicked; about 0.2% of DNS queries and under 1% of HTTP requests affected; fix: discard negative durations.
5. [Leap Smear](https://developers.google.com/time/smear), Google Public NTP. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: smearing since 2008; proposed 24-hour linear noon-to-noon smear; about 11.6 ppm; AWS uses the same smear; smeared time up to just under 0.5 s from UTC around the leap; quartz oscillators' own rate errors.
6. [Go 1.9 Release Notes](https://go.dev/doc/go1.9), The Go Authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: time package tracks monotonic time in each Time value, so durations are safe across wall clock adjustments.

Extra: [package time](https://pkg.go.dev/time), Go 1.27.1 docs. Seen: "wall clock is for telling time and the monotonic clock is for measuring time"; monotonic reading stripped when serialised. Not given a note; the release notes carry the version.
Extra: [Google Public NTP FAQ](https://developers.google.com/time/faq). Seen: don't mix smeared and non-smeared NTP servers. Not given a note.

#### `lamport-clocks` (short)

1. [Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/time-clocks.pdf), Leslie Lamport, CACM 21(7), 1978. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: happened-before as a partial order; concurrency; clock condition (one way only); rules IR1 and IR2; total order with process-id tie-break, not unique; mutual exclusion without a central process; state machine replication; the phone-call anomaly and the user-carried-timestamp fix; physical clock synchronisation in the second half. Scan with OCR errors.
2. [Logical Physical Clocks and Consistent Snapshots in Globally Distributed Databases](https://cse.buffalo.edu/tech-reports/2014-04.pdf), Kulkarni et al., 2014. See `hybrid-logical-clocks` #1. Section 1.1: what Lamport clocks and vector clocks can't do.

#### `vector-clocks` (short)

1. [Virtual Time and Global States of Distributed Systems](https://www.vs.inf.ethz.ch/publ/papers/VirtTimeGlobStates.pdf), Friedemann Mattern, 1988 (author's edited version). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: defect of linear time; vector of length n; tick own entry; componentwise max on receive; comparison test for causality (theorems 10, 11); version vectors for replicated files (Parker et al.). Text layer drops ligatures.
2. [Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf), DeCandia et al., SOSP 2007. Paper, primary: yes (note already existed, appended). Seen: (node, counter) pairs; ancestor rule; D1 to D5 example; client-side merge, deleted items resurface; truncation at a threshold "(say 10)"; 99.94% of cart requests saw one version.

Extra: [Version Vectors are not Vector Clocks](https://haslab.wordpress.com/2011/07/08/version-vectors-are-not-vector-clocks/), Carlos Baquero, 2011. Blog by a researcher on the topic, primary: yes. Seen: vector clocks order events, version vectors order replica states; integers over-expressive for replicas; dotted version vectors. Not given a note (short node already at 2 sources); good for `conflict-resolution`.
Extra: [Vector Clocks Revisited](https://riak.com/posts/technical/vector-clocks-revisited/index.html), Russell Brown, Riak, 2015. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: actor explosion with client ids before Riak 1.0; vnode version vectors; false concurrency and sibling explosion fixed in Riak 2.0. Not given a note; belongs to `conflict-resolution`.

#### `hybrid-logical-clocks` (short)

1. [Logical Physical Clocks and Consistent Snapshots in Globally Distributed Databases](https://cse.buffalo.edu/tech-reports/2014-04.pdf), Kulkarni, Demirbas, Madeppa, Avva, Leone, 2014. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: LC, VC, PT and TrueTime compared; naive algorithm drifts unboundedly; HLC rules (figure 5); theorems: hb implies smaller HLC, l ≥ pt, |l − pt| ≤ ε, c bounded; HLC reads but never sets the clock; ignore out-of-bounds messages and alert; AWS runs (max l − pt 90.5 ms at 16 ms average NTP offset); 48 + 16 bit layout; external consistency possible with a client-notification wait.
2. [Transaction Layer](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/architecture/transaction-layer), Cockroach Labs, CockroachDB v26.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: every transaction timestamp is an HLC value; HLC ≥ wall time; nodes pass HLC timestamps on requests; nodes crash when out of sync with half the cluster by 80% of the max offset; skew past the bound breaks single-key linearizability for causally dependent transactions, not serializability; uncertainty window.

Extra: [Living without atomic clocks](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/blog/living-without-atomic-clocks/), Spencer Kimball, Irfan Sharif, 2022. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: causal reverse example with a lagging clock; Spanner waits after writes, CockroachDB sometimes retries reads; uncertainty restarts; causality tokens; NTP bounds of 100 to 250 ms quoted. Not given a note by this group (another group created `cockroach-living-without-atomic-clocks-2022`).
Extra: [cockroach start](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/cockroach-start). Seen: `--max-offset` default 500ms, servers crash when exceeded. Not given a note; the number isn't used.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Spanner vs HLC: Spanner waits out clock uncertainty to get external consistency; HLC orders by messages and skips the wait, giving up ordering for causes outside the system unless a client-notification wait is added. CockroachDB accepts the weaker guarantee and documents it.
- Leap seconds: step (NTP, CLOCK_REALTIME) vs smear (Google, AWS). Smeared and stepped clocks differ by up to about half a second around a leap; Google's FAQ says not to mix them.
- Version vectors vs vector clocks: Dynamo calls its per-object vectors vector clocks; Mattern and Baquero keep the terms apart.
- PACELC labels vs configuration: Abadi classifies products by 2012 defaults; MongoDB's default is now `w: majority`.

**Couldn't open:**

- Nothing needed failed to open. Fidge's 1988 vector clock paper was not looked for (Mattern covers it).

**Rejected:**

- Wikipedia and secondary explainers on NTP, Lamport and vector clocks: the primary sources were readable.
- Riak and Baquero blogs for `vector-clocks`: better homes in `conflict-resolution`.

**Gaps:**

- No source opened for measured NTP accuracy on modern cloud VMs or with chrony; the article uses RFC 5905's typical figures and Spanner's numbers.
- No source for when MongoDB's default write concern changed (the 8.3 manual only states today's default).
- The Kulkarni sentence about NTP errors of 100 ms or more from asymmetric routes is split by a footnote in the PDF; the asymmetry point in `clock-skew` is derived from the RFC's formula instead.

## Phase 12: Distributed systems II, consensus and coordination

Researched by 5 parallel passes, one per group below.

### Detecting failure + Consensus

#### `failure-detection` (deep)

1. [The φ Accrual Failure Detector](https://dspace.jaist.ac.jp/dspace/bitstream/10119/4784/1/IS-RR-2004-010.pdf), Hayashibara, Défago, Yared, Katayama, JAIST research report, 2004. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: boolean vs accrual detectors; conservative vs aggressive tradeoff; heartbeat interval, timeout and transmission time (Fig. 1); ◇P properties; detection time and mistake rate; monitoring / interpretation / action split; φ = −log10(P_later); φ 1, 2, 3 ≈ 10%, 1%, 0.1% chance of a wrong suspicion; sliding window, normal distribution; week-long UDP run Japan to Switzerland, nearly 6 million samples; not a way around FLP.
2. [Unreliable Failure Detectors for Reliable Distributed Systems](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~lorenzo/corsi/cs380d/papers/p225-chandra.pdf), Chandra and Toueg, JACM, 1996. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: introduction, sections 5, 6.3, A.3. Failure detector as a local suspect list that can be wrong; completeness and accuracy; ◇W can make infinitely many mistakes; a misbehaving detector costs liveness, not safety; timeout-and-back-off implementation; Isis forces wrongly suspected processes to crash; eventual accuracy needs a majority of correct processes; consensus ≡ atomic broadcast. Scan has OCR errors.
3. [Distributed Systems lecture notes](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2122/ConcDisSys/dist-sys-notes.pdf), Kleppmann, Cambridge. Course notes, primary: no.
