Seen: 2.4, slides 40 and 41: timeout detector can't tell crashed, paused, lost or delayed; perfect detector only in synchronous crash-stop with reliable links; none in asynchronous; eventually perfect detector. Already a note (`kleppmann-dist-sys-notes`), appended.
4. [Phi Accrual Failure Detector](https://doc.akka.io/libraries/akka-core/current/typed/failure-detector.html), Akka core docs, version 2.10.22. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: heartbeats every second by default, request/reply; φ formula; steadier heartbeats give a steeper curve; acceptable-heartbeat-pause margin for GC pauses; flapping UNREACHABLE/REACHABLE means false positives; default threshold 8, 12 suggested on EC2.
5. [cassandra.yaml file configuration](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/5.0/cassandra/managing/configuration/cass_yaml_file.html), Apache Cassandra 5.0 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `phi_convict_threshold`, default 8, "most users should never need to adjust this". Page shows a prerelease banner even at the 5.0 path.
6. [Lifeguard: Local Health Awareness for More Accurate Failure Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.00788), Dadgar, Phillips, Currey, HashiCorp, 2017 (arXiv v2). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: slow members wrongly declare healthy peers dead; flapping triggers costly failovers; local health multiplier backs off probes (memberlist 1 s / 500 ms up to 9 s / 4.5 s); suspicion timeouts shrink as others agree; 50x to 100x fewer false positives in their tests; 100 Azure VMs, one stressed member already causes false positives.

#### `gossip-protocols` (short)

1. [SWIM](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/projects/Quicksilver/public_pdfs/SWIM.pdf), Das, Gupta, Motivala, Cornell, DSN 2002. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: all-to-all heartbeats grow quadratically; separate detection from dissemination; ping, ping-req to k members, ack; updates piggybacked on pings and acks; logarithmic spread; suspect / alive / confirm with incarnation numbers; round-robin targets bound detection to 2× group size periods; weakly consistent lists. Some symbols missing from the PDF text.
2. [Epidemic Algorithms for Replicated Database Maintenance](https://bitsavers.org/pdf/xerox/parc/techReports/CSL-89-1_Epidemic_Algorithms_for_Replicated_Database_Maintenance.pdf), Demers et al., Xerox PARC, PODC 1987 (tech report CSL-89-1). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: abstract, sections 0, 1.1, start of 2. Direct mail vs anti-entropy vs rumor mongering; spread in time proportional to log n; pull and push-pull beat push at the tail; death certificates for deletes; used in Clearinghouse.
3. [Lifeguard](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.00788): see `failure-detection` #6. memberlist (Consul, Nomad) is SWIM; >6,000 members in one group; gossip makes membership weakly consistent.
4. [Gossip (Consul docs)](https://developer.hashicorp.com/consul/docs/concept/gossip), HashiCorp, Consul v2.0.x. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Serf gossip for membership and failure detection; LAN pool port 8301, WAN pool 8302; gossip encryption key; Lifeguard. Not used (the Lifeguard paper covers what matters).

#### `consensus` (deep)

1. [Distributed Systems lecture notes](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2122/ConcDisSys/dist-sys-notes.pdf): see `failure-detection` #3. Seen: 6 and 6.1: manual failover slow, consensus automates it; definition (validity, agreement, finality); equivalence with total order broadcast; Paxos vs Multi-Paxos/Raft/VR/Zab; partial synchrony + crash-recovery + fair-loss; FLP; clocks only for liveness; terms, one vote per term, quorum elects; two leaders from different terms; leader must ask a quorum per decision.
2. [Paxos Made Simple](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/paxos-simple.pdf), Lamport, 2001. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: safety requirements; asynchronous non-Byzantine model; single acceptor is a single point of failure; any two majorities share an acceptor; dueling proposers; leader election needs randomness or timeouts, safety never depends on it. Note already existed (`lamport-paxos-simple-2001`), appended section 3 claims.
3. [Unreliable Failure Detectors](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~lorenzo/corsi/cs380d/papers/p225-chandra.pdf): see `failure-detection` #2. Seen: consensus spec (termination, uniform integrity, agreement, uniform validity); majority needed with eventually accurate detectors.
4. [Consensus in the Presence of Partial Synchrony](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Lynch/jacm88.pdf), Dwork, Lynch, Stockmeyer, JACM, 1988. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: GST model; safety must hold under full asynchrony, termination only after GST; fail-stop needs N ≥ 2t + 1, Byzantine N ≥ 3t + 1. Note already existed (`dwork-partial-synchrony-1988`).
5. [In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf), Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: section 2 (five servers tolerate two failures; safety independent of timing), 5.6 (broadcastTime ≪ electionTimeout ≪ MTBF; 10 to 500 ms). Note already existed (`ongaro-raft-2014`), appended.
6. [Flexible Paxos](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.06696), Howard, Malkhi, Spiegelman, 2016. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: majorities not required, only phase 1 and phase 2 quorums must intersect; 10 nodes with 3 for replication and 8 for leader change. Note already existed (`howard-flexible-paxos-2016`).

#### `flp-impossibility` (short)

1. [Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Lynch/jacm85.pdf), Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, JACM, 1985. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: abstract, sections 1 to 3, theorem 2, conclusion: reliable network, no clocks, no death detection; weak one-bit consensus; bivalent initial configuration; admissible run that never decides; window of vulnerability in every commit protocol; possible with no deaths during the run; "doesn't mean unsolvable in practice".
2. [Distributed Systems lecture notes](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2122/ConcDisSys/dist-sys-notes.pdf): see `failure-detection` #3. Seen: FLP as slide 107; ways around: randomization, or clocks for timeouts with safety independent of timing.
3. [Consensus in the Presence of Partial Synchrony](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Lynch/jacm88.pdf): see `consensus` #4. The standard escape hatch from FLP.
4. [Paxos Made Simple](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/paxos-simple.pdf): see `consensus` #2. Seen: 2.4, FLP means electing a proposer needs randomness or real time.

#### `replicated-state-machine` (deep)

1. [Implementing Fault-Tolerant Services Using the State Machine Approach](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/fbs/publications/SMSurvey.pdf), Schneider, ACM Computing Surveys, 1990. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: introduction, sections 1, 2 and start of 3: outputs determined only by the request sequence; the sensor-loop counterexample; t + 1 replicas for fail-stop, 2t + 1 for Byzantine; Replica Coordination = Agreement + Order; read-only and commuting requests relax it.
2. [In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf): see `consensus` #5. Seen: section 2 and figure 1: replicated log, consensus keeps it consistent, deterministic machines give same outputs; GFS/HDFS/RAMCloud use a separate RSM; Chubby and ZooKeeper.
3. [Paxos Made Simple](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/paxos-simple.pdf): see `consensus` #2. Seen: section 3: server as deterministic state machine, bank withdrawal example, i-th instance chooses i-th command, no-op gap filling, membership in the state.
4. [Distributed Systems lecture notes](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2122/ConcDisSys/dist-sys-notes.pdf): see `failure-detection` #3. Seen: 5.3: SMR via total order broadcast; even errors deterministic; active vs passive (primary-backup) replication; commutative updates for weaker broadcasts.
5. [Paxos Made Live](https://research.google.com/archive/paxos_made_live.pdf), Chandra, Griesemer, Redstone, Google, 2007. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: introduction (identical log gives identical database), 5.5 snapshots, 6.2 checksum-in-the-log consistency check and three inconsistency incidents, section 9 gaps between theory and practice. Note already existed (`chandra-paxos-made-live-2007`), appended.
6. [etcd-io/raft README](https://github.com/etcd-io/raft), etcd maintainers, main branch. Code, primary: yes. Seen: the library implements only Raft; transport, storage and state machine are the user's; the library is itself a deterministic state machine for testing; users (etcd, Kubernetes, CockroachDB, TiDB).

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- How many replicas? Schneider's tutorial says t + 1 replicas suffice for fail-stop failures. Consensus under partial synchrony (Dwork, Lynch, Stockmeyer; Chandra and Toueg with eventually accurate detectors) needs 2t + 1. They're answering different questions: Schneider's fail-stop assumes failures are detectable and agreement is already solved; ordering commands when crashed and slow look the same needs a majority.
- Majorities. Paxos and Raft are taught with majority quorums; Flexible Paxos shows only the phase 1 / phase 2 intersection is required, so replication quorums can shrink if leader-change quorums grow.
- Where to put failure detection. Chandra and Toueg say reason about detectors as abstract properties, not timeouts; the φ paper and Akka say expose a continuous suspicion level and let each application choose; Lifeguard says the detector must also suspect itself. They agree the answer can be wrong; they differ on who decides what "dead" means.
- FLP's weight. The FLP authors themselves say it doesn't make consensus unsolvable in practice; Kleppmann's notes and Lamport both treat it as the reason leader election needs timeouts or randomness. No real disagreement, but it's often overstated as "consensus is impossible".

**Couldn't open:**
- Chandra, Hadzilacos, Toueg, "The weakest failure detector for solving consensus" (1996): not opened; only cited through Chandra and Toueg's introduction, and not used.
- Das, Gupta, Motivala SWIM PDF opened, but some symbols (member names, formulas) are missing from its text layer; claims that depend on formulas were left out.

**Rejected:**
- [Demers slides, Cornell CS6410](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs6410/2016fa/slides/19-p2p-gossip.pdf): course slides summarising Demers and others; the paper itself was opened instead.
- Consul gossip docs (see `gossip-protocols` #4): nothing beyond the Lifeguard paper for our purposes.
- Cassandra "latest" cassandra.yaml page: marked prerelease; used the 5.0 path instead (same banner, same value).

**Gaps:**
- No measured detection times or false-positive rates from a production system other than HashiCorp's own Lifeguard tests. A phase 12 lab run (heartbeats over the phase 11 fault injector) would give us our own.
- No source opened for "gray failure" (a node that passes health checks but fails real work); it would fit `failure-detection` or `health-checks`.
- `replicated-state-machine` would benefit from one production write-up on nondeterminism bugs (e.g. a replica diverging because of floating point, map order or time); Paxos Made Live's three incidents are the closest found.

### Raft

#### `raft` (deep)

1. [In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf), Diego Ongaro, John Ousterhout, Stanford, 2014. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: abstract (equivalent to Multi-Paxos, decomposition, user study 33 of 43); 2 replicated state machines, five servers tolerate two failures, safety under non-Byzantine conditions; 5 Figure 2 summary and Figure 3 properties (election safety, leader append-only, log matching, leader completeness, state machine safety); 5.1 roles, terms as logical clock, stale term steps down; 5.2 to 5.4 election, replication, election restriction, Figure 8 commit rule, safety argument with "the voter"; 5.5 idempotent RPCs; 5.6 broadcastTime ≪ electionTimeout ≪ MTBF, 0.5 to 20 ms broadcast, 10 to 500 ms timeouts; 6 joint consensus; 7 snapshots and InstallSnapshot; 8 client serial numbers, no-op entry, read-only via heartbeats or lease; 9.2 TLA+ spec and proof of the section 5 core; 9.3 election measurements; 10 strong leadership as the main difference from Paxos.
2. [Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/papers/OngaroPhD.pdf), Diego Ongaro, Stanford PhD dissertation, 2014. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: 3.8 persisted state (term, vote, log), commit index rebuildable, lost disk means new identity; 3.9 timing; 3.10 leadership transfer (TimeoutNow); chapters 4, 5, 6.2 to 6.4, 9.6, 10.2 (see the other nodes). GitHub README errata point to a bug in chapter 4.
3. [Paxos vs Raft: Have we reached consensus on distributed consensus?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05074), Heidi Howard, Richard Mortier, PaPoC, 2020. Paper, primary: no. Seen: simplified Multi-Paxos in Raft's terms; differ only in leader election (Paxos divides terms between servers and sends log entries in votes; Raft votes only for up-to-date logs, keeps original terms, commits old-term entries only indirectly); Raft elections expected slower with more variance but lighter; understandability mostly from presentation.
4. [Distributed Systems lecture notes](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2122/ConcDisSys/dist-sys-notes.pdf), Martin Kleppmann, University of Cambridge, 2021. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: 6.1 Raft gives FIFO-total order broadcast; partially synchronous crash-recovery model; FLP; clocks only for timeouts; unique leader per term but not one leader at a time (slide 109); leader must get quorum confirmation for every decision; BFT algorithms more complicated and less efficient; 6.2 Raft as nine slides of pseudocode.
5. [etcd-io/raft README](https://github.com/etcd-io/raft), etcd maintainers. Code docs, primary: yes. Seen: algorithm only, network and disk left to the user; deterministic state machine for testing; powers etcd, Kubernetes, CockroachDB, TiDB and more; ReadIndex and lease reads; optional pipelining, batching, flow control, parallel leader disk write, step down on lost quorum; Ready loop order (persist, send, apply); proposals may be dropped; node IDs never reused; membership changes applied on apply, one at a time; use three or more nodes. (Note already existed as `etcd-raft-library`; claims appended.)
6. [Students' Guide to Raft](https://thesquareplanet.com/blog/students-guide-to-raft/), Jon Gjengset, 2016. Blog by an MIT 6.824 TA, primary: no. Seen: figure 2 is MUST not SHOULD; heartbeats aren't special; truncate only on conflict; timer reset rules; up-to-date check exactly; commitIndex only for current-term entries; nextIndex vs matchIndex; term confusion on stale replies; snapshot crash gap; fast backup with conflictTerm/conflictIndex.

Extra: [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/), opened; links to the paper, thesis and implementations list. Not given a note.

#### `raft-elections` (deep)

1. [Raft paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf). See raft #1. Sections 5.2, 5.4.1, 5.6, 9.3 (five servers, broadcast about 15 ms, 1000 trials per line, 100 for 150-150 ms; no randomness over 10 s; 5 ms randomness median 287 ms; 50 ms randomness worst 513 ms; 12 to 24 ms gives 35 ms average; recommend 150 to 300 ms).
2. [Ongaro dissertation](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/papers/OngaroPhD.pdf). See raft #2. 9.6 Pre-Vote (inspired by ZooKeeper; recommended; doesn't hurt election performance); 6.2 leader steps down after an election timeout without a majority (CheckQuorum); 3.10 leadership transfer; 4.2.3 Pre-Vote doesn't stop removed servers.
3. [Raft does not Guarantee Liveness in the face of Network Faults](https://decentralizedthoughts.github.io/2020-12-12-raft-liveness-full-omission/), Heidi Howard, Ittai Abraham, Decentralized Thoughts, 2020. Blog, primary: no. Seen: five-server partial-connectivity counter-example for plain Raft; Pre-Vote fixes it but adds a stuck isolated leader; CheckQuorum fixes that; both together give liveness.
4. [A Byzantine failure in the real world](https://blog.cloudflare.com/a-byzantine-failure-in-the-real-world/), Tom Lianza, Chris Snook, Cloudflare, 2020. Postmortem, primary: yes. Seen: 6 h 33 min API outage; partial switch failure; etcd node 1 reaches node 2 but not leader node 3; repeated elections, read-only etcd; database failover chain; postscript says omission fault, not Byzantine. Doesn't say whether PreVote/CheckQuorum were on.
5. [etcd-io/raft raft.go](https://github.com/etcd-io/raft/blob/main/raft.go), etcd authors. Code, primary: yes. Seen: Config comments for ElectionTick (suggest 10 × HeartbeatTick), CheckQuorum, PreVote (thesis 9.6), ReadOnlyOption; randomized timeout in [et, 2et-1]; StatePreCandidate; lease reads require CheckQuorum; MaxInflightBytes bandwidth-delay example; pending ReadIndex until current-term commit; joint configs.
6. Howard and Mortier (raft #3) and Gjengset (raft #6) for the Paxos comparison and timer-reset livelocks.

#### `raft-log-replication` (deep)

1. [Raft paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf). See raft #1. 5.3 (consistency check, log matching, nextIndex back-off, optional fast backup "we doubt this optimization is necessary"), figure 7 (follower log scenarios, nextIndex 11), 5.4.2 and figure 8 (commit rule).
2. [Ongaro dissertation](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/papers/OngaroPhD.pdf). See raft #2. 10.2: disk write 100 µs to 10 ms, RTT 5 µs to 400 ms; leader writes in parallel and can commit before its own write; batching vs pipelining; LogCabin 1 MB batches; one TCP connection per follower.
3. [etcd-io/raft design.md](https://github.com/etcd-io/raft/blob/main/design.md), etcd authors. Code docs, primary: yes. Seen: progress match/next; probe, replicate, snapshot states; new leader starts all in probe; flow control limits.
4. [etcd-io/raft raft.go](https://github.com/etcd-io/raft/blob/main/raft.go). See raft-elections #5. MaxInflightMsgs/MaxInflightBytes.
5. [etcd-io/raft README](https://github.com/etcd-io/raft). See raft #5. Persist-send-apply order, dropped proposals.
6. [Students' Guide to Raft](https://thesquareplanet.com/blog/students-guide-to-raft/). See raft #6.

#### `raft-snapshots` (short)

1. [Raft paper](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf). See raft #1. Section 7, figures 12 and 13: last included index/term, config in snapshot, InstallSnapshot chunks as sign of life, discard whole log vs keep suffix, leader-only snapshots rejected, fixed-size trigger, copy-on-write with fork.
2. [Ongaro dissertation](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/papers/OngaroPhD.pdf). See raft #2. Chapter 5 intro, 5.1 to 5.2: independent compaction, session data in snapshots, 10 GB copy about 1 s, expansion factor (4 → about 20% disk bandwidth, about 6× space), temp file then rename, "entry i present" assumption, snapshot every entry in development, disk-based state machines, transfer speed usually unimportant.

Extra: Gjengset (raft #6) on the crash between saving a snapshot and trimming the log. Not cited to keep the short node at two sources.

#### `raft-membership-changes` (short)

1. [Ongaro dissertation](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/papers/OngaroPhD.pdf). See raft #2. Chapter 4: single-server changes and overlap (figures 4.2, 4.3), config used as soon as logged, fall back if removed, non-voting catch-up in rounds (10 rounds, last under an election timeout), abort on unreachable server, removing the leader, disruptive servers and the RequestVote-within-minimum-timeout rule, joint consensus (3 → 9 needs 2 of 3 and 5 of 9), automatic removal is dangerous.
2. [bug in single-server membership changes](https://groups.google.com/g/raft-dev/c/t4xj6dJTP6E/m/d2D9LrWRza8J), Diego Ongaro, raft-dev list, 2015. Mailing-list post, primary: yes. Seen: bug found by Huanchen Zhang and Brandon Amos (CMU) while formalizing; three counter-examples from a 4-server cluster; needs even size, concurrent changes, leadership loss; joint consensus unaffected; fix: no new configuration entry until the leader commits an entry in its term; no formal proof of membership changes yet.

Extra: [etcd learner design (v3.6 docs)](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/learning/design-learner/), Gyuho Lee, Joe Betz. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: new members overload the leader; adding a 4th to 3 raises quorum to 3; misconfigured member add can lose quorum irreversibly; "member remove" first; learners (v3.4) as non-voting members, promote only once caught up, one learner max, 1/10 of snapshot count threshold. Note written then removed so the short node stays at two sources; good candidate if the node grows.

#### `linearizable-reads` (short)

1. [Ongaro dissertation](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/papers/OngaroPhD.pdf). See raft #2. 6.3 sessions and at-least-once; 6.4 stale reads from a partitioned leader, stale-read bugs in two third-party implementations, ReadIndex steps, batching heartbeats, follower reads; 6.4.1 lease reads (start + election timeout / drift bound), not recommended unless needed, monotonic reads via client-tracked index, expire lease before transfer.
2. [etcd-io/raft raft.go](https://github.com/etcd-io/raft/blob/main/raft.go). See raft-elections #5. ReadOnlySafe (default) vs ReadOnlyLeaseBased; lease mode requires CheckQuorum; pending reads until current-term commit.
3. [Jepsen: etcd 3.4.3](https://jepsen.io/analyses/etcd-3.4.3), Kyle Kingsbury, 2020. Analysis, primary: no. Seen: etcd 0.4.1 stale reads by default (local reads on any leader); 3.0 API made linearizable default except watches; serializable flag allows stale committed reads; 3.4.3 key-value operations appear strict serializable; locks unsafe.

Extra: [How TiKV Uses "Lease Read"](https://tikv.org/blog/lease-read/), Siddon Tang, TiKV, 2020. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: log read vs ReadIndex vs lease read; TiKV renews the lease on writes; election timeout 10 s, lease 9 s (at the time); raw monotonic clock because NTP slews the normal one. Not cited (short node at three sources already); good source if leases get more depth.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Understandability: the Raft paper's user study says Raft is significantly easier than Paxos; Howard and Mortier say the algorithms differ only in leader election and much of the gain is presentation. Covered in `raft`.
- Liveness: the Raft paper says consensus systems stay available while a majority can communicate; Howard and Abraham show plain Raft doesn't under partial connectivity, and the Cloudflare outage is a real case. Covered in `raft-elections`.
- Membership changes: the paper uses joint consensus; the dissertation recommends single-server changes; the raft-dev post then found a bug in them (fixed by one rule). The etcd README describes single-node changes while raft.go also supports joint configurations.
- Cloudflare first called its failure Byzantine, then corrected it to an omission fault in a postscript.
- Leases: the dissertation doesn't recommend lease reads unless needed; TiKV uses them by default (not cited).
- etcd's API docs (per Jepsen) once claimed only sequential consistency; Jepsen found strict serializability.

**Couldn't open:**

- Nothing needed failed to open. The raft-dev post needed a browser user agent with curl; its full text was read.

**Rejected:**

- [MIT 6.5840 Lab 3: Raft](https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.824/labs/lab-raft1.html) (opened, current course page): useful for the lab harness (heartbeats at most ten per second, election within five seconds), not for the articles; it belongs to the phase 12 build.
- The Secret Lives of Data visualisation and other tutorials: secondary, nothing the paper doesn't cover.

**Gaps:**

- No source opened measures etcd or LogCabin write latency on current hardware; the articles give only the dissertation's latency ranges. The lab's etcd comparison should fill this.
- No source says whether etcd enables PreVote or CheckQuorum by default at the server level (only that they're library options); the articles don't claim a default.
- Chapter 9 of the dissertation (election evaluation beyond 9.6) wasn't read in full.
- Joint consensus in etcd (EnterJoint/LeaveJoint) seen only in code comments, not in docs.

### Other ways to agree

#### `paxos` (deep)

1. [Paxos Made Simple](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/paxos-simple.pdf), Leslie Lamport, 2001. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: the consensus problem and its three safety rules; proposers, acceptors, learners; why one acceptor fails and why "accept the first proposal" splits the vote; proposal numbers; derivation P2 to P2c; phase 1 (prepare, promise) and phase 2 (accept); acceptor must remember highest promise and highest accepted proposal on stable storage; two proposers can duel forever; a distinguished proposer and FLP; proposers pick numbers from disjoint sets; section 3: Multi-Paxos as a sequence of instances, phase 1 for all future instances in one short message, gaps filled with no-ops (the 135 to 140 example), steady-state cost is phase 2 only, membership changes through the state machine (alpha commands ahead).
2. [Paxos Made Live: An Engineering Perspective](https://research.google.com/archive/paxos_made_live.pdf), Chandra, Griesemer, Redstone, Google, 2007. Paper by the builders, primary: yes. Seen: Chubby's Paxos log replacing a third-party database; five replicas per cell; one page of pseudo-code becomes several thousand lines of C++; five disk writes per instance vs one with a stable master; batching; disk corruption and non-voting catch-up; master leases for local reads, lease shorter on the master for clock drift; master churn and sequence-number boosting; epoch numbers; group membership not spelled out in the literature; snapshots; MultiOp; state-machine specification language; seeded single-threaded random-failure test on hundreds of machines; a misspelled replica name silently lowering fault tolerance; Linux 2.4 fsync stall; 100 machine-years in production; throughput table vs 3DB.
3. [Paxos vs Raft: Have we reached consensus on distributed consensus?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05074), Heidi Howard and Richard Mortier, 2020. Paper, primary: no (analysis of both). Seen: a simplified Multi-Paxos written in Raft's terms; the two differ only in leader election (terms split by t mod n, vote for any candidate, entries sent back with votes, old entries re-stamped with the new term); Raft's election is lighter; understandability comes mostly from Raft's presentation; table of the three differences; glossary mapping ballot/proposal/view to term and prepare/accept to RequestVote/AppendEntries.
4. [Flexible Paxos: Quorum intersection revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.06696), Howard, Malkhi, Spiegelman, 2016. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: only phase 1 and phase 2 quorums need to intersect; example of 10 nodes with 3 for replication and 8 for leader changes; with an even n, phase 2 quorum can shrink by one; LibPaxos3 latency rises and throughput falls with more replicas (figure 1); TLA+ spec model-checked.
5. [Paxos Made Moderately Complex](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs7412/2011sp/paxos.pdf), Robbert van Renesse and Deniz Altinbuken, ACM Computing Surveys, 2015. Paper, primary: no. Seen: full multi-decree Paxos with pseudocode; ballots vs slots are orthogonal; 2f+1 acceptors to tolerate f crashes; the "ping-pong" duel between leaders and FLP; pinging plus timeouts that grow with ballot numbers (AIMD); power loss with a surviving disk counts as slow, not crashed; read-only commands; state on disk.
6. [In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf), Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout, 2014. Paper, primary: yes (for Raft; secondary on Paxos). Seen: section 3 "What's wrong with Paxos?": hard to understand, no agreed Multi-Paxos, single-decree foundation, symmetric peer-to-peer core; Chubby and Spanner algorithms unpublished; user study with 43 students, 33 did better on Raft; Raft's leader election is part of consensus, in Paxos it's an optimization.

#### `chain-replication` (short)

1. [Chain Replication for Supporting High Throughput and Availability](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/home/rvr/papers/OSDI04.pdf), Robbert van Renesse and Fred B. Schneider, OSDI, 2004. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: fail-stop servers; head takes updates, tail answers queries and sends replies; state changes forwarded over reliable FIFO links; t servers tolerate t-1 failures; a master (itself replicated with Paxos) detects failures and relinks the chain; head, middle and tail failure cases; Sent list and acks; new servers added at the tail; comparison with primary/backup (serial vs parallel dissemination, outage lengths in message delays); weak-chain variant reading from any server.
2. [Object Storage on CRAQ](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/usenix09/tech/full_papers/terrace/terrace.pdf), Jeff Terrace and Michael J. Freedman, USENIX ATC, 2009. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: CR's tail is a read hot spot and may be far away across datacenters; CRAQ keeps clean and dirty versions, any node serves clean reads, dirty reads trigger a version query to the tail; read throughput scales with chain length for read-mostly loads; ZooKeeper for chain membership; optional weaker reads with bounded staleness.

#### `byzantine-fault-tolerance` (short)

1. [Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance](https://pdos.csail.mit.edu/6.824/papers/castro-practicalbft.pdf), Miguel Castro and Barbara Liskov, OSDI, 1999 (MIT 6.824 course copy). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: 3f+1 replicas for f faulty, and why that's the minimum; primary and views; pre-prepare, prepare, commit; client waits for f+1 matching replies; safety doesn't depend on synchrony, liveness does; independent failures need different code, OS, passwords and admins; MACs in the normal case, signatures only with faults; BFT NFS only 3% slower than unreplicated NFS on the Andrew benchmark; no fault-tolerant privacy.
2. [The Byzantine Generals Problem](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/byz.pdf), Lamport, Shostak, Pease, ACM TOPLAS, 1982. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: the generals story; with oral messages the problem is solvable only if more than two-thirds are loyal (3m+1); with unforgeable signed messages, any number of traitors; majority voting among replicas needs agreement on inputs.
3. [Distributed Systems lecture notes](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2122/ConcDisSys/dist-sys-notes.pdf): see phase 11 `failure-models`. Seen here: Byzantine generals needs 3f+1 with unpredictable delays; same software means the same bug on every node, so "Byzantine" usually means deliberate misbehaviour; trust between customer, shop and payments service; BFT popular with blockchains; BFT consensus more complicated and less efficient, crash-recovery algorithms enough for trusted datacenter networks.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Is Paxos hard? Its author calls it simple and nearly obvious; the Raft authors call it exceptionally difficult and cite a user study; Howard and Mortier find the two about equally understandable once Paxos is written in Raft's style.
- Is Paxos a good base for real systems? Lamport's paper sketches Multi-Paxos and reconfiguration in a few paragraphs; the Chubby team found large gaps (membership, disk corruption, leases, snapshots) and ended with an "unproven protocol".
- Majority quorums for both phases: classic Paxos uses them; Flexible Paxos shows only cross-phase intersection is needed.
- Byzantine: PBFT argues BFT will matter more because of attacks and software errors; Kleppmann's notes point out a shared bug breaks the one-third assumption, so the term is kept for deliberate misbehaviour.

**Couldn't open:**
- `https://pmg.csail.mit.edu/papers/osdi99.pdf` (PBFT at the authors' group) returned an HTML error page; used the MIT 6.824 copy instead.
- `https://www.cs.cornell.edu/home/rvr/Papers/paxos.pdf` returned 404; used the Cornell course copy of Paxos Made Moderately Complex.

**Rejected:**
- The Part-Time Parliament (Lamport, 1998): not opened; Paxos Made Simple covers the same algorithm in plain terms, and the article doesn't use anything only the original has.

**Gaps:**
- No official docs from a current Paxos-based system (Spanner, Megastore, WeChat PaxosStore) were opened; the article stays with papers.
- No production write-up of chain replication beyond the two papers was opened.
- No modern BFT protocol (HotStuff, Tendermint/CometBFT) was opened; the BFT node stays with PBFT and the generals paper.

### Leases and locks

#### `leases` (short)

1. [Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency](http://web.stanford.edu/class/cs240/readings/leases.pdf), Cary G. Gray, David R. Cheriton, Stanford, 1989. Paper (SOSP), primary: yes. Seen: scanned PDF with OCR text; section 2 lease definition (rights over data for a limited term), write deferred until holders approve or terms expire, unreachable holder only delays, server honors leases after crash by waiting max term, short terms reduce false sharing, long terms cut traffic; section 3 analytic model (effective client term shortened by propagation, processing and clock allowance ε), V system numbers (10 s term cuts consistency traffic to 10% of a zero term at S = 1); section 4 lease management options; section 5 fault tolerance: fast server clock or slow client clock breaks consistency, the opposite only costs traffic, bounded drift suffices if the term is sent as a duration; section 6 Xerox DFS breakable locks degenerate to zero-term leases.
2. [The Chubby lock service for loosely-coupled distributed systems](https://research.google.com/archive/chubby-osdi06.pdf), Mike Burrows, Google, 2006. Paper (OSDI), primary: yes. Seen: see coordination-services #1. For leases: 2.2 master lease, 2.8 session lease, KeepAlive default 12 s, master may only move lease forward, conservative client timeout with bounded clock-rate assumption, jeopardy and 45 s grace period, figure 2.
3. [Leader election in distributed systems](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/leader-election-in-distributed-systems/), Marc Brooker, Amazon Builders' Library. Blog by the builders, primary: yes. Seen: see leader-election #1. For leases: leases depend on local elapsed durations, a clock that seems to go backwards breaks them, GC pauses between check and work.

#### `fencing-tokens` (short)

1. [How to do distributed locking](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html), Martin Kleppmann, 2016. Blog, primary: no. Seen: see distributed-locks #1. The token 33/34 diagram, storage must check, ZooKeeper zxid or znode version as token, Redlock's random value isn't monotonic.
2. [The Chubby lock service](https://research.google.com/archive/chubby-osdi06.pdf), Burrows, 2006. See leases #2. Seen: 2.1 acquisition count passed with writes and an if-statement at the file server; 2.4 sequencers (name, mode, generation number), checked against Chubby cache or the last sequencer seen; lock-delay up to one minute, called imperfect.
3. [etcd 3.4.3](https://jepsen.io/analyses/etcd-3.4.3), Kyle Kingsbury (Jepsen), 2020. Test report, primary: no. Seen: see distributed-locks #4. Lock key revision as a globally ordered fencing token; fencing gives non-interleaving, not atomicity.

#### `coordination-services` (short)

1. [The Chubby lock service for loosely-coupled distributed systems](https://research.google.com/archive/chubby-osdi06.pdf), Mike Burrows, Google, 2006. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: 1 Paxos for safety, clocks for liveness; ad hoc primary election before Chubby; 2.1 rationale for a lock service over a consensus library (retrofit, advertise results, familiarity, one client can progress), five replicas three needed, coarse-grained locks held hours or days; 2.2 system structure (replicas in different racks, master lease, master-only reads, elections 4–6 s, up to 30 s); 2.4 advisory locks, sequencers, lock-delay; 2.6 primary election recipe; 2.8 sessions and KeepAlives; 4.3 most popular use was naming; 4.5 abusive clients (1.5 MB file rewritten per user action, 256 kB limit, a year to migrate; pub/sub too slow); 5 grace period vs Boxwood; 6 summary.
2. [ZooKeeper: Wait-free coordination for Internet-scale systems](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/atc10/tech/full_papers/Hunt.pdf), Hunt, Konar, Junqueira, Reed, Yahoo!, 2010. Paper (USENIX ATC), primary: yes. Seen: intro (primitives not locks, no blocking primitives, FIFO client order plus linearizable writes, Zab, local reads, watches vs Chubby's leases, 2:1 to 100:1 read ratios); service overview (regular, ephemeral, sequential znodes, one-time watches, sessions and timeouts); guarantees and sync; examples (config, rendezvous, group membership, simple locks and herd effect, no-herd locks, read/write locks, double barrier); implementation (in-memory tree, 1 MB per znode default, WAL and fuzzy snapshots, heartbeat after s/3).
3. [etcd versus other key-value stores](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/learning/why/), etcd authors, etcd v3.6 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: name origin; never tolerate split brain; use cases (locksmith semaphore, Kubernetes state); comparison chart vs ZooKeeper, Consul, NewSQL (linearizable reads, MVCC, max DB size several GB vs hundreds of MB); improvements over ZooKeeper; Consul KV weaknesses; NewSQL for more than a few GB; single Raft group without sharding; revisions; built-in lock/election primitives; "Notes on the usage of lock and lease": lock API isn't mutual exclusion by itself, revision is the fencing token, leases are an optimization, can't protect external resources.
4. [etcd API](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/learning/api/), etcd authors, etcd v3.6 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: KV/Watch/Lease services; response header (revision, raft_term); create/mod revisions, lock client waits on create_revision; 64-bit store revision as logical clock; Lease API (keepAlive within TTL, attached keys deleted on expiry, advisory TTL, bidirectional keepalive stream).

Extra: [ZooKeeper overview](https://zookeeper.apache.org/doc/current/zookeeperOver.html), ZooKeeper 3.9 docs. Seen: in-memory znodes, data in the byte to kilobyte range, ensemble majority, ordering by transaction stamps, reads best at about 10:1, ephemeral nodes, persistent recursive watches since 3.6.0, guarantees list. Not given a note; the paper covers it.
Extra: [etcd API guarantees](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/learning/api_guarantees/), v3.6 docs. Opened, skimmed; not used.

#### `leader-election` (short)

1. [Leader election in distributed systems](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/leader-election-in-distributed-systems/), Marc Brooker, Amazon Builders' Library. Blog by the builders, primary: yes. Seen (Wayback copy, the live page redirects to a JavaScript-only builder.aws.com page): definition; alternatives first (Step Functions, idempotent APIs, optimistic locking); pros and cons (single point of failure, scaling, trust; partial deployments); sharding into many leaders; leases as Amazon's most used mechanism with a database and heartbeats; durations not wall clock; DynamoDB lock client; GC pauses between check and work; examples (RDBMS, EBS, KCL); zero or two leaders during failures; idempotent redrive; best practices (check lease before side effects, no background heartbeat thread, metrics, audit log of leadership changes, TLA+).
2. [ZooKeeper Recipes and Solutions](https://zookeeper.apache.org/doc/current/recipes.html), Apache ZooKeeper 3.9 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: recipes are client-side; barriers, queues, locks (guid, sequential ephemeral, watch the next lowest, no herd), recoverable errors and the guid, shared locks, revocable locks, two-phase commit, leader election (smallest sequence number, watch predecessor, lowest znode doesn't mean the process knows it's leader).
3. [Package leaderelection](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/client-go/tools/leaderelection), Kubernetes authors, client-go v0.37.1. Code docs, primary: yes. Seen: no fencing; only local timestamps; tolerates clock skew but not skew rate; LeaseDuration/RenewDeadline ratio (60 s/30 s example); defaults 15 s, 10 s, 2 s; JitterFactor 1.2; ReleaseOnCancel warning; alpha API disclaimer; overview still mentions endpoints annotations.

Extra: [Leases](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/leases/), Kubernetes docs (v1.36 era). Seen: Lease objects in coordination.k8s.io; node heartbeats in kube-node-lease; kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler leader election; alpha lock release on exit (v1.36); API server identity leases (beta since v1.26). Not given a note; could back a sentence in `kubernetes`.

#### `distributed-locks` (deep)

1. [How to do distributed locking](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html), Martin Kleppmann, 2016. Blog, primary: no (primary for the argument). Seen: efficiency vs correctness locks; single Redis for efficiency; broken lease pattern with GC pause, HBase, pause causes, GitHub 90 s packet delay; fencing tokens (33/34); Redlock lacks tokens, consensus needed to make them; asynchronous model, safety vs liveness; Redis gettimeofday; clock-jump and GC-pause counterexamples on five nodes; synchrony assumptions; conclusion (neither fish nor fowl, use ZooKeeper/Curator plus fencing); update noting antirez's rebuttal.
2. [Is Redlock safe?](http://antirez.com/news/101), Salvatore Sanfilippo (antirez), 2016. Blog by Redlock's designer, primary: yes. Seen: auto-release needed for liveness; five objections to fencing (resource with no other control, linearizable store could make IDs, random token plus check-and-set, token order vs action order, non-transactional resources); system model: count elapsed time with bounded error; agrees to switch to monotonic time; steps 1 and 3 catch delays during acquisition; delayed restarts vs fsync; GPS digression; asks for Jepsen testing.
3. [Distributed Locks with Redis](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/clients/patterns/distributed-locks/), Redis docs (DELEX in Redis 8.4). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: implementations list; three properties; failover race with async replication; SET NX PX with random value; DELEX IFEQ or Lua compare-and-delete; Redlock steps with N = 5; clock-rate assumption; retry with random delay; safety argument MIN_VALIDITY; liveness and TTL penalty on partitions; fsync=always vs delayed restarts; lock extension; disclaimer (implement fencing tokens, TTL not on a monotonic clock).
4. [etcd 3.4.3](https://jepsen.io/analyses/etcd-3.4.3), Kyle Kingsbury, Jepsen, 2020. Test report, primary: no. Seen: KV strict serializable; doc claims corrected; test design with partitions, pauses, crashes, clock skew, membership changes; 3.2 "Locks Aren't Real": two holders in a healthy cluster, ~18% lost updates (2 s TTLs, 5 processes, pauses every 5 s), missing lease re-check bug, locks unsafe in asynchronous systems, revision as fencing token, guarded transactions; 4.1 recommendations.
5. [etcd versus other key-value stores](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/learning/why/). See coordination-services #3.
6. [The Chubby lock service](https://research.google.com/archive/chubby-osdi06.pdf). See coordination-services #1.
7. [ZooKeeper paper](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/atc10/tech/full_papers/Hunt.pdf). See coordination-services #2 (the no-herd lock).

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Redlock: Kleppmann says its safety rests on a synchronous timing model and it lacks fencing, so it's unsafe for correctness; antirez says it only needs bounded clock-rate error, catches acquisition delays by re-reading the clock, and that fencing assumes a resource that can check. The Redis docs now side with fencing and admit the non-monotonic TTL clock. Explained in `distributed-locks`.
- Whether fencing is realistic: antirez says most resources can't check tokens; Kleppmann and Jepsen say then the lock can't make it safe. Both agree an unchecked resource has no real mutual exclusion.
- Lock service vs primitives: Chubby exposes locks; ZooKeeper deliberately doesn't (blocking primitives hurt fast clients); etcd ships lock and election RPCs but documents them as not being mutual exclusion.
- Reads: etcd's comparison table says ZooKeeper has no linearizable reads; ZooKeeper's paper says local reads plus sync suffice for coordination.

**Couldn't open:**

- The live Builders' Library article (builder.aws.com) renders only with JavaScript; read the Wayback Machine copy of the aws.amazon.com URL instead.
- The Gray and Cheriton paper at `web.stanford.edu/class/cs240/readings/89-leases.pdf` (404) and the ACM DL PDF (blocked); the `readings/leases.pdf` copy opened.

**Rejected:**

- Wisconsin and Princeton course copies of the leases paper: dead links or HTML stubs.
- Consul's lock docs: not opened; etcd and ZooKeeper cover the pattern and etcd's page already quotes Consul's "not a bulletproof method".

**Gaps:**

- No source opened for the DynamoDB lock client or Curator; articles mention them only as named clients (Brooker, Kleppmann).
- No measured numbers for lock throughput or latency on Redis, etcd or ZooKeeper; antirez's "hundreds of thousands locks per second" is a claim, left out.
- The Builders' Library article has no year on the page.
- The client-go package doc still describes the old endpoints-annotation lock; the current Lease object wording comes from the Kubernetes Leases page, not given a note.

### Transactions across machines + Testing

PDFs were fetched with `curl -sL` and read with pdftotext; HTML pages
with curl and pandoc. The Sagas paper is an old scan with an OCR text
layer, so its quotes were checked against rendered page images.

#### `two-phase-commit` (deep)

1. [Consensus on Transaction Commit](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/video/consensus-on-transaction-commit.pdf), Jim Gray and Leslie Lamport, Microsoft Research, 2006 (ACM TODS; MSR-TR-2003-96, copy revised 2017). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: the commit problem stated as stability and consistency plus non-triviality and non-blocking; RM state machine (working, prepared, committed, aborted); 2PC message flow with a TM; every process logs its state before sending a message in it; normal case four message delays and 3N − 1 messages (three delays and 3N − 3 with co-location); three stable-storage write delays, two if RMs prepare concurrently; TM failure after all Prepared blocks; no complete, proven three-phase commit known; Paxos Commit with 2F + 1 acceptors; for 5 RMs and F = 1, 12 vs 17 vs 20 messages; 2PC is Paxos Commit with one acceptor. Existing note: none, created `gray-lamport-consensus-commit-2006`.
2. [Distributed Systems lecture notes](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2122/ConcDisSys/dist-sys-notes.pdf), Martin Kleppmann, University of Cambridge (2021/22 run). Course notes, primary: no. Seen: section 7.1 slides 122 to 127: atomic commit vs consensus table; 2PC vs 2PL; 3PC assumes a synchronous model; prepare means data on disk, constraints checked, locks held; in-doubt transactions; fault-tolerant 2PC over total order broadcast, counting only each node's first vote. Existing note `kleppmann-dist-sys-notes`, appended.
3. [PREPARE TRANSACTION](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-prepare-transaction.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: state stored on disk and detached from the session; COMMIT/ROLLBACK PREPARED from any session; failed PREPARE becomes ROLLBACK; id under 200 bytes; "you probably shouldn't be using" it unless writing a transaction manager; prepared transactions keep locks, block VACUUM, risk wraparound; keep `max_prepared_transactions = 0` without a manager; `pg_prepared_xacts`.
4. [Two-Phase Transactions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/two-phase.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18 (section 67.4). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: follows X/Open XA partly; short-lived prepared transactions in shared memory and WAL, longer ones in `pg_twophase`.
5. See `distributed-transactions` #1 (Spanner) for 2PC over Paxos and its scaling test, and `sagas` #3 (Helland) for the case against distributed transactions.

Also opened: [MySQL XA transactions](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/xa.html), which returned a "technical difficulty" page. Not used.

#### `sagas` (deep)

1. [Sagas](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/andru/cs711/2002fa/reading/sagas.pdf), Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem, SIGMOD 1987 (scan hosted by Cornell). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: long-lived transactions of hours or days; saga = sequence of transactions that can interleave with others; either all Ti run or T1..Tj then Cj..C1; compensation is semantic (the airline seat); partial sagas are visible and nobody is notified on compensation; backward vs forward recovery, save-points; pure forward recovery assumes every step eventually succeeds; a failing compensation leaves the system stuck, recovery blocks as a possible fix; compensate a letter with a second letter; a missile can't be undone; put in-transit state in the schema; the name was suggested by Bruce Lindsay.
2. [The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations](https://jimgray.azurewebsites.net/papers/thetransactionconcept.pdf), Jim Gray, 1981. Paper, primary: yes. Existing note `gray-transaction-concept-1981`: compensating transactions, real actions that can't be undone, long-lived transactions. Re-used, not re-opened beyond the existing note.
3. [Life beyond Distributed Transactions: an Apostate's Opinion](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2007/papers/cidr07p15.pdf), Pat Helland, CIDR 2007. Position paper, primary: no (opinion, but by a builder of transaction systems). Seen: distributed transactions founder on cost and fragility; 2PC can block; atomic transactions stop at one machine or cluster (entities); at-least-once messaging forces idempotence; uncertainty moves into business logic as workflow; tentative operations that confirm or cancel; warehouse reservation and escrow examples.
4. [Saga distributed transactions pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, revised 2025. Docs, primary: no. Seen: compensable, pivot and retryable steps; choreography vs orchestration tables; compensations can fail; no isolation across services; lost updates, dirty reads, fuzzy reads; countermeasures (semantic lock, commutative updates, pessimistic view, reread values, version files, risk-based concurrency).
5. [Pattern: Saga](https://microservices.io/patterns/data/saga.html), Chris Richardson, microservices.io. Pattern page, primary: no. Seen: database per service; "2PC is not an option"; order with credit limit example in choreography and orchestration; drawbacks: no automatic rollback, no isolation, must update DB and publish atomically (outbox), client must learn the outcome by waiting, polling or notification.

#### `distributed-transactions` (deep)

1. [Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf), Corbett et al., OSDI 2012. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: each tablet is a Paxos group; participant leaders and a coordinator group run 2PC, transaction manager state replicated in Paxos; single-group transactions skip 2PC; "Running two-phase commit over Paxos mitigates the availability problems"; 2PL with wound-wait; client buffers writes and drives 2PC; prepare records through Paxos, coordinator skips prepare; TrueTime interval, error bound about 1 to 7 ms; commit wait about 5 ms in their benchmark; 2PC reasonable to 50 participants, rising at 100. Existing note `corbett-spanner-2012` (clocks), appended.
2. [Parallel Commits](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/blog/parallel-commits/), Nathan VanBenschoten, Cockroach Labs, 2019 (CockroachDB 19.2). Blog, primary: yes. Seen: intents = prepare, record = commit; 2PC over consensus to avoid blocking; costs two sequential consensus rounds; first secondary index doubled insert latency; STAGING record listing in-flight writes; status recovery via the timestamp cache; heartbeats keep recovery rare; latency slope 2x RTT before, 1x after; TLA+ spec; Flexible Paxos framing, Calvin comparison.
3. [Transaction Layer](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/architecture/transaction-layer), Cockroach Labs, v26.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: write intents as replicated lock plus provisional value; transaction record in the first write's range with four states; heartbeats; HLC timestamps; max clock offset self-termination; uncertainty pushes; read refresh and retries; random abort on deadlock; Parallel Commits halves commit latency but intents still take two rounds to resolve; SERIALIZABLE default. Existing note `cockroach-transaction-layer`, appended.
4. [Living without atomic clocks](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/blog/living-without-atomic-clocks/), Spencer Kimball and Irfan Sharif, Cockroach Labs, 2022. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: TrueTime bounds offset; Spanner waits; CockroachDB uses an uncertainty interval and restarts reads, at most once per node; causal reverse and its conditions; CockroachDB claims serializability, not linearizability; causality token; nodes self-terminate past the max offset.
5. See `two-phase-commit` #2 (Kleppmann), sections 8.2 on Spanner's commit wait and why Lamport clocks can't order transactions linked through a user.

Also opened: [TrueTime and external consistency](https://cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/true-time-external-consistency), Google Cloud docs. Not used; the paper and Kleppmann cover the mechanism. The CockroachDB SIGMOD 2020 paper on dl.acm.org returned a Cloudflare block.

#### `deterministic-simulation-testing` (deep)

1. [FoundationDB: A Distributed Unbundled Transactional Key Value Store](https://www.foundationdb.org/files/fdb-paper.pdf), Zhou et al., SIGMOD 2021. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: section 4: real code with randomized workloads and fault injection in a deterministic discrete-event simulation; no multithreading, one node per core; network, disk, time, PRNG abstracted; production shim; oracles (invariants, recoverability); fault injection incl. corruption of unsynced writes; tuned fault rates; buggification; swarm testing; coverage macros; fast-forwarded time; embarrassingly parallel; limits (performance, third-party code, weaker OS contracts); 6.2: logging doesn't change replay, wild bugs first reproduced in simulation, ZooKeeper replaced, 0.5M disk years without corruption.
2. [Simulation and Testing](https://apple.github.io/foundationdb/testing.html), FoundationDB docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: whole cluster in one thread; tens of thousands of simulations nightly; estimate of about a trillion CPU-hours; cycle test for isolation; swizzle-clogging; plus Circus performance tests and hardware failure tests.
3. [Deterministic Simulation Testing (docs/internals/vopr.md)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tigerbeetle/tigerbeetle/main/docs/internals/vopr.md), TigerBeetle, main branch. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: seed plus Git commit replays; clock, network and disk stubbed; seed tunes faults; thousands of assertions kept on in production; byte-identical replica checker; inspired by FoundationDB and Antithesis.
4. [Safety](https://docs.tigerbeetle.com/concepts/safety/), TigerBeetle docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: VOPR runs whole clusters of real code under network, storage and process faults at 1000x speed, 24/7 on 1024 cores.
5. [We Put a Distributed Database In the Browser](https://tigerbeetle.com/blog/2023-07-11-we-put-a-distributed-database-in-the-browser/), Phil Eaton and Joran Dirk Greef, TigerBeetle, 2023. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: VOPR inspired by fuzzing, Dropbox Nucleus and FoundationDB; "3.3 seconds of VOPR simulation gives you 39 minutes"; all I/O mocked; checks linearizability; three fault levels up to 8%/9% storage corruption.
6. [What's the big deal about Deterministic Simulation Testing?](https://notes.eatonphil.com/2024-08-20-deterministic-simulation-testing.html), Phil Eaton, 2024. Blog, primary: no (reviewed by Alex Miller and Will Wilson). Seen: inject clock and seed; single thread plus async I/O; Go's random goroutine scheduling, Polar Signals' WASM and forked runtime; tokio/turmoil; multi-node in one process; determinism is a spectrum; limits: mocked edges, workload quality (Will Wilson on coverage), knowledge of mocks, seeds rot as code changes, compute; Jepsen can't replay.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Is 2PC worth using? Helland (2007) says large applications abandon distributed transactions as too fragile and slow; the Spanner paper (2012) says offer transactions and fix bottlenecks as they arise, with 2PC over Paxos to fix availability. microservices.io lists "2PC is not an option" for microservices. The articles present this as a difference in setting: inside one database built for it vs across independently owned services.
- Three-phase commit: Kleppmann dismisses it for assuming synchrony; Gray and Lamport say no published version has a complete proof. Neither describes the protocol in detail, so the article doesn't either.
- Spanner vs CockroachDB on clocks: wait out a tight hardware-backed bound on every commit (linearizable) vs retry reads within a looser NTP bound (serializable, linearizable only within the configured offset). Cockroach's post calls the leftover anomaly (causal reverse) marginal in practice; that's the vendor's view.
- The NTP figure (100 to 250 ms) and Spanner's "7ms" in the Cockroach post are round numbers; the Spanner paper's own 1 to 7 ms sawtooth and about 5 ms commit wait were preferred.
- DST value: FoundationDB and TigerBeetle report very strong results; Eaton's post (with Will Wilson) warns a simulator can look busy and explore little, and seeds stop reproducing when code changes. FoundationDB itself lists limits (no performance bugs, weaker-than-believed OS contracts).
- FoundationDB docs' "about a 10-1 factor of real-to-simulated time" is ambiguous in direction and wasn't used; TigerBeetle's "1000x" is a vendor figure and is attributed as such.

**Couldn't open:**
- ACM Queue version of Helland's "Life Beyond Distributed Transactions" (queue.acm.org, Cloudflare block). Used the CIDR 2007 PDF instead.
- CockroachDB SIGMOD 2020 paper on dl.acm.org (Cloudflare block).
- Gray-Lamport at the Microsoft Research URL (redirected to a removed page) and one Lamport-site path (404); the `/video/consensus-on-transaction-commit.pdf` copy opened.
- MySQL 8.4 XA page (site returned "technical difficulty").

**Rejected:**
- Google Cloud "TrueTime and external consistency": correct but adds nothing to the paper and Kleppmann.
- arXiv copy of Gray-Lamport: same content as the Lamport-site copy, which is the revised version.
- Will Wilson's Strange Loop talk (video, not watched); only quoted through Eaton's post.
- TigerBeetle "Simulation testing for liveness" blog: not opened in time; the VOPR doc covers what the node needs.

**Gaps:**
- No primary source describing XA itself (the X/Open spec); Postgres's pages describe its XA-style support only.
- No first-hand source for the "presumed abort" and other 2PC optimizations (R* paper not opened), so they're left out.
- No source for how long in-doubt transactions last in practice or how teams resolve them; the article gives advice without numbers.
- No source measuring saga failure rates or compensation bugs; left qualitative.
- Richardson's book (chapter 4, saga countermeasures) not opened; the Microsoft page lists the same countermeasures.
- No measured cost of DST (cores, time to find a known bug) other than vendor figures. The lab can measure one: plant a bug in the Raft build and count seeds to find it.

## Phase 13: Reliability engineering

Researched by 5 parallel passes, one per group below.

### Targets

#### `availability-math` (short)

1. [Embracing Risk](https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/), Marc Alvidrez (error budgets: Mark Roth), Google SRE book, 2016. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: nines, each one an order of magnitude; 99.99% is 52.56 minutes a year; time-based vs aggregate (request success) availability and why Google uses the second; 2.5M requests at 99.99% allows 250 errors; same error count can mean a trickle or a full outage; cost example 99.9% to 99.99% worth $900 on $1M; ISP background error rate 0.01% to 1%.
2. [Availability Table](https://sre.google/sre-book/availability-table/), Google SRE book appendix A, 2016. Book appendix, primary: yes. Seen: downtime allowed per year, quarter, month, week, day, hour for 90% to 99.999%, assuming no planned downtime; aggregate "X% of operations failed" is better for partly-up services.
3. [The Calculus of Service Availability](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/sre.google/en//static/pdf/calculus_of.pdf), Treynor, Dahlin, Rau, Beyer, ACM Queue, 2017. Paper (practitioner article), primary: yes. Seen: availability = MTTF/(MTTF+MTTR); a service can't beat its critical dependencies; rule of the extra 9; the extra 9 doesn't compound per level, count unique dependencies once, each gets 1/N; worked 53-minute budget with five 99.999% dependencies (26 min) leaving 17 minutes per outage; three copies at 99.9% give nine 9s only with zero correlation; geography isn't a good proxy for independence. The queue.acm.org page (id=3096459) returned 403; read as the PDF on sre.google.
4. [Availability and Beyond](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/availability-and-beyond-improving-resilience/understanding-availability.html), Michael Haken, AWS whitepaper, 2021. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: marked "historical reference only"; A = MTBF/(MTBF+MTTR), MTTD inside MTTR; series availability is the product of hard dependencies but real systems beat it because dependencies beat their SLAs, so treat it as an order of magnitude; parallel: two 99% give 99.99%; s spares fail only when s+1 fail; diminishing returns after three spares; count spares at the unit of failure (a spare AZ, not 10 spare instances); 3 AZs x 5 instances vs 2 x 10.

#### `sli-slo-sla` (deep)

1. [Service Level Objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/), Jones, Wilkes, Murphy, Smith, Google SRE book ch. 4, 2016. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: SLI, SLO, SLA definitions; SLA overloaded; "what happens if the SLOs aren't met?" test; yield; SLI ≤ target shape; can't set an SLO on QPS; Chubby planned outage to stop over-reliance; tighter internal SLO; don't overachieve; start loose; few SLOs; control loop; multiple latency thresholds.
2. [Implementing SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/), Thurgood, Ferguson, Hidalgo, Beyer, SRE Workbook ch. 2, 2018. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: SLI as good events / total events; SLI specification vs implementation (server logs miss requests that never arrive; probes; client JS); quality, coverage, cost; SLI types per component (request-driven, pipeline, storage); worked mobile game example with real numbers (97% availability, 90% < 450 ms, 99% < 900 ms) and budgets over four weeks; four-week rolling window, whole weeks; three-party agreement; error budget policy; bucketing by tier; dependencies share failure domains so two zones don't multiply out.
3. [The Calculus of Service Availability](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/sre.google/en//static/pdf/calculus_of.pdf): see `availability-math` #3. Seen: lower external commitment, 99.99% internal; stricter internal target because users get unhappy before the contract breaks.
4. [Amazon Compute Service Level Agreement](https://aws.amazon.com/compute/sla/), AWS, current version. Docs (a real SLA), primary: yes. Seen: region-level 99.99% monthly uptime for instances across 2+ AZs, instance-level 99.5%; credit tiers 10/30/100%; credits only against future bills, must be claimed with your own request logs, sole remedy; exclusions; "unavailable" means no external connectivity, per minute.
5. [Embracing Risk](https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/): see `availability-math` #1. Seen: time-based vs request-based availability; targets quarterly, tracked weekly.
6. [Alerting on SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/), Steven Thurgood, SRE Workbook ch. 5, 2018. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: six alerting strategies ending in multiwindow multi-burn-rate; burn rate definition and table. Used by `error-budgets` only; belongs mainly to phase 14 `alerting`.

#### `error-budgets` (short)

1. [Embracing Risk](https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/): see `availability-math` #1. Seen: motivation (dev vs SRE incentives); budget from the SLO measured by monitoring; releases continue while budget remains; 99.999% example where 0.0002% failures spend 20%; bang-bang vs gradual slowdown; outages you didn't cause spend it too; team can loosen the SLO; needs authority to stop launches.
2. [Example Error Budget Policy](https://sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/), Steven Thurgood, SRE Workbook appendix B, 2018. Book appendix, primary: yes. Seen: not a punishment; halt changes except P0 and security fixes when over budget for the preceding four weeks; exceptions (company-wide network, other team's service, out-of-scope load tests); single incident over 20% needs a postmortem; escalation to CTO; changes cause roughly 70% of outages.
3. [The Calculus of Service Availability](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/sre.google/en//static/pdf/calculus_of.pdf): see `availability-math` #3. Seen: budget = 1 - SLO; period often a month; freeze except security fixes and fixes for the cause; sliding windows grow back gradually; quarterly reset above 99.99%; splitting the budget half own bugs, half dependencies.
4. [Implementing SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/): see `sli-slo-sla` #2. Seen: 99.9% on 3M requests is 3,000 errors, a 1,500-error outage is 50%; ranking incidents by budget spent (bad release 13%, 20-hour restore 65%); two schools on dependency-caused misses.
5. [Alerting on SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/): see `sli-slo-sla` #6. Seen: burn rate; 99.9% over 30 days, burn rate 10 empties it in 3 days, 1,000 in 43 minutes.

#### `failure-domains` (short)

1. [Availability in Globally Distributed Storage Systems](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/osdi10/tech/full_papers/Ford.pdf), Ford et al., Google, OSDI 2010. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: failure domain definition (machines sharing a switch or power cable); 37% of failures in bursts of 2+; large bursts are rack or multi-rack events, only 3% of 10+ node bursts all on different racks; rolling reboots and upgrades as correlated failure; planned reboots the biggest source of unavailability; rack-aware placement triples stripe MTTF; independence assumption overestimates availability by two or more orders of magnitude; more replicas help less under correlation.
2. [AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-fault-isolation-boundaries/availability-zones.html), Michael Haken, AWS whitepaper, 2022. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: AZ = one or more data centers with separate redundant power and networking; up to about 100 km apart, single-digit ms apart; don't share generators, cooling, substations; deploys staggered across AZs; Regions have 3+ AZs and are isolated; data stays in a Region unless replicated.
3. [CRUSH Maps](https://docs.ceph.com/en/latest/rados/operations/crush-map/), Ceph docs (latest, marked development version). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: hierarchy mirrors physical layout to model correlated failures; types osd, host, chassis, rack, row, pdu, pod, room, datacenter, zone, region, root; rule picks the failure domain; default host; racks typical for mid to large clusters.
4. [Regions and zones](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/regions-zones), Google Cloud Compute Engine docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: zones designed to minimize correlated failures from power, cooling, networking; regions give more independence; "failure domains" named. Not used (AWS covers the same with more detail).
5. [Regions and Zones (EC2 user guide)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-regions-availability-zones.html), AWS. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Regions isolated, AZs isolated locations; spread instances across AZs. Not used (thin; the fault isolation whitepaper has the physical detail).
6. [Implementing SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/): see `sli-slo-sla` #2. Seen: two zones share dependencies, failure domains, control planes.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Series math: the AWS paper says multiplying dependency availabilities gives a theoretical ceiling, but real workloads often beat it because dependencies beat their SLAs; the Calculus paper treats the product as a hard cap and asks for an extra 9 per critical dependency. Both agree the math is a rough guide.
- Parallel math: every source gives the independent-failure formula and then warns it's wrong in practice. Ford et al. put a number on it (independence overestimates by at least two orders of magnitude for their storage).
- Time-based vs request-based availability: EC2's SLA counts minutes of no connectivity; Google counts failed requests. They measure different things and disagree about partial outages.
- Picking a target from current performance: the SRE book says don't; the Workbook says it's fine as a start if you iterate.
- Dependency-caused misses: freeze your releases or not? The Workbook lists both schools and leans to freezing; the example policy lets the team keep shipping when another team's service caused it and that team has frozen.
- Budget windows: SRE book uses quarters, Calculus paper often a month (quarter above 99.99%), Workbook recommends a four-week rolling window.

**Couldn't open:**
- [The Calculus of Service Availability on ACM Queue](https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=3096459): 403 from Cloudflare (curl and WebFetch). Read the PDF copy on sre.google instead.

**Rejected:**
- Google Cloud regions-zones page and the EC2 regions/zones user guide for `failure-domains`: accurate but thin next to the fault isolation whitepaper.

**Gaps:**
- No source for rack-level details of power (PDUs, top-of-rack switches) beyond Ford et al. and the Ceph type list. Enough for a short node.
- No independent (non-Google) source on SLO practice; the SRE books dominate. Fine for the concepts, but the style of SLI (good/total) is Google's convention.
- Latency SLOs as percentiles vs as "fraction under a threshold": both forms appear in Google's own books; no source compares them head on.

### Calls between services

All pages below were opened with `curl -sL` and converted to text with
pandoc (the SRE book chapters with a small HTML stripper, because pandoc
dropped their body). Raw copies were kept in the scratchpad while writing.

#### `deadline-propagation` (short)

1. [Deadlines](https://grpc.io/docs/guides/deadlines/), gRPC authors, page last modified 2025. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: deadline is a point in time, timeout a duration; no deadline by default, client can wait "effectively forever"; server cancels the call but the app must stop its own work; propagation on by default in Java and Go, opt-in in C++; the deadline travels as a remaining timeout to dodge clock skew; client → user server → billing sequence with a 2 s budget. Already a note (`grpc-deadlines`).
2. [Addressing Cascading Failures](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/), Mike Ulrich, Google SRE book, 2016. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: "Deadline propagation" section: one absolute deadline for the whole RPC tree, 30 s then 23 s then 19 s; the counter-example where B hard-codes 20 s and C works on a request that's already dead; shave a few hundred milliseconds off the outgoing deadline; cap outgoing deadlines to non-critical backends; check the remaining time before each stage; exceptions for checkpointed catch-up work; "Cancellation propagation" for hedged requests and doomed trees; "you don't get credit for late assignments". Already a note (`google-sre-cascading-failures`); re-opened and appended.
3. [context package](https://pkg.go.dev/context), The Go Authors, go1.27.1. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Context carries deadlines and cancellation "across API boundaries and between processes"; incoming requests create one, outgoing calls accept one; cancelling a parent cancels every derived context; `WithDeadline` can only move the deadline earlier ("no later than d"); `WithTimeout` is `WithDeadline(now+timeout)`; failing to call cancel leaks the child; `WithoutCancel` (Go 1.21) for work that must outlive the request.
4. [Router filter](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/configuration/http/http_filters/router_filter), Envoy docs, 1.40.0-dev. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: the route timeout "includes all retries" (3 s budget, first try 2.7 s, retry gets 0.3 s) "to avoid an exponential retry/timeout explosion"; per-try timeout must be below the route timeout; `max_grpc_timeout` lets `grpc-timeout` set the route timeout; `x-envoy-expected-rq-timeout-ms` sent upstream so the service can exit early.

Also opened: [gRPC and Deadlines](https://grpc.io/blog/deadlines/), Gráinne Sheerin (Google SRE), gRPC blog, 2018. "Always set a deadline"; servers should check whether the client is still waiting before expensive work; it says the default deadline "is a very large number", where the current guide says there's none. Not used; the guide is newer and covers the same points.

#### `retry-budgets` (short)

1. [Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/), Alejandro Forero Cuervo, Google SRE book, 2016. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: "Deciding to Retry": per-request budget of three attempts; per-client budget, retry only while retries are under 10% of requests; worst case just under 3x with only the per-request cap, about 1.1x with the 10% budget; attempt counter in metadata and "overloaded; don't retry"; retry only at the layer above the one rejecting. Also "Client-Side Throttling" (adaptive throttling, requests vs K × accepts over two minutes). Already a note (`google-sre-handling-overload`); re-opened and appended the throttling claims.
2. [Clients (Finagle user guide)](https://twitter.github.io/finagle/guide/Clients.html), Twitter, Finagle 24.2.0. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Retries module sits above load balancers, circuit breakers, timeouts and pools; default RetryBudget allows "approximately 20%" of requests to be retried plus 10 retries per second "to accommodate clients that have just started"; `RetryBudget(ttl, minRetriesPerSec, percentCanRetry)` backed by a leaky token bucket; share one budget between RetryFilter and RequeueFilter "to prevent retry storms"; NonRetryable flag; request timeouts not retried by default because Finagle can't know idempotency.
3. [Retry behavior](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdkref/latest/guide/feature-retry-behavior.html), AWS SDKs and Tools reference guide, the retry behavior behind `AWS_NEW_RETRIES_2026` (opt-in when this was written). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: standard mode has a retry quota, a token bucket of 500 tokens; a transient retry costs 14, a throttling retry 5; a successful retry refunds its cost, a first-try success adds 1; with 3 attempts the quota drains above about 22% sustained transient failures or 32% throttling; quota never delays first attempts; scoped to one SDK client, not shared across processes; legacy mode had no standard quota.
4. [Circuit breakers (proto)](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/api-v3/config/cluster/v3/circuit_breaker.proto), Envoy docs, 1.40.0-dev. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `retry_budget` limits concurrent retries as a percentage of active plus pending requests (default 20%), with `min_retry_concurrency` (default 3); overrides `max_retries` (default 3 parallel retries); `budget_interval` to count recent requests instead of only active ones.
5. [Fixing retries with token buckets and circuit breakers](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2022/02/28/retries.html), Marc Brooker, 2022. Blog, primary: no (an AWS engineer's own simulation, not a spec). Seen: four strategies (no retries, N retries, adaptive token bucket, retry circuit breaker) simulated with 100 clients; N retries does 1+N times the work at 100% failure; token bucket acts like N retries at low failure and like "0.1 retries" above 10%; per-client estimates: with many small clients the breaker trips too early and the bucket drains too slowly; the breaker is "modal", the bucket isn't.

Also opened: [Retries and Timeouts](https://linkerd.io/2-edge/features/retries-and-timeouts/), Linkerd docs (2.16+). Retries configured with HTTPRoute annotations; retries are opt-in, only for idempotent methods, and "by definition will increase the load". The page no longer describes a retry budget (that lived in ServiceProfiles). Not used. gRPC's `retryThrottling` is already in the note `grpc-retry` and in `retries-with-backoff`.

#### `circuit-breakers` (deep)

1. [CircuitBreaker](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CircuitBreaker.html), Martin Fowler, 2014. Blog, primary: no (popularised by Nygard's Release It!, which I couldn't open). Seen: wrap the call, count failures, trip at a threshold, then fail without calling; Ruby example with failure_threshold 5 and a timeout; a third "half open" state makes a trial call after a reset timeout; count-that-resets vs error rate ("say, a 50% failure rate"); different thresholds per error type; break when a thread pool or queue fills; log state changes, let operators trip and reset; clients must decide what to do on a breaker error.
2. [Circuit Breaker pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/circuit-breaker), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center. Docs, primary: no (a pattern write-up, not a library). Seen: Closed, Open, Half-Open with a time-based failure counter and a consecutive-success counter in half-open; half-open stops a recovering service being "flooded"; increasing open timeout; ping or health endpoint instead of a timer; "Resource differentiation" for shards; accelerated breaking on a 429/503 with a retry hint; retries should stop when the breaker says the fault isn't transient; not suitable where platform health checks already handle it.
3. [How it Works](https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix/wiki/How-it-Works) and [Configuration](https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix/wiki/Configuration), Netflix Hystrix wiki (Hystrix 1.5). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: trip needs both request volume over threshold and error percentage over threshold; open short-circuits; after the sleep window one request goes through (half-open); defaults 20 requests in the rolling window, 50% errors, 5,000 ms sleep window, 1,000 ms timeout; thread-pool and semaphore isolation (see `bulkheads`). The [README](https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix) says Hystrix is in maintenance mode (final 1.5.18) and Netflix moved to "adaptive concurrency limits" and recommends resilience4j.
4. [CircuitBreaker](https://resilience4j.readme.io/docs/circuitbreaker), resilience4j docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN plus METRICS_ONLY, DISABLED, FORCED_OPEN; count-based or time-based sliding window; trips on failure rate or slow-call rate; `minimumNumberOfCalls` (9 failures out of 9 don't trip with a minimum of 10); defaults 50% failure rate, window 100, minimum 100, 60 s open, 10 calls in half-open; half-open transition only on the next call unless `automaticTransitionFromOpenToHalfOpenEnabled`; the breaker doesn't limit concurrency, "please use a Bulkhead".
5. [Clients (Finagle user guide)](https://twitter.github.io/finagle/guide/Clients.html), Finagle 24.2.0. See `retry-budgets` #2. Seen for this node: "Circuit Breaking" section: per-endpoint breakers that the load balancer routes around; Fail Fast (session-driven, fails closed, disabled when only one host) and Failure Accrual (request-driven, fails open, one probe request on recovery); default 5 consecutive failures or 80% success rate, marked dead for a jittered 5 to 300 s.
