6. [Circuit breaking](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/circuit_breaking), Envoy docs, 1.40.0-dev. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Envoy's "circuit breakers" are limits on connections, pending requests, requests, retries and connection pools per cluster and priority, default 1024; "fully distributed (not coordinated)"; worker threads share limits; overflow sets `x-envoy-overloaded`. The error-rate kind of breaker is Envoy's outlier detection (existing note `envoy-outlier-detection`).
7. [Will circuit breakers solve my problems?](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2022/02/16/circuit-breakers.html), Marc Brooker, 2022. Blog, primary: no. Seen: sharded store where only the A-H shard is overloaded; a client-side breaker either makes things worse for everyone else or never trips; same in cell-based systems; fixes: tight coupling (breakers per shard or per customer), server hints, or statistical guessing; "Circuit breakers are designed to turn partial failures into complete failures."
8. See `retry-budgets` #5 (Brooker's retry breaker vs token bucket) and the existing note `brooker-timeouts-retries-backoff-2019` (breakers add hard-to-test modal behaviour; Amazon uses a local token bucket instead).

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- **What a circuit breaker is.** Fowler, Azure, Hystrix and resilience4j mean an error-rate state machine. Envoy calls its concurrency limits "circuit breaking", which is closer to a bulkhead; Envoy's error-rate breaker is outlier detection, per host. Finagle's breakers are per endpoint and steer the load balancer instead of failing calls.
- **Should you have one at all.** Azure and Fowler recommend breakers; Brooker argues a client-side breaker turns a partial failure (one shard, one cell) into a complete one, and Amazon prefers a retry token bucket. Brooker's simulation also shows a retry-only breaker trips early with many small clients.
- **Retry budget shape.** Google: ratio of retries to requests (10%). Finagle: 20% plus 10 per second. Envoy: concurrent retries as 20% of active requests. AWS: a token bucket that drains above about 22% transient failure. Same idea, different numbers and units, none derived from a model.
- **gRPC default deadline.** The gRPC guide says there's no default deadline; the older gRPC blog says the default is "a very large number". The guide is newer.
- **Bulkhead vs cells.** The Azure bulkhead page says the pattern is "also known as a cell-based architecture"; the tentative shape keeps `cell-based-architecture` as its own node (splitting a service into full copies), which is the server-side end of the same idea.
- **Threads or semaphores for bulkheads.** Hystrix defaults to a thread pool per dependency (can walk away from a hung call; costs a context switch); resilience4j's main bulkhead is a semaphore; a semaphore can't time out the call itself.

**Couldn't open:**
- Michael Nygard, *Release It!* (the book that popularised the pattern): not opened. Mentioned by name only, as the origin both Fowler and Brooker point to.
- Netflix's original "Fault Tolerance in a High Volume, Distributed System" blog post: not tried; the Hystrix wiki covers the design from the builders.

**Rejected:**
- gRPC and Deadlines blog (2018): older than the guide and partly out of date on the default.
- Linkerd retries page: no longer describes a budget.
- Polly (.NET) docs: same state machine as resilience4j; one library's docs is enough.

**Gaps:**
- No source measures how much a breaker helps or hurts in a real outage; Brooker's simulation is the only data, and it's about retry breakers. The phase 13 lab could measure it.
- No primary source on how to size a bulkhead beyond "the same way as a thread pool" (Hystrix). Left to `thread-pool` and `littles-law`.
- No source on trusting deadlines sent by untrusted clients (an external caller sending a huge `grpc-timeout`). Envoy's `max_grpc_timeout` caps it, but the docs don't frame it as a security point. Left out.

### Overload

#### `goodput` (short)

1. [Using load shedding to avoid overload](https://d1.awsstatic.com/builderslibrary/pdfs/using-load-shedding-to-avoid-overload.pdf), David Yanacek, Amazon Builders' Library, 2019. Engineering article from the builders, primary: yes. Read as the PDF (the web page redirects to builder.aws.com, JavaScript only). Seen: throughput vs goodput defined ("handled without errors and with low enough latency for the client to make use of the response"); latency rises to an inflection point; median latency equal to the client timeout means 50% availability; the "Goodput vs. throughput" graph (rises, peaks, collapses to zero); the ideal load test has goodput plateau and stay flat; shedding isn't free, so goodput eventually drops; late replies count as success on the server and error at the client; fast failures make median latency look good (60% shed example). Note: `yanacek-load-shedding-2019`.
2. [Metastable Failures in Distributed Systems](https://sigops.org/s/conferences/hotos/2021/papers/hotos21-s11-bronson.pdf), Bronson, Aghayev, Charapko and Zhu, HotOS 2021. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: goodput "(i.e., throughput of useful work)"; Figure 2, goodput against load in stable, vulnerable and metastable states; the retry example (fast below 300 QPS, one retry after 1 s, 280 QPS, a 10 s outage, then 560 QPS and zero goodput; stable below 150 QPS); keeping goodput high during overload by changing policy. Note: `bronson-metastable-failures-2021`.

Extra: [Addressing Cascading Failures](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/) (existing note): "you don't get credit for late assignments"; used for the late-work point.

#### `load-shedding` (deep)

1. [Using load shedding to avoid overload](https://d1.awsstatic.com/builderslibrary/pdfs/using-load-shedding-to-avoid-overload.pdf). See goodput #1. Also: cheap rejections (an accidental log line makes dropping expensive); load balancer pings are the most important request; crawler vs human priority; per-request deadlines and timeout hints; bound queue time and throw out old requests; LIFO where the protocol allows; Classic Load Balancer surge queue vs Application Load Balancer spillover; NGINX `max_conns` as last resort; iptables rejects cheaper than any process; shed in layers; shedding at the autoscaling CPU target stops reactive scaling.
2. [Addressing Cascading Failures](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/), Mike Ulrich, Google SRE book ch. 22, 2016. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: "Load Shedding and Graceful Degradation" section: goal, 503 above N in-flight requests, LIFO or CoDel, prioritizing; rate limiting ignores service health; queue sizing (50% of thread pool or less, Gmail queueless). Existing note `google-sre-cascading-failures`, appended.
3. [Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/), Alejandro Forero Cuervo, Google SRE book ch. 21, 2016. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: degraded responses; per-customer limits in CPU seconds; client-side (adaptive) throttling, rejection probability max(0, (requests − K × accepts)/(requests + 1)) as an image, K = 2 preferred; four criticalities (CRITICAL_PLUS, CRITICAL, SHEDDABLE_PLUS, SHEDDABLE), propagated, set near the user; executor load average; keep serving the provisioned rate at 2x to 10x overload; don't stop accepting everything. Existing note `google-sre-handling-overload`, appended.
4. [Fail at Scale](https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=2839461), Ben Maurer, Facebook, ACM Queue 13(8), 2015. Article from the builders, primary: yes. queue.acm.org returned a JavaScript challenge; read through the Wayback Machine snapshot. Seen: CoDel-style queue timeout (M = 5 ms, N = 100 ms, "tends to work well across a wide set of use cases"); adaptive LIFO; client-side cap on outstanding requests per service; the 1%-of-users experimental service that takes all threads. Note: `maurer-fail-at-scale-2015`.
5. [Keeping Netflix Reliable Using Prioritized Load Shedding](https://netflixtechblog.com/keeping-netflix-reliable-using-prioritized-load-shedding-6cc827b02f94), Correa, Gonigberg and West, Netflix, 2020. Engineering blog, primary: yes. 403 to curl and WebFetch; read through the Wayback Machine snapshot. Seen: NON_CRITICAL / DEGRADED_EXPERIENCE / CRITICAL buckets, priority 1 to 100 in Zuul; service vs global throttling and their signals; cubic curve for the priority threshold; `maxRetries` and `retryAfterSeconds` sent to devices; failure injection by priority found a client race condition. Note: `netflix-prioritized-load-shedding-2020`.
6. [The Site Reliability Workbook, ch. 11: Managing Load](https://sre.google/workbook/managing-load/), Bethea, Sheerin, Mace, King et al., Google, 2018. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: "When Load Shedding Attacks": shedding keeps CPU flat, the utilization-aware balancer reads errors as cheap requests and piles traffic on; count an error as 120% utilization; autoscale before shedding; deadlines. Note: `google-sre-workbook-managing-load`.

Extra: [Admission Control filter](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/configuration/http/http_filters/admission_control_filter), Envoy docs (1.40.0-dev). Seen: a port of SRE client-side throttling with an `aggression` exponent and success-rate threshold. Not used; the SRE chapter covers the idea.

#### `admission-control` (short)

1. [Performance Under Load: Adaptive Concurrency Limits @ Netflix](https://netflixtechblog.medium.com/performance-under-load-3e6fa9a60581), Landau, Thurston and Bozarth, Netflix, 2018. Engineering blog, primary: yes. 403 to curl and WebFetch; read through the Wayback Machine snapshot. Seen: Little's law for concurrency; hand-measured limits went stale; TCP congestion control borrowed; gradient = RTTnoload/RTTactual; newLimit = currentLimit × gradient + queueSize, queueSize = sqrt(limit); per-server limits, one retry nearly 100% successful with client-side balancing. Note: `netflix-adaptive-concurrency-2018`.
2. [Adaptive Concurrency](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/configuration/http/http_filters/adaptive_concurrency_filter), Envoy docs (1.40.0-dev). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: gradient controller, minRTT measured by pinning concurrency to `min_concurrency` (3 by default) with jitter, 503s during measurement, gradient = (minRTT + B)/sampleRTT, headroom pinned to sqrt(limit), needs full control over the cluster's concurrency. Note: `envoy-adaptive-concurrency`.

Extra: [Netflix/concurrency-limits README](https://github.com/Netflix/concurrency-limits). Seen: Vegas and Gradient2 algorithms, simple and percentage (partitioned) enforcement, server limiter rejects with gRPC `UNAVAILABLE`, client limiter as backpressure. Read for context, not cited.

#### `graceful-degradation` (short)

1. [Addressing Cascading Failures](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/). See load-shedding #2. Graceful degradation reduces the work per request (search a subset in memory, cheaper ranking); trigger rarely; unused paths break, so run a few servers near overload; alert, and keep an off switch; the Shakespeare example drops pictures and maps.
2. [Avoiding fallback in distributed systems](https://d1.awsstatic.com/builderslibrary/pdfs/avoiding-fallback-in-distributed-systems.pdf), Jacob Gabrielson, Amazon Builders' Library, 2019. Engineering article, primary: yes. Seen: Amazon almost never uses fallback; the shipping-speed cache whose database fallback took down the site and the fulfillment centers around 2001; alternatives (improve the main path, let the caller handle it, push data, turn fallback into always-on failover). Note: `gabrielson-avoiding-fallback-2019`.

Extra: [REL05-BP01 Implement graceful degradation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_mitigate_interaction_failure_graceful_degradation.html), AWS Well-Architected, Reliability Pillar. Seen: turn hard dependencies into soft ones; anti-patterns (serving nothing when partial results are possible); degraded paths should be simpler than the primary one and "fallback strategies should be avoided". Not used, covered by the two above.

#### `thundering-herd` (short)

1. [The Site Reliability Workbook, ch. 11: Managing Load](https://sre.google/workbook/managing-load/). See load-shedding #6. Pokémon GO: a single immediate retry then constant backoff; bursts of quick errors synchronized clients into a "thundering herd"; spikes 20x the previous global peak; rate limiting at the load balancer, then jitter and truncated exponential backoff.
2. [Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter](https://d1.awsstatic.com/builderslibrary/pdfs/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter.pdf), Marc Brooker, Amazon Builders' Library, 2019. Already a note (`brooker-timeouts-retries-backoff-2019`). Correlated failures back off to the same time; jitter on all timers and periodic jobs; consistent per-host jitter for scheduled work.

Extra: [Exponential Backoff And Jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/) (existing note `brooker-backoff-jitter-2015`): clusters of calls with plain backoff. Linked through `retries-with-backoff` instead.

#### `cascading-failures` (deep)

1. [Addressing Cascading Failures](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/). See load-shedding #2. Definition (positive feedback), cluster A/B example (1,000 to 1,200 QPS), resource exhaustion chains, GC death spiral, crash loops (10,000 / 11,000 / 9,000 QPS and 10% healthy), balancers avoiding error servers, cold caches (latency vs capacity cache), intra-layer calls, triggers, testing past the breaking point, recovery steps (drop to 1%, disable health checks, remove batch load).
2. [Fail at Scale](https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=2839461). See load-shedding #4. Large latency causes cascading failures; resource exhaustion lets a failure in a subset of requests fail all of them; client-side concurrency caps.
3. [Avoiding fallback in distributed systems](https://d1.awsstatic.com/builderslibrary/pdfs/avoiding-fallback-in-distributed-systems.pdf). See graceful-degradation #2. A fallback spread a partial outage to the whole site and the fulfillment network.
4. [The Site Reliability Workbook, ch. 11](https://sre.google/workbook/managing-load/). See load-shedding #6. Pokémon GO as a "classic cascading failure"; the load balancer's own capacity fell by 50%; autoscaling a service whose dependency is failing.
5. [Panic threshold](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/panic_threshold), Envoy docs. Already a note (`envoy-panic-threshold`). Below 50% healthy hosts, ignore health so failures don't cascade.
6. [Metastable Failures in Distributed Systems](https://sigops.org/s/conferences/hotos/2021/papers/hotos21-s11-bronson.pdf). See goodput #2. Trigger vs sustaining effect; the contagious feedback loop. For the comparison with `metastable-failures`.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- **Fallback vs degradation.** Google's SRE book recommends degraded modes and cheaper answers; Amazon's Builders' Library says it almost never uses fallback, because rarely used paths break and can pile load on what's already failing. Both agree the degraded path must be exercised regularly (Google: run some servers near overload; Amazon: run both paths all the time, which makes it failover).
- **Where to shed.** Facebook and Google say the server knows most and is the best place; Amazon sheds in layers and says the earliest layer is cheapest but sees least; Netflix sheds at the API gateway. Amazon calls proxy connection caps (NGINX `max_conns`) a last resort, because in-flight counts can mislead.
- **Fixed vs adaptive limits.** Netflix and Envoy compute a concurrency limit from latency; Facebook's CoDel values (5 ms, 100 ms) are fixed but "tend not to need tuning"; Google uses CPU-based utilization and executor load average. Amazon found a single max-connections number never stayed right.
- **Shedding vs autoscaling.** Amazon warns that shedding at the same CPU target disables reactive autoscaling; Google's workbook says autoscale before shedding and shows shedding fooling a load balancer.
- **Retrying after a rejection.** Google and Netflix both say a quick retry on another server usually works when only a few servers are overloaded; the Pokémon GO case shows quick errors synchronizing retries into a herd.

### Overload + Testing and recovery

All pages below were opened with `curl -sL` and converted to text with
pandoc (papers with pdftotext). The Amazon Builders' Library pages and
the AWS post-event summary render with JavaScript, so they were read
with headless Chromium (`--dump-dom`). queue.acm.org blocked the fetch
(Cloudflare), so the Krishnan article was read from the Wayback Machine

#### `metastable-failures` (deep)

1. [Metastable Failures in Distributed Systems](https://sigops.org/s/conferences/hotos/2021/papers/hotos21-s11-bronson.pdf), Nathan Bronson, Abutalib Aghayev, Aleksey Charapko, Timothy Zhu, HotOS 2021. Paper, primary: yes (written from operating Facebook's systems). Seen: definition ("a bad state that persists even when the trigger is removed"); stable, vulnerable and metastable states (figure 1); retry example with a database fast below 300 QPS, one retry after 1 s, 280 QPS load, a 10 s outage, then 560 QPS and zero goodput; stable below 150 QPS; recovery needs load under 150 QPS or retries under 20 QPS (figure 2); look-aside cache with 90% hit rate, 3,000 vs 300 QPS, 10x amplification; slow error handling; link imbalance fixed by one line in a connection pool after two years; fixes: root cause is the loop, policy changes under overload (retry budget, LIFO, smaller queues, priorities, shedding, circuit breaker), CoDel-style minimum queueing delay, read-through cache, fast error paths; worst-case amplification over 100x despite priorities; characteristic metric, hidden vs advertised capacity, trigger intensity; reconfiguration lowers capacity short term; systematic approach still open. Note `bronson-metastable-failures-2021` was created by another group while I worked; I appended my claims.
2. [Metastable Failures in the Wild](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi22-huang-lexiang.pdf), Lexiang Huang and others (Penn State, UNH, Twitter), OSDI 2022. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: 22 metastable failures from 11 organizations in public incident reports; at least 4 of 15 major AWS outages in a decade; ~45% of triggers engineer errors, ~35% load spikes, 45% more than one trigger; outages 1.5 to 73.53 hours; retry policy the sustaining effect in more than 50%; recovery often needs load shedding; load-spike vs capacity-decreasing triggers, workload vs capacity-degradation amplification (GC at Twitter); many names (retry storms, death spirals, cascading failures, persistent congestion); smaller headroom and longer triggers mean more vulnerability.
3. [Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption and Related Impacts in the US-East Region](https://aws.amazon.com/message/5467D2/), AWS, 2015 (year from Huang's Table 1, incident AWS3). Post-event summary, primary: yes. Seen: storage servers retry membership requests and take themselves out of service on timeout; membership responses grown by GSIs, unmonitored; brief network disruption, retries kept the metadata service overloaded, healthy servers dragged in; error rate ~55%; couldn't add capacity because admin requests failed; pausing requests broke the loop; fixes include longer timeout, fewer requests, and many metadata service instances each serving part of the fleet.
4. [Metastability and Distributed Systems](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2021/05/24/metastable.html), Marc Brooker (AWS), 2021. Blog, primary: no (review of #1). Seen: queue example, "up but down"; agrees on loop as root cause; mode changes under overload are hard to reason about; priorities hard to get; retries lower daily error rate but make systems more vulnerable; not new outside computing (control systems); earlier framed as bistability.
5. See phase 9 `caching`: [Caches, Modes, and Unstable Systems](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2021/08/27/caches.html) (existing note `brooker-caches-modes-2021`): load tests don't show the bad mode; the bad test needs a heavier-tailed key mix.

Also opened: [Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/avoiding-insurmountable-queue-backlogs/) (async queue backlogs, LIFO, constant work). Not used; better for `load-shedding` or phase 10. [Fixing retries with token buckets and circuit breakers](https://brooker.co.za/blog/2022/02/28/retries.html) (Brooker): simulation comparing no retries, N retries, adaptive token bucket and retry circuit breaker. Not used; belongs to `retry-budgets`.

#### `cell-based-architecture` (short)

1. [Reducing the Scope of Impact with Cell-Based Architecture](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reducing-scope-of-impact-with-cell-based-architecture/reducing-scope-of-impact-with-cell-based-architecture.html), AWS Well-Architected, 2023. Docs, primary: yes. Seen (intro, what/why/when, partition, routing, router resilience, sizing, deployment, best practices, FAQ): a cell is an isolated full copy sharing no state; 10 cells, 90% of requests unaffected; contains bad deploys and poison pills; router, cell, control plane; same 30 hosts possible; fixed max cell size, grow by adding cells, test a cell past its breaking point; canary cell; "100% of customers see 5% failures, or 5% see 100%"; costs; big customers may not fit a cell; cross-cell calls go through the router; the router is shared, a single point of failure, must stay thin; sizing trade-offs table; start with cell zero and migration from day one; shuffle sharding is not cells, use it within a cell.
2. [Workload isolation using shuffle-sharding](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/workload-isolation-using-shuffle-sharding/), Colm MacCárthaigh (Amazon Builders' Library). Blog, primary: yes. Seen: no sharding cascades through all workers; 4 shards of 2, 25% impact, more slack needed; shuffle shards of two random workers, 28 pairs from 8, 1/28 impact, 7x better; needs clients that retry elsewhere; Route 53: 2048 virtual name servers, 4 per domain, ~730 billion shards, no two domains share more than two; recursive shuffle sharding; Infima library.

Also opened: #3 under `metastable-failures` (DynamoDB's fix of segmenting the metadata service is cell-like). Not cited in the short article, to stay at two sources.

#### `chaos-engineering` (deep)

1. [Principles of Chaos Engineering](https://principlesofchaos.org/), chaos engineering community (Netflix origin), last updated 2019. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: definition; four steps (steady state, hypothesis on control and experimental groups, real-world variables, try to disprove); advanced principles: hypothesis on measurable output not internals, vary real-world events including non-failures like traffic spikes, run in production, automate continuously, minimize blast radius with some short-term harm allowed.
2. [Chaos Engineering](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1702.05843), Ali Basiri and others (Netflix), IEEE Software 2016 (arXiv copy). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: Chaos Monkey (working hours only), Chaos Kong (region, monthly), FIT; system perspective; SPS as steady state; fine-grained metrics can end an experiment early; inputs list; region failure simulated, not real; subset of users; why production (synthetic clients, DNS); unbounded client queue failure; confidence decays; bookmark experiment with control and experiment groups; combinations of events; which experiments to run is open.
3. [Weathering the Unexpected](https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=2371516), Kripa Krishnan (Google), ACM Queue 2012, with a sidebar by Thomas A. Limoncelli. Article, primary: yes. Seen: DiRT annual multi-day company-wide test; breaks live systems and removes key people; caused outages and revenue loss; start small; earthquake scenario broke authentication; communications plan found by one person, bridge held 40 callers; approvers all in the lost site; docs don't prove anything; reviewed tests with revert plans; sandboxes less realistic; prefail but no prepass; command center; fix, don't blame; sidebar restore talk-through found two bugs (fictionalized).
4. [What is AWS Fault Injection Service?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fis/latest/userguide/what-is.html), AWS. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: FIS based on chaos engineering principles; guardrails to stop or roll back; recommends planning and pre-production first; template = actions, targets, stop conditions; stop condition is a CloudWatch alarm threshold.

Also: phase 11 `fault-injection` is the comparison point (Jepsen, netem); not re-cited.

#### `backups` (short)

1. [25.3 Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/continuous-archiving.html), PostgreSQL 18.6 manual. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: base backup plus archived WAL; inconsistency fixed by replay; stop anywhere; warm standby; pg_dump output can't be replayed; whole cluster only; test archiving before first base backup; 16MB segments; archive_command returns zero only on success, must not overwrite; pg_wal fills and PANICs if archiving fails; lag increases disaster loss; config files not restored; archive_timeout ~1 minute; keep several backup sets; incremental backups need the chain and pg_combinebackup, no built-in tracking; recovery targets (time, restore point, xid); timelines.
2. [25.1 SQL Dump](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/backup-dump.html), PostgreSQL 18.6 manual. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: dump is SQL that recreates the database; runs from any host; loads into newer versions, only cross-architecture method; consistent snapshot, non-blocking; psql continues after errors (partial restore) vs single transaction; ANALYZE after restore; pg_dump skips roles and tablespaces; pg_dumpall snapshots not synchronized; custom format allows selective table restore; parallel dump needs directory format.
3. [25.2 File System Level Backup](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/backup-file.html), PostgreSQL 18.6 manual. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: server must be stopped or use an atomic snapshot; tar isn't atomic; tables can't be restored alone (pg_xact); snapshot restore looks like a crash and replays WAL; multi-filesystem snapshots must be simultaneous; bigger than a dump but possibly faster.

#### `disaster-recovery` (deep)

1. [Disaster Recovery of Workloads on AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws.html), AWS Well-Architected, 2021. Docs, primary: yes. Seen (what is a disaster, HA vs DR, BCP, options, detection, testing): natural, technical, human disasters; HA is components, DR is whole copies; replication copies deletes and corruption; DR is part of BCP; time-dependent impact (payroll); no DR can be valid; RTO and RPO definitions (figure 3); cost vs loss; four strategies; data-plane failover; backup frequency sets recovery point; back up code, config, infrastructure; test backups; pilot light vs warm standby; manual failover with automated steps; active/active still needs backups, recovery point before discovery; detection counts against RTO; only frequently tested paths work; capacity and quota drift; manage config drift.
2. [Data Integrity: What You Read Is What You Wrote](https://sre.google/sre-book/data-integrity/), Raymond Blum and Rhandeev Singh, Google SRE book (2016), chapter 26. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: people want restores, not backups; replication isn't recoverability; replicas spread corruption; seconds / 40 minutes / hours for copies at different layers, restore as long as backup; late discovery needs older backups and merging; defense in depth (soft deletion, backups, validation); tiered backups; latent broken recovery; full end-to-end tests, automated, continuous; recovery checklist; Gmail 2011 tape restore, practised before, 99%+ recovered before the estimate.
3. [GitLab.com database outage postmortem](https://about.gitlab.com/blog/2017/02/10/postmortem-of-database-outage-of-january-31/), GitLab, 2017. Postmortem, primary: yes. Seen: one primary, one hot standby; replication broke under load with no WAL archiving; data directory wiped on the primary, ~300 GB; pg_dump 9.2 vs 9.6 failed silently, alert emails rejected (DMARC); disk snapshots not enabled for DB; LVM snapshot 6 hours old used instead of 24; ~18 hours to copy from throttled staging disks; ~5,000 projects, 5,000 comments, 700 accounts affected; nobody owned testing backups; fixes include automated restore testing. The page's real title names the day of the outage; the note uses a shortened title.
4. See `chaos-engineering` #3 (Krishnan): the restore-drill sidebar and people/process failures.
5. See `backups` #1: WAL archiving lag raises what a disaster loses.

Also opened: [Disaster recovery planning guide](https://cloud.google.com/architecture/dr-scenarios-planning-guide), Google Cloud. Downloaded but not read closely; the AWS paper covered the same ground. Not used.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Metastable failures: Bronson et al. list policy changes under overload as a fix; Brooker argues modes are bad and hard to reason about. Priorities help in theory, but one priority-protected system still failed at over 100x amplification.
- Metastable vs cascading: Huang et al. note "cascading failures" is one of the names used for metastable failures in reports; the graph keeps two nodes, and the article separates them by the "stays down after the trigger" test.
- Novelty: Brooker says the paper overstates novelty (control systems, operations research); the paper claims to be first to frame it.
- Cells and shuffle sharding: the node note ties them together, AWS's own guidance says they're different and shuffle sharding belongs inside a cell.
- Chaos in production: the principles strongly prefer production; AWS FIS docs recommend pre-production first; DiRT uses sandboxes for untried tests while admitting they're less realistic. Netflix simulates region loss rather than causing it.
- DR automation: AWS warns automatic failover can cause damage on false alarms and suggests manual initiation with automated steps; SRE book pushes automating recovery tests. Not a contradiction, but readers mix the two up.

**Couldn't open:**
- queue.acm.org directly (Cloudflare block, also in headless Chromium). Read the Wayback Machine copy of the same URL instead.
- github.com/lexiangh/Metastability (Huang's reproduction code): not opened.
- The Route 53 Infima library: not opened.

**Rejected:**
- Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs (Builders' Library): about async queue backlogs, not metastability as such.
- Brooker's retries-with-token-buckets post: belongs to `retry-budgets`.
- Google Cloud DR planning guide: duplicate of the AWS paper for this node.

**Gaps:**
- No primary numbers for how long real restores take per GB; the SRE chapter's 40-minute and hours figures are illustrative. The phase 13 restore drill is meant to produce real ones.
- No source measured the cost or overhead of running cells; the article stays qualitative.
- No source on WAL archiving tools (pgBackRest, WAL-G); left out.
- Chaos engineering results (how many bugs found, at what cost) aren't quantified in any source opened.

### Incidents

#### `incident-response` (deep)

1. [Managing Incidents (Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 14)](https://sre.google/sre-book/managing-incidents/), Andrew Stribblehill, Google, 2017 (online edition copyright). Book chapter (free online), primary: yes. Seen: the "Mary" story of an unmanaged incident (sharp technical focus, poor communication, freelancing); roles based on the Incident Command System: incident command, ops, communication, planning; only ops changes the system; a recognized command post; live incident state document kept by the IC; explicit handoff ("You're now the incident commander, okay?"); when to declare (second team needed, customer-visible, unsolved after an hour of analysis); best practices: prioritize (stop the bleeding, restore service, preserve evidence), prepare, trust, introspect, consider alternatives, practice, rotate roles.
2. [Incident Response (The Site Reliability Workbook, chapter 9)](https://sre.google/workbook/incident-response/), Jennifer Mace, Jelena Oertel, Stephen Thorne, Arup Chakrabarti (PagerDuty) and others, Google, 2018. Book chapter (free online), primary: yes. Seen: resolving vs managing an incident; ICS founded by firefighters in 1968; the "3Cs" (coordinate, communicate, control); IC, Communications Lead, Ops Lead; IC holds every undelegated role; four case studies: Google Home (no incident declared, weekend rollout), GKE CreateCluster (6 h 40 min, 41 IRC users, 28 action items; formal structure two hours late; a generic rollback would have mitigated by about 10 a.m. instead of 12:11 p.m.), lightning at a Belgian datacenter (well-managed), PagerDuty NTP drift (IC and on-calls rotated every four hours); the mitigation-first order (assess, mitigate, root-cause, fix and write postmortem); drills (DiRT, Wheel of Misfortune).
3. [Different Roles](https://response.pagerduty.com/before/different_roles/), PagerDuty Incident Response docs. Docs from the team that runs it, primary: yes. Seen: IC is the single source of truth and "NOT a resolver"; Deputy (hot standby IC), Scribe (timeline in chat), Subject Matter Expert with CAN reports (condition, actions, needs), Customer Liaison, Internal Liaison; roles collapse onto fewer people for small incidents. Also opened: What is an Incident? (major incident = needs coordinated response between teams; "peacetime vs wartime" shift; any employee can trigger), Severity Levels (if unsure, treat it as the higher severity), During an Incident (IC steps; typical repair actions: roll back a bad deploy, rolling restart, drain a data center; "If in doubt, post it out").
4. [Incident Commander training](https://response.pagerduty.com/training/incident_commander/), PagerDuty Incident Response docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: IC's purpose "Keep the incident moving towards resolution"; IC doesn't check graphs or logs; deep technical knowledge not required; size-up, stabilize, update, verify loop; "a wrong decision is better than no decision"; "Are there any strong objections?"; assign tasks to a named person with a time box, never "Can someone..." (bystander effect); clear over concise.
5. [Generic mitigations](https://www.oreilly.com/content/generic-mitigations/), Jennifer Mace, O'Reilly (a Google collaboration), 2020. Blog, primary: yes (Google SRE writing about Google practice). Seen: a mitigation reduces impact; a generic one works without understanding the outage; list: rollback, data rollback, degrade, upsize, block list, drain, quarantine; measure "time to mitigate" not "time to fix"; unpractised mitigations don't work; timeline figure of mitigate-first vs investigate-first.
6. [Emergency Response (SRE book, chapter 13)](https://sre.google/sre-book/emergency-response/), Google. Seen: downloaded and skimmed (test-induced and change-induced emergencies, "all problems have solutions"). Not used; chapter 14 and the workbook cover the concept.

#### `on-call` (short)

1. [Being On-Call (Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 11)](https://sre.google/sre-book/being-on-call/), Andrea Spadaccini, Google, 2017 (online edition copyright). Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: response times of 5 minutes (user-facing) and 30 minutes (less time-sensitive); 99.99% a quarter allows about 13 minutes of downtime; primary and secondary rotations; at most 25% of SRE time on-call, so at least 8 engineers for a single-site 24/7 rotation, 6 per site for two sites; an incident takes about 6 hours of work on average, so at most 2 per 12-hour shift; compensation capped; stress pushes people toward intuitive, habitual action; resources: escalation paths, incident procedures, blameless postmortems; noisy alerts, aim for 1 alert per incident; "give back the pager"; operational underload (be on call at least once or twice a quarter).
2. [On-Call (The Site Reliability Workbook, chapter 8)](https://sre.google/workbook/on-call/), Ollie Cook, Sara Smollett, Andrea Spadaccini, Cara Donnelly, Jian Ma, Garrett Plasky (Evernote) and others, Google, 2018. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: recap of the two-incident target; playbooks (general vs step-by-step is contentious; a deterministic list of commands should become automation); Evernote's P1/P2/P3 alert tiers; pager load defined; table of response times (5 min, 30 min, ticket); every alert immediately actionable, with a playbook entry; new alerts run in a non-paging test mode about a week; shift length at most 12 hours; "survive the week" culture scenario.
3. [Monitoring Distributed Systems (SRE book, chapter 6)](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/), Rob Ewaschuk, Google. Already a source note (`google-sre-monitoring`). Seen now: pages are expensive; questions to ask of each paging rule; every page actionable, needs intelligence, about a novel problem; page on symptoms more than causes; rote pages are a red flag.
4. [Being On-Call](https://response.pagerduty.com/oncall/being_oncall/) and [Alerting Principles](https://response.pagerduty.com/oncall/alerting_principles/), PagerDuty docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: prepare, triage, fix, improve, support; "Never hesitate to escalate"; backup schedule directly after the primary shift; escalation timeout 5 minutes; alert vs notification; High/Medium/Low/Notification table; alert content should link a run book; an untested alert is no alert. Not used (short node; the SRE chapters cover it), but good further reading.

#### `postmortems` (short)

1. [Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure (Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 15)](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/), John Lunney and Sue Lueder, Google, 2017 (online edition copyright). Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: what a postmortem records; common triggers (user-visible downtime, data loss, on-call intervention, long resolution, monitoring failure), defined in advance; blameless means assuming good intentions; blameless culture came from healthcare and aviation; "You can't 'fix' people"; review criteria; "An unreviewed postmortem might as well never have existed"; reading clubs, Wheel of Misfortune.
2. [Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure (The Site Reliability Workbook, chapter 10)](https://sre.google/workbook/postmortem-culture/), Daniel Rogers, Murali Suriar, Sue Lueder, Pranjal Deo, Divya Sudhakar and others, Google, 2018. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: a bad and a good postmortem of the same satellite diskerase outage; bad one: missing context, vague action items ("Improve"), equal priority, no owners, individuals blamed, animated language, one team audience, published four months late; good one: glossary, numbers, owners and tracking bugs, measurable preventive action items, published within a week; reward closing action items not just writing; failure signs (avoiding association, repeating incidents).
3. [How Complex Systems Fail](https://how.complexsystems.fail/), Richard I. Cook, MD, University of Chicago Cognitive Technologies Laboratory, 1998-2000. Short treatise, primary: yes (the author's own work). Seen: 18 points; catastrophe needs multiple failures; root-cause attribution is "fundamentally wrong"; hindsight bias; all practitioner actions are gambles; post-accident remedies often add coupling and complexity.
4. [Each necessary, but only jointly sufficient](https://www.kitchensoap.com/2012/02/10/each-necessary-but-only-jointly-sufficient/), John Allspaw, 2012. Blog, primary: no. Seen: "there is no root cause" in complex systems; Five Whys assumes one sufficient cause per symptom; a single root cause is easy to pin on a person. Not used (makes Cook's point for a web ops audience; Cook is the original).
5. [Postmortem Process](https://response.pagerduty.com/after/post_mortem_process/) and [Effective Postmortems](https://response.pagerduty.com/after/effective_post_mortems/), PagerDuty docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: IC assigns one owner; meeting within 3 calendar days (SEV-1) or 5 business days (SEV-2), 15 to 30 minutes; timeline first, every item backed by a graph or log link; avoid "human error"; keep "what happened" apart from "how to fix it". Not used (short node), good further reading.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- "Root cause". Google's templates keep "Root Causes and Trigger" sections and ask whether "the root cause" was deep enough; Cook calls root-cause attribution fundamentally wrong, since failure needs several causes that are only jointly sufficient. PagerDuty sits between: "drill down to the underlying causes", avoid "human error".
- Playbooks. The workbook calls it contentious: short general entries that age slowly, or step-by-step lists that cut variation. It agrees a fixed list of commands should become automation.
- Should the IC also fix things? Google lets the IC hand off command and take the Ops Lead role or vice versa, and in small incidents one person holds all roles; PagerDuty's IC "is NOT a resolver" and shouldn't look at graphs.
- Roles differ by name: Google has IC, Ops Lead, Comms Lead, planning; PagerDuty has IC, Deputy, Scribe, SMEs, Customer and Internal Liaison.

**Couldn't open:**
- Etsy's "Blameless PostMortems and a Just Culture" (John Allspaw, codeascraft): etsy.com returns a bot check (403 to WebFetch, captcha page to curl); the Wayback Machine didn't answer from here. Not cited.
- Rob Ewaschuk's "My Philosophy on Alerting" (Google Doc): not tried; the SRE monitoring chapter contains its core.
- Atlassian incident management handbook: page came back as a 1.5 MB script bundle with no readable text.

**Rejected:**
- SRE book chapter 13 (Emergency Response): useful stories, but not needed for these three concepts.
- Allspaw's kitchensoap post: secondary to Cook.
- PagerDuty on-call and postmortem pages: primary and good, but the short nodes stay at the Google chapters plus one; listed above as further reading candidates.

**Gaps:**
- No source opened on the legal or compensation side of on-call beyond Google's (time off in lieu or capped cash).
- No measured data on whether blameless postmortems reduce repeat incidents; Google's claim ("fewer outages") is its own, not measured in a published study.
- No source for status pages or public incident communication beyond PagerDuty's short rules.

## Phase 14: Running it: containers, deploys, observability

Researched by 5 parallel passes, one per group below.

### Containers and orchestration

#### `linux-namespaces` (deep)

1. [namespaces(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/namespaces.7.html), Michael Kerrisk and man-pages contributors, man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: definition (wraps a global resource so members see their own instance); table of the eight types with flags; clone, unshare, setns; CAP_SYS_ADMIN needed except for user namespaces since Linux 3.8; /proc/pid/ns handles and the inode-equality test; handles for cgroup since 4.6 and time since 5.6; /proc/sys/user limits since 4.9; namespace lifetime and what pins it.
2. [pid_namespaces(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/pid_namespaces.7.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: PIDs start at 1; init adopts orphans; init's death SIGKILLs the namespace; init only receives signals it has handlers for (SIGKILL/SIGSTOP from ancestors forced); nesting limit 32 since 3.7; one PID per level; unshare(CLONE_NEWPID) moves children not the caller; remount /proc.
3. [network_namespaces(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/network_namespaces.7.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: what's isolated (devices, stacks, routes, firewall, ports, abstract Unix sockets); a physical device lives in one namespace; veth pairs; veths destroyed with the namespace.
4. [mount_namespaces(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/mount_namespaces.7.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: per-namespace mount list, new one is a copy, later changes don't cross; shared subtrees since 2.6.15 and propagation types.
5. [user_namespaces(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/user_namespaces.7.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: root inside, unprivileged outside; nesting limit 32 since 3.11; full capabilities in the new namespace only; capabilities only reach resources the namespace governs; module loading, clock, mknod need initial-namespace privilege; mountable filesystems per version (overlayfs since 5.11); uid_map ranges.
6. [pivot_root(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/pivot_root.2.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: swaps the root mount of the caller's mount namespace; restrictions (not MS_SHARED) so nothing propagates; container setup named as a modern use.
7. [Namespaces in operation, part 1](https://lwn.net/Articles/531114/), Michael Kerrisk, LWN, 2013. Blog by the man-pages maintainer, primary: yes. Seen: the six types that existed then, in order, with kernel versions (mount 2.4.19 in 2002, UTS/IPC 2.6.19, PID 2.6.24, net 2.6.24 to about 2.6.29, user 2.6.23 to 3.8); unprivileged user namespaces in 3.8; warning that user namespaces may hide security issues. Comments: Eric Biederman says namespaces and cgroups are orthogonal by design (comment, not cited).
8. [Network namespaces](https://lwn.net/Articles/580893/), Jake Edge, LWN, 2014. Blog, primary: no. Seen: `ip netns` walk-through; new namespace has only a down loopback; veth pair; bridge or NAT on the host to reach the internet; empty namespace as a sandbox.

#### `cgroups` (deep)

1. [Control Group v2](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html), Tejun Heo, Linux kernel docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: the whole reference. Single hierarchy; cgroup.procs, subtree_control; top-down and no-internal-process rules; weights, limits, protections, allocations; cpu.max default "max 100000", cpu.stat throttling fields; memory controller counts page cache, kernel structures, socket buffers; memory.high vs memory.max, memory.events, memory.oom.group; memory ownership (first toucher charged); io.max example; writeback per cgroup only on ext2/ext4/btrfs/f2fs/xfs; pids.max and fork bombs; "Issues with v1" rationale (multiple hierarchies, soft limit, why memory.high).
2. [cgroups(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/cgroups.7.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: first release 2.6.24; v2 work from 3.10, official in 4.5; per-controller arrival versions (memory 2.6.25, CPU bandwidth 3.2).
3. [Memory Controller](https://facebookmicrosites.github.io/cgroup2/docs/memory-controller.html), Meta cgroup2 docs. Docs from the team behind much of cgroup2 and PSI, primary: yes. Seen: memory.current includes page cache; fbtax2 case study: memory.high on system services caused thrashing, switched to memory.low for the workload; read memory.current under pressure because the kernel hoards memory when idle; memory.pressure.
4. [The container throttling problem](https://danluu.com/cgroup-throttling/), Dan Luu, David Mackey and others, 2019. Blog, excerpt of a Twitter internal doc, primary: yes. Seen: services failing at about 50% reserved CPU; quota limits average not instantaneous cores; thread pools bigger than the reservation; JVM GC threads; case study 20-core quota, 8 cores average, 100 ms period; 2x capacity after shrinking thread pools; list of candidate fixes (period tuning, pinning).
5. [About cgroup v2](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/cgroups/), Kubernetes docs, v1.36. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: kubelet and runtime enforce limits with cgroups; v2 stable since v1.25; Linux 5.8+; page cache writeback accounting; runtimes without v2 support read host memory (Node.js v20.3.0+ OK, Java versions listed); `stat -fc %T`; v1 deprecated in v1.35.
6. [PSI](https://docs.kernel.org/accounting/psi.html): already a note (`kernel-psi`). Per-cgroup pressure files. Linked through `use-method` instead of cited.

#### `overlayfs` (short)

1. [Overlay Filesystem](https://docs.kernel.org/filesystems/overlayfs.html), Linux kernel docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: upper/lower merge, directories merged; whiteouts (0/0 char device or xattr) and opaque directories; copy-up and parent creation; multiple lowers (leftmost on top), read-only without upperdir; sharing lowers; non-POSIX list (atime, MAP_SHARED, ETXTBSY); st_dev/st_ino instability, xino; changes to underlying layers undefined; copy-up fsync + rename; volatile mount.
2. [OverlayFS storage driver](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/overlayfs-driver/), Docker docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: lowerdir/upperdir/merged mapping for image and container layers; 128 lower layers in overlay2; whole-file copy-up, once per file; many layers slow lookups; shared page cache; volumes for write-heavy data; open(2) two-fds problem, rename(2) EXDEV.
3. [Linux 3.18](https://kernelnewbies.org/Linux_3.18), KernelNewbies. Release notes, primary: no. Seen: overlayfs merged in 3.18; live CDs as the first use; operations go straight to the underlying filesystem after open.

Extra: [Hybrid union filesystems](https://lwn.net/Articles/403012/), Jake Edge, LWN, 2010. Seen: the RFC patches that became overlayfs, the name change from "hybrid union" to overlayfs, whiteout/opaque xattrs, readdir caveats. Not used; history only.

#### `containers` (deep)

1. [namespaces(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/namespaces.7.html): see `linux-namespaces` #1.
2. [Control Group v2](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html): see `cgroups` #1.
3. [OCI Runtime Specification](https://github.com/opencontainers/runtime-spec), Open Container Initiative, main after v1.3.0. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: config-linux.md says the Linux container is built from namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, LSM and filesystem jails; namespace types and `path` to join; cgroupsPath. See `container-runtimes` #1.
4. [Storage drivers](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/), Docker docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: one layer per filesystem-changing instruction; thin writable container layer; deleted with the container; many containers share an image; shared layers not pulled twice; Docker Engine 29 uses the containerd image store by default.
5. [Setting the Record Straight: containers vs. Zones vs. Jails vs. VMs](https://blog.jessfraz.com/post/containers-zones-jails-vms/), Jessie Frazelle, 2017. Blog, primary: yes (container tooling and security author). Seen: a container is a term for namespaces plus cgroups, not a first-class object; Zones, Jails and VMs are; sharing namespaces (wireshark, strace from another container); complexity leads to escapes.
6. [CVE-2019-5736: runc container breakout](https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2019/02/11/2), Aleksa Sarai, oss-security, 2019. Maintainer disclosure, primary: yes. Seen: container root overwrites the host runc binary; triggers (attacker image, exec into attacker-writable container); not blocked by default AppArmor; blocked by user namespaces without host root mapped; CVSS 7.2.
7. [capabilities(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: root bypasses checks; split into capabilities since 2.2; per-thread; CAP_SYS_ADMIN overloaded, CAP_BPF/CAP_PERFMON/CAP_CHECKPOINT_RESTORE split out.
8. [seccomp(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/seccomp.2.html), man-pages 6.19. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: strict mode; filter mode with a BPF program; needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN or no_new_privs.
9. [Firecracker](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi20-paper-agache.pdf): already a note (`agache-firecracker-2020`, from the `virtual-machines` group). Used for the VM side: own virtual hardware, page tables and kernel; shared-kernel trade-off; seccomp-bpf as the main container boundary; Lambda's containers-inside-VMs.

#### `container-images` (short)

1. [OCI Image Format Specification](https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec), Open Container Initiative, main after v1.1.1. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: spec.md (manifest, index, layers, config; verified by hash, unpacked into a runtime bundle); manifest.md (content addressing, one platform, schemaVersion 2 for Docker compat, layer order and media types, zstd SHOULD); image-index.md; descriptor.md (media type, digest, size; digest grammar; verify from untrusted sources); layer.md (tar changesets, `.wh.` whiteouts, opaque whiteouts, applying vs extracting); config.md (no settings in layers, DiffID vs layer digest, ChainID).
2. [OCI Distribution Specification](https://github.com/opencontainers/distribution-spec/blob/main/spec.md), Open Container Initiative, main after v1.1.1. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: based on Docker Registry HTTP API V2; tag as movable pointer; pull manifest then blobs, endpoints; client digest verification; Docker-Content-Digest header; push blobs first, manifest last; layer upload de-duplication; tag length 128.
3. [Storage drivers](https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/): see `containers` #4 (deleting in a later layer doesn't shrink the image).

#### `container-runtimes` (short)

1. [OCI Runtime Specification](https://github.com/opencontainers/runtime-spec), Open Container Initiative, main after v1.3.0. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: spec.md (scope, platforms); bundle.md (config.json plus rootfs); runtime.md (state JSON, statuses, 13-step lifecycle with hooks, create without running the program, delete undoes create, operations not a CLI); config-linux.md (namespaces, join by path, inherit if absent, cgroupsPath).
2. [Runtime v2](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/main/docs/runtime-v2.md), containerd maintainers. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: containerd doesn't launch containers; snapshotter lays out layers; shim listens on a socket with ttRPC; shim+engine pattern; containerd-shim-runc-v2 invokes runc; one shim can serve many containers.
3. [crun README](https://github.com/containers/crun), Giuseppe Scrivano and contributors. Code docs, primary: yes. Seen: C runtime; runc re-execs itself with a C module; author's 100 × /bin/true timing (1.69 s vs 3.34 s); runs with a 512k memory limit where runc failed at 4M.
4. [Container Runtime Interface (CRI)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/cri/), Kubernetes docs, v1.36. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: plugin interface, gRPC, kubelet as client; stable since v1.23; v1 API required since v1.26; alpha list streaming in v1.36.
5. [Container Runtimes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/production-environment/container-runtimes/), Kubernetes docs, v1.36. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: dockershim removed in 1.24; containerd and CRI-O; cgroup drivers must match; systemd driver with systemd and with cgroup v2.

Extra: [runc README](https://github.com/opencontainers/runc), runc maintainers. Seen: "CLI tool for spawning and running containers on Linux according to the OCI specification"; not meant for end users; `runc spec`, `runc run`, default config with a short capability list. Not used (the OCI spec and crun README cover it). [containerd README](https://github.com/containerd/containerd). Seen: daemon for the full lifecycle, designed to be embedded, overlay snapshotter default, any OCI Distribution registry. Not used; runtime-v2.md covers the part the article needs.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- **CPU limits or not.** The kernel docs present `cpu.max` as the bandwidth limit; Twitter's write-up shows quotas throttling bursty services at about half their reservation and costing latency. Both agree on the mechanism; the disagreement is whether to set quotas at all or rely on weights, and it isn't settled in any source opened.
- **memory.high vs memory.max.** The kernel docs call memory.high the main control and memory.max the backstop; Meta's own production attempt at memory.high on system services made them thrash, and they switched to memory.low protections for the main workload.
- **Are containers a security boundary?** Frazelle: complexity from composing primitives causes escapes; the Firecracker paper: shared kernel means a security vs compatibility trade-off, seccomp-bpf is the main boundary; CVE-2019-5736 shows a real escape blocked only by user namespaces. Kerrisk's 2013 article also warned that user namespaces themselves may hide security bugs, so user namespaces both help and widen the kernel surface.
- **runc vs crun.** crun's README claims about 2x faster sequential starts; that's the author's single machine with no versions. The lab's runtime comparison is meant to settle it on this machine.

**Couldn't open:**

- Nothing failed. The first batch of fetches (docs.kernel.org overlayfs, LWN 531114, pivot_root) came back empty once and loaded on retry.

**Rejected:**

- LWN "hybrid union filesystem" (2010): history only.
- runc README and containerd README: read, but the OCI runtime spec and containerd's runtime-v2 doc carry the same claims with more precision.
- unshare(2) and setns(2) man pages: opened; namespaces(7) and pid_namespaces(7) say what's needed.

**Gaps:**

- No source opened on the time namespace or cgroup namespace beyond the namespaces(7) table; the article only names them.
- No source opened with numbers on container start time or overhead versus VMs other than crun's README and Firecracker's (from the other group). The lab comparison is the real gap.
- Rootless containers (unprivileged overlay, slirp-style networking) aren't covered by any opened source beyond the 5.11 overlayfs line in user_namespaces(7).
- No source opened on Docker/OCI media-type compatibility (the image spec's media-types.md matrix); the article avoids claiming anything about it.
- Seccomp default profiles (which syscalls Docker blocks) not opened.

### Containers and orchestration

#### `virtual-machines` (short)

1. [Firecracker: Lightweight Virtualization for Serverless Applications](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi20-paper-agache.pdf), Agache, Brooker, Florescu, Iordache, Liguori, Neugebauer, Piwonka, Popa (AWS), NSDI 2020. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: abstract (VMs secure but heavy vs containers light but weaker); 1 intro (containers share one kernel, security vs compatibility; keep KVM, replace QEMU; < 5 MB overhead, < 125 ms boot, up to 150 microVMs/s per host with a minimal guest kernel; QEMU > 1.4M LOC as of 4.2); 1.1 what it leaves out (no BIOS, PCI, legacy devices, migration; replaces QEMU, not Docker or Kubernetes); 2 Lambda's first design (containers per function, VMs per customer); 2.1 figure 1 container vs KVM model; 2.1.1 seccomp-bpf the main container boundary; 2.1.3 hardware virtualization (own page tables and kernel), startup in seconds, type 1 vs type 2, ~50k lines of Rust, security boundary moves to hardware plus small VMM; 3 one process per microVM, relies on Linux scheduler, memory manager, TUN/TAP, ps/top/kill work; 3.1 virtio net and block, serial, partial i8042; 3.2 REST API over a Unix socket, kill the process to stop; 3.3 token-bucket rate limiters; 3.4 side-channel mitigations (SMT off etc.); 3.4.1 jailer (chroot, pid and net namespaces, seccomp); 4.1 Lambda slots, one function per slot, hundreds or thousands of microVMs per worker.
2. [The Definitive KVM API Documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/virt/kvm/api.html), Linux kernel documentation. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: 1 general description (/dev/kvm, KVM_CREATE_VM, vCPU fds, VM ioctls from the creating process, vCPU ioctls from the creating thread); 4.10 KVM_RUN runs a guest vCPU; 5 kvm_run exits KVM_EXIT_IO and KVM_EXIT_MMIO hand I/O to user space.

Extra: [Firecracker design doc](https://github.com/firecracker-microvm/firecracker/blob/main/docs/design.md), Firecracker maintainers. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: API, VMM and one vCPU thread per guest core running KVM_RUN; network backed by TAP, block by host files; jailer required in production; 5 microVMs per host core per second mutation rate. Not given a note; the paper and KVM docs covered the short node.

#### `control-loops` (short)

1. [Controllers](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/controller/), Kubernetes documentation, Kubernetes 1.37. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: thermostat example; controllers watch and make or request changes; spec is desired state; most controllers act through the API server (Job controller creates Pods, doesn't run them); direct control of outside systems then report back; cluster may never be stable; many simple controllers; labels keep controllers apart; built-ins run in kube-controller-manager.
2. [Writing Controllers](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-api-machinery/controllers.md), Kubernetes SIG API Machinery. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: the three-line loop, watches are optimizations; one item at a time via work queue; no ordering between watches; level driven not edge driven (shell-script analogy); shared informers; don't mutate cached objects; wait for cache sync; other actors; leader election still imperfect; requeue with backoff; periodic resync; ObservedGeneration; owner references.
3. [API Conventions](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md), Kubernetes SIG Architecture. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: spec and status, separate authorization for each; system drives to the latest spec, 2 to 5 to 3 need not touch 5, level-based not edge-based; spec fields declarative; conditions are observations, open world.

#### `kubernetes` (deep)

1. [Borg, Omega, and Kubernetes](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//pubs/archive/44843.pdf), Burns, Grant, Oppenheimer, Brewer, Wilkes (Google), ACM Queue 2016. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: Borg monolithic master, Omega shared Paxos store with optimistic concurrency, Kubernetes shared store behind a REST API server; container isolation imperfect (L3 cache, memory bandwidth), needs an extra layer like VMs against malicious tenants; application-oriented infrastructure; alloc vs pod; metadata/spec/status; replication controller vs autoscaler decoupling; reconciliation loops, choreography; IP per pod instead of Borg's port allocation; labels and selectors, quarantine a pod by removing a label; ownership conflicts; configuration and dependency management as open problems.
2. [Kubernetes Components](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/components/), Kubernetes documentation, Kubernetes 1.37. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: control plane (kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, optional cloud-controller-manager); node (kubelet, optional kube-proxy, container runtime); addons (DNS, dashboard, monitoring, logging).
3. [Kubernetes API Concepts](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/), Kubernetes documentation, Kubernetes 1.37. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: resourceVersion, list then watch, 5 minutes of history with etcd 3, 410 Gone and re-list, Reflector; bookmarks; streaming lists (large lists cost control-plane RAM); alpha sharded list and watch in 1.37; 409 Conflict on stale resourceVersion, clients retry; server-side apply.
4. [Pods](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/), Kubernetes documentation, Kubernetes 1.37. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: smallest deployable unit; shared namespaces, cgroups, volumes; one container per pod is common; use workload resources; pods disposable, not a process; node failure means a replacement pod; template changes replace pods; pod networking (one IP, localhost); requests for scheduling, limits enforced by throttling and OOM kills; CPU limits can throttle with spare CPU; static pods; sidecars.
5. [Kubernetes Scheduler](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/kube-scheduler/), Kubernetes documentation, Kubernetes 1.37. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: watches unassigned pods; filter then score, random tie-break, unschedulable pods wait; binding; policies vs profiles and plugins.
6. [Pod Lifecycle](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/), Kubernetes documentation. Note already existed; re-opened. Seen: scheduled once, never rescheduled, replaced with a new UID; CrashLoopBackOff; restart backoff 10 s doubling to 300 s, reset after 10 minutes; termination flow (SIGTERM and endpoint removal together, 30 s grace, SIGKILL).
7. [Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes/), Kubernetes documentation. Note already existed; re-opened, quotes still match.
8. [etcd versus other key-value stores](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/learning/why/), etcd v3.6. Note already existed; re-opened, the quotes used (no sharding, several gigabytes, API server persists state into etcd) still match. The page itself never says Raft.

Extra: [Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/), Kubernetes documentation, Kubernetes 1.37. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Deployment creates a ReplicaSet per template, rolling update scales new up and old down, pod-template-hash label, defaults 25% max unavailable and 25% max surge. Not given a note; belongs to `deployment-strategies`.
Extra: [Kubernetes overview](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/), Kubernetes documentation. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: open-sourced 2014; "not a mere orchestration system", independent control processes; history of deployment eras. Not used.
Extra: [Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//pubs/archive/43438.pdf), Verma et al., EuroSys 2015. Paper, primary: yes. Downloaded, not read closely. Not used.

#### `kubernetes-networking` (short)

1. [Services, Load Balancing, and Networking](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/), Kubernetes documentation, Kubernetes 1.37. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: the network model (IP per pod, shared netns, pod to pod without proxies or NAT, node agents reach pods); Service API and EndpointSlices; service proxy programs the data plane; Gateway API and Ingress; NetworkPolicy; old systems mapped container ports to host ports; which parts are CNI plugins, kube-proxy or others; NetworkPolicy has no effect without plugin support.
