3. [DNS for Services and Pods](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/dns-pod-service/), Kubernetes documentation, Kubernetes 1.37. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: kubelet writes pod resolv.conf; search list with namespace, svc, cluster domain; ndots:5; A/AAAA for normal (cluster IP) and headless (pod IPs); SRV for named ports; pod A records.
4. [resolv.conf(5)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/resolv.conf.5.html), man-pages. Note already existed; appended ndots. Seen: ndots threshold, default 1, capped at 15; search list tries.
5. [gRPC Load Balancing on Kubernetes without Tears](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2018/11/07/grpc-load-balancing-on-kubernetes-without-tears/), William Morgan, 2018. Note already existed; re-opened, quotes still match. Used for "connection-level balancing pins gRPC to one pod".

Extra: [Cluster Networking](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/networking/), Kubernetes documentation. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: four networking problems; why not dynamic ports; non-overlapping ranges for pods, services, nodes; IPv4, IPv6, dual-stack; CNI plugins implement the model. Not given a note; the Services overview page says the same more directly.
Extra: [Service](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/), Kubernetes documentation. Note `kubernetes-service` already existed; re-opened, quotes still match. Not cited here (the overview page covered EndpointSlices).

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Kubernetes calls itself not an orchestration system (overview page: control processes, not a workflow), while the same docs and the whole industry call it an orchestrator. The Burns et al. paper frames it as choreography vs central orchestration. The control-loops article uses the choreography framing without the naming fight.
- CPU limits: the Pods page itself says they prevent noisy neighbours but can throttle with spare CPU, and leaves the choice to you. The `cgroups` node covers the mechanism.
- DNS vs virtual IPs for Services: Kubernetes proxies by default because clients mishandle TTLs, but offers headless Services for clients that want pod IPs (gRPC). Both covered.
- Containers vs VMs as a security boundary: Burns et al. and the Firecracker paper agree containers need an extra layer for hostile tenants; Firecracker still wraps its VMM in container tools (jailer), so it's layering, not a choice.

**Couldn't open:**

- [Borg, Omega, and Kubernetes on queue.acm.org](https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=2898444): behind a Cloudflare check. Used Google Research's PDF of the same article instead.

**Rejected:**

- Kubernetes overview page: marketing-level, and its history section adds nothing the Burns et al. paper doesn't say better.
- Firecracker README: the design doc and paper say the same with more detail.

**Gaps:**

- No source opened says how fast endpoint removal reaches kube-proxy on other nodes after a pod is deleted, so the shutdown race is described without a number.
- The Firecracker numbers (125 ms boot, 5 MB, 150 per second) are from the 2020 paper; no newer measurement opened.
- No source opened on gVisor or Kata Containers; the VM node mentions only KVM and Firecracker.
- No source opened on CoreDNS itself; cluster DNS is described from the Kubernetes docs only.

### Observability

#### `observability` (deep)

1. [Monitoring Distributed Systems (SRE book, chapter 6)](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/), Rob Ewaschuk, Google SRE book. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: definitions (monitoring, white-box, black-box, dashboard, alert, root cause); why monitor (trends, comparisons, alerting, dashboards, ad hoc debugging); "what's broken, and why?" symptoms vs causes with table 6-1; black-box is symptom-oriented, white-box catches imminent problems and failures masked by retries; one person's symptom is another's cause; the four golden signals; tail latency and bucketed histograms; resolution of measurements; Google avoids "magic" systems that learn thresholds. Note already exists (`google-sre-monitoring`).
2. [Metrics, tracing, and logging](https://peter.bourgon.org/blog/2017/02/21/metrics-tracing-and-logging.html), Peter Bourgon, 2017. Blog, primary: yes (his own framing, written at the Distributed Tracing Summit). Seen: Venn diagram; metrics defined by being aggregatable (gauge last-writer-wins, counter by addition, histogram by buckets); logs defined by discrete events; tracing defined by request scope; not all instrumentation is request-scoped; volume gradient: metrics cheapest, logs heaviest, tracing in the middle; logs can surpass the traffic they report on.
3. [Observability primer](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/observability-primer/), OpenTelemetry docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: observability as asking questions from outside about "unknown unknowns"; "properly instrumented" means no new instrumentation needed to debug; telemetry = traces, metrics, logs; metrics are aggregations over time; SLI/SLO in one paragraph each; logs lack context unless tied to a span; span attributes table (HTTP semantic conventions); trace = tree of spans with a root span; waterfall view.
4. [It's Time to Version Observability: Introducing Observability 2.0](https://www.honeycomb.io/blog/time-to-version-observability-signs-point-to-yes), Charity Majors, Honeycomb, 2024. Blog, primary: yes (from the company that pushed the term into software). Seen: Honeycomb borrowed "observability" from control theory in 2016; "three pillars" called observability 1.0, wide structured events as one source of truth called 2.0; aggregation at write time vs read time; metrics discard context and can't take high cardinality; cost grows with cardinality for metrics tools; head or tail sampling as the cost lever for events; strong vendor stance, so treat as one side of a debate.
5. [Context propagation](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/context-propagation/), OpenTelemetry docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: context lets traces, metrics and logs be correlated; default propagator is W3C traceparent; SDKs inject trace and span IDs into log records; metrics can be aggregated by caller path; security: forged incoming context, leaking IDs outward; baggage and PII. Also used for `distributed-tracing`.
6. [Canonical log lines](https://stripe.com/blog/canonical-log-lines), Brandur Leach, Stripe, 2019. See `structured-logging` #2. Useful here for why logs answer questions nobody planned for, where metrics dashboards can't.

#### `structured-logging` (short)

1. [Structured Logging with slog](https://go.dev/blog/slog), Jonathan Amsterdam, Go blog, 2023. Blog by the Go team, primary: yes. Seen: log/slog in Go 1.21; key-value pairs so logs can be parsed, filtered, searched; text and JSON handlers with example output; levels are integers; LogAttrs to cut allocations; Logger.With pre-formats common attributes; a context argument lets handlers pull trace IDs; LogValuer for redaction; over 95% of calls pass five or fewer attributes; frontend Logger vs backend Handler.
2. [Canonical log lines](https://stripe.com/blog/canonical-log-lines), Brandur Leach, Stripe, 2019. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: plain vs key=value lines for one payments request; "structured" is ambiguous (JSON or logfmt); logs flexible where metrics dashboards are designed in advance; information spread across lines is slow to query; one wide line per request at the end; emitted in an ensure block, never fails the request; stable field names codified in a protocol buffer; shipped to Kafka, S3, Redshift for analytics.

Extra: [XI. Logs (The Twelve-Factor App)](https://12factor.net/logs), Adam Wiggins. Opened: logs as an event stream written unbuffered to stdout, routing left to the environment. Not given a note; a short node doesn't need it.

#### `metrics` (deep)

1. [Metric types](https://prometheus.io/docs/concepts/metric_types/), Prometheus docs (3.15). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: counter, gauge, histogram, summary; server flattens all but native histograms into untyped float series; counter only goes up or resets on restart; never a counter for something that decreases; classic histogram as _bucket{le}, _sum, _count series, cumulative buckets; native histograms atomic and always mergeable; summary quantiles over a sliding window.
2. [Data model](https://prometheus.io/docs/concepts/data_model/), Prometheus docs (3.15). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: time series identified by metric name and labels; any label change creates a new series; sample = float64 or native histogram + millisecond timestamp; notation `name{label="value"}`; UTF-8 names since v3.0.0.
3. [Instrumentation](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/), Prometheus docs (3.15). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: instrument everything; online-serving, offline-processing, batch job metrics; a counter for every log line; failures plus total attempts; thread pool and cache metrics; one metric with labels rather than many names; cardinality guidance (below 10, investigate above 100, node_exporter example); if it can go down it's a gauge; never rate() a gauge; export timestamps not "time since"; a Java counter increment 12-17 ns; export 0 for series that may exist.
4. [Pull doesn't scale - or does it?](https://prometheus.io/blog/2016/07/23/pull-does-not-scale-or-does-it/), Julius Volz, Prometheus blog, 2016. Blog by a Prometheus co-founder, primary: yes. Seen: who opens the connection doesn't matter for scale; 800,000 samples/s record at SoundCloud; 10 s interval, 700 series per host, over 10,000 machines per server; pull fails loudly; Prometheus isn't event-based, it samples current state every 15 or 30 s; monitoring must know the desired targets anyway; pull lets you run a copy on a laptop and run two servers for HA; push makes rogue jobs more likely to flood; Borgmon; pull is hard across firewalls.
5. [When to use the Pushgateway](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/pushing/), Prometheus docs (3.15). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: only for service-level batch jobs; single point of failure; loses the `up` metric; never forgets pushed series; for firewalls move Prometheus or use PushProx; node exporter textfile collector for machine-level batch jobs.
6. [Metrics data model](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/metrics/data-model/), OpenTelemetry specification 1.61.0. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: temporal and spatial reaggregation; delta vs cumulative temporality with time ranges; cumulative needs sender memory proportional to cardinality, deltas push that cost out of the process; Prometheus cumulative, StatsD delta; StartTimeUnixNano for resets; exemplars link a metric point to a trace.
7. [Histograms and summaries](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/histograms/). Note exists (`prometheus-histograms`); the `histograms` node covers it, so `metrics` links there instead of citing it.

Extra: [Overview](https://prometheus.io/docs/introduction/overview/) and [FAQ](https://prometheus.io/docs/introduction/faq/), Prometheus docs. Opened: pull over HTTP, push via a gateway, not for 100% accurate per-request billing, "pulling is slightly better than pushing" but not a major point, don't feed logs into Prometheus. Not given notes; the blog post and the Pushgateway page carry the argument.

#### `cardinality` (short)

1. [Instrumentation](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/instrumentation/). See metrics #3. The "Do not overuse labels" section: every labelset is a series with RAM, CPU, disk and network cost; keep cardinality below 10; investigate above 100; node_filesystem_avail: 10,000 nodes gives about 100,000 series, adding per-user quota for 10,000 users gives double-digit millions; start with no labels.
2. [Metric and label naming](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/naming/), Prometheus docs (3.15). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: base units, unit suffix, _total; sum or avg over all labels should be meaningful; caution box: each unique label combination is a new series, never user IDs, emails or unbounded values in labels.

#### `distributed-tracing` (deep)

1. [Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure](https://research.google/pubs/dapper-a-large-scale-distributed-systems-tracing-infrastructure/), Sigelman et al., Google Technical Report dapper-2010-1, 2010. Paper, primary: yes. Seen (PDF): the universal search example; ubiquity, always on; low overhead and application transparency; instrumentation only in threading, callback and RPC libraries; trace tree, spans, span id, parent id, trace id, 64-bit ids; client and server annotations in one span, clock skew bounded by send/receive order; annotations and a per-span volume cap; out-of-band collection via local logs, median under 15 s; 426 bytes per span; root span 204 ns, non-root 176 ns; table 2 latency cost by sampling rate; 1/1024 uniform sampling, adaptive sampling by target rate; second sampling at collection by hashing trace id; limitations: coalescing/batching, batch workloads, queueing root causes, kernel events.
2. [Trace Context](https://www.w3.org/TR/trace-context/), W3C Recommendation (Level 1), 2021 (editorial update of the 2020 Recommendation). Spec, primary: yes. Seen: problem of vendor-specific propagation; traceparent (version, 16-byte trace-id, 8-byte parent-id, flags) and tracestate; all-zero ids invalid; sampled flag is a recommendation; forwarding vs participating; processing model: no traceparent -> new trace, invalid -> restart; privacy: no PII in headers, may restart at trust boundaries; DoS from blindly honouring sampled; randomness of trace-id lets vendors sample on it. Level 2 (Candidate Recommendation Draft, 2024) opened: adds the random-trace-id flag (right-most 7 bytes random).
3. [Traces](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/traces/), OpenTelemetry docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: spans with trace_id, span_id, parent_id; root span has no parent; span contents (name, parent, timestamps, span context, attributes, events, links, status); span context is what gets propagated; add attributes at creation so samplers can see them; span events vs attributes; links for async work; status Unset/Error/Ok; span kinds client, server, internal, producer, consumer.
4. [Context propagation](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/context-propagation/). See observability #5. Inject into a carrier on send, extract on receive; default W3C propagator; security of incoming and outgoing context.

#### `trace-sampling` (short)

1. [Sampling](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/sampling/), OpenTelemetry docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: sampled vs not sampled terminology; representativeness; 1% often enough at high volume; when to sample (1000+ traces/s) and when not; three costs of sampling; head sampling, consistent probability on trace ID; can't guarantee error traces; tail sampling rules (errors, latency, attributes); tail sampler is stateful, can need dozens or hundreds of nodes, may fall back; head then tail in a pipeline.
2. [Tail Sampling Processor README](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-contrib/blob/main/processor/tailsamplingprocessor/README.md), OpenTelemetry Collector contrib (main branch; latest release v0.162.0 when read). Code docs, primary: yes. Seen: beta for traces; all spans of a trace must reach the same collector; keeps spans in memory; decision_wait default 30 s, num_traces default 50000; policies (latency, status code, probabilistic, rate limiting); two layers with the load-balancing exporter; circular buffer drops traces before decision; late spans need decision caches.

Also used for context: Dapper (distributed-tracing #1) sections 4.4 to 4.6 on uniform, adaptive and collection-time sampling; W3C Trace Context (distributed-tracing #2) on the sampled flag. Cited in `distributed-tracing`, not here.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Three pillars vs wide events. Bourgon (2017) draws metrics, logs and traces as overlapping circles with different costs; Majors (2024) argues storing them separately is the problem and wide structured events should be the single source of truth, with metrics demoted to cheap summaries. Majors writes as a vendor. The articles present both designs and what each costs.
- Majors attributes the "three pillars" phrase to a Bourgon post from 2018. The Bourgon post opened here is from 2017 and doesn't use the phrase. Left out of the articles.
- Pull vs push. The Prometheus blog argues pull scales fine and push is more likely to let rogue jobs flood the server; the FAQ softens it ("slightly better", not a major point). OpenTelemetry pushes OTLP from SDKs by design. Presented as a trade-off.
- Cumulative vs delta temporality: Prometheus is cumulative (simple, survives dropped scrapes, sender memory grows with cardinality); StatsD and OTel delta push that cost out of the process. Spec states both sides.
- Head vs tail sampling: OpenTelemetry says large systems almost always need tail sampling, and lists its operational costs in the same page. Dapper found 1/1024 head sampling adequate for high-volume services. Both are in the sampling node.
- Prometheus names carry unit and type suffixes; OpenTelemetry conventions don't. The naming page argues for suffixes. Not expanded.

**Couldn't open:**

- Nothing needed failed to open. Ben Sigelman's piece on metrics, logs and traces being "just telemetry" (linked from Majors) wasn't looked for; the argument is carried by Majors.

**Rejected:**

- Brandur's own copy of the canonical log lines post (brandur.org): same text as the Stripe post; the Stripe one is cited.
- Prometheus overview and FAQ: opened, facts overlap the blog and Pushgateway page.
- Twelve-Factor logs: opened; nothing a short node needs beyond slog and Stripe.

**Gaps:**

- No measured cost numbers for log volume vs metrics; Bourgon's gradient is qualitative, so the article says "more" and "less" without numbers.
- No source gives per-series memory cost in Prometheus; the cardinality node uses the docs' series counts only.
- Dapper's overhead numbers are from a 2.2 GHz x86 server in 2010; nothing newer with numbers for OTel SDK span cost was opened.
- No primary source on log sampling or log level dynamics; left out.

### Observability

#### `opentelemetry` (short)

1. [What is OpenTelemetry?](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/what-is-opentelemetry/), OpenTelemetry authors, CNCF. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: framework for generating, exporting and collecting traces, metrics, logs; vendor-neutral, works with Jaeger, Prometheus and commercial backends; "not an observability backend itself", storage and UI left to other tools; two principles (own your data, one set of APIs and conventions); component list (spec, OTLP, semantic conventions, APIs, SDKs, instrumentation libraries, auto-instrumentation, Collector, Operator); extensibility (receivers, exporters, custom propagators); history: merger of OpenTracing and OpenCensus.
2. [Overview (OpenTelemetry specification)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/overview/), OpenTelemetry authors, spec 1.61.0. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: signals share context propagation; cross-cutting concern; four package types (API, SDK, semantic conventions, contrib); instrumentation MUST NOT reference the SDK; trace as DAG of spans, span fields, SpanContext (16-byte TraceId, 8-byte SpanId, TraceFlags sampling bit, tracestate); links for batch and scatter/gather; metrics: Meter, Instrument, Measurement, counters/gauges/histograms, sync vs async instruments, views; log data model; baggage; resources (Kubernetes cluster, namespace, pod, container); TextMapPropagator; Collector agent vs standalone, enrich/transform/scrub PII, smart sampling; instrumentation library naming.
3. [OTLP Specification](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otlp/), OpenTelemetry authors, OTLP 1.11.0. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: stable for traces, metrics, logs; development for profiles; Protobuf over gRPC (port 4317) or HTTP (4318, /v1/traces etc., binary or JSON); gzip required; size limits (4 MiB typical gRPC default, 64 MiB recommended); throughput formula with 200 spans/s example; concurrent requests; full success, partial success (never retried), retryable vs non-retryable (gRPC code table; HTTP 429/502/503/504 only); throttling via UNAVAILABLE + RetryInfo or 429/503 + Retry-After; exponential backoff with jitter; per-hop acknowledgement only, no end-to-end guarantee; duplicates accepted as the right tradeoff; no explicit version numbers.
4. [Collector](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/), OpenTelemetry authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: vendor-agnostic receive/process/export; accepts Jaeger, Prometheus, Fluent Bit formats; direct export fine to start; recommended to run a collector alongside the service for retries, batching, encryption, sensitive-data filtering; default OTLP exporters assume a local collector; status "mixed"; components: receivers, processors, exporters, connectors, extensions.

Extra: [Status](https://opentelemetry.io/status/), OpenTelemetry authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: per-language maturity table (e.g. Go traces and metrics stable, logs release candidate; Java profiles in development; Rust beta); Collector and Operator "mixed". Not given a note; would support a sentence on per-language maturity if the node grows.

#### `continuous-profiling` (short)

1. [Google-Wide Profiling: A Continuous Profiling Infrastructure for Data Centers](https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/36575.pdf), Ren, Tune, Moseley, Shi, Rus, Hundt, Google, IEEE Micro 2010. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: owners won't tolerate more than a few percent latency degradation; two-dimensional sampling (random subset of machines, event sampling per machine); per-machine rates capped at "less than a few percent"; aggregate overhead "less than 0.01 percent"; no full stacks for machine-wide profiles; per-process profiles via a common library with an HTTP server; binaries deployed stripped, unstripped copies kept in a repository, MapReduce symbolization; JIT code can't be symbolized offline; profiles tagged with job/machine/datacenter; OLAP profile database, query and call-graph views; entropy-based stability analysis; zlib nearly 5% of fleet CPU cycles; "dollar amount per performance change"; platform affinity scheduling (10-15% potential); comparing profiles across versions; FDO from live profiles. (First download was truncated; re-downloaded in full.)
2. [Parca overview](https://www.parca.dev/docs/overview), Parca authors (Polar Signals). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: definition; sampling because it can always be on; stacks plus values; sampling misses parts, continuous collection makes it significant; three uses (saving money, differences over time/process/version, incidents after the fact); labelled series, label-selector queries; push from agent or pull over HTTP, "Go has popularized" HTTP profile endpoints; Parca Agent is eBPF whole-system; icicle graphs.
3. [What is continuous profiling? (Grafana Pyroscope)](https://grafana.com/docs/pyroscope/latest/introduction/continuous-profiling/), Grafana Labs. Docs (vendor), primary: yes for its own product. Seen: on-demand vs continuous; stores sampled profiles in a database; overhead "~2-5% depending on a few factors"; marketing-heavy benefits list (MTTR, cost).
4. [OpenTelemetry Profiles Enters Public Alpha](https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2026/profiles-alpha/), OpenTelemetry Profiling SIG (Alexandrov, Anjo, Geisendörfer, Kalkanis, Lehner, Mathieu), 2026. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: no common protocol before, despite pprof and JFR; deduplicated stacks, dictionary tables, timestamped events for off-CPU; trace_id/span_id on samples; lossless pprof round trip; Elastic's eBPF agent as a Collector receiver, Collector v0.148.0+; Go on-target symbolization; not for critical production; no production backends yet; symbolization API still being standardized.

Extra: [OpenTelemetry announces support for profiling](https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2024/profiling/), Austin Parker, 2024. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: profiling SIG, data model OTEP merged, Elastic eBPF agent and Splunk .NET profiler donations pledged; superseded by the 2026 alpha post, not given a note.
Extra: [Profile-guided optimization](https://go.dev/doc/pgo), the Go team. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: PGO since Go 1.20; uses CPU pprof profiles; production profiles recommended; 2-14% gains as of Go 1.22; default.pgo. Not given a note; a natural link if a PGO or build-optimization node ever exists.
Reused: [Diagnostics](https://go.dev/doc/diagnostics) (note `go-diagnostics` exists): profiling production is safe but costs; profile a random replica; one profile at a time. Not cited in the article to keep it at 4 sources; the phase 9 `profiling` node already covers it.

#### `alerting` (deep)

1. [Alerting on SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/), Steven Thurgood and others, Google SRE Workbook, 2018. Book chapter (free online), primary: yes. Seen: precision, recall, detection time, reset time; six strategies with Prometheus rules and pros/cons tables (10-minute window: 0.6 s detection, 144 alerts/day; 36-hour window: 36 h reset; `for` duration: 140% budget before paging, spikes never fire; burn rate 36: 58 min reset, burn 35 never fires; multiple burn rates; multiwindow with 1/12 short window); Table 5-8 parameters; low-traffic services (10 req/h example, synthetic traffic, combining services, client retries, lower SLO); extreme targets (90% never fires, 99.999% in 26 s); alerting at scale with request-class buckets. Note already existed; appended.
2. [Monitoring Distributed Systems](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/), Rob Ewaschuk, Google SRE book, 2016. Book chapter, primary: yes. Seen: definitions of alert/ticket/email/page; noise makes people ignore pages; avoid "magic" threshold-learning systems; symptoms vs causes table; black-box vs white-box; four golden signals; questions for every paging rule; every page actionable, needs intelligence, novel; remove rarely used config; Bigtable over-alerting and Gmail rote-response case studies; email alerts of limited value. Note already existed; appended.
3. [My Philosophy on Alerting](https://docs.google.com/document/d/199PqyG3UsyXlwieHaqbGiWVa8eMWi8zzAn0YfcApr8Q/edit), Rob Ewaschuk. Essay (Google Doc, opened via its plain-text export), primary: yes. Seen: urgent/important/actionable/real; over-monitoring harder than under-monitoring; what users care about; why cause alerts are bad and when they're needed; alerting from the client/load balancer; "also firing" cause summary in pages; tickets, reports and email; short playbooks; alerts under 50% accurate are broken; quota example with page vs ticket thresholds.
4. [Alerting (Prometheus best practices)](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/alerting/), Prometheus authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: summary of Ewaschuk; as few alerts as possible; slack for blips; page on latency at one point; low-traffic request types drowned out; offline processing, batch jobs (2 full runs, 10 h example), capacity, metamonitoring with end-to-end black-box test.
5. [Alerting rules](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/configuration/alerting_rules/), Prometheus authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: rule syntax; `for` and pending state; `keep_firing_for` against flapping; labels and annotations (runbook links); templating; ALERTS series; Prometheus isn't a notification system, Alertmanager is.
6. [Alertmanager](https://prometheus.io/docs/alerting/latest/alertmanager/), Prometheus authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: dedupe, grouping (partition example), inhibition, silences, HA (don't load-balance to Alertmanagers), per-alertname limits.

Extra: [Practical Alerting](https://sre.google/sre-book/practical-alerting/), Google SRE book chapter 10. Downloaded, skimmed the headings only (Borgmon history). Not used; the monitoring chapter and workbook cover the ideas.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Duration clauses: the SLO workbook says not to use `for` in SLO alerts (poor recall, resets on dips), with a footnote allowing it for very short noise; Prometheus's docs use `for` in every example, advise "slack" for blips, and added `keep_firing_for` against flapping. The article presents the multiwindow short window as doing the job a duration tries to do.
- Cause-based alerts: the SRE chapter and Ewaschuk say avoid them, but both carve out imminent resource exhaustion (disk, quota, N+0). The article keeps both halves.
- "Smart" anomaly detection vs simple rules: Google's chapter avoids threshold-learning systems; vendor tools sell them. Nothing opened argues the other side with evidence, so the article only states Google's position.
- Profiling overhead: GWP's "less than 0.01 percent" is fleet-wide and averaged over mostly unprofiled machines; per profiled machine it's "less than a few percent"; Pyroscope quotes "~2-5%" per process. Different denominators, not a contradiction; the article says so.
- OTel collector: docs say direct export is fine to start but recommend a collector in general. Not really a disagreement; both stated.

### Deploying and scaling

All pages below were opened (HTML fetched with curl and read as text
through pandoc; the Facebook paper as PDF through pdftotext).

#### `ci-cd` (short)

1. [Continuous Integration](https://martinfowler.com/articles/continuousIntegration.html), Martin Fowler, martinfowler.com, 2024 revision (first version 2000). Article, primary: yes (one of the people who named and spread the practice). Seen: definition, everyone merges to mainline at least daily, each integration verified by an automated self-testing build; every push to mainline triggers a build; fix broken builds immediately, usually by reverting to the last good build; pending head / gated commit as an alternative; XP guideline of a ten-minute build; deployment pipeline with a fast commit build and slower later stages; running a CI service on feature branches "isn't Continuous Integration"; hide work in progress with keystone interfaces, feature flags, branch by abstraction; CI vs continuous delivery (always releasable, release is a business decision) vs continuous deployment (every green build goes out automatically); automated rollback; show the build id in every running version.
2. [Release Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/release-engineering/), Dinah McNutt, *Site Reliability Engineering* chapter 8, Google/O'Reilly, 2016. Book chapter from the builders, primary: yes. Seen: hermetic builds (same revision gives identical results, no dependence on the build machine); release from a branch cut at a revision, fixes cherry-picked; continuous test system on every mainline change; re-run tests on the release branch; packages versioned with a hash and signed, labels like canary and production; "Push on Green" (deploy every build that passes all tests) vs picking from hourly builds; rollout by Sisyphus, from one cluster expanding exponentially, or over several days for sensitive infrastructure; configuration kept in the source repo with code review, four ways to ship it.
3. See `deployment-strategies` #4 (Liguori): Amazon's four pipeline phases (source, build, test, prod), builds with no network access, pre-production stages alpha/beta/gamma, one pipeline per kind of change.

#### `configuration` (short)

1. [III. Config](https://12factor.net/config), Adam Wiggins, The Twelve-Factor App, last updated 2017. Manifesto, primary: yes (Heroku's authors). Seen: config is whatever varies between deploys (resource handles, credentials, per-deploy values); strict separation of config from code; litmus test: could the code be open-sourced now without leaking credentials; internal wiring (Rails routes) isn't config; store config in environment variables; don't group env vars into named "environments", which explode combinatorially.
2. [Holistic Configuration Management at Facebook](https://sigops.org/s/conferences/sosp/2015/current/2015-Monterey/printable/008-tang.pdf), Chunqiang Tang et al., SOSP 2015. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: runtime configs changed live thousands of times a day without redeploying; config errors "a major source of site outages"; config treated as code (Python/Thrift compiled to JSON, validators, code review, CI in a sandbox, automated canary on 20 servers then a full cluster, auto-rollback); Gatekeeper for feature rollouts; incident stories (old code can't read new config schema, canary caught it on 20 servers; engineer overrode the canary as a "false positive" and caused crashes; small canary missed a load problem so a cluster-sized phase was added); 16% of high-impact incidents over three months were config-related; breakdown 42% common errors, 36% subtle, 22% valid changes exposing code bugs; config commit to servers about 14.5 s baseline, canary about ten minutes.
3. [Cloudflare outage, the Bot Management feature file](https://blog.cloudflare.com/18-november-2025-outage/), Matthew Prince, Cloudflare, 2025. Postmortem, primary: yes. Seen: a database permissions change made a query return duplicate rows, the generated Bot Management feature file more than doubled, was pushed to the whole network within minutes, and the proxy hit its hard limit of 200 features and panicked (`Result::unwrap()` on an Err); file regenerated every five minutes so good and bad versions alternated; fix was stopping propagation and inserting a known-good file; follow-ups: treat internally generated config like user input, more global kill switches.
4. See `ci-cd` #2 (McNutt): four ways Google ships config (mainline config, config in the binary's package, separate config packages, external store), and config changes as "a potential source of instability".

#### `feature-flags` (short)

1. [Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags)](https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html), Pete Hodgson, martinfowler.com, 2016 (revised 2017). Article, primary: no (practitioner, well-cited). Seen: toggle point, toggle router, toggle configuration; four kinds by longevity and dynamism (release, experiment, ops, permissioning); release toggles should last a week or two; ops toggles as kill switches, a manual circuit breaker; per-request cohorts (1% by user id modulo); "separating release from deployment"; prefer static config in source control; config file, app DB, or ZooKeeper/etcd/Consul; test the production config plus the flags you mean to flip, both on and off; flags as inventory with a carrying cost, expiration dates, time bombs; Knight Capital's $460 million loss mentioned as a cautionary tale.
2. See `configuration` #2 (Tang et al.): Gatekeeper releases code disabled and turns it on for employees or 1% of a device model, billions of checks per second, a big share of frontend CPU.

#### `infrastructure-as-code` (deep)

1. [InfrastructureAsCode](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/InfrastructureAsCode.html), Martin Fowler, martinfowler.com, 2016. Bliki, primary: no (summarises Kief Morris's book). Seen: definition; practices: definition files, no hand edits on servers (snowflake servers), version everything, test continuously, small changes, keep services available (blue-green, parallel change); phoenix and immutable servers.
2. [State](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state), HashiCorp, Terraform docs v1.16. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: state maps real objects to resource instances; refresh before any operation; default local `terraform.tfstate` plus backup; don't keep state in version control (no locking, secrets in state); JSON, don't edit by hand; one-to-one mapping, broken by `import` or `state rm` done wrong.
3. [Purpose of Terraform State](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state/purpose), HashiCorp, Terraform docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: early prototypes used cloud tags instead of state and it failed (not everything supports tags); state keeps dependencies so deleted resources can be destroyed in order; attribute cache for performance, round trips of hundreds of milliseconds per resource and rate limits, big users run with `-refresh=false` and `-target`; remote state with locking so two people don't run at once.
4. [terraform plan command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan), HashiCorp, Terraform docs v1.16. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: plan reads current remote objects, compares config to prior state, proposes actions; speculative plan vs saved plan (`-out`) applied later; others' changes can make an earlier speculative plan wrong; destroy and refresh-only modes (0.15.4+); `-refresh=false` can give an incorrect plan; `-detailed-exitcode` 0/1/2; `-lock=false` dangerous.
5. [Manage resource drift](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/tutorials/state/resource-drift), HashiCorp tutorial. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: drift defined; if state and config don't match reality Terraform "may unintentionally destroy or recreate resources"; worked example of a security group changed by hand; `plan -refresh-only` to see drift; normal apply would revert the hand change; import to adopt it; drift detection is a paid HCP Terraform feature.
6. [terraform refresh command](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/refresh), HashiCorp. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: deprecated; alias for `apply -refresh-only -auto-approve`; with bad credentials Terraform may think everything was deleted and drop it all from state without asking.
7. [OpenGitOps principles v1.0.0](https://opengitops.dev/), OpenGitOps (CNCF working group). Spec, primary: yes. Seen: declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled by software agents. The contrast with Terraform's run-when-asked model.
8. [OpenTofu FAQ](https://opentofu.org/faq/), OpenTofu project, 1.12 current. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: fork of Terraform after HashiCorp moved to the BUSL licence; given to the Linux Foundation; works with Terraform state files up to 1.5.x; same providers, separate registry.
9. [Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Configuration Files](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-kubernetes-objects/declarative-config/), Kubernetes docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `kubectl apply` on a directory, `last-applied-configuration` annotation, `kubectl diff` as preview, apply sets fields in the file and clears fields removed from it. Read for research; not cited.

#### `deployment-strategies` (deep)

1. [Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/), Kubernetes docs v1.35. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: RollingUpdate (default) vs Recreate; maxUnavailable and maxSurge default 25% each (unavailable rounds down, surge rounds up); example with 3 replicas; the controller stops scaling a stuck new ReplicaSet; rollout only when the pod template changes; `kubectl rollout undo`, `--to-revision`; revisionHistoryLimit 10; progressDeadlineSeconds default 600, but Kubernetes only reports the stall and takes no action; minReadySeconds; canary with two Deployments.
2. [BlueGreenDeployment](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BlueGreenDeployment.html), Martin Fowler, 2010 (updated 2015). Bliki, primary: no. Seen: two identical environments, switch the router, switch back to roll back; missed transactions problem; read-only mode trick; environments swap roles; separate schema changes from app upgrades.
3. [CanaryRelease](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CanaryRelease.html), Danilo Sato, 2014. Bliki, primary: no. Seen: route a few users first, choose by random sample, employees or profile; roll back by rerouting; capacity testing in production; region or brand partitioning; don't conflate canary with A/B testing (days for significance vs minutes or hours); cluster immune system from IMVU; managing several versions; database changes need parallel change.
4. [Automating safe, hands-off deployments](https://builder.aws.com/content/3ErTKQOTKc5NIw031UePBPxTQ6I/automating-safe-hands-off-deployments), Clare Liguori, Amazon Builders' Library (now on AWS Builder Center). Article from the builders, primary: yes. Seen: four phases; one-box stage (single VM or container, about 10% of traffic in a ten-box gamma, at most 10% of a region's requests in prod); rolling deploys replacing at most 33% of boxes with 66% capacity kept; some teams 5% at a time with 33% fast rollback; waves by region, first a low-traffic region, one AZ or cell at a time; aggregate high-severity alarms roll back automatically; one-box alarms scoped to the one box; bake time (at least 1 h after one-box, 12 h after first wave, 2 to 4 h after later ones), wait for N data points; global rollout in about four or five business days.
5. [Ensuring rollback safety during deployments](https://builder.aws.com/content/3F04j2yRAAMBuPSPs50xwXZqg01/ensuring-rollback-safety-during-deployments), Sandeep Pokkunuri, Amazon Builders' Library. Article, primary: yes. Seen: during a rolling deploy two versions talk to each other; protocol changes are the most common reason a rollback fails; heartbeat 5 s to 10 s example; two-phase prepare/activate deploy (XML to JSON); verify every server reached prepare; bake days between phases; readers before writers when rolling forward; test environments with one server hide the problem.
6. [Canarying Releases](https://sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/), Alec Warner and Štěpán Davidovič, *The Site Reliability Workbook* chapter 16, 2018. Primary: yes. Seen: definition (partial, time-limited deployment plus evaluation); majority of Google incidents triggered by binary or config pushes; 5% canary with 20% errors gives 1% overall; blue/green needs twice the resources and is a before/after canary; before/after evaluation is risky; one canary at a time; traffic teeing and artificial load.

#### `canary-analysis` (short)

1. See `deployment-strategies` #6 (Canarying Releases): canary vs control, metrics must indicate problems and be attributable, use SLIs, no more than about a dozen metrics, exclude 4xx, split metrics by population, metric window no longer than the canary, gradual multi-stage canaries, shared failure domains mean a bad canary can hurt the control, also check absolute SLOs.
2. [How canary judgment works](https://spinnaker.io/docs/guides/user/canary/judge/), Spinnaker docs (NetflixACAJudge). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Kayenta fetches metrics, judge compares; NaN handling; outlier removal with IQR fences; Mann-Whitney U test at 98% confidence, plus effect size threshold; labels Pass/High/Low/Nodata.
3. [Best practices for configuring canary](https://spinnaker.io/docs/guides/user/canary/best-practices/), Spinnaker docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: compare against a fresh baseline, not production (same time, size, traffic; controls for cache warm-up, heap); at least 50 data points per metric, plan for hours; 3 h lifetime, 1 h interval starting point; marginal 75 and pass 95 starting thresholds; too many metrics in one group hides one failure, use `critical`; latency, errors, saturation; retrospective analysis.
4. [Introducing Kayenta](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/introducing-kayenta-an-open-automated-canary-analysis-tool-from-google-and-netflix), Nikhil Kaul and Andrew Phillips, Google Cloud blog, 2018. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: Google and Netflix open-sourced Kayenta; route e.g. 1% to canary and a new baseline, typically three instances each; score 0 to 100, success/marginal/failure; manual canary analysis is slow and biased. Not cited (the Spinnaker docs cover the same points, current).
5. See `configuration` #2 (Tang et al.): canary spec phases, predicate like "CTR no more than x% lower than control", log spew caught on 20 servers.

#### `autoscaling` (short)

1. [Horizontal Pod Autoscaling](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/autoscaling/horizontal-pod-autoscale/), Kubernetes docs v1.35. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: control loop every 15 s by default; `desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × current/desired)`; 0.1 tolerance; utilization as a share of the pod's resource request, no request means no action; not-ready pods and missing metrics dampen scale-up; CPU of starting pods ignored for up to 5 min, 30 s readiness delay; highest of several metrics wins; scale-down stabilization 300 s; default scale-up has no window, at most 4 pods or 100% per 15 s; thrashing/flapping.
2. [Managing Load](https://sre.google/workbook/managing-load/), *The Site Reliability Workbook* chapter 11, 2018. Primary: yes. Seen: autoscaling section: unhealthy instances still counted in the average stop scaling; "Creating new instances is never instant"; scale up eagerly, down cautiously; keep far from bottlenecks and reserve spare capacity; a CPU-burning bug or a stuck dependency makes the autoscaler grow forever, so set min and max; kill switch; autoscaling pushes load onto backends and shared quota; stateful systems don't benefit. (Note already existed; appended.)
3. See existing note `yanacek-load-shedding-2019`: shedding at the same CPU target as autoscaling can starve the scaler of its signal.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- **Config in env vars or in a reviewed pipeline?** Twelve-factor says env vars set per deploy, outside the code repo. Google, Facebook and Amazon keep config in source control, code-reviewed, built and canaried like code. They answer different questions: the first keeps secrets and per-environment values out of the build, the second makes changing config as safe as a deploy.
- **Feature branches with CI.** Fowler says running a CI service on feature branches isn't CI at all; most teams using pull requests call it CI. The article explains the difference in integration frequency.
- **Blue-green is a canary?** Fowler presents blue-green as a fast cut-over with instant rollback; the SRE workbook calls it a before/after canary with double resources, and before/after evaluation risky.
- **Compare with production or with a baseline?** Kayenta/Spinnaker say always a fresh baseline; the SRE workbook's example compares canary against the rest of the fleet (control), Facebook compared 20 servers' logs with the rest of production. The baseline removes warm-up effects.
- **Terraform's cached state vs live reads.** Terraform refreshes by default, but its own docs say large users skip refresh and treat the cached state as truth, which is where drift hides.

- SEC order on Knight Capital (sec.gov returned "Request Rate Threshold Exceeded" to curl; WebFetch couldn't extract the PDF). The only Knight Capital fact used is Hodgson's one line.
- Netflix tech blog on Kayenta (Medium, Cloudflare challenge page).
- HashiCorp's licence change blog (Vercel security checkpoint). The fork is described from the OpenTofu FAQ.
- research.facebook.com page for the Tang et al. paper (error page); the PDF on sigops.org opened.

**Rejected:**

- Kubernetes declarative config task page: good background on `kubectl apply`, but Kubernetes' own controllers are the `kubernetes` node's story.
- Kayenta announcement: superseded for the article by the current Spinnaker docs.
- SRE workbook chapters 14 and 15 (Configuration Design, Configuration Specifics): fetched, about config languages (Jsonnet, templating); more than a short node needs.

**Gaps:**

- No primary source on how long a new pod takes to start and serve; the autoscaling article gives the HPA's own timers and leaves pod startup as "not instant".
- No source for how often config changes cause incidents outside Facebook's 2015 numbers and Google's "majority of incidents from binary or config pushes".
- No DORA/Accelerate research opened; no numbers on deploy frequency across the industry.
- No primary source on GitOps tools (Argo CD, Flux) opened; the principles page only.

## Phase 15: Security, authentication and authorization

Researched by 5 parallel passes, one per group below.

### Who you are

#### `threat-modeling` (deep)

1. [Threat Modeling Manifesto](https://www.threatmodelingmanifesto.org/), Braiterman, Shostack, Marcil, Wuyts et al., threat modeling working group (no year on the page). Community statement by practitioners, primary: yes. Seen: the definition (analyzing representations of a system to highlight security and privacy concerns); the four questions; five values ("continuous refinement over a single delivery"); patterns (systematic approach, varied viewpoints) and anti-patterns (hero threat modeler, admiration for the problem, tendency to overfocus, perfect representation).
2. [Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Threat_Modeling_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Docs, primary: no. Seen: four steps mapped to the four questions; data flow diagrams with trust boundaries, data flows, data stores, processes and external entities; STRIDE table with the property each category violates and an example each (one is tampering with a JWT to change a role); ranking by likelihood times impact and why that's hard; responses mitigate, eliminate, transfer, accept; review checklist; no single standard process (PASTA, OCTAVE, LINDDUN).
3. [The Ultimate Beginner's Guide to Threat Modeling](https://shostack.org/resources/threat-modeling), Shostack + Associates. Guide from the author of the four-question framework, primary: yes. Seen: threat modeling vs risk management; four questions with prompts ("can an unintended user get access to it?"); responses including a tongue-in-cheek "ignore"; DFDs, STRIDE and kill chains as the three most common techniques; STRIDE's last letter given as "Expansion of Authority"; a DFD is sometimes mistaken for the whole threat model.
4. [Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/develop/threat-modeling-tool-threats), Microsoft Learn. Docs from the team that made STRIDE, primary: yes. Seen: STRIDE category table with Microsoft's own definitions; the tool as part of the Microsoft SDL; example questions ("how can an attacker change the authentication data?").
5. [Threat Modeling Guide for Software Teams](https://martinfowler.com/articles/agile-threat-modelling.html), Gayathri Mohan and Jim Gumbley, martinfowler.com, 2025. Practitioner guide, primary: no. Seen: start from data flows and where data enters your boundary; STRIDE as prompts per data flow; "little and often", 15 to 30 minute team sessions on the feature in hand; a worked order-management example with assets (order information, customer details) and the UI as the least trusted component; one threat per sticky note, specific. Only the first half of the page rendered as text; the later workshop sections weren't read.

#### `password-hashing` (deep)

1. [Password Storage Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Docs, primary: no. Seen: hash, don't encrypt; how cracking works (guess, hash, compare); salt per password; pepper (pre- and post-hash, stored apart, rotating means forcing resets); work factor, under one second, login DoS risk; upgrade on next login; Argon2id minimums (m=19 MiB, t=2, p=1 and four equivalent settings); scrypt N=2^17, r=8, p=1; bcrypt cost 10 or more and the 72-byte limit; pre-hashing pitfalls (null bytes, password shucking); PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 600,000 iterations for FIPS; PHC string format; layering old hashes (bcrypt(md5)).
2. [RFC 9106](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9106), Biryukov, Dinu, Khovratovich, Josefsson, 2021. Spec (Informational, CFRG), primary: yes. Seen: Argon2 as memory-hard; Argon2d vs Argon2i vs Argon2id and why; Argon2id must be supported; 16-byte salt recommended, unique per password; first recommended option t=1, p=4, 2 GiB; second t=3, p=4, 64 MiB; backend server example 0.5 s on a 2 GHz CPU with 4 GiB; time-space trade-off attacks in section 7.
3. [RFC 7914](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7914), Percival and Josefsson, 2016. Spec (Informational), primary: yes. Seen: history of password KDFs (crypt, PBKDF2, bcrypt); iteration counts keep up only if attackers use the same software; custom parallel hardware drops the cost of brute force every year; scrypt's aim is to take that advantage away. Section on parameters not read closely.
4. [NIST SP 800-63B-4](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html), NIST, 2025. Government standard, primary: yes. Seen: passwords "SHALL be salted and hashed" with a password hashing scheme; salt at least 32 bits; store scheme and cost with each hash; cost as high as practical and raised over time; SHOULD add a keyed hash with a secret stored apart (in an HSM or TEE); rate limiting on failed attempts; blocklists; attackers compute "many billions of hashes per second" offline.
5. [A Future-Adaptable Password Scheme](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/usenix99/provos/provos_html/node1.html), Niels Provos and David Mazières, USENIX, 1999. Paper (the bcrypt paper), primary: yes. Seen: introduction only (HTML version): password entropy doesn't scale with computing power; crypt did fewer than 4 hashes per second in 1976 and over 200,000 on a fast workstation by 1999; bcrypt as a hash with adjustable cost.
6. [golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt), Go authors, x/crypto v0.57.0. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: MinCost 4, DefaultCost 10, MaxCost 31; ErrPasswordTooLong past 72 bytes; cost stored in the hash (`Cost` reads it back). The x/crypto/argon2 page was also read: IDKey is Argon2id, and it quotes RFC 9106's two recommended options. Not used separately.

#### `cookies` (short)

1. [Cookies: HTTP State Management Mechanism (draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22), Mike West and John Wilander (editors), IETF HTTPBIS. Spec draft, primary: yes. Seen: in the RFC Editor queue when read, will obsolete RFC 6265; Set-Cookie and Cookie; Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite (Strict, Lax, None) semantics; unknown SameSite value means Lax enforcement; "Lax-allowing-unsafe" and its 2-minute window; `__Secure-` and `__Host-` prefixes with examples of accepted and rejected headers; 4096-octet name+value limit; 400-day lifetime cap; security considerations: ambient authority, clear text, session identifiers, weak confidentiality (no isolation by port or scheme), weak integrity (sibling domains, network attacker injecting over HTTP), SameSite is defense in depth.
2. [Using HTTP cookies](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies), MDN. Docs, primary: no. Seen: the login flow with a session cookie; Secure (localhost exception, not in Safari); HttpOnly blocks `Document.cookie`; SameSite values with examples; "If no SameSite attribute is set, the cookie is treated as Lax by default"; third-party cookies being blocked by browsers; regenerate session cookies on login; Clear-Site-Data.
3. [RFC 6265](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265), Barth, 2011. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: downloaded, skimmed the contents. Not used: the bis draft obsoletes it and covers SameSite and prefixes, which 6265 lacks.

#### `sessions` (deep)

1. [Session Management Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Docs, primary: no. Seen: a session ID after login is as strong as the login itself; at least 64 bits of entropy from a CSPRNG (128 if you make your own); ID must be meaningless, data lives server side; cookies over URLs; TLS for the whole session; Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, `__Host-` example; strict vs permissive session handling; regenerate the ID on login and privilege change (session fixation); idle, absolute and renewal timeouts, enforced server side, with typical ranges; logout must invalidate on the server; `Cache-Control: no-store`, Clear-Site-Data; don't keep tokens in localStorage.
2. [Cookies: HTTP State Management Mechanism (draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22): see `cookies` #1. Seen: section 8.4, session identifiers (a nonce as lookup key limits damage and prevents splicing; the three steps of session fixation); 8.3 encrypting and signing doesn't stop replay.
3. [NIST SP 800-63B-4](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html): see `password-hashing` #4. Seen: section 5, session management: session secret from an approved RNG, at least 64 bits; erased on logout; not in localStorage; cookie rules (Secure, HttpOnly, `__Host-`, SameSite Lax or Strict, opaque value only); overall and inactivity timeouts (AAL2: 24 hours and 1 hour; AAL3: 12 hours and 15 minutes); device-bound session credentials as proof of possession.
4. [How to use sessions](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/topics/http/sessions/), Django 6.1 docs. Framework docs, primary: yes. Seen: default store is the database; cache, cached_db (write-through), file and signed-cookie backends; cache-only sessions log users out on eviction; signed cookies are readable, can exceed 4096 bytes, give no freshness and aren't invalidated on logout; `cycle_key()` called by login against fixation; `clearsessions` to purge expired rows; no session IDs in URLs by design.

#### `jwt` (deep)

1. [RFC 7519](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519), Jones, Bradley, Sakimura, 2015. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: JWT as compact claims in a JWS or JWE; worked HS256 example (header, claims, MAC, three base64url parts); registered claims iss, sub, aud (must reject if not the audience), exp and nbf with a few minutes' leeway, iat, jti for replay; contents can't be trusted unless cryptographically secured.
2. [RFC 8725](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725), Sheffer, Hardt, Jones, 2020. BCP, primary: yes. Seen: attacks: alg none, RS256 to HS256 confusion, weak HMAC keys brute-forced offline, substitution and cross-JWT confusion, kid injection and jku SSRF; practices: allowlist algorithms, one key one algorithm, validate iss/sub/aud, explicit typing, mutually exclusive validation rules.
3. [JSON Web Token Best Current Practices (draft-ietf-oauth-rfc8725bis-10)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-rfc8725bis-10), Sheffer, Hardt, Jones, IETF OAuth WG. Spec draft, primary: yes. Seen: in the RFC Editor queue when read; will obsolete RFC 8725; new threats: huge PBES2 counts, blocklist bypass with "noNE", JWE decompression bombs, compact vs JSON serialization confusion; allowlists over blocklists; reject tokens with characters outside base64url and dots.
4. [Critical vulnerabilities in JSON Web Token libraries](https://auth0.com/blog/critical-vulnerabilities-in-json-web-token-libraries/), Tim McLean, Auth0 blog, 2015. Blog by the researcher who found the bugs, primary: yes. Seen: how a JWT is built, step by step; the none algorithm accepted as verified; the RSA public key used as an HMAC secret; fix is a verify call that takes the expected algorithm; proposal to drop `alg`.
5. [JSON Web Token Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/JSON_Web_Token_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Docs, primary: no. Seen: JWTs for "stateless" sessions are "frowned upon"; logout needs a deny list, which makes them stateful again; signature vs MAC and who can mint tokens; Token Status Lists; deny list keyed on (iss, jti), not the raw token (malleability); signed JWTs are readable by anyone; short expiry and sender-constrained tokens (DPoP) against theft.
6. [RFC 7515](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7515), Jones, Bradley, Sakimura, 2015. Seen: downloaded, read only where RFC 8725 quotes section 5.2 (the application decides which algorithms are acceptable). Not used separately.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Argon2id memory: RFC 9106's "uniformly safe" options are 2 GiB or 64 MiB per hash, while OWASP's minimum is 19 MiB with t=2 (or 46 MiB with t=1). The RFC is written for one hash; a login server hashing many passwords at once can't spend 2 GiB on each. Both are floors from different angles, not a contradiction, but the numbers differ by two orders of magnitude.
- bcrypt's place: OWASP now says bcrypt only "in legacy systems", yet NIST SP 800-63B doesn't name algorithms and points to SP 800-132 (PBKDF2), which OWASP ranks last except for FIPS.
- Peppers: NIST 800-63B says verifiers SHOULD add a keyed hash with a secret stored apart; OWASP calls a pepper optional defense in depth that "provides no additional secure characteristics" alone and costs a forced reset for everyone if it leaks.
- JWTs as sessions: OWASP says using JWTs for "stateless" sessions is "frowned upon" because logout needs a deny list; many tutorials recommend exactly that. RFC 8725 is silent on sessions.
- SameSite default: MDN says a cookie without SameSite "is treated as Lax by default"; OWASP says the default "varies across browsers and versions" and not to rely on it; the bis draft allows "Lax-allowing-unsafe" for recent cookies as a transition. Set it explicitly.
- STRIDE's last letter: Microsoft and OWASP say Elevation of Privilege; Shostack's guide says "Expansion of Authority". Shostack also marks non-repudiation with a shrug emoji.
- Ranking threats: OWASP says ranking should in theory be likelihood times impact but both are hard to estimate and ignore the cost of the fix.

**Couldn't open:**
- The rest of the Mohan and Gumbley page (the workshop sections after "Identify Threats" didn't render as text).
- The original STRIDE memo (Kohnfelder and Garg, "The threats to our products", 1999): not searched for further; Microsoft's own doc was used instead.

**Rejected:**
- OWASP JWT for Java cheat sheet (old URL returns 404; replaced by the general JWT cheat sheet).
- The x/crypto/argon2 docs page as a separate source: it repeats RFC 9106.

**Gaps:**
- No measured bcrypt or Argon2id hash times on real hardware: the article gives no timing numbers beyond the RFC's example. A small benchmark on the lab machine would fill this (lab is on hold).
- No primary source on how often real breaches involved unsalted or fast hashes; left out.
- Browser-by-browser SameSite defaults aren't in any source opened here.

### Who you are

#### `api-keys` (short)

1. [Behind GitHub's new authentication token formats](https://github.blog/engineering/platform-security/behind-githubs-new-authentication-token-formats/), Indigo K, GitHub, 2021. Engineering blog from the team that built it, primary: yes. Seen: old tokens 40 hex chars indistinguishable from SHA hashes; 3-letter prefixes (ghp, gho, ghu, ghs, ghr) plus `_`, which isn't Base64; expected false positive rate down to 0.5% from the prefix alone; 32-bit CRC32 checksum in the last 6 chars, Base62, lets scanners drop fakes without a database hit; entropy 160 to 178 bits for OAuth tokens (30 Base62 chars) in the same length; invites other issuers to join secret scanning. Says nothing about how GitHub stores tokens.
2. [Authentication development guidelines](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/authentication/), GitLab Docs. Docs from the builders, primary: yes. Seen: token prefix table with storage per type: glpat- SHA-256 digest, gldt- and glcbt- AES-256-GCM encrypted, gloas- SHA-512 digest; new token types must use digest or encrypted storage, not plaintext; default PAT lifetime 365 days.
3. [API keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys), Stripe Docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: pk_/rk_/sk_ prefixes with _test_/_live_; publishable keys safe in front-end code, can't create charges or read data; restricted keys with chosen permissions, recommended over secret keys; a new secret key shown once ("You can't retrieve it later"); rotation revokes and replaces, old and new both work up to 7 days; expired key gives an authentication error.
4. [Best practices for managing secret API keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys-best-practices), Stripe Docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: never in source code, search code for sk_live_/rk_live_, pre-commit hooks, secrets vault or env vars, least privilege, rotate periodically, audit request logs. Not used (overlaps `secrets-management`).
5. [Best practices for managing API keys](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/api-keys-best-practices), Google Cloud docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: add restrictions; don't send keys as query parameters (use the x-goog-api-key header); API keys are bearer credentials and obscure the end user in audit logs; one key per team member per app; rotate periodically. Not used (Stripe covers restriction and rotation with more detail).
6. [Secret scanning partner program](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/secret-scanning/secret-scanning-partnership-program/secret-scanning-partner-program), GitHub Docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: how token issuers register patterns and receive leak reports; can report back raw token or its SHA-256. Not used.

#### `oauth2` (deep)

1. [RFC 6749](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749), Dick Hardt (editor), IETF, 2012. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: problems with sharing passwords (stored in clear text, too broad, can't revoke one app); four roles; access tokens opaque to the client, either a lookup id or self-contained signed; refresh tokens only to the authorization server; confidential vs public clients; TLS MUST at authorization and token endpoints; figure 3 code flow A to E; code lifetime at most 10 minutes recommended, single use, reuse should revoke tokens; implicit grant for in-browser JavaScript; CSRF against the redirect URI (10.12); codes leak via history and referrer (10.5). Updated by RFC 8252, 8996, 9700; not obsoleted.
2. [RFC 7636](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7636), Nat Sakimura (editor), John Bradley, Naveen Agarwal, IETF, 2015. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: code interception attack via a shared custom URI scheme on one device (figure 1); code_verifier 43 to 128 chars, 32 random bytes recommended; S256 challenge; S256 mandatory if possible, plain only for technical reasons, no downgrade; server recomputes at the token endpoint.
3. [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700), Lodderstedt, Bradley, Labunets, Fett, IETF, 2025. BCP, primary: yes. Seen: exact redirect URI matching (loopback port exception); no open redirectors; CSRF via PKCE, nonce, or state; PKCE MUST for public, RECOMMENDED for confidential clients, servers MUST support; implicit SHOULD NOT; password grant MUST NOT (can't do 2FA, WebAuthn may be impossible); sender-constrained tokens (mTLS, DPoP); refresh token rotation or binding for public clients, with the replay-detection explanation; audience-restricted, least-privilege tokens; asymmetric client auth; server metadata recommended; no authorization responses over plain HTTP.
4. [RFC 6750](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6750), Michael B. Jones, Dick Hardt, IETF, 2012. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: bearer token definition; `Authorization: Bearer`; no bearer tokens in page URLs.
5. [RFC 8252](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8252), William Denniss, John Bradley, IETF, 2017. BCP, primary: yes. Seen: embedded web views can copy credentials, MUST NOT be used; system browser gives SSO; private-use scheme, claimed https and loopback redirects.
6. [The OAuth 2.1 Authorization Framework](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1/), Hardt, Parecki, Lodderstedt, IETF draft -16. Spec draft, primary: yes. Seen: would obsolete RFC 6749 and 6750; section 10 list of changes (PKCE in the code flow, exact redirect match, implicit and password grants removed, no bearer tokens in query strings, public-client refresh tokens sender-constrained or one-time, PKCE plain removed); client credentials grant kept. Still a draft when this was written.
7. [RFC 9068](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9068), Vittorio Bertocci, IETF, 2021. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: header and abstract only, JWT profile for access tokens. Not used; belongs with `jwt`.
8. [RFC 9449](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449), Fett et al., IETF, 2023. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: header and abstract only (DPoP). Not used; DPoP is named through RFC 9700.

#### `oidc` (short)

1. [OpenID Connect Core 1.0](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html), Sakimura, Bradley, Jones, de Medeiros, Mortimore, OpenID Foundation, errata set 2. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: identity layer on OAuth 2.0; ID token is a JWT; openid scope required; iss/sub/aud/exp/iat/auth_time/nonce definitions; ID token exp unrelated to session lifetime; code flow keeps tokens out of the user agent; validation steps 3.1.3.7 (exact iss, aud contains client_id, TLS may replace signature check for token endpoint responses, exp, nonce); UserInfo endpoint; iss+sub the only stable identifier; email not unique; email_verified meaning left to the provider.
2. [OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-discovery-1_0.html), Sakimura, Bradley, Jones, Jay, OpenID Foundation, errata set 2. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: /.well-known/openid-configuration; jwks_uri holds signing keys; issuer must equal iss in ID tokens.

#### `passkeys` (deep)

1. [Web Authentication, Level 3](https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-3/), Cappalli, Kumar, Lundberg, Miller, Pascoe, Satragno (editors), W3C. Spec, now a W3C Recommendation (previous: Level 2, 2021; Level 1, 2019), primary: yes. Seen: credentials scoped to an RP, enforced by user agents and authenticators; RP ID default and registrable-suffix rule; registration and authentication ceremonies; challenge at least 16 bytes (13.4.3); server verification steps 7.1/7.2 (type, challenge, origin, rpIdHash, UP, UV, BE/BS, signature over authData + hash of clientData, signCount); flag bits; backup eligibility and state; multi-device credentials = synced passkeys; signature counter and clones, zero when unimplemented.
2. [Terms](https://passkeys.dev/docs/reference/terms/), passkeys.dev (W3C WebAuthn Adoption Community Group, FIDO Alliance). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: passkey = discoverable credential; synced vs device-bound; platform vs roaming authenticators (USB, NFC, Bluetooth); CDA over CTAP hybrid, persistent linking; UP vs UV; conditional mediation; conditional create; Credential Exchange; one login challenge can collect several factors.
3. [What are passkeys?](https://passkeys.dev/docs/intro/what-are-passkeys/), passkeys.dev. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: unique per service; RP servers store public keys; sync servers can't view or use private keys; browsers and OS enforce the right service.
4. [Create a passkey for passwordless logins](https://web.dev/articles/passkey-registration), Eiji Kitamura, Google (web.dev). Docs from a team that builds passkey support, primary: yes. Seen: four components; registration steps; don't gate creation on a password alone; creation options (RP ID example, user.id without PII, algs -7 and -257, excludeCredentials, userVerification "preferred" can be skipped); what to store (credential ID, public key, AAGUID, BE flag); Signal API; notify the user because a rogue passkey survives a password change.
5. [NIST SP 800-63B-4](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html), Temoshok et al., NIST, 2025. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: phishing resistance by channel binding or verifier name binding; manual entry never phishing-resistant; syncable authenticators (Appendix B): keys encrypted in the sync fabric, access MFA-protected, not allowed at AAL3; notify on binding a new authenticator. See also `mfa` #1.
6. [Passkeys](https://fidoalliance.org/passkeys/), FIDO Alliance. Marketing page, primary: yes. Seen: definition, "80% of breaches" claim without a source. Not used.
7. [Passkeys](https://developers.google.com/identity/passkeys), Google for Developers. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: landing page with links only. Not used.

#### `mfa` (short)

1. [NIST SP 800-63B-4](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html), Temoshok et al., NIST, 2025. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: something you know/have/are; AAL2 two distinct factors and must offer a phishing-resistant option; AAL3 non-exportable key; OTP from shared key plus time or counter, verifier holds the key; OTP and out-of-band not phishing-resistant (manual entry, relay); authentication fatigue, secret transfer now required, limit push rate; PSTN the one restricted authenticator, SIM change and porting checks; look-up secrets under 112 bits need a password hash; four recovery classes.
2. [Implementing Phishing-Resistant MFA](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/fact-sheet-implementing-phishing-resistant-mfa-508c.pdf), CISA, 2022. Government fact sheet, primary: no. Seen: MFA definition; any MFA stops password spraying; attacks (phishing a 6-digit code, push bombing, SS7, SIM swap); table 1 ranking FIDO/WebAuthn and PKI, then app OTP and push with number matching, then push without, then SMS/voice as last resort; FIDO can include biometrics or PIN; PIV/CAC smart cards.
3. [RFC 6238](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238) (TOTP) and [RFC 4226](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4226) (HOTP), IETF, 2011 and 2005. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: downloaded, headers only. Not used; NIST's OTP description was enough at this depth.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Synced passkeys. WebAuthn, passkeys.dev and Google present synced passkeys as the phishing-resistant default for consumers; NIST accepts them at AAL2 but bans them at AAL3 because the key is exportable, and moves the risk to the provider account (sync fabric must be MFA-protected).
- CSRF in OAuth. RFC 6749 relied on `state`; RFC 9700 lets clients rely on PKCE instead, but only once they know the server enforces it, and still requires state-based tokens otherwise.
- Push with number matching. CISA ranks it with app OTP as the best non-phishing-resistant option; NIST treats plain approve prompts as unacceptable and requires a secret transfer, which number matching is a form of. Both agree it's still phishable.
- What counts as phishing-resistant. CISA says FIDO/WebAuthn is the only widely available kind and PKI the other; NIST defines it by channel binding or verifier name binding, which covers both.
- Hashing tokens. GitLab stores PATs as plain SHA-256; NIST requires a slow password hash only for random secrets under 112 bits. Secondary API-key guides seen in search results mix the two; no primary source says to use bcrypt for long random keys.
- OAuth version. RFC 6749 is not obsoleted, but RFC 9700 changed its defaults and the OAuth 2.1 draft removes grants. Older write-ups still show the implicit flow.

**Couldn't open:**
- None failed. The FIDO Alliance passkeys page loaded but was mostly navigation and marketing.

**Rejected:**
- apikeys.guide, randomkeygen.com, safeguard.sh and similar API-key guides from a web search: secondary, no named authors or sources; not opened.
- FIDO Alliance passkeys page and Google's passkeys landing page (little content). RFC 9068, RFC 9449, RFC 6238, RFC 4226 (headers only; not needed at this depth).

**Gaps:**
- No primary source says how GitHub or Stripe store their own API keys; the hashed-storage claim rests on GitLab's docs.
- No source opened for OAuth for browser-based apps (the backend-for-frontend pattern, draft-ietf-oauth-browser-based-apps); the article doesn't cover where a single-page app should keep tokens.
- No passkey adoption numbers, and no source for how often synced passkeys report a zero signature counter.
- WebAuthn related origin requests (sharing passkeys across domains) seen in the spec but not written up.
- No source on TOTP clock drift windows or code length; left out.

### What you're allowed to do

#### `authorization-models` (deep)

1. [Authorization Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series contributors. Docs (community guide), primary: no. Seen: authorization vs authentication; broken access control ranked first in the 2021 OWASP Top 10; horizontal privilege elevation common; least privilege (horizontal and vertical), privilege creep; deny by default; validate on every request, one missed check is enough; RBAC, ABAC (NIST SP 800-162 definition) and ReBAC defined; recommends ABAC and ReBAC over RBAC (fine-grained logic, robustness against chained role checks, role explosion overflowing headers, multi-tenancy, ease of management); IDOR / CWE-639 with `acct_id` example; access to one object of a type isn't access to all; never rely on client-side checks; exit safely; logging; unit and integration tests.
2. [NIST SP 800-162](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/NIST.SP.800-162.pdf), Hu, Ferraiolo, Kuhn, Schnitzer, Sandlin, Miller, Scarfone, NIST, 2014 (editorial updates 2019). Spec (guide), primary: yes. Seen: §1.4 subject/object attributes, environment conditions, PDP and PEP; §2 MAC/DAC history, IBAC/ACLs (per-object lists, privilege accumulation), RBAC (role as a subject attribute), ABAC (ACL = identity attribute, RBAC = role attribute; boolean policies over many attributes; XACML with PDP/PEP/PAP/PIP; NGAC); §2.1 role explosion, RBAC can't easily do multi-factor decisions (location, HIPAA training), cross-organization access without pre-provisioning; §3.1.2 ACL vs ABAC trust chains, ABAC needs many more trust relationships and depends on attribute authorities.
3. [Role-Based Access Controls](https://csrc.nist.gov/files/pubs/conference/1992/10/13/rolebased-access-controls/final/docs/ferraiolo-kuhn-92.pdf), David Ferraiolo, Richard Kuhn, NIST, 1992. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: DAC vs MAC vs RBAC; RBAC bases decisions on job function, users can't pass permissions on (the difference from DAC); a role is a set of transactions; formal rules (role assignment, role authorization, transaction authorization) and an optional fourth rule for object access modes; central administration is mostly membership changes; role hierarchy (Healer, Intern, Doctor); least privilege; static vs dynamic separation of duty (dynamic needs user ID too).
4. [Zanzibar](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/atc19-pang.pdf). See `zanzibar` #1. §5: roles are similar to Zanzibar relations; several clients built RBAC on top; Cloud IAM built on Zanzibar.
5. [OpenFGA Concepts](https://openfga.dev/docs/concepts), OpenFGA authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: types, type definitions, authorization model (JSON syntax follows the Zanzibar paper, plus a DSL), stores (data can't be shared across stores), objects, users (incl. usersets and `*`), relations, directly related user types, conditions in CEL, relationship tuples, direct vs implied relationships, check returns `allowed`.

Extra: [The NIST Model for Role-Based Access Control](https://csrc.nist.gov/CSRC/media/Publications/conference-paper/2000/07/26/the-nist-model-for-role-based-access-control-towards-a-unified-/documents/sandhu-ferraiolo-kuhn-00.pdf), Sandhu, Ferraiolo, Kuhn, 2000. Downloaded; the PDF is a scanned image with no text layer. Not read, not used.

#### `zanzibar` (deep)

1. [Zanzibar: Google's Consistent, Global Authorization System](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/atc19-pang.pdf), Ruoming Pang and 13 others, Google, USENIX ATC 2019. Paper, primary: yes.
