Seen: goals (correctness, flexibility, low latency, availability, scale); relation tuple notation and Table 1; usersets and nested groups; §2.2 consistency model, new enemy examples A and B, external consistency and bounded-staleness snapshots via Spanner TrueTime, zookie protocol, at-least-as-fresh freedom; §2.3 namespace configs and userset rewrites (`_this`, `computed_userset`, `tuple_to_userset`, union/intersection/exclusion), Figure 1; §2.4 Read, Write (OCC with lock tuple), Watch, Check, content-change check, Expand; §3 architecture (aclservers, watchservers, Leopard, Spanner DBs, changelog), tuple storage keys and GC window, replication (5 voting replicas), default staleness from out-of-zone read stats, config snapshot, check evaluation as boolean expression with concurrent leaves and early cancel, Leopard (GROUP2GROUP, MEMBER2GROUP, skip lists, incremental layer), hot spots (distributed cache via consistent hashing, snapshot timestamp in cache key, quantized timestamps of 1 or 10 s, lock table against cache stampede, hot object prefetch, delayed cancellation), performance isolation, hedging (not between Zanzibar servers); §4 numbers from a 7-day sample in 2018 (1,500+ namespaces, 2 trillion+ tuples near 100 TB, 10M+ QPS, Safe vs Recent, latency percentiles, Table 2, availability 99.999%, cache hit rates); §4.5 lessons; §5 related work (RBAC, IAM, TAO, Lamport clocks, Chubby, ZooKeeper).
2. [Schema Language Reference](https://authzed.com/docs/spicedb/concepts/schema), AuthZed (SpiceDB docs). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: definitions, caveats, relations and subject relations, wildcards (only for read), permissions vs relations (easy to change a permission, not a relation), operators `+ & - ->`, union precedence trap, arrows vs subject relations, `.any`/`.all`, `self` keyword (v1.49.0), typechecking catching silent always-false permissions.
3. [Consistency](https://authzed.com/docs/spicedb/concepts/consistency), AuthZed (SpiceDB docs). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: caches and the New Enemy Problem; defaults (writes fully_consistent, others minimize_latency); minimize_latency, at_least_as_fresh, at_exact_snapshot (Snapshot Expired after GC), fully_consistent (bypasses cache); CockroachDB caveat (fully_consistent isn't read-after-write, max_offset default 500 ms); ZedTokens = zookies; when to store them (varchar(1024) suggestion); Zanzibar needs ContentChangeCheck; quantization interval flag for ignoring tokens.
4. [OpenFGA Concepts](https://openfga.dev/docs/concepts). See `authorization-models` #5.
5. [Query Consistency Modes](https://openfga.dev/docs/interacting/consistency), OpenFGA authors. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: MINIMIZE_LATENCY (default) vs HIGHER_CONSISTENCY; write-then-check may miss the write when served from cache; caching disabled by default (then always strong); cache flags (check-query-cache, iterator cache, cache controller); zookie-like tokens only "considered" for future releases.

#### `new-enemy-problem` (short)

1. [Zanzibar](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/atc19-pang.pdf). See `zanzibar` #1. §2.2 is the definition, examples A and B, and the zookie protocol; §5 why Lamport clocks don't fit (humans as "processes").
2. [Enforcing Causal Ordering in Distributed Systems: The Importance of Permissions Checking](https://authzed.com/blog/new-enemies), Jake Moshenko, AuthZed, 2021. Blog by SpiceDB's builders, primary: yes. Seen: door-code story; replication delay breaking causal order; permissions and data as an ad-hoc distributed system; showing an old copy leaks nothing new; zookie portmanteau; write/read pseudocode storing the zookie with content; false negatives allowed, no false positives; optionally refresh the zookie on permission changes. Says it uses Zanzibar terms and will be updated.
3. [Consistency](https://authzed.com/docs/spicedb/concepts/consistency). See `zanzibar` #3. Used for how a real system exposes the choice per request.

#### `multi-tenancy` (deep)

1. [Multi-tenant SaaS partitioning models for PostgreSQL](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/saas-multitenant-managed-postgresql/partitioning-models.html), AWS Prescriptive Guidance. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: overview trade-off table for silo, pool, bridge; sub-pages silo.html (instance per tenant, eliminates noisy neighbor, driven by compliance, cost/onboarding/mapping downsides), pool.html (single instance with RLS, cheaper, per-tenant monitoring needs instrumentation, noisy neighbor can't be eliminated, some customers want more than RLS), bridge.html (database or schema per tenant on shared instance; same noisy-neighbor issues as pool).
2. [Tenancy models for a multitenant solution](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/tenancy-models), John Downs and others, Microsoft. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: defining a tenant (B2B, B2C); commercial decision; tenants vs deployments (stamps), mapping layer; isolation as a spectrum per tier; security (tenant and user identity in authz), cost, performance, reliability; automated single-tenant, fully multitenant, vertically and horizontally partitioned deployments; test your isolation.
3. [Multitenant SaaS database tenancy patterns](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/saas-tenancy-app-design-patterns), Microsoft (Azure SQL docs). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: switching models is costly; standalone app, database per tenant (customization, per-tenant restore, elastic pools, 20 indexes to 20,000), multi-tenant database (tenant ID columns, no per-tenant resource view, noisy neighbors, hard single-tenant restore), sharded multi-tenant (catalog, split/merge, tenant ID leads the primary key), hybrid (move tenants between shared and dedicated databases), comparison table.
4. [Noisy Neighbor antipattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/antipatterns/noisy-neighbor/noisy-neighbor), Microsoft. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: definition; many small tenants peaking together; can't completely avoid; client and provider actions (per-tenant monitoring, quotas, throttling, rebalancing, restricting expensive operations, QoS); treat as resource governance; detection.
5. [Multi-tenant data isolation with PostgreSQL Row Level Security](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/multi-tenant-data-isolation-with-postgresql-row-level-security/), Michael Beardsley, AWS, 2020. Blog, primary: no (AWS didn't build RLS). Seen: silo/bridge/pool; pool relies on the right WHERE clause in every statement; RLS as an automatic WHERE clause, since 9.5; SELECT silently filtered, UPDATE/DELETE 0 rows, INSERT errors; table owner and BYPASSRLS bypass; role per tenant doesn't scale; `current_setting('app.current_tenant')` pattern; set on every pool checkout; session variables vs pgBouncer; test views and functions. Its Java example builds the SET statement by string concatenation.
6. [Authorization Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html). See `authorization-models` #1. RBAC poorly suited to multi-tenant and cross-organization access.

#### `row-level-security` (short)

1. [5.9. Row Security Policies](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: default deny; TRUNCATE and REFERENCES not covered; policy evaluated before user conditions except leakproof functions; superusers, BYPASSRLS and table owners bypass (FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY); permissive OR vs restrictive AND; implicit WITH CHECK; passwd example; restrictive policy for local-socket admin; referential integrity bypasses RLS (covert channel); `row_security = off` errors instead of filtering, for backups; policies reading other tables can race under READ COMMITTED (mallory example) and the fixes.
2. [CREATE POLICY](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createpolicy.html), PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: USING vs WITH CHECK; silent filter vs error; PERMISSIVE/RESTRICTIVE semantics; per-command rules (ALL, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, ON CONFLICT, RETURNING); Table 300; combining policies; notes on constraint side channels, LEAKPROOF, views using the owner's rights unless security_invoker; a PostgreSQL extension.
3. [Multi-tenant data isolation with PostgreSQL Row Level Security](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/multi-tenant-data-isolation-with-postgresql-row-level-security/). See `multi-tenancy` #5.

Extra: [PostgreSQL 9.5 release notes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/9.5.0/), note already existed. Opened E.26.3.5: "Add row-level security control" with CREATE/ALTER/DROP POLICY. Claim appended to the note.

#### `audit-logging` (short)

1. [Logging Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series contributors. Docs, primary: no. Seen: security vs operational uses; audit trails; non-repudiation hard for logs; audit logs kept separate; PCI DSS audit log definition; the app as main event source; separate write-only DB account; which events to always log (authn/authz failures, admin actions, privilege changes, exports); when/where/who/what attributes, interaction identifier; data to exclude; log injection; logging failures shouldn't stop the app; can't disable compliance logging; protection at rest and in transit (tamper detection, read-only media); retention both ways; attacks on logs.
2. [Validating CloudTrail log file integrity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html), AWS CloudTrail User Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: SHA-256 hashes and SHA-256 with RSA signatures; hourly digest files listing log hashes; digests signed per Region; each digest carries the previous digest's signature; separate folder; S3 MFA Delete; enabling doesn't validate; CLI or custom validation.

Extra: [Efficient Data Structures for Tamper-Evident Logging](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/sec09/tech/full_papers/crosby.pdf), Scott Crosby, Dan Wallach, USENIX Security 2009. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: untrusted logger model with clients and auditors; tamper evidence requires auditing; hash chains need linear proofs, history tree gives logarithmic membership and incremental proofs; Merkle aggregation for safe deletion. Not given a note: a short node doesn't need it, but it's the core source for a tamper-evident-log node if one is added.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- RBAC vs ABAC/ReBAC: OWASP says prefer ABAC and ReBAC for applications; NIST SP 800-162 (by some of RBAC's authors) stresses that ABAC needs far more trust relationships and depends on attribute authorities. The article presents both costs.
- Consistency in Zanzibar clones: SpiceDB has ZedTokens and per-request levels; OpenFGA, when this was written, has only "skip the cache" and says zookie-like tokens are under consideration. SpiceDB's own docs say fully_consistent isn't read-after-write on CockroachDB. So "Zanzibar-style" doesn't imply "solves the new enemy problem".
- Staleness defaults: Zanzibar and SpiceDB default to a recent, cache-friendly snapshot; the price is late grants (false negatives), accepted on purpose (AuthZed blog).
- Silo vs pool: AWS says silo "completely eliminates" noisy neighbors (at the database), while Azure frames isolation as a per-tier spectrum where shared tiers still carry the risk.
- Logging failures: OWASP says a logging failure shouldn't stop the application, while also saying compliance logging must not be deactivatable. For audit trails these pull in different directions.

**Couldn't open:**

- Nothing needed failed to open. The NIST RBAC model paper (Sandhu, Ferraiolo, Kuhn 2000) downloaded but has no text layer, so it wasn't read.

**Rejected:**

- [SaaS Tenant Isolation Strategies](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/saas-tenant-isolation-strategies/saas-tenant-isolation-strategies.html), AWS whitepaper, 2020. The page says it's "for historical reference only" and may be outdated; the Prescriptive Guidance pages cover the same models.
- MDN and vendor marketing pages on RBAC/ABAC: secondary, and NIST plus OWASP cover the same ground.

**Gaps:**

- No primary source opened for policy-as-code engines (OPA/Rego, AWS Cedar) or XACML beyond NIST's mention; the authorization-models article leaves them out.
- The Zanzibar paper doesn't give its default staleness value, only that it's tuned from measurements; the article gives none.
- No source opened with numbers on how common cross-tenant leaks are; the multi-tenancy article has none.
- No first-party Postgres docs page for PgBouncer's pooling modes was opened here; the RLS article defers to `db-connection-pooling` for which modes break session variables.
- AWS's bridge page opens with "you provision a single PostgreSQL instance for each tenant", which contradicts its own diagrams (one shared instance); treated as a typo and not quoted.

### Attacks and defenses

#### `owasp-api-top-10` (short)

1. [OWASP Top 10 API Security Risks – 2023](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10/), OWASP API Security Project, 2023. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: the ten 2023 risks with a paragraph each (API1 BOLA, API2 broken authentication, API3 broken object property level authorization = 2019's Excessive Data Exposure + Mass Assignment, API4 unrestricted resource consumption incl. paid SMS/email, API5 BFLA, API6 sensitive business flows "doesn't necessarily come from implementation bugs", API7 SSRF, API8 misconfiguration, API9 improper inventory, API10 unsafe consumption of APIs); page navigation shows the 2019 list (API8:2019 Injection, API10:2019 Insufficient Logging & Monitoring); site lists only 2019 and 2023 editions, so 2023 is current.
2. [Methodology and Data](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xd0-about-data/), OWASP API Security Project, 2023. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: public call for data produced nothing usable for statistics; incident data from bug bounty platforms and public reports, 2019 to 2022; OWASP Risk Rating Methodology, prevalence by team consensus; "Injection" and "Vulnerable and Outdated Components" left out as generic risks that don't behave differently in APIs; doesn't replace other Top 10 lists; "forward-looking awareness document for the next three or four years".

Extra: [Release Notes](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x04-release-notes/) and [Introduction](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x03-introduction/), 2023. Opened: second edition four years after the first; merge of API3; new API6 and API10; list of other OWASP Top 10 projects. Not given notes; the list page and methodology cover the node.

#### `bola` (short)

1. [API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/), OWASP API Security Project, 2023. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: exploitability easy, prevalence widespread, detectability easy; IDs can be integers, UUIDs, strings, in path, query, headers or body; common because servers rely on client-sent IDs; comparing session user ID with the ID parameter isn't sufficient; BOLA vs BFLA; scenarios (shop revenue by shop name, car VIN, GraphQL deleteReports); prevention: check per function, prefer random GUIDs, write tests and block deploys.
2. [Insecure Direct Object Reference Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Insecure_Direct_Object_Reference_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Docs, primary: no. Seen: three ingredients of an IDOR; /users/123 to 124, hidden form field, file names; complex IDs still need checks; testing with User A and User B across read/create/update/delete/export/admin; scope lookups to the user's dataset (Rails `@current_user.projects.find`); random IDs as defense in depth; don't encrypt identifiers.
3. [RFC 9562](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9562). Note exists. Section 8: UUIDs "MUST NOT be used as security capabilities"; use UUIDv4 over v7 for anything security-related.

#### `sql-injection` (short)

1. [SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Docs, primary: no. Seen: cause is string concatenation with user input; four defenses (parameterized queries, safe stored procedures, allow-list validation for identifiers and sort order, escaping "STRONGLY DISCOURAGED"); `tom' or '1'='1` matched literally; HQL injection; stored procedures safe only without dynamic SQL; map parameters to fixed table/column names; convert input to non-string types; least privilege, views, never DBA for app accounts; validated data isn't safe for string building.
2. [Command Execution Functions (libpq)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/libpq-exec.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, PostgreSQL 18. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: PQexec accepts multiple statements separated by semicolons; PQexecParams sends parameters separately, "avoiding the need for tedious and error-prone quoting and escaping"; PQexecParams allows at most one statement, a protocol limit that helps against injection; PQescapeLiteral/PQescapeIdentifier; escaping a value passed as a parameter is "neither necessary nor correct".

Extra: [PREPARE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-prepare.html), PostgreSQL 18. Opened: server-side prepared statements, `$1` parameters, session lifetime, performance motivation. Not given a note; libpq-exec covers the injection side.

#### `ssrf` (deep)

1. [API7:2023 Server Side Request Forgery](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa7-server-side-request-forgery/), OWASP API Security Project, 2023. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: basic vs blind SSRF; impact incl. port scanning, bypassing firewalls; webhooks, URL fetch, custom SSO and previews make it common; cloud, Kubernetes and Docker control channels over HTTP make it dangerous; can't always be eliminated; profile-picture port scan via timing; webhook test request leaking `169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/...`; prevention: isolate the fetcher, allow-lists, disable redirects, well-tested URL parser, no raw responses.
2. [Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Docs, primary: no. Seen: SSRF over other schemes (file, phar, gopher, data, dict); two cases (known destinations: allow-list; any destination: block-list); disable redirects; IP parsers tested against hex/octal/dword/URL/mixed encodings; DNS resolution during validation can be abused ("DNS pinning"); resolution happens again when the request runs; don't accept full URLs, match host and build the request yourself; parser disagreement example `http://example.com\@evil.com` (WHATWG vs CPython urllib); network segregation; check all A and AAAA records; HTTP/HTTPS only; IMDSv2 as defense in depth; minimum deny-list table.
3. [Server-side request forgery (SSRF)](https://portswigger.net/web-security/ssrf), PortSwigger Web Security Academy. Docs, primary: no. Seen: localhost trust (access check in a front component, recovery login, admin port); weaker internal systems; bypasses: 2130706433, 017700000001, 127.1, own domain resolving to 127.0.0.1, URL encoding, redirects, `@`, `#`, `expected-host.evil-host`, open redirects; blind SSRF; URLs in XML (XXE) and Referer headers.
4. [Add defense in depth against open firewalls, reverse proxies, and SSRF vulnerabilities with enhancements to the EC2 Instance Metadata Service](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/defense-in-depth-open-firewalls-reverse-proxies-ssrf-vulnerabilities-ec2-instance-metadata-service/), Colm MacCárthaigh, AWS, 2019. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: IMDS on link-local 169.254.169.254 hands out temporary role credentials; IMDSv2 session via PUT and secret token; PUT stops most open WAFs; X-Forwarded-For refused (open reverse proxies); static-header defenses fail when SSRF lets attackers set headers; PUT + token protects against "the vast majority" of SSRF (AWS analysis, no numbers); IP TTL 1 on token response; v1 and v2 both on by default at launch; ec2:RoleDelivery IAM condition key.
5. [Use the Instance Metadata Service to access instance metadata](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/configuring-instance-metadata-service.html), Amazon EC2 User Guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: by default either v1 or v2 works; can require v2 per instance; token TTL 1 s to 6 h; PUT `/latest/api/token`, `X-aws-ec2-metadata-token` header; 401 without valid token when required; PUT with X-Forwarded-For rejected; hop limit 1 by default; IPv6 endpoint `[fd00:ec2::254]` on Nitro.
6. [Smokescreen](https://github.com/stripe/smokescreen), Stripe. Code (README), primary: yes. Seen: HTTP CONNECT egress proxy for most of Stripe's outbound traffic incl. webhooks; resolves each name and allows only publicly routable IPs, to stop webhooks scanning the internal network; mTLS client identity and per-client ACLs; `--deny-range`/`--allow-range`; stable egress IPs for partners; warning that a hostname deny-list doesn't block the destination IP.

Extra: [RFC 6890](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6890). Note exists (special-purpose address blocks). Not cited; the OWASP deny-list and the phase 2 `ip-addressing` node cover the ranges.
Extra: [Configure instance metadata options for new instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/configuring-IMDS-new-instances.html), Amazon EC2 User Guide. Opened: account-level default to make new instances IMDSv2-only, hop limit 2 for containers. Not given a note.

#### `same-origin-policy` (short)

1. [RFC 6454](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6454), Adam Barth, 2011. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: section 3 principles (trust by URI; origin = scheme, host, port; why scheme and why full host; granularity "a historical artifact"; authority by media type; object access only same-origin; reading cross-origin forbidden, sending permitted, embedding scripts/images/styles allowed; CORS as opt-in; image height and width leak; sending requests gives rise to CSRF; blocking would break hyperlinks); section 7 Origin header and "null" for privacy-sensitive contexts; section 8 reliance on DNS, cookies predate origins, ambient authority and XSS.
2. [Same-origin policy](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Same-origin_policy), MDN Web Docs. Docs, primary: no. Seen: webmail and intranet motivation; origin comparison table; inherited and file origins; document.domain deprecated; cross-origin writes allowed, embedding allowed, reads disallowed but leaked by embedding; CORS to allow, CSRF tokens to block writes; postMessage.

#### `csrf` (short)

1. [Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Docs, primary: no. Seen: definition; browsers include cookies automatically; XSS defeats all mitigations; tokens "still essential" for cookie-authenticated apps; Fetch Metadata allowed when targeting modern browsers, with a mandatory fallback; Go 1.25 CrossOriginProtection; synchronizer tokens, signed double-submit bound to the session (HMAC), naive double-submit bypassable by cookie-writing subdomains; custom headers subject to same-origin policy; no state change on GET; SameSite as defense in depth.
2. [Cross-Site Request Forgery](https://words.filippo.io/csrf/), Filippo Valsorda, 2025. Blog, primary: yes (research behind Go 1.25's middleware). Seen: CSRF as confused deputy using cookies or network position; CSRF vs CORS; same-site vs same-origin (subdomains, schemeless vs schemeful); tokens turn forgery into a leak problem; Origin header caveats, null means cross-origin; SameSite not cross-origin, Lax-by-default "mostly failed"; non-simple requests; Sec-Fetch-Site in all major browsers since 2023, only sent to trustworthy origins; five-step algorithm; Go 1.25 CrossOriginProtection; Private Network Access for network-position attacks; API traffic generally not a CSRF target.

Extra: [net/http CrossOriginProtection](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#CrossOriginProtection), Go 1.25. Opened: rejects non-safe cross-origin browser requests using Sec-Fetch-Site or Origin vs Host; safe methods always allowed; requests without either header allowed. Not cited (the `go-net-http` note exists but wasn't appended; Valsorda's post covers the same algorithm).

#### `cors` (deep)

1. [Fetch Living Standard](https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/), WHATWG. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: 3.3 CORS protocol for server developers: opt-in to protect intranets and credentialed data; preflight for anything beyond a form; Origin also sent on all non-GET/HEAD requests; ACAO is the literal Origin or `*`; Max-Age default 5 s, browsers may cap; preflight needs ok status; side channels like timing; preflight never has credentials; credentials table (no `*`, `true` case-sensitive, no trailing slash); Expose-Headers; safelisted methods GET/HEAD/POST, safelisted Content-Type values, 128-byte limit; CORS unsafe for IP/firewall-protected resources, `*` otherwise safe ("curl and wget" rule); `Vary: Origin`; supersedes RFC 6454's Origin semantics.
2. [Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS), MDN Web Docs. Docs, primary: no. Seen: why simple requests skip preflight (HTML forms could always send them); "simple request" is a term from the obsolete CORS spec; Safari preflights nonstandard Accept/Accept-Language/Content-Language values; preflight example with Max-Age 86400; Authorization header triggers preflight; no credentials by default; credentialed simple GET isn't preflighted but the response is hidden; preflights never include credentials.
3. [How to win at CORS](https://jakearchibald.com/2021/cors/), Jake Archibald, 2021. Blog, primary: no. Seen: no-CORS embeds leak (Yahoo Mail CSS example); SOP from Netscape 2; origins vs sites and the public suffix list; why dropping credentials wasn't enough (intranets, routers, IoT); Flash crossdomain.xml history; header opt-in; Vary with Origin and Cookie, cloud storage hosts getting it wrong; preflight has no credentials, must be 2xx; preflight only approves the request; Max-Age caps in 2021 (Chrome 600 s, Firefox 86400 s).
4. [Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS)](https://portswigger.net/web-security/cors), PortSwigger Web Security Academy. Docs, primary: no. Seen: CORS is not a CSRF defense; reflected Origin with credentials; prefix/suffix/regex matching errors; `null` origin via sandboxed iframes; trusting XSS-prone subdomains; trusting http:// subdomains breaks TLS; without credentials only public content, except intranets where `*` turns browsers into proxies.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- CSRF tokens vs Fetch Metadata: OWASP's cheat sheet still calls tokens "essential" for cookie-authenticated apps and allows Fetch Metadata only when targeting modern browsers; Valsorda (and Go 1.25) argue Sec-Fetch-Site plus an Origin fallback makes tokens unnecessary. The csrf article presents both.
- Random IDs for BOLA: OWASP API1 lists "prefer random GUIDs" under prevention; the IDOR cheat sheet calls them defense in depth; RFC 9562 says UUIDs must not be security capabilities. The bola article treats them as an extra layer only.
- IMDSv2: AWS says PUT plus token stops "the vast majority" of SSRF, from its own analysis with no numbers; the OWASP cheat sheet says it "mitigates some of the instances". The article reports AWS's claim as AWS's.
- OWASP API Top 10 ranking is team consensus, not measured data (the call for data failed). The owasp-api-top-10 article says so.
- SameSite: Lax-by-default was meant to end most CSRF; Valsorda says the rollout "mostly failed" and current defaults aren't a defense. No browser vendor source opened.
- Naming: the OWASP SSRF cheat sheet calls the check-then-resolve-again trick "DNS pinning"; Valsorda's post and common usage say DNS rebinding. The ssrf article gives both names.

**Couldn't open:**

- https://owasp.org/www-project-api-security/ (the project home page) returned 404 with and without a trailing slash. The edition pages under /API-Security/ opened fine.

**Rejected:**

- MDN's CSRF glossary and PortSwigger's CSRF page: not opened, since the OWASP cheat sheet plus Valsorda's post (primary for Go's design) cover the short node.
- OWASP Top 10 (general web, 2021/2025 editions): not opened; the API list is the node. Mentioned only as "OWASP's other Top 10 lists" from the methodology page.
- Capital One breach write-ups as an SSRF case study: not researched, and no primary source opened, so no incident story in the article.
- Orange Tsai's "A New Era of SSRF" talk (linked from both OWASP and PortSwigger): a PDF of slides; the parser-disagreement example the article uses is in the OWASP cheat sheet itself.

**Gaps:**

- No source opened on drivers that "emulate" prepared statements by interpolating on the client (e.g. some PHP or Go simple-protocol modes). The sql-injection article doesn't discuss it.
- No source on Postgres's extended query protocol messages (Parse/Bind/Execute); the article stays at the libpq level.
- Current (not 2021) per-browser Access-Control-Max-Age caps: only Archibald's 2021 numbers; the article dates them.
- Private Network Access (browser protection for intranets and routers): mentioned in one line from Valsorda's footnote; no Chrome/WICG source opened.
- No source on GCP or Azure metadata protections beyond the OWASP deny-list naming their addresses; the ssrf article only details AWS.
- IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses as an SSRF bypass: not in any opened SSRF source (RFC 6890 lists `::ffff:0:0/96` but doesn't discuss SSRF), so not claimed.

### Attacks and defenses (secrets, keys, trust, supply chain)

#### `secrets-management` (short)

1. [Secrets Management Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Docs, primary: no. Seen: secrets hardcoded and shared across services; least privilege on the store; dynamic secrets that expire on restart; automated rotation (and that rotating encryption keys can force re-encryption); lifecycle creation, rotation, revocation, expiration; user passwords excluded from scheduled rotation; audit list; secrets store as a dependency, break-glass credentials; consumer fetches its own secret; no secrets in docker ENV/ARG, env vars discouraged; keys not next to what they encrypt unless wrapped (envelope encryption); KMS API limits; incident steps revoke, rotate, delete, log; detection with pre-commit hooks.
2. [Lease, renew, and revoke](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/concepts/lease), HashiCorp, Vault v2.x docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: every dynamic secret gets a lease with a TTL; expired leases revoked automatically; leases force check-ins, making audit logs and key rolling easier; KV store issues no leases; renewal increment is advisory and counted from now; revoking by path prefix after an intrusion; revoking a token revokes its leases.
3. [Database secrets engine](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/secrets/databases), HashiCorp, Vault v2.x docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: dynamic roles create a database user per request with a lease; unique credentials per service instance make audits traceable to one instance; Vault's own privileged "root" database user creates and revokes the others; static roles rotate one existing user's password; rotating root credentials placed in a static role breaks every managed user.
4. [What is Vault?](https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/about-vault/what-is-vault), HashiCorp, Vault v2.x docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: authenticate, get a token tied to policies, access secrets by path, every request audited; storage options. Not used (the lease page carries the concrete mechanism).
5. [Secrets](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/secret/), Kubernetes docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: Secrets stored unencrypted in etcd by default; anyone who can create a Pod in a namespace can read its Secrets; base64 "obscured but not secret"; immutable Secrets since v1.21; short-lived ServiceAccount tokens via TokenRequest since v1.22. Not used (short node, three sources were enough; OWASP 5.3 carries the "encrypt the orchestrator's store" point). Good for `kubernetes` or a future Kubernetes-security node.

#### `envelope-encryption` (short)

1. [Envelope encryption](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/envelope-encryption), Google Cloud KMS docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: DEK and KEK definitions; DEK practices (generate locally, new DEK per write so no rotation, one DEK per user, AES-256-GCM, store near the data, never plaintext); KEK stored centrally, never leaves KMS; KMS Encrypt/Decrypt capped at 64 KiB; encrypt and decrypt flows; Google Cloud encrypts stored data this way by default.
2. [AWS KMS cryptography essentials](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/kms-cryptography.html), AWS KMS developer guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: definition; key chains end in a plaintext root key that stays in the HSM; encrypted data key stored next to the data; re-encrypt only the data key to put data under another key; symmetric HSM operations are AES-256-GCM.
3. [Rotate AWS KMS keys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html), AWS KMS developer guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: yearly automatic rotation by default, custom periods, on-demand; old key material kept and picked automatically on decrypt; rotation doesn't rotate data keys or re-encrypt data, doesn't help if a data key leaked; data keys best used once or a few times (key exhaustion); wrapping keys rarely at risk; rotation often required by rules.
4. [Generate data keys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/data-keys.html), AWS KMS developer guide. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: GenerateDataKey returns plaintext and encrypted copies; KMS doesn't store or use data keys; remove plaintext key from memory after use. Not used (Google's page covers the same flow).

#### `zero-trust` (short)

1. [SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-207.pdf), Rose, Borchert, Mitchell, Connelly, NIST, 2020. Spec, primary: no. Seen: definition (no implicit trust from location or ownership; per-request least-privilege decisions; network viewed as compromised); PDP/PEP and shrinking the implicit trust zone (airport example); seven tenets; service identity counts as client identity; components PE, PA, PEP; threats (PE/PA subversion, PE/PA outage stops everything, stolen credentials still work within their grants); hybrid perimeter/ZT for a long time.
2. [BeyondProd](https://cloud.google.com/docs/security/beyondprod), Google Cloud, 2024 version. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: zero trust between production services; no inherent trust between services; edge perimeter kept for DoS; ALTS mutual auth with identities bound to services not hosts; Binary Authorization for Borg (code provenance at deploy); end-user context tickets forwarded along call chains; every hop checks caller, ticket and user.
3. [BeyondCorp: A New Approach to Enterprise Security](https://research.google/pubs/beyondcorp-a-new-approach-to-enterprise-security/), Ward and Beyer, ;login: 2014. Paper, primary: yes. Seen (PDF): castle-and-moat critique; treat the internal network like the internet; access from user and device credentials, not location; device certificates plus inventory; internet-facing access proxy; per-request access control engine; phased migration off the VPN.

#### `supply-chain-security` (short)

1. [Supply chain threats](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.2/threats-overview), SLSA v1.2, OpenSSF. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: integrity first, availability second; source vs build integrity; lettered attack points A to I with incidents (SushiSwap, PHP git server, The Great Suspender, SolarWinds, CodeCov, package mirrors, Browserify typosquatting, default credentials); dependency threats recursive (event-stream); what SLSA doesn't cover (malicious producers, typosquatting, disappearing packages).
2. [Build: Track Basics](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.2/build-track-basics), SLSA v1.2. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: L0 to L3; L1 provenance exists but is trivial to forge; L2 signed by a hosted platform, consumer verifies; L3 hardened, signing key out of reach of build steps; v1.0 dropped the source track and v1.2 brings it back.
3. [Go Modules Reference](https://go.dev/ref/mod), Go docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: no lock file, MVS deterministic; go.sum SHA-256 (h1) hashes of all dependencies; mismatch is a security error; checksum database (sum.golang.org), a Merkle-tree transparent log, makes untrusted proxies safe and catches retagged versions; GOPRIVATE/GONOSUMDB/GOSUMDB=off skip verification.
4. [2026 Minimum Elements for an SBOM](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/2026-minimum-elements-software-bill-materials-sbom), CISA, NSA, FBI and partners, 2026. Spec, primary: no. Seen: replaces NTIA's 2021 minimum elements; SBOM as nested ingredient list; coverage includes transitive dependencies so a missing component rules out a CVE; new fields (author signature, component hash, license, generation context); SPDX and CycloneDX; "will not resolve all" supply chain concerns.
5. [Module Mirror and Checksum Database Launched](https://go.dev/blog/module-mirror-launch), Katie Hockman, Go blog, 2019. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: go.sum alone is trust on first use; the checksum database makes everyone's go.sum lines the same; on by default from Go 1.13. Not used (the Go Modules Reference covers the current behaviour).
6. [Supply chain threats (v1.0)](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/threats-overview), SLSA. Seen: marked "Status: Retired". Replaced by #1.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Rotation. OWASP pushes regular rotation of secrets; AWS says wrapping keys are almost never used enough to need rotating for cryptographic reasons, and that rotating the KMS key doesn't touch data keys or data. Both hold: rotate what's exposed and used a lot (data keys, credentials), and know that rotating a KEK doesn't protect old data from a leaked DEK.
- Environment variables. Passing config through the environment is common practice (not checked against a source here); OWASP discourages env vars for secrets (visible to all processes, can end up in logs and dumps). `configuration` should point secrets to `secrets-management`.
- Perimeter or not. NIST and BeyondCorp say drop implicit trust from the network; BeyondProd still keeps an edge perimeter for DoS. Zero trust removes trust from the network, not the network controls.
- Lock files. npm, Cargo and others record exact versions in a lock file; Go deliberately has none (MVS is deterministic) and relies on go.sum plus a public checksum log. Both aim at "the same bytes every build".

**Couldn't open:** none.

**Rejected:**
- Vendor product pages (Vault marketing, AWS Secrets Manager landing page): no mechanism.
- NTIA's 2021 minimum elements PDF: opened, but replaced by the 2026 CISA guidance.

**Gaps:**
- No primary source read on Sigstore (keyless signing, Rekor); the article talks about signed provenance at the SLSA level only.
- No source on npm/Cargo lock files was opened; the article uses Go as the worked example.
- No measurement of KMS call latency; the envelope article gives no number for it.

## Phase 16: Data systems

Researched by 4 parallel passes, one per group below.

### Analytical storage

#### `oltp-vs-olap` (deep)

1. ["One Size Fits All": An Idea Whose Time Has Come and Gone](https://cs.brown.edu/~ugur/fits_all.pdf), Stonebraker and Çetintemel, ICDE, 2005. Position paper by database builders, primary: yes. Seen: early relational systems built for OLTP (rows, B-trees, cost-based optimizer, ACID); warehouses from the early 1990s; about 50 operational systems per large enterprise; admins keep ad-hoc BI queries off them; BI wants history and cross-system data; star schema figure (SALES fact table, STORE/TIME/PRODUCT/CUSTOMER dimensions); bitmap indexes vs B-trees; materialized views "never in OLTP"; vendors ship two engines behind one parser; state coded in six bits; section 5.1 row stores write-optimized, warehouses read-optimized, column stores.
2. [C-Store: A Column-oriented DBMS](https://www.vldb.org/archives/website/2005/program/paper/thu/p553-stonebraker.pdf), Stonebraker, Abadi et al., VLDB, 2005. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: row store = write-optimized, one disk write per record, suits OLTP; read-optimized for warehouses (bulk load then long query periods); trade CPU for disk bandwidth; six-bit states, dense packing N*K bits; operate on compressed data; tension between updates and read layout; writeable store + tuple mover + read-optimized store; projections in several sort orders.
3. [What is OLAP?](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/olap), Al Brown, ClickHouse docs. Vendor docs, primary: yes (vendor of an OLAP engine). Seen: OLAP vs OLTP definitions; Codd 1993; "online" means interactive; OLTP/OLAP comparison table (storage, read and write patterns, concurrency, schema); cubes (MOLAP/ROLAP/HOLAP) to columnar engines; Sybase IQ 1994, Vertica 2007; wide-column stores are row stores; Postgres is OLTP, Citus/Timescale/pg_duckdb add limited analytics; Postgres + CDC + OLAP pattern; HTAP named; OLAP is not the same as a data warehouse.
4. [What is ClickHouse?](https://clickhouse.com/docs/intro), ClickHouse docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: OLTP reads/writes a few rows in milliseconds vs analytics over billions of rows; row vs column orientation; blocks read whole from disk; example query over 100 million rows reading a few of 100+ columns (92 ms on their playground, hardware unstated).
5. [DuckDB: an Embeddable Analytical Database](https://mytherin.github.io/papers/2019-duckdbdemo.pdf), Raasveldt and Mühleisen, SIGMOD demo, 2019. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: embedded vs stand-alone grid against OLTP vs OLAP; SQLite row-major engine on B-trees, poor on OLAP; requirement: OLAP efficiency without completely sacrificing OLTP (dashboards updating and querying); vectorized interpreted engine chosen over JIT for portability; vectors of 1024.
6. [The Design and Implementation of Modern Column-Oriented Database Systems](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-column-stores.pdf): see `column-storage` #2 (row vs column seek trade-off, updates).

#### `column-storage` (deep)

1. [Column-Stores vs. Row-Stores: How Different Are They Really?](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-sigmod08.pdf), Abadi, Madden, Hachem, SIGMOD, 2008. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: emulating a column store in a row store (vertical partitioning, index-only plans, materialized views) on SSBM scale 10; C-Store 6x faster than the row store, 3x faster than its materialized views; per-row overhead of vertical partitioning (about 8 bytes header, 4 bytes record id; 0.7 to 1.1 GB per column vs 240 MB in C-Store); compression up to an order of magnitude, late materialization about 3x, block iteration and invisible joins about 1.5x; virtual ids (i-th value is i-th row); RLE on sorted columns; light vs heavy compression.
2. [The Design and Implementation of Modern Column-Oriented Database Systems](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-column-stores.pdf), Abadi, Boncz, Harizopoulos, Idreos, Madden, Foundations and Trends in Databases, 2013. Survey monograph by the builders of C-Store, MonetDB and VectorWise, primary: yes. Seen: every major vendor shipped a column store by late 2013; figure 1.1 row vs column layouts; seek trade-off for single records; virtual ids and fixed-width arithmetic; late materialization; PAX; section 4.1 vectorized processing (vector of N tuples, N = 1000 in VectorWise, calls drop by the vector size, SIMD, parallel cache misses, not tied to column storage); 4.2 RLE, bit-vector, dictionary, frame of reference (1003... to 1000, 3, ...), patching; 4.7 updates: read-store and write-store, MonetDB delta columns, VectorWise positional delta trees. Tried the Harvard copy first (Access Denied); the UMD copy opened.
3. [C-Store: A Column-oriented DBMS](https://www.vldb.org/archives/website/2005/program/paper/thu/p553-stonebraker.pdf): see `oltp-vs-olap` #2.
4. [ClickHouse - Lightning Fast Analytics for Everyone](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p3731-schulze.pdf), Schulze et al., VLDB, 2024. Paper by ClickHouse's developers, primary: yes. Seen: immutable sorted parts, background merges, compared with LSM trees; bulk inserts (e.g. 20,000 rows) or async insert buffering; one file per column; granules of 8192 rows; 1 MB compressed blocks, LZ4 by default, chained codecs; sparse primary index (1000 entries for 8.1 million rows); mutations rewrite all parts, lightweight deletes via bitmap column; X100-style vectorized execution; SIMD kernels picked by cpuid; LLVM compilation of hot expressions; Photon paper on code generation being harder to debug. Features as of v24.6.
5. [What is OLAP?](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/olap): see `oltp-vs-olap` #3 (wide-column is not columnar).
6. [Apache Parquet format specification](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format): see `parquet` #1 (row groups of column chunks as the sliced layout).

#### `vectorized-execution` (short)

1. [MonetDB/X100: Hyper-Pipelining Query Execution](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2005/papers/P19.pdf), Boncz, Zukowski, Nes, CIDR, 2005. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: low IPC of databases on analytical work; Volcano tuple-at-a-time interpretation overhead; MySQL 4.1 TPC-H Q1 profile (10% real work, 28% hash table, rest record navigation; 38 instructions per addition); MonetDB/MIL memory-bound by full materialization; X100 vectors of about 1000 values in cache; primitives; selection vectors; default vector size 1024, 128 to 8K work well, degrades out of cache (figure 10).
2. [Execution Format](https://duckdb.org/docs/current/internals/vector.html), DuckDB docs (current). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: vectorized model with fixed-size vectors; STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE 2048; DataChunk; flat, constant, dictionary and sequence vectors; unified vector format; string_t with 12-byte inlining. The /stable/ URL redirects to /current/.
3. [DuckDB: an Embeddable Analytical Database](https://mytherin.github.io/papers/2019-duckdbdemo.pdf): see `oltp-vs-olap` #5 (vectorized over JIT for portability; 1024 then vs 2048 now).
4. [ClickHouse - Lightning Fast Analytics for Everyone](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol17/p3731-schulze.pdf): see `column-storage` #4 (SIMD kernels, LLVM compilation alongside vectorization).
5. [The Design and Implementation of Modern Column-Oriented Database Systems](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-column-stores.pdf): see `column-storage` #2, section 4.1. Not cited in the article (kept it to four sources), but it's the best single summary of the advantages.

#### `parquet` (short)

1. [Apache Parquet format specification](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format), Apache Parquet contributors (README of parquet-format, master when read). Spec, primary: yes. Seen: glossary (row group, column chunk, page); unit of parallelization; file layout with PAR1 magic, footer, 4-byte little-endian footer length; footer written last for single-pass writes; Thrift compact protocol; minimal physical types (no int16); logical types; min/max statistics at several levels; Dremel definition and repetition levels; nulls in definition levels (1000 nulls = one run); dictionary page first; optional page index; CRC32 page checksums; error recovery (corrupt footer loses file); row groups 512 MB to 1 GB, pages 8 KB.
2. [Parquet encoding definitions](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/Encodings.md), Apache Parquet contributors. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: PLAIN (little-endian, 4-byte length prefix for byte arrays); dictionary with fallback to plain; RLE/bit-packing hybrid; DELTA_BINARY_PACKED (varints, zigzag, miniblocks; all-equal block packs to zero bits); delta-length and delta strings; byte stream split; ALP (in preview when read); BIT_PACKED deprecated.
3. [Parquet Page Index](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/PageIndex.md), Apache Parquet contributors. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: ColumnIndex and OffsetIndex; problem with page stats inside page headers; goals for point lookups and range scans on the sort column. Not used (the README covers what the article needs).
4. [Compression.md](https://github.com/apache/parquet-format/blob/master/Compression.md), Apache Parquet contributors. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: codec list (UNCOMPRESSED, SNAPPY, GZIP, LZO, BROTLI, LZ4 deprecated, ZSTD, LZ4_RAW); pages compressed as-is. Not used.

#### `data-warehouse` (short)

1. ["One Size Fits All"](https://cs.brown.edu/~ugur/fits_all.pdf): see `oltp-vs-olap` #1 (why warehouses exist, star schema, warehouse-specific features).
2. [Fact Tables and Dimension Tables](https://www.kimballgroup.com/2003/01/fact-tables-and-dimension-tables/), Ralph Kimball, Kimball Group (Intelligent Enterprise), 2003. Article by the originator of the techniques, primary: yes. Seen: measurements vs context; facts numeric; dimensions as clumps of context; fact table = foreign keys + facts; surrogate keys, not natural keys; slowly changing dimensions mentioned; dimensions left flat in second normal form.
3. [The Snowflake Elastic Data Warehouse](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15721-f24/papers/Snowflake.pdf), Dageville et al., SIGMOD, 2016 (copy on the CMU 15-721 page). Paper, primary: yes. Seen: traditional warehouse data came from internal systems; new semi-structured external data; deep ETL pipelines; shared-nothing couples compute and storage; loading vs querying want different hardware; immutable PAX files on S3, ranged GETs; min-max pruning instead of indexes (worked example); VARIANT enables ELT, "schema later"; ETL schema changes take months.
4. [What is a Data Warehouse?](https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/data-warehouse/), AWS. Vendor explainer, primary: no. Seen: central repository fed from transactional systems; tiers; data marts; data lakes. Thin; not used.
5. [Star Schemas and OLAP Cubes](https://www.kimballgroup.com/data-warehouse-business-intelligence-resources/kimball-techniques/dimensional-modeling-techniques/star-schema-olap-cube/), Kimball Group. Primary: yes. Seen: star schema definition; cubes derived from star schemas. Not used (the 2003 article covers it).

#### `etl-vs-elt` (short)

1. [The Snowflake Elastic Data Warehouse](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15721-f24/papers/Snowflake.pdf): see `data-warehouse` #3, section 4.3.
2. [Understanding ELT: Extract, Load, Transform](https://docs.getdbt.com/terms/elt), dbt Labs. Vendor glossary (makers of a transform tool), primary: no. Seen: ELT definition; transform uses the warehouse's compute; raw data kept; changed definitions applied to all history; idempotent rebuilds; ETL for strict governance (finance, healthcare); layered stored procedures as the real pain; typical transforms; dbt brings version control and tests.
3. [What's the Difference Between ETL and ELT?](https://aws.amazon.com/compare/the-difference-between-etl-and-elt/), AWS. Vendor explainer, primary: no. Seen: ETL uses a secondary processing server; ELT transforms in the warehouse; ETL needs up-front definition; PII masking; when ETL still fits (legacy, IoT filtering and averaging at the edge, mixed use); flat "ELT is faster" claim.
4. [What is ETL?](https://docs.getdbt.com/terms/etl), dbt Labs. Primary: no. Seen: downloaded and skimmed; same material as #2 from the other side. Not used.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Vectorized interpretation vs query compilation. DuckDB (2019) chose vectorized interpretation for portability, avoiding LLVM. ClickHouse (2024) uses both: vectorized by default, LLVM compilation for repeated hot expressions. The ClickHouse paper relays the Photon paper's view that code generation is harder to build and debug. No source compares them head to head.
- Vector size. X100 (2005) defaulted to 1024 and found 128 to 8K fine; DuckDB's 2019 paper says 1024; its current docs say 2048. VectorWise's "N = 1000" in the 2013 survey is the same idea rounded.
- How much of the column-store win is layout. The 2008 study says plain column layout without compression and late materialization doesn't beat a well-tuned row store by much; vendor pages credit columns alone. The article follows the 2008 study.
- ETL vs ELT framing. AWS calls ELT faster and "the standard choice" flatly; dbt concedes that much of ETL's pain was stored procedures, not the order of steps. Both are vendors with a stake. The Snowflake paper's argument (schema later, transforms in parallel SQL) is the most concrete.
- Cubes. ClickHouse calls cubes "largely a legacy pattern"; Kimball's techniques page still treats a cube as a common final deployment step. Different eras and different vendors.

**Couldn't open:**
- stratos.seas.harvard.edu copy of the 2013 column-store monograph (Access Denied); used the UMD copy.
- event.cwi.nl copy of the Snowflake paper (404); used the CMU 15-721 copy.
- Amazon Redshift Re-invented (SIGMOD 2022): the assets.amazon.science PDF link returned an empty file and the publication page is HTML only. Not used.

**Rejected:**
- DuckDB "Why DuckDB" page: opened and noted, then not needed (its claims duplicate the 2019 paper and the execution-format page); note removed.
- AWS "What is a Data Warehouse?" (thin), Kimball star-schema techniques page (covered by the 2003 article), dbt "What is ETL?" (duplicate), Parquet PageIndex.md and Compression.md (README is enough for a short node), parquet.apache.org configurations page (same text as the README's Configurations section).

**Gaps:**
- No measured numbers from this project. Every number in these articles is from a paper's own setup (2005 CPUs, a 2008 SSBM run, ClickHouse v24.6 defaults).
- No primary source opened for BigQuery/Dremel or Redshift; Dremel is only mentioned through the Parquet spec.
- No source on slowly changing dimensions beyond Kimball's one-line mention; the article only names the technique.
- No source for real-world Parquet writer defaults (row group sizes in Arrow, DuckDB or Spark). The article only gives the spec's HDFS-era recommendation.
- No HTAP primary source (TiDB, SingleStore, HyPer); HTAP is only named.
- DDIA chapter 3 (column-oriented storage) not opened.

### Analytical storage + Batch

#### `object-storage` (deep)

1. [What is Amazon S3?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html), Amazon Web Services. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: buckets, objects (data + metadata name-value pairs), keys, versions ("bucket + key + version" map); four bucket types (general purpose, directory, table, vector); directory buckets have hierarchical directories, general purpose are flat; S3 Express One Zone uses directory buckets; "Amazon S3 data consistency model": strong read-after-write for PUT and DELETE in all Regions, LIST included, HEAD/ACL/tags strongly consistent; single-key updates atomic; no locking, concurrent PUTs latest timestamp wins, last-writer-wins, order unpredictable; no atomic updates across keys; bucket configurations eventually consistent, wait 15 minutes after enabling versioning; W1/W2/R1/R2 concurrency examples; "Paying for Amazon S3" is pay-per-use.
2. [Naming Amazon S3 objects](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-keys.html), Amazon Web Services. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: UTF-8 keys up to 1,024 bytes; flat data model, no sub-buckets or sub-folders; console and SDKs infer folders from prefixes and `/`; console folder = zero-byte object; `./` and `../` key pitfalls.
3. [How to prevent object overwrites with conditional writes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-writes.html), Amazon Web Services. Docs, primary: yes. Note already existed (phase 5). Seen again: If-None-Match `*`, If-Match ETag, 412, first write to finish wins, 409 on concurrent delete, PutObject/CompleteMultipartUpload/CopyObject, bucket policy can require conditional writes.
4. [Uploading and copying objects using multipart upload](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html), Amazon Web Services. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: initiate/upload parts/complete; upload ID; part numbers 1-10,000, any order, parallel, retransmit one part; recommended from 100 MB; parts concatenated by part number; no expiry, billed until complete or stop; concurrent multipart uploads to one key; conditional writes on complete; checksums (CRC64NVME default). Companion pages opened, not given notes: [limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/qfacts.html) (max object 48.8 TiB, parts 5 MiB to 5 GiB) and [uploading objects](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/upload-objects.html) (5 GB single PUT, "up to 50 TB" multipart).
5. [Best practices design patterns: optimizing Amazon S3 performance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/optimizing-performance.html), Amazon Web Services. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE or 5,500 GET/HEAD per second per partitioned prefix; no limit on prefixes; 10 prefixes → 55,000 reads/s; scaling gradual, 503 Slow Down meanwhile; small-object latency roughly 100-200 ms; up to 100 Gb/s per EC2 instance for data lake apps.
6. [Amazon S3 Pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/), Amazon Web Services. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: cost components list; storage by size, duration, class; requests per request by type; LIST at PUT rate, DELETE free; IA 128 KB minimum billable size and 30-day minimum, Glacier 90/180-day minimums; transfer in free, same-Region to AWS services free, out to internet paid; RenameObject only on Express One Zone; S3 Tables worked example ($0.005 per 1,000 PUT, $0.0004 per 1,000 GET). The main S3 Standard price table is loaded by script and wasn't in the page text.
7. [Diving Deep on S3 Consistency](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2021/04/s3-strong-consistency.html), Werner Vogels, 2021. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: eventual consistency came from a resilient metadata cache (writes and reads on different cache paths); s3mper (Netflix, DynamoDB) and S3Guard (Hadoop) as workarounds; strong consistency default for every request, free, no performance trade-off; witness component as read barrier; proofs and model checking; over 100 trillion objects, tens of millions of requests per second.
8. [Delta Lake paper](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol13/p3411-armbrust.pdf). See open-table-formats #4. Section 2 on object store APIs (no cheap rename, LIST 1,000 keys and tens to hundreds of ms per call, byte ranges, whole-object rewrites, 5-10 ms base latency then 50-100 MB/s, 8-10 parallel reads for 10 Gbps).

Extra: [Building and operating a pretty big storage system called S3](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2023/07/building-and-operating-a-pretty-big-storage-system.html), Andy Warfield, 2023. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: frontend fleet, namespace service, storage fleet of hard disks, background fleet; hundreds of microservices; HDD seeks improved only 150x since RAMAC, about 120 random ops per second per drive; heat management; erasure coding (k data + m parity shards); spreading each bucket's objects across very many drives; ShardStore and lightweight formal methods. Not given a note: it explains S3's insides, not what a user of S3 relies on. Good for a future "how S3 is built" section.

#### `open-table-formats` (deep)

1. [Iceberg Table Spec](https://iceberg.apache.org/spec/), Apache Iceberg project. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: format versions 1-3 adopted, 4 in development; v2 row-level deletes (position/equality delete files), v3 deletion vectors, variant, geo types, row lineage; goals (serializable isolation, O(1) remote calls for planning, schema and partition evolution); tracks files not directories; metadata file → snapshots → manifest list → manifests → data files; manifests reused; optimistic concurrency and retry rules per operation; sequence numbers; only needs in-place write, seekable reads, deletes ("compatible with object stores, like S3"); file-system rename commit deprecated as unsafe; metastore check-and-put commit.
2. [Maintenance](https://iceberg.apache.org/docs/latest/maintenance/), Apache Iceberg project (Java 1.11.0 docs). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: expire snapshots (time travel lost, files deleted when unreferenced); old metadata files and `write.metadata.delete-after-commit.enabled`; orphan files from failed jobs and the danger of a short retention; compacting small data files; rewriting manifests.
3. [Delta Transaction Log Protocol](https://github.com/delta-io/delta/blob/master/PROTOCOL.md), Delta Lake project. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: goals (serializable writes, snapshot-isolated reads, self-describing); MVCC over files; two-phase write; vacuum default 7 days; contiguous version numbers; commit files zero-padded to 20 digits; checkpoints (classic, multi-part, V2), log compaction files, version checksum; actions (metaData, add, remove, txn, protocol, commitInfo, domain metadata); transaction identifiers for idempotent writes; table features; deletion vectors; catalog-managed tables (catalog decides commit success; PUT-if-absent as one publish option).
4. [Delta Lake: High-Performance ACID Table Storage over Cloud Object Stores](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol13/p3411-armbrust.pdf), Michael Armbrust and others, VLDB 2020. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: object store APIs and performance (section 2); eventual consistency of S3 LIST at the time; three approaches (directories of files, closed-world engines like Snowflake, metadata in the object store); log format, checkpoints every 10 commits, `_last_checkpoint`; read and write protocols; put-if-absent on GCS and Azure, HDFS rename, S3 needed a coordination service; serializable writes, snapshot-isolated reads, single-table only; several commits per second; half of early support escalations storage-related; Hudi and Iceberg use the same design; streaming exactly-once via txn.
5. [Lakehouse](https://www.cidrdb.org/cidr2021/papers/cidr2021_paper17.pdf), Armbrust, Ghodsi, Xin, Zaharia, CIDR 2021. Paper, primary: yes (Databricks' own argument). Seen: definition (open formats, ML support, performance); first-generation warehouses, second-generation lakes, two-tier lake + warehouse; four problems (reliability, staleness, limited advanced analytics, cost); survey numbers on stale data (not used).
6. [S3 conditional writes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/conditional-writes.html). See object-storage #3. S3 now has put-if-absent, which the Delta paper said it lacked.

#### `batch-processing` (deep)

1. [MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//archive/mapreduce-osdi04.pdf), Jeffrey Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, OSDI 2004. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: model and types; word count; execution overview (M splits 16-64 MB, master, local partitioned output, RPC fetch, sort, reduce, R output files); master data structures; worker failure and re-execution; deterministic semantics via atomic commit and rename; weaker semantics for non-deterministic functions; locality with GFS; task granularity (M=200,000, R=5,000, 2,000 workers); backup tasks (sort 44% slower without); partitioning function, ordering, combiner, side effects, skipping bad records; 1 TB sort, 200 of 1,746 workers killed adds 5%; 2004 hardware.
2. [Resilient Distributed Datasets](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/nsdi12/nsdi12-final138.pdf), Matei Zaharia and others, NSDI 2012. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: reuse between MapReduce jobs goes through stable storage; RDDs, lineage, immutability; up to 20x faster than Hadoop for iterative apps; narrow vs wide dependencies; stages cut at shuffles; shuffle output materialized on map side; delay scheduling.
3. [RDD Programming Guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/rdd-programming-guide.html), Apache Spark 4.2.0 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: lazy transformations, actions; shuffle operations section (see shuffle #1); persistence; groupByKey vs reduceByKey note; accumulators and laziness.
4. [Performance Tuning](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-performance-tuning.html), Spark SQL 4.2.0 docs. Docs, primary: yes. See shuffle #2. Used here for skew handling in AQE.

#### `shuffle` (short)

1. [RDD Programming Guide, "Shuffle operations"](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/rdd-programming-guide.html), Apache Spark 4.2.0 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: definition (regroup across partitions, all-to-all); operations that shuffle; order within a partition not deterministic after a shuffle; disk I/O, serialization, network; map side sorted by target partition into one file; spilling and GC; shuffle files kept until RDDs are garbage collected, can fill disks; map/reduce naming from MapReduce.
2. [Performance Tuning](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-performance-tuning.html), Spark SQL 4.2.0 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` default 200; broadcast join threshold; AQE on by default since 3.2.0; coalescing post-shuffle partitions (advisory 64MB); skew join (factor 5, threshold 256MB); converting sort-merge to broadcast or shuffled hash join.

Also cited: RDD paper (batch-processing #2) for why wide dependencies shuffle and cut stages.

#### `backfills` (short)

1. [Dag Runs](https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/core-concepts/dag-run.html), Apache Airflow 3.3.2 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: data interval (run after interval ends; logical date = interval start); manual triggers and data intervals; catchup (off by default via `scheduler.catchup_by_default=False`; don't use for jobs not limited to their interval); backfill via UI or `airflow backfill create` with reprocess behaviour, max active runs, run backwards; clearing tasks with past/future/upstream/downstream/recursive/failed.
2. [Best Practices](https://airflow.apache.org/docs/apache-airflow/stable/best-practices.html), Apache Airflow 3.3.2 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "Creating a task": treat tasks like database transactions, same outcome on every re-run, UPSERT not INSERT, read a specific partition not the latest, don't use `now()`, partition writes in S3/HDFS the same way.

Extra: [Backfilling data](https://docs.dagster.io/guides/build/partitions-and-backfills/backfilling-data), Dagster docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: backfills for first setup and after logic changes; one run per partition by default vs single-run backfill policy for engines like Spark or Snowflake. Not given a note; Airflow's two pages cover a short node.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- S3 latency: AWS's performance guide says small-object latency is "roughly 100-200 milliseconds"; the Delta Lake paper (2020) says each read has 5-10 ms of base latency. Different sources, contexts and years; the article says both and tells you to measure.
- Lakehouse vs warehouse: the lakehouse paper argues warehouses will be replaced; it's written by Databricks, which sells a lakehouse. No independent source opened on the other side. The article says whose argument it is.
- Commit mechanism: the Delta paper (2020) used a separate coordination service on S3 because S3 lacked put-if-absent; S3 now has `If-None-Match: *`. The Iceberg spec deprecates rename-based commits as unsafe on object stores; Delta now adds catalog-managed tables. The formats are moving from "storage decides" toward "catalog decides".
- Object size limit: Delta paper says 5 TB; AWS's limits page says 48.8 TiB and its upload page says "up to 50 TB". Left out of the article.

- [Functional Data Engineering](https://maximebeauchemin.medium.com/functional-data-engineering-a-modern-paradigm-for-batch-data-processing-2327ec32c42a), Maxime Beauchemin: Medium returned a Cloudflare challenge to curl and 403 to WebFetch. It's the best-known essay on idempotent partitions and backfills; not cited.

**Rejected:**

- Hadoop MapReduce tutorial: secondary to the MapReduce paper for the concepts.
- DDIA chapter 10 (batch processing): not opened.
- Iceberg/Delta vendor blogs comparing formats: marketing; the specs and the Delta paper were enough.

**Gaps:**

- No S3 Standard storage or request prices: the price table didn't load as text. The article uses the S3 Tables worked example and labels it.
- No year for when S3 became strongly consistent, only Vogels' 2021 post describing it.
- No source on Apache Hudi was opened; it's only named (via the Delta paper).
- No source opened on what S3-compatible servers (MinIO and others) support, notably conditional writes. The phase 16 lab writes to "a local S3-compatible store", and its output commit protocol needs put-if-absent or a catalog; check before the build.
