### Streams

#### `stream-processing` (deep)

1. [Streaming 101: The world beyond batch](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/the-world-beyond-batch-streaming-101/), Tyler Akidau, O'Reilly Radar, 2015. Blog by the MillWheel and Cloud Dataflow engineer, primary: yes. Seen: "streaming" should mean only an engine designed for infinite data (true streaming and micro-batch); unbounded vs bounded data; the Lambda Architecture as streaming + batch side by side, and Kreps's Kappa proposal; two things streaming needs to match batch: correctness (consistent checkpointed state, exactly-once) and tools for reasoning about time; event time vs processing time and the causes of skew (network, software, the data itself, a plane full of phones); four ways to process unbounded data: time-agnostic (filtering, inner joins), approximation algorithms, processing-time windows, event-time windows; event-time windows cost buffering and have a completeness problem; footnote: the batch/stream efficiency gap comes from bundling and shuffle transports, not an inherent limit.
2. [What is Apache Flink? Architecture](https://flink.apache.org/what-is-flink/flink-architecture/), Apache Flink project. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: all data is produced as a stream of events; unbounded streams have a start and no end and must be processed continuously; you can't wait for all input; bounded streams can be ingested whole and sorted, which is batch processing; Flink runs on YARN, Kubernetes or standalone.
3. [Kafka Streams core concepts](https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/core-concepts/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: a stream is an unbounded, continuously updating, ordered, replayable, fault-tolerant sequence of immutable records; processor topology = graph of stream processors connected by streams; source and sink processors; one-record-at-a-time processing for millisecond latency; event time, processing time, ingestion time; stream time advances only when records arrive; stream-table duality; aggregations output a KTable so out-of-order records can update results; grace period drops records past window end plus grace; out-of-order handling differs for stream-stream, stream-table, table-table joins.
4. [MillWheel: Fault-Tolerant Stream Processing at Internet Scale](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//pubs/archive/41378.pdf), Akidau et al., Google, VLDB 2013. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: user code runs per key over a directed computation graph with persistent state; requirements list (data available as soon as published, persistent state in the consistency model, out-of-order data handled, monotonic low watermark, constant latency as it scales, exactly-once delivery); Zeitgeist spike/dip detection; per-key processing serialized; low watermark definition (min of oldest work and upstream watermarks); injectors seed watermarks; late records ~0.001% dropped by Zeitgeist; timers on wall time or low watermark; measured single-stage median 3.6 ms, p95 30 ms on 200 CPUs without exactly-once, 33.7 ms / 93.8 ms with it; watermark lag 1.8 s at first stage of a 3-stage pipeline, under 200 ms more per stage.
5. [The Log](https://web.archive.org/web/2025/https://engineering.linkedin.com/distributed-systems/log-what-every-software-engineer-should-know-about-real-time-datas-unifying), Jay Kreps, LinkedIn, 2013. Note exists (`kreps-the-log-2013`). Used for the log as the buffer that lets readers go at their own pace and replay.

Extra: [Flink Concepts overview](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/concepts/overview/), Flink 2.3 docs. Seen: layered APIs (ProcessFunction, DataStream, Table API, SQL). Read for context, not given a note.

#### `event-time-vs-processing-time` (short)

1. [Streaming 101](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/the-world-beyond-batch-streaming-101/). See stream-processing #1. The time-domain section, the skew diagram, the mobile-app and transcontinental-link examples, why processing-time windows are wrong for event-time questions and right for monitoring.
2. [Timely Stream Processing](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/concepts/time/), Apache Flink 2.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: processing time = system clock of the machine running the operator, hourly processing-time window example starting 9:15; simplest, lowest latency, not deterministic; event time = time on the producing device, embedded in the record; progress depends on data not wall clocks; event time costs latency waiting for out-of-order events; replaying historic data can move through weeks of event time in seconds; Watermark(t) definition; operator event time is the min of its inputs; late elements; windows can be time or data driven.
3. [Kafka Streams core concepts](https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/core-concepts/). See stream-processing #3. Ingestion time (broker append time), the topic-level choice between event time and ingestion time, and "stream time".

#### `windowing` (short)

1. [Windows](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/operators/windows/), Apache Flink 2.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: window lifecycle (created on first element, removed at end + allowed lateness), keyed vs non-keyed (parallelism 1), assigners: tumbling, sliding, session, global; start inclusive, end exclusive; epoch alignment and offsets for time zones; sliding elements copied into several windows; session windows created per record and merged; global window needs a custom trigger; ReduceFunction/AggregateFunction aggregate incrementally, ProcessWindowFunction buffers everything; triggers (FIRE, PURGE), default EventTimeTrigger; evictors; allowed lateness default 0; side output for late data; late firings; state size advice (size 1 day slide 1 second is a bad idea).
2. [Kafka Streams DSL](https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/developer-guide/dsl-api/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: hopping (size + advance), tumbling (hop = size), sliding (record-difference based, both bounds inclusive, aligned to records), session windows (inactivity gap, merge on out-of-order records); "hopping windows are sometimes called sliding windows in other tools"; windows aligned to the epoch; default window retention one day; grace period (ofSizeAndGrace); suppress(untilWindowCloses) for final results.
3. [The Dataflow Model](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p1792-Akidau.pdf), Akidau et al., Google, VLDB 2015. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: section 1.2 windowing (fixed = sliding with size equal to period; aligned vs unaligned; windows sometimes phase-shifted per key to spread load); tuple-based windows are time windows over a logical clock; section 2.2 AssignWindows and MergeWindows; session merging walk-through (30-minute gap).

Extra: [Structured Streaming Programming Guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/streaming/apis-on-dataframes-and-datasets.html), Spark 4.2.0. Seen: tumbling, sliding and session windows via `window` and `session_window`. Not needed for windowing; used under late-data.

#### `watermarks` (deep)

1. [MillWheel](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//pubs/archive/41378.pdf). See stream-processing #4. Low watermark definition, injectors, late records, timers, measured watermark lag.
2. [Watermarks in Stream Processing Systems: Semantics and Comparative Analysis of Apache Flink and Google Cloud Dataflow](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p3135-begoli.pdf), Akidau, Begoli, Chernyak, Hueske, Knight, Knowles, Mills, Sotolongo, VLDB 2021. Paper, primary: yes (Flink and Dataflow builders). Seen: formal definition (monotonicity, conformance, liveness); conformant vs non-conformant = perfect vs heuristic; uses: readiness (single correct answer, data absence/dip detection, non-incremental computation), obsolescence (garbage collecting state), health monitoring; alternatives: ordered processing, timestamp frontiers, punctuations; generation (per-partition max minus one for monotonic Kafka partitions; bounded disorder t minus delta; timeout; statistical model of lag with a quantile such as 0.999); propagation (min over inputs; aggregation holds the watermark); consumption through watermark timers; late-data strategies (drop and monitor, or recompute); Flink in-band vs Dataflow out-of-band aggregator; idle sources; bottlenecks; watermark skew and alignment; measured ~100 ms median per shuffle in Flink 1.12.1 and ~500-1000 ms in Dataflow (Beam 2.27.0).
3. [Streaming 102: The world beyond batch](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/the-world-beyond-batch-streaming-102/), Tyler Akidau, O'Reilly Radar, 2016. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: what/where/when/how; watermark as F(P) -> E; perfect vs heuristic watermarks; too slow (late 9 holds back the watermark, nearly seven minutes to first output) and too fast (5 instead of 14); triggers (watermark, processing time, counts, punctuations, composites); early/on-time/late firings; allowed lateness as garbage collection; accumulation modes table (discarding 3/4/8, accumulating 7/14/22, retracting); processing-time windowing via triggers vs ingress time; same event-time results (14, 22, 3, 12) under different arrival orders.
4. [Generating Watermarks](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/event-time/generating_watermarks/), Apache Flink 2.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: WatermarkStrategy = TimestampAssigner + WatermarkGenerator; forBoundedOutOfOrderness; generate at the source (knows partitions) rather than after; idle sources hold back the min, withIdleness; watermark alignment pauses fast sources; periodic vs punctuated generators; BoundedOutOfOrdernessGenerator code (max timestamp minus bound minus 1); per-Kafka-partition watermarks; an operator fires windows before forwarding the watermark; two-input operators take the min.
5. [Timely Stream Processing](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/concepts/time/). See event-time-vs-processing-time #2. Watermark(t) definition, watermarks in parallel streams, lateness.

Extra: [Structured Streaming Programming Guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/streaming/apis-on-dataframes-and-datasets.html). See late-data #3. Spark's watermark = max event time seen minus a threshold.

#### `late-data` (short)

1. [Windows](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/operators/windows/). See windowing #1. Allowed lateness (default 0, late elements dropped), side output for late data, late firings, results must be treated as updates, session windows can merge on a late firing.
2. [Streaming 102](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/the-world-beyond-batch-streaming-102/). See watermarks #3. Late firings with AtCount(1), allowed lateness horizon (the 6 is accepted, the 9 dropped), perfect watermarks need zero lateness, global aggregates over few keys need none; accumulation modes.
3. [Structured Streaming Programming Guide](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/streaming/apis-on-dataframes-and-datasets.html), Apache Spark 4.2.0 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: withWatermark(column, threshold); watermark = max event time seen minus threshold, set at the start of each trigger; (12:09, cat) counted, (12:04, donkey) ignored; update vs append output mode; the guarantee is one-directional (data less delayed than the threshold is never dropped, later data may or may not be); withWatermark on a batch Dataset is a no-op.
4. [Kafka Streams DSL](https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/developer-guide/dsl-api/). See windowing #2. Grace period: the 09:00-10:00 window accepts records until 10:10; suppress for final results.

Extra: [Watermarks in Stream Processing Systems](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p3135-begoli.pdf). See watermarks #2. Section 4.5: drop late data and monitor how much, or recompute.

#### `dataflow-model` (short)

1. [The Dataflow Model](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p1792-Akidau.pdf). See windowing #3. What/where/when/how; unbounded/bounded vs streaming/batch; watermarks too fast and too slow; triggers and the three refinement modes (discarding, accumulating, accumulating and retracting); worked examples on batch, micro-batch and streaming engines; design principle "never rely on any notion of completeness"; motivating experiences (backfills with a separate FlumeJava implementation, a team that stopped trusting weakly consistent Lambda results, billing teams, percentile watermarks for abuse detection).
2. [Streaming 102](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/the-world-beyond-batch-streaming-102/). See watermarks #3. The four questions with running examples and the accumulation-mode table.
3. [Apache Beam Programming Guide](https://beam.apache.org/documentation/programming-guide/), Apache Beam project. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: windowing sections 8.1-8.4, default global window, grouping an unbounded PCollection without a window or trigger fails at construction; fixed, sliding, session, global windows; watermark and late data (30 s lag example); allowed lateness propagates downstream; triggers: event time, processing time, data-driven (count only), composite; completeness vs latency vs cost; default trigger fires at watermark then on every late element, but with default windowing allowed lateness is 0; accumulating vs discarding example.

#### `lambda-vs-kappa` (short)

1. [How to beat the CAP theorem](http://nathanmarz.com/blog/how-to-beat-the-cap-theorem.html), Nathan Marz, 2011. Blog by Storm's creator, primary: yes. Seen: query = function(all data); data is immutable facts; batch layer on Hadoop precomputes views, queries hours out of date; realtime layer (Storm + Cassandra) covers the last few hours; merge the two at query time; realtime complexity is transient because batch overrides it; human fault tolerance (redeploy and recompute); story of Cassandra running out of space; exact algorithm in batch, approximate in realtime ("eventual accuracy"). The post doesn't use the word "Lambda".
2. [Questioning the Lambda Architecture](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/questioning-the-lambda-architecture/), Jay Kreps, O'Reilly Radar, 2014. Blog by a Kafka and Samza creator, primary: yes. Seen: describes Lambda (same logic twice, stitched at query time); credits it for immutable input and reprocessing; argues streams need not be approximate; CAP claim doesn't hold; the pain of keeping two code bases in sync, Summingbird-style abstractions only give the intersection; LinkedIn's experience; the alternative: retain the log (e.g. 30 days), start a second job from the beginning, write to a new table, switch, delete the old; "Kappa Architecture"; costs: 2x output storage temporarily, a database that takes high-volume writes; the real advantage is one framework.
3. [The Dataflow Model](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p1792-Akidau.pdf). See dataflow-model #1. Lambda fails on simplicity; batch output is only correct if input is complete when it runs; a MillWheel customer who ran weak streaming plus nightly MapReduce found users stopped trusting the fast results.

Extra: [Streaming 101](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/the-world-beyond-batch-streaming-101/). See stream-processing #1. Lambda credited as a good idea for its time, Kappa "not convinced that notion itself requires a name".

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- Watermarks as the trigger for results: MillWheel and the watermarks paper treat the watermark as the completeness signal for single final answers; the Dataflow paper's design principle is "never rely on any notion of completeness" and adds triggers and refinements instead. Both come from the same team at different times; the 2021 paper says eventually-consistent approaches serve alerting, dip detection and non-incremental models poorly.
- Simple watermark heuristics: Flink, Spark and Kafka Streams ship bounded-out-of-orderness (max seen minus a fixed delay). The 2021 paper says fixed delay and timeout heuristics were problematic in practice (too slow when healthy, too fast in trouble) and a statistical model of lag worked better.
- "Sliding window" means two things: Flink, Beam, Spark and the Dataflow paper call size-plus-period windows sliding; Kafka Streams calls those hopping and reserves "sliding" for windows defined by the difference between record timestamps.
- Lambda vs Kappa: Marz argues the batch layer's recompute-from-scratch gives human fault tolerance and hides CAP complexity; Kreps says the CAP claim doesn't hold and two code bases are the real cost; Akidau says Kappa doesn't need a name and streaming is a superset of batch.
- Is streaming a superset of batch? Akidau and Flink's docs say yes in semantics; Streaming 101's own footnote and Flink's architecture page admit batch engines still have efficiency advantages (bundling, shuffle, sort-based algorithms).

**Couldn't open:**

- Nothing needed failed to open. The Kafka docs URL without a version (`/documentation/streams/core-concepts`) now redirects by script; the versioned 4.3 pages opened.

**Rejected:**

- *Streaming Systems* (Akidau, Chernyak, Lax, O'Reilly book): not opened; the two O'Reilly posts and the two VLDB papers are by the same authors and cover what the nodes need.
- DDIA chapter 11: not opened for this project.
- Flink Concepts overview: context only.

**Gaps:**

- No source opened gives a measured throughput comparison between batch and streaming engines on the same job; the articles state the efficiency gap only as the sources' claim, without numbers.
- No source opened gives a typical real-world allowed lateness or grace period; the articles use the sources' illustrative values (Flink's 1 minute, Kafka Streams' 10 minutes, Beam's 2 days) as examples only.
- Kafka Streams' default grace period isn't stated on the pages opened (the DSL examples use explicit `ofSizeWithNoGrace` / `ofSizeAndGrace`); the articles don't claim a default.
- Streaming 102's accumulation table says summing the accumulating panes gives 51; the panes shown (7, 14, 22) add to 43. The article avoids the number and says only that summing double counts.
- MillWheel's 0.001% late-record rate is for one pipeline (Zeitgeist) in 2013; not generalised.

### State, checkpoints and output

#### `stateful-stream-processing` (deep)

1. [Stateful Stream Processing](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/concepts/stateful-stream-processing/), Apache Flink, Flink 2.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: what counts as state (pattern sequences, pending aggregates, model parameters); keyed state as an embedded key/value store partitioned with the stream, so every update is local and needs no transaction; key groups are the unit of redistribution, as many as the max parallelism; fault tolerance is replay plus checkpointing; checkpointing off by default; source must be able to rewind; state backends (in-memory hash map or RocksDB).
2. [Working with State](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/fault-tolerance/state/), Apache Flink, Flink 2.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: keyBy partitions both state and records, keys must be deterministic; ValueState, ListState, ReducingState, AggregatingState, MapState scoped to the current key; state handles aren't where state lives; TTL on keyed state (processing time only, best-effort cleanup, compaction filter on RocksDB); TTL migration since 2.2.0; operator state (Kafka source offsets per partition) and broadcast state.
3. [State Backends](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/ops/state/state_backends/), Apache Flink, Flink 2.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: HashMapStateBackend (Java heap objects, the default), EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend (serialized bytes on local disk, state size limited by disk, "order of magnitude slower" on average, incremental checkpoints), ForStStateBackend (SST files on S3/HDFS, experimental); 2^31-byte key/value limit; savepoint format unified in 1.13; incremental checkpoints record only changes.
4. [Parallel Execution](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/execution/parallel/), Apache Flink, Flink 2.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: max parallelism is the upper bound for rescaling because state is split into key groups; default about 1.5x parallelism, at least 128, at most 32768; changing it on restore breaks state compatibility.
5. [State Management in Apache Flink](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol10/p1718-carbone.pdf), Carbone, Ewen, Fóra, Haridi, Richter, Tzoumas, VLDB, 2017. Paper by the builders, primary: yes. Seen: state used to live in a shared database; keyed vs operator state; key-group formula h(k) mod max-parallelism, contiguous ranges per task, and the trade-off it sits on (scan everything vs index every key); local vs external backends; copy-on-write snapshots in the heap backend and version marking in RocksDB; queryable state is read-uncommitted; King's RBEA deployment numbers (Flink 1.2.0, parallelism 70, 100 to 500 GB state, 1.3 s average alignment per snapshot).
6. [Kafka Streams Architecture](https://kafka.apache.org/43/streams/architecture/), Apache Kafka, Kafka 4.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: tasks fixed by input partitions (max parallelism = partition count); local state stores per task; each store backed by a compacted changelog topic, replayed on restore; standby replicas to cut restore time; since 2.6 tasks go to a caught-up instance if one exists. Used as the contrast to Flink's snapshot approach.
7. [Disaggregated State Management](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/ops/state/disaggregated_state/), Apache Flink, Flink 2.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: local-disk limits, spiky checkpoint I/O, recovery time proportional to state size; Flink 2.0 ForSt plus async State V2 API; experimental. Not used (the State Backends page covers ForSt enough for one paragraph).

#### `distributed-snapshots` (deep)

1. [Distributed Snapshots: Determining Global States of Distributed Systems](https://lamport.azurewebsites.net/pubs/chandy.pdf), K. Mani Chandy and Leslie Lamport, ACM TOCS, 1985. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: a process can only record its own state and its messages; no common clock; the photographers analogy; FIFO, error-free channels; the single-token example that records two tokens or none; marker-sending and marker-receiving rules; channel state is the messages received between recording and the marker; the recorded state may never have happened but is reachable from the start and can reach the end; usable for checkpointing.
2. [Lightweight Asynchronous Snapshots for Distributed Dataflows](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1506.08603), Carbone, Fóra, Ewen, Haridi, Tzoumas, arXiv, 2015. Paper by the builders, primary: yes. Seen: existing snapshots stall the job or log all in-transit records; Naiad's synchronous stop-snapshot-resume; Chandy-Lamport with upstream backup; ABS keeps only operator state on acyclic graphs, a small log only for cycles; barriers emulate stages; evaluation on EC2 (up to 40 m3.medium, 1 billion records, 3 shuffles), synchronous snapshots pause in 1 to 2 s bursts.
3. [Stateful Stream Processing](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/concepts/stateful-stream-processing/): see `stateful-stream-processing` #1. Seen: barriers flow in line and never overtake records; several snapshots in flight at once; source position Sn (a Kafka offset); alignment on multi-input operators and after shuffles; sinks acknowledge, then the checkpoint is complete; recovery from the latest completed checkpoint; unaligned checkpoints (since 1.11) store overtaken in-flight data and are closer to Chandy-Lamport; alignment usually costs a few ms; skipping alignment gives at-least-once.
4. [Checkpointing under backpressure](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/ops/state/checkpointing_under_backpressure/), Apache Flink, Flink 2.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: under backpressure barrier travel time dominates; buffer debloating (1.14); unaligned checkpoints add I/O; aligned-checkpoint timeout switches to unaligned; no concurrent unaligned checkpoints; watermark caveat on recovery; a slow single record still delays the barrier.
5. [Checkpoints vs. Savepoints](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/ops/state/checkpoints_vs_savepoints/), Apache Flink, Flink 2.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: checkpoints are like a database's recovery log, savepoints like backups; who owns and deletes each; native vs canonical format (native savepoints since 1.15); capability table (unaligned checkpoints can't survive a job-graph change or a minor version upgrade; all kinds support rescaling).
6. [State Management in Apache Flink](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol10/p1718-carbone.pdf): see `stateful-stream-processing` #5. Seen: protocol assumptions (replayable input, reliable FIFO channels that can be blocked); Algorithm 1 (block, forward marker, snapshot, unblock); alignment can spill buffered records to disk; relaxed at-least-once mode; alignment cost grows with shuffles and parallelism, not state size.

#### `transactional-sinks` (short)

1. [An Overview of End-to-End Exactly-Once Processing in Apache Flink (with Apache Kafka, too!)](https://flink.apache.org/2018/02/28/an-overview-of-end-to-end-exactly-once-processing-in-apache-flink-with-apache-kafka-too/), Piotr Nowojski and Mike Winters, Apache Flink blog, 2018. Blog by the builders, primary: yes. Seen: checkpoint start is the pre-commit phase, the checkpoint-complete notification is the commit phase; a commit must eventually succeed or data is lost; the file-sink example (temp file, flush and close on pre-commit, atomic move on commit, delete on abort); the crash between pre-commit and commit, handled by committing again on restore, so commit must be idempotent; TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction since Flink 1.4.0.
2. [FileSystem connector](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/connectors/datastream/filesystem/), Apache Flink, Flink 2.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: part files are in-progress, pending or finished; finished only on a successful checkpoint; without checkpointing files stay in-progress forever; bulk formats (Parquet) roll on every checkpoint; compaction since 1.15; S3 uses multipart uploads, and an aggressive abort-MPU lifecycle rule can break restoring from a savepoint; never overwrites committed data; last in-progress files not finished on normal termination.
3. [Apache Kafka Connector](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/connectors/datastream/kafka/), Apache Flink, Flink 2.3 docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: KafkaSink default guarantee NONE; EXACTLY_ONCE writes a Kafka transaction committed on checkpoint; readers must use read_committed; visibility waits for the checkpoint; unique transactionalIdPrefix; transaction.timeout.ms must exceed checkpoint plus restart time or data can be lost; ProducerFencedException after a timeout.
4. [Committer (sink2 API)](https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/api/java/org/apache/flink/api/connector/sink2/Committer.html), Apache Flink Javadoc. Code docs, primary: yes. Seen: the Committer does the second step of a two-phase commit for data staged by the CommittingSinkWriter; commits must be idempotent because Flink re-commits after a restart; FileCommitter implements it.
5. [Apache Flink 2.0.0: A new Era of Real-Time Data Processing](https://flink.apache.org/2025/03/24/apache-flink-2.0.0-a-new-era-of-real-time-data-processing/), Xintong Song, Apache Flink blog, 2025. Release notes, primary: yes. Seen: SourceFunction, SinkFunction and Sink V1 removed, use Sink V2; TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction in the removed class list; disaggregated state and ForSt.
6. [State Management in Apache Flink](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol10/p1718-carbone.pdf): see `stateful-stream-processing` #5. Seen: section 4.4, idempotent vs transactional sinks; the printer example; WAL-then-commit vs eager append with pre-commit by flagging a directory; the bucketing file sink commits by atomic rename. Not used (the blog and the FileSystem docs cover the same, more current).

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- The State Backends page recommends HashMapStateBackend for "jobs with large state, long windows, large key/value states", the same words it uses for RocksDB, while the "choose" section says heap state is limited by memory. Looks like a copy-paste in the docs; the article follows the "choose" section.
- The same page says RocksDB is "the only backend that offers incremental checkpoints", then says ForSt "always performs asynchronous incremental snapshots". ForSt is experimental, which may explain it.
- Aligned checkpoints cost "a few milliseconds" per the docs, but "can reach hours" with a slow path under backpressure; King's production numbers (2017) average 1.3 s of alignment per snapshot at parallelism 70. The cost depends on backpressure and shuffles, not on state size.
- Carbone 2015 counts Chandy-Lamport as logging all in-transit records; Flink's own docs call unaligned checkpoints (which store in-flight data) "closer to Chandy-Lamport". Both are true: aligned checkpoints trade a little blocking for storing no channel state.
- Kafka Streams restores state by replaying a changelog topic, Flink by loading a snapshot file; different answers to the same problem.

#### `system-design-method` (deep)

1. See `back-of-envelope-estimation` #1 (Google SRE workbook, NALSD). The method itself: two phases, four questions ("Is it possible?", "Can we do better?", "Is it feasible?", "Is it resilient?"); "in practice, we bounce around between the questions and phases"; the design evolves one machine → MapReduce (fails the 5-minute freshness SLO) → LogJoiner → sharded LogJoiner with duplicate shards → multi-datacenter with Paxos; "we separated software components based on how we expected the system to grow".
2. [Design Docs at Google](https://www.industrialempathy.com/posts/design-docs-at-google/), Malte Ubl, 2020. Blog by a Google engineer, primary: yes. Seen: sections (context and scope, goals and non-goals, the actual design with APIs and data storage sketched not pasted, alternatives considered, cross-cutting concerns); non-goals are "things that could reasonably be goals"; 10-20 pages for a larger project, 1-3 page mini docs; don't write one when there's no ambiguity; "I tried it out and it works" is a strong argument; review's value is timing.
3. [System Design in a Hurry: Delivery Framework](https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/delivery), Evan King and Stefan Mai, Hello Interview, 2024. Interview guide, primary: no. Seen: Requirements (~5 min), Core Entities (~2), API (~5), Data Flow (~5), High Level Design (~10-15), Deep Dives (~10); top 3 functional requirements; quantified non-functional requirements tied to a part ("low latency search, < 500ms"); checklist (CAP, environment, scalability incl. read/write ratio, latency, durability, security, fault tolerance, compliance); argues against up-front estimates unless they change the design; REST by default; user from the auth token; build the design endpoint by endpoint; complexity too early is the common failure.
4. [A Framework For System Design Interviews](https://bytebytego.com/courses/system-design-interview/a-framework-for-system-design-interviews), Alex Xu, ByteByteGo. Book chapter, primary: no. Seen: four steps (scope, high-level design and buy-in, deep dive, wrap up); "Over-engineering is a real disease"; write down assumptions; back-of-the-envelope in step 2; API and schema "depends on the problem"; wrap-up covers bottlenecks, errors, operations, next scale step; 45-minute time split (3-10, 10-15, 10-25, 3-5).
5. [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer), Donne Martin and contributors. Community guide, primary: no. Seen: four steps (use cases/constraints/assumptions, high level design, core components, scale the design); questions incl. read-to-write ratio; "Everything is a trade-off"; appendix with powers-of-two table and a copy of the latency numbers plus derived rules (2,000 round trips a second inside a data center).

#### `monolith-vs-microservices` (deep)

1. [Microservices](https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservices.html), James Lewis and Martin Fowler, 2014. Article, primary: yes (they wrote the common definition). Seen: definition (suite of small services, own process, lightweight mechanisms, business capabilities, independently deployable); monolith as "a single logical executable" scaled by copying behind a load balancer; services as out-of-process components; remote APIs must be coarser; Conway's Law quote; decentralized data management; "transactionless coordination" and eventual consistency; naive RPC conversion is chatty; team size up to a dozen.
2. [Microservice Trade-Offs](https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservice-trade-offs.html), Martin Fowler, 2015. Primary: yes. Seen: benefits (strong module boundaries, independent deployment, technology diversity) and costs (distribution, eventual consistency, operational complexity); monoliths make it easy to "sneak around the barrier"; integration databases; chains of half-a-dozen calls; async helps but is hard; Facebook and Etsy deliver monoliths continuously; coordinated deploys are a common failure; complexity "shifted around to the interconnections".
3. [MonolithFirst](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/MonolithFirst.html), Martin Fowler, 2015. Primary: yes. Seen: successful microservice stories started as monoliths, built-from-scratch ones ended in trouble; boundaries hard to get right early; routes (peel off at edges, coarse services first, sacrificial monolith); the counter argument (modular monolith takes a lot of discipline); "early days", few anecdotes.
4. [Goodbye Microservices](https://segment.com/blog/goodbye-microservices/), Alexandra Noonan, Segment, 2018. Primary: yes. Seen: head-of-line blocking on one queue; one service and queue per destination; 140+ services; diverging shared-library versions; per-service autoscaling "more art than science"; 3 engineers keeping it alive; merged into one service, one version of 120 dependencies; Centrifuge keeps queue isolation; 32 vs 46 shared-library improvements; trade-offs (fault isolation, caches spread over 3000+ processes, dependency updates).
5. [Deconstructing the Monolith](https://shopify.engineering/deconstructing-monolith-designing-software-maximizes-developer-productivity), Kirsten Westeinde, Shopify, 2019. Primary: yes. Seen: Rails monolith, over a decade, more than a thousand developers; problems (coupling, unrelated test failures, onboarding); why not microservices; modular monolith definition; reorganised ~6000 classes by business domain; public APIs and data ownership per component; Wedge flags cross-boundary calls from a CI call graph; tax engine swapped out.
6. [Towards Modern Development of Cloud Applications](https://sigops.org/s/conferences/hotos/2023/papers/ghemawat.pdf), Sanjay Ghemawat and others, Google, HotOS 2023. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: survey reasons for splitting; challenges C1-C5 (performance, correctness across versions, management, frozen APIs, slow cross-service changes); "conflate logical boundaries ... with physical boundaries"; components become RPCs only when placed apart; atomic deploys; Table 2 at 10,000 QPS: 28 cores / 2.66 ms vs 78 cores / 5.47 ms; co-located 9 cores / 0.38 ms; most gain from unversioned serialization; persistent state still couples versions; code at github.com/ServiceWeaver.
7. [Conway's "How Do Committees Invent?"](https://www.melconway.com/Home/Committees_Paper.html), Melvin Conway, Datamation, 1968. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: the thesis "organizations which design systems ... are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations"; author's later note restating it. Not cited: Lewis and Fowler quote the law, and the article needs only one line.
8. [MicroservicePremium](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/MicroservicePremium.html), Martin Fowler, 2015. Primary: yes. Seen: "The majority of software systems should be built as a single monolithic application"; complexity sources (team size, multi-tenancy, sheer size); Inverse Conway Maneuver; service counts vary (team of 60 with 20 services to team of 4 with 200). Not cited separately; MonolithFirst covers the argument.

#### `service-mesh` (short)

1. [What is a service mesh?](https://linkerd.io/what-is-a-service-mesh/), Linkerd project, docs for Linkerd 2.20. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: definition (features "at the platform layer rather than the application layer"); data plane of proxies, control plane; one request step by step (routing incl. canary, latency-aware instance choice from Kubernetes discovery, pooled mTLS connection, HTTP/2 between proxies, retries only if idempotent and within a retry budget, eviction of failing instances, metrics); off Kubernetes the cost "starts increasing rapidly"; history from Finagle, Hystrix, Stubby; bound at runtime instead of compile time.
2. [Istio architecture](https://istio.io/latest/docs/ops/deployment/architecture/), Istio project, Istio 1.31 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: data plane of Envoy sidecars, control plane istiod; Envoy features (routing, retries, failovers, circuit breakers, fault injection); istiod converts routing rules into Envoy config and pushes at runtime, does discovery, acts as CA for mTLS; policy by service identity rather than L3/L4 identifiers.
3. [Istio ambient mode overview](https://istio.io/latest/docs/ambient/overview/), Istio project, Istio 1.31 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: per-node L4 ztunnel (Rust; mTLS, authentication, L4 authorization, telemetry; no HTTP parsing; HBONE over HTTP CONNECT) and optional per-namespace L7 waypoint (Envoy); "sidecar-less" informally; sidecar and ambient pods can share a mesh; some uses need only the L4 overlay; waypoints heavier than ztunnel.
4. [The Istio service mesh](https://istio.io/latest/about/service-mesh/), Istio project. Marketing page, primary: yes. Seen: definition, founded by Google, IBM and Lyft in 2016, CNCF graduated, two data plane modes. Not cited; the docs pages cover the mechanism.

#### `id-generation` (short)

1. [Snowflake](https://github.com/twitter-archive/snowflake/tree/snowflake-2010), Twitter, 2010 (archived 2021). README and `IdWorker.scala`, primary: yes. Seen: moving from MySQL to Cassandra, which has no sequence; minimum 10k IDs/s per process, 2 ms; uncoordinated; k-sorted within 1 s (aiming for tens of ms); under 64 bits; 41 bits time with custom epoch (69 years), 10 bits machine (5 datacenter + 5 worker in code), 12 bits sequence (4096 per ms); refuses to generate when the clock moves backwards; spins to next ms on sequence wrap; run NTP so it never steps back.
2. [RFC 9562: UUIDs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9562), K. Davis, B. Peabody, P. Leach, 2024. Spec, primary: yes (note already existed; appended). Seen: UUIDv7 layout; 6.1 implementations must decide what to do when the clock moves back; 6.2 monotonic counters for batches; 6.4 distributed generation, node IDs and central registries (NOT RECOMMENDED), rely on every host's randomness.
3. [Ticket Servers: Distributed Unique Primary Keys on the Cheap](https://code.flickr.net/2010/02/08/ticket-servers-distributed-unique-primary-keys-on-the-cheap/), Flickr engineering, 2010. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: sharded MySQL needs globally unique keys (rows move between shards); GUIDs big and index badly; `REPLACE INTO` on a one-row table plus `LAST_INSERT_ID()`; two servers with odd/even (`auto-increment-increment = 2`); they drift; "dumbest possible thing that will work".

#### `feed-fan-out` (short)

1. [Feeding Frenzy: Selectively Materializing Users' Event Feeds](https://jeffterrace.com/docs/feeding-frenzy-sigmod10-web.pdf), Adam Silberstein, Jeff Terrace, Brian F. Cooper, Raghu Ramakrishnan, SIGMOD 2010. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: push vs pull defined as materialize vs query on demand; per producer/consumer decision by ratio of consumer view rate to producer event rate against H/L (Lemma 1); local decisions give global minimum cost (Theorem 1); latency-constrained version is knapsack-like; flash loads handled by switching pairs to pull; feed properties (gapless, no duplicates); tested on PNUTS.
2. [The Architecture Twitter Uses to Deal with 150M Active Users](https://highscalability.com/the-architecture-twitter-uses-to-deal-with-150m-active-users/), High Scalability, 2013, summarising Raffi Krikorian's QCon talk. Secondary, primary: no. Seen: 300K QPS reads vs 6000 RPS writes; fan-out on write into Redis lists of 800 entries (tweet ID, user ID, 4 bytes of flags), 3 replicas; only users active in 30 days kept in RAM, others reconstructed; hydration by multiget; O(n) write vs O(1) read, search the inverse; celebrity accounts (31 million followers), 3.5 s p50 to 1M followers, up to 5 min p99; replies before tweets; stop fanning out the biggest accounts and merge at read time; posting goes to a queue and fan-out runs asynchronously.
3. [Timelines at Scale](https://www.infoq.com/presentations/Twitter-Timeline-Scalability/), Raffi Krikorian, QCon, InfoQ. Talk, primary: yes. Seen: page is the video with a short abstract only; no transcript. Not cited; the High Scalability write-up is used instead.
4. [Design A News Feed System](https://bytebytego.com/courses/system-design-interview/design-a-news-feed-system), Alex Xu, ByteByteGo. Book chapter, primary: no. Seen: fanout on write (push) vs on read (pull); "hotkey problem" for users with many friends; hybrid (push for most, pull for celebrities); feed cache holds only IDs with a configurable limit. Not cited: same content as the primaries.

#### `distributed-rate-limiting` (short)

1. [How we scaled the GitHub API with a sharded, replicated rate limiter in Redis](https://github.blog/engineering/infrastructure/how-we-scaled-github-api-sharded-replicated-rate-limiter-redis/), Robert Mosolgo, GitHub, 2021 (updated 2023). Blog, primary: yes. Seen: old fixed-window limiter in a shared Memcached (evictions gave fresh windows; per-datacenter Memcached would split counts); new: Redis sharded in the app, primary plus replicas, Lua for atomicity, TTL cleanup; feature-flag rollout; bug 1 "wobbling" reset time from TTL plus Ruby clock; bug 2 replica didn't expire keys so rejections showed a full quota; fixes; still counts after the request finishes.
2. [Global rate limiting](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/other_features/global_rate_limiting), Envoy docs, 1.40.0-dev. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: when global limits are needed (many hosts to few, low latency, e.g. a database); per-request gRPC service with a Go/Redis reference implementation; quota-based mode with load reports for large uneven fleets (no open-source quota service when read); local token bucket in front to absorb bursts and reduce load on the global service.
3. See phase 5 `rate-limiting-algorithms`: [Cloudflare, "How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains"](https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/), Julien Desgats, 2017 (note existed): per-PoP counting thanks to anycast, memcache shards, asynchronous counting, cached mitigation flag, 0.003% wrong on 400 million requests.
4. See phase 5 `rate-limiting`: [Stripe, "Scaling your API with rate limiters"](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters), Paul Tarjan, 2017 (note existed): token bucket per user in Redis; fail open.
5. [INCR](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/incr/), Redis docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "Pattern: rate limiter" with INCR+EXPIRE per IP per second in MULTI/EXEC; the single-counter variant's race and its Lua fix (EVAL since Redis 2.6); a list-based variant. Not cited; GitHub's scripts show the same idea in production.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- **Estimate up front or not?** ByteByteGo and the System Design Primer put back-of-the-envelope estimates early; Hello Interview says most candidates compute QPS and storage only to conclude "it's a lot" and should estimate only when a number changes the design. The SRE workbook does both: an early estimate kills the one-machine design, and every later estimate answers a specific question. The article sides with "estimate to decide".
- **Monolith first or services first?** Fowler (MonolithFirst, 2015) reports that successful microservice systems almost all started as monoliths; he also reports the counter-argument (a splittable monolith takes too much discipline). Shopify stayed a modular monolith; Segment split and merged back; Ghemawat et al. argue the split should be a runtime decision, not a code one.
- **Continuous delivery needs microservices?** Fowler (Trade-Offs) says no, citing Facebook and Etsy.
- **Where a global rate limit is counted.** GitHub left per-datacenter Memcached because counts would split across datacenters; Cloudflare counts per data centre deliberately (anycast keeps one client in one PoP), asynchronously, accepting some overshoot.
- **Which clock.** GitHub chose the application's clock (for testability) and stores reset times as data; Brandur (phase 5) points to the store's own `TIME`. Both agree: one clock.
- **Service mesh cost.** Linkerd presents meshes as cheap on Kubernetes and costly elsewhere; Istio's ambient mode exists because a proxy beside every pod is heavy. No source read gives overhead numbers.

**Couldn't open:**

- Twitter's "Announcing Snowflake" blog post (blog.x.com / blog.twitter.com, 2010): 403 and a JavaScript shell. The GitHub README and code are cited instead.
- Instagram's "Sharding & IDs at Instagram" (instagram-engineering.com): curl timed out twice. Not cited.
- Krikorian's "Timelines at Scale" is video only on InfoQ; no transcript.

**Rejected:**

- ByteByteGo's rate limiter chapter (fetched, not read closely): secondary, and the primaries cover it.
- Istio "The Istio service mesh" about page: marketing, no mechanism.
- Conway's paper and MicroservicePremium: opened, but the articles need only what Lewis/Fowler and MonolithFirst already say.

**Gaps:**

- No measured overhead for sidecar vs ambient meshes (latency, CPU, memory) from a primary source.
- No primary source (paper or official docs) on Facebook's or Instagram's feed design; Twitter's is known only through a secondary summary of a talk.
- No measurement of index locality for Snowflake vs UUIDv7 vs UUIDv4; RFC 9562's "one order of magnitude or more" has no benchmark.
- The Segment post has no numbers on latency or cost before and after the merge, only engineering-effort measures.
- Nothing here was run in the lab; `back-of-envelope-estimation` would benefit from an estimate checked against a measured lab number when phase 17's system design write-ups are done.

### Designing a system

#### `long-polling` (short)

1. [RFC 6202](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6202), Loreto, Saint-Andre, Salsano, Wilkins, IETF, 2011. Spec (informational), primary: yes. Seen: short vs long polling defined; the four-step life cycle; issues: header overhead, average latency about one transit and worst over three, a connection and a request held per client, graceful degradation by batching, timeouts, caching; best practices: one shared long poll per browser (browsers then allowed 6 or 8 connections), proxies that share backend connections get starved, asynchronous servers handle long polls cheaply, 30 s a safe timeout and 120 s workable, 408/504 when too long, `Cache-Control: no-cache`; DoS risk from many open requests. New note `rfc-6202`.
2. [Blocking Queries](https://developer.hashicorp.com/consul/api-docs/features/blocking), HashiCorp, Consul v2.0.x docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: `X-Consul-Index` header passed back as `?index=`; request hangs until a change or the wait; a return is no guarantee of change; wait capped at 10 min, default 5 min, plus up to wait/16 jitter; reset the index if it goes backwards (raft snapshot restore); index 0 causes busy loops; rate limit the loop with a token bucket of burst 2 instead of sleeping; streaming backend since Consul 1.10 replaces long polling for some endpoints; hash-based blocking for agent endpoints. New note `hashicorp-consul-blocking-queries`.

#### `realtime-sync` (deep)

1. [High-Latency, Low-Bandwidth Windowing in the Jupiter Collaboration System](https://lively-kernel.org/repository/webwerkstatt/projects/Collaboration/paper/Jupiter.pdf), Nichols, Curtis, Dixon, Lamping, Xerox PARC, UIST 1995. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: central server; clients apply their own edits at once; each client syncs only with the server, which serializes and echoes, turning n-way sync into two-way; figure 3 (ABCDE, del 4 vs del 2, transformed to del 3); xform(c, s) and its convergence property; the "delete everything" transform that converges but is useless; delete-delete rule. New note `nichols-jupiter-1995`; figure 3 redrawn.
2. [Google Wave Operational Transformation](https://svn.apache.org/repos/asf/incubator/wave/whitepapers/operational-transform/operational-transform.html), Wang, Mah, Lassen, Google, version 1.1, 2010. Whitepaper, primary: yes. Seen: started from Jupiter; plain OT makes the server keep a state space per client; Wave clients wait for acknowledgment before sending more, caching and composing local operations; server keeps a single history, transforms against it, applies, broadcasts; trade-off: others' edits arrive in chunks about once per round trip; streaming document operations (retain, insert, delete...). New note `google-wave-ot-2010`.
3. [How Figma's multiplayer technology works](https://www.figma.com/blog/how-figmas-multiplayer-technology-works/), Evan Wallace, Figma, 2019. Blog by the builder, primary: yes. Seen: skipped OT as too complex; WebSockets, one process per document; reconnect by downloading a fresh copy and reapplying offline edits; OT powers most text apps such as Google Docs; CRDT properties; not true CRDTs because the server is the authority; document as Map<ObjectID, Map<Property, Value>>; server-ordered last-writer-wins per property; AB/BC never ABC; discard incoming changes that conflict with unacknowledged ones (flicker); client IDs in object IDs; server rejects cycles on reparenting; fractional indexing; undo rule. New note `figma-multiplayer-2019`.
4. [Making multiplayer more reliable](https://www.figma.com/blog/making-multiplayer-more-reliable/), Darren Tsung, Figma, 2022. Blog by the builders, primary: yes. Seen: authoritative in-memory server; checkpoints to S3 every 30-60 s, up to 60 s lost on crash; journal with per-file sequence numbers in DynamoDB, written asynchronously, goal under 1 s loss; recovery = checkpoint + newer entries; clients send every 33 ms, journal batches; split brain if clients reach two instances; lock UUID and conditional journal writes; DynamoDB global tables would cost 6x, so S3-replicated checkpoints within 30 min instead; about 400K validations; >2.2B changes/day, 95% persisted within ~600 ms. New note `figma-multiplayer-reliable-2022`.
5. [Local-first software](https://www.inkandswitch.com/essay/local-first/), Kleppmann, Wiggins, van Hardenberg, McGranaghan, Ink & Switch, 2019. Essay/paper by CRDT builders, primary: yes. Seen: CRDTs sync over any channel including a server; the one unresolvable conflict (same property of same object); Automerge prototypes (Trellis, Pixelpusher, PushPin); conflicts rarer than feared; CRDT history grows and can't be truncated (reconnect after six months); networking unsolved; servers as "cloud peers", closed-laptop problem; OT (ShareDB) as the established alternative. New note `kleppmann-local-first-2019`.
6. [Real Differences between OT and CRDT under a General Transformation Framework](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.01518), Sun, Sun, Ng, Cai, Cho, PACMHCI GROUP 2020. Paper, primary: no (OT authors analysing CRDTs). Seen: OT from the late 1980s, WOOT around 2006; claim that CRDT is rarely found in working co-editors; CRDTs transform indirectly via identifiers and tombstones; CRDT commutativity achieved indirectly with correctness and complexity issues; explicitly argues against CRDT claims. New note `sun-ot-crdt-2020`.
7. [y-websocket](https://github.com/yjs/y-websocket), Yjs project, README. Code docs, primary: yes. Seen: classic client-server provider; server distributes document updates and awareness (cursors); the bundled in-memory backend can't be scaled easily, @y/hub is the scalable one; rooms; reconnect with exponential backoff up to 2500 ms; close codes 4400-4499 are permanent. Not used (the article didn't need a CRDT library's server details).

#### `search-architecture` (short)

1. [Reading and writing documents](https://www.elastic.co/docs/deploy-manage/distributed-architecture/reading-and-writing-documents), Elastic, Elasticsearch docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: primary-backup after PacificA; routing by document ID; primary waits for all in-sync replicas; coordinating node fans out to one copy per shard and merges; adaptive replica selection; retries another copy on failure; partial results with 200 OK and `_shards`; a slow shard slows the group and unlucky searches; read-unacknowledged; dirty reads from an isolated primary. New note `elastic-reading-writing-documents`.
2. [Near real-time search](https://www.elastic.co/docs/manage-data/data-store/near-real-time-search), Elastic, Elasticsearch docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: searchable within 1 s; Lucene per-segment search; refresh writes and opens a new segment without a full commit; default refresh every second, only on indices searched in the last 30 s; `?refresh` and the refresh API. New note `elastic-near-real-time-search`.
3. [Using logs to build a solid data infrastructure](https://www.confluent.io/blog/using-logs-to-build-a-solid-data-infrastructure-or-why-dual-writes-are-a-bad-idea/): see phase 10 `dual-writes`. Reused note `kleppmann-dual-writes-2015` for why a search index fed by dual writes drifts and CDC fixes it.
4. [Clusters, nodes, and shards](https://www.elastic.co/docs/deploy-manage/distributed-architecture/clusters-nodes-shards), Elastic, Elasticsearch docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: each shard a self-contained Lucene index over a subset of documents; primaries and replicas; primary count fixed at index creation, replicas changeable any time. Not used (kept the short node to three sources).
5. [Size your shards](https://www.elastic.co/docs/deploy-manage/production-guidance/optimize-performance/size-shards), Elastic, Elasticsearch docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: oversharding; 10-50 GB and under 200M documents per shard; one search thread per shard; deleted documents linger until merges; split index or reindex plus alias to change shard counts. Not used.

#### `multi-region` (deep)

1. [AWS multi-Region fundamentals](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pdfs/prescriptive-guidance/latest/aws-multi-region-fundamentals/aws-multi-region-fundamentals.pdf), John Formento, AWS Prescriptive Guidance (PDF, copyright 2026). Docs, primary: yes. Seen: three reasons (bounded recovery, sovereignty, latency); most workloads fine in one Region with several AZs; can lower availability if built badly; 99.99% = 53 min/year, 5 min to detect + 10 to engage, 30-45 min to recover; roughly double cost; async replication leaves pending writes and needs business-logic reconciliation; sync needs three Regions and a 2-of-3 quorum, write latency up an order of magnitude; read local write global; Aurora global database up to five read-only Regions; active-active needs routing, session affinity, idempotency, conflict handling; most don't need it; shard clients across Regions as cells; no cross-Region calls; Route 53 control plane in us-east-1; per-Region certificates with staggered expiry; untested recovery equals none; deploy one Region at a time. New note `aws-multi-region-fundamentals`. The HTML landing page served only a JS redirect to curl; fundamentals 1 and 2 HTML pages loaded and match.
2. [AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-fault-isolation-boundaries/availability-zones.html), Michael Haken, AWS, 2022. Docs, primary: yes. Seen (re-opened, Regions and AZ pages): Regions isolated, data doesn't leave a Region unless replicated, AZ deploys staggered. Reused note `aws-fault-isolation-boundaries`.
3. [How DynamoDB global tables work](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/V2globaltables_HowItWorks.html), AWS docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen (re-opened): MREC async with per-item last writer wins, local-only conditional writes and transactions, RPO equal to replication delay; MRSC synchronous across exactly three Regions or two plus a witness, ReplicatedWriteConflictException. Reused note `aws-dynamodb-global-tables`.
4. [Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf), Corbett et al., OSDI 2012. Paper, primary: yes. Seen (re-opened): placement controls read latency, write latency and durability; per-directory placement (user A three replicas in Europe, user B five in North America); F1 five replicas across the US, 2 west and 3 east; most apps 3-5 datacenters in one geographic region. Appended to note `corbett-spanner-2012`.
5. [Table Localities](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/table-localities), Cockroach Labs, CockroachDB v26.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: regional, regional-by-row and global tables; home region = leaseholder plus voting replicas; users table as the regional-by-row example; global tables read fast everywhere and write slowly. New note `cockroach-table-localities`.
6. [Multi-Region Capabilities Overview](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/multiregion-overview), Cockroach Labs, CockroachDB docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: cluster and database regions, survival goals (zone default, region), super regions for data domiciling, secondary regions for failover. Not used.
7. [Making multiplayer more reliable](https://www.figma.com/blog/making-multiplayer-more-reliable/): see `realtime-sync` #4. Used for a real cross-Region replication decision made on cost.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- OT vs CRDT. CRDT work long portrayed OT as incorrect, complex and inefficient; Sun et al. (OT researchers) argue CRDTs transform indirectly with their own correctness and complexity issues, and that OT still runs most co-editors. Figma found OT overkill and full CRDTs unnecessary with a central server; Ink & Switch report CRDTs working well in prototypes but with history growth problems.
- Where the server belongs. Jupiter, Wave and Figma make the server the authority; local-first wants servers as "cloud peers" off the critical path.
- Active-active as a goal. AWS's guidance says most multi-Region workloads don't need it and that multi-Region done badly lowers availability; product docs (DynamoDB, CockroachDB) present multi-active writes as a feature. DynamoDB's own two modes show the trade: last writer wins silently vs rejected conflicts with higher latency.
- Long poll timeouts. RFC 6202 calls 30 s safe for the open web; Consul defaults to 5 min and caps at 10 on networks it controls.

**Couldn't open:**
