### Durable execution

#### `orchestration-vs-choreography` (short)

1. [Choreography pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/choreography), Microsoft, Azure Architecture Center. Official docs, primary: no. Seen: orchestrator vs broker diagrams; orchestrator consolidates status but must know every service's job, can be a bottleneck and SPoF; choreography via a broker; failure messages trigger compensations; sequences get awkward (delivery service waits for two messages, correlated by a session id); no component sees an in-flight operation, so tracing and correlation ids; event schema evolution; idempotent consumers; outbox; event storms and feedback loops; choreography between bounded contexts, orchestrator inside one.
2. [What do you mean by "Event-Driven"?](https://martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html), Martin Fowler, 2017. Blog, primary: no. Seen: four patterns (event notification, event-carried state transfer, event sourcing, CQRS); a flow over event notifications is "not explicit in any program text" and often only visible in a live system; the "passive-aggressive command".
3. [Pattern: Saga](https://microservices.io/patterns/data/saga.html): see `sagas` (phase 12). Seen: choreography and orchestration versions of the order saga. Not used here (the node reuses the order example through `sagas`).
4. [Saga distributed transactions pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga): see `sagas`. Seen: orchestration introduces a point of failure. Not used (the choreography page says the same).

#### `durable-execution` (deep)

1. [Durable orchestrations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-functions/durable/durable-functions-orchestrations), Microsoft, Azure Functions docs. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: orchestrators as procedural code; checkpoint at every await/yield; event sourcing in an append-only store; function unloaded after each commit, re-executed from the start on the next message or timer; completed tasks replayed from history; local variables restored; must be deterministic; duplicate logs on replay; real history table (ExecutionStarted, TaskScheduled, TaskCompleted...); Azure Storage provider has no transaction between tables and queues; unhandled exception = Failed, can't retry; I/O only in activities.
2. [Temporal Workflow Execution](https://docs.temporal.io/workflow-execution), Temporal. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: durability = "effectively once and to completion", seconds or years; replay checks commands against the Event History; commands vs events; two sequential activities = 11 state transitions; worker-side workflow cache and sticky queues, replay after eviction; replay APIs per SDK.
3. [Events and Event History](https://docs.temporal.io/workflow-execution/event), Temporal. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: history is an append-only log; the seven activity events; ActivityTaskScheduled puts a task on a task queue that workers poll; while retrying only the scheduled event is in history; warning at 10,240 events, termination past 51,200; Continue-As-New; no time limit on a workflow.
4. [Temporal Activity Definition](https://docs.temporal.io/activity-definition), Temporal. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: activities not recorded until they return, so they can rerun; crash between completion and report; smaller activities vs longer history; idempotency keys enforced by the called service; run id + activity id as a key; "observed as completed exactly once" but may execute more than once; backoff survives worker crashes.
5. [DBOS Architecture](https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture), DBOS. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: library checkpointing to Postgres, no orchestration server; one write per step plus two per workflow; large outputs make large writes, return pointers; recovery scans PENDING workflows, re-calls with checkpointed inputs, returns checkpointed step outputs; two rules (deterministic workflow, idempotent steps); breaking change = which steps or their order; patching and versioning; durable queues polled by workers; Conductor off the execution path. Also a vendor benchmark (>40K workflows or steps per second on one Postgres), no setup: not used.
6. [Key concepts](https://docs.restate.dev/foundations/key-concepts), Restate. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: the old URL /concepts/durable_execution redirects here; server in front of services like a reverse proxy or broker, one Rust binary; journal of every step and its result, replayed on failure; idempotency-key deduplication; cluster uses consensus, needs a majority; suspension on FaaS.
7. [Demystifying Determinism in Durable Execution](https://jack-vanlightly.com/blog/2025/11/24/demystifying-determinism-in-durable-execution): see `workflow-determinism` #1. Seen: "the durable function is not an atomic transaction". Used in `workflow-determinism` only, to keep this node at six.

#### `workflow-determinism` (short)

1. [Demystifying Determinism in Durable Execution](https://jack-vanlightly.com/blog/2025/11/24/demystifying-determinism-in-durable-execution), Jack Vanlightly, 2025. Blog, primary: no. Seen: framework-neutral model (control flow vs side effects); recovery reruns from the top; promo-date and loyalty-points double-charge bugs; side effects need idempotency, not determinism; Temporal explicit split vs Restate/Resonate function trees; some examples would be a non-determinism error in Temporal.
2. [Temporal Workflow Definition](https://docs.temporal.io/workflow-definition), Temporal. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: same API calls in the same sequence; which calls produce commands; replay compares each command with the event at the same position; timer/activity swap example; safe changes (timer duration except to/from 0 in Java, Python, Go; activity inputs, not types or ids); intrinsic non-determinism (local time, random); Worker Versioning (recommended) and patching; workflows fail only when code throws.
3. [Determinism during replay](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/durable-execution/patterns/best-practices/determinism/), AWS, Lambda durable functions guide. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: code outside steps must be a pure function of inputs and completed results; the list (wall-clock time, random, external service, local file system, mutable global state); random id outside a step double-charges; step bodies writing to outer variables lose the write on replay; feature flags and env vars read in a step.
4. [Orchestrator function code constraints](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-functions/durable/durable-functions-code-constraints), Microsoft. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: no DateTime.Now, use context time; context NewGuid gives Type 5 UUIDs; seeded RNG is fine; no bindings, env vars, static variables, threads; NonDeterministicOrchestrationException detection doesn't catch everything; JS/Python orchestrators must be generators, not async. Not used (the three above cover it); good for a future re-check.
5. [Patching](https://docs.temporal.io/patching), Temporal. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: patched() writes a marker on first run, returns false when replaying a history without it; put the newest patch first. Not used (too SDK-specific for a short node).
6. [Versioning in Durable Functions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-functions/durable/durable-functions-versioning), Microsoft. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: breaking-change checklist; inserting a call between Foo and Bar causes a non-deterministic orchestration error; strategies: orchestration versioning (recommended), side-by-side deployments, stop all in-flight instances. Not used.

#### `durable-timers` (short)

1. [Timers in Durable Functions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-functions/durable/durable-functions-timers), Microsoft. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: timers for delays and timeouts; a timer is a queue message visible only at the due time, which also wakes an app scaled to zero; JS/Python/PowerShell timers limited to six days; long timers split into shorter ones internally (three-day example); compute due time from the context clock; cancel unawaited timers or the orchestration won't complete; timing out doesn't stop the activity.
2. [Timers and Start Delays](https://docs.temporal.io/workflow-execution/timers-delays), Temporal. Official docs, primary: yes. Seen: timers persisted, fire when workers and service come back; workers use no resources while waiting ("millions" of timers, vendor claim, not used); one second to several years; duration is a minimum (11.97 s ends up closer to 12 s); Start Delay for one-off later workflows.
3. [Durable orchestrations](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-functions/durable/durable-functions-orchestrations): see `durable-execution` #1. Seen: an expired timer wakes the orchestrator and replays it; timer messages enqueued at checkpoints; external events for human interaction. Used for the replay-after-timer step.

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Where the orchestrator lives. Temporal runs a separate service with task queues; Restate puts a server in front of services like a proxy; DBOS is only a library plus Postgres and presents "no separate orchestration server" as a feature. Azure sits in between with pluggable storage, and its Azure Storage provider has no transaction across tables and queues.
- "Exactly once". Restate says an invocation "runs exactly once"; Temporal says an activity is *observed* as completed exactly once but may execute more than once. Both still need idempotent side effects in the crash window.
- Versioning. Temporal recommends Worker Versioning over patching; Azure recommends its built-in orchestration versioning over side-by-side deployments; DBOS offers patching and versioning without ranking them.
- Determinism checks. Temporal compares every command against the history and fails on mismatch; Vanlightly notes that in the general model the same bug quietly runs a new step. Azure's detection of thread misuse "won't catch all violations".
- Orchestration's central point of failure (Azure choreography page) vs the durable execution view that a durable orchestrator removes the memory-loss problem; the availability dependency on the engine stays.

**Couldn't open:**
- Nothing failed to open. docs.restate.dev/concepts/durable_execution redirected to /foundations/key-concepts; that URL is the one cited.

**Rejected:**
- The Temporal limits page (docs.temporal.io/workflow-execution/limits): read; adds 50 MB size limits. Not made a note; the event-count limits come from the Events page.
- Temporal Continue-As-New page: read; the concept is covered from the Events page.
- Temporal "Idempotency and Durable Execution" blog: linked from the activity page, not opened.
- Uber Cadence history (Temporal's origin): no source opened, so the history of the idea is left out.

**Gaps:**
- No primary source on the academic roots (e.g. workflow systems before Cadence) or any paper on durable execution; everything is vendor docs plus one independent blog.
- No measured cost per step for any engine except DBOS's write count and Temporal's state-transition count. The lab's Temporal comparison will fill this.
- No source opened on how Temporal stores timers internally (a timer queue in its persistence layer); the article describes only Azure's delayed-message design and Temporal's external guarantees.
- AWS Lambda durable functions only via the determinism page; not described as an engine in `durable-execution`.

## Added after writing

Eight short nodes split out of written articles after the phase 4 to 17 pass: `backwards-compatibility` (phase 5), `latches` (7), `redis-transactions` (9), `share-groups` (10), `session-guarantees` and `split-brain` (11), `shuffle-sharding` (13), `dns-rebinding` (15). Researched by 2 passes.

### Added after writing (1)

#### `backwards-compatibility` (short)

1. [AIP-180: Backwards compatibility](https://google.aip.dev/180), Google API Improvement Proposals. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: source, wire and semantic compatibility; new components allowed in the same major version; no new required fields; client-set fields default to old behavior; server keeps populating old fields; enum values free in request-only enums, documented in responses; rename is remove plus add, so add the new one and keep the old; no type changes even if wire-compatible; string length increases are breaking; resource name formats can't get stricter or looser; default and format changes are breaking; limited-scope APIs may set their own rules; guidance is indicative, not complete.
2. [RFC 9745](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9745), Dalal and Wilde, 2025. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: Deprecation header (structured-field date, past or future); deprecation link relation to docs and migration guides; Sunset (RFC 8594) must not be earlier than Deprecation; deprecation changes no behavior; it's a hint clients must work without; after the date clients can't assume behavior stays the same.
3. [Hyrum's Law](https://www.hyrumslaw.com/), Hyrum Wright. Essay, primary: yes. Seen: every observable behavior gets depended on; performance as an implicit interface; tests detect but can't remove the dependency. Already a note (used by api-versioning).

#### `latches` (short)

1. [Lecture #10: Index Concurrency Control](https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/fall2024/notes/10-indexconcurrency.pdf), Andy Pavlo, CMU 15-445, 2024. Course notes, primary: no. Seen: locks vs latches (contents vs internal structures, transaction vs short operation, deadlock detection vs programmer discipline); read and write latch modes; latches built from CAS; spin latch, futex-based OS mutex (about 25 ns per lock/unlock), reader-writer latches and starvation; hash table page vs slot latches; latch crabbing; top-down can't deadlock; leaf scans need no-wait and restart.
2. [src/backend/storage/lmgr/README](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/REL_18_STABLE/src/backend/storage/lmgr/README), PostgreSQL 18 source. Code docs, primary: yes. Seen: four lock kinds; spinlocks for a few dozen instructions, busy-wait, no deadlock detection or release on error; LWLocks with shared/exclusive modes, a few dozen instructions uncontended, semaphore wait in arrival order, released on error, no timeout; heavyweight locks with deadlock detection; query cancel held off while holding LWLocks.
3. [src/backend/storage/buffer/README](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/REL_18_STABLE/src/backend/storage/buffer/README), PostgreSQL 18 source. Code docs, primary: yes. Seen: pins vs short content locks; single BufMgrLock before 8.1 was a bottleneck; buffer mapping lock partitioned since 8.2. Already a note (buffer-pool).

#### `redis-transactions` (short)

1. [Transactions](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/using-commands/transactions/), Redis docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: MULTI/EXEC/DISCARD/WATCH; isolation and all-or-nothing on EXEC; queue-time errors abort EXEC since 2.6.5; run-time errors don't stop the rest; no rollbacks and why; WATCH as optimistic check-and-set, including expiry and eviction since 6.0.9; AOF single write but partial transactions after hard crash; Redis 8.4 SET IFEQ/IFNE/IFDEQ/IFDNE and DELEX; scripts can do everything a transaction can.
2. [Scripting with Lua](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/programmability/eval-intro/), Redis docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: atomic execution; KEYS vs ARGV and why keys must be declared; volatile SHA1 script cache and NOSCRIPT; effects replication default since 5.0, verbatim removed in 7.0; maxmemory behavior; shebang flags and cross-slot keys.
3. [Redis programmability](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/programmability/), Redis docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: EVAL since 2.6.0, Functions since 7.0; scripts block all clients; five-second busy-reply-threshold; BUSY replies, SCRIPT KILL only before writes, SHUTDOWN NOSAVE after; read-only scripts.
4. [Redis cluster specification](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/reference/cluster-spec/), Redis. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: hash slots and hash tags for multi-key operations. Already a note.
5. [Redis Lua API reference](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/programmability/lua-api/), Redis docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: redis.call vs redis.pcall error handling; script flags (no-writes, allow-oom, allow-stale, no-cluster, allow-cross-slot-keys; declared keys must share a slot). Not used; eval-intro covered what the article needs.
6. [Redis functions](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/programmability/functions-intro/), Redis docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: functions are atomic, keys must be declared, functions must be loaded on every cluster node by the admin. Not used (one line in the article, covered by the programmability page).

#### `share-groups` (short)

1. [KIP-932: Queues for Kafka](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/KAFKA/KIP-932%3A+Queues+for+Kafka), Andrew Schofield. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: motivation (over-partitioning); share-partition and its leader; share coordinator and internal state topic; four record states and transitions; delivery count and the attempt limit (5 by default); at-least-once; approximate counts; ordering example (100–109 redelivered with count 2); in-flight window SPSO to SPEO capped by max.record.locks, no max queue depth; SPSO starts at latest; reset wipes state; retention can drop undelivered records; read_committed stalls on open transactions; InvalidRecordStateException for late acks; no transactional acks; DLQ as future work.
2. [Kafka design](https://kafka.apache.org/43/design/design/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: "The Share Consumer": accept, release, reject, renew, or do nothing; 30-second lock; per-partition acquired-record limit; independent share groups on one topic.
3. [Broker Configs](https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/broker-configs/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: group.share.delivery.count.limit 5 (2–10), group.share.record.lock.duration.ms 30000 (1000–3600000), group.share.partition.max.record.locks 2000 (100–10000).
4. [Upgrading](https://kafka.apache.org/43/getting-started/upgrade/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: preview in 4.1, production-ready in 4.2, per-record acks and delivery counting. Already a note.
5. [Consumer and Share Consumer Configs](https://kafka.apache.org/43/configuration/consumer-configs/), Apache Kafka 4.3 docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: share.acknowledgement.mode (implicit by default, explicit). Not used.

**Disagreements and tensions:**

- The KIP lists four things a consumer can do with an acquired record; the Kafka 4.3 design docs list five, adding "renew". The KIP page as read doesn't mention renew; the article follows the 4.3 docs.
- The KIP calls the delivery limit `group.share.delivery.attempt.limit` in its state diagram, while the 4.3 broker config is `group.share.delivery.count.limit`. The article only names the default (5), not the key.
- Redis calls MULTI/EXEC a "transaction" but it has no rollback; scripts are called "transactional". Both mean isolated, not atomic in the ACID sense. The article says so.
- Latch vs lock naming: CMU says latch/lock; Postgres says LWLock/spinlock vs heavyweight lock. Same split, different words.

**Couldn't open:**

- Nothing failed.

**Rejected:**

- RFC 8594 (Sunset header): not opened separately; RFC 9745 section 4 says what the article needs about Sunset.
- Redis Lua API reference and Redis functions pages: opened, not needed for a short node (see above).

**Gaps:**

- No source states outright that a failing Lua script's earlier writes stay. The article says scripts give no undo, backed by the programmability page's time-limit section (a script that has written can't be stopped without losing the data set). Worth a primary line if one turns up.
- No primary source for how common databases other than Postgres name their latches (InnoDB, SQL Server). Left out.

### Added after writing (2)

#### `session-guarantees` (short)

1. [Session Guarantees for Weakly Consistent Replicated Data](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs734/2000FA/cached%20papers/SessionGuaranteesPDIS_1.html), Terry, Demers, Petersen, Spreitzer, Theimer, Welch, Xerox PARC, 1994. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: re-opened (HTML copy on a Cornell course page); all four guarantees with formal definitions and examples (Grapevine password, deleted mail reappearing, calendar, bibliography entry, bulletin board replies, text editor versions, library before application code); WFR and MW affect users outside the session; read-set and write-set in a client session manager; version vectors; checks skipped while latched to one server; shared client cache can break monotonic reads; guarantees give consistency, not isolation. Existing note `terry-session-guarantees-1994`, appended; one old quote in it corrected to match the page.
2. [PRAM](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/pram), Jepsen. Reference docs, primary: no. Seen: PRAM is exactly read your writes + monotonic reads + monotonic writes; sticky available; causal adds writes follow reads and is just as available; for total availability drop read your writes. Sibling pages (read your writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes) opened: RYW sticky available, MR and MW totally available.
3. [Causal Consistency and Read and Write Concerns](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/causal-consistency-read-write-concerns/), MongoDB manual. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: re-opened; causally consistent client sessions give the four guarantees only with majority read and write concern; local/w:1 gives none. Existing note.
4. [Causal Consistency](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/causal), Jepsen. See `causal-consistency`. Seen: total availability means giving up causal and read your writes, keeping the other three. Not cited (PRAM page says the same about availability).

#### `split-brain` (short)

1. [Pacemaker Explained, 8. Fencing](https://clusterlabs.org/projects/pacemaker/doc/3.0/Pacemaker_Explained/html/fencing.html), ClusterLabs, Pacemaker 3.0. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: fencing and STONITH defined; power fencing vs fabric fencing; split brain defined (lost communication but still able to run resources); effect by resource type (IP useless, database corrupts or diverges); fence devices must not share the cluster network or the node's power, and must not rely on the target (ssh shutdown for testing only); fencing needs quorum by default.
2. [High availability with Redis Sentinel](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/sentinel/), Redis docs. Docs, primary: yes. Seen: re-opened; majority needed to fail over, no failover in the minority partition; two-Sentinel setups never shown; permanent split brain without agreement; old primary's data discarded when it rejoins; min-replicas-to-write bounds the window (10 s example); configuration epochs, higher wins. Existing note.
3. [An Analysis of Network-Partitioning Failures in Cloud Systems](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi18-alquraan.pdf), Alquraan et al., OSDI 2018. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: re-opened; leader election affected by 40% of 136 failures; most common flaw two leaders at once; election by longest log, newest timestamp or lowest id can erase the majority's writes. Existing note.
4. [26.3. Failover](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby-failover.html), PostgreSQL 18 docs. Docs, primary: yes. See `failover`. Seen: STONITH named; both think they're primary leads to data loss. Not cited (Pacemaker's chapter says it in more depth).
5. [How to do distributed locking](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html), Martin Kleppmann, 2016. See `fencing-tokens`. Seen: re-opened; a paused lease holder writes after expiry; storage that remembers the highest token and rejects older ones. Cited for the token kind of fencing and for pauses.

#### `shuffle-sharding` (short)

1. [Workload isolation using shuffle-sharding](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/workload-isolation-using-shuffle-sharding/), Colm MacCárthaigh, Amazon Builders' Library. Blog from the team that built it, primary: yes. Seen: re-opened (redirects to builder.aws.com, read with headless Chromium); eight workers, plain vs shuffle, 28 pairs, 7 times better; still lose a quarter of the workers; gets better as the fleet grows; Route 53's 2,048 virtual name servers, 4 per domain, 730 billion shards, overlap capped at two; attacked domain moved to dedicated capacity; recursive shuffle sharding. Existing note, appended.
2. [Amazon Route 53 Infima](https://github.com/awslabs/route53-infima), AWS (awslabs). Code (README), primary: yes. Seen: Alice C/F/L vs Bob B/F/M example; impact 1/(N choose K); needs clients with multiple endpoints and short timeouts or DNS failover; stateless hash sharder vs stateful sharder that caps overlap; zone-aware shards.
3. [Reducing the Scope of Impact with Cell-Based Architecture](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reducing-scope-of-impact-with-cell-based-architecture/reducing-scope-of-impact-with-cell-based-architecture.html), AWS Well-Architected. See `cell-based-architecture`. Seen (through the existing note): shuffle sharding within a cell, not across cells.

#### `dns-rebinding` (short)

1. [Protecting Browsers from DNS Rebinding Attacks](https://crypto.stanford.edu/dns/dns-rebinding.pdf), Jackson, Barth, Bortz, Shao, Boneh, Stanford, CCS 2007. Paper, primary: yes. Seen: the basic attack (short TTL, rebind to internal address, same origin so the script reads the reply); no DNS compromise, so DNSSEC doesn't help; DNS pinning and why 2007 browsers and plug-ins broke it; pinning breaks VPN names; defenses: dnswall on resolvers, Host header checks on servers, finer-grained origins.
2. [Local Network Access](https://wicg.github.io/local-network-access/), Chris Thompson, Hubert Chao (Google), WICG Draft Community Group Report. Spec, primary: yes. Seen: permission gate for public-to-local requests; replaces Private Network Access (preflights); 5.2, the check runs on the address actually connected to, for each new connection, because of rebinding; 5.3, only a mitigation; Chromium does public-to-local only.
3. [New permission prompt for Local Network Access](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access), Chris Thompson, Chrome, 2025. Blog, primary: yes. Seen: launching in Chrome 142; address ranges that count as local or loopback; secure contexts only; PNA put on hold.
4. [Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP. See `ssrf`. Seen (existing note): an allow-listed name is resolved again when the request is made; the resolve-twice bypass it calls "DNS pinning".

**Disagreements and tensions:**
- Names. OWASP's SSRF cheat sheet calls the server-side trick a "DNS pinning bypass"; the 2007 paper uses "DNS pinning" for the browser's defense and "rebinding" for the attack. The article uses rebinding for the attack in both places.
- Browser defense: pin names to addresses (breaks failover and VPN names) vs check the address at connect time (Local Network Access). Private Network Access (preflights the device opts into) was paused in favour of a user permission prompt.
- Split brain: majority voting stops a second election but not the old leader; fencing stops the old leader but needs out-of-band hardware or a resource that checks tokens. Sentinel's min-replicas-to-write only bounds the window.
- Shuffle sharding: stateless hashing (no storage, probabilistic overlap) vs stateful assignment (guaranteed overlap limit, needs a datastore).
- Session guarantees: Terry lets each session pick; MongoDB bundles all four as "causal consistency" and only keeps them with majority read and write concern.

**Couldn't open:**
- Nothing needed was unreachable. The Builders' Library page needs JavaScript; read with headless Chromium.

**Rejected:**
- Postgres 26.3 for split brain (covered better by Pacemaker, and already cited by `failover`).
- Jepsen causal page for session guarantees (the PRAM page covers the availability point).

**Gaps:**
- No current source on how other browsers (Firefox, Safari) handle local network requests; the article describes Chrome only.
- No source on whether `fetch` in current browsers can set the Host header; the Host-check defense is sourced to the 2007 paper, which states it for XMLHttpRequest.
- No source on how Route 53 keeps virtual name servers apart on physical hosts (a reader asks under the article; no answer).
- No experiment; the shuffle-sharding arithmetic (28 pairs, 1/(N choose K)) is from the sources.

Twenty-eight short nodes split out of written articles, plus four nodes
made deep (`benchmarking-pitfalls`, `anti-entropy`,
`kubernetes-networking`, `container-runtimes`). Sources per node, all
opened for these articles; details are in each source note.

#### `atomics` (short, phase 4)

1. [Atomic vs. Non-Atomic Operations](https://preshing.com/20130618/atomic-vs-non-atomic-operations/), Jeff Preshing, 2013. Torn reads and writes at the instruction level, alignment, and what relaxed atomics do and don't promise.
2. [sync/atomic package documentation](https://pkg.go.dev/sync/atomic), The Go Authors, go1.27. Go's atomic operations, their sequentially consistent ordering, and the alignment rules.
3. [Programming Language Memory Models](https://research.swtch.com/plmm), Russ Cox, 2021. Why atomics are really about ordering, and the three kinds of atomics in C++.

#### `table-partitioning` (short, phase 6)

1. [PostgreSQL documentation, 5.12 Table Partitioning](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-partitioning.html), PostgreSQL Global Development Group, version 18. Range, list and hash partitioning, pruning, the limitations, and how many partitions is too many.

#### `overflow-pages` (short, phase 7)

1. [TOAST](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/storage-toast.html), PostgreSQL docs, version 18. The thresholds, chunking, the four storage strategies, and why out-of-line storage keeps the main table small.
2. [Database File Format](https://www.sqlite.org/fileformat2.html), SQLite developers. Sections 1.6 and 1.7: how a too-big cell spills onto a linked list of overflow pages.

#### `hot-updates` (short, phase 8)

1. [Heap-Only Tuples (HOT)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/storage-hot.html), PostgreSQL documentation, version 18. The two conditions, what HOT saves, pruning without vacuum, fillfactor and monitoring.
2. [Why Uber Engineering Switched from Postgres to MySQL](https://www.uber.com/blog/postgres-to-mysql-migration/), Evan Klitzke, Uber, 2016. Write amplification from updates that touch every index, on Postgres 9.2.

#### `universal-scalability-law` (short, phase 9)

1. [A General Theory of Computational Scalability Based on Rational Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/0808.1431), Neil J. Gunther, 2008. The USL, what σ and κ mean, the peak, and how Amdahl and Gustafson follow from a queueing bound.

#### `hedged-requests` (short, phase 9)

1. [The Tail at Scale](https://www.barroso.org/publications/TheTailAtScale.pdf), Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso, CACM, 2013. Hedged and tied requests, why they work, and the BigTable and file-system results.
2. [gRPC Retry Design (A6)](https://github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A6-client-retries.md), Noah Eisen and Eric Gribkoff, gRPC. How gRPC's hedging policy works, and its limits.
3. [HTTP routing](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/http/http_routing), Envoy docs. Envoy's hedging on per-try timeout.

#### `stack-walking` (short, phase 9)

1. [The Return of the Frame Pointers](https://www.brendangregg.com/blog/2024-03-17/the-return-of-the-frame-pointers.html), Brendan Gregg, 2024. How frame pointers disappeared from Linux, what that broke, what they cost, and the alternatives.
2. [perf-record(1)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/perf-record.1.html), Linux perf developers. The fp, dwarf and lbr call-graph methods, and the warning about binaries without frame pointers.
3. [CPU Flame Graphs](https://www.brendangregg.com/FlameGraphs/cpuflamegraphs.html), Brendan Gregg. Why JIT runtimes break stacks and symbols, and the perf map and PreserveFramePointer fixes.

#### `quantile-sketches` (short, phase 9)

1. [DDSketch: A Fast and Fully-Mergeable Quantile Sketch with Relative-Error Guarantees](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10693), Charles Masson, Jee E. Rim, Homin K. Lee, PVLDB, 2019. Why rank error fails on heavy tails, the geometric buckets, merging, and a comparison with other sketches.
2. [Computing Extremely Accurate Quantiles Using t-Digests](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04023), Ted Dunning and Otmar Ertl, 2019. The t-digest: clusters sized so the tails stay accurate, and merging digests.

#### `exemplars` (short, phase 14)

1. [Metrics Data Model](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/metrics/data-model/), OpenTelemetry specification 1.61.0. What an exemplar contains and how it relates to the histogram point.
2. [Metrics SDK](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/metrics/sdk/), OpenTelemetry specification 1.61.0. Exemplar filters, the default reservoirs, and exported filtered attributes.
3. [Feature flags](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/feature_flags/), Prometheus docs. Exemplar storage in Prometheus: the flag, the ring buffer and its memory cost.

#### `merkle-trees` (short, phase 11)

1. [Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf), DeCandia et al., SOSP 2007. Section 4.7: Merkle trees for comparing replicas, and the cost of rebuilding them when ranges move.
2. [RFC 9162: Certificate Transparency Version 2.0](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9162), B. Laurie, E. Messeri, R. Stradling, IETF, 2021. The exact tree hash, inclusion proofs and consistency proofs.

#### `tombstones` (short, phase 11)

1. [Tombstones](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/managing/operating/compaction/tombstones.html), Apache Cassandra docs, version 5.0. Zombies, the grace period, and the three-replica walkthroughs with and without tombstones.
2. [Repair](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/managing/operating/repair.html), Apache Cassandra docs, version 5.0. Why repair has to run within the grace period.
3. [Epidemic Algorithms for Replicated Database Maintenance](https://bitsavers.org/pdf/xerox/parc/techReports/CSL-89-1_Epidemic_Algorithms_for_Replicated_Database_Maintenance.pdf), Demers et al., Xerox PARC, PODC 1987. Death certificates, and why a plain delete gets undone.

#### `strict-serializability` (short, phase 11)

1. [Linearizability versus Serializability](http://www.bailis.org/blog/linearizability-versus-serializability/), Peter Bailis, 2014. The two guarantees side by side, and why combining them gives strict serializability.
2. [Strict Serializability](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/strict-serializable), Jepsen. The definition, its other names, and why it can't stay available during a partition.
3. [Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf), James C. Corbett et al., OSDI 2012. External consistency, and the clocks and commit wait that provide it.

#### `soft-deletion` (short, phase 13)

1. [Data Integrity: What You Read Is What You Wrote](https://sre.google/sre-book/data-integrity/), Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 26, Google. Soft deletion, lazy deletion and trash as the first layer of defense, and the delays Google uses.

#### `flexible-quorums` (short, phase 12)

1. [Flexible Paxos: Quorum intersection revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.06696), Heidi Howard, Dahlia Malkhi, Alexander Spiegelman, 2016. The intersection rule, simple and grid quorums, and the availability price.

#### `leadership-transfer` (short, phase 12)

1. [Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice](https://web.stanford.edu/~ouster/cgi-bin/papers/OngaroPhD.pdf), Diego Ongaro, 2014. Section 3.10 describes the leadership transfer extension, step by step, and why it's safe.
2. [etcd-io/raft](https://github.com/etcd-io/raft), etcd authors. A Raft library that implements leadership transfer.

#### `total-order-broadcast` (short, phase 12)

1. [Distributed Systems lecture notes](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/2122/ConcDisSys/dist-sys-notes.pdf), Martin Kleppmann, University of Cambridge. Sections 4.2 and 4.3 on broadcast orders and algorithms, 5.3 on replication through broadcast, and 6.1 on its equivalence with consensus.

#### `commit-wait` (short, phase 12)

1. [Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//archive/spanner-osdi2012.pdf), James C. Corbett et al., OSDI 2012. TrueTime, the commit-wait rule, and its measured cost.
2. [Living without atomic clocks](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/blog/living-without-atomic-clocks/), Spencer Kimball and Irfan Sharif, Cockroach Labs, 2022. Causal reverse, why waiting out NTP offsets is too slow, and uncertainty intervals as the alternative.

#### `seccomp` (short, phase 14)

1. [seccomp(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/seccomp.2.html), man-pages 6.19. The filter data, the actions, inheritance, and the caveats (allow-lists, vDSO calls).
2. [Seccomp security profiles for Docker](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/seccomp/), Docker docs. The default profile, what it blocks and why, and how to replace it.

#### `linux-capabilities` (short, phase 14)

1. [capabilities(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html), man-pages 6.19. The list of capabilities, the thread capability sets, and how they change across execve.
2. [Running containers](https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/run/), Docker docs. The capabilities a container keeps by default, --cap-add and --cap-drop, and what --privileged grants.

#### `kube-proxy` (short, phase 14)

1. [Virtual IPs and Service Proxies](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/networking/virtual-ips/), Kubernetes documentation, Kubernetes 1.37. How kube-proxy works, its modes and their status, sync behaviour and the conntrack caveat.
2. [gRPC Load Balancing on Kubernetes without Tears](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2018/11/07/grpc-load-balancing-on-kubernetes-without-tears/), William Morgan, 2018. Why connection-level balancing pins gRPC calls to one pod.

#### `noisy-neighbor` (short, phase 15)

1. [Noisy Neighbor antipattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/antipatterns/noisy-neighbor/noisy-neighbor), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center. How the problem shows up, how to detect it per tenant, and the governance, monitoring and rebalancing that contain it.

#### `egress-proxy` (short, phase 15)

1. [Smokescreen](https://github.com/stripe/smokescreen), Stripe. An HTTP CONNECT egress proxy that resolves and checks every destination, with per-client rules over mTLS.
2. [Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP. Why URL and IP checks fail, the DNS pinning bypass, and network-layer controls.

#### `tamper-evident-logs` (short, phase 15)

1. [Validating CloudTrail log file integrity](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html), AWS CloudTrail User Guide. A production hash chain: hourly signed digests, chained signatures, and what validation proves.
2. [Efficient Data Structures for Tamper-Evident Logging](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/event/sec09/tech/full_papers/crosby.pdf), Scott A. Crosby and Dan S. Wallach, USENIX Security 2009. Untrusted loggers, auditors, and the history tree with logarithmic proofs.
3. [RFC 9162: Certificate Transparency Version 2.0](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9162), B. Laurie, E. Messeri, R. Stradling, IETF, 2021. Merkle-tree logs in production, with inclusion and consistency proofs.

#### `account-recovery` (short, phase 15)

1. [NIST SP 800-63B-4: Digital Identity Guidelines, Authentication and Authenticator Management](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html), NIST, 2025. The account recovery section: what counts as recovery, the four methods and their rules, and how much proof each assurance level needs.

#### `sender-constrained-tokens` (short, phase 15)

1. [RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700), T. Lodderstedt et al., IETF, 2025. The recommendation to sender-constrain access and refresh tokens.
2. [RFC 9449: OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449), D. Fett et al., IETF, 2023. The DPoP proof JWT, the jkt binding, and its security considerations.
3. [RFC 8705: OAuth 2.0 Mutual-TLS Client Authentication and Certificate-Bound Access Tokens](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8705), B. Campbell et al., IETF, 2020. Binding tokens to a client certificate, and what happens on rotation and TLS termination.

#### `star-schema` (short, phase 16)

1. [Fact Tables and Dimension Tables](https://www.kimballgroup.com/2003/01/fact-tables-and-dimension-tables/), Ralph Kimball, 2003. Facts and dimensions, flat dimensions, and surrogate keys.
2. [Declare the Grain](https://www.kimballgroup.com/data-warehouse-business-intelligence-resources/kimball-techniques/dimensional-modeling-techniques/grain/), Kimball Group. What a fact table row represents, and why to start atomic.
3. [Type 1: Overwrite](https://www.kimballgroup.com/data-warehouse-business-intelligence-resources/kimball-techniques/dimensional-modeling-techniques/type-1/), Kimball Group. Overwriting a dimension attribute, and what it destroys.
4. [Type 2: Add New Row](https://www.kimballgroup.com/data-warehouse-business-intelligence-resources/kimball-techniques/dimensional-modeling-techniques/type-2/), Kimball Group. Keeping history with new rows and new surrogate keys.

#### `operational-transformation` (short, phase 17)

1. [High-Latency, Low-Bandwidth Windowing in the Jupiter Collaboration System](https://lively-kernel.org/repository/webwerkstatt/projects/Collaboration/paper/Jupiter.pdf), David A. Nichols, Pavel Curtis, Michael Dixon, John Lamping, Xerox PARC, UIST 1995. The paper behind client-server OT: the transform function and the server that serializes and echoes.
2. [Google Wave Operational Transformation](https://svn.apache.org/repos/asf/incubator/wave/whitepapers/operational-transform/operational-transform.html), David Wang, Alex Mah, Soren Lassen, Google, 2010. How waiting for acknowledgments lets the server keep a single history.
3. [How Figma's multiplayer technology works](https://www.figma.com/blog/how-figmas-multiplayer-technology-works/), Evan Wallace, Figma, 2019. A production design that borrows from CRDTs with a server in charge, with its edge cases.
4. [Real Differences between OT and CRDT](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.01518), Chengzheng Sun, David Sun, Agustina Ng, Weiwei Cai, Bryden Cho, 2020. The OT side of the argument: CRDTs as indirect transformation.

#### `workflow-versioning` (short, phase 17)

1. [Versioning](https://docs.temporal.io/develop/go/versioning), Temporal Go SDK docs. Patching with GetVersion, Worker Versioning, and cutting over to a new workflow type.
2. [Versioning in Durable Functions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-functions/durable/durable-functions-versioning), Microsoft Azure docs. The breaking-change checklist, what happens with no plan, and orchestration versioning.
